WASHINGTON, Feb. 10.—Impeachment charges against Andrew W. Mellon were dropped by the house judiciary committee today as the veteran financier prepared to step from the treasury direction into England's Court of St. James. Equivalent to Ouster Upon this exchange of duties and Mellon's impending resignation from the cabinet to take the oath of ambassador, the 23 lawyer representatives based their agreement that "nothing justified further proceedings." Chairman Sumners announced his committee was unanimous on this point, viewing impeachment proceedings as virtually equivalent to an ouster suit. Representative Patman, Democrat, Texas, sponsored the charges to obtain Mellon's removal from the treasury post he occupied 11 years. But the committee was not unanimous on the actual resolution adopted, and during the two-hour meeting the voices of members in heated discussion often could be heard

Beverly Hills, Cal... Feb. 9 (2) Edgar Wallace, 56, who rose from a home in the slums of London to world-wide fame as an author, was stricken here today with double pneumonia. Attending physicians said Wallace had a chance for recovery if his vitality could outlast the disease. They said he had been in excellent health prior to the illness. Wallace, one of the most prolific of modern writers, came here three months ago to write film scenarios. Arriving on Friday, he met studio executives, asked them what they wanted, and upon learning their wishes, appeared Monday with a 60,000 word novel. Mystery Author Hollywood still gasps at the amazing productive speed of the Englishman. Wallace contracted a cold last week during unseasonable weather. Influenza developed and his condition suddenly became worse today. His wife, who is living at the family home in London with their four children, was

San Francisco, Feb. 10 (UP)—Storm clouds spent their fury in Southern California yesterday, inundating thousands of acres of farm lands, washing out bridges, disrupting transportation and driving hundreds from homes, while a new storm, sweeping down the coast from British Columbia was promised. San Diego was cut off from rail transportation following heavy washouts. In the vicinity of Los Angeles an average of 3.21 inches of rain fell between Sunday night and Tuesday evening, and records of 17 years’ standing were shattered.

1932-12-23.text: NEW YORK, (UP).—Andrew Mellon, former secretary of the treasury and now ambassador to Great Britain, is positive he will be off the public payroll after March 4. He said so yesterday when he returned home from England to spend the Christmas holidays at his home in Pittsburgh. Reporters suggested that perhaps President-Elect Franklin D. Roosevelt would like Mellon to remain ambassador. “That,” said Mellon with a hearty laugh, “would hardly be within the realm of possibility.”

GLASGOW, Scotland. (?). Christmas shoppers hurried to places of safety when a riot developed as several thousand persons were marching through the city in an unemployment demonstration. Five policemen were injured, two of them seriously. The demonstrators started their march after seven labor members of the city council had been suspended from the council as the result of a dispute over whether to receive a deputation from the jobless. All of the injured policemen were taken to the hospitals. A detective, thrown into the Clyde, was rescued with difficulty. The rioters chased several other policemen.

WINGATE, Dec. 22. (#)—A fusillade of shots fired by a cashier and aroused citizens brought death for one bank robber and left another dying after the two had entered the Security Bank of Wingate, locked the young woman bookkeeper in the vault and scooped up all the money in the tills, between $1,500 and $2,000. Employes at Lunch The robbery occurred at 12:40 p.m., while all employes of the bank excepting Miss Leliah Harter, the bookkeeper, went out to lunch. Parking a sedan at the curb, the two men entered and drew guns as they approached the window. "Give us all your money," Miss Harter was commanded and all the currency and silver in the tills and vault was scooped up and hastily packed in sacks by the bandits. The men, both very young, passed Duncan Hensley, the cashier, as they were leaving the bank. He sensed it was a robbery and opened fire on them, alarming the neighborhood. Citiz

New York, Dec. 22. (4?)-—Andrew Mellon said today he would retire to his Pittsburgh home “soon after March 4.” To get a “fresh perspective on affairs in Washington” and to spend Christmas with his family, the Ambassador to England arrived aboard the Europa, insistent that it “is not appropriate for me now to discuss the war debt situation in any way.” Asked if he had any intention of resigning while in America for the holidays, Mellon said: “I wouldn't have any reason not to go back and it is hardly within the range of possibility that I would not do so.” The former Secretary of the Treasury, saying he was “somewhat tired and anxious for a rest,” said he expected to be replaced at the Court of St. James “as soon as Roosevelt is inaugurated.” The Ambassador said he would telephone the White House tonight and arrange to confer with President Hoover before the latter leaves for a vacation i

London, Dec. 22.— (P) — David Lloyd-George, the former liberal leader, made a sensational declaration in the house of commons, this afternoon, intimating that he was ready to go to jail, if it came to that, on the issue of further disclosure by him of cabinet proceedings which he threatened should any further "partial disclosures" be made. What led up to this was the recent partial disclosure by several members, including Mr. Lloyd-George himself, during debate in the house of proceedings in Lloyd-George's own cabinet in connection with the 1923 debt settlement with America. PARIS, 22.—Joseph Paul-Boncour intends to follow the policies of the Herriot government with regard to negotiations in connection with the American debt, he revealed today in his first appearance as premier before the chamber of deputies. His primary objective will be a conference to effect a general settlement, but he warned that the political situation in the United States makes it advisable to conduct the negotiations with the greatest care. His disarmament policy also will be a continuation of his predecessor’s. In domestic matters he intends to effect administrative economies which probably will take the form of salary and pension reductions. In his foreign relations, he said, he desires particularly to cultivate the friendship between France and Great Britain, at the same time granting to Germany so far as he can consistently do so, the status of equality which she demands. TOKYO, DEC. 23. (AP).—Nineteen persons were dead, eighteen injured and 32 still unaccounted for as police continued a search for bodies in the ruins of a fire which razed a tenement section today in the Tukagawa slum district of Tokyo. The majority of the casualties were Korean coolies. Twenty tenements housing 92 families were destroyed within half an hour after the blaze started before dawn.

1932-08-11.text: LONDON. (). A report from Madrid that a general arrested there and two other officers would be shot at dawn Thursday was received by Reuter's (British) news agency. The report lacked official confirmation.

- Lendon, Aug. 11.—()—Under a blazing sun which produced the hottest day England has had in two years, Mr. Vidtar Bruce shuttled back and forth in her “flying bungalow,” completing forty-eight hours in the air in an attempt to set a new world’s record for endurance flying. Mrs. Bruce broke the British endurance record of fifty hours and thirty-eight minutes at 3 p.m. The world’s record established in 1930 by Forest O’Brine and Dale Jackson is more than 647 hours.

OTTAWA, Aug. 11—(#)—The Canadian and British delegations to the imperial economic conference were reported preparing today to make additional tariff preference concessions in an attempt to reach a final trade agreement. It was indicated Great Britain now was ready to accept a program whereby extensive preferences would be accorded dominion natural products, notably lumber, meat and possibly wheat, while Canada was reported ready to go further than first suggested on iron, steel, coal and a limited range of textiles. Readiness by Great Britain to curb lumber imports from Russia in some measure, through orders in council, for Canada’s benefit also was given as a new development.

| PARIS, Aug. 11 (P)—It was reliably reported here today that Soviet Russian oil interests will be represented at the international oil conference in New York next month. An agreement among members of the Russian syndicate and the English, American, Dutch and Romanian group was reported likely, Such an agreement, it is held, would result in an immediate rise in the price of gasoline.

BY NORRIS J. HARNIS (Copyright, 1932, by The Associated Press.) SHANGHAI, Aug. 11 (#)—China was a nation virtually adrift today. Chiang Kai-Shek, former president and virtual commander-in-chief of the army, appeared to be drifting toward the role of Fascist dictator, favoring a tolerant foreign policy, especially with respect to Manchuria. China’s government was at a standstill. In political circles it was indicated that leaders were urgently attempting to solve the crisis resulting from the resignation of Wang Ching-Wei, president of the executive Yuan, and the Nanking cabinet. Without warning, Wang Ching-Wei quit Saturday. Chiang Kai-Shek, instead of assuming the dictatorial role and commanding his one-time subordinates to remain in their respective jobs, telegraphed to Nanking that he, too, would be forced to resign unless various leaders resumed their duties. BERLIN, Aug. 10 (7)—Adolf Hitler, former Austrian paper-hanger who has made his National Socialists party the most powerful political organization in Germany, seemed tonight to be within striking distance of the chancellorship. Chancellor Franz Von Papen requested the leaders of the Centrist party to call on him tomorrow and discuss their attitude toward turning the most important post in the Government over to the fiery Nazi. Hindenburg Is Favorable Persons in a position to know the details of the intricate political maneuvering that has been going on the last few days asserted that the Centrists and President Paul Von Hindenburg were agreed on one thing: that Herr Hitler, as chief of a coalition cabinet, would be far more innocuous than he is as the leader of a movement which has no political responsibility. BERLIN, Aug. 11.—()—Adolf Hitler, whose bid for the German chancellorship appears to grow stronger daily, is coming to Berlin tomorrow to talk with President Von Hindenburg. The president, who is reported to be wavering from his determination to maintain a non-party cabinet, invited the National Socialist leader to come in and talk things over. Hitler is on a vacation in Bavaria with other leaders of his party, while the country celebrated the 13th anniversary of the founding of the republic.

Associated Press Staff Correspondent MADRID, Aug. 10—(AP)—Monarchist leaders of the army, who rose in rebellion today against the sixteen months old Republic of Spain, failed in an attempt to seize the principal government offices in Madrid after street fighting in which at least eight persons were killed, but they captured the city of Seville. Tonight the entire nation was under what amounted to martial law. Loyal troops were being concentrated for an attack on Seville from the north and 200 persons were under arrest for participating in the rebellion. There was an unofficial report from Seville that federal planes were bombarding the city. This report was not confirmed, but it was certain the government was using airplanes in a pacific mission in an endeavor to get the rebels to surrender. 1932-06-15.text: Englewood, N. J., June 18—Attended by Gerald Shepherd, acting British consul general who brought a wreath of red roses to be placed on the casket, funeral services were conducted today in an undertaking establishment for Violet Sharpe, English servant who committed suicide at the home of Mrs. Dwight W. Morrow Friday. Arthur Springer, one of Mrs. Morrow's secretaries, represented the Morrow family, Mrs. Morrow and her son and a daughter, Dwight Morrow, Jr., and Constance, sailed for England early today. Servants from the Morrow estate also attended the funeral. An automobile from the Morrow estate brought a number of floral pieces which were placed about the casket. The Rev. Joseph R. Lyons, rector of St. Paul's Episcopal church, conducted the service. The body was placed in a grave about 200 yards from that of the late Senator Morrow.

London, June 14 ()— Widespread protests in the British press against American police methods have been followed by a government investigation into the suicide of Violet Sharpe, an English servant girl employed in the Morrow home in Englewood, N. J., it was learned today. The British consul general in New York has been instructed to draw up a report on the suicide for the foreign office here. Last Saturday, the day after Violet killed herself in Englewood, her sister Emily declared the American police “drove her crazy” by their insistent questioning about the kidnapping of the Lindbergh baby. Emily, who was in New York at the time of the abduction, has since returned home. "The police never let her alone,’ she said. ‘They questioned her for hours. They drove her crazy. She knew nothing, but they'll never believe what you tell them over there." Emily herself was questioned by Scotland Yard

NEW YORK, June 15 (UP) — Mrs. Dwight Morrow, Constance and Dwight, Jr., sailed for England after boarding the Europa behind a flying wedge of bodyguards. The Morrows planned to visit Elizabeth Morrow, who arrived in England the day their English servant at Englewood, Violet Sharpe, killed herself when notified she was to be questioned again in the Lindbergh kidnapping. Mrs. Morrow is the grandmother of the kidnapped Lindbergh baby, Charles A., Jr.

RIO DE JANEIRO, BRAZIL, June 15—(AP)—The Greek Steamer Artemis, which sent out an SOS early this morning, radioed later that she was sinking and the crew had taken to the boats. The British motorship Eastern Prince, speeding to the rescue, was not far off. The government radio station at Arpador learned that the Artemis was bound for Buenos Aires from Torre Vieja, Spain, and that she was rapidly sinking in South latitude 17.44 and west longitude 37.28. This would place her off Southern Bahia North of the Abrolhos islands. The Artemis, formerly the Contessa Adelma, is 3,587 tons gross register, is listed as owned in Andros, Greece, and was built in 1907 at Glasgow, Scotland.

Englewood, N. J., June 14.--(AP) —The funeral of Violet Sharpe, maid in the Dwight W. Morrow home, who committed suicide Friday and whose marriage was disclosed in her death certificate today, will be held here tomorrow. She will be buried here. E. H. G. Shepherd, acting British consul general who has been asked to report to his government about charges in the press there that she was “hounded to death” by police, will attend, he said, in New York. The death certificate stated Violet was married, ‘name of husband unknown.” Lieutenant Nathan Allyn of the prosecutor's staff, said servants in the Morrow household, questioned after the suicide, told him they believed the girl was married, but had been separated from her husband several years. . LONDON, June 15. (AP) — Ellsworth Vines, United States singles champion, was defeated by Harry Hopman, Australia, in the third round of the London tennis championships today.

ENGLEWOOD, N. J., (UP).—The British government in the person of its acting consul general, Edward H. G. Shepherd, Wednesday placed a bouquet of red roses on the casket of Violet Sharpe, servant girl in the home of Mrs. Dwight W. Morrow, who killed herself rather than submit to further police questioning in the kidnaping and murder of Charles A. Lindbergh Jr. Funeral services for the girl were held in an undertaker’s chapel. Mingling with the servants from the Morrow household was Shepherd and Arthur Springer, secretary to Mrs. Morrow, representing the Morrow family. LONDON, (UP).—The question of possible British representations to the United States over the suicide of Violet Sharpe during questioning in the Lindbergh kidnaping case was raised in the House of Commons Wednesday. Beenham, England, June 15 — (AP) — Violet Sharpe, English waitress in the Morrow home in New Jersey who committed suicide following questioning by police in connection with the Lindbergh kidnapping, was married in London before she went to America. Violet's husband was a man named George Payne, her sister Emily revealed. She said she herself knew nothing about him and never met him. Violet's mother said she did not know her daughter was married.

1932-01-25.text: Associated Press Staff Writer Dartmoor, Devon, England, Jan. 24 (#)—Three hundred convicts at grim Dartmoor prison—enraged over a mess of unsweetened porridge, waged a bitter, futile battle with prison guards and police today in the most violent penal outbreak in British history. Two Reported Dead Two convicts were understood to have been killed, ninety-five were wounded, and one was believed to have escaped in an all-day conflict in which the prisoners burned the principal buildings and attempted a wholesale escape over the walls; Twelve warders and police were injured. The home office in London issued a statement, however, saying no inmates had been killed and none had escaped. Only about twenty remained in the hospital according to this source and none of the injuries to guards or police were serious. | LONDON (P)—Prison rioting which the press declared ‘out-rivalled the imagination of a Hollywood film producer,’ an outbreak unprecedented in British prison history, failed to free a single convict. One hundred long-term inmates of Dartmoor prison in the loneliest section of the Devon Moors attacked their warders Sunday, set fire to the warden’s office and main cell block, and were only prevented from gaining control of the prison by truckloads of police from Plymouth. Damage was estimated at £12,000. Some of the convicts were reportedly maddened with liquor which they seized in a raid on the prison canteen. Fifty “bobbies” from Plymouth arrived at the prison gates, just as the convicts, armed with sticks, stones and improvised weapons, were inviting the warders to ‘come and get it.’ The policemen shed their great coats, drew their truncheons, and with shouts of ‘Come on, lads,’ charged

NEW DELHI, Jan. 25—(4)—The British government can make no compromises in its decision to put down Mahatma Gandhi's civil disobedience movement, Viceroy Lord Willingdon said today in his inaugural address to the Indian legislature. “While the government will take the necessary steps to guard against any abuse of the special powers vested in the authorities,” he said, “there can be no relaxation of the measures now in force against civil disobedience so long as the circumstances exist which make them necessary.” After declaring the work of the last round table conference would be carried forward and details of the new constitution for India fully and rapidly explored by the three committees which are due here from London Jan. 29, the viceroy said: “I feel it a great privilege, toward the end of my public life, to be leading India on to her promised position as an absolutely equal partner w

New York, Jan. 24. (AP)—While his brother leaned from a window of an adjoining suite and begged him not to jump, Erroll O’Brien, 43, an attorney and former magistrate in the British West Indies, plunged to his death today from the tenth floor of The body crashed through a glass marquee, narrowly missing a doorman. LONDON, Jan. 25.—(?)—Today's newspapers laid part of the responsibility for yesterday's riot at Dartmoor prison to recent outbreaks in American prisons, accounts of which had been communicated to long-term prisoners by newcomers. The Daily Herald, in an article signed “by a released Dartmoor convict,” laid part of the blame on American motion pictures which dramatized prison revolt. Some of the new men at Dartmoor had seen one such film and told the other prisoners about it, the article said. The writer also told of other sources of discontent, asserting that the porridge at Dartmoor often tasted mouldy.

Princetown, England. Jan. 25. (INS). —Bleak Dartmoor prison, where England sends her most dangerous criminals, was wrecked to-day as a result of the most serious penal riot in the country’s modern history. Eighty-five persons, including several guards, were wounded in a battle which lasted for nearly twelve hours Sunday. The outbreak came as a climax to weeks of unrest, the immediate cause being the convicts’ dissatisfaction with their morning porridge. Despite the seriousness of the riot, in which several portions of the institution were set afire, not one prisoner escaped. The uprising was checked without a death, an official report stated, although twenty of the injured were seriously hurt and two critically. Approximately half of the 450 Dartmoor convicts took part in the riot. For several hours the rioters were in complete control of the prison except for the outer walls, where guar

Detroit, Jan. 24, (4). -- A dozen thugs who beat and kicked Noel W. English to death early today in the crowded Merry Gardens ballroom, attacking with fists and knives other dancers who attempted a rescue, were sought by police today. Before police arrived and locked the approximately 1,000 dancers in the ballroom for questioning, the slayers escaped.

SHANGHAI, Jan. 25—(U.P.)—The Chinese foreign minister and premier both resigned today while 1,400 Japanese marines patrolled the waterfront here, and 10 Japanese warships lay off shore prepared to enforce Japanese ultimatum by “drastic naval action.” Eugene Chen, foreign minister and Premier Sun Fo resigned, it was announced, because they could not break diplomatic relations with Japan, could not invoke an international boycott against her, or otherwise take positive effective action. It was believed that serious trouble could be avoided by Chinese officials agreeing to officially disown the anti-Japanese boycott and to prosecute members of boycott societies. This would appease Japan but would not completely wipe out the boycott which could be carried on by individuals.

1932-08-23.text: FLOYD BENNETT FIELD, BROOKLYN, N. Y., Aug. 23.—(U.P.)—The Hutchinson family left today on a 4,500-mile trip to London that will take them over the North Atlantic. Their giant, bi-motored amphibian plane, christened “The Flying Family,” took off for St. John, N. B., the first leg of the flight, at 11:07 a.m. with George R. Hutchinson, Richmond, Va., aviator at the controls. Hutchinson was accompanied by his wife, Mianche, his daughters, Kathryn, 8, and Janet Lee, 6; Peter Redpath, navigator; Joseph Ruff, mechanical engineer; Gerald Altissish, radio operator and Norman Alley, motion picture cameraman. They hope to reach St. John within six hours.

NEW YORK, AUG. 23. (AP)—George Hutchinson’s flying family took off in the Sikorsky amphibian “City of Richmond” from Floyd Bennett Field at 10:07 a. m., Eastern Standard time, on the first leg of an easy stage flight to London. In addition to the Hutchinson family, which included himself, his wife and two daughters, Kathryn, 8, and Janet Lee, 6, the crew of the flight consists of Peter Redpath, navigator; Joseph Ruff, motor engineer; G. J. Altfilisch, radio operator, and Norman W. Avey, cinema cameraman. The first stop scheduled is St. John, New Brunswick, 511 miles from New York. Unless weather conditions are bad the expedition plans to reach Labrador on the second day, Greenland on the third, Ireland on the fourth and London on the fifth day. New York, Aug. 23 (AP)—George Hutchinson’s flying family took off in the Sikorsky amphibian “City of Richmond” from Floyd Bennett field at 10:07 a.m. for the first leg of an easy stage flight to London. In addition to the Hutchinson family, which includes himself, his wife and two daughters, Kathryn, 8 and Janet Lee, 6, the rest of the flight consists of Peter Redpath, navigator, Joseph Ruff, motor engineer, G. J. Alsfisch, radio operator, and Norman W. Alley, cinema cameraman. The first stop scheduled is St. John, N. B., 512 miles from New York. Unless weather conditions are bad the expedition plans to reach Labrador on the second day, Greenland on the third day, Iceland on the fourth and London on the fifth day. | PLYMOUTH, England, Aug. 23.—(AP)—Robert Beal was attached to his pipe: So much so that when told he must give up smoking or go blind, he committed suicide.

NEW YORK, Aug. 23, (/P)—Senator David I. Walsh, of Massachusetts, said today, democrats of New England will be as loyal on election as those of any other section of the country. The senator visited James A. Farley, democratic national chairman, and said he would speak for the ticket wherever Governor Roosevelt's campaign managers wish to send him. Senator Walsh said that there was some disappointment in Massachusetts and other New England states over the failure of the national convention to nominate farmer Governor Alfred I. Smith, but added that this feeling was gradually disappearing. Asked about the outlook for the Maine election Sept. 12, Senator Walsh said: "My advices are that the democrats are going to give the republican party a desperate fight."

New York, Aug. 23. pt. Jas. A. Mollison, English air ace, prepared today for an eastward crossing of the Atlantic in his little plane within the next forty-eight hours. He was practically ready, the only thing detaining him was that the weather man hadn't said “Go.” And when he does Mollison will begin his return flight.

BERLIN. (UP). A “struggle against the government” to free five fascist storm troopers, sentenced to be beheaded, was promised by Adolf Hitler, national socialist party leader. A short time after he addressed a petition to the government of Chancellor Von Papen, asking that the death sentences be commuted, Hitler sent a pithy message to the five condemned men. The action was viewed as an open challenge of the Von Papen regime, and of the government's right to set up arbitrary courts to handle cases involving political terrorism. Hitler's sudden action followed a period of frenzied activity in which nazi storm troopers fairly expressed their indignation at the penalty. Mobs of Hitler followers fought with steel helmeted police in the streets of Beuthen, where the five were sentenced. Hitler left no doubt that if his five followers are executed all chance of his resuming negotiation with Vo

Tokyo, Aug. 22 (#)—Expectations that Japanese troops will be moving against Chinese armies again this fall received semi-official confirmation today on the heels of dispatches telling of a sharp battle near Peipiao in Jehol, the Chinese province which lies west of Manchuria. A foreign office spokesman intimated that the favorable questionably as part of the newly created state of Manchukuo, which was set up by power of Japanese arms to rule Manchuria.

1932-12-09.text: Set FY 5200OUC FIR PRESS. Developments in Europe indicate that both England and France will pay the money they owe the United States next Thursday. There was no flat statement from an official quarter either in London or Paris that this decision has been reached, but in both capitals the cabinets gave their attention to evolving the most practical method of payment. An official statement in London said that this matter will be considered at a cabinet meeting early next week when Prime Minister MacDonald comes back from the disarmament meeting at Geneva. In Paris the minister of finance advised the foreign affairs committee and the finance committee of the chamber of deputies that the government is disposed to pay with the understanding that this will be the last payment, pending reconsideration of the entire debt structure. Washington, Dec. 8—(P)—The United States insisted on payment of the Dec. 16 war debt installment, in its latest note to Great Britain, but left the way open to have it done in the manner considered least disruptive to world finance. Made public tonight, Secretary Stimson’s communication expressed confidence Congress would “be willing to consider any reasonable suggestion” from the English “which will facilitate payment” of the $95,500,000 due 4 weeks from today. It also revealed informal suggestions have been made to Great Britain as to how the payment might best be met, but did not show the nature of the proposals. The note was studied with interest on Capitol Hill, but leaders were cautious in commenting on the reference to the acceptability of a new form of making the transfer. Those who did speak expressed the view that Congress was adamant and not likely to consider any but the regu

LONDON, Dec. 8 (7)—It was stated authoritatively today that the Soviet government has refused to accede to a British demand for an apology for statements published in the newspaper Izvestia, official organ of the Soviet regime. The Soviet ambassador, in disclaiming government responsibility for the objectionable articles, was said to have refrained from stressing agreement with their substance. The Izvestia article accused the British intelligence service of having instructed its agents in Riga, Latvia, to obtain documents "real or bogus" establishing a relationship between the Soviet government and the communist Third Internationale. This was linked with British claims of evidence that the Third Internationale directed the recent hunger march on London and was working against the British rule in India. The Soviet ambassador was reported to have declined under the circumstances to offer

(AP) The Captain Walter Wanderwell murder mystery unfolded like a the crew of Wanderwell’s yacht, Carma, were forbidden to discuss events preceding the slaying, and a scion of British nobility was arrested. "the developments, William tates Guy, young Australian soldier of fortune held as a suspect in the killing Monday night of the colorful globe-trotter, clung to his alibi that he was 30 miles away from the scene of the shooting on the Carma. Owen Murphy that "certain persons, for reasons best known to themselves, have been withholding information from the police." His charges were followed by an order issued by the Long Beach police forbidding any member of the crew, consisting of seven women and eight men, from talking to anyone but authorities about the slaying. (UP) — The net result today of new United States notes to Great Britain and France was that while the two debtors have America’s promise of later relief they still are expected to pay $125,000,000 on December 15, Asked For Plan Britain was invited to submit its own method of payment. London reports indicated, however, she decided to pay in gold. Secretary of State Stimson in his note to London promised a “close examination” of the whole debt problem. But he warned this offer did not imply a willingness to cancel the debt. He again suggested that disarmament would help Europe’s debt case. The note to France was handed to Ambassador Paul Claudel last night. Its publication was delayed until it had time to reach Paris. WASHINGTON, Dec. 8.—(P)—A second firm, polite refusal to extend the war debt moratorium was in the hands of the British today, while the American government waited to see how much of the nearly $125,000,000 due Dec. 15 would be paid by foreign debtors. A few hours after renewed opposition to reducing these obligations had been heard in Congress, Secretary Stimson last night gave Sir Ronald Lindsay, the British ambassador, the United States reply to that country’s newest request for suspension of payments this month. While the contents were not made public, it was assumed in official quarters that the note said again that Congress alone could change the debt situation, that the president would ask creation of an agency to study it, and advised that payment be made. At least six countries have asked for a new moratorium, the Belgian government making a second appeal yesterday. President Ho

APY B&F SAMA & SUR Again yesterday the United States insisted in a note to Great Britain on payment of the $95,550,000 war debt installment due December 15. Secretary Stimson said in the note he was confident Congress would be “willing to consider any reasonable suggestion” which would facilitate payment. In London it was learned on high authority arrangements would be made immediately to make the payment in gold. The American reply to the second French note, asking postponement of the $20,000,000 payment due from France December 15, was presented to the French ambassador at Washington. In Paris Prime Minister MacDonald of Britain and Premier Herriot went over the debt question at a four-hour conference, at the conclusion of which it was indicated Britain was planning to pay the December installment and M. Herriot would recommend payment to parliament with reservations.

1932-08-04.text: | OTTAWA, ONT., Aug. 3—(?)—Bilateral agreements between the dominions and preference rates for empire wheat in Great Britain were set up today as two of the most important results of the imperial trade conference. This program, which includes four other major items, appeared to have grown out of an interview granted by Premier Bennett of Canada yesterday and a session of the British delegation which lasted well into last night. The other four objectives are: 1. A curb upon Russian trade with Great Britain. 2. Creation of an empire bank to clear empire trade balances. 3. Freer dominion markets for British products which do not compete with home industries. 4. Lower preferential tariffs within the empire.

MIAMI, Fla., Aug. 3. (The tangled and tragic love affairs of Mrs. Jessie M. Keith-Miller, Australian aviatrix, with Capt. W. N. Lancaster, former British army flier, and Haden Clarke, young writer, were recounted by her from the witness chair Wednesday in Lancaster's trial for the murder of Clarke. She expressed confidence in the innocence of Lancaster, whom she said she had “always intended to marry” during the five years of intimate association, and said Clarke had often threatened suicide. She declared Lancaster's reaction to information that Clarke had taken his place in her affection while he was away on a business trip seeking to bolster their finances was one of “sadness” and that he planned to kill himself so she and Clarke might collect $1,000 insurance on his life as a “wedding present.”

DUBLIN, Aug. 3. (P)—The Irish Free State passed a motion Wednesday night calling for the reopening of negotiations with Great Britain regarding the Irish land annuities, which President Eamon de Valera's government has failed to pay. Declaring the policy of the De Valera government to be one of creating an Irish republic, including Ulster, Senator Joseph Connolly, Minister of Posts and Telegraphs, said he could “tell Ramsay MacDonald (British prime minister) that he has no hope of getting his war debts even considered by America so long as this question remains unsettled.”

Miami, Fla., Aug. 4 -- The story of a strange love triangle drew crowds today to the trial of Capt. W. N. Lancaster, former British Army flier, for murder of Haden Clarke, his rival for the affections of Mrs. Jessie M. Keith-Miller. Mrs. Keith-Miller, Australian aviatrix who was Lancaster's flying partner and once his fiancée, was called back to the witness stand for cross-examination after a three and one-half hour session in which she told of her love for the aviator and Clarke to whom she became engaged as he wrote a story of her life. The woman gave a graphic picture of the loves of the trio in her testimony as a court's witness. She said she had loved and admired Lancaster, and planned for almost five years to marry him. Then she told of her sudden infatuation for Clarke, during Lancaster's absence on a business trip, and of subsequent intimacy when she and the author decided to mar

| Berlin, Aug. 3.—()--Rioting, with guns, knives and clubs for weapons, has suddenly flared anew in Germany. Three men are dead and several others severely injured. At Koenigsberg, communists retaliated for the attacks by national socialists last Monday which resulted in the death of the communist leader and another man in the party councils. They fired a volley into a Nazi meeting, killing one. Four were stabbed or shot during the riot which followed. A socialist laborer, father of ten children, was killed at Zweibruecken when a squad of Nazis leaped from a group of pedestrians, some of whom had been taunting them. The Nazis beat the crowd with clubs, spades and stones. A Reichsbannerman was shot dead by Nazis at Olendorf. Police arrested 200 armed Nazi storm troops at Frensheim after breaking up a disturbance. Windows of the Hungarian consulate at Frankfurt-am-Main were smashed by a gr

BERLIN, Aug. 4. ()—The prospect of a serious break between Chancellor von Papen’s government and Adolph Hitler, national socialist leader, over the recent riots in Germany, was intimated in the rightist press today. This was coupled with evidence that Hitler was spreading his organization efforts into other European countries and planning a powerful Nordic European alliance. The ultra-rightist Boersen-Zeitung said the government is considering a smashing emergency decree to end the rioting, in practically all of which Hitler’s Nazis and his storm troops had a part. That the decree would meet a protest from Hitler’s forces was indicated by William Kube, head of the powerful Nazi delegation in the Prussian diet. Herr Kube severely criticized Chancellor von Papen, minister of interior Baron von Gayl, and Franz Bracht, Prussian dictator, for what he said was an attempt to “sabotage the Nazi
Warsaw, Poland, Aug. 4. (AP)— Lightning struck a detachment of soldiers on the march near Powursk, Volhynia, today, killing six and injuring six more.

STOCKHOLM, Aug. 4. (f)— Greta Garbo, noted film actress, who is on her way home from the United States, will begin producing films here soon with the assistance of Victor Sjöström and Ludwig Berger, it was reported. It was reported she planned also to buy the summer residence of the late Ivan Kreuger, Swedish match king, on the islet of Aengsholmen.

1932-06-18.text: NEW YORK, June 18 (#)—The New York World-Telegram today states that Nicholas Murray Butler, who led the fight for a repeal plank in the Republican national platform, will lead a movement to bring about repudiation by New England and middle Atlantic Republican state conventions of the plank finally adopted in Chicago. If he succeeds, Dr. Butler said, President Hoover may have “a sporting chance” of re-election. If he fails, he predicted, the Republican party will “go over the dam.” Adoption of the present plank by the Republican national convention in Chicago was described by Dr. Butler as “the most shocking exhibition of patronage control of a convention since 1872, when Ulysses S. Grant won his second nomination.” “I was told,” he said, “that six cabinet members were at the convention, that 37 of the 97 delegates from New York and upward of 400 of the convention's membership were office

LAUSANNE, SWITZERLAND, June 17.—(?)—Great Britain offered to wipe the slate clean of reparations and war debts at the international economic conference here today, but France insisted that elimination of trade barriers was more important than cancellation of the war payments. Germany's spokesman, in a temperate address, made no reference to repudiation of reparations, but indicated it might be necessary to declare a moratorium on private debts, most of which are owed to Americans. The most important concrete achievement of today’s session was the acceptance by Great Britain, France, Italy, Belgium and Japan of a temporary agreement to suspend reparation payments from June 30, when the Hoover moratorium ends, to the close of the present conference. This sidetracked a suggestion that the Hoover holiday be extended another six months. It assured continuation of the conference at least until

London, June 18.—(A.P.)—Stanislaus Hausner, Polish-born American flyer who was rescued from the Atlantic a week ago, today, after failing to fly from New York to Warsaw, plans to try the flight again this year, he said in a message received from him today. The message was sent from the freighter Circe Shell which picked him up out of the sea 500 miles off the coast of Portugal and which is taking him back to the United States. Hausner asked if it were possible for the British government to send a training ship to salvage his plane, which was abandoned at the spot where he was rescued. He said it could keep afloat for a week or more. Hausner revealed that he flew 28 hours before he was forced down into the ocean.

London, June 18.— (A.P.)—The United States liner Leviathan was aground for less than three quarters of an hour today off the isle of Wight, a message received by Lloyds Agency here said, but she got away again without difficulty or known damage. The liner was reported hoisting the signal “not under control” at 7:40 a. m. on the Dean sand approaches to Spithead. Within less than three quarters of an hour, however, another message said, the ship had hauled down its distress signal and proceeded to the nearby Cowes roads where, by mid-forenoon, it was discharging and receiving passengers.

MONTREAL, June 18 — Divers and firemen risked their lives today among smoking steel plates and twisted wreckage of the British oil tanker, Cymoline, seeking bodies buried by three explosions which killed a score or more in drydock here yesterday. Officials of Canadian Vickers, Ltd, who checked the casualty lists, said they believed the death toll in the million dollar fire would reach 25. Some bodies may never be recovered, because the explosion destroyed all trace of some men, they said. The list of known dead included four Montreal firemen and six Vickers workmen who died in hospitals. Fifteen Vickers men are missing, believed dead, "blown to bits or buried in the debris." The four dead firemen included Fire Chief Raoul Gauthier, noted for his bravery. Flames 100 Feet High Eyewitnesses described the disaster, one of the greatest in the history of this city. They said workmen were busy

MONTREAL, June 18—(P)— The blast-torn tanker Cymbaline was searched today for bodies of 14 persons believed dead. Eleven already have been recovered. Of the more than three score men injured when explosions shattered the British vessel yesterday, 37 were still in hospitals. Several million dollars damage was done, officials estimated, in the blasts and fire that inflicted one of Montreal's major disasters. A $5,000,000 Canadian Vickers drydock, in which the British vessel was undergoing repairs when it blew up, was partly wrecked. Officials believe a hot rivet may have come in contact with gas accumulating over oil inside the vessel. The bodies recovered were those of three firemen and eight Vickers repair men. The fourteen missing and presumed dead were Vickers employees.

Dublin, June 18.—(A. P.)—Dublin was giving last minute touches today to her more than a year’s preparation for the Eucharistic congress which will be held here next week. For weeks pilgrims to the great religious convention have been trickling into Ireland, but in the last three days the trickle has swollen into a rushing stream, taxing housing, but not Irish hospitality. Dublin itself wears a festive air, a kind of quiet gaiety. The streets are garlanded with Irish flowers—old roses often—house fronts are newly painted, yards are neat and pavements swept clean. And, however humble the cottage, the curtains at the window are as snowy and stiff as washings and starch can make them. Saturday is a bustling day ordinarily in Dublin, but with the congress visitors adding their thousands today, broad and monumented O’Connell street became so packed this afternoon that it was almost like a foot

(United Press Staff Correspondent.) LAUSANNE, June 18 — The Lausanne slate, showing $50,000,000 in war debts and reparations payments due July 1, suspended, was turned to the wall today as statesmen decided whether to wipe the slate clean or fill it with new figures. Great Britain, Italy, and Germany stood for cancellation. France and her allies wanted alteration. The statesmen will hold private conversations until the conference meets again Tuesday, but a private moratorium for Europe appeared to be the only possible development until the United States modifies its attitude. The Germans were at first pleased by the suspension, thinking it indicated that a final solution would be found by the conference. ‘The speeches of Edouard Herriot and Neville Chamberlain impressed me as animated by goodwill, the best indication for success of the conference,” Chancellor Von Papen said. But the Germ

1932-03-22.text: DUBLIN, Ireland, March 22, (U.P.)—The Irish Free State formally notified Great Britain today that it intends to remove the oath of allegiance to the king required of members of the Dáil Éireann,

SHANGHAI, March 22 (/P)—A complaint against Japanese air patrols continuing to fly over the area behind the Chinese lines was filed with the League of Nations inquiry commission today by twenty-five American and British residents of Shanghai. Japanese army officials declared, however, they had no intention of stopping the patrols until a truce is finally effected. Such reconnoitering flights are justified by military necessity, a Japanese spokesman said. Peace negotiations, which heretofore have been participated in by diplomats, will be monopolized tomorrow by military leaders, not only of China and Japan but of the United States, Great Britain, France and Italy.

| SHANGHAI, Mar. 21. (P)—New parleys for peace and new trenches for war were under way here today. Japanese and Chinese negotiators continued peace parleys under the auspices of neutral observers, while out along the Japanese front line to the northwest Japanese soldiers worked feverishly on new trenches, barbed wire barricades and sandbag redoubts. Those actually connected with the negotiations, the Chinese and Japanese representatives and the foreign officials, all professed to see hope for success of the parleys, but there were widely circulated reports on the outside that the negotiators were deadlocked over the question of withdrawal of Japanese troops. Officials declined to reveal the terms suggested for the armistice but they were reported to have centered on three points: 1. Chinese troops to remain in their present positions about 20 miles west of Shanghai. 2. Japanese forces to

CHANGCHUN, Manchuria, Mar. 22.—(#)—A widespread revolt against the new Manchurian state of Ankuo has resulted in clashes on the edge of the Soviet Siberian border between Japanese and Chinese insurgents, Japanese military authorities said in messages received today. The most severe fighting occurred Monday, the messages said, when Chinese insurgents engaged an infantry detachment of Gen. Jiro Tamon’s Japanese brigade at Nanhuto, on the southern end of Lake Birten. This is only a short distance from the Russian border, 50 miles northeast of Tunhua, eastern terminus of the uncompleted branch of the railway leading toward the Korean border. The Chinese lost 150 killed and the Japanese 15, the Japanese military reported. Fifteen Japanese were wounded. Lesser affrays over a wide area were reported at the same time. In an interview with the Unit- ed Press, bearing on the present conflict in the far east, Trotzky said that Japan is going to stick up to the knees in the “fat soil of Manchuria.” The energetic little revolution- ist, who performed a modern military miracle by creating the Soviets’ red army when he stood beside Lenin at the head of the Bolshevist state, is well qualified to analyze the Russian position in the orient conflict, which has now spread along the Siberian frontier. SHANGHAI, March 21.—(4°—Chinese and Japanese negotiations reached a basis for peace today, after long parleys here, while League of Nations investigators viewed the scars of recent battle. Members of the league's commission of inquiry returned, grimy and weary, from an all-day tour of the battlefields. They found the rival disputants ready for a formal peace conference, scheduled to begin Wednesday. Quo Tai-Chi, representing China, said the terms on which the two sides apparently agreed provided: 1. The Chinese troops would remain where they now are, about 20 miles west of Shanghai. 2. The Japanese troops would withdraw according to a fixed program not yet announced. 3. A joint commission, including representatives of neutral powers would oversee the execution of the foregoing conditions. JAPAN'S PROMISE! BOV aAS MOSCOW (4) — The Soviet foreign office said today it had been reassured by the Japanese government that massing of Japanese troops on the Soviet border was not intended as a threat to Soviet territory and that the Japanese stood ready to suppress the activities of "White" Russian guards in Manchuria, should these become menacing. The assurance was given the foreign office by Koki Hirota, Japanese Ambassador, the statement said. M. Hirota said his government had no intention of pursuing aggressive measures along the Chinese Eastern railway, operated jointly by China and Russia. Recently a controversy arose between Russia and Japan when Japanese military officials asked to move troops northward over it. Russia asked where the troops were going and what they intended to do.

Rome—(#)— Paoli De Bene, 13-year-old student, his head almost severed from the body by a knife wound, was found dead in bed in a dormitory at the Catholic institute of Pius IX, yesterday. Paolo Sociarelli, a priest, was held by the police, who said he admitted that he must have killed the boy “in a moment of unconsciousness.” The dormitory was occupied by 40 boys and four priests.

1932-06-30.text: London, June 30.—The Prince of Wales was confined to his rooms with a chill today but an official statement from York House said he was “going on well.” Because of his illness the prince cancelled an engagement to attend the Canadian Dominion Day dinner tonight.

London, July 1 (UP)—Reprisals against the Irish Free State for its failure to pay the land annuities due Great Britain were announced in the House of Commons today by J. H. Thomas, Dominions Secretary. Thomas said no payment on the annuities due today had been received, and therefore he would introduce in the House on Monday "proposals to deal with the situation."

Washington, June 29 (AP)—Heading the voice of Borah of Idaho, the Senate today refused President Hoover's request for funds for American participation in a world economic conference to be called by Great Britain later in the year. Instead it voted $40,000 for paying expenses of United States delegates to a conference confined to a discussion of monetary questions including the restoration of silver, if one should be called. The action was taken after Senator Borah, chairman of the foreign relations committee, had told the Senate that “since the breakdown of the Lausanne conference there is directly nothing to be gained by calling another economic conference.” He also pointed to a plank in the recently adopted Republican platform which declares for participation in “an international conference to consider matters relating to monetary questions,” and remarked that it does not mention a gen

Edinburgh, Scotland, June 30— Andrew W. Mellon, United States ambassador to Great Britain, was granted an honorary degree of doctor of laws by Edinburgh University today. Tribute was paid to Mellon by Dr. James MacIntosh, professor of civil law, in granting the degree.

WIMBLEDON, Eng., June 30,— Helen Wills Moody, four times women’s singles tennis champion at Wimbledon, swept into the final round again today by defeating Miss Mary Heeley, an English girl, 6-2, 6-0. Mrs. Moody will meet Helen Jacobs, a hometown rival from Berkeley, Calif., in the final round.

Associated Press: Staff Writer LAUSANNE, Switzerland, June 29.—Franz Von Papen, German chancellor, laid before the powers at the war debts reparations conference today a demand for revision of the Versailles treaty as a necessary preliminary for German participation in the economic reconstruction of the world. In a statement to the press, Chancellor Von Papen demanded that all discrimination against Germany be revised out of the treaty. His statement was a reply to a question proposed by Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald of Great Britain yesterday asking what concessions Germany was ready to make in order to facilitate a definite settlement of the reparations problem. “World confidence cannot be re-established,” the chancellor said, “if the powers which emerged victors from the World War do not decide to eliminate the discrimination created by the treaty of Versailles. “If, by revision of

Lausanne, Switzerland, June 28. —(AP) — Every effort to bring about a Franco-German reparations agreement failed today and the international statesmen who gathered here in a spirit of hope two weeks ago prepared to give the Lausanne conference decent burial. Unless there is an unforeseen change of front overnight, the six leading powers will meet tomorrow to prepare for adjournment and to arrange the usual gesture of appointing a committee of experts to solve the problems they have been unable to solve. To Meet in Fall In the fall another attempt will be made to compose the reparations conflict at another international conference. Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald of Great Britain made almost superhuman efforts to bring about an agreement between Premier Édouard Herriot of France, who insisted that reparations must not be cancelled, and Chancellor Franz von Papen of Germany, who insisted t

LAUSANNE, Switzerland, June 29. (®)—After the reparations conflict between France and Germany had reached its high point today with a forthright demand by Chancellor Franz von Papen that the Versailles treaty be revised to eliminate all discriminations against Germany, there was evidence of calmer counsels and a possible eventual agreement. The French, who were greatly displeased by the declaration for treaty revision, reported the German chancellor modified his tone in subsequent discussions.

1932-03-06.text: Glasgow, Scotland, March 5. (P)— Betty Gow, nursemaid to the kidnapped Lindbergh baby, cabled her mother here today not to worry. “I'm heart broken, but cheer up, mother,” the message said. The young woman and her mother have communicated by cable frequently since the kidnapping.

Shanghai, March 5. (4?) — Approximately 10,600 additional Japanese troops were landed in the Shanghai area today and the crackle of machine guns and occasional crashes of heavy artillery fire still resounded over the countryside between Kiangwan and the banks of the Yangtze. Army units totaling 8,000 men were landed at Liuho on the southern bank of the Yangtze and 2,000 more were put ashore at Woosung. It was understood that bluejackets who have been on duty in those areas were returning to their ships. Japanese Forces. Japanese military and naval authorities continued to maintain there has been no serious fighting since the Japanese advance was through the Kiangwan and Woosung area today supported Chinese claims that there has been considerable skirmishing along the northwest sector. Gunfire was heard frequently and a squadron of Japanese planes roared overhead in the direction of the Y

Shanghai, March 5.— (UP) —The Chinese Nationalist government issued a virtual declaration of war on the new independent Manchurian state today while rioting threatened foreign concessions here and Japanese and Chinese forces planned further fighting. The first act of a new military council created by the central executive committee of the Chinese government was to order a punitive expedition against the Manchurian state. The committee meeting at Loyang was attended by government and military leaders. According to the opinion of Chinese leaders here, the expedition will be headed by Marshal Chang Hseuh-Liang, ousted as Manchurian overlord by the Japanese, and Feng Yu-Hsiang, the “Christian General.” He still heads a powerful military force. Marshal Chang had a loyal army of 25,000 men in the Chinchow area before he ordered his men to retire within the great wall of China at Shanhaikwan. I

- SHANGHAI, March 5 (UP). Miss E. Rose Marlow, American teacher at a Baptist mission school, was severely beaten yesterday by reservist troops while inspecting the ruins of her school at Chapei, American consular officials were informed today. Miss Marlow, it was learned, was struck in the face and beaten with sticks. It was not learned what provoked the attack. The teacher, affiliated with the Southern Baptist mission, has been a resident of the Orient for some time.

TOKYO, March 5 (F)—Gen. Sadao Araki, minister of war, told the members of the League of Nations Manchurian investigating commission that Japan has no intention of invading Soviet Russian territory, but that if the Soviet army menaced Manchurian territory, Japan would have no choice but to defend it. Members of the commission conferred with the war minister at the war office for two hours today. The war office declared that "documents" published yesterday in the Moscow newspaper Izvestia purporting to elucidate plans of Japanese military leaders for an invasion of Siberia were "entirely fabrications."

Oslo, Norway, March 5. (P)— Prime Minister M. Kolstad died today. He had been in all health for a long time. His death means the resignation of the government, which is expected within the next few days. The announcement of his passing reached the parliament while it was in session and an adjournment was voted immediately. Mr. Kolstad was 54 years old. He entered parliament in 1922 and last year he formed Norway's first agrarian government.

GENEVA, March 5—China accused Japan before the League of Nations today of planning to take the entire region between Shanghai and Nanking. The League announced at the same time that United States participation in an international commission of military officials at Shanghai to supervise cessation of hostilities was assured. Dr. W. W. Yen, Chinese delegate, read submitted official telegrams stating that Japanese were pouring reinforcements into the region beyond Liuho on the Yangtze and that ‘some 35,000 more, with tanks and cavalry, have landed to outflank our present positions near Kuansan.’ The Chinese said eight more Japanese transports entered the Yangtze yesterday and that severe fighting was in progress. ‘Our regiments defending Woosung were killed to the last man rather than surrender,’ the official telegram said. ‘Foreign eyewitnesses saw our peasants being forced at bayonet poin

Shanghai, March 5, — Chinese casualties during the engagements in the Chapei, Kiangwan and Woosung areas reached a total greater than 20,000, the press union estimated today. This total, according to the press union estimate, was about ten times greater than Japanese casualties and it included approximately 7,000 killed. Japanese military and naval authorities continued their insistence that there has been no serious fighting since the advance was halted two days ago, but an inspection of the Kiangwan and Woosung areas supported the Chinese contention that there has been considerable skirmishing along the northwest sector. This correspondent frequently heard gunfire and a squadron of Japanese planes roared overhead, going in the direction of the Yangtze river. A large detachment of cavalry was being unloaded at the Woosung docks, and trackloads of troops and civilians were being moved to

1932-03-12.text: London, March 11.—(A.P.)—Prince Lennart, grandson of King Gustav of Sweden, and Miss Karin Nissvandt, daughter of a wealthy Stockholm businessman, were married at the prince’s Row Registry office at 11 a.m. today. The prince and his fiancée came to London a fortnight ago for their wedding, because King Gustav refused his consent to the marriage and it could not be solemnized in Sweden. The prince’s mother, the Grand Duchess Marie of Russia, came from New York a week ago but did not attend the ceremony. He renounced his rights to the succession to the Swedish throne in order to marry his bride, who is a commoner. They plan to live in Switzerland where the prince has an estate. He will devote his time

NEW YORK, March 12.—(U.P)— The distressed coast guard patrol boat, 218, has been taken in tow by the British steamer Dakotian which is proceeding toward Nantucket, a radio marine message reported today. The message said the seven members of the crew which has been battling a storm the past five days since leaving Cape May, N. J. were safe. The steamer first sighted the patrol boat about 400 miles southeast of New York.

Washington, Mar. 12—(A P)—The United States stands ready to cooperate with Great Britain, France and Italy in effecting an arrangement for the evacuation of Japanese troops from Shanghai under the plan adopted yesterday by the League of Nations assembly. As yet, however, the state department has no advices from Shanghai as to any definite steps having been taken to put the plan into effect. Sir Eric Drummond, secretary of the League of Nations, officially informed Secretary Stimson of yesterday’s action in the assembly looking to a peaceful settlement of the Sino-Japanese dispute. The secretary’s statement expressing the willingness of the United States to cooperate in the League effort was communicated to Sir Eric Drummond. Consequently the league and the United States are waiting for the Chinese and Japanese to act on the plan and stop fighting.

London, March 11—(P)—An unsmiling young prince of the blood, Lennart of Sweden, Friday sacrificed his royal privileges, quarreled with his mother and married a commoner. A colorless British civil ceremony in Princes' Row Register office united the grandson of the King of Sweden and Miss Karin Nissyandt, a beautiful girl with corn-colored hair, the daughter of a wealthy Stockholm businessman. No sooner had the ceremony ended than a representative of the Swedish legation stepped up and handed the prince a new passport which certified "that he was plain 'Mr. Bernadotte,'" the bespectacled young man’s symbol of sacrifice—an exchange of titles and royal highness for the girl he loved. No member of the prince's family was present, and the small wedding party included only the bride's mother, aunt and uncle. The young man's mother, the Grand Duchess Marie Pavlova, who made an eleventh-hour prot

London, March 12.--(4?)-—"The Economist,” important British financial journal, said today the kidnaping of Charles Augustus Lindbergh, Jr. was a result of American business policy. “The inability of the police to find the slightest trace of the missing child,” it said, “the appeals by Colonel Lindbergh to the underworld and his despairing recourse to the services of two well-known gangsters as potential intermediaries in the negotiations with undisclosed leaders of the supposed kidnaping racket—the whole extraordinary chronicle is a curiously revealing commentary on one angle of social life in the United States. “America ‘big business’ individualist by strong inclination and disposition, has stood consistently for weak and compliant administration. A nation-wide organization of rackets is the price which the public is now paying for that policy. From the doctrines of ‘100 per cent pure’

PARIS, March 12.--(AP)--Just before the Briand funeral today the foreign office issued a communique announcing that France and Great Britain had reached an agreement to “work together to appease Europe's political rivalries and hasten the day of economic reconstruction.” The announcement followed a two-hour conference between Premier Tardieu and Sir John Simon, the British foreign secretary. They talked over outstanding issues, including the reparations problem, projected commercial treaties and the Mediterranean naval dispute. It was said they gave special consideration to the French plan for extending economic assistance to the central European and Danubian states and that they had reached an accord on this and all other questions declaring that “Franco-British cooperation should have the double object of achieving amelioration of European political and accelerating

By The Associated Press Shanghai, March 11.—Chinese authorities were adamant today in refusing to accept any peace settlement which did not include an unconditional withdrawal of Japanese troops from the Shanghai area. As a result, although both the Chinese and Japanese accepted the resolution of the League of Nations adopted March 4 looking toward a settlement of hostilities there, no peace was in sight today. The Chinese reiterated they were unwilling to enter into a conference on any other basis than unconditional withdrawal of troops by the Japanese and Japanese diplomatic circles—although they said they were not only willing but anxious to enter into a conference with the Chinese—indicated it was imperative that the two sides get together on an interpretation of the League's resolution.

Berlin, Mar. 15. —(AP)— Republican Germany stood at the crossroads today as nearly 3,000,000 voters, the last din of a bitter election campaign sounding in their ears, pondered which road to take. Down one road lay the way to communism akin to that of Soviet Russia. On another, the sign pointed to Adolf Hitler's camp of Fascism. A third way, the face of the nationalists, swerved backward toward the old monarchy. On the fourth road stood the octogenarian former warrior, now President Paul Von Hindenburg, seeking reelection with a promise to maintain the moderation of the republic. The veteran president was slated to close the exciting campaign this evening with a last appeal on a nationwide radio broadcast. Throughout the nation tomorrow is looked upon as one of the most decisive days in German history. Nothing has been left undone by the radical forces to achieve control of the nation. B

1932-05-16.text: LONDON, (P)—A mutiny has broken out in the Japanese navy and in part of the army. Private advices from Tokio said today. A general censorship has been established in Tokio.

Bombay, May 16 (UP)—The third day of Hindu-Moslem rioting—murder, pillage and arson—with British troops firing into fighting mobs has boosted the death toll to 34 with the injured estimated at 400. Four more victims were added to the death toll when fighting broke out again this morning. The entire northern city resembled a battlefield in which troops were handicapped by the guerilla tactics of bloodthirsty crowds. The traditional rivalry between Hindus and Moslems flared into violence Saturday, touched off when Moslem boys allegedly stoned Hindu homes. Street fights began, pedestrians were stoned or stabbed, houses were set on fire, and soon an entire street was in flames. Police said many women and children were in the blazing houses and that numerous occupants preferred to die in the flames rather than rush into the streets and be attacked. The assassins raced through Tokyo streets in motor cars as they hurled their bombs, throwing the populace into a panic. Seventy-seven-year-old Tsuyoshi Inukai, premier and the “old fox” of Japanese politics, was executed in his home by six men wearing military uniforms who battered their way past police guards. Hold, Shoot Him - They called Inukai from a room where he was chatting with a visitor. Two men held the premier, another fired twice, one bullet entering the temple and another penetrating a nostril. By United Press MARSEILLES, France — Rescue liners have saved nearly 600 passengers from the steamer, Georges Philippar, abandoned in flames in the Gulf of Aden. The Jetee wireless station was informed today. No information on the number of dead was available. The station reported four liners and three freighters arrived near the burning vessel and picked up the passengers as they took to the boats.

Poona, India — () — Armored cars were rushed early Monday to Bombay to assist in breaking up the bloody fighting between Hindus and Moslems which has been going on since Saturday. An Indian regiment was ordered to stand by prepared to leave for Bombay at a moment's notice. (Early story on Page 12.)

TOKYO, May 15, (Monday)— Premier Suyoshi Inukai died shortly before midnight from bullet wounds inflicted by an assassin, a member of a group of military terrorists responsible for serious bombings. The moment the premier was attacked, bombs were exploded in the office of the metropolitan police board, the Bank of Japan, headquarters of the Seiyūk or government party, and the home of the Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal. The outrages took place simultaneously at 5:30 p.m. No serious damage was done. After the outburst of terrorism which climaxed a long series of political crimes including an attack on the life of the emperor, 18 men, five naval lieutenants in uniform and the others former army cadets also in uniform surrendered to police. A handbill left at the police board office was signed, “The Young Army and Navy Officers’ Association.” They condemned the present state of political part

BOMBAY, May 16 — (INS)— Cold-blooded daylight murders, widespread incendiarism, looting, and the wanton destruction of property today featured the third day of Moslem-Hindu warfare. The fighting was entirely beyond control of police and government troops and gave no indication of an early end. Deaths had mounted to 44 and the injured was well above 500 toward the middle of the day, while government troops were rushed into the city from all available ports. The city was paralyzed, with streets deserted except for police patrols or sudden appearances of Hindus or Moslems conducting a guerrilla war.

BY DELOS SMITH (United Press Staff Correspondent) TRENTON, N. J., May 16. —Leaders in the futile hunt for the killers of the Lindbergh baby met here today to decide who shall direct the investigation and thus end the official quibbling that began the day after the kidnapping. Governor A. Harry Moore, who early retained for his office supervision over official news releases in the case, called the conference. Among the attendants were two county prosecutors, the attorney general's representative, state police heads, and a representative of the department of justice. J. Edgar Hoover, chief of the bureau of investigation of the department of justice, is charged with coordinating the work of his own men, the secret service, the internal revenue agents and post office detectives with the New Jersey state police. 1932-03-23.text: LONDON, March 23 (A. P.)—Great Britain is determined that Ireland shall never abolish the oath of allegiance to the British crown nor the payment of the Irish land annuities. To that end the government has sent a communication to the Free State government which will make the British standpoint "clear beyond the possibility of a doubt," he said. Eamon De Valera, new Free State president, informed London officially yesterday that he intends to abolish the oath, and, although there had been no official communication regarding the annuities, his public statements during and since the recent Irish election made it clear that he intends to discontinue their payment to England. LONDON, March 22.—The Irish Free State served notice on an anxious England today that the oath of allegiance to the king, almost the last tie that binds Erin to Great Britain, would be abolished. The Irish situation, which J. H. Thomas, British Secretary for Dominions, described in Parliament as grave, will be discussed at a cabinet meeting tomorrow. Lord Dulanty, high commissioner in London for the Free State, informed Thomas that the Irish people by overwhelming vote in the last election had made mandatory the oath's removal. His statement, which admittedly made the Irish situation serious after 10 years of peace between the two nations, was in answer to a request of the Dominions Secretary for “correct information” as to the intentions of the new Irish government of President Eamon De Valera. Dulanty said that whether the oath to the British crown should be retained was purely an Iris

LONDON: MAR. 23. (AP).—Great Britain is sending Ireland a communication "which will make the British standpoint clear beyond the possibility of a doubt" in connection with proposed abolition of the oath of allegiance to the crown, J. H. Thomas informed the House of Commons today. The Secretary for Dominions made this announcement in informing the House that he had received official notification from the Free State government that it considered the oath of allegiance not mandatory. The view of the British government set forth that it is manifest that the oath is an integral part of the treaty signed when the Free State was created ten years ago. Mr. Thomas said there had been no official communication from the Free State with regard to the land annuity, but he added that "judging from the statement reported to have been made by Mr. De Valera in the Free State Senate, we understand that th

(United Press Staff Correspondent) LONDON, MAR. 23,—(U.P)—Announcement of a firm British policy toward the Republican government of the Irish Free State was expected today as the cabinet considered Eamon De Valera’s plan to renounce the oath of allegiance to the crown and land annuities paid to England. Britain was expected to stand firmly on the terms of the Anglo-Irish Treaty, to indicate in the clearest language the consequences of any such breach in the treaty. King George received J. H. Thomas, Secretary for Dominions, in audience at Buckingham Palace for an hour, after which Thomas hurried to the cabinet meeting at No. 10 Downing Street. The British government, it was understood, desires that any controversy be conducted with dignity and patience. It was considered possible that the dispute might be referred to a tribunal. (Continued on Page Two)

SHANGHAI, March 22. — Disease and famine, two others of the four horsemen of the Apocalypse, rode roughshod over China today in the path of the havoc of war. As a result of the crowding of millions of refugees during the hostilities at Shanghai, an epidemic of smallpox is now sweeping the Orient, according to Dr. Wu Lien-teh, Director of Chinese Maritime Quarantine. Sir John Hope-Simpson, British Director of the China Famine Commission, said at the same time that famine conditions had again reached such a pass in some parts of the country that the people were eating the bark of trees, the chaff of thrashed grain, and weeds, in order to ward off starvation. Dr. Wu said the smallpox epidemic was the most widespread, and taking the heaviest toll in this vicinity of any two days and the native quarters are crowded with patients, the number of whom is not known, he said.

By The Associated Press Changchun, Manchuria, March 23—A new battle in which five Japanese and 42 Chinese were killed broke out today in the wide-spread revolt in Kirin province against the new Manchurian state.

Harbin, Manchuria, March 2—(U. P.)—Travellers arriving here from Europe today via the Trans-Siberian Railroad reported large numbers of Soviet troops between Irkutsk and Chita and many airplanes flying along the Mongolian frontier. Both Japanese and Soviet officials said they had not the slightest intention of fighting. It was obvious, however, that the Soviet troops were ready for battle. Gen. Hasebe, Japanese Commander here, said Japan was doing everything possible to avoid offending the Soviets. Gen. Tamon said practically the same thing. Correspondents returning from Mukden said residents of the city considered the new Manchurian state a joke. They told how Gen. Chang Ching-Hui, set up at Mukden by the Japanese, summoned correspondents for an interview, then allowed his Japanese advisor to do all the talking while he passed the time admiring his new shoes and socks.
