SALZBURG, Austria, Sept. 12. (P)—Winston Churchill, former British chancellor of the Exchequer, was taken from his hotel to a hospital today with a slight case of paratyphoid. The doctor said his condition was not alarming.

COPENHAGEN, Sept. 12—An extended search was along the southeast Greenland coast today for the “Flying Hutchinsons.” The British Trawler Lord Talbot failed to find the plane of George Hutchinson, his wife, and two daughters and four other members of the party when it raced to a point where the distress signals flashed yesterday. The party was attempting a New York-London flight.

HARBIN, Manchuria, Sept. 12 (4). Twenty-four persons were killed, upwards of 70 injured, and an undetermined number kidnapped and 600 robbed in a series of three combination bandit raids and train wrecks near here within 24 hours. In addition to these casualties more than 200 were killed and several wounded in a battle between Japanese troops and Chinese bandits.

BERLIN, Sept. 12, (4)—Caught napping the Reichstag opposition, which passed a motion of non-confidence before he could promulgate a decree of dissolution, Chancellor Von Papen found himself today in a position of great uncertainty. He will remain in charge of the government for at least several weeks, however, for the Court will be asked to rule on the constitutionality of the events which made today’s session of the Reichstag one of the most dramatic in a long time. A single dissenting voice could have forestalled consideration of a Communist motion coupling a declaration of non-confidence with a demand that the government's last emergency decree be rescinded. But the government had not expected this turn of events and was caught off guard. Realizing too late what was going on, the Chancellor sprang to the rostrum with his decree of dissolution, but the speaker waved him aside, assertin

(United Press Staff Correspondent) Berlin. - (UP) — The Reichstag, amid tumultuous scenes, was dissolved by the von Papen government today but broke into open rebellion and refused to consider itself dissolved. A “state of emergency,” similar to martial law, was expected to be declared. As soon as the Reichstag convened to hear the maiden ministerial declaration of Chancellor Franz von Papen, the communists and Hitler's fascists declared war on the government, Calls For Vote Without awaiting von Papen's speech, Hermann Goering, the speaker, who is a Hitlerite deputy, called for immediate vote on communist motions rescinding President von Hindenburg’s emergency decree of Sept. 4, providing a rigid one-year plan of economy to save the country's finances, and also of misconfidence in the government. Von Papen immediately read a decree of dissolution. Goering refused to leave the rostrum, ho

BERLIN, Sept. 12.—(/--A communist motion of non-confidence in the cabinet of Chancellor Franz Von Papen was voted by the reichstag today 513 to 32, with 50 members abstaining. The motion was carried after the chancellor had promulgated a decree dissolving the reichstag and Hermann Wilhelm Goering, national socialist speaker, had declined to enforce the decree pending action of a technicality before the house. Coupled with the non-confidence motion was a demand for the emergency decree by which President Von Hindenburg legalized the economic program of Chancellor Von Papen be rescinded. This dramatic turn in events left parliamentarians uncertain regarding the exact status of the reichstag. This confusion was increased by Speaker Goering, who declared that the chancellor's decree of dissolution would be ignored in view of the fact that the government had already been overthrown.

1932-10-25.text: London, Oct. 23—(UP)—Thousands of hunger marchers battled their way toward London today to the music of fife and drum corps and the strains of “Keep the Home Fires Burning,” plodding over muddy roads through a cold, drenching rain. Groups already on the road totaled more than 3,000. Many others were preparing to start the trek. Pipers, bands and fifers and drummers cheered the marchers on their way to protest dole reductions in an immense demonstration planned for Thursday. Although roads were submerged in many places, and marchers were drenched by cold rains that have swept the country for a week, they maintained their march on schedule with a minimum of “grousing.” “We will sleep at Buckingham Palace or at Claridge's Hotel when we get to London,” some of the marchers said jocularly. They have been sleeping in dance halls, school houses and community centers during the march. London pol

New York—(Y)—Miss Betty Gow, who was nursemaid for the kidnapped and slain Lindbergh baby, arrived from England today on the liner Caledonia and sped away from the pier in an automobile bearing New Jersey license plates. Miss Gow declined to say whether her destination was the home of Col. Charles A. Lindbergh at Hopewell, N. J., or the estate of Mrs. Dwight Morrow, mother of Mrs. Lindbergh at Englewood, N. J. Miss Gow sailed for England last August and visited her parents. The car in which she was taken from the pier was reported to have come from the Morrow estate.

LONDON, Oct. 25.—(UP)—The Prince of Wales will be given the largest armed bodyguard he ever had when he visits Belfast next month, the Daily Herald said today. According to the Herald's Belfast correspondent, Belfast authorities ordered all police leave cancelled during the prince’s visit. They are arranging the utmost precautions to ensure the prince's safety when he opens the new Northern Ireland Parliament building. The Sinn Fein standing committee at Dublin already has protested the prince's visit as the latest “English act of defiance of the rights and liberties of the Irish people in a further attempt to stabilize the partition of Ireland.”

Bucharest, Rumania, Oct. 25—(A. P.)——Michael of Rumania, the youngest ex-king in Europe, was back with his mother to celebrate his eleventh birthday today. Princess Helen, in her own palace, had set a party table with even candles grouped about a huge birthday cake. She came from London yesterday to spend this day with her boy, and because of the complicated domestic situation in which she and King Carol are involved, there is much talk about the possibility of a reconciliation with the king. They brought Michael from Sinaia by automobile this afternoon and drove right to his mother’s door. She was waiting and as the boy stepped from the car she took him in her arms, kissed him fervently on both cheeks and hurried inside.

ENIPUIN, Oct 24 (H)— Gathering converts as they advanced, nine groups of British unemployed continued their march on London today from many points in the country. LONDON, Oct. 24. (>)—Dismayed by a week-end of severe weather, nine contingents of Great Britain's unemployed prepared today to continue their march on London as the rains and gales subsided. London police estimated 2,000 persons to reach the capital by Thursday to protest their plight. The various “battalions” started their marches from Manchester, Burnley, Glasgow, Sheffield, Newcastle, Norwich, Hereford, Cardiff and Plymouth. The Manchester-Lancashire contingent was within 55 miles of the goal today despite a week-end buffeting from boisterous gales and almost incessant rains. When the Lancashire group of 230 reached Oxford, fifty sympathetic undergraduates tried to make the week-end comfortable. The students obtained billet

London—(F)—Two thousand jobless "hunger marchers" closed in upon London today to present demands for abolition of the "means test" which obliges every recipient of the dole to prove that he has no other means of support. It has been hard going through incessant rain along muddy roads from Scotland, Wales and many parts of England, and early this morning the sun shone only to hide behind clouds which threatened another downpour. Tonight the marchers will camp at such nearby places as Croydon and St. Albans, converging tomorrow afternoon at Hyde Park where there will be a great demonstration of welcome by the London unemployed. Then on Sunday afternoon the jobless will gather in Trafalgar Square where there will be speeches. Many in the ranks are wearing new red rosettes and the charge is openly made in several London newspapers that the march was fostered by funds from Moscow.

LONDON, Oct. 24.—(AP)—The United States and Great Britain were believed in official circles to be closer to complete agreement on disarmament today than at any time in recent years as a result of conversations between Prime Minister MacDonald and Norman Davis, American disarmament representative. Meanwhile Sir John Simon, foreign secretary, who talked two hours today with Mr. Davis and the premier, went before the House of Commons and placed responsibility for the disarmament impasse squarely upon France and Germany. He said these nations still were unable to agree on the site for a four-power emergency disarmament conference proposed to bring Germany into the general conference called for Nov. 3. The disarmament conversations carried on by Davis, both in regard to naval and land strength, have progressed materially. It was pointed out, however, that the present discussions were not of a

ENGLEWOOD, N. J., Oct. 25.—(>)— Betty Gow, nurse to the slain Lindbergh baby, returned from Great Britain today to the home of Mrs. Dwight W. Morrow where Col. and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh are staying with their infant son.

1932-03-04.text: SHANGHAI, March 4. (%) — Thousands of orphaned and homeless babies, left in the wake of the month of fighting, constituted one of the city’s greatest problems today. One British lady alone was caring for 80 of them whose parents and families vanished during the hostilities. Thousands of them are being cared for by other citizens of the international settlement as well as possible, but heads of charitable organizations feared unless some definite arrangement were made they would gradually grow up into a horde of wild urchins such as once swarmed over Russia.

LONDON, Mar. 4. (W?P)—Lady Hall Caine, widow of the famous novelist Sir Hall Caine, died last night from pneumonia. Sir Hall died last August 31. They were married in 1882 and had two sons, Ralph and Derwent Hall Caine.

London, March 3, (). -- Great Britain today tentatively sliced $18,342,036 off the cost of her army, navy and air force for 1932 but left her naval construction program at last year’s level. Total expenditures for the three branches of the service were estimated in a government statement at £104,264,000 ($373,188,064), a reduction of £5,270,700.

LONDON, March 46 (UP) => Scotland Yard’s world famed criminal investigation machinery was put to work on the Lindbergh case today. The yard referred to its Glasgow Criminal Investigation department a cablegram from New Jersey authorities asking information about certain persons. Glasgow detectives started on the

London, March 4. (/P)—Credits for longer than one year will no longer be extended to Soviet Russia on British exports, except under more stringent conditions than have prevailed in the past, the government has declared. The announcement was made in the House of Commons yesterday. The exact nature of the conditions was not set out and it was explained these were still under negotiation with Moscow. The general assumption in political quarters was that Great Britain is insisting on greater purchases of British manufactures.

SHANGHAI, Mar. 4. — (#) — The Chinese national government late today rejected the series of new Japanese demands presented yesterday as a basis for further peace parleys just as the city of Shanghai, surrounded by war for a month, had begun quietly to get down to work again. The announcement was made by Lo Wen-Kan, foreign minister. Another disturbing report came in Chinese official advices from Nanking which said that a new battle was under way at Taitsang, 25 miles northwest of here. The dispatches said the Japanese eleventh division attacked the Chinese forces there and a severe battle was under way. Japanese naval and military officials denied late in the afternoon that any fighting was taking place at Taitsang, however. Military officials issued the following statement: “The Japanese forces are maintaining the same position as yesterday, calling a halt to their hostilities and conce

Shanghai, March 4.—(UP)—Warfare was resumed in the Shanghai area today within 24 hours after the Chinese and Japanese high commands had ordered an armistice, to be broken only to resist attack. A bloody encounter began at Nanziang, 20 miles from Shanghai on the Shanghai-Nanking railroad at 10 a.m. The Japanese 5th division was ordered to attack the town after Japanese charged that Chinese had opened fire on their occupation forces. The Japanese claimed the Chinese began firing from trenches at Wangtu, near Nanziang. The order to attack was given by Gen. Yoshinori Shirakawa, who arrived from Japan with the 11th division to command all Japanese military activities. An earlier communique from the Chinese headquarters said fighting had started near Nanziang and in the region of Liuho, on the Yangtze river above the Woosung forts and debarkation point for the 11th Japanese division.

MOSCOW, U. S. S. R., March 4. (UP)—The Soviet government admitted for the first time today it had strengthened military forces on its far eastern frontiers. Simultaneously it was charged that representatives of military and non-military groups in Japan were planning to seize far eastern Soviet possessions. Through a leading editorial in the newspaper Izvestia it was revealed Moscow possessed documents allegedly emanating from Japanese leaders urging early attack against the Soviet. These urged attacks allegedly were aimed at the destruction of the Soviet Union with the aid of Poland, Rumania and other western nations. Izvestia admitted that “the documents perhaps can be considered personal opinions of the authors,” but said the authors were too influential to be disregarded and deserve “serious political weight.”

1932-05-06.text: LONDON, May 5.—(AP)—A surgeon’s knife today removed Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald from international and domestic politics for a period of six weeks. An operation to relieve glaucoma, an ailment which might eventually lead to blindness, was performed on his right eye. Four months ago a similar operation was performed on the left eye. It was officially announced that today’s surgical treatment had been carried out successfully.

LONDON, May 6 (AP)--Guests at a luncheon of bankers and business men where United States Ambassador Andrew W. Mellon spoke today observed that the ambassador drank whiskey and soda during the meal. When he first came to London recently Mr. Mellon, questioned as to whether there would be a cellar in the embassy said he would follow the custom of the country,

LONDON, May 6.—J. P. Morgan’s four-word sermon: “Never sell America short,” was preached again today by United States Ambassador Mellon to a gathering of bankers and business men at a luncheon in London's city hall. “A great and patriotic American who lived much in England and loved this country once said to a compatriot, ‘never sell America short,’” said Mr. Mellon. “I would reiterate what Mr. Morgan said then, and I would apply it to England no less than to my own country. “None of us has any means of knowing when or how we shall emerge from the valley of depression in which the world is now traveling. But I do know that as in the past a day will come when we shall find ourselves on a more solid economic foundation and the onward march of progress will be resumed.”

PARIS, May 6.—President Paul Doumer, 74-year-old head of the French republic, was critically wounded today by an assassin identified as a “white” Russian. Two blood transfusions and a trepaning operation were performed immediately and the doctors held out some hope that the president might recover. Motive Was Revenge The police hammered at the assassin until they learned that his name is Paul Gouguloff, that he had come here from Monaco especially to commit this crime and that his motive was revenge for the French refusal to intervene in Russia against the Bolsheviks. M. Doumer had come from the Elysee palace with Claude Farrere, the noted author. Together they entered the grand hall of the Baron De Rothschild foundation near the palace. Farrere walked with him up the grand staircase where the president paused to sign a copy of a book by a contemporary author. Suddenly a man sprang, seem

Vienna, May 6—(AP)—The Austrian cabinet, headed by Chancellor Karl Buresch, resigned today. The resignations, presented to President Miklas by Chancellor Buresch, were accepted, but the chancellor consented to the president's request that he continue in office until a new government is formed.

“~~ I (United Press Staff Correspondent) Paris. —(UP) —President Paul Doumer was shot and critically wounded by a crazed Russian at an afternoon charity event today. He was considered by his physicians tonight to have a fighting chance to recover, although the outcome was in doubt after two blood transfusions. At 5:41 p. m. (10:41 CST.) the following official bulletin was issued at the Beaujon hospital by the attending physicians: “The president received two bullets, one at the cranium and the other under the right shoulder. There were no hemorrhages, but serious shock. Already there have been two blood transfusions. His condition is still most grave.” Attending Book Exhibition The interior ministry issued the following communique: “President Doumer was shot twice while attending a ‘book afternoon’ by a Russian anarchist, seemingly without full mental faculties. One bullet entered the he

PARIS, May 6. (P)--President Paul Doumer was shot and critically wounded by a fanatical Russian assassin today. Little hope was held for his recovery. The assassin, Gol Gorguloff, also shot and slightly wounded Claude Farrere, a prominent author of Paris, and Paul Guichard, director of the Paris police. Doumer was taken to the hospital. At 4:20 p. m., a blood transfusion was performed in an effort to save him. Professor Gunciet performed the transfusion after which the president underwent an operation for his injury. Doctors there said there was little hope he would survive. Gorguloff is a doctor who had established himself in Paris. Police believe he went temporarily insane. The shooting occurred at an afternoon charity function where many prominent guests gathered in celebration of "book week" to aid needy authors and their families. Gorguloff entered the house, pushing through the cro
By United Press May 6.—Premier Ismail Sidky Pasha escaped from an attempt against his life when a bomb placed to blow up the train on which he was traveling exploded prematurely.

1932-06-28.text: LAUSANNE, June 29, —Prime Minister MacDonald of Great Britain called in the French and German delegations and told them that if the reparations conference is to get anywhere they will have to bury the hatchet. He is making a determined effort to prevent the conference from breaking up without accomplishing anything. Collapse threatened yesterday when Chancellor Von Papen of Germany told Premier Herriot of France that his country insisted upon cancellation of reparations.

LONDON — The British cabinet was understood today to have turned down more or less diplomatic thumbs on Pres. Hoover’s disarmament proposals. After a discussion of the Hoover plan for more than two hours last night the ministers were reported to have agreed the plan did not provide for enough naval vessels for the needs of the empire. Sir John Simon, foreign secretary, and Sir Herbert Samuel, who remained here for the conference last night, prepared today to return to Geneva to report on the conference to Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald.

Hongkong, June 27.—(A.P.)—The British gunboat Moorhen was bombed by mistake today by Chinese airplanes sent by General Chan Chaitong to recover a quantity of munitions captured by Admiral Chan Chak, rebel commander of the Cantonese navy. Admiral Chan Chak’s gunboats earlier in the day had captured a Chinese steamer carrying a quantity of rifles valued at $500,000 which belonged to the regular Cantonese forces. The planes were sent out to bomb Chan Chak’s boats, but near Kiau island they apparently mistook the British boat for a rebel craft. Six bombs were dropped near her, but she was not struck.

By Associated Press DUBLIN, June 28.—The Irish senate today passed the De Valera bill to abolish the oath of allegiance to the English crown, but carried an amendment to nullify the purpose of the free state government. The minister telegraphed Connolly and said — the government had no intention of accepting the measure in the present form, but let it go dail for action.

Germany Takes Arrogant Position at Lausanne Conference. } Lausanne, June 27.—Germany categorically informed France today that reparations must be cancelled,— This declaration, deadlocking the Lausanne conference, came from German Minister of Finance von Krosigk, at a critical meeting attended only by representatives of the two governments. Germany, the finance minister said, was determined not to yield an inch in enforcing the policy of no more reparations. This firm attitude—the strongest taken by the Berlin delegation since the Lausanne conference opened—was believed to have resulted from cabinet conferences held by Chancellor Von Papen in Berlin over the week-end. Even before the finance minister informed the French that there would be no yielding, news got about Lausanne that both Germans and French were considering shelving the conference until next fall. Back of this proposal was t

BERLIN, June 29 (UP)—The alarming spread of political chaos, street fighting and rioting throughout Germany indicated Tuesday the government might have to resort to martial law to prevent more serious disorders. Although election of a new Reichstag is five weeks away and the campaign is not even started, newspapers daily devote columns to an increasing toll of disorders. The situation became steadily worse after the government lifted the ban on Adolf Hitler’s brown shirt army. Pres. Von Hindenburg appealed to extremists to settle their differences less belligerently, but political foes, chiefly nazis and communists, continued to resort to fists, stones, and revolvers.

SUANGHAT, June 28,—(UP)— The President Jefferson of the Dollar Steamship lines crashed into the line's wharf here today while attempting to berth without a pilot. The huge passenger liner penetrated the wharf 36 feet, stoving a hole in her bow above the water line. No one was reported injured.

MOSCOW, June 29—(P)—Five employees of Moscow's state retail stores were sentenced to death today after a six-day trial on charges of defrauding the state of 1,000,000 rubles (nominally $500,000) by theft, illegal raising of prices and by supplying speculators with goods. Seven others were sentenced to 10 years in prison and eight were sent to jail for three to five years. Three other defendants were acquitted.

1932-03-24.text: BEVERLY HILLS, Cal, March 22.-Phar Lap sounds like a mouth wash, but runs like a race horse. All American horses saw of him Sunday was his tail and his dust. England, which holds a mandate over Australia, now has the auto and airplane; and Williams of Canada won the Olympics. Now this race horse makes a sucker out of us, but the good old U. S. A. still holds one international record. Our international bankers have loaned more of other people's money to foreign countries than was ever loaned before. Now there is a record we want to see beat. Yours, Will Roesers

LONDON, Mar. 23.—(AP)—Great Britain took a decisive stand today against the announced intention of Eamon DeValera, president of the Irish Free State, to abolish the oath of allegiance to the British crown and to withhold payment of the Irish land annuities. Speaking in the House of Commons, J. H. Thomas, secretary for dominions, asserted that the oath is an integral part of the treaty which established the Irish Free State ten years ago and that payment of the annuities constitutes a bargain between two peoples and England is determined that it shall not be violated. A formal communication to this effect will be sent to Dublin immediately. It will be published as soon as possible thereafter. The Irish treaty provides the form of an oath to be taken by all Free State office holders. DeValera con- (Continued on Page Eleven)

Pittsburgh, March 24.—(AP)— Andrew W. Mellon, newly-appointed ambassador to Great Britain, observed his seventy-seventh birthday quietly with his family today. He arrived here last week to be with his brother, Richard B. Mellon, on the latter's seventy-fourth birthday, and also to arrange personal matters before sailing for the court of St. James. He leaves tonight for Washington.

MYUNUYUN, Mar. 29. — (UF) J. H. Thomas, Dominions secretary, informed the House of Commons today that the British government stands firmly against abolition of the oath to the king and non-payment of the land annuities, as proposed by the republican government of Eamon de Valera in the Irish Free State. ‘The government is addressing to the Free State government a communication which will make their standpoint clear beyond the possibility of a doubt on the question of the oath,” he said. “Failure to pay the land annuities would be a manifest violation of an agreement which is binding in law and honor on the Irish Free State, whatever administration

By The Associated Press Pittsburgh, March 24.—Andrew W. Mellon will quietly celebrate his 77th birthday today with his family in their Woodlawn home. The former secretary of the treasury, who recently became ambassador to England, came to Pittsburgh last week to be with his brother, R. B. Mellon, on the latter’s 74th birthday.

LONDON, March 24 (P)—For the first time in more than 200 years the King of England today distributed in person the traditional Royal Maundy (Holy Thursday) pence to the poor persons at Westminster Abbey. James II was the last English sovereign personally to perform this office. The recipients are selected from the aged and infirm poor throughout England. Each received 67 pence today, as many as there are years in King George’s age. There were 67 men and 67 women recipients. Queen Mary accompanied the king.

DUBLIN, March 24— (INS) — The British government's reply to Eamonn de Valera’s proposal to abolish the oath of allegiance and withhold land annuities from the British treasury was received in Dublin this afternoon. President de Valera of the Irish Free State executive council immediately summoned a cabinet meeting for tonight at which the ministry is expected to consider the British note and possibly draft a reply. While de Valera refrained from commenting, it was ascertained that the Irish reply probably would constitute a restatement of the free state government's views, despite the fact that Britain has served formal notice it will not consent to de Valera’s proposals.

LONDON, Mar. 24. (P)—The British press today endorsed the government’s attitude toward Eamon de Valera’s intention to dispense with land annuities and the oath to the king as part of the Irish Free State’s policy. Yesterday J. J. Thomas, secretary for the dominions, told the house of commons that the British government regarded the oath and annuities as a part of the Anglo-Irish treaty of 1922 and that Britain is determined that instrument shall not be violated. Among other things, the press pointed out that the Laborites, upon whom De Valera depended for his balance of power, have stated through their leader, Wilson Norton, that they would not tolerate abrogation of the Anglo-Irish treaty, although they were prepared to stand for negotiation of the land annuities.

1932-04-15.text: London, April 14. (4)—Hailing a new era, Andrew W. Mellon, America’s ambassador to Great Britain, tonight told the Pilgrims Society there was nothing in world conditions so unprecedented as to justify a lack of faith “in our capacity to deal with them.” This was the first public address as ambassador of the man who made millions in business and then administered the United States treasury under three presidents. He spoke before a distinguished audience of 400 or more, including the Prince of Wales, Sir John Simon, foreign secretary, and Lord Derby, who presided. Before his address the ambassador drank toasts in champagne to King George and the president of the United States, in accordance with his previously expressed intention to conform to the customs of the country to which he had been named ambassador. Those Englishmen who had hoped for some indication that Mr. Mellon's mission to Gr

Auckland, New Zealand, April 15—Vicious fighting broke out in the streets again tonight and for three hours crowds of jobless men and women who rioted all day yesterday held their own against police, volunteer reinforcements and a landing party from a British cruiser. Mounted men charged the rioters and foot police advanced in close formation with drawn clubs, but they were beaten back by the jobless who fought with clubs, rocks and their fists. During the melee fire broke out in the Church of the Epiphany and the building was badly damaged. Police said the blaze had been started by the rioters. At least 30 persons were injured, some of them seriously. The mayor, who marshaled civilian volunteers to assist the police yesterday, said tonight that if the fighting continued he would read the riot act.

LONDON, April 10. [AP] -- The portion of British officialdom and the British public which looked for some indication that the mission of Ambassador Andrew W. Mellon was to arrange a revision, or perhaps cancellation, of war debts were disappointed today. At the annual dinner of the Pilgrims Society last night, Mr. Mellon drank champagne toasts to the King and to the President of the United States and reaffirmed his faith in capitalism, "or whatever name may be applied to the system which has been evolved in adapting individual initiative to the machine age." But he said nothing about war debts or reparations. Referring to the financial situation, he said he did not believe in

- DUBLIN, April 15.—The Free State government will move next Wednesday toward abolishing the oath of allegiance to King George and probably will have the support of the labor members of the Dail, it became known today. The government announced last night that a bill to abolish the oath will be introduced Wednesday in the Dail. The government's announcement diverted attention, momentarily, at least, from the question of the land annuities payments.

Columbus, O., April 15.—(AP)—Theft of 300 pounds of dynamite from a power storehouse near London, O., was being investigated by State authorities today in the belief that the explosive might have been used to blow up the state office building. The dynamite was stolen last week from the Hercules Co., and since that time authorities of Madison and Franklin county (London and Columbus, respectively) have been investigating the case. An unnamed man was said to be under suspicion in the theft. The dynamite was of the “high powered” variety. LeRoy Keene, an official of the powder company, said 100 pounds of the explosive contained sixteen quarts of T. N. T., and he pointed out that about 80 percent of the T. N. T. can be extracted from the sticks by one familiar with the dynamite. Keene said tests showed about 100 pounds of the dynamite would have been sufficient to cause the damage which resu

AUCKLAND, N. Z., April 15. UP - Rioting by unemployed who looted stores and smashed hundreds of windows in Queen Street last night was renewed tonight. Mounted police and naval reinforcements repeatedly charged the crowds and cleared the streets. Groups re-formed elsewhere as soon as dispersed in one spot.

Warsaw, April 15.—Edith Gral-Mott, 40, head of the United States Baptist mission in Warsaw, was murdered in her home here, police announced today. Mrs. Gral-Mott was found with her throat cut. Police said the murderer or murderers had searched her home for mission funds. Her throat was cut with a razor. Police said they had no cause to suspect suicide. Mrs. Gral-Mott had run the mission alone for the past year.

Warsaw, Poland, April 15.---(4P) The body of Mrs. Grace Edna Mott, a Baptist missionary from New York City, was found in her apartment today, the throat deeply slashed by a knife or a razor. In her hand police found a tuft of hair apparently pulled from the head of the person who killed her. A small cash box in Mrs. Mott's wardrobe had been broken open and rifled.

1932-07-31.text: GLASGOW, July 30,—INS—Nine women and children were taken to hospitals with serious injuries today when a mob of 8,000 enthusiastic fans stampeded at a railway station in welcoming Stanley Laurel and Oliver Hardy, comedy team of the American screen, Thirty were injured in all. Women and children were trampled as the crowd surged to catch a glimpse of the two actors. During the excitement a stone balustrade of a nearby hotel fell away from the building, and many were injured by the falling debris.

Ottawa, Ont., July 30. (*)—The extent to which Great Britain will be allowed to cut in on American sales to Canada of textiles and iron and steel products, valued at $200,000,000 in 1931, was under consideration by the British imperial economic conference today when it adjourned until Tuesday. With the exception of India—that politely aloof and potentially great purchaser of empire goods for her 300,000,000 people—almost every nation of the empire has seen definite trade overtures to the United Kingdom and to Canada. Another phase of the kaleidoscopic problems before the conference came before the heads of delegations today when it was understood they were studying the methods of stabilizing the Canadian dollar as against the pound sterling. This apparently came from the monetary committee, which today organized a subcommittee. It was known no definite scheme had been worked out, all the

WASHINGTON, July 30.—UP—The British government, in inviting the United States to attend the world economic conference under the auspices of the League of Nations, specifically assured the United States that debts, reparations and tariff rates would not be discussed, it was revealed today when the state department made public the invitation.

OXFORD, England. (H. G. Wells publicly criticized King George V. for meddling in politics. In England such criticism of royalty is almost unheard of. The eminent novelist said his say to an audience at the Oxford liberal summer school, which heard him in silence. His objections were based on the part the king played in the formation of the national government last year. “The king was so ill advised as to depart from his proper social and political neutrality and to lead the movement for cheese-paring and grinding the faces of the needy in the interests of the debt collector,” he asserted. “And not a soul in the labor party said what ought to have been said about the king or the miserable campaign of economy which cast its shadow over the closing months of 1931.”

Berlin, July 30. (AP)---More than 7,000,000 voters sharpened their pencils to mark at the voting booths on the ballots their final decision of the bloodiest and noisiest election ever staged in the Reich. The question whether Germany will go the right or left way is yet to be decided. The voters heard the living voice of Adolf Hitler, the former Austrian army corporal and paper hanger, saying "we're through with democracy and the election will end the democracy." Alfred Hugenberg, old time nationalist leader, voiced the call for the return of the kaiser and the re-establishment of the monarchy which is pursued by the present government of Chancellor von Papen, the noted Junker and former soldier General Kurt von Schleicher. On the left there were the German socialists, chief supporters of the republican constitution and still farther leftward the communist powers under Ernst Thälmann who

Berlin, July 30 (UP)—Four persons were killed and 10 wounded in clashes in Germany today on the eve of the Reichstag elections. Two members of the republican Reichsbanner organization were shot dead and one wounded when a group came into conflict at Reisensburg near Königsberg, East Prussia, with Nazi troopers who suffered five wounded. Meantime at Esslingen in Württemberg police fighting off a communist onslaught killed two communists and wounded one. Two police were wounded in this struggle.

Berlin, July 30.—(4)—With bloodshed and blistering oratory, Germany today closed the campaign for tomorrow's momentous elections which will result in an entirely new reichstag and may decide whether the nation will choose the paths of dictatorship or monarchy or remain in the way of republicanism. During the closing hours of the campaign, five persons were killed in political brawls in the provinces. Here in Berlin 250 persons were arrested for taking part in street fights. The army stood ready to act in case of major disorders tomorrow and the entire Berlin police force of 20,000 men was under mobilization orders to stamp out riots. On Air The last appeals to the nation were made tonight over the radio by Chancellor Franz von Papen and by Karl Severing, who was ousted as Prussian minister of the interior when the federal government set up a dictatorship over the reich’s most important s

HARBIN, Manchuria, July 30. (P)—Travelers arriving from Vladivostok, Siberia, report that the Soviet Russian authorities are fortifying that city’s harbor approaches on a large scale in anticipation of a possible attack by Japan. Troops are arriving every day, they said, transported in closed railway cars and disembarking at night. Ten armored trains were reported to be in the railway yards, and nearby are fifty tanks, sixty airplanes and numerous artillery units. The travelers said trains arrive every day with munitions, food and miscellaneous supplies including material for building steamers, piers and small warcraft. It was said that the people of Vladivostok have been trained in the use of gas masks, in rifle fire and in seeking safety in underground shelters already prepared. Similar activities are reported at Khabarovsk and Blagoveshchensk. Meanwhile the Soviet authorities are rapi

1932-03-15.text: LONDON, Mar. 18 (UP) — Zaro Agha, aged Turk, who claims to be the oldest man in the world, was dangerously ill today at St. Mary Abbott's hospital suffering from heart trouble. Agha collapsed in a Kensington tea shop late yesterday. He was placed in a small, dimly lighted hospital room with three other occupants who apparently did not know their neighbor was the oldest man on earth.

TOKYO, March 15 (P)—News from Manchuria today led Japanese officials to express the belief that Soviet Russia will soon recognize officially the new Manchurian state under the dictatorship of Henry Pu-Yi, former Chinese boy emperor. A dispatch to the Rengo News Agency from Changchun, capital of the new state, said Russia "informally indicated" it would accept Dictator Pu-Yi's nominees for directors of the Chinese Eastern railway, instead of the directors appointed by the Chinese National government at Nanking. This, Mr. Pu-Yi's followers were reported as saying, would be equivalent to a de facto recognition of the new regime. Changchun authorities already have approached Moscow with the proposal, the dispatch said. The Chinese Eastern railway is jointly operated by Russia and China. The indication here was that Tokyo would be considerably relieved if Russia would accept the new regime an

Berlin, Germany, March 14.—President Von Hindenburg, still first in the hearts of the Reich, agreed today to the formality of running again for re-election and the opposition parties began dickering for advantage on the second vote April 10. The venerable former field marshal expressed satisfaction over the seven million vote margin he rolled up in Sunday’s election over Adolf Hitler, his nearest competitor, and informed a delegation he would continue to stand as a candidate in the compulsory run-off. While his re-election is considered certain, the maneuvering of political leaders indicated that he would fight his major battle with Hitler, head of the National Socialists (fascists) who already has announced he would run again in an effort to increase his eleven million votes. Hitler issued a fervent appeal to his followers from Munich to “resume the fight in the fiercest form. We can no
Canton, China, March 15—This city was shaken as though by an earthquake today when four ordinance buildings were blown up, presumably by the communists. No loss of life was reported.

Tokyo, March 15—UP—Tokugoro Nakahashi, home minister in the cabinet of Premier Inukai, resigned late today. Nakahashi's resignation followed a conference with Premier Inukai. Observers saw in the move an attempt to strengthen the cabinet’s defenses in preparation for expected attacks of the opposition in the special session of the parliament which opens March 18. The home minister, as head of the police, was severely criticized because he continued in office after the explosion of a bomb near the carriage of Emperor Hirohito January 8. According to the orthodox Japanese procedure in such cases, he would have taken responsibility for the incident and handed in his resignation. He is expected to be succeeded by Kesaiburo Suzuki, minister of justice.

SHANGHAI, Match 14.--The League of Nations commission of inquiry, led by the Earl of Lytton, arrived in Shanghai today to seek out the reasons why Japan and China have been at each other's throats for the past six months. Coming up the Whangpoo River on the liner President Adams from Japan, the five members caught a first-hand view of the destruction wrought at Woosung. They looked through binoculars to inspect the ruins of the forts and village and to see a line of Japanese warships still stripped for action. On disembarking, Lord Lytton said that the commission's plan of investigation had not been fully mapped out, but that it would willingly arrange a truce in the present warfare and a subsequent round-table conference if both sides solicited its assistance. The commission was willing to extend its cooperation within the limits of its authority, he said, but its members could not part
By The Associated Press Paris, March 15.—The body of Ivar Kreuger, Swedish “match king” who committed suicide last week, will be taken to Stockholm for burial, it was announced today.

HOPEWELL, N. J., March 15—Investigators went to New York City to question Frank Berg, a prominent figure in a fantastic kidnapping years ago to determine whether any new clues might be obtained from him in the Lindbergh mystery. Berg was arrested in 1925 in connection with a reported attempt to lure Max Phillips, rich collar manufacturer, aboard Berg’s yacht. A woman, who represented herself as a countess, but was his wife, was aboard. The charges were dropped. Phillips last week visited the New Jersey police head and after a lengthy conference it was announced that every effort would be made to find if there was any possible connection between the Phillips attempt and the kidnapping of the Lindbergh baby.

1932-07-08.text: London, July 8. (AP)—Rev. H. F. Davidson, gray-haired rector of Stiffkey, was found guilty today on charges of immoral conduct with young women which he faced at the recent church trial. The clergyman with his daughter "Paddy" and son Neugent were present in the courtroom when the verdict was returned. It is thought that the clergyman may appeal his case. The rector denied all the charges filed against him and said that he came from his country parish to (Continued on Page 7.)

French Premier Elated The World War really ended at Lausanne today. It ended when Édouard Herriot, premier of France, emerged beaming from the conference of statesmen and shouted: "It's done. It's done. It's done." Then he seized a blond German woman and a brunet French one, both reporters covering the conference, hugged them to him and kissed them with fervor, while the crowd roared its approval. The agreement ended a dozen years of international wrangling, during which the leading statesmen and financial men of the world met for weary week after week in the capitals and summer resorts of Europe. More than 40 such conferences were held. The United States, which refused to associate

London (U.P.)—The Rev. Harold F. Davidson, 60-year-old rector of Stiffky, was found guilty today of immoral conduct and improper relations during his “rescue work” among young London girls. The rector was found guilty on three charges, the first of alleged immoral conduct and relations with Rose Ellis, alleged by the prosecution to have extended over a period of 10 years; the second, of misconduct with a waitress in a tea shop, and a third, of misconduct with a girl in a Bloomsbury restaurant.

Geneva, OWLUZEMiand — (P) — A move to summon another five-power naval conference to achieve further reductions in sea forces was discreetly launched by British authorities today simultaneously with the announcement in London of the government's counter-proposal to President Hoover's one-third arms reduction program. Meanwhile American spokesmen criticized the program announced in London as an attempt to reduce the size of American ships and therefore force them to remain in home waters.

GENEVA, Switzerland, July 8. American naval experts united today in criticizing a move for a new five-power naval parley launched from British sources yesterday. The British plan was broached shortly after a set of counter-proposals to the Hoover disarmament plan was announced in the House of Commons at London. It was contained in a press interview given anonymously by a high British authority. The United States, Japan, Great Britain, France, and Italy would be expected to join in the parley. The British program, one of the American critics said, was merely a renewal of a 10-year-old controversy in which the British had sought to reduce the size of our ships to keep our navy in home waters.

(By Associated Press) LONDON, July 7—Great Britain officially today defined her attitude toward President Hoover's proposals to cut arms one-third. She declared herself in general accord, but drew the line at his naval program. In a White paper read before the House of Commons by Stanley Baldwin, acting prime minister, the government asserted Britain's far-flung interests made it impracticable for her to reduce the number of her naval units beyond a certain point. "But if there is a limit to numerical reduction, it is still possible, and highly desirable, to secure by other means a large diminution in naval armaments," Mr. Baldwin said. The government lined up with Mr. Hoover by opposing air bombing with reservations, and by pointing out that the British standards of land disarmament already more than cover the American aims. LONDON. —(#) —Lady Louis Mountbatten won a libel action Friday against the Odham Press Ltd., publisher of “The People,” a Sunday newspaper, which accused her inferentially of scandalous associations with a negro. The defendants apologized and paid all costs. Lady Mountbatten was said to have refused to accept heavy damages which the paper was willing to pay. Many prominent society people occupied seats in the court room. When the case was called Lady settled. She and her husband hurried back to England unexpectedly Thursday from a long vacation in Malta where they entertained Former King Alfonso XIII of Spain. During the brief proceedings Friday morning, the plaintiffs’ attorney informed the court that although it was unusual he wanted to read into the record the libelous article on "I'll do that," he said, "so that its full enormity may be known and every fact in this case plainly state

| LONDON, July 8—(—)—By a vote of 222 to 30 the House of Commons today passed on third reading a measure empowering the government to levy a duty up to 100 percent on all imports from the Irish Free State. The bill was approved at the request of J. P. Thomas, Secretary for Dominions, who described it as the only means of retaliation for the Free State’s refusal to meet installments on the Irish land annuities. It was rushed through all the parliamentary stages with unusual dispatch.

1932-11-17.text: Geneva—(?)—The British foreign secretary, Sir John Simon, proposed to the world disarmament conference Thursday that the German demand for arms equality be satisfied by allowing the Reich to have the same kind of armaments as other nations. The British government also proposed as a part of a scheme to solve the equality problem that all the European states join in a solemn affirmation that under no circumstances will they attempt to resolve any present or future differences among them by force. Sir John declared the limitation of Germany's armaments should be contained in the same disarmament convention which defines limitations on the armaments of others. Norman Davis, the American representative, recalled the long months of the disarmament conference and its scanty results. He said the delegates were in Geneva to reduce armaments and not merely to talk about them. Recalling the economi

BY STEWART BROWN United Press Staff Correspondent GENEVA, Nov 17.--(UP)-- British Foreign Secretary Sir John Simon invited Germany back to the world disarmament conference today on the basis of recognition of the principle of armament equality for all nations. The British proposals provide that the present limitation of German armaments under the Versailles treaty be superseded by a new convention and that German limitation “would be arrived at by the same process and expressed in the same document as those of all other countries.” Sir John proposed that Germany have the legal right to possess all weapons granted other powers under a system of disarmament by stages. In a telegram to Franklin D. Roosevelt, President Hoover Sunday invited him to confer at the White House late next week on pressing international debt questions. Hoover quoted to his Democratic successor a note from the British government asking for a suspension of the war debt payment due December 15, of approximately $95,000,000.00. Secretary Stimson informed the president that similar requests have been received from the other nations for debt payments due December 15. Mr. Hoover stated that “thus our government is now confronted with a world problem of major importance to this nation.” Because of the questions, disarmament and other problems affecting the world economic situation, and continued postponement of payment of war debts, Mr. Hoover added, it seemed ‘an interchange of views would be in the public interest.” The chief executive reviewed to Roosevelt the war debt question as

By The Associated Press LONDON, Nov. 17—D. A. Mollison received a cablegram today from his wife, Amy Johnson, who is flying to beat his record from London to Cape Town. It indicated that she had run into trouble. "Forced landing Benguela," the message said, "no oil pressure. Doubt if can be rectified here but writing later. Terribly disappointed.

Geneva (U.P.) -- The United States warned Europe today the heavy burden of armaments must be lightened if the world economic crisis is to be solved. At the same time Great Britain took the lead in attempting to solve the deadlock on arms reduction by promising Germany equality of treatment and inviting her to return to the disarmament conference. Hint on War Debts The American position was presented by Norman H. Davis, United States delegate, in a speech to the steering committee of the arms conference, and was regarded as a veiled hint that Europe must reduce arms if she expects any consideration on war debts. Britain’s offer was made by Sir John Simon, foreign secretary. In addition to the invitation to Germany he made the important proposal that all air forces be reduced to the level of Great Britain’s, and then cut one-third. Deplores Bombing Sir John said no aspect of international

PARIS, Nov. 16.—The creation of an economic consortium by France, Germany and Great Britain, which is designed to assist in coping with the unemployed problem, was announced today by Raymond Patenotre, who will be in charge of its operations. “We foresee,” said M. Patenotre, “a return of prosperity by the natural process of the development of industrialization. “The unemployed in the smaller depressed countries will be given work, while the jobless in the larger countries will be relieved by the operation of factories.” Capital, Labor Combine The plan was described as a combination of French capital and German industry, with guarantees covering the subjects of insurance, security and non-competition. M. Patenotre, who was born in the United States and whose father served as French ambassador at Washington, is France's undersecretary for national economy. As vice-president in actual charg

DAKAR, French West Africa, Nov. 18. (}—-Amy Johnson, who is flying a tiny plane from England to the Cape in an effort to better the record of her husband, Captain J. A. Molison, successfully crossed the Sahara desert yesterday and today she was speeding toward Douala, on the Gulf of Guinea. Miss Johnson made the 1,400-mile flight from Oren, Algeria, to Gao, on the upper Niger in French West Africa, in a little more than 13 hours. She landed at Gao at 12:30 p. m. yesterday. The flight to Douala from Gao is 1,200 miles.

LONDON, Nov. 17. — (UP) — Arthur Loew, American motion picture executive, was injured, and the pilot of his monoplane "Spirit of Fun" was killed when the plane crashed near Victoria Falls, Rhodesia, Africa, the Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer offices here advised the United Press today. Loew's pilot was believed to be a Capt. Dickson, an American. Another passenger named Raosthal, believed to be a lawyer, also was injured, according to information received at the motion picture company’s offices. The extent of Loew's injuries was not revealed. The "Spirit of Fun" was en route to Assuan, Egypt, from Johannesburg, Transvaal.

1932-01-26.text: To Editor of Gazette-Republican: LONDON, Jan. 25.—I got the dope on these international bankers that are crying for us. A commissioner and business man over here tell of the flock of bankers' representatives over in Germany and Europe in the last few years. Hotel lobbies are full of ’em offering all kinds of commissions to help put over loans for American banks. The loans were forced over here as much as the sales of ’em were forced over home. Now they want the government to cancel to make up for their mistakes. Now if this is not the real showdown on it, then Borsh is a republican, Yours, WILL.

LONDON, Jan. 26.—President signed another loan bill, this one only for $125,000,000 for land banks. Then last week two billion. You can tell this is an election year from the way these appropriation bills are passing. It will take the taxpayers 50 years to pay for the votes in this election. Our only solution of relief seems to be to fix it so people who are in a hole through borrowing can borrow some more. Borrowing is what's the matter with the world today. If no individual or country could borrow a dime for five years, that would be the greatest five-year plan ever invented. Yours, WILL, P. S. But what about Morgan and company? That would be discriminating against them wouldn't it? Well, we won't do it then. Just let it go.

Princetown, England, Jan. 26—(P)—A force of 100 steel-helmeted infantrymen, armed with machine guns and rifles, augmented the regular guard over Dartmoor prison and all approaches to it today, following reports that the frustrated revolt of Sunday was to be followed by a concerted attack from the outside. The soldiers were hurried from Plymouth last night. The extra precautions were the result of reports that confederates of the prisoners on the outside were congregating, armed with machine guns, and prepared an attack which was intended to end in a general jail delivery. Prison officials said strange cars were seen patrolling the roads during the last few days and these had been seen to flash light signals at night. An inquiry into the causes of Sunday’s outbreak is under way. One of its consequences, it was reported, might be the abandoning of the prison, partly because of the difficul

CARDIFF, Wales, Jan. 26 (fP) — Eleven men were dead today as a result of an explosion in the Llwynpia colliery in the Rhonda Valley last night. Thirty men were working in the mine at the time. Rescue parties went down immediately. One rescuer was overcome by gas and died before aid could reach him. Other members of the party, working under the handicap of the fumes, brought out the injured, some of whom died after reaching the surface, and the bodies of those who died below.
Cardiff, Wales, Jan. 25.—()-— Four men were killed and about 10 were injured in an explosion tonight in the Llwynypia coal mine in the Rhondda valley,

LONDON, (Tuesday morning,) Jan. 26 (@)—A Princetown dispatch to the Daily Mail today said the establishment of a military guard outside Dartmoor prison had followed reports that friends of the convicts planned to attack the prison. The Mail's correspondent said there was evidence that Communists were behind the plot, which had been confirmed by 5 of the convicts. The attack was to have been made coincidentally with a renewal of rioting inside the prison early this morning.

GENEVA, Jan. 25 CP — Sir Drummond, who has been secretary general of the League of Nations since its formation, submitted his resignation at a meeting of the League council, but the council deferred action.

Tokyo, Jan. 26— (A.P.)—Thirteen additional Japanese warships were ordered by the navy office today to proceed immediately to Shanghai from the Sasebo naval base. The new order, it was stated, was issued because of the increasing gravity of the Shanghai situation. Eleven Japanese warships previously were reported lined up in the Whangpoo river opposite the Chinese city, awaiting the outcome of the Japanese demand that Chinese officials suppress the anti-Japanese societies alleged to be supporting the boycott against Japanese goods. The cabinet yesterday decided that the first step, in case the Japanese demands were not met and occupation of Shanghai seemed necessary, would be to take over the headquarters of the anti-Japanese associations.

1932-03-16.text: TOKYO, March 16.—(AP)—A tentative agreement for peace at Shanghai, reached Monday at a conference between representatives of the two nations in the presence of envoys of the United States, Great Britain, France and Italy, was approved by the Japanese government today "in principle." The government instructed Mamoru Shigemitsu, Japanese minister to China and its representative in the parleys, to confer again with Chinese spokesmen on the details of the plan, which was taken to be an agreement concerning withdrawal of troops from the Shanghai zone. (The parleys Monday were held before the League of Nations investigating commission arrived from Japan, but the Earl of Lytton, chairman of the commission, was reported from Shanghai as saying the members of the league group were willing to assist other neutral mediators and to remain in Shanghai until all danger of further hostilities was past.

London, March 16 (UP)—Two Japanese steamers with a total of 160 passengers and crew were believed lost today, the Kobe correspondent of the Daily Herald reported. The coastal steamer Choan Maru struck a submerged rock in a dense fog near Chefoo Saturday and had disappeared when rescue ships reached the scene Monday, the Herald said. There were 110 passengers and seamen aboard. The steamer Yankei Mari, with 50 aboard, had not been heard from since sending an SOS call during a blizzard several days ago en route to Vladivostok.

SAO PAULO, Brazil, March 16 — British officials are considering a new search for Colonel H. P. Fawcett who entered the “great jungle” of Brazil seven years ago in search of a ‘lost civilization,’ and was lost to civilization himself, swallowed by trackless wilds. The new hope that the explorer is alive and held captive by Indians was inspired by a report by a jungle trapper, Stephen Rattin, who has spent years in the Matto Grosso (great jungle). “I have seen a white man who claimed to be Fawcett,” Rattin reported to British consular officials. “He asked that I report to you.” The British consulate general considered Rattin’s word the most de- (Turn To Page Nine—No. 4.)

WASHINGTON, March 16—(4)—Ambassador Mellon sat at the right of President Hoover last night with the cabinet and other former associates gathered around the White House dinner table to wish him Godspeed to London. It was an intimate dinner, despite the 36 guests. All cabinet members were there with their wives; so were General and Mrs. Dawes; Governor Meyer of the Federal Reserve Board; Paul Bastor, the farm loan commissioner, and the ranking officials of the treasury. Mellon expects to sail for his post in London by April 1 but has not set the exact date.

Tokyo, March 16 (Wednesday) — The government announced today that it approved “in principle” a tentative agreement for a Sino-Japanese armistice reached on Monday at a Shanghai conference between the Chinese and the Japanese with neutral mediators present. The Monday meeting was held at the British Consulate General with Mamoru Shigemitsu, Japanese Minister to China representing his country and Kuo Tai-Chi, Nationalist commissioner at Shanghai, representing China. Nelson T. Johnson, United States Minister to China, and the British, French and Italian envoys were present.

RIO DE JANEIRO, March 16 (AP). —Arthur Abbott, British consul general at Sao Paulo, said today that a man reported to him that he had seen Colonel P. H. Fawcett, British explorer who disappeared in the jungles seven years ago, but that investigations he is carrying on have not yet confirmed the story. Fawcett disappeared while searching for a lost civilization in the jungle. There have been many reports since then that he was seen, but General Candido Rondon, head of the Brazilian Indian service, said several years ago, after an investigation of his own, that he was convinced the explorer was dead.

PARIS, March 16.—(4#)—Pierre Vau-laer flew his airplane out over a departing ocean liner to wave goodbye to his fiancée. The plane fell into the Atlantic. Pierre was rescued by the liner’s crew and had all the way to Plymouth, England, to say goodbye.

GENEVA, Mar. 16. (4)—The League of Nations assembly committee of 19 on the Sino-Japanese problem was informed this afternoon that Japanese and Chinese authorities at Shanghai had reached a secret agreement, tentative in nature, calling for an armistice and the summoning of a peace conference. This information came from Paul Hymans, president of the assembly and foreign minister of Belgium, who explained he received it from Naotake Sato, Japan’s delegate. The committee will hold a public meeting tomorrow afternoon. If peace discussions are moving successfully at that time a three week recess may be taken for the Easter holidays. In the preliminary discussions over the teacups in Shanghai, the conditions of peace have included: 1. That the Chinese maintain their present military positions about 12% miles outside Shanghai, 2. That the Japanese withdraw their troops to the international sett

1932-05-07.text: LONDON, May 6.— A medical bulletin issued from Down Street today said Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald, who underwent an operation on his right eye for glaucoma yesterday, had a somewhat restless night but that the condition of his eye was satisfactory.

Washington, May 6, (#).—A Navy as big as treaties will allow was voted today by the Senate. By 44 to 21, the Hale bill to authorize building up the United States fleet to the limits set by the London and Washington conferences was approved and sent to the House. A bi-partisan line-up shoved it through despite the strong objections of opponents from both parties who described the bill as “militarism” and “a program of national suicide.” The bill carries no appropriation but the program that it would authorize involves approximately a billion dollars. The President would be authorized to suspend it upon conclusion of any new disarmament agreement.

London, May 7 (AP)—London morning newspapers all expressed profound regret and deep sympathy today over the death of President Paul Doumer of France. The tragedy dominated all other news. Associated Press Staff Writer Paris, May 7.—(AP)—The body of Paul Doumer, beloved and venerable 71-year-old president of France, lay in state in the green room of the presidential palace today, the victim of an assassin’s gun, while France was bowed in sadness and in horror. After lingering throughout the night in a coma and delirium, while a staff of physicians worked feverishly in a vain attempt to save his life, the aged president died at 4:37 a.m. just as the first light of dawn crept over the cold stone walls of Beaujon hospital, where he was taken after the tragic shooting yesterday. The funeral will be held Thursday, it was decided shortly before noon today. An election to select a new president will be held at Versailles next Tuesday. PARIS, May 7, (Saturday) (P)—Paut Doumer, venerable president of France, died at 4:40 a. m. today (0300 Re Friday, Central Standard Time) from two bullet wounds inflicted by a “white” Russian fanatic who shot him Friday as he was attending a war veterans charity exhibition. He was 75 years old. The president lingered almost exactly 12 hours. Seven physicians did their utmost to save him, resorting to numerous blood transfusions and to the use of oxygen to assist his failing heart. French Cabinet Assembled. When the end came the entire French cabinet was assembled in his room at Beaujon hospital adjoining the one occupied by M. Doumer. At the bedside were the president's wife, one of his daughters and several of his physicians. Mme. Doumer, who gave four sons to the republic on the battlefields of the great war, collapsed. The president was shot by Dr. Paul Gorgulov, who told police his p

Paris, May 7 (UP) — President Paul Doumer died today, the victim of a crazed Russian assassin, as dawn broke over a saddened France which mourned the loss of its venerable and beloved "Pere." The 13th president of the French Republic, in his 75th year, regained consciousness for only a few minutes during the 14 hours that the most skilled French physicians battled to save his life. He was shot at the base of the cranium and under the right shoulder. The end came peacefully. Doumer had fallen into a coma from which four blood transfusions and an emergency operation failed to revive him. Members of the president's cabinet, Premier Andre Tardieu, and government officials were at his bedside. Police held that the assassin, Dr. Paul Gorgouloff, self-styled "chief of the Russian Fascists," was insane and that the assassination had no political significance. Gorgouloff will be charged with firs

Parts, May i—a}—raul Goreclovy, who assassinated President Doumer, was described today by the head of the French secret service as a “member of a Bolshevik organization.” When he was arrested yesterday the man admitted he was a Russian, but said he was the head of a “Fascist” organization which was opposed to Bolshevism. By killing M. Doumer, he said, he hoped to involve France in a war with Soviet Russia. The first statement by the police yesterday said the prisoner was not in possession of all his faculties, but today three alienists examined him and pronounced him sane and responsible for his crime. Shortly after that he was arraigned before a magistrate and formally charged with the assassination. It was expected that he would be brought to trial quickly. On Monday the court will appoint an attorney for the defense. Pierre Jullien, head of the Sûreté Générale, told the Associated Pre

1932-05-13.text: DUBLIN, Irish Free State, May 18 (GP) — The weather outlook for Lou Reichers, flying from Newfoundland, is uncertain. Tralee reported threatened rain but no wind. Visibility was fair. Galway, which is in direct line between Newfoundland and Dublin, reported showers with slight wind and fair visibility.

Marseilles, France, May 13. (AP) Former King Alfonso of Spain stepped off a steamer from Malta today into a rain of blows from a roughly dressed man on the pier. The incident was so unexpected that the man punched the former monarch several times, about the head and body before anybody could stop him. He was arrested immediately and identified as a Spaniard.

MARSEILLES, May 15. (UP) Former King Alfonso of Spain was attacked today by an enraged countryman. He was pummeled with fists and almost pushed off the boat from which he was debarking before bystanders pulled off his assailant. He was uninjured.

Marseilles, May 13.--Ex-King Alfonso of Spain narrowly escaped a ducking in the Mediterranean today when an enraged countryman sought to push him from the gangplank of a boat from which he was debarking. Failing in this, he tried to beat and choke the former king, screaming: “Alfonso needs a lesson!” The king's son, Prince Juan, who accompanied him, pulled the assailant from his sire and held him until police took the man into custody. He was identified as Gonzales Maseanares. Somewhat but slightly ruffled, Alfonso and his entourage went to a hotel where he will stay until he goes to Paris. During hold-up and robbery of Donald Stoneburner, Licking View, at 1:30 o'clock Friday morning on Timber Run creek bridge, Licking View road, was reported to police today. Two men, one of whom wielded a gun in a menacing manner, are said to have secured $28, and escaped in Stoneburner's Chrysler sedan

By The Associated Press. PARIS, France, May 12.-Paul Doumer, France's assassinated president, was buried today with public ceremonials of great majesty and impressiveness and with private rites of the utmost simplicity. Fully a million persons thronged streets and squares to watch the funeral procession pass from Elysee palace to Notre Dame cathedral where the requiem mass was sung, and then to the Pantheon where the dead statesman was eulogized by Premier Andre Tardieu as “the supreme type of democrat.” Soldiers In Ceremony Among the participants in the public ceremony were thousands of the soldiers of France, a king and four royal princes, and the diplomats of virtually every nation of the world. When the public funeral was over the body was taken from the Pantheon to the Doumer family vault at Vaugirard cemetery. There it was laid to rest beside the four sons whom M. Doumer gave to Fr

WASHINGTON, May 13 (*) — President Hoover today directed the law enforcement agencies and secret service of the Federal government to set out upon a hunt for the murderers of the Lindbergh baby, “never to be relaxed until those criminals are implacably brought to justice.” The President issued the following statement: Never to Relax. “I have directed the law enforcement agencies and the several secret services of the Federal government to make the kidnapping and murder of the Lindbergh baby a live and never-to-be-forgotten case, never to be relaxed until these criminals are implacably brought to justice. “The Federal government does not have police authority in such crimes but its agencies will be unceasingly alert to assist the New Jersey police in every possible way until this end has been accomplished.” Deeply shaken at the tragedy, the nation’s legislators strove to throw a barrier o

Harbor Grace, N. F., May 13.—(AP)—Lou Reichers hopped for Dublin, Ireland, at 8:30 a. m., Newfoundland daylight time (4:50 a. m. C. S. T.) today, after effecting repairs to his stabilizer, broken in landing on his hop from Newark, N. J., to Harbor Grace. Harbor Grace was the Arlington, N. J., speed flier’s first scheduled refueling stop on a three-hop flight from Newark, N. J., to Paris. From Harbor Grace he proposes to fly to Dublin, Ireland, where he will pick up a second supply of fuel and continue to Paris. It was at first believed that repairs to a stabilizer he had broken in landing would hold him here for several hours, but mechanics began work on the broken part immediately and repairs were completed within two hours. The speed flier is attempting to halve the time of Colonel Lindbergh's nonstop flight from New York to Paris in 1927. Reichers expected to make the flight in “about

1932-09-06.text: Copenhagen, Denmark, Sept. 6 (AP)—George Hutchinson, American flier leading a party of eight from New York to London over the Arctic air route, was fined 1,000 kroner (approximately $180) by the governor of southern Greenland for landing in Greenland without a permit. The governor notified the Danish government of the penalty today and said Hutchinson's conduct since arriving at Godthaab had been exemplary and that he had expressed sincere regret for his error. The governor said he did not know yet when the Hutchinsons would continue their flight.

YORK, Eng., Sept. 6. (P)—England is gradually sinking to sea level at the rate of nine inches every one hundred years, Captain T. E. Longfield, ordinance survey expert, told the British Association of Scientists today. “The evidence seems conclusive,” he said, “that the level of high tide 2,000 years ago must have been at least 15 feet lower than at present.” The Bank of England in London has sunk more than six inches since 1868, and St. Paul's Cathedral is gradually tilting over from the effects of the subsidence, he said.

HYDE PARK, N. Y., Sept. 5. (4) Armed with further assurances that party differences in New England will heal before election, Governor Roosevelt was preparing today for two more campaign appearances, one of them in Vermont, within the next two days. Resting at his Hyde Park home before proceeding to the New York state fair at Syracuse tomorrow, Roosevelt yesterday received Peter P. Gerry of Rhode Island and Mrs. Frances P. Sayre, vice president of the Massachusetts state committee. Gerry, who was a pre-convention supporter of former Governor Alfred E. Smith, told the candidate he believed feeling which grew out of Smith’s failure to obtain the democratic nomination would soon fade.

ROTTERDAM, Sept. 6 (P) — Dutch marines put to sea today to meet the trans-Atlantic liner Rotterdam to deal with what the captain reported as a mutiny inside Dutch territorial waters. (Previously London shipping circles had heard the Rotterdam’s crew refused to dock her anywhere but at Rotterdam, her home port, where a seamen's strike was on. There was no explanation of why the Rotterdam called for marines, since the captain had already agreed to the crew’s stipulation to proceed to the home port.) The Holland America Line asked for the marines when the captain reported that part of the crew had refused to stoke the fires. Protection was sought for those willing to work.

Sep. 6 (AP)—Mayor Cermak of Chicago, touring Buffalo in the interest of next year’s Chicago Fair, was introduced to a gathering of distinguished British and American business men as the “First Mayor of America.” “He heads the government of the second city of the United States,” said Francis Powell, who introduced him, “But because of the political situation in New York he ranks as the first mayor of America.” The mayor gave facts and figures about the Chicago administration and plans for the Fair. There was applause when he promised that Chicago would have real beer for those who visit the exposition. Whoever wins the national election in November, he said, the Volstead Act will be changed.

DETROIT, Sept. 6 UPi—The seventh attempt of a foreign challenger to lift the Harmsworth trophy failed today—as have all others in the last decade—in the disabling of the challenging craft, Miss England III, piloted by Kaye Don. For Gar Wood, veteran defender of the historic bronze plaque, today's heat, like the first Saturday, was merely a workout in his Miss America X. After mechanical difficulties had brought Don to a complete stop before he could finish 13 miles of the 35-mile course, Wood coasted along to an uncontested victory. Don Out For 1932: Before Wood had finished his fourth lap of the seven-mile semi-ellipse Don accepted a tow to his boatwell and was automatically eliminated from further competition this year. Wood's big mahogany-hulled Miss America X, generally credited with a potential speed of around 125 miles an hour, never was opened up, except possibly for a mile at the

Rotterdam, Sept. 6—(#)—The “mutiny” aboard the Holland-America liner Rotterdam, near the end of the ship's voyage from New York, ended today in the hands of the police. When the liner entered this port this morning under escort of the minelayer Meerlandt, four policemen went aboard immediately with arrest warrants for the rebellious members of the crew, charging insubordination. On request of the captain, 30 Dutch marines met the liner yesterday, near West Hindes lightship when members of the crew reported to have insisted on proceeding to Rotterdam from Boulogne in spite of the fact that the company’s and the captain's orders were to debark passengers at Southampton. Fears that the crew would join a seaman's strike here if they came to this port were given as the reason for the order to proceed to Southampton. Yesterday's reports said the captain finally acquiesced in the demand to proc

BERLIN. Sept. 6—(#)—Chancellor von Papen will face the new Reichstag for the first time next Monday, prepared for a possible vote of no confidence with an undated decree of dissolution signed by President von Hindenburg. Hermann Goering, the National Socialist speaker of the house, issued the formal call for assembly this afternoon.

1932-10-28.text: By The Associated Press London, Oct. 27.—Rioting unemployed shouting defiance at police participated today in the most serious disturbance of the kind that London has seen in years. Fifty thousand people massed inside Hyde Park and at the several entrances as a column of several thousand jobless marched in for a demonstration in protest against administration of the dole system. In Great Cumberland Place, opposite the marble entrance of Edgeware Road, a brick was thrown through the post office window. Mounted police charged swinging their clubs and the mob fell back cursing and booing. Police retired and the crowd swept in again upon them. Time after time the horses pressed back the mob withdrew and the mob surged in again. Stones and mud whizzed past the policemen’s heads. Several persons were injured. This fighting took place over a 300-yards section along the bridle path from the marb

LONDON, Oct. 28. ()—Sixty or 70 persons were nursing injuries today in the wake of a riot that raged in Hyde Park as a climax of a “hunger army’s” march on London. Twelve of the casualties, including three policemen, were seriously hurt in furious melees that transformed the fashionable park into a battleground yesterday. The home secretary in a report to the House of Commons, said the real trouble had been caused by London toughs. Nearly all the men arraigned today before magistrates were Londoners.

WASHINGTON, Oct. 27. (AP). A navy built to the London Treaty limit and “equal to that of the most powerful in the world” is considered by President Hoover a necessity if arms limitation efforts fall. The president's view was expressed in a formal statement commemorating the eleventh annual observance today of Navy Day.
