This year, on the bicentennial anniversary of his birth, George Washington's relation to the navy was made the theme of the nation-wide celebration led by the chief executive and Secretary Adams. President Hoover's statement follows in full: “I take the occasion of Navy Day to remind the nation that the national defense is the first and most solemn obligation placed upon the government by the Constitution. Our people have ever been lovers of peace and they have consistently pursued a policy designed to preserve national rights by peaceful negotiation wherever possible, rat

NEW YORK, Oct. 5.--Five world powers —the United States, Great Britain, France, Russia and Japan —were breaking trail today toward new alignments intended to promote peace and security. As reflected in Associated Press dispatches from several capitals, their activity also introduced three powerful factors into the international problem. These factors were: 1. Improved relations between Russia and Japan despite the troublesome Manchuria that lies between them. 2. The proximity of a treaty of non-aggression between France and Russia stipulating that France will give no aid to a country attacking Russia, and vice versa. 3. Apparent Anglo-American unity at Geneva, having reached an agreement in principle to harmonize their views on disarmament. Manchurian Problem Considered Moscow reports told of better relations between Japan and Russia, especially affecting their mutual trouble spot, Manch

LONDON, Oct. 27.—Rioting occurred on Edgeware Road where thousands of 'hunger marchers' were entering Hyde Park today to organize for their protest against revision of the British dole system. Police charged the crowds, swinging long batons to the right and left. Several were injured. The rioting broke out opposite the marble arch entrance to the huge park on the Edgeware Road. It was estimated that 50,000 persons, mostly spectators, were massed in the park where many of the marchers were assembling and their leaders were making speeches.

- LONDON, Oct. 28.— The house of commons, the prime minister’s residence and the home of Montagu Norman, governor of the Bank of England, were strongly guarded today after the hunger marchers who rioted in Hyde Park yesterday and threatened renewed sabotage. Guards at Buckingham Palace, residence of the king, also were on the alert. Extra police were sent to Montagu Norman's after a telephone threat had been received in which the caller said “We are sending unemployed to wreck the house.” The streets of London were heavily patrolled, and in many sections the constables walked their beats by twos instead of singly. The unemployed organizers planned scattered demonstrations today and tomorrow before their next mass demonstration, scheduled for Trafalgar Square on Sunday. It was feared outbreaks at separated points, if well-timed by the jobless, would be more difficult to cope with than a c

Hyde Park, London, Oct. 27 (CUP) — Two riots were broken up by police when the British “hunger marchers” reached Hyde Park today. London hoodlums who awaited the marchers in the park were credited with starting the disturbances which attracted a crowd of 100,000 persons. Many were injured and demonstrators threw stones at police and smashed the windows of automobiles and shops. Sixty Injured. The injured list inside Hyde Park was given as 60 at 6 p. m. but many others were injured outside the park. One hunger marcher was found to be almost dead from starvation. Two dozen persons were carried on stretchers to St. George’s hospital. Police casualties included Chief Inspector Oger of Scotland Yard and two underofficers, all suffering from serious head injuries. Carry Red Banners. London, Oct. 27 (UP)—Thousands of unemployed, carrying red banners and openly flaunting the sickle and hammer of

A TTS Cte LOS ANGELES, Oct. 28.—() ~Three-year-old Nancy Irene Buchanan was happily back in her nursery today unaware she was the central figure of a storybook tale of real life which combined, kidnapping, attempted extortion, a tragedy of mother love and the wealth of an old English estate. The circumstances which brought her into the midst of this strange picture began a few hours after her birth as the daughter of Ruth Borman, unmarried mother and former Iowa girl, who sat brokenly in a jail cell today awaiting threatened prosecution for kidnapping. Nancy did not know Miss Borman, 20 years old, as 'mother.' That was the name to her of Mrs. Violet C. Buchanan, her guardian; a wealthy divorcee and daughter of an aristocratic family of England and the California Spaniards, from whose home she was abducted Wednesday. The child was found yesterday asleep in the arms of her real mother, who

1932-10-12.text: (EDITOR'S NOTE: The complete text of former President Calvin Coolidge’s endorsement of President Herbert Hoover and his plea for the latter’s re-election will be found on page 8.) New York, Oct. 12 —(AP)—Calvin Coolidge, coming from his New England retreat to praise President Herbert Hoover as a man who saved the country from disaster, has signaled the start of the final phase of his party's campaign, A drive which would reach a climax in the appearance of the president here later was started by eastern leaders today after Mr. Coolidge told a throng in Madison Square Garden last night that the public welfare requires the re-election of Mr. Hoover. “Tf saving the country from one impending disaster after another provides any basis for gratitude, President Hoover is entitled to gratitude,” he said. He stated that the country “knows that its worst troubles are probably past and economic rec

BELFAST, Northern Ireland, Oct. 12 (AP)—British army troops were rushed to Belfast today after rioting, similar to that which resulted in one death and more than thirty serious injuries yesterday, broke out again shortly before noon. Quiet was restored by the police by midnight last night after quasi-military rule was clamped down on the city. The quiet continued throughout the early morning and forenoon until about 11 A.M. when shooting broke out again in the Falls area west of the city. A bus was wrecked by the mob and every available armored car was brought into use by the police. The milling crowds retreated before the charge of armored cars manned by police, however, and quiet was restored again.

LEWES, Del., Oct. 12.—The crew of the salvage ship Cape, grounded on Pea Patch Island dyke, were about ready today to concede that some sort of curse must hang over the Spanish gold that went down with the British sloop Debraak in 1798. The Cape, sister ship of the salvage vessel Katie Durm which burned and sank two weeks ago, went aground and was wrecked last night, with the loss of valuable diving apparatus, and the crew was picked up by a government boat and landed at New Castle, Del. The Katie Durm and the Cape, owned by a Baltimore salvaging company, started late in the summer on a quest for the sunken gold, said to have been seized by the Debraak from two Spanish galleons off the West Indies and estimated to be worth $10,000,000. For more than 130 years all efforts to salvage the gold have failed. It was announced the quest may be resumed in the spring.

MUKDEN, Oct. 12.—(UP)—Unconfirmed reports received here today said Mrs. C. T. Woodruff, wife of a British accountant for the British America Tobacco Company, had been shot and killed at Witaiskaya near Harbin, and her two children kidnapped. Officials of the company here were attempting to check the report.

London, Oct. 12.—(AP)—Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald celebrated his sixty-sixth birthday at work today at No. 10 Downing Street, where his attention was demanded by matters connected with various pending conferences. There was one short break this afternoon, however, when the members of his family participated in a birthday tea party. The party brought poignant memories to the prime minister, for the little sewing circle started twenty-eight years ago by his wife held its regular Wednesday afternoon meeting in Downing Street with his daughter, Ishbel, as hostess. Every Wednesday afternoon since Mrs. MacDonald started the circle, her friends have met at the MacDonald home. Always the women sew and knit in aid of a clinic which Mrs. MacDonald helped to establish. Today he talked over with them the early days of the clinic which now commemorates his wife’s memory.

Harbin, Manchuria, Oct. 12. (>)— Mrs. C. T. Woodruff, an Englishwoman, was killed today as she attempted to prevent the kidnapping of her three children. After shooting her, the kidnappers fled with the children and seriously injured two Russians who attempted to pursue them, but finally they were forced to give up the children by Chinese police. Two of the bandits were killed by the police and two others escaped. Acting in behalf of the consular corps, George C. Hanson, American consul-general, protested to the authorities of Japan and the new state of Manchukuo, emphasizing the need for greater police protection. Citizens of Harbin, he said, are afraid to venture into the streets. The killing of Mrs. Woodruff, whose husband is chief accountant for the British-American Tobacco Company, took place on one of the principal streets. Bandit raids have been frequent during the last few weeks.

CHANGCHUN, Manchuria, Oct. 12—A possibility that a large part of northern China might be annexed to the new state of Manchukuo, with the aid of the Japanese army, and at least part of the old Chinese monarchy restored under the former “boy emperor,” Henri Pu-Yi, was predicted today by sources close to Pu-Yi's palace. These sources described the move as a cherished ambition of Pu-Yi and his followers and said they hoped to be able to bring it about next spring after the Japanese army has occupied the province of Jehol, which was described as ‘inevitable.’ After that, the “boy emperor” and his associates were represented as believing the extension of the Japanese military operations southward to the Peiping and Tientsin districts would be an inevitable sequel. Pu-Yi, now dictator of the new Manchukuo state, under the advice of dozens of Japanese counsellors, recently received emissaries fr

ATHENS, Oct. 12—(4)—Samuel Insull, entirely free following his brief detention by the police, awoke today in fine spirits at the Petit Palais, a leading hotel of Athens, and said he planned to stay here for some time enjoying the glory that was Greece. Meanwhile, officials at the American legation said the necessary warrant was on the way to secure his detention again and that as soon as it arrived a fight would begin in the courts to take the erstwhile power master. (Continued on Page 2, No. 3)

1932-09-16.text: LONDON, Sept. 15 (UP).—Military equality of Germany with the other powers was advocated today by Arthur Henderson, former foreign minister and chairman of the world disarmament conference. Henderson, on the eve of leaving for Geneva to preside over the resumption of the conference, proposed that the signatories of the Versailles treaty and associated powers assemble publicly and declare their intention of restoring Germany to a position of military equality.

COPENHAGEN, Denmark, Sept. 15.— George R. Hutchinson and his “flying family” will leave Angmagssalik, Greenland, today for England on the trawler Lord Talbot, the Danish administrator there informed the government today. The Hutchinsons, attempting a flight from New York to London over the Arctic route, wrecked their plane near Angmagssalik and were rescued by the Lord Talbot on Tuesday.

London, Eng., Sept. 15.—Germany’s demand for equality in armament received enthusiastic support today from Arthur Henderson, president of the world disarmament conference. Speaking before the national peace council, Mr. Henderson, who was foreign secretary in the last British labor cabinet, called upon the allied powers of the world to carry out the disarmament provisions of the treaty of Versailles. “Why shouldn't the World War allies get together and recognize that what was said in their names in 1929 must bind them?” Mr. Henderson demanded. “Why should they not publicly declare their intention to remove Germany’s position of inferiority with all possible haste and to restore Germany’s equality in military status?” Saturday Henderson will leave for Geneva to prepare for the resumption of the disarmament conference. Admitting frankly that he was dissatisfied with the results of the conf

POONA, India, Sept. 15. Mahatma Gandhi still is determined to begin his “fast unto death,” he told official visitors who saw him in Yjoda jail here today. He is determined to refuse food until Great Britain’s adjustment of the Indian communal problem is to his satisfaction.

LONDON, Sept. 16—Release of Mahatma M. K. Gandhi from prison will not alter his intention to starve himself to death in protest against the government's communal settlement for India, Gandhi indicated in a cablegram to an intimate friend here, Rev. C. F. Andrews. “I regard fasting as God’s call to me,” Gandhi cabled. “Only the certain prospect of withdrawal of separate electorates for the depressed classes (the government's provision which Gandhi opposes) can warrant postponement.”

GORLESTON, England, Sept. 15 —(AP)— A lifeboat and tugs went out from this suburb of Yarmouth tonight in search of an airplane reported to have come down and exploded in the North Sea. There was no immediate indication whether this could be the missing transatlantic airplane, American Nurse. The plane was sighted by the Nicholas Lightship about a mile or so off shore. The Lightship fired distress signals. When the lifeboat and tug reached the spot the master of the lifeboat reported to them he had seen the plane on the water with its engines running. There was an explosion followed by two white lights, he said. The tug and lifeboat cruised for some time but found no trace of the ship. Visibility was very poor.

By The Associated Press Five Farms Course, Baltimore County Club, Sept. 16.—An international final for the United States amateur golf team championships seemed virtually assured today. Ross (Sandy) Somerville, of London, Ontario, four times former Canadian champion, shot into a lead of six up over Jesse Guilford, Boston veteran, in the first half of the 36-hole semi-finals. The 39-year old defending champion, Francis Ouimet, of Boston, meanwhile is deadlocked in a spectacular duel with 22 year old Johnnie Goodman, of Omaha, in a match to determine the other finalist. They finished the first 18 holes all square, each with five medal scores of 72, only two over par. Goodman's marvelous recovery shot and brilliant putting repeatedly saved him as he waged a give and take struggle with the title holder.

PLYMOUTH, Mass., Sept. 16.—A grim band of National Guardsmen and country officials trudged through the woodland around Great Herring Pond today, seeking a clue which would untangle the most amazing mystery of recent years in New England. They were hunting for the body of Mrs. Edith Du Bois, wife of a well-to-do salesman. They were under orders to keep looking “inch by inch” through the countryside until they have succeeded or definitely proved that the effort to solve the mystery of Mrs. Du Bois’ disappearance must be shifted to some other locality. Authorities have been convinced the woman is dead. But they have only a tangled strand of hair, taken from Plymouth Harbor, and a few less tangible clues to guide their search. Mrs. Du Bois, 40, dark haired and attractive, drove with her husband and two other persons from the Du Bois cottage at Great Herring Pond to Providence, R. I., railroa

1932-11-26.text: London—(#)—The British government proceeded Saturday in the belief that arrangements could yet be made to pass the December war debt payment to the United States, despite advice from Washington to the contrary. To that end a new note to Washington was in the making. It will follow up a note sent earlier in the month requesting suspension of the $95,550,000 installment—a note to which Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson replied yesterday. What the new note may contain was a matter of conjecture, but before its framers was an expression of good will by Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald. “The discussions with the United States are arousing no bad feeling between us,” was the prime minister's statement. Sums up Viewpoint As summed up for the British taxpayer, the British viewpoint was expressed thus by Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer: “We never contemplated a state of things i

Great Britain today planned a new appeal to the United States for suspension of its Dec. 15 war debt payment. Prime Minister MacDonald said he was still hopeful the postponement could be arranged, although the United States in notes to Britain, France and Belgium said such concessions were impossible. MacDonald was reported to have summoned leading cabinet members to a special meeting Sunday to begin drafting a new note to America. The American notes, while refusing Europe's request for delaying December payments, promised that President Hoover would ask Congress to create a commission to re-examine the whole debt situation, as the allied powers asked. OPPOSE HOOVER Congressional leaders and President-elect Roosevelt oppose Mr. Hoover's plan. Congressional sentiment strongly opposes any reconsideration or reduction of the debts. Roosevelt recently said any negotiations should be confined

Europe is considering the problem of its debts to the United States in every phase before the next move to obtain re-consideration of the whole issue. Members of the British cabinet are studying Secretary Stimson’s reply to the request for postponement of the December installment. A new note, advancing additional grounds for the request, is in preparation. The chancellor of the exchequer probably will make a statement of the government’s position in the House of Commons on Monday. The French cabinet was called into special session, presumably to consider the advisability of sending a supplementary note to Washington. In Berlin the government is watching developments closely, but the current negotiations do not directly concern Germany.

DUBLIN, IRISH FREE STATE, Nov. 26.—(7)—Donald Buckley, former member of the Dáil Éireann for Kildare, was appointed governor-general of the Irish Free State today to succeed James McNeill, who resigned last month.

London, Nov. 26—(U.F.)—Postponement of British debt payments to the United States, and an exchange of views on the world economic situation are necessary to save the world from “economic madness,” according to British government officials. The British government still considers postponement of the debts due December 15 possible if the two nations will have “a real meeting together—if both sides can put themselves in the shoes of the other,” Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald said. Hope for U. S. Agreement, “We hope the United States will agree to postponement of the war debt payments,” MacDonald said in the first official reference to the present stage of the debts question. “We asked that the date of payment be postponed while there is an opportunity for an exchange of views on the general situation... While war debts are legal obligations, they are tantamount to economic madness.” Chan

LONDON, Nov. 25 () — While Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald was expressing confidence tonight a new debt agreement could be made with the United States, Chancellor of the Exchequer Neville Chamberlain revealed if Britain resumes her payments December 15, it will be necessary to boost the income tax from 25 to 30 per cent. The prime minister said he could not believe that a real effort on both sides would fail to result in a solution "to enable December 15 to be passed."

London, Nov. 26 (INS)—Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald endeavored today to reconcile the divergent views of his cabinet ministers on the war debt question. Plainly on record as favoring postponement of the December 15 payment to the United States, the prime minister held a series of telephone conversations with his colleagues in an attempt to swing the government into a unified position. He faced no easy task, since some cabinet members have persistently advocated default on the payment, while others have insisted the instalment must be paid no matter what the consequences. With several members of the cabinet out of town over the weekend, it appeared there would be no decisive developments until Monday, when an emergency meeting of the full cabinet will be held. At that meeting the ministers will have an opportunity to air their views before approving or amending the new British reply

Paris, Nov. 26 - (4) - The text of a pact of conciliation and non-aggression between France and Soviet Russia was approved today by the cabinet, Premier Herriot said it will be signed on Tuesday. The agreement provides that neither country, alone or in conjunction with a third power, will resort to arms against the other, and that each will respect the territories under the sovereignty of the other. It also stipulates that if either party is the subject of aggression by a third power, the other will not aid the aggressor directly or indirectly. If one party should commit an act of aggression against a third power, the other party to the agreement can immediately withdraw from the pact.

1932-10-20.text: Mukden, Manchuria, Oct. 20 (P)— Mrs. Kenneth Pawley and Charles Corkran, British subjects who have been in the hands of Chinese bandits several weeks, were liberated today. It was reported they had reached Panshan today and would be at Newchang tomorrow on the way back here, Mrs. Pawley and Corkran and another Englishman named Duncan McIntosh, all employees of the Asiatic Petroleum Company, were riding together near Newchang in the first week of September. They stopped to change horses and were immediately surrounded by the bandits.

BOSTON, Oct. 19.—(#)-A howling northeaster that had already taken the lives of three increased in intensity today as it swept down the New England coast. Storm warnings were flying from Block Island to Boston Light and in greater Boston a three inch rainfall was reported for a 24 hour period ending at 6 a. m. Many of the vessels scheduled to leave port yesterday remained at their berths. Streets were flooded in many sections of greater Boston and at sea winds of 50-mile velocity were reported. The three deaths occurred at Jamestown, R. I., yesterday when a fishing party was swept into the sea from the jagged rocks off the Harrison Morris estate. The drowned were Ernest Vierre, 40; Manuel Madeiros, 20, and Joseph Mello, 50.

London, Oct. 18.—(4)—The police intercepted a rush on Parliament Square by an organized army of several thousand jobless men today and a bloody riot ensued. The disorder occurred in the poorer class Lambeth section just across the Thames from the historic House of Parliament where the national government had just reassembled. The police were successful in turning back the demonstrators but not until six or seven hours of battling in hand-to-hand fashion had disturbed the peace of ancient Lambeth. Then came looting by rowdy youths, and when order was restored around 11 p.m., scores had been injured, at least twenty of them seriously. March on Commons The demonstration began late in the afternoon when several thousand unemployed began to march toward the parliament buildings from various thoroughfares on the south side of the Thames. The authorities said the men had been marshalled by the

LONDON, Oct. 20 (4) — Extension of the ‘dole’ payments to unemployed has been demanded by Labor party leaders as a result of Tuesday's riots in the Lambeth district. The demand was made yesterday in the House of Commons by George Lansbury. Prime Minister MacDonald, taking note of the disturbance Tuesday, cleared the way for debate. ‘I demand that the damnable means test be abolished,” Lansbury said, and that every man be given a chance of decent existence.’ The so-called means test in the ‘dole’ regulations provides that before a person can receive unemployment insurance he must show proof that he has not the means to subsist normally, even though he is not employed. Lansbury's demand was supported by George Buchanan, Glasgow labor member, who declared further demonstrations by the unemployed would ‘wreck the existing social system or be itself wrecked in the attempt,’ unless concessions

| BOSTON, Oct. 20. (4)—For the third day a driving rainstorm beat its way down the New England coast and today the northeaster had brought death to nine. Yachting fleets along the Massachusetts coast suffered, roads were flooded, in many places power lines were down and many shore communities were flooded by rising tides and pounding surf. At midnight last night five inches of rain had fallen in greater Boston since the start of the storm Monday but the force of the northeaster was abating and predictions were that it would pass out to sea during the night. Of the deaths, six were drownings and three the result of automobile accidents.

MUKDEN, Manchuria, Oct. 20. (UP)—Mrs. Muriel Pawley and Charles Corkran, young Britons captured by Chinese bandits on Sept. 7, have been released and arrived at Panshan today. Mrs. Pawley and Corkran obtained their freedom through negotiations by British and Japanese authorities. It was understood a small ransom was paid, although the original demands of the bandits were fantastic. Mrs. Pawley is 19, bride of Kenneth Pawley, an employee of the Asiatic Petroleum company at Tientsin.

Boston, Oct. 19 ()—The number of deaths incidental to the northeast gale which for two days has raged over New England mounted to nine tonight as the storm continued, unabated. Three high school students were killed at Sharon, in a collision of their automobile and a train. A crossing tender told police he was unable to lower the gates because of the pressure of the wind. The victims were Burton Peck, 17; Henry Stone, 16; and Martha Burlinghame, 14. The other lives were taken by the angry sea. Stanley E. Bassett, 24, of Harwich, drowned in a vain attempt to swim ashore from a small boat off Orleans; two duck hunters drowned off Anisquam Light, Gloucester, and yesterday three fishermen were swept to their deaths from a rock at Jamestown, R. I. by a huge wave. The Gloucester men, Robert Wonson and Clyde Robinshaw, drowned when their skiff overturned in heavy seas. The storm caused thousand

London, Oct. 19.—(4?)—Less than 24 hours after 10,000 jobless men and women had rioted across the Thames from Parliament square, the House of Commons engaged in sharp debate tonight over the government’s policy of handling the unemployed. Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald, taking note of the disturbance across the river, cleared the way for the debate early today and it was opened by George Lansbury, laborite leader. Test Unjust “TI demand that the damnable ‘means test’ be abolished,” Mr. Lansbury said, “and every man be given a chance of decent existence.” (Before an unemployed person can receive unemployment insurance, he must show the government proof that he has not the means to subsist normally.) Mr. Lansbury was supported by George Buchanan, the Glasgow laborite, who declared future demonstrations by the unemployed.

1932-10-07.text: LONDON, UP). The British government still stood by its suggestion that a four-power conference take up the question of Germany's demand for arms equality, but it was said in official circles that if either France or Germany declined to participate the plan would be dropped. The French foreign office announced in Paris that Britain had postponed indefinitely its plan to call the conference. This announcement was issued after Lord Tyrrell, the British Ambassador, had conferred with Premier Herriot. Paris reports received in London to the effect that the British ambassador had informed France that London had decided to postpone the conference were regarded in official circles as a misinterpretation. Government spokesmen were reticent about discussing the apparent breakdown in the British plan to take up the German arms demand at a meeting attended by representatives of Germany, Britain, Fra
BERLIN, (UP). Germany has accepted unconditionally a proposal for a four power arms conference in London, it was said authoritatively. The reply was sent to Great Britain.

Santa Monica, Calif. —(UP)— Miss Agnes M. Mitchell, nurse, had a lot on Twelfth street. She saved her money to build a house. “Build it here,” she told a contractor, pointing out one of 48 series of vacant lots. The contractor built a $2,200 English cottage. Y. Naumoff also had a lot on Twelfth street. He inspected his property today and was amazed to find on it Miss Mitchell’s cottage. Her lot adjoined. Legally, the building is his, but attorneys said an arrangement had been made to trade lots, if Miss Mitchell paid the attorneys’ and transfer fees.

TORONTO, ONT., OCT. 7, (AP) — John Hampton, assistant state's attorney for Cook County, Ill., who was successful in having Martin Insull indicted in Chicago for embezzlement, lodged in an Ontario jail, said today that Illinois authorities are going to Europe and will bring back Samuel Insull, former head of the Insull utilities interests. Samuel Insull, also under indictment in Chicago on charges of embezzlement and larceny, was reported missing today from his Paris residence. Hampton said Chicago authorities will leave for Paris within two or three weeks. Hampton said he would resist bail for Martin Insull, who was held in a jail cell at Barrie, Ont., while procedure was begun to secure his extradition. Samuel Insull is an American citizen. Martin Insull still retains his British citizenship.

| Orilla, Ont., Oct. 6 (4)—John Hampton, assistant states attorney of Cook County, Illinois, said early today that Martin Insull, indicted public utility magnate, had refused to waive extradition proceedings and return voluntarily to Cook County. Hampton said he would go to Barrie, 22 miles from here to start legal procedure for extradition.

BARRIE, Ont., (P)—Martin J. Insull, once powerful Chicago multi-millionaire and operating chief of the two-billion dollar Insull utilities, occupied a jail Friday with vagrants, bootleggers and petty robbers. He was held as a fugitive from justice awaiting extradition to Chicago on charges of embezzlement and larceny. Insull, a weary old man, surrendered to authorities at 9:30 p.m. Thursday night. After a meeting at the home of Judge Dudley Holmes, of Simcoe county, Insull was taken to the Barrie jail, an old fortress, known as a “tough” place. He must remain there for at least eight days, the judge ruled in convening a court in the front parlor of his home. Judge Holmes set hearing for Oct. 14. If extradition papers have not arrived by that time, Insull will be remanded to jail for another eight days. Just 25 minutes after the court (Continued on Page Two)

TORONTO, Ont., Oct. 6 ()—Raward Bayly, deputy attorney general of Ontario, was retained today as private counsel by John Hampton, assistant state's attorney of Cook County, Illinois, in extradition proceedings against Martin Insull, former public utilities magnate who is under indictment for embezzlement and larceny. Hampton, who said today he had been unable to induce Insull to waive extradition, explained he would now lay his evidence before a county judge in Canada and ask for a provisional warrant for Mr. Insull’s arrest. He said that if the application is successful he would arrest Insull immediately.

PARIS, Oct. 7—()—Samuel Insull, former Chicago utilities magnate who is under indictment there on charges growing out of the investigation of the collapse of some of his interests, still was missing, for the third day, from his hotel here today. Mrs. Insull, who is still at the hotel, refused to answer any questions about him. The American embassy also declined to say whether a request for extradition for Insull had been received from the United States. Embassy officials said they were not permitted to discuss extradition cases.

1932-11-20.text: CAPE TOWN, Union of South Africa, Nov. 19. (AP)—Amy Johnson, feeling better after 12 hours sleep, talked by telephone this morning with her husband, J. A. Mollison, in London, about flying back to England for another speed record. He said he would have to think it over and would let her know tomorrow. Miss Johnson now holds the speed record for the flight from England to Cape Town, having clipped nearly eleven hours off her husband's record when she reached here yesterday.

CAPE TOWN (UP).—Amy Johnson arranged an appointment with a hair dresser yesterday as soon as she awoke from a sleep of 14½ hours. Miss Johnson, who broke her husband's record for an England-Cape Town flight, received congratulatory messages from all over the world. Mechanics who examined Miss Johnson’s light plane, the ‘Desert Cloud,’ found it in good condition.

BERLIN, Nov. 19.—(47—Adolf Hitler, making what may be his most powerful bid for leadership in the German government, talked for an hour today with President Von Hindenburg, emerged with a broad smile and let it be known that he would see the president again next Tuesday. Persons close to the president said the meeting was “extraordinarily cordial,” and there was a prevailing feeling in political circles that the day's conference and the ones which are to follow may produce a “national concentration” cabinet in which Hitler's national socialists will have an important part. Last August when the president received Hitler for the first time the Nazi leader made a blunt demand for the chancellorship or nothing. He was turned down and the interview lasted only 15 minutes.

BERLIN, Nov. 19.—(U.P.)—President von Hindenburg is willing to appoint Adolf Hitler Chancellor on condition that he continue the general policies of the Von Papen cabinet and leave the composition of the new cabinet in the president's hands, the United Press was informed in reliable quarters today. The president told Hitler in their conversations today that he had no objection in principle to entrusting the government to the Nazis, but would not appoint Hitler unconditionally. Hitler told the president he wanted several days to think over the proposition, and Von Hindenburg agreed to see him again next week. The president specified that Hitler adopt a definite economic scheme such as the “one year plan” inaugurated by Von Papen.

Berlin, Nov. 19. —(P)—Adolf Hitler applied today to Field Marshal Paul von Hindenburg, president of Germany, to be made chancellor of the Reich. It was the second time in three years. This time, in marked contrast to their meeting August 13, Hitler was invited to sit down for an hour and to talk with frank cordiality. As he departed from the president's residence, the formal corporal in the World War was asked to come back for another conference next Tuesday. Suggestion of President After listening patiently to the national socialist leader, the president suggested Hitler lay his aims before other party leaders and tell the president at their next audience how they reacted to them. A government statement issued tonight said “personal questions were not considered. Hitler merely gave a summary of the aims of his movement.” Political commentators said today’s meeting in no wise indicated (

TOKYO, Nov. 19 (AP).—It was officially learned today that Japan will remind the council of the League of Nations next week that Manchukuo is not the first state separated from its "parent state" and given independence through the actions of another power. This argument will be contained in Japan's answer to the Lytton report on Manchuria, which will be made public tomorrow night, an official told The Associated Press today. "I cannot affirm," the informant said, "the assertions in vernacular newspapers that our reply to the Lyttton report will cite Panama and Estonia in this connection, but certainly Panama is one of the incidents we had in mind. I can assure you however, this portion of the document is in no wise construable as derogatory to the United States." Rejects Lytton Report The document emphatically rejects the proposal of the Lytton commission for restoration of Chinese sovere

| Moscow, Nov. 19. (AP).—Thirty thousand white collar workers in various government offices have been laid off under an order issued last month directing their transfer to farms and factories. All government bureaus have cut the payroll ten to twenty per cent and a slightly smaller reduction has been made in the offices of all government trusts and syndicates. The authorities have promised to find new jobs for all those affected, providing suitable work for those unfit for manual labor.

SADSEW VERE, ONE NEG NOV, LOLA. Col. Raymond Robins, prohibition and peace advocate, found in the western North Carolina mountains yesterday after a disappearance of more than two months, was brought to Asheville today and placed in a sanatorium under the care of a physician. Col. Robins, who is suffering from amnesia, was brought here by automobile from Whittier, a small village in Swain county, where he lived for more than two months under the name of "Raymond Rogers." John Dreier of New York, a nephew, who identified the missing philanthropist yesterday, issued the following statement: "Colonel Raymond Robins is at present at Norburn hospital in Asheville, and under the care of Dr. Mark A. Griffin of Asheville. Allowed to See No One, "The doctor has given orders that no one is to be allowed to see or speak with Colonel Robins, but that he is to be kept quiet and free from disturbances

1932-10-10.text: LEIGH, Lancashire, England, Oct. 10 (‘UP)—Nineteen of twenty miners descending in a cage at the Plank Lane colliery were killed today when the cage crashed to the bottom of a 700-foot pit. The man who escaped forced the cage door open and had freed himself when rescuers reached him.

RANGOON, Burma, Oct. 10—The British steamship Karagola reached Capt. Wolfgang Von Gronau, round the world flier forced down in the Gulf of Martaban, off the Burmese coast near Ye and about 100 miles south of Moulmein. The steamer reported efforts were being made to tow Von Gronau's seaplane. “S. S. Karagola comes to our rescue, thanks for your help. Sorry we could not finish our program,” the message from the flier said. Von Gronau was flying north along the Burmese coast from Mergue in lower Burma to Akyab in upper Burma at the time he was forced to descend.

Lendon, Oct. 10 (4—Winston Churchill, former chancellor of the exchequer, today left the hospital where he was under treatment for pneumonia. “They carried him out to his automobile on a stretcher, but he smiled broadly and waved a big cigar as he told the doctor he was feeling better.

DUBLIN. (?). Nearly a score of persons were injured in a riot at Kilmallock, County Clare, during a meeting of the oppositionists of former President William Cosgrave. The partisan struggle developed among the audience, which was addressed by Gen. Richard J. Mulcahy, and the police were outnumbered from the start. Members of the "white army" attempted to eject a group of youths apparently sympathizers of President De Valera and a free for all developed during which several revolver shots were fired.

LONDON, Oct. 10—Sir Malcolm Campbell, holder of the world’s land speed record, is building a 1,000 horsepower automobile equipped with a Rolls-Royce airplane engine with which he hopes to reach 300 miles an hour.

Newchwang, Manchuria, Oct. 9 —(/P)— A fresh effort to rescue Mrs. Kenneth Pawley and Charles Corkran, British citizens captured by bandits and held for ransom Sept. 7, was made by Japanese authorities today. A Japanese army captain and a detail of 30 men left for Panshar under orders to open direct negotiations with the bandits and to cooperate with the British authorities. Death Threat Sent In Go-betweens have brought several letters from Mrs. Pawley and her companions asserting the bandits plan to kill them unless heavy ransom is paid.

Athens, Greece, Oct. 28 (AP)— Samuel Insull left the capital today accompanied by 19 members of the Greco-American League for a luncheon at Sunion. The former Chicago utilities magnate, who is under indictment in Chicago for larceny and embezzlement in connection with the crash of his companies, was accompanied by a bodyguard. The precaution was taken by police at the request of Insull who recalled his recent announcement that he had recounted that attempts would be made to kidnap him to facilitate his removal to the U. S. It was stated the luncheon was not given officially by the league but only by some members who have been assisted by Insull in the U. S. "We are only performing our humanitarian duty to an unfortunate man who, according to Greek and American traditions of hospitality, should be befriended during his stay regardless of legal or political consideration," an announcement

Athens, Greece (U.S.)—Samuel Insull, arrested here today for probable deportation to the United States, told Greek police he had lost personally $100,000,000 in the collapse of the Insull utilities interests in connection with which he and his brother Martin have been indicted in Cook County, Illinois. Insull said his losses were exclusive of those sustained by his wife and son. Have Consular Agreement Insull was arrested on request of United States authorities. Police conferred with the United States legation before making the arrest. Insull, it was understood, would be deported either direct by steamer to the United States or to Italy from which country he could be extradited. Although the Greek-United States extradition treaty has not been ratified there is in operation a consular agreement providing for the mutual exchange of fugitives under which his case could be handled. Insull to

1932-11-01.text: Lendon, Nov. 1 (P) — W. A. B. Hannington, communist organizer of the unemployed "hunger march" on London, was arrested today on a charge of inciting mutiny among the London police and placed in the Bow Street police station pending arraignment. Twenty detectives swarmed into the office from which he had been directing activities of thousands of unemployed who engaged in serious rioting in Hyde Park and Trafalgar Square last week. Hannington was arrested as he was talking at his desk with a newspaperman. The office records were seized and another man was arrested on a charge of distributing seditious literature. Hannington threatened Monday that he would lead 50 of his men to the House of Commons tonight and demand revision of the dole system, scorning the tradition that any petition for the House must be presented by a member of parliament.

STOCKHOLM, Nov. 1. (#)— Stockholm newspapers openly discussed rumors today that the engagement of Princess Ingrid to Prince George or the Prince of Wales will be announced in London on November 11. The newspapers added that the announcement might be made at a dinner in the British capital celebrating the 50th anniversary of the birthday of the princess’ father. The time and circumstance of the dinner was accepted as unusually propitious for (Continued on Page Eight)

(United Press News Service) LONDON, Nov. 1.—Scotland Yard raided the dingy, smoky field headquarters of England's hunger marchers today and arrested leaders of London’s unemployed demonstrators, while police were mobilizing to prevent a march on parliament. Serious rioting which began with a mass demonstration in Hyde Park Thursday has been suppressed. - W. A. Lloyd Hennington, one of the organizers of the march on London was charged with inciting mutiny. Another leader was arrested on a charge of distributing ‘seditious literature.

MANCHESTER, Eng., Oct. 31. (P) — Many thousands of spinners and cardroom hands declined to go to work in the spinning section of the Lancashire cotton textile industry this morning, rejecting a provisional agreement for a wage cut of five to eight percent. At Leigh, 2,900 spinners and cardroom hands appeared for duty, but on learning the 16 mills there would open at the reduced rate of pay, returned to their homes. None of the spinners at Rochdale started to work, and the situation was similar in other centers. It has been estimated that if all the spinners walk out 200,000 will be affected.

LONDON. (CP). Communist agents directing a campaign for increased unemployment benefits announced they intend to march up to the House of Commons Tuesday night and demand a hearing of their case without going through the formality of presenting a petition. W. A. L. Hannington, one of the leaders of the “hunger march” of unemployed into London last week, said he would take 100 men with him and present a demand with a million signatures for abolition of the means test from the dole system and restoration of cuts in government aid to the jobless. John McGovern, left wing labor member of parliament, was rebuffed when he offered to present a petition in the traditional manner and to assist in obtaining a hearing for the idle at the bar of the House of Commons. There had been no reply from the government to a letter from unemployed leaders asking that their case be heard in the House. Last wee

| BENGLEWOOD, N. J. Nov. 1 (UP) — Elizabeth Morrow, older sister of Ann Morrow Lindbergh, will marry Aubrey Niel Morgan, a Welsh businessman whom she met during the London naval conference in 1930. Formal announcement of the engagement was made by Mrs. Dwight Whitney Morrow, wife of the late senator, but no date for the wedding has been set. Miss Morrow's engagement is a culmination of a romance that began when the Morrow family accompanied Senator Morrow to London to witness the international disarmament discussion more than two years ago. At that time Morgan, son of Mr. and Mrs. John Llewellyn Morgan of Wales, was frequently seen in her company. In the two years that have intervened since that event, Miss Morrow has been reported engaged to various prominent Americans, but on each occasion denial has been forthcoming.

LONDON, Nov. 1.—The police raided the headquarters of the National Unemployed Workers' movement today and arrested W. A. J. Hannington, organizer of the “hunger” army's march on London, which has precipitated two bloody riots within a week. It was understood Hannington, who planned to defy tradition by leading a deputation on parliament tonight, would be taken to Bow Street station and charged with violating the laws in connection with the Trafalgar Square riots of Sunday. Meanwhile, London's volunteer police, which were called to duty for the first time since the general strike of 1926 for the Trafalgar riots, reported today to many parts of London to relieve regular police and traffic officers. The regulars will rest until tonight awaiting the demonstration of the jobless in Camberwell Green in the south of London.

London.— () — Mounted police hidden in the alleys and corners about Parliament Square swarmed out into Whitehall tonight and began thrusting back a great crowd assembled before the houses of Parliament for a demonstration by the unemployed. It was about 8 o'clock when the hobbies appeared from all directions. With the fear of the man on foot for the man on horse, the crowd fell back. Up to now there had been no indication that there was any organized spirit among the crowd which might lead to repetition of the riots which occurred last week in Hyde Park and Trafalgar Square.

1932-10-17.text: LONDON, Oct. 17 UP—A fierce battle between the ancient British principle of free trade and the newer policy of empire tariff protection is promised when parliament reassembles here tomorrow to act on the new tariff deals between Great Britain and the dominions reached at the Ottawa trade conference last summer. Victory for the new policy is as certain as anything in politics, for the national government musters a plurality of 500 in commons, Free trade may be making its last stand, but its friends are the sort who never surrender. They have split Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald's national cabinet during recent weeks and in the shadowy halls of Westminster they will launch a campaign looking toward new elections and a reversal of the basic fiscal policy the government has embraced. The session, originally planned as a three-day cleanup of routine, probably will last a myota.

London — (7) — Disarmament, not rearmament, is the basis of Great Britain's whole policy regarding the disarmament issue, Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald said today at a luncheon attended by several cabinet ministers and 300 of his followers in the National Labor party. “Germany knows perfectly well,” he said, “that Great Britain does not oppose her claim to be regarded as an equal at the disarmament conferences. Our policy is not rearmament, but disarmament. “I profoundly regret that Germany has refused to come to Geneva for preliminary disarmament discussions because of reasons the substance of which is difficult for me to detect. The British government is continuing to pursue its purpose and hopes to make a further announcement in a few days.”

LONDON, Oct. 15.—INS—With matrimonial rumors persistently linking Princess Ingrid of Sweden and the British royal family, the Prince of Wales was nearly mobbed by feminine admirers when he arrived here today at the conclusion of his Scandinavian tour. The heir apparent to the throne was greeted boisterously by 100 girls, who spied him while on their way to work as he disembarked from his train at the Liverpool Street station. They overwhelmed his escort of detectives, compelling him to dash toward a waiting automobile while they followed in hot pursuit. The girls then swarmed over his car and remained there until police reinforcements cleared them away.

LONDON, Oct. 17.-G)—The Express says under a Newchang, Manchuria, date that Mrs. Kenneth Pawley, who, with Charles Corkran, were in the hands of Chinese bandits, had saved her own life and that of her companion by threatening to haunt the bandits after death. Both of the captives are British subjects and were taken at Newchang several weeks ago. Since then the British Government and the Japanese and Manchukuo authorities have been trying to negotiate their release. The Express said Mrs. Pawley, who speaks Chinese fluently, struck terror into the hearts of her captors by threatening to pursue them after death and change their spirits and those of their ancestors into turtles. This courageous move, the paper said, proved more effective than all the elaborate negotiations that have been taking place, and occurred in an interview between Mrs. Pawley and Pei Patlen, the chief of the brigands.

London, Oct. 17,—A telegram from a close advisor informing him that a plot has been hatched by Chicago authorities to kidnap and shanghai him to the United States has been received by Samuel Insull, indicted ex-utilities magnate, now a refugee in Athens, International News Service learned today. The telegram reads as follows: "Have reliable advice that Chicago authorities have hired four Greek detectives in America, planning to send them to Athens to kidnap and remove you to a country more favorable to their ends." "The four have not left America yet but Chicago believes authorities there may alternatively try to arrange with other residents to do this job. "Chicago says their reports to be confirmed or otherwise will cable."

ATHENS, Greece, Sept. 8 — Premier Eleutherios Venizelos resigned today with his cabinet. President Zaimis will request him to remain at the head of the government. A serious political situation was brewing as a result of growing antagonism between Premier Venizelos and P. E. Tsaldaris, Royalist leader. The controversy came to a head when the premier attacked the former royal family in Greece in an election speech early in the week.

ATHENS, Oct. 17. (AP).—Samuel Insull, under indictment in Chicago following the collapse of his utilities interest, told correspondents today he had been informed that Chicago authorities had hired four Greek detectives to kidnap him and take him back to the United States. “It doesn't seem possible that such a thing could even be contemplated anywhere where there is an orderly government,” he said. “But I have just informed the police of the receipt of a telegram, which although it seems to me absolutely preposterous, I cannot afford to ignore in the present situation.”

Berlin, Oct. 17 (AP)—Three were killed and a score injured in political riots in Germany over the weekend. At Leipzig a national socialist was killed and four wounded. Two were killed and twelve seriously injured at Dortmund in clashes between national socialists and communists. In Berlin a comparatively long spell of political tranquillity was broken by pre-election fights in which three were injured and 25 arrested. The trouble at Dortmund started when 400 national socialists, staging a propaganda march through the working-class district, were met by a stone barrage from the communists.

1932-11-02.text: Albany, N. Y., Nov. 2.—()—Governor Roosevelt Wednesday prepared for the final bid of his presidential campaign with a week-end of speech-making in New York City. He returned to the capital Tuesday night after a whirlwind three-day motor trip through all of the six New England states. He said he was “assured that all of the New England states” would be Democratic this fall. “When the Democratic presidential candidate passed through the last of the Massachusetts cities toward 10 o'clock Tuesday night and entered New York state, the record of the Roosevelt campaign away from home was closed. Thursday Roosevelt will go to New York City for a speech that night. Friday and Saturday nights will come rallies in the Brooklyn Academy of Music and Madison Square Garden in New York. Since he stepped into an airplane here July 2 for his acceptance speech at Chicago, Roosevelt has traveled more than 1

LONDON, Nov. 2.—(@)—Balked last night in their third attempt to enforce their demands by violence, the unemployed "hunger marchers" who straggled into London last week turned homeward today. W. A. L. Hannifigton, the communist agent who organized the march of the idle from Scotland, Wales and the industrial centers of England, was in jail. His associates who precipitated a riot in Parliament Square last night also were in the hands of the police. So this morning 30 ragged men who had trudged with the others through the rain last week climbed aboard a charabanc and started back for Brighton, whence they came. Other contingents prepared to go back home before the end of the day. Meantime, the historic precincts of Parliament Square were in the hands of police after a mass attack by thousands of jobless had precipitated the bloodiest of four recent riots. The disorders began at dusk in the

in a state of semi-siege today with mobs of unemployed threatening outbreaks in all halves of the capital. Police raided the headquarters of the unemployed council and warned them they must soon cease their demonstration or else be forcibly escorted from the city. Days of sporadic rioting reached a climax last night with fighting between police and unemployed at Trafalgar Square and other important centers. Thirty were arrested and held by police.

London, Nov. 2.—Thousands of rioting unemployed men and women and their sympathizers fought a series of savage battles with mounted and foot police for more than three hours last night in many of the chief streets of London. The sharpest fighting occurred when strong groups of mounted men charged mobs in Trafalgar Square, Pall Mall, The Strand, Whitehall and Victoria Embankment. Many persons were arrested and scores were injured. The rioters had been chased away from Trafalgar Square, the vortex of the fighting, by the time the theatres let out, but groups of theatregoers in silk hats and tail coats had to call for police protection from angry detachments of snarling men. Sixth Day of Disorders. The riots were the bitter conclusion of six days of uneasiness in London resulting from the columns of hunger marchers who converged on the capital from all parts of the island to protest against

LONDON, Oct. 30.— (AP) — Mounted and foot police saved the king’s palace and official residences on Downing Street from attack by thousands of unemployed and “hunger marchers” after a hard battle today at Trafalgar Square. Booed to the echo by an angry crowd of the unemployed and sympathizers, British “bobbies” were forced to retreat at least once as the mob attempted to swarm streets leading to Buckingham Palace and Westminster. The crowd was finally forced back into Trafalgar Square where the loudest voices of British Communism and unemployed leaders were condemning the government. Today’s casualty list hardly exceeded ten or 12 persons injured, although ambulances were kept busy for a while, as compared with the 60 or 70 injured when “hunger marchers” from all parts of the country gathered Thursday in Hyde Park. More serious fighting is anticipated Tuesday before the House of Commons

ALBANY, N. Y., Nov. 2 (UP).— Gov. Franklin D. Roosevelt was at “home” in Albany again today, to spend a comparatively restful 24 hours before he enters the home stretch of his race for the presidency. On his day's program, in contrast to the whirlwind finish of his Southern campaign in New England, which ended last night after he had spurted homeward at 66 miles an hour over rain-soaked roads, were only a few conferences with his advisers, and one public address, scheduled for this evening. Tomorrow, the governor will make three speeches, two in Newark and Jersey City, and the third in the Metropolitan Opera House in New York Saturday.

ALBANY, N. Y., Nov. 1—(P)—Franklin D. Roosevelt came back to the executive mansion tonight from a three-day campaign swing by automobile that took him into every New England state. The trip marked the first time that any candidate has made so long a campaign journey by automobile. It took the democratic presidential candidate more than 700 miles through a stretch of Vermont and across Massachusetts, New Hampshire, into Maine, back across Massachusetts and through Rhode Island and Connecticut. The last two days of the journey swept him to hearty welcomes in Portland and Boston and through a succession of applauding throngs in various Rhode Island, Massachusetts and Connecticut towns. For many miles in Rhode Island and Massachusetts today the candidate’s automobile crept through lines of drenched humanity that stood in a pelting rain to catch a glimpse of Mr. Roosevelt and hear him say a f

| LONDON Nov 2) — What was believed to be an attempt to do violence to Prime Minister MacDonald or to rob his home was revealed in a case in Hampstead police court today. Ivan Seruva, described as a British subject, was arraigned on a charge of loitering. He was arrested, the police said, in the garden of Mr. MacDonald's house at 3 a.m. Mr. MacDonald rarely uses his lodge at Frognal near Hampstead, while Parliament is in session, preferring to remain in his official residence at No 10 Downing Street. He was believed to have been at Frognal last night, however, during the disturbance in Whitehall! Seruva is a well-dressed thickset youth, who speaks English with a foreign accent. He was carrying bricks under his arms when the police found him. The prisoner said he had just entered the garden for a look around. He did not resist arrest.

1932-10-03.text: LIVERPOOL, Eng. Oct. 3—Samuel Insull, Jr. arrived today and said his trip is merely a holiday that occurred simultaneously with investigation of the Insull companies only by coincidence. Insull took the boat train for London. He planned to proceed to Paris to join his father and mother this afternoon. Although it is known here that Samuel Insull, Sr. has purchased an estate of approximately 100 acres at Theale, near Reading, the younger Insull said he was ignorant of his father's plans. He thought the family would remain in France or England. Insull said he planned to return to the United States in November. He said he had promised not to discuss the affairs of the Insull companies during his European visit.

- LONDON, Oct. 3 (P).—An official announcement on behalf of the Irish Free State Government said today that James McNeill has relinquished the office of Governor-General of the Free State. John W. Dulanty, Free State high commissioner to London, issued a statement saying: “In accordance with advance tendered his majesty by the president of the executive council of the Irish Free State, the King has approved of Mr. James McNeill relinquishing the office of Governor-General of the Free State. It was understood that the King took this step on advice from President De Valera of the Free State. Mr. McNeill had lunch with the King and Queen at Buckingham Palace. He reached London this morning, went to the palace at noon and remained there until shortly before 3 o'clock. The procedure which was understood to have been adopted is in accordance with a resolution passed at the Imperial Conference

London, Oct. 3—(P)—It was understood on good authority today that James McNeill, governor general of the Irish Free State, had relinquished that office and that King George had approved his decision. It was understood that the king took this step on advice from President de Valera of the Free State. Mr. McNeill had luncheon with the king and queen at Buckingham palace.

MILWAUKEE, Wis., Oct. 3.—(4)—Smoke of the density of a London fog hung over highways and cities of southeastern Wisconsin last night causing numerous traffic jams and forcing residents of the area to sleep in tightly closed bedrooms. A high southwest wind which fanned the smoldering Horicon marsh fires to new heights sent heavy clouds of smoke and swirling cinders into Fond du Lac shortly before midnight and left a mantle of smoke over the city and nearby highways. Waukesha county was the scene of the worst traffic tie-up, where a marsh known as the “Huckleberry marsh” was burning. Some 2,500 cars carried crowds into the area. A marsh fire which threatened cottages in the vicinity of Lake Geneva was checked by the Genoa fire department. A peat fire near Lake Como which had been smoldering for a month got out of bounds and spread over an area of 100 acres. Unless it rains, these fires are

WASHINGTON, Oct. 3—(UP)—Analysis of foreign trade of the United States for the first eight months of this year today revealed Great Britain as the largest foreign customer, but showed a decrease in purchase of American exports of $104,000,000. Canada ranked second with purchases of $170,432,422, a decrease of approximately $125,000,000 from the eight month period last year.

Geneva, Oct. 3.—(A. P.)—Irak became a member of the League of Nations today, and at the same time attained sovereign independent statehood by release from its status as a mandate to Great Britain. As the first mandated territory to be graduated into statehood since the league was formed, the precedent was historic, and was augmented by Irak’s ancient history, which according to tradition, began with the Garden of Eden. The chief importance of Irak is its vast oil fields, control of which has been the cause of fierce rivalry by the world’s powerful petroleum interests. It is the first Arab state to enter the league.
A, Oct. 3—The organizing committee of the League of Nations council decided today to call the proposed world economic conference in London. December is the probable date.

GENEVA, Oct. 3—(#) — The League of Nations was definitely at grips today with the Manchurian problem — perhaps the greatest test it has faced in its history — following publication of the report of the Lytton investigating commission which inferentially condemned Japan's military occupation and turned thumbs down on the Japanese-advised regime of Henry Pu-Yi. The commission, in an exhaustive analysis of the situation which began with the opening of the Japanese army’s drive in September of last year, found that the military campaign was unjustified and that the new state of Manchukuo is not supported by the Manchurian people. It proposed a special autonomous regime for the territory, with China retaining full sovereignty over the three provinces, and suggested a special Sino-Japanese conference to work out the basis of a permanent settlement, with the provision that the League Council ta

1932-10-26.text: PORT OF SPAIN, Oct. 26— if you think that Amazon River ain't big? We was from just daylight to after lunch ferrying over it in an airplane. There is an island in it as big as New York state. ‘Don’t you all remember looking on a map and seeing those little countries called French Guiana and British Guiana? Well, we found and stopped at both of ’em today. We also flew (but not too close) to Devil Island, the French prison off French Guiana.

Converging from all parts of England tonight threatened to seize quarters for the marchers after they enter London tomorrow unless city and government authorities guarantee them shelter. LONDON (UP).—Thousands of “hunger marchers” besieged London today, ready for an impressive demonstration demanding that the government feed and care for them and their unemployed families. Police were mobilized to prevent disorders. It was announced no demonstrations could be held within a mile of the House of Commons while Parliament is in session. The wet, weary marchers from the provinces, totaling more than 3,000, converged on London from points hundreds of miles away. Footsore, half-fed and poorly clothed, they pressed on in their determination to force the government into extending a greater bounty. The main point of their protest was against the “means test,” under which unemployed are required to

London, Oct. 26.—(AP)—Reconsideration of some phases of the national government's dole system came as a promise from Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald today as 2,000 members of a nationally-recruited “hunger army” moved within a stone’s throw of London. It is the “means test” in the dole, or unemployment benefits administration, which has brought much of the rising tide of discontent that has culminated recently in protest riots and now the march on London. The prime minister spoke during debate yesterday on a motion of censure against the government's dole policy introduced in the House of Commons by the labor opposition. The motion was defeated, 462 to 565. Mr. MacDonald defended the government's policy and declared the means test, which is given to determine the means of a dole applicant to subsist normally, cannot be abolished. But some questions, the premier said, would be reconsidere

FOOCHOW, China, Oct. 26.—(?)—American and British missionaries in the northwestern region of Fukien province are hastily withdrawing toward this city as a result of the advance of communist outlaws from Kiangsi province, whence they were driven by National government troops. It was understood that the two American groups principally involved are missionaries of the Congregational church with headquarters in New York. These two maintain numerous missionary stations in northwestern Fukien. Two British missions have been abandoned.

TOKYO, Oct. 25—-(AP)—A new disarmament plan, distinctly Japanese and differing from the American and British suggestions for naval reduction is to be advanced by the Japanese representative when the disarmament conference resumes next February at Geneva, the Associated Press learned today. Its details are a closely guarded secret, and not even an idea of its general character was offered. A high official said, however, that the plan will embrace all naval categories and will be sufficiently complete to stand alongside the proposals by President Hoover and Stanley Baldwin of Great Britain. The naval ministry already has drafted the plan and the cabinet approved it today. Immediately it was cabled to the Japanese delegation at Geneva. It has not been decided whether the plan will be made public before the disarmament conference resumes, but the delegation at Geneva or the ambassadors in va

London, Oct. 26. (INS).—Britain’s weary but militant hunger marchers, closing in on London from all sides, today were given an official rebuttal by the Trades Union Council, national governing body of the country’s Trade Unions. The council put its definite stamp of disapproval on the hunger marchers by an official statement aimed at dissuading London's unemployed from joining the ranks of those marching from the rest of England and Scotland. “The march is a communist enterprise for the exploitation of the unemployed,” the council warned. Thus the council, representing more than 5,000,000 workers throughout Great Britain, joined the national government and London authorities in opposing the dramatic march of the 2,000 unemployed men and women. As a result, a cold welcome awaited these jobless, and, although attempts will be made to house and feed them, they will be discouraged in their e

LONDON, Oct. 26 (4NS)—Marshalling all its forces in anticipation of riots and disorders, Scotland Yard today suspended leaves to all members of London's police force during the period that Britain’s unemployed hunger marchers remain in the capital. The demonstrators, advancing along fourteen different routes, are drawing near the city and expected to reach here by nightfall.

sacidine Mreag. “LONDON, -' Oct; 25. — Accommodations for 2,000 “hunger marchers" nearing London tonight were promised by London county council authorities in event organizers of the march failed to make adequate preparations. Council officials made it plain they expected leaders of the demonstration to obtain accommodations for the dozen or so parties of the jobless army who were to camp tonight at such nearby places as Croydon and St. Albans. When the marchers converge tomorrow at Hyde Park, London's unemployed plan a great demonstration of welcome. A nation-wide demonstration in their behalf has been organized by the National Unemployed Workers’ movement, which a government spokesman in parliament has branded as a Communist organization. Many of the marchers were reported wearing red rosettes and the charge was made in several London newspapers that the march was fostered by funds fro

1932-10-18.text: LONDON, Oct. 18. WM—J. H. Thomas, secretary for dominions, announced in the house of commons today that Great Britain has abrogated its commercial treaty with Soviet Russia. Under article 21 of the tariff agreement reached at the recent Ottawa imperial conference, he said, renunciation of the temporary commercial agreement with Russia was made necessary.

London, Oct. 17. — The Daily Herald tonight quoted "close personal friends" of the Mahatma Gandhi as asserting the frail nationalist leader of India had suffered a paralytic stroke in Yeroda jail at Poona, Bombay. These friends, who were in London, said the Mahatma was stricken soon after he had ended his recent "fast unto death" in the interests of Indian unity, and this was why the government had suddenly stopped visitors at Yeroda jail.

POONA, India, Oct. 18. (4)—Reports published in London saying that Mahatma Gandhi suffered a paralytic stroke here were denied officially today. Gandhi was thoroughly fit last night, the statement said.

OTTAWA, Ont., Oct. 18 --- The Canadian Liberal Party opened a drive today against the tariff preference agreements negotiated by Great Britain and Canada at the recent imperial trade conference and hinted that a general election might be demanded to carry the issue to the people. The agreements were attacked in the House of Commons last night in a two and a half hour speech by former Premier MacKenzie King, Liberal leader, who assailed them as "protection gone mad" and as more likely to injure imperial trade than to help it. At the close of his speech, he proposed an amendment which would have the effect of rejecting the treaty. The Speaker of the House reserved judgment on its admissibility.

MANSFIELD, Oct. 15, (4?) + Four Mansfield Reformatory convicts were indicted today for first degree murder in connection with the attempt of 12 convicts to escape from the reformatory correction cell block in which Guard Frank B. Hanger, of Mount Vernon, was beaten fatally. - The four, Merrill E. Chandler, 22, negro, of Columbus; Charles Willis, 29, of Hamilton county; James Allen, 20, of Hamilton county and Chester Prohoski, Cuyahoga county, were alleged to have been the ring leaders of the escape plot. * Chandler is alleged to have confessed that he wielded the iron bar inflicting fatal injuries on Hanger.

London, England, Oct. 17.-Speaking on the eve of the reconvening of Parliament, Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald today proclaimed Britain’s arms policy to be “not rearmament but disarmament.” The prime minister spoke at a luncheon attended by most of his cabinet and by 300 of his followers in the national labor party. His speech took on special significance because tomorrow parliament will assemble for speedy action on the tariff deals between Britain and the dominions made at last summer’s Ottawa conference. Debate on these measures will be the occasion for another conflict between advocates of the ancient British policy of free trade and supporters of the new policy of empire protection. The overwhelming government majority in the house of commons makes approval certain for the new system. In his speech today the prime minister gave Germany reassurances regarding the nature of the propo

LONDON, Oct. 18. (UP)—Parliament reassembled today to ratify the Ottawa trade agreement presenting a united empire trade front against the world, and was informed almost immediately the existing trade agreement with Soviet Russia would be cancelled. J. H. Thomas, dominions secretary, informed the House of Commons that Britain yesterday had given the Soviet charge d'affaires in London the requisite six months notice of denunciation of the agreement. The step was taken, he said, “to maintain the effectiveness of the Ottawa conference preferences against action of any foreign country which might stultify the interests of preference.”

LONDON, Oct 18 —(UM)— Mounted and foot police clashed today with unemployed demonstrators attempting to march on the County Council Hall, at the opposite end of Westminster Bridge from the House of Commons. With heavy guards around Parliament, the first clash was at St. George's Circus, where one demonstrator was knocked unconscious while the leaders shouted: "All to County Hall,"

1932-10-30.text: LONDON, Oct. 31.—London’s bobbies surveyed their third victory within a month over rioting jobless today after repulsing an attack by thousands on Buckingham Palace and Westminster. But the disorders, which began yesterday in Trafalgar Square, brought only a dozen minor casualties, as compared to the 70 hurt in Hyde Park last week and the 30 injured in the Lambeth section Oct. 21. The weary police expected only a 24-hour breathing spell, however, for Tuesday the jobless plan a march on forbidden Parliament Square to present a petition of protest against the means test in the dole system. The bobbies are prepared for more serious trouble with a relief system employed in the general strike of 1926. The plan employs London’s 12,000 special constables for routine police work as needed, freeing hundreds of police for use in riot squads. More than 2,000 of these special patrolmen, who are volu

LONDON, Oct. 20—Mindful of the rioting that has wrecked London’s calm twice within recent weeks, police today arranged elaborate precautions against trouble when the nation’s “hunger marchers army” converges on Trafalgar Square tomorrow. The marchers will stage their second demonstration tomorrow morning, reiterating their demand for abolition of what they declare to be abuses of the dole system.

By The Associated Press. London, Eng., Oct. 29.--Where Nelson's column rises in Trafalgar Square thousands of Great Britain’s unemployed will gather tomorrow for a mass meeting, and the police are prepared for trouble. There may be some street fighting, as there was last Thursday at Hyde Park. Since Thursday’s troubles the jobless here have been entirely orderly. Two thousand men who came into the city in the “hunger march” from many parts of the island have been sleeping in various institutions, spending part of their time soliciting funds in the streets. Today a delegation of two men and a woman appeared at the House of Commons to ask that they be permitted to plead the case of the idle in the House on Tuesday. But Parliament was not in session and they were taken over to Prime Minister MacDonald's office where they left a letter asking his assistance and urging the release of the men

London, Oct. 29 (UP)—The army of “hunger marchers” which invaded London this week to protest against restriction of unemployment relief urged the government today to act in their behalf. A delegation will seek to plead hunger marchers’ case in the House of Commons next week. It also was announced that in addition to small borough demonstrations today, a monster protest meeting will be held at Trafalgar Square tomorrow when more than 100,000 are expected to participate. The meeting will be similar to that in Hyde Park which led to rioting in which 77 were injured.

CHICAGO, Oct. 29.--The price of wheat futures went to the lowest price in world records today on the Chicago board of trade, falling fractionally below the minimum price set when Queen Elizabeth was on England's throne, more than 300 years ago. At the low point, December wheat at 43 7-8c was the lowest price known since records have been kept. The world wheat war was held accountable. With the United States and Canada in a race to dispose of their surplus wheat abroad, prices fell.

By United Press KNOXVILLE, Tenn., Oct. 23. — Earl Devon, professor of English at the University of Tennessee, was found shot to death in his residential hotel bedroom today. Police said he killed himself.

LONDON, Oct. 29. (UR)—A German air mail liner was forced down in the English Channel late tonight in high seas and a 60-mile gale. A lifeboat put out from Dover on the supposition that the liner came down between Dover and Deal, The air ministry received reports that the liner had sent out S.O.S. calls. The wireless signals from the plane did not give her position, it was said at the air ministry, where no further details were available. The air ministry assumed that the plane in distress was the German liner that left Croydon Aerodrome at 8:15 p.m. with mails and freight for Cologne, manned by a pilot and mechanic. There were believed to be no passengers aboard.

PROTEST MEETINGS DUBLIN, Oct. 29.—(UP)— The forthcoming visit of the Prince of Wales to Belfast to open the new Northern Ire- land Parliament building will be greeted with protest meet- ings throughout Ireland, the Republican Sinn Fein organi- zation announced today. LAW MAKER ARRESTED ST. JOHNS, N. F. Oct. 29. —(UP)—Roland G. Starkes, a member of Parliament, was charged today on 17 counts with falsifying and forging re- lief fund accounts, with intent to defraud the government. DISCUSS REUNION BUCHAREST, Roumania, Oct. 29.—(UP)—The troubles of the Roumanian royal fam- ily will be discussed by a special crown council composed of representatives of all political parties, it was an- nounced today. The special council will determine the status of Princess Helene, di- vorced wife of King Carol, es- pecially with regard to her contacts with their son, Crown Paul.

1932-10-31.text: London, England.
