Hotels, restaurants and clubs were crowded with gay parties. The newspapers flashed the latest returns to the celebrating crowds. The general expectation of a heavy dry vote in the farming districts and among laborers failed to materialize. In both rural and urban districts

(By the Associated Press) The menace of an apparently widespread bomb plot directed against Italian officials and public figures prompted federal and other officials today to begin an extensive hunt for the perpetrators following the discovery of five or more infernal machines. The bombs were delivered by mail or express yesterday in Chicago, Cleveland, Detroit, and Youngstown, O., but none of them caused any loss of life or property damage because they were all intercepted in time. Their discovery followed closely upon the heels of the explosion of two bombs in the Easton, Pa., post office, which killed two men last Wednesday. A third victim, Charles Weaver, died of injuries last night. Powerful Explosives Three packages, one of which is known to have contained powerful explosives, were received in Chicago. One of them, which reached the office of Oscar Durante, editor of L'Italia, a pr

Mukden, Manchuria, Jan. 1—()—Japanese cavalry clattered across the ice on the Taling river today and stopped at the outskirts of Chinchow, China’s last Manchurian stronghold. This was an advance patrol from the main body of the brigade encamped on the north side of the river. There was no resistance. The Chinese defenders continued leaving the walled city in great numbers and presumably the Japanese intended to take it over tomorrow. Most of the Japanese brigade was to cross the Taling tonight, go as to be in position to move on with the dawn. It was obvious that the Chinese had no intention of resisting this side of the Great Wall and it was altogether possible that the Japanese would keep on the heels of the retreating army clear down to Shanhaikwan, at the very edge of the Great Wall. Major General Miyake, chief of staff for General Honjo, told the Associated Press tonight: “Our campa

1932-01-04.text: MEET IN POONA, India, Jan. 4. (P— Mahatma Gandhi was walled up today in the British jail at Yerawda, a few miles from here, for the third time in his career as leader of the Indian nationalists. The little Indian leader was brought here this morning from Bombay, where he was arrested dramatically in the early morning hours for what the warrant said were "good and sufficient reasons." At the same time that Gandhi was arrested, Vallabhai Patel, president of the Indian National Congress, also was taken into custody and a new series of repressive decrees against various acts associated with the civil disobedience type of "warfare" were promulgated at New Delhi by Viceroy Lord Willingdon. It was Gandhi's day of silence and this kept him from speaking, but he gave his old jailer a broad smile of recognition, beaming upon him like an old friend. Once inside the jail, he turned without hesitatio

London, Jan. 4. (AP)—In one of the most daring holdups which has occurred in London in many years, several men in an automobile today robbed the manager of a jewelry store in the heart of Mayfair, of $100,000 worth of gems. They drew up to the curb in Regent Street as the manager was walking to his shop from a bank not more than fifty yards away, carrying his firm’s most valuable jewels which had been stored in the vaults over the weekend. They yanked his hat down over his face, threw him to the sidewalk, seized the gems, dashed back into the car and sped away. The holdup took only about twenty seconds and none of the passersby could provide a good description of the car or the robbers.

BOMBAY, Jan. 4—Mahatma Gandhi was arrested early today for the second time within a year and a half and Nationalist India once more girded itself for “non-violent” war on Great Britain. President Vallabhbhai Patel of the All-India Nationalist Congress also was taken into custody. Both were arrested under a Bombay regulation of 1827 and the warrant stated that they were being removed to Yerawda jail at Poona for “good and sufficient reasons.” Viceroy Lord Whittingdon’s drastic move was made after eleventh hour attempts of moderate Nationalist leaders to bring about a compromise (Continued on Page 3)

BOMBAY (UP). — Mahatma Gandhi and his chief lieutenant, Vallabhbhai Patel, were in jail today as the government planned further strict measures to crush an imminent “non-violence” war on Great Britain. But before Gandhi went to jail he issued instructions to guide the faithful in their non-violent war for independence. First observe prayer and fasting, follow with civil disobedience, and fulfill the resolutions of the working committee, he urged, “even if hardships include injury or loss of life or property.” While it appeared that imprisonment at Poona of the leader and idol of India’s millions would make resumption of civil disobedience inevitable, the government prepared to issue four new all-India ordinances which may be applied by provincial regimes to curb the independence movement.

{by the Associated Press; Great Britain struck back at the Indian civil disobedience campaign today, clapped Mahatma Gandhi back into jail, imprisoned Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru, his second in command, and prepared to deal vigorously with any further manifestations. The country remained outwardly calm and it probably will be some days before the nationalists show their hand. The leaders were lying low, awaiting developments. From London came word that the British government views the nationalist campaign as a challenge to the fundamentals of law and order and intends to deal with it as such. The developments at Bombay had repercussions elsewhere. There was a split in the All India Muslim Conference at New Delhi where the president and secretary resigned on the grounds that they wanted the conference to give full discretion to Muslims who wanted to join the Congress party movement. London, Jan. 4.—The government of Great Britain, operating through the government of India, will use all its statutory power to combat Mahatma Gandhi's civil disobedience campaign, it was learned today on the highest authority.

BOMBAY, Monday, Jan. 4.—U.P)—British authorities dramatically raided the headquarters of Mahatma M. K. Gandhi in the darkness of early morning today, and placed the little revolutionary leader under arrest. Their action, coming as a surprise

BOMBAY, India, Jan. 4.—(4)— That the British government is determined to deal with the Indian situation with an iron hand was shown today by the sentencing at Allahabad of Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru to two years at hard labor on a charge of violating one of the new restrictive ordinances. Pandit Nehru ranks only second to Mahatma Gandhi himself in political importance among the nationalists, and he is idolized by the Indian youth. Declare Congress Illegal. The working committee of the Indian nationalist congress was declared illegal today by British officials, but despite this nationalist congress leaders today began launching a movement to boycott the round table conference committee from London, which are slated to carry on the task of working out India’s new federal constitution. A similar “boycott” was applied to the previous Simon commission, with serious results. The provincial congre

1932-10-05.text: ALBANY, N. Y., ‘P—Alfred E. Smith, grinning, fighting, and happy, shook hands with Franklin D. Roosevelt last night, urged his election as president and dramatically ended a personal feud that also may reunite party factions in New England and elsewhere before November 8. It was a moment of high drama for delegates to the State Democratic convention, and for the two New York Democratic leaders, when they met for the first time since Smith returned from the Chicago National convention, defeated for the presidential nomination by his former campaign manager. The two men had been battling for two days in behalf of a mutual friend, Colonel Herman H. Lehman, the lieutenant governor they wished to make governor. They were fighting a common enemy to their cause, John F. Curry, boss of Tammany Hall. Curry wanted to give the place to John Boyd Thacher, but failed as Lehman was nominated. The gove

PARIS... The government is understood to be sponsoring a four-year conference which would take up Germany's demand for equality in armaments. Sir John Simon, the British foreign minister, conferred today with Premier Edouard Herriot, and it was reported that the subject of their discussion was the proposed conference. Provision would be made, it was understood, for the United States to be invited to send an observer. The British government suggested that the meeting be held in London. At the conclusion of his talk with the British foreign secretary, which lasted an hour and a half, M. Herriot said that their conversation had been “cordial and intimate.”

LONDON, O., Oct. 5.—Ten year old Crown Prince Michael of Romania started home today without knowing if he ever would see his mother again, and without knowing why his father, King Carol, ordered his immediate return to Bucharest. The ten-year-old boy travelled by motor to Dover with his mother, Princess Helene, and his aunt, Princess Irene of Greece. Helene feared that Carol would not permit her to see her son again, It was understood that Carol would not allow the boy to return to England, because Michael first learned of his father’s love affair through reading an English language newspaper in Paris. At Dover, Michael will board the cross channel steamer to France. It was not considered likely that Helene would accompany the boy beyond Dover. The mother was expected to bid her boy a tearful farewell on the quay at the historic port, where bleak chalk cliffs overlook the gray, troubled

Bucharest, Rumania, Oct. 9 (AP)—King Carol bitterly denounced today the accusation credited to his former wife, Princess Helen, by a London newspaper, that he had cut short the visit of Crown Prince Michael to London because of the publicity given it. "How untrue, unjust and unfair!" the king exclaimed to those near him after he had been given the gist of his former wife’s remarks in a long telephone conversation yesterday. "To think that this should be thrown in my face," he said, "when during the two years of my exile in Paris I was not permitted to see Michael once, although I repeatedly sought permission to do so. Helen, he said, has the privilege of coming to Rumania any time she wishes to see Michael and in this case, when she asked that he be allowed to visit her in London instead, the wish was readily granted. New London, Conn. —(?)— Coast guard destroyers were rushing today to the assistance of a seaplane reported down at sea and in distress 17 miles southeast of Shinnecock, L. I. Lighthouse. The identity of the plane was not known at destroyer forces headquarters.

London, Oct. 6—(A.P.)—Crown Prince Michael of Rumania, who has been visiting his brother, Princess Helen, estranged wife of King Carol, here for two weeks, left today by motor for Dover to return home. Princess Helen was quoted by the Daily Mail yesterday as saying the king cut short the prince's visit because he resented the publicity given the event. She seemed lonely as they left in a big automobile. Michael, bareheaded, smiling, and apparently excited, sat upright with the chauffeur as the car rolled away toward the Kentish coast. General Grigorescu, Michael’s aide, took a train for Dover to accompany the prince on the trip back to Bucharest. Both Michael and his mother were in tears as the youngster boarded the cross-channel steamer at Dover.

LEICESTER, Eng. Oct. 5 P—Sweeping aside the objections of its leader, Arthur Henderson, the Labor Party Conference today carried a resolution declaring the establishment of a socialistic state to be the main objective of the party. The program in achieving this end probably would include nationalization of the Bank of England and Joint Stock Banks, but would not affect the constitutional position of the Crown should the Labor party come into power. Mr. Henderson warned the conference against adopting the resolution, but it was warmly supported by Sir Charles Trevelyan, formerly a Liberal and once Minister of Education in a Labor government. Mr. Henderson was reelected secretary and treasurer of the party by acclamation.

| BERLIN, Oct. 4. (2) — The British charge d’affaires verbally submitted to the foreign office today an official invitation to a conference of the powers to be held in London to pave the way for Germany’s return to the world disarmament conference at Geneva. In replying to the invitation, Germany emphasized that unless certain guarantees were given that her demand for arms equality would be fulfilled, the government of the Reich would not participate.

1932-04-01.text: Oklahoma City, April 1. (AP) The big number three Holmes gas well of the British American Oil company, only three blocks from the Wheeler grade school, in the northwest part of the Oklahoma City oil field, caught fire this afternoon. Friction was believed to have ignited escaping gas while the well was flowing open. Immediately the flow was shut off, but the fire spread to tanks and was threatening other tanks in the vicinity whipped by a stiff wind. The section is covered with small residences, most of which have wells in back yards. The fire was being fought with chemicals by oil field and city firemen.
LONDON; March 31. (P)—A surplus of 364,000 — ($1,830,000 at par) showed on the books of the United Kingdom tonight at the close of the fiscal year 1931-32...

NAPLES, April 1 (#)—Ten thousand inhabitants of the city of Villa Santa Stefano began abandoning the town this afternoon when it started to sink into the ancient Roman caves over which it is built. Santa Stefano is an agricultural community approximately halfway between Naples and Rome. Today 10 buildings in the center of the town slowly sank out of sight into the earth and many others gave signs of caving in. Their disappearance was slow enough to give the inhabitants time to escape and so far as was known there were no casualties. The wholesale exodus began immediately and all the inhabitants fled with as much of their possessions as they could gather together in a hurry and carry away on their backs and in donkey carts. Tonight many of them had pitched camp at a safe distance from the town but others pressed on to the neighboring towns and villages and farmhouses. It was thought the c

Bombay. April 1 (UP)—Dock workers on strike and Pathan strike breakers clashed in serious rioting near the Bombay docks today and later fired many dwellings in the Pathan section. First police reports listed one man killed, 12 seriously injured and 20 slightly hurt. Police fired on the rioters. Water from fire hose was played on the battling mob.

(By ASSOCIATE Press) Moscow, Apr. 1—A sweeping reorganization of Soviet Russia’s livestock and dairy industries, including prosecution and dismissal of scores of directors of state breeding farms, has been decreed by the council of peoples’ commissars, the central committee of the communist party and the commissariat for agriculture. The order, bearing the signatures of Premier Molotov, Joseph Stalin and M. Ykavlev, coincides with the presence here of Robert P. Lamont, Jr. of the United States, who is considering an offer to undertake rehabilitation and development of Soviet cattle breeding operations. The decree charges gross inefficiency and carelessness from top to bottom, from the cattle, swine and sheep breeding trust and butter and chicken trusts down to the state farms devoted to these purposes. It cites unsatisfactory care of livestock resulting in the death of large numbers, was

| By Associated Press: SHANGHAI—Skirmishing between Chinese and Japanese troops in the vicinity of Taitsang, 30 miles northwest of here, is continuing with increasing seriousness, Chinese reports said tonight. The Japanese, on the other hand, said there had been no engagement between the opposing armies, but that there had been fighting between the main Chinese body and a Chinese detachment which mutinied. Meantime, conferences continued among the delegates trying to effect a formal armistice, but the deadlock over the withdrawal of Japanese troops and the policing of the evacuated area remained.

(Copyright, 193%, by the Associated Press; MOSCOW, Mar. 31 (4?)—Members of the communist party, including the highest government officials, as well as factory workers who heretofore have been limited to the most meager salaries, may soon cash in on substantial raises in pay. The political bureau, it was learned today, is considering trebling the maximum monthly income allowed party members from 300 to 900 rubles (about $150 to $450). The raises are planned in accordance with the policy outlined by Joseph Stalin months ago when he decided on the abolition of the system of “equal wages for all.” Factory workers heretofore have been limited to the smallest salaries in order to set an example for the rest of the proletariat. Three factors were said to be inspiring the action. The first is the enormous loss of time and energy by party members holding important posts due to the necessity for s

Paris — (#) — The French parliament after a session which lasted all night and through the entire morning approved a balanced budget today for the period from April 1 to Dec. 31. The budget calls for receipts of 2,100,883,000 francs and expenditures of 4,197,501,000. The chamber adopted the final draft of the offer 485 to 55.

1932-01-22.text: London, Jan. 22. (AP)—Great Britain's cabinet today split on the tariff issue, but contrary to precedent the government will not resign. The break was precipitated by a proposed flat rate tariff of 10 to 15 per cent on manufactured and partially manufactured imports. Liberals in the cabinet were believed to have held out for free trade, and conservatives were said to be for a protective tariff. The cabinet action means that the tariff will be thrown into the House of Commons for a free vote, and indications are that its enactment will be only a matter of time.

BERLIN, Jan. 21.—Announcement (of postponement of the Lausanne conference, made in London yesterday, caused no surprise in official circles here but Chancellor Bruening informed the British ambassador that Germany could accept no proposal for a one year extension of a moratorium as a substitute. Germany has taken the stand that a prolongation of the moratorium would mean an indefinite delay of efforts to reach a final settlement and would mean the acceptance of
By The Associated Press. Inkpen, Berkshire, England Jan. 21.—Lytton Strachey, 52 one of the most prominent biographers of his time, died to- day after an illness of many weeks,

Pings EE LONDON, To the Tribune-Times — Flew from Paris today. Americans always make this trip, but won't fly at home. Yet we have 20 lines as good. I sure miss Charley Dawes. The trouble is there is not enough of Dawes to go round everywhere we need him. I bet you they call the Lausanne reparations conference off as we were not there. You can’t have a picnic lunch unless the party carrying the basket comes. Yours, I WILL.

BOSTON, Jan. 16.—(AP)—Four important liquor seizures today marked concerted efforts by rum runners to land contraband on the New England coast under cover of fog. Liquor which fell into federal hands was valued at more than $150,000 at “trade” prices. Three vessels, including one suspected foreign supply ship, and two speed boats, were captured. On the beach at Cohasset, a pistol battle between rum runners and hijackers was broken up. The combatants fled as police approached, leaving 400 cases of liquor on the strand. The alleged supply ship, The Cadet, was captured by the patrol boat Thetis, off Nantucket, and brought to the New London, Conn., coast guard base. Only a thousand sacks of liquor remained aboard her, (Continued on Page 2, Col. 1.)

By The Associated Press. Europe has reached another deadlock over reparations and war debts with the second postponement of the conference at Lausanne originally scheduled for Jan. 15, then deferred to Jan. 26. Great Britain, which originally proposed the meeting and then changed the date because of political difficulties in France, announced the second postponement. France maintains that she will not forgo German reparations unless the United States makes a corresponding reduction in the amount due her from France. It is understood the American government has informed France that it cannot agree to such a proposal. France also suggested extension of the “Hoover moratorium” for another year, but the American position is that it can have no part in extension, until Europe agrees on reparations. Germany, speaking through Chancellor Bruening, asserted that she cannot meet reparations paymen

CAIRO, Egypt, Jan. 22—(AP)—Lord Reading, noted British statesman and foreign secretary in the first national government of Prime Minister MacDonald, is seriously ill at Luxor, according to word received here today. An army airplane left here with a doctor and nurse to go to his bedside. He is 71 years old. Lord Reading married his secretary last year. They left Haifa by train for Egypt on Jan. 6.

1932-10-04.text: London, Oct. 4. (AP).—Dispatches from Dublin to London newspapers today reported rumors which, however, could not be confirmed, that President De Valera does not intend to nominate a successor to former Lieut. Gov. McNeill, who resigned yesterday and that the free state planned to cut away entirely from the British commonwealth. A dispatch to the Daily Mail said the question of continued membership of the free state in the commonwealth probably would be raised tomorrow if negotiations were resumed by De Valera and J. H. Thomas, British secretary for the dominions, on the question of the abolition of the oath of allegiance and the Irish annuity payments.

PARIS, Oct. 4.—King Carol of Roumania has recalled his son, Crown Prince Michael, from London because the boy learned for the first time of his father’s love affairs from an English language newspaper published in Paris, the United Press learned today. Carol was understood to be determined never to allow Michael to set foot in England again, or even to see his mother, Princess Helen, with whom he had been visiting in London. It was during Michael's brief stay in Paris en route to London that the boy first encountered a printed version of his father’s private affairs, according to the story told here today. Michael, who reads and speaks English fluently, picked a copy of an English language paper before his father’s aide de camp, who accompanied him from Pucharest, realized it. Madame Magda Lupescu, a beautiful red-haired woman with whom Carol once lived in exile, was referred to in the n

LONDON, Oct. 4 (AP).—King Carol of Roumania has cut short the visit of Crown Prince Michael in London with his mother, Princess Helen, the princess was quoted by the Daily Mail as saying today, and has threatened her with never seeing her son again. She charged her former husband with “persecution and bad faith” for the action which, she said, was taken because the king was resentful of the sympathy the British people have shown her since Michael arrived in London two weeks ago. Michael came to stay six weeks, he said, but she was informed by an aide that he had been ordered to return to Roumania with the boy tomorrow.

By The Associated Press London, Oct. 4—James McNeill submitted his resignation as Governor General of the Irish Free State to King George and the press association (British) reported that President Eamon de Valera might nominate either himself or some colleague high in Irish Republican political life as his successor. The Irish cabinet has the sole right to nominate the governor general. A 1930 resolution after the imperial conference failed to leave the crown any loophole in this matter. The king has no power to veto or to control the choice of a dominion.

PARIS, Oct. 4—(4)—Sir John Simon conferred today with Premier Herriot, and it was understood that he had proposed a four-power conference at London to study Germany’s demand for equality of armaments. It was said the proposal included provision for attendance by an American observer. BERLIN, Oct. from Geneva that has suggested a way for Germany's return to the disarmament conference has caused great interest here among those who regard the proposal as a way out of the present deadlock. Official circles insist, however, that because of the acute situation created by differences at Geneva between Germany, France and Great Britain, this country must have guarantees that any future discussions in which it is to participate will not be.

LONDON, Oct. 4.—-(UP)—Eamon De Valera was credited today with a political maneuver which may make him both governor general and president of the executive council of the Irish Free State and create an unparalleled situation between the crown and a dominion. Observers believed there was nothing to prevent De Valera advising his own appointment to succeed Governor General James MacNeill, who resigned at De Valera’s suggestion. Since the 1930 imperial conference prescribed that dominion governments recommend their governors-general, King George would hardly do other than agree. De Valera comes to London tomorrow to confer with Dominion Secretary J. H. Thomas.

LONDON, Oct. 3.—(AP)—"We were actuated throughout by the desire to make peace," the Earl of Lytton, who headed the League of Nations commission which drew up the controversial report on the Manchurian conflict, asserted tonight when he got back home from Shanghai. He had been traveling since Sept. 5. Lord Lytton said it was no surprise to him that Japan had indicated she could not accept the suggestions of the report. "That fact was made clear to the commission in Tokyo," he explained. "Our object was to try to find a basis for peace in the future. We hope all countries of the League will follow the lead which the commission has given them and will treat the matter in the same spirit."

TOKYO, Oct. 4—(P)—The cabinet decided today, after a session called to consider the League of Nations commission's report on Manchuria, that there was no reason to alter its Manchurian policy, the keystone of which is the separation of Manchukuo from China and the maintenance of its independence. Accounts of the meeting published in local newspapers agreed that War Minister Sadao Araki led the critics and was joined by several ministers. Araki said the report was merely “a diary of a fortnight’s journey through Manchuria” and showed inability to grasp fundamentals. As such, he said, it was unworthy of Japan's serious attention. Japanese newspapers quoted a spokesman for the foreign office today as saying Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson's speech at Philadelphia last Saturday, in which he recounted the high spots of the foreign relations record of President Hoover's administration, was

1932-03-08.text: SHANGHAI, March 8, — Central mediators who have not met in several days gathered to renew efforts to put an end to the fighting. They are meeting on 2 British warships. Meanwhile a new offensive of major character is reported to be developing along a new battle line northwest of Shanghai. Both armies are strengthening their positions. Inauguration CHANG CHUN, Manchuria, Mar- 8, — Henry Pu-yi, former boy emperor of China, who went into exile 20 years ago, arrived for his inauguration tomorrow as the head of the new Manchuria federated State. He was accompanied by his wife and several founders of the new state, including Chang Ching-hul.

HOPEWELL, N. J., Mar. 8.—(A.P.)—The searchlight of the Lindbergh baby kidnapping investigation swung its full glare into New England today. Two men were arrested in a Boston railroad station while putting through a long distance call to the Lindbergh home. One of the men told police he believed his father-in-law knew more about the case than he would tell and he wanted to inform Col. Lindbergh. In New Haven, Conn., a contractor was held in $25,000 bond for state police investigating what they said was an entirely new angle of the case. There was little development elsewhere, though three long term kidnap convicts were questioned at length in Philadelphia.

London, March 8—(4)—Prince Lennart of Sweden, who lost the prerogatives of royalty because of his love for a commoner, will marry the young woman, Miss Karin Nisandt, on Friday, it was learned Monday. The prince and his fiancée came here more than a week ago for the ceremony, after King Gustav of Sweden had forbidden the marriage in that country. His mother, the Grand Duchess Marie of Russia, came over from New York last week to be present. The marriage will be performed at the Princes Row register office, with the mother and a few intimate friends present. After a motor honeymoon on the continent, the couple will settle down on an estate on Lake Constance.

BY MOTS ¢d. SiArris SHANGHAI, Mar. 8 (P—A new offensive of major character was reported developing today along a newly established battle line west and northwest of Shanghai. Two thousand Japanese soldiers who arrived at Woosung yesterday, were taken up to the front lines on the west. They followed larger detachments which entered the lines yesterday. The Japanese also took forward large amounts of ammunition, field guns and supplies. Independent reports indicated that considerable fighting was going on at various points from Nanziang northward, and that both armies were strengthening their positions with increased forces. Japanese consular officials said they were investigating the beating of Miss Rose Marlowe, Baptist missionary from Williamsburg, Kentucky, and that if they found circumstances warranted it the perpetrators would be punished. SHANGHAI (UP) -— Wearied armies battled along a wide front in the Yangtze valley Tuesday as China brushed aside world-wide peace overtures and recalled from exile her greatest military leader, General Chiang Kai-shek, to direct the defense against invading Japanese. Chinese government leaders, meeting Japanese charges that defending armies were responsible for the renewed hostilities, flatly announced their refusal to attend the long-awaited peace conference unless Japanese troops are withdrawn. At the same time, the central executive committee meeting at the temporary capital of Loyang announced that General Chiang had been appointed chairman of the military council, a post tantamount to command of the nation’s armies. The Sino-Japanese clash in the Yangtze valley, which sprang up shortly after commanders on both sides had announced cessation of hostilities, apparently encouraged the go

SHANGHAI, March 8 (Tuesday) — (AP)—Heavy fighting on a broad scale was reported today to be developing out of skirmishes between the Chinese and Japanese armies along the newly established inland battle line. The Japanese and Chinese accused each other of resuming the offensive on the front west and northwest of Shanghai, threatening to precipitate a renewal of general conflict. Independent reports indicated that considerable fighting was going on at various points from Nanzhang northward, while both armies strengthened their positions with increasing forces. Service over the Shanghai-Hangchow railway was broken off today when the personnel of the Shanghai station suddenly left for Hangchow. Before their departure, they removed the telegraph and telephone instruments from the station. Soldiers were reported to have severed the line 35 miles southwest of Shanghai. PARIS, March 6 (UP).—France will honor Aristide Briand in the most brilliant and pompous of state funerals such as accorded national military heroes. Then the veteran man of peace will be buried among the peasants in a rustic village cemetery overlooking the peaceful valley of the Eure river. Messages expressing sympathy of the world poured into the foreign office on the passing of the greatest French statesman since Richelieu and one of the greatest peacemakers of all time.

STOCKHOLM, Sweden, Mar. 8. — Frederick Von Svyrow, a young law student, committed suicide today after killing his father, his wife, and two maid servants. His father, Hjalmar Try Sydow, was a well-known figure in Swedish industrial circles. The young man battered his father and the two maid servants to death at his father’s home and then went with his wife to Upsala and joined a festive party of his fellow students. After the bodies were found at Stockholm a detective was sent to Upsala. When the detective arrived the young man shot his wife dead with a revolver and then turned the gun on himself. He was believed to have been insane.

1932-03-05.text: (Copyright, 1932, by The Associated Press.) Shanghai, March 4. —(AP)— The rumble of artillery in Taitsang, 25 miles to the northwest, and a Nanking government announcement that the Chinese had rejected the latest Japanese peace terms, today disturbed the rehabilitation of war-weary Shanghai. Official Chinese advices from Taitsang late in the day said the Japanese 11th division had attacked the Chinese forces there and that a severe battle was under way. Demands Rejected Low Wen Kan, Nanking foreign minister, was authority for rejection of the new Japanese series of demands, which have been charac- (Continued on Page 10)

By The Associated Press. Tokyo, March 5.--(Saturday) Baron Takuma Dan, managing director of the vast Mitsui commercial interests, died shortly after noon today from wounds inflicted by an assassin. He was attacked as he alighted from an automobile in front of the Mitsui bank. Whether he was stabbed or shot could not immediately be learned from the police authorities. The baron was probably the foremost figure in the Japanese financial world.

MOSCOW. UP. Soviet Russia admitted Friday she was concentrating an army near the far eastern Siberian border to defend herself "against a Japanese attack." The admission was made in the government organ Izvestia and was inspired by a statement of the Tokyo foreign office on Feb. 29. As published here, the foreign office statement quoted the Japanese consul in Vladivostok as saying that Soviet Russia was concentrating large bodies of troops and munitions there and predicting a "collision" soon between Japan and Russia. Asserting that the Japanese information was obtained from "foreigners" in Vladivostok, the newspaper said the Japanese report clearly showed "specific provocative aims" and that it was unnecessary to deny the prediction of a collision. "It is much more interesting to note that Japanese politicians are trying to use information from 'poisoned wells' instead of being more att

By The Associated Press. Geneva, Switz, March 4--The assembly of the League of Nations unanimously called on China and Japan tonight to negotiate a cessation of hostilities around Shanghai including withdrawal of Japanese forces. The assembly spoke in the form of a three point resolution which also provided for assistance in the negotiations from representatives of the great powers. Faced with certain defeat by a determined concert of fifty states, Naotake Sato, the Japanese representative, joined in supporting the resolution and smilingly abandoned an effort to put the movements of Chinese forces within the terms of the proposed negotiations. The assembly's action came after the Chinese delegate, W. W. Yen, had delivered an impassioned appeal for measures to halt the Japanese military advance around Shanghai, which he declared was continuing.

Tokio, March 8—(UP)—Baron Taketina Dan, 74, engineer and head of the powerful Mitsui interests, was assassinated today by Goro Hishingma, a young Japanese from Ibaraki prefecture. The murder was believed to have been in connection with protests made last December by patriotic factions when the Mitsui interests reportedly made immense profits dealing in foreign exchange. Certain Japanese elements considered the dealings unpatriotic because Japan was on the gold standard and the value of the yen was unstable. Ibaraki prefecture was the home of the man who assassinated former finance Minister Junnosuki Inouye in February. Baron Dan was shot as he was leaving his automobile in front of his office. He died within a few hours. The baron received part of his education in America and was graduated from an engineering school in Boston. The Mitsui interests control banks, mines, and many commercia

GENEVA, Switzerland, March 5 — The smaller nations raised their voices today, urging the League of Nations assembly to exert its authority for the restoration of peace in the Far East. Some, like the delegate from Colombia, announced they were prepared to support any and all measures provided by the league covenant to halt the Sino-Japanese conflict. Others, such as the representative from Mexico, declared the league's moral forces were sufficient to solve the problem without resort to other means.

(Copyright, 1932, Associated Press) Tokyo, March 4—A Japanese brigade in Northeast Manchuria left Imienpo today over the Chinese railway and arrived in Hallin. The brigade under General Amano was en route northward for the express purpose of putting down insurgents against the new federated Manchukuo. The Japanese planned to proceed on foot from Harbin. HELSINGFORS, Finland, March 5 — Kustaa Latvala, one of the most prominent of the Lapua (fascist) group in Finland, committed suicide today in disappointment over failure of the recent rebellion. He was a former school teacher. The government published a presidential proclamation today commanding all the fascist rebels to return to their homes and promising cent leaders of the rebellion.

1932-05-12.text: NORFOLK, Va., May 12. (Still maneuvering behind a screen of secrecy, John Hughes Curtis, Norfolk negotiator in the Lindbergh kidnapping case, today was believed to be seeking in New England waters the contact with kidnappers which numerous cruises off the Virginia coast had apparently failed to procure. The new center of the negotiator’s work was reported to be in the vicinity of Block Island, off the Rhode Island coast. Reports from that locality, however, said no such activities had been noted there.

LONDON, May 11.—Twelve American debutantes and matrons, who crossed the Atlantic to be introduced to Britain’s King and Queen, participated in a free show outside Buckingham Palace Wednesday night with much of London as an audience. United States Ambassador Andrew W. Mellon was one of the late arrivals in the queue. Mr. Mellon served the precedent set by Charles G. Dawes and turned his back on that of the late Col. George Harvey. He wore ordinary evening dress, including ordinary trousers, eschewing the silk breeches in which Colonel Harvey appeared at court. Ray Atherton, counselor to the American Embassy, wore the breeches with cotton stockings and silver buckled pumps prescribed by court etiquette. The main event of the evening—for which the Americans had received gilt-engraved invitations from the palace—was their presentation to Their Majesties beneath a golden canopy in the State b

LONDON, May 12 (4)—The Bank of England reduced its discount rate today from 3 to 2% per cent. It was the second reduction within less than a month. The rate was lowered on April 21 from 3% to 3 per cent. With the budget details completed at that time, it was announced, the bank was able to make a further move for cheaper money in the hope of checking the influx of foreign money for short term investment.

————- LONDON, May 12.—(4)—Ambassador Andrew W. Mellon established himself definitely last night as of the Dawes trousers persuasion rather than the Harvey breeches cult, in the matter of wearing breeches when one goes to court. The ambassador appeared in plain republican pantaloons, eschewing the silk breeches which are the ordinary court mode. In this he followed the precedent set by his unconventional predecessor, former Ambassador Charles G. Dawes. The late George Harvey, when he was ambassador at London, wore breeches and was widely lampooned for it in the United States.

DUBLIN, Irish Free State, May 12 (AP) — Irish bachelors found themselves threatened today with grievously increased tax burdens, proposed in the new Free State tax bill introduced last night in the Dail Eireann. Under a new income tax schedule which calls for a general increase in rates, a bachelor with an income of 300 Pounds (about $1,100) a year would pay nearly 19 Pounds (about $70) tax, while the good fortune of having an income of 1,000 Pounds ($3,670) a year would entail a tax of about $683.

LONDON, May 11—(UP)—The king and queen, hand in hand, led the royal procession into the ballroom at Buckingham Palace tonight to hold the first court of the season at which 400 debutantes, including 13 Americans, were presented to their majesties. Save for the Prince of Wales, almost all of the prominent figures of England's royal and political life were there. Among them was slight, grey-haired Andrew Mellon, the American ambassador to the court of St. James. And all eyes, momentarily, were on the ambassador because there had been much speculation—and considerable mystery—as to whether he would follow the example of brusk, popular Charles G. Dawes, who began his ambassadorial career in London by declining to wear the formal court uniform of knee breeches and stockings. Mellon definitely approved the attitude of Dawes by appearing in ordinary full dress suit, with long trousers. Among th

LONDON, (®) The British government served notice on the government of Eamon de Valera that if the Irish Free State abolishes the oath to the crown, there will be no Anglo-Irish trade agreement at the Ottawa imperial conference this summer. This in effect was the gist of a reply by J. A. Thomas, secretary of dominions, to a questioner in the House of Commons. If the abolition bill should be made law in the Free State, De Valera's government will find itself in the same position as a foreign country, so far as trade with Great Britain is concerned, under Mr. Thomas's pronouncement. The present imperial preferences act expires on Nov. 15, and unless renewed or replaced by a new agreement, the new British tariffs, averaging 20 percent, would be reared against the Free State.

LONDON, May 12—(U2)— Ambassador Andrew W. Mellon was represented as not exactly happy today over his choice of long pants at last night’s court, in preference to the prescribed knee breeches. He commented to a neighbor in the ballroom of Buckingham Palace, “I feel rather out of place not having knee breeches the same as everyone else.” Mellon was said to have obtained a special dispensation from King George through the Lord Chamberlain, permitting him to wear trousers.

1932-07-15.text: London, July 159 —(America) Britain pondered President Hoover's letter to Senator Borah today, in which he declared the United States would not be pressed on the debt question by any combination in Europe, but the general attitude seemed to be that the question was cleared up by the official explanations here yesterday. The letter was the big news of the day in morning papers. Although it came too late for extended editorial comment in London papers, it was pointed out that the Downing Street statement of yesterday showed there was no intention in the Lausanne gentlemen’s agreement or the later Anglo-French accord, to form a united front against the United States. “It hardly needed an official statement to show no such alignment ever was contemplated by the British government,” the Times said. Surprise was expressed at the contrary interpretation placed upon the agreement by Premier Herr

LONDON, July 14 (2) — The British government made a double attempt today to wipe out any impression in the United States that a concerted European move was being made to nullify the war debts owed to Washington. The government issued two official statements. One of them denied that the new Anglo-French accord bound Britain not to negotiate an individual debt settlement with the United States. The other reiterated and strengthened the recent denial that American representatives were consulted before the European powers wrote the Lausanne treaty, which greatly scaled down the German reparations with which they meet a large part of their debts to the United States. During the day the Italian and Belgian charge d'affaires notified the foreign office that their governments agreed with the ideas expressed in the Anglo-French pact and intended to adhere to it. DUBLIN, Irish Free State. President Eamon de Valera for London Friday morning to discuss with Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald the differences between the Free State and Great Britain which have arisen out of de Valera's refusal to pay $11,000,000 a year in land annuities. The president said he could not discuss the situation. — “I was invited to go to London by Mr. MacDonald and I have accepted. The rest remains to be seen,” he said. Meanwhile the Dail, after heated discussion, voted 69 to 59 to shut off debate on the emergency tariff bill which would retaliate for Great Britain’s new customs levies on imports from the Free State. It is expected the measure would be put through all parliamentary stages.

DUBLIN, July 15. —-(UP)—The Dial passed the emergency bill retaliating for the new British tariff by a vote of 68 to 67 today. Government supporters cheered loudly. Sean McEntee, finance minister, assured William Davin, Laborite, that it would be repealed if an agreement was reached with Britain to arbitrate the dispute. The Dial then adjourned to Oct. 18.

DUBLIN, Irish Free State, July 1 (P)—While President de Valera was on the way to London to confer with Prime Minister MacDonald on differences between Great Britain and the Free State, the Daily rushed through all stages a measure taxing British imports. The final government majority was 68 to 57. During the debate, the finance minister, describing enactment of the measure as ‘due to British penal legislation,’ said the powers which it confers will be used primarily to open new channels of trade, to establish new industries in the Free State, and to reimburse the nation for any possible losses due to the new tariff enacted by Great Britain.

By United Press WASHINGTON, July 15.—Sir Ronald Lindsay, British ambassador, today officially advised Under-Secretary of State Castle that the Anglo-French agreement had no reference to a united front on the two nations’ policy toward war debts owed America.- On instruction of the British Foreign Office, Sir Ronald gave Castle a copy of its statements that the accord did not affect non-European countries.

DUBLIN. (Friday). P. A scheme for arbitration of differences between the Irish Free State and Great Britain was understood to have been proposed after the Free State had gone ahead with plans for a tariff war with Britain. Acceptance by President De Valera of an invitation to confer with Prime Minister MacDonald in London at the same time was regarded in political circles here as hopefully altering the situation arising out of the Free State's failure to pay land annuities to the British treasury and the subsequent retaliatory tariff measures. William Norton, chairman of the Free State labor party, after a consultation early Wednesday with President De Valera, carried a plan to London, which he said was acceptable to the Free State. It is understood the plan provided for a tribunal of four members, two nominated by the British government and two by the Free State, who would discuss the s

1932-07-10.text: LAUSANNE, Switzerland. July 9—(UP)—The Lausanne Treaty, ending Germany's war reparations payments, was signed today, with Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald, of Great Britain, declaring “our agreements must have response elsewhere.” It provides that Germany pay in one lump sum one cent for every dollar demanded by the victorious Allies—if she can sell the bonds to raise the money. Collection and payment of inter-European war debts was declared suspended until ratification of the treaty. Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald, of Great Britain, was the first statesman to sign. As president of the conference, he declared the treaty open to signature, walked around a square formed by tables, and signed the document which lay on a translators’ table in the hollow of the square. The other delegates approached and signed. The signatures took considerable time because of the multitude of documents. Chanc

LAUSANNE, July 9—-(INS)— A call to the United States to join Europe in a united effort to lift the world from its present economic distress formed the keynote of an address delivered here today by Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald of Great Britain as he signed the reparations-ending treaty of Lausanne. MacDonald, although not directly, inferentially asked the United States to drastically reduce the war debts owed her by the allies just as the allies reduced the reparations owed them by Germany. "The most self-contained country in the world, the United States, is as hard hit as Europe," MacDonald said. "No country so strong can separate itself from other nations economically. "Europe cannot build barriers and live prosperously inside them. "An agreement for a solid economic foundation will bring greater security and wealth. CHERBOURG, France, July 9 (3). A diver descended to the sunken submarine Promethee today, knocked repeatedly on the hull and received no reply, a wireless message received from the rescue party by the maritime prefecture, said. The submarine had been on the bottom more than 56 hours and there was very little hope that any member of the crew remained alive.

By The Associated Press Cherbourg, France, July 9.—Divers descended to the sunken French submarine Prométhée today and thumped away at her armor, but no answering taps came from within and all but the faintest hope of rescuing the more than 60 men who went down with her was abandoned. Little knots of sailing men and townspeople gathered around the bulletin board of the Maritime Prefecture, discussing in gloomy tones of the ever-diminishing chance of getting any of the luckless bluejackets out alive. Three dives were made during the day. First a French diver went down in a steel case, but he could not locate the hull of the sunken vessel. He was followed by two divers from the Italian salvage ship Artiglio II, which recently lifted gold from the hulk of the sunken liner Egypt off Brest. The first Artiglio diver also failed to locate the hull. The second, who went down in special apparatus

ABOARD WARSHIP AILETTE, off Cherbourg (UP)—The sunken submarine Promethee, which carried 63 men to their death while on a test cruise, was found Saturday lying in a mudhole 40 fathoms down. The craft sank Thursday with only seven members of the crew escaping. They were on deck when the big new submarine dropped suddenly under the water, carrying the crew to their deaths. A diver who has been working on the gold recovery project from the steamer Atiglio, went down Saturday to find what had happened to the big submarine. While hundreds of navy men, technicians and others stood anxiously on the decks of a dozen craft, the diver put on a bell uniform and slipped into the water. Forty fathoms down he found the vessel, sunken into the mudhole. There was no trace of life. After the diver came up, technicians started working on a plan to bring the craft to the surface. KELVINGTON, Sask. (CP)—The trail of William Miller, fugitive from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, ended Saturday in a clump of muskeg, where his crumpled body was found, apparently a suicide. Miller was the leader of a gang of three who Mounties said murdered Corporal Leonard V. Ralls, Foam Lake. Two others were overtaken by the greatest manhunt in the history of the province.

SHANGHAI, July 9—@—The slaying of William Simpson, an American missionary and a Russian named Horvath, by Chinese bandits, reported from Lanchow last week, was confirmed by further dispatches today. Simpson was attached to the Assemblies of God mission, American headquarters of which are at Springfield, Mo.

1932-02-05.text: WASHINGTON, Feb. 5 (AP)—Andrew Mellon was confirmed today as ambassador to England. WASHINGTON, Feb. 5 (AP)—The Senate Foreign Relations Committee unanimously approved the nomination of Andrew Mellon to be ambassador to Great Britain today, within an hour after President Hoover forwarded the name to the Senate. The committee, out of deference to the veteran secretary of the treasury, held a special meeting to report his name.

WASHINGTON, Dec. 0 (UP) - A consultation with Great Britain and other powers and a thorough analysis of Japan's reply to American-British peace plans were expected today to precede further overtures to the Tokyo government from Washington. Haste was made, however, in accordance with the urgent desire for cessation of hostilities at Shanghai. Secretary Stimson and his aides pushed their study of Ambassador Forbes’ digest of the Japanese answer which came yesterday. It was accompanied by assurance that further proposals for effecting peace would be welcomed. There was no indication here what form such proposals might take; in fact, Stimson and the other officials have reserved all comment on the Japanese reply. It was clear there was disappointment that the answer was not more favorable but thought was concentrated on the constructive possibilities of the situation.

London, Feb. 4.—(4)—In an historic session of Commons today, Great Britain’s free trade policy, the nation’s cornerstone for a century, was thrown overboard by Neville Chamberlain, who wore the mantle of his famous father, Joseph, as he proclaimed the financial revolution. On March 1, a general tariff of 10 per cent will be levied on all British imports with the exception of wheat, meat, fish, grain, cotton and wool, under the national government’s program. A tariff commission something like that of the United States will be established to levy additional duties up to 100 per cent. Conference Planned Preferential treatment for British dominions will be worked out at an imperial conference in Ottawa in June, but meanwhile the Dominions will be unaffected. The Associated Press. Washington, D. C., Feb. 4. — Secretary Mellon made ready today to yield to his closest assistant and colleague the office he has held through eleven troubled, significant years and then assume new duties as America’s envoy to the British government. Meanwhile, the senate’s newest member, Huey P. Long of Louisiana, declared himself opposed to both the Mellon and Mills appointments. He said he would endeavor to prevent their confirmation. Administration leaders freely predicted approval of the nominations by an overwhelming vote. From the house there came a reiteration of Representative Patman’s opposition to Mellon. The Texas Democrat is the author of a resolution seeking the treasury secretary's impeachment. This is now in the hands of a house sub-committee. Washington, Feb. 4. (#)—Japan definitely left the door open for further negotiations in delivering to Ambassador Forbes and the ambassadors of Great Britain, France and Italy at Tokyo its refusal to accept two of five American-British peace proposals. In a message to the Department of State accompanying a digest of the Japanese reply, Forbes said Foreign Minister Yoshizawa told him Japan will be glad to consider further proposals from the powers which are endeavoring to bring about peace in Shanghai. Secretary Stimson will not formulate a reply to Japan tonight, and possibly not even tomorrow, as it will be necessary for him to confer with other interested powers and make a thorough analysis of the digest of the Japanese reply before preparing any counter- The terms of the reply were made public in Tokyo yesterday. - BOSTON, Feb. 5.—(#)—An old-fashioned New England blizzard swept in from the northeast today, ripping down power lines, crippling communication in the outlying districts and bringing heavy seas off the coast. Lightning interrupted the broadcasting of two of Boston’s largest radio stations, clinging sleet bore down wires and drifting snow clogged highways and made automobile driving impossible in many sections.

Washington, Feb. 5 (P)—Andrew Mellon was confirmed today as ambassador to England. The Senate waived its rules to speed through the nomination of the man who for almost 11 years has run the treasury. No attempt was made for a record vote. A chorus of “ayes” answered the presentation of Mr. Mellon’s name for the court of St. James. Senator Reed, Republican of Pennsylvania, close friend of the veteran Mellon, asked unanimous consent for consideration of the nomination. Senator McKellar, Democrat of Tennessee, an old foe of Mellon, told the Senate he was voting “against confirmation.” The question then was put to the Senate, but there was such a chorus of “ayes” that no roll call was demanded.

1932-12-24.text: NEW YORK, Dec. 24.—(#)—The British freighter Newbrough broadcast an SOS early today, stating it was sinking off the Island of Jamaica, with its engine room flooded. The call, picked up by station WAX at Miami, Fla., was rebroadcast to the liner President McKinley, which replied that she would proceed to the position given, 125 miles, or about eight hours, away. The Miami station's call also was picked up by the coast guard in New York.

BIRMINGHAM, England, Dec. 24. ()—Seven of the eight young children of an unemployed man were burned to death when trapped on the upper floor by a fire which destroyed the family’s tiny two-room house today. The father, Lake Weir, a crippled ex-service man, and his wife, who were sleeping downstairs with a four months old baby, were seriously burned and were taken to a hospital. The tinder-like interior of the dwelling flared up so rapidly that by the time firemen arrived it was impossible even to attempt to rescue the other children, their ages ranging from four to 13 years, who were sleeping, crowded together, in the upper room.

LONDON, Dec. 24.—UP—Great Britain led the world today in a four-day celebration of Christmas, which was made one of the longest vacations on record by proclamation of Tuesday as an additional bank holiday. After tonight, not a door will open in London until Wednesday. The royal family is at Sandringham for four days, and every member is expected to be at dinner tomorrow. NEW YORK, Dec. 24.—UP—Peggy Hopkins Joyce broke into the newspapers again by taking 12 Salvation Army Santa Clauses to luncheon at the Waldorf Astoria. NEW YORK, Dec. 24.—(UP)—Lucrezia Bori and Giovanni Martinelli, Metropolitan opera stars, will sing for immigrants held at Ellis Island over Christmas day. Miss Bori was born on Christmas. NEWARK, N. TEHERAN, Persia. (UP) — Little Persia has challenged the British lion on the question of oil for the British Navy. Representatives of Persians, from Teheran, merchants and politicians to chiefs of the wild interior tribes, have pledged their support to Shah Riza Khan Pahlevi on cancellation of the Anglo-Persian Oil company’s concession a most vital link in the British worldwide naval fuel supplies. Country Aroused The whole country is aroused. The Shah, himself a former cossack - and once a guard at the portals of the royal palace, is said to be extremely grateful for this display of confidence in him. LONDON, Dec. 24.—U.P)—Great Britain led the world today in a four-day celebration of Christmas, which was made one of the largest vacations on record by proclamation of Tuesday as an additional bank holiday. After tonight, not a door will open in London until Wednesday. The royal family is at Sandringham for four days, and every member is expected to be at dinner tomorrow.

England, Ark., Dec. 24.-(@)-A tornado struck the southwestern section of England early today, unroofing or damaging about thirty dwellings and injuring two persons. Property damage was estimated at $35,000 to $40,000. Woman Suffers Head Injury Mrs. Bee McCarthur, 45, suffered a head injury. A negro woman was struck by a falling timber as her home collapsed and she suffered a fractured arm. Most of the homes which suffered the greatest damage were occupied by negroes. The business section escaped with little damage. Windows on the south side of the England high school were broken out. Among the homes virtually destroyed were those of John Whitehead and Wayne Pledger. Mrs. Pledger and a child were alone at her home when the house collapsed. They were imprisoned by the fallen walls and were at the mercy of the rain and cold for some time before they were rescued by neighbors. The tornado al

WELLINGTON, New Zealand, Dec. 23 P)--Replying to New Zealand's voluntary offer to resume payment on its war debt to the United Kingdom, the British government said today that it does not wish to withdraw or qualify its offer of suspension extended to debtor dominions at the time of the general Hoover moratorium.

London, Dec. 22,—(#)—Capt. J. A. Mollison, the long-distance flier, will start from England on February 7 for a flight to Rio de Janeiro by way of Africa, it was announced today. Captain Mollison and his wife, Amy Johnson, are now in France on a belated wedding trip.

1932-07-30.text: WASHINGTON, July 36 (P)—An invitation to the United States to attend the proposed monetary and economic conference has been received by the state department from the British embassy. It provides that reparations, debts and tariff rates are not to be discussed at the parley. The invitation says that among the monetary matters to be discussed is the question of silver. No time or place for the conference was given, The United States was invited to name a member of the organizing committee at Geneva which is arranging for the conference. This country also was advised to name an economist and a financial expert to assist the preparatory committee drawing up the program, The state department has already indicated it would accept such a conference invitation provided that debts and tariffs were not on the agenda.

Ottawa, Ont., July 30. (UP)— Publication of the secret hopes held by empire units for diverting United States trade to the British Empire will be discussed by the chief delegates to the Empire Economic Conference today. These hopes are included in the statements the chief delegates made during secret meetings this week. The belief of some is that the statements should be published at once. They then would explain as frankly as possible the views of their governments on an empire currency, an empire bank, stabilization of currency, and increase in commodity prices. An empire bank would coordinate the finances and currencies of the great dominions and the little islands, and other colonial possessions, that dot the world in all continents. Los Angeles (A.P.)—Many of the foreign athletes in the Olympic village don't know much English but they can all grin and say “O. K.” Four Argentines said they knew a great deal of American. When asked to illustrate, they chorused: “G. M., hot dog, you bet.”

BERLIN, May 30, (4)~- Chancellor Heinrich Bruening and the members of his cabinet resigned today and the resignations were accepted by President Paul Von Hindenburg. The stern, hard-fisted chancellor, combination of soldier and student, who in the little more than two years he has guided the German republic through unprecedented storms and financial near collapse, finally lost an uphill fight against growing nationalism and dissatisfaction with government by emergency decrees. He was forced at last to make way for a cabinet in which conservatives are likely to predominate and which, in turn, probably soon will have to give way to one dominated by the phenomenally rising national socialists of the young fascist leader, Adolf Hitler, who romped away with the recent state diet elections. OTTAWA, July 30.—(#)—A general agreement that the most necessary task of the imperial trade conference is to boost the general price levels of basic commodities pervaded every special committee today. The committee on monetary and financial questions brought the question to a head after 24 hours of talk. As long as it takes twice as much of any commodity to pay off a debt as it did when the debt was contracted, the committee decided, there could be no basic stability of money, trade or tariffs or any attempt to equalize values. The committee’s announcement came almost simultaneously with reports that Canada and Great Britain were believed to have agreed in principle on a wheat preference plan. (By United Press). Geneva, August 2.—Jose Matos, president of the League of Nations council, telegraphed to Bolivia and Paraguay today, urging them to avoid war. He sent a similar telegram Saturday, reminding them of their world obligations to keep the peace.

Minto, N. B. July 29--(A.P)— Three boys who had been told that they could see the moon in broad daylight if they climbed to the bottom of an old mine shaft are dead and two miners lost their lives trying to rescue them. Four youngsters made the experiment, clambering down a rickety ladder in an abandoned shaft not far from town yesterday. The first one down choked as gas seeping from the worked-out vein overcame him. He lost his hold on the ladder and dropped 40 feet into a pool of water at the bottom. Two of the others had started right behind him. They too lost consciousness and fell. Six-year-old Joe O'Leary, the fourth, had lingered a little. He saw his friends drop and fled terrified, coming back with his father and several other men. Two of the men started down the ladder. Both succumbed to the gas and fell. Berlin. July 29. (#—Chancellor Franz Von Papen, whose cabinet is made up of men powerful in the junker and military caste of the old imperial government, assured the United States in a trans-Atlantic broadcast tonight that neither he nor his ministers were maneuvering for a German dictatorship. His address, in which he assailed the Versailles treaty, took on added significance because of two factors. At home Germany is embroiled in the campaign for the Reichstag elections Sunday, and abroad she is involved in a new difference with France. A few hours before the chancellor went on the air, his foreign minister, Baron Konstantin Von Neurath, told the French ambassador that when defense Minister Kurt Von Schleicher threatened the other day to arm Germany if the other nations did not disarm, he spoke for every member of the German cabinet and for the whole German nation. 1932-09-05.text: DETROIT, SEPT. 5. (AP).—The jinx rode again with Kaye Don's Miss England III today and eliminated him from the second and final heat of the Harmsworth Trophy race after a thrilling start against Gar Wood, trophy defender. Developing mechanical difficulties almost as he crossed the starting line a little less than a second ahead of Wood's Miss America X, Don made a heroic effort to keep his craft in the race. Steadily losing power, however, he came to a complete stop about a mile from the end of the second seven-mile lap of the course. Wood, meanwhile, loafed around the course at an average of only 69.034 statute miles per hour to win the heat and retain the noted British international trophy for at least another year. Contrasting with the trouble he had in the first heat Saturday, Don was unable to finish today’s heat. With his mechanic, Dick Garner, he tried vainly to get his craft goin

HARMSWORTH COURSE, Lake St. Clair, Mich. Sept. 5 >The United States today retained possession of the Harmsworth International Trophy emblematic of world speed supremacy on the water when a motor mishap disabled the challenger, Miss England II. Den's boat became disabled on the second lap and the Briton was unable to complete the lap. Wood's average speed for the thirty miles was 69.036 miles an hour. This was twenty miles an hour slower than the record set last year by Don in Miss England II. As patrol boats towed the Miss England to her well with the disappointed Briton riding in the towing boat, Wood received the finish gun. He swung the Miss America, her exhaust belching smoke and fire, as he slowed her down, and came past the press stands. LONDON, Sept. 5 (4)—The government intervened today in the Lancashire cotton textile strike, which already resulted in approximately 150,000 operatives walking out and threatens to involve at least that many more. After numerous business leaders had declared the labor warfare might well mean the death of the industry if it lasted any length of time, Sir Henry Betterton, minister of labor, communicated with both employers and employees. Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald was scheduled to return tonight from Scotland, and Sir Henry arranged to inform him of the steps taken to effect peace. The contents of letters sent by the labor minister to the two parties to the conflict were not divulged, but it was understood he suggested methods of bringing them together for negotiations.

| Detroit, Sept. 4 (P)—Having di- | rected more than 24 hours of labor on his disabled challenger, “Miss England III” Kaye Don, British speed ace, announced tonight that he and his craft were ready to meet Gar Wood and his “Miss America X” in the second heat of the Harmsworth trophy race. Wood took the opening heat Saturday after training Don for four laps of the 35-mile course. Don later explained his boat had begun to ship a huge volume of water and that one of his engines went out of commission. Unless weather conditions necessitate a postponement the second heat will be run at 6:30 a.m., Monday. Regatta officials announced that the starting and timing barges which broke loose from their moorings during a violent storm on Lake St. Clair last night had been replaced and that everything again was in readiness for the battle between the world’s two fastest hydroplanes. GENEVA, Sept. 6 (4)—Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald of Great Britain has suggested a first meeting of the preparatory commission for the world economic conference could be held sometime during the last two weeks of September... Mr. MacDonald's suggestion was revealed in a letter he wrote to the secretary general of the League of Nations. He said he had ascertained that the interested powers, including the United States, would approve of this arrangement. The letter was sent in Mr. MacDonald’s capacity as president of the Lausanne conference. Besides scaling down German reparations to $714,000,000, the Lausanne conference suggested that a world economic and financial discussion be arranged in the near future. The conference would include, besides the European creditor nations, the other European states and the United States. The Lausanne negotiators defined the questions to be examined as

TOKIO, SEPT. 5. (AP).—Captain Wolfgang von Gronau, German aviator, and his three companions were resting at the German embassy here today after completing this much of their round-the-world flight from Germany by way of the United States. They arrived here at 3:35 p.m. yesterday after a 600-mile flight from Nemuro to Lake Kasumigaura, the naval base near Tokio. They said they would remain at least a week before taking off for Manila, Shanghai and Indo-China.

ROTTERDAM, Sept. 5 —(AP)— Captain Holland of the American liner, Rotterdam, radioed today for 30 marines to meet the vessel to deal with what he said was mutiny of the crew. The marines left in a pilot steamer to meet the liner at sea. Previous advices said the crew, against the orders of the steamship company, had refused to dock at any port other than Rotterdam. Officials wished to land the passengers at Bruinigne and Southampton because it was feared the crew might join the seamen’s strike now in progress at Rotterdam.

Berlin, Sept. 5—(U.R)—Allegiance of Germany’s gray clad war veterans for the old aristocracy’s von Papen government has been sworn in a great demonstration in which they goose stepped, 160,000 strong, before members of the government, members of the royal family, and 300,000 spectators, seven of whom were killed in the traffic congestion. The veterans revived the traditions of imperial militaristic Germany in their steel helmet parade at Tempelhof airdrome where their leader rejected a bid for allegiance with the Fascist chieftain, Adolf Hitler. The parade lasted six hours. Chancellor Franz von Papen and most of the members of his official family were in the reviewing stand. 1932-08-18.text: (By The Associated Press) London, Aug. 18—The Cunard liner Ascania today reported that Captain J. A. Mollison, flying from Ireland to Newfoundland, passed that vessel at 4 p.m. (11 a.m. E.S.T.) at 52.22 north latitude, 20.32 west longitude. He seemed to be going well. There was a light northerly wind, and fine, clear weather. The position reported by the Ascania is about 650 miles west from Galway. Mollison, noted British distance flier, took off at 11:35 a.m. (5:35 a.m., Eastern Standard Time.) He planned to make his first stop at Harbor Grace, Newfoundland, and after refueling to dash on immediately to Roosevelt Field, Long Island. Then his schedule called for a quick turnaround and a dash back again, this time without a stop, to Croydon, England. James A. Mollison, who holds the Australia-to-England and the England-to-Capetown speed records, and who was married last July to Amy Johnson, famous British girl flier, took off at 4:35 EST and headed into a dreary haze. A large crowd cheered, among them Amy Johnson. Mollison, who is to England what Lindbergh is to America, hoped to reach Harbor Grace, Newfoundland in 20 hours, and to fly on to New York after refueling. He planned to stop only briefly before heading back across the North Atlantic. His ship is a baby Puss Moth, so small that he has trouble pushing his shoulders through the cabin door. MIAMI, Fla. Aug. 18—(AP)— Captain W. N. Lancaster, British aviator, acquitted yesterday of murder in the death of his rival in love, Haden Clarke, a young American writer, rested at the home of his attorney today before starting to hunt a job. He was without definite plans for the future, he said, and declined to discuss what attitude he would adopt toward Mrs. Jessie M. Keith-Miller, Australian flying companion whose affections Clarke won from him. “Please do not ask me about her,” he begged questioners who sought to learn if his plans would include the aviatrix. “I don’t know now what answer I would give you!” Lancaster, arrested May 2 on a first degree murder charge, was acquitted yesterday on one complete ballot that followed 4 hours and 58 minutes of debate by a jury made up solely of men. His trial lasted more than two weeks.

Miami, Fla., Aug. 17 (P)— Captain W. N. Lancaster, British flier, was freed today of a charge of murdering Haden Clarke, young writer and his rival in love, by a verdict which precipitated a courtroom demonstration that threatened to go beyond the control of bailiffs. The twelve-man jury deliberated 4 hours and 48 minutes before acquitting him on one complete ballot. He had been on trial since August 2 in one of the most sensational hearings in the history of South Florida—a trial that brought out the secret love lives of himself, Haden Clarke and Mrs. Jessie M. Keith-Miller, Australian aviatrix, in detail. Fashionably gowned women wept and shrieked in delight as F. R. B. Leatherman, clerk of Circuit Court, read aloud the jury's verdict of "not guilty." It became obvious the plenary session could not be held Thursday when Stanley M. Bruce and J. G. Coates, leaders of the Australian and New Zealand delegations, joined forces with Prime Minister Bennett of Canada in demanding dominion products be protected against Soviet “dumping” in British markets.
