| CONWAY, N. H. (#) — They are selling the Aug. 31 eclipse of the sun to vacationists in the New England summer resorts. | Selling an eclipse proves to be about like selling apples, those who started earliest and worked hardest have the most profits. The profits already in prospect are sufficient to qualify the rare celestial spectacle as one of the 1932 comebacks from 3:30 P. M., Eastern Standard Time. Sufficient reservations already are in sight to make up partly for a “season” thus far showing the characteristic 1932 curtailment. No one around here has had previous experience in “selling” an eclipse. Estimates of possible visitors at Conway, a town of a few hundred, range from everything filled to wild guesses of 10,000. A large number already have reservations.

LONDON, Aug. 17. (P)—The British cabinet took the bit in its teeth in the Indian situation today as Prime Minister MacDonald announced its plan for solving the critical problem of electoral representation. The plan called for allotting seats to Hindus, Moslems, Sikhs, Untouchables, and other bitterly antagonistic races, creeds and classes in the future provincial legislatures of India. Predicating roars of criticism and that the plan would be displeasing to all Indian communities, the prime minister said it was necessary, if the building of an Indian constitution were to proceed. The Indians should have agreed upon the question themselves, he said, but they failed three times so the cabinet proceeded at the request of the communities involved.

- Washington, D. C., Aug. 18.— (AP)— Andrew W. Mellon has been granted permission by the state department to remain away from his ambassadorial post in London for another week or so. Mellon had originally planned to begin his return trip tomorrow. In asking for the extension he pointed out that parliament is not in session and said his immediate presence in England was not necessary.

1932-09-08.text: CHERBOURG, France, Sept. 8 (AP) — J. A. Mollison, who recently flew from Ireland to New York, arrived here today aboard the liner Empress of Britain. He was met by his wife, Amy Johnson, also a noted British long-distance flier. She flew here from England to accompany her husband home aboard the ship.

LONDON, Sept. 7.— The upward trend in American business is well under way, Ambassador Andrew W. Mellon said today when he received American press representatives for the first time since his return from the United States. The ambassador noted a marked improvement of confidence in the United States. He said he was sure of President Hoover's reelection, and that the president’s reconstructive measures were producing ‘very satisfactory results.’ Mellon insisted that the measures did not constitute inflation, which he condemned as being ‘like taking dope; one dose necessitates another.’ He said it made no difference to the United States which of the tentative dates, December or February, was selected for the world economic conference here.

LONDON, Sept. 8—(/)—President Hoover's chances for re-election at the present time, Ambassador Andrew W. Mellon said on his return from the United States today, are equally good as they were two months before the election in 1928. The president's efforts to remedy the depression and unemployment, he said, already are taking effect.

LONDON, Sept. 8. UP—Gresg Britain has decided to pass up the opportunity of giving the United States notice on September 15 that she will not pay her war debt annuity due on December 15, it was reported today. Great Britain was animated by two considerations. First, officials are still confident that at a propitious moment, the United States would offer a readjustment or another moratorium. Second, Britain has been given to understand that the United States Treasury would be satisfied with 30 days’ notice, on the assumption that President Hoover's ban on war debt discussions after the election has in effect superseded the war debt clauses requiring 90 days' notice.

| NEWCASTLE, Eng., Sept. 8 (>-Disappointment and dissatisfaction is widespread in England and other countries over the meager results of the first six months of effort at the world disarmament conference at Geneva, Arthur Henderson, British labor leader and president of the arms conference, told the trade union congress here today. It was Henderson’s first public pronouncement of disarmament since the adjournment of the Geneva conference.

LONDON, Sept. 8—(4)—It was stated today in well-informed quarters that the British government will allow its option for postponement of the next payment on the American debt to expire next Thursday without taking any action. The option applies to the payment on the principal of the debt, due Dec. 15.

LONDON, Sept. 8.—Lancashire cotton weavers continued balloting today on whether to accept proposed wage cuts or add their 200,000 members to the 106,000 weavers already on strike in the cotton trades. Aside from a threatened strike of London grade, a of the present statement Sept. bend were 20

MANCHESTER, Eng, Sept. 7—(AP)—A ray of hope appeared in the Lancashire textile situation today when employers expressed a willingness to arbitrate. During a meeting lasting half an hour, the cotton spinners and manufacturers association central committee drafted its reply to the offer of Sir Henry Betterton, minister of labor, to sponsor a meeting with union leaders. The association said it would attend such a meeting, if invited. A union representative commented that the action was a surprise and the employers had gone further toward settlement of the issues than was expected.

MANCHESTER, Ky., Sept. 19. —(#)—National guard troops were on duty here today following the killing of two men and the wounding of another yesterday in the outbreak of a feud that started during the civil war. The dead were commonwealth attorney Frank H. Baker, 39, of London, Ky., and John Brockman about 25 years old, formerly of Breathitt county and southern Indiana. Frank Young, 40, was shot in the left hip and was in a serious condition today. Rifle shots fired by men barricaded in the Clay county courthouse felled Baker as he stepped from the home of his uncle, Wiley Baker, 62. As Brockman went to Baker's aid, he too was shot down and killed instantly. During the next four hours the two bodies lay in the street while the snipers in the courthouse fired intermittently at the Wiley Baker home. One bullet pierced Wiley Baker’s shoe but did not wound him. Another whizzed over the head of

BOMBAY, Sept. 19. (4)—Mahatma Gandhi began training today for his 'fast to the death' which is slated to begin tomorrow as a protest against the British government's solution of the knotty problem of Indian communal elections. In Yeroda jail, at Poona, where he is imprisoned, he began by cutting down the amount of food he takes at a meal and widening the space between meals. He has been studying ways, he said, for extending his life as long as possible after his hunger strike begins.

(United Press Staff Correspondent.) LONDON, Sept. 19—The British government had lined up solidly today with France against Germany’s demand for armament equality, as a result, political observers said, of a surprisingly blunt foreign office statement. The statement was not even tempered with the usual courteous diplomatic phraseology. In many respects it was more devastating than the French reply to the Reich's equality demand. Britain considers the demand unwise in view of Germany’s economic difficulties; untimely in view of financial concessions recently granted Germany; and holds that even if a disarmament convention is not concluded by the world conference at Geneva, Germany will not be entitled to abrogate the restrictions placed on her by the Versailles treaty, the statement said. Germany, after being advised that questions involving national pride and dignity could be best settled

BRIGHTON, England, Sept. 19—()—"Alpha” the electric mechanical man invented by Harry May, had made good his threat today to wreak vengeance upon his inventor. During a demonstration of the robot at an electrical exhibition yesterday, one of May's hands was severely burned by the premature discharge of the gun the robot fires. May was inserting the cartridge in the gun, during which the robot customarily says: “Look out, or I'll blow your hand off!” As it uttered the words the gun was fired. It was the inventor's third injury at the robot's hands. Twice before, it raised its steel fist and crashed it down on his head. May was unable to explain how yesterday's accident occurred unless somebody in the audience said something which affected the iron man’s mechanism.

Manchester, Ky., Sept. 19.—Two men were killed and two others wounded Sunday in what authorities said was the renewal of an old feud. Governor Ruby Laffoon ordered 25 National Guardsmen here. One of the men slain was Frank H. Baker, 39 years old, London, Ky., commonwealth attorney. The other was identified as John Brock, 23, of Cincinnati. The wounded are Frank Young, 40, and Wiley Baker, 62, an uncle of the commonwealth attorney. The troops were ordered at the request of Judge William C. Lewis of London. The assassins apparently escaped. The commonwealth attorney, Judge Lewis said, came to Manchester Saturday from London and stopped at Wiley Baker’s home. When he and the other three men walked out of the house Sunday morning, the judge was informed they were shot down by rifle and shotgun fire apparently directed from the Clay County courthouse across the street. Sunday's shooting added

London, Sept. 19.—Great Britain responded Sunday to Germany’s demand for arms equality by proposing a new international convention to wipe out inequalities, but insisted Germany had no legal right to seek readjustment outside the world disarmament conference. It was further proposed in an official statement ultimately to replace the military restrictions of the Versailles treaty with the new convention, which also would include the limitations on armaments imposed by existing treaties. The British statement was inspired by the German aide memoire, sent to France Aug. 29, which threatened withdrawal from the disarmament conference unless Germany’s demands were considered. Since then Germany has informed Arthur Henderson, president of the conference, that she could not participate in the next meeting of the conference unless it was established that Germany would be included in any solution

BOMBAY, Sept. 18—(AP)— Mahatma Gandhi made further reductions in his diet and began abstaining from all physical exercise today in preparation for his “fast unto death.” Having set Tuesday as the day he will begin the fast in protest against British Government plans for communal elections in India, the Mahatma has been preparing for the event for weeks. It was learned at Yeroda jail at Poona, where he is held, that he has been studying ways to extend his life as long as possible after beginning the hunger strike. He declared, however, he still hoped the situation might change and relieve him of the necessity of fulfilling his vow. The only condition on which he offered to withdraw from his plan was abandonment of the British elections scheme. Meanwhile he has started cutting down his diet of staple foods and milk and today ate only sparingly and between long intervals. He was also eating

1932-10-13.text: Harbin, Manchuria, Oct. 13 — An infuriated crowd last night hung the Chinese bandit accused of killing Mrs. C. T. Woodruff, an English woman yesterday as she tried to prevent the kidnapping of her three children. The bandit was strung up on a tree where the kidnapping occurred. Later his head was cut off and stuck up upon a pole as an example.

Ottawa, Ont., Oct. 13—LP)—New preference tariffs negotiated at the recent imperial trade conference between Canada and Great Britain became effective throughout the Dominion today. Manufacturers generally hailed the new rate in favor of Canadian-British trade as marking the first step in an agreement which is expected to give Canada an advantage over American and other foreign competition and confine much British trade within the empire. The new schedule covers a wide list of products agricultural and industrial, including Canadian wheat, which will enter the United Kingdom free while a tariff of about 4.32 cents a bushel will be levied on American and other foreign wheat. Other Canadian agricultural products which will be on the free list entering the United Kingdom in comparison with a considerable tariff tax levied on similar products from foreign countries, are flour, rye, barley, oa

LONDON, Oct. 13. (AP).—Discussions of the demand of the German government for equality of armaments, a problem which has become one of the major difficulties of the world disarmament conference at Geneva, was begun here today by Premier Herriot of France and Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald of Great Britain. Where the discussions will end, no one in authority here would venture to predict. The French premier arrived from Paris last night and was greeted by MacDonald, Sir John Simon, foreign secretary, Miss Ishbel MacDonald, the prime minister’s daughter and the French ambassador. American Watches. Norman H. Davis, American delegate to the Geneva arms conference will be on the sidelines during the parleys, ready to assist in any way possible. The only engagement he has at present for meeting Premier Herriot, however, is a luncheon at the French embassy tomorrow. Ambassador Andrew W. Mellon

BELFAST, Northern Ireland, Oct. 18—(UP)—British troops cooperating with Belfast police preserved order in Belfast today after two days of rioting, looting and hand-to-hand fighting between police and unemployed. “Seven truckloads of Royal Inniskilling Fusiliers were moved into the city late yesterday and went on patrol duty armed with machine guns. The troops are normally stationed at Hollywood, nearby. The second battalion of the King’s Royal Rifles are due tomorrow from Tidworth in the course of normal military relief. The War Office in London stated the arrival of the battalion was “purely a coincidence and merely in accordance with arrangements made some time ago,” and denied reports that British troops were being “rushed” here. In any event, the arrival of the Fusiliers and the word that the King’s Rifles were on their way was a welcome relief to Belfast citizens. The police force a

Belfast, Northern Ireland, Oct. 13.—British troops were hurried into Belfast yesterday to cope with new unemployment riots following in the wake of Tuesday’s outburst of violence in which one man was killed and more than 30 persons wounded seriously. A unit of the Iniskilling Fusiliers was brought in from the barracks at Holywood. The King’s Royal Rifles, it was announced, will arrive Friday. Yesterday afternoon, after there had been considerable shooting in the Falls Road area in the western part of the city and armored cars manned by police had gone into action, the authorities said they had the situation well in hand. Many arrests were made. In one street alone the police took 39 prisoners. It was said that plain clothes constables mingled with the mob during Tuesday’s outbursts and marked the leaders for subsequent arrests. Police enforced curfew restrictions at 8 last night in the a

Mea Vl Ed, VOL. £0 UB mA dispatch from Vera Cruz today said all telegraph lines in the Isthmus of Tehuantepec were down and it was feared that high winds, reaching there from Belize, British Honduras, had caused extensive damage. Torrential rains and high winds lashed Vera Cruz all day. The government weather bureau here said the storm apparently would decrease in intensity as it approached the Pacific Ocean.

London, Oct. 12. —-(P)— The British cabinet ended a virtual two-day session late this afternoon preparatory to Premier Edouard Herriot's visit to lay the new French disarmament plan before Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald. The cabinet dealt with the whole range of important problems which will face the government this week and next, when parliament opens. In addition to the disarmament discussions with M. Herriot, there are the negotiations over the Anglo-Irish controversy with President Eamon de Valera, which begin Friday. Norman H. Davis, American delegate to the Geneva disarmament conference, stands ready to assist in any way possible in the Franco-British disarmament negotiations, but the only engagement he has at present for meeting M. Herriot is a luncheon at the French embassy Friday. Ambassador Andrew W. Mellon also will attend the luncheon.

Athens, Greece, Oct. 13. (AP)— Samuel Insull, under indictment in Chicago in connection with the collapse of his utilities interests, refused today to surrender his passport to the American consul until he had consulted his lawyer. The attorney continued to refuse any statement on the case for publication. It was said at the American legation that the staff was without official notification in writing of Mr. Insull’s release from detention or the reasons for his release. He was liberated on Tuesday after a brief detention by the Athens police when the courts ruled that since formal ratification of the Greco-American extradition treaty had not been completed there was no legal warrant for keeping him in custody.

1932-09-04.text: SAULCHINSONS 10 GUCemanc. | Ottawa, Sept. 3. (AP)—George R. Hutchinson and his party of seven, flying from New York to London over the Arctic route, reached Godthaab, Greenland, at 7:00 p.m. yesterday, the department of marine was informed by radio today.

Manchester, Eng., Sept. 3.—No break in the textile strike situation is expected during the weekend. The leaders of the operatives organizations have gone to Newcastle for Monday’s session of the trade union congress in the hope of obtaining pledges of financial assistance for the cotton workers from the general trade union organization.

PLEASURE BEACH PARA, Bridgeport, Conn, Sept. 3—Governor Franklin D. Roosevelt carried his presidential campaign into New England tonight with a veiled appeal for the support of the Al Smith Democrats and a reiteration of his determination to fight for the “forgotten man” if he is elected chief executive of the nation. Addressing a crowd estimated at 20,000 and composed of Democratic leaders from all parts of New England, Governor Roosevelt flayed the Republican leadership at Washington, and charged that it has failed to understand that government “must consider the high, the middle and the low.” “Millions of voters are turning today to the leadership of a revitalized Democracy,” he declared. Governor Roosevelt said that under his principle and that of the Democratic party “the small farmer and the small homeowner must be the object of our careful solicitude in these times of distress and

Berlin, Aug. 2.—(AP)—The German republic, as a result of Sunday's election, faced a situation today resembling the days of Bismarck, with Gen. Kurt von Schleicher in the role of iron chancellor. Chancellor Franz von Papen, head of the present cabinet, the power behind which is the decisive junker-General von Schleicher, informed the Associated Press his government intended to stay in power, defying the Reichstag if necessary. Referring to the post-election riots yesterday in which four were slain, the chancellor said whoever is found responsible for the "regrettable events" would find the cabinet "determined to deal swiftly and summarily with them." Dr. Franz Bracht, dictator of Prussia under Von Papen, warned that swift retribution would be meted out to offenders. The chancellor made it clear that he would continue to rule Germany without party support. "My colleagues and I," he continu

SHANGHAI, Sept. 3. (UP)—After trapping him by a ruse the Japanese chief of police of Antung, Manchuria, attempted to force R. M. Talbot, American acting customs commissioner, to hand over customs revenues, the customs inspector general here was advised today in a telegram from Talbot. "Securing my presence at a dinner supposedly sponsored by Chinese, the Manchukuo police chief and his aide, both of them Japanese, bullied me for three hours to hand over the balance of customs revenues," Talbot's telegram stated. "I refused to sign a check for the revenues and only secured my release by signing a promise to again telegraph you the seriousness of their demands." Talbot advised that he feared force would be used against him. The American customs agent has steadfastly refused to turn over customs revenues of the Antung port to officials of Manchukuo, recently established government in Manchur

PARIS, Sept. 2 (4)—Although the United States is not a signatory to the Versailles treaty, France intends to consult the American Government in connection with Germany's new demand for equality in arms with the other European powers. In official quarters today it was explained the reason for consulting America is that the clauses of the Versailles treaty covering German arms are embodied also in the separated peace treaty which the United States negotiated with Germany in 1921. Meantime the French government will take its time examining the German aide-memoire which demands revision of the Versailles armaments clauses. This consideration will be undertaken in collaboration with the other Versailles signatories, Will Consult League The belief was expressed here that France will not depart from the traditional policy of turning over to the League of Nations or to the disarmament conference

Nemuro, Japan, Sept. 8.--(2)-- Capt. Wolfgang von Gronau and his three companions on a round-the-world flying jaunt, were ready here today for a flight to Kasumiguara naval base, 2 miles northeast of Tokyo. The flight from Nemuro to Kasumiguara is 600 miles, and the take off was set for 10 a.m. Sunday. The captain had expected to rest here until Monday, but the funeral of a Japanese navy flier will be held at Kasumiguara Monday; and the navy suggested that it might be inconvenient.

1932-07-19.text: Ottawa, Ont., July 19.—(AP)—Stanley Baldwin, former prime minister of Great Britain and leading delegate to the imperial trade conference which opens Thursday, believes the conference should not confine itself to the British empire, but should point the way back to prosperity to the world. “The delegates at Ottawa,” he said at Montreal yesterday, as he left the steamer and boarded the special train prepared to bring the British delegation here, “can reach agreements which will increase trade between different parts of the empire and so promote the well-being of every unit of the empire. “But we also believe that, by the methods we adopt, we can set an example for the whole world in breaking down obstacles to commerce, in aiding a revival of agriculture, industry and trade and so bringing peoples safely through the tragic depression of recent times.” The British, Northern Ireland, India,

LONDON, July 19—(?)—Ambassador Andrew W. Mellon said today he would leave for New York tomorrow on the steamer Majestic to spend several weeks on an unofficial visit. His son, Paul, will accompany him. Mr. Mellon said nothing but personal affairs took him back to the United States and that he did not contemplate engaging in any political activity. He said he had promised his son he would go back with him if he could and since official business was dull at this time he was doing so.

GENEVA, (U.P)— ‘Substantial reduction in world armaments applied to land, naval and air armaments,' has been agreed upon by the United States, Great Britain and France. Their agreement was noted in the draft of the disarmament resolution which will be adopted, it is expected, by the world disarmament conference, after which the world powers will negotiate settlement of certain armament differences. The resolution declared that the conference was “guided by the underlying principles of the Hoover Declarations.” It did not, however, cite any specific reduction in any type of armament. President Hoover’s suggestion called for approximately 33 1-2 percent reductions. The resolution recommended the arms truce, expiring November 1, be renewed for four months. Reducing means of aggression was given as the primary objective of the conference. The world disarmament conference was expected to adjo

(Associated Press Staff Writer) - WITH GOVERNOR, ROOSEVELT, LITTLE BOARS HEAD, N. H., July 18.—(P)—Governor Franklin D. Roosevelt, homeward bound after a vacation cruise along the New England coast, today faced the job of overseeing completion of his presidential campaign organization. He expects to announce his campaign plans within a few days. His vacation cruise culminated Saturday night at Portsmouth, and Sunday he spoke at a large Democratic demonstration at Hampton Beach. He planned to return home today by automobile after a visit to Colonel Edward M. House, former adviser to President Wilson. Mayor James J. Walker's answer to Samuel Seabury’s contention that the chief executive of New York City is unfit to hold office was to be one of Gov. Roosevelt's first considerations on his arrival in Albany. It was expected that Walker's reply would be laid on Roosevelt's desk this week. The

BOSTON, July 19 — A plan which its sponsors believe would add three million persons to the nation’s payrolls on the basis of the current business volume, will be projected for nation-wide discussion at a meeting to be held here tomorrow, the New England council announced today. The meeting is to be held under the auspices of the New Hampshire unemployment relief committee and the Massachusetts commission on the stabilization of employment. It is to be called the joint conference on the flexible work day and week and will be attended by the governors of the New England states and nationally known industrialists and educators. They will discuss a plan known as the New Hampshire plan for re-employment, developed by Harold M. Davis, industrial engineer of Nashua, N. H. It involves application to units of government and business of the principle of flexible working hours. The objective, accor

LOCH LAMOND, Scotland (DP) — Kaye Don, daring British racing driver, broke the world’s speedboat record twice Monday when he sent the powerful Miss England III bulleting over the choppy waters of Loch Lomond at the amazing speed of 119.81 miles an hour on his second attempt. - He wrested the world mark from the United States on his first attempt this morning, beating Gar Wood's record of 111.71 with a speed of 117.43. Don dared unfavorable weather to zoom over the official course again at the still greater speed. On one of the two official runs which registered the fast average of 119.81, the long, streamlined craft roared over the official one-mile course at 120.50 miles an hour. This made Don the first to travel two miles a minute on the water. In addition to breaking the world record twice, Don also beat the British national record of 98.96 miles an hour, established by Sir Henry Seag

former French Ambassador to the United States, died this morning. He was 77 last February. For some time he had been suffering from a kidney ailment, but although his health was delicate, his death was not expected. Death came peacefully as he lay in his Paris home. It was learned he had been under the care of a physician for the past eight days because of a constitution weakened by a series of kidney operations some years ago. Madame Jusserand was with him when he died.

By The Associated Press Berlin, July 18.—The German government issued a decree today banning all outdoor demonstrations following a weekend of political rioting in which 15 persons were killed and scores injured. The cabinet faced a number of other possibilities such as declaring a state of emergency demanded by various political groups forbidding the wearing of uniforms as the Centrists and trade unions want, or outlawing the Communists as the Nazis demanded, but it considered a general ban on all outdoor processions and demonstrations, the most effective method of avoiding further bloody weekends. Permission to wear uniforms continued, however. The cabinet reinstated them under pressure from Adolf Hitler, Nazi leader, and could hardly afford politically to rescind its own orders. In some quarters it was maintained that as long as the uniforms are permitted, the possibility of further c

1932-04-10.text: WINDSOR, Eng., April 9. (UP)— Andrew W. Mellon presented his credentials to King George today as U. S. ambassador to the court of St. James. The ceremony took place at historic Windsor Castle. Mellon arrived by motor from London. He was met by Major Harding, the king's private secretary, and conducted to the king.

WINDSOR, Eng., April 9. UP United States Ambassador Andrew W. Mellon presented his credentials to King George today and was accorded the unusual honor of being asked to luncheon in the famous old castle on the hill above the Thames. Sir John Simon, British Foreign Secretary, escorted Mr. Mellon on his ceremonial visit to the king.

Los Angeles, April 9—(#7)—A woman, so certain her husband is not dead that she shows no sign of grief, waited today at an undertaking establishment for the man, John David Guleph, 71, physician and claimant to the English throne, to show signs of life. She has ordered the body held five days by the undertaker before burial, declaring her husband is not dead, but is in a state of suspended animation. “Why, he has been in this same condition five times before; four times while a soldier in India and a fifth time at our home here in California,” she said. Three physicians have announced Guleph dead, but Mrs. Guleph refuses to consider herself a widow. Guleph claimed to be a son of King Edward VII. of England by a morganatic marriage. In 1910, he published a book in England setting forth his claims. He was ignored by English royalty.

LONDON, April 9 ().—The Sunday Express said tonight it understood a delegation of Jugoslavian deputies, led by a former cabinet minister, was coming to London to offer the throne of Jugoslavia to Prince Arthur of Connaught, nephew of King George. The newspaper said King Alexander of Jugoslavia does not feel too secure on his throne. He was understood to have placed 7,000,000 pounds to his credit in London in case of eventualities, the story added.

BERLIN, April 9. (4)—The second political battle of Von Hindenburg vs. Hitler, the greatest electoral contest in the history of Germany, was all but ended today as more than 37,000,000 voters prepared again to elect a president of the reich. In contrast with that which preceded the first (and indecisive) election four weeks ago, the campaign for tomorrow's voting has been brief but bitter. Held down by the decree proclaiming a political truce over the Easter holidays, it did not begin until last Sunday, Followers of Von Hindenburg, the 84-year-old former field marshal of the Kaiser’s armies, were confident today that he would win. They based their confidence on the fact that he fell short of a clear majority over all candidates in the election of March 13 by only 174,328 out of 37,658,036 votes. In tomorrow's election a simple plurality will reelect him. The battle is between Hindenburg

| Rome, Apr. 5—Italy advanced a “five-year plan” for world peace today, suggesting renunciation of war debts and reparations, revision of peace treaties, elimination of tariff barriers and fewer international conferences. The five-year plan of disarmament was sent to the League of Nations. The other resolutions were adopted by the Fascist Grand Council in its capacity of supreme advisory body of the nation. The grand council met under the presidency of Premier Benito Mussolini. Its resolutions regarding the world crisis, “which now has a moral and political rather than economic aspect,” were: 1. The necessity of renunciation of reparations and cancellation of war debts, 2. Suppression of restrictions of international trade before they result in the strangling trade of all countries, 3. Relief of the Danubian countries, representing 70,000,000 inhabitants. 4. Revision within the spirit of

BERLIN.—(#)—Dr. Hans Luther, president of the Reichsbank, narrowly escaped assassination by a bullet fired at him Saturday night while he was pacing the platform of the Potsdamer station in Berlin waiting for a train to take him to Basel, Switzerland. The bullet, fired at close range by one of two men who had been quietly walking up and down the platform, passed through one sleeve of Dr. Luther's coat and inflicted a slight scratch about an inch and a half below his elbow. The bullet then entered the heel of a nearby railway porter’s boot. The man who fired the shot told police his name was Dr. Max Roosen and that he was 58. He said he was born in Buenos Aires, went to London in 1930 and had been only a short time in Berlin. He smilingly surrendered his pistol. Both he and his companion, who gave the name of Werner Kertscher, admitted cheerfully, police said, that they planned to shoot D

MOSCOW, April 9. (#)—Judas Stern and Sergei Vassiliev, convicted last week of the attempted assassination of Dr. Fritz von Twardowski, counsellor to the German embassy, were executed today by a firing squad.

1932-04-21.text: GENEVA, April 21.—(4)— Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald of Great Britain and Premier Andre Tardieu of France met with Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson today in a private conference at Secretary Stimson’s villa shortly after the arrival of the two premiers from Paris on a morning train. Immediately after the British and French premiers arrived, a bustle of preparation began for the conferences of the officials.

LONDON. —(4)— Ambassador Mellon’s answer Thursday to the protest of American women dry leaders against serving liquor in the American embassy here was that he had no statement to make. At the embassy it was said there was nothing to add to the statement Mr. Mellon made when he arrived in England that he would probably follow the custom of the country.

Amoy, China, April 21 (Ar)—The evacuation of this treaty port was begun by the government forces today in anticipation of its capture any hour by the communists under General Sun Liang-Chen who has routed the government troops in city after city along his march. The British cruiser Devonshire was standing by to protect British inhabitants, among whom are a number of women and children. Many Chinese fled to the countryside, fearing looting and bloodshed, although the city was still comparatively quiet. Hongkong, April 21 (AP)—The British warship Devonshire at Amoy reported today that refugees were flocking into the city, driven by the advancing communist army, and that the government troops were retreating toward Changpu and Tungon. Chinese reports said the communists were expected to capture the city any moment.

London, April 21. (4)—Failure of the national government to provide in the new budget for war debt payments to the United States has brought down on the administration an attack from the labor opposition. The omission was assailed in the House of Commons yesterday by Maj. C. R. Attlee, labor spokesman, who said Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer, who presented the budget Tuesday, apparently proceeded on the principle that no American payments would have to be made. “There is already a reminder from the United States,” Major Attlee said, “that there is not the slightest chance of getting any relief from that quarter, therefore the chancellor hasn’t really met the budget situation in this respect at all.” The public has paid little attention to the debts phase of the budget. It has been pointed out that the chancellor announced his decision to hold these accounts in suspense

LONDON, April 21.—()-—Sir Francis Laurence John Barrow, 69, Great Britain's missing baronet who had not been heard from by friends or relatives for 18 years until yesterday, was married today at the registry office to Edith Townsend, 52, of London. His “reappearance” occurred at the registry office yesterday when he called there to secure his marriage license. He denied he had been missing and said he had been living in England all the time. In January of last year the British radio system broadcast an appeal to him to come home when his eldest son was critically ill. He said he renounced his title twenty years ago.

Dublin, Irish Free State, April 20. President Eamon de Valera today got past the first legislative barricade in his battle to scrap the oath of allegiance to the British crown. The Dail Eireann passed on first reading the abolition measure he promised to the Irish voters when he asked them to turn the government of the Free State over to his Fianna Fail party. The action postponed until next Wednesday the fiery debate that advocates and opponents of the proposal alike expect. Deputy McDermott, independent, served formal notice of objection to the measure. De Valera party leaders expressed confidence that they would be able to swing the required votes when the bill finally is acted on. The British government has held that the Free State is bound to retain the oath as well as to continue payment of land annuities, which Mr. De Valera has informed London will be discontinued.

WASHINGTON, April 21.-- Great Britain has no intention of repudiating her war debts, the United Press was told on highest authority in London, after failure to provide in the budget for such payments caused worldwide comment. The United Press found that the only other indication new budgets might not include reparations payments came from Germany, where newspapers hailed the British decision as 'the death sentence for reparations.' At Washington it was made known that the United States had asked all war debtor nations to sign formally agreements previously only initialed by which they would resume payments suspended by the Hoover moratorium. The French budget adopted April 1 made allowance for reparations receipts and payments to the United States. Radicals there contended that the budget would show a deficit because Germany was considered certain to default on reparations, while France

LONDON, April 21—(WP)—Anglo-American cooperation to solve the world crisis was strongly urged by Winston Churchill, former Chancellor of the Exchequer, during debate on the British budget in the House of Commons today. Churchill, in a powerful speech lasting an hour, said the crisis was due primarily to a rise in the price of gold and poor distribution of gold stocks. If the U.S. and Great Britain reached an agreement, Churchill said, ‘France in spite of her hoards of gold would have to ask admission to our councils the next morning.’ It was Churchill's first important public utterance in more than a year of political silence.

1932-04-23.text: LONDON, April 23.— (UP) —The Daily Mail reported today that Greta Garbo, Swedish film star, would be married soon to Wilhelm Soerenson, son of a Stockholm financier and close friend of Prince Sigvard of Sweden. According to the Daily Mail correspondent at Stockholm, the wedding will be in Berlin. It was understood that Sorenson and Prince Sigvard arrived in Berlin to complete arrangements for it. HOLLYWOOD, April 23.—(UP)—That Greta Garbo, film star, will marry Wilhelm Sorenson, son of a Swedish financier, as reported in London, was doubted today by her motion picture associates. Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer officials said they "doubted if there was any truth to the reports." Miss Garbo, who holds a contract with M-G-M, could not be reached for a statement.

London, April 22.—(#)—Beginning at midnight next Monday the British tariff wall against foreign products goes up to twice its present height. The import duties advisory committee recommended last night that the duty be raised from ten to twenty per cent on almost every kind of manufactured product imported into the country effective at midnight April 25. On a limited number of articles the duty will be 15 per cent and for some articles in the luxury or semi-luxury goods the committee placed a duty of 33 1-2 per cent for three months until it has had an opportunity to fix a more permanent schedule.

Stratford-On-Avon, England, Apr. 23—William Shakespeare was honored by the world today as the hometown boy who made good when the Prince of Wales opened the new and modernistic Shakespeare Memorial Theatre here. The theme of the occasion was not merely the pride of this quaint Warwickshire market town in its most famous son, but there was more than a touch of that sentiment in its picturesque and winding streets. Here Shakespeare lived and loved and laughed; here he was born and here he died. And here he lies buried under a simple stone in Holy Trinity Church. Tradition has it, too, that this was both his birth and death day. Great and near great made pious pilgrimages here today, but all seemed dim against the luster of the butcher’s son who wrote pieces for the theatre 300 years ago. The Prince of Wales made a speech and unfurled the king’s flag. An ode, composed for the occasion by Jo

Ottawa, April 23 (P)—A member of Scotland Yard, London’s famous police agency, is reported to be in the United States aiding in the search for the kidnapped son of Col. Charles A. Lindbergh. Friends of Inspector T. Gallagher, of Scotland Yard, have received word that he has been in the United States for two weeks. He is said to be there at the invitation of United States police officials to assist in the search for the Lindbergh baby.

Amoy, China, April 23.—(AP)—Chinese Communist army occupied Chaowei, fifteen miles east of Chanchow today, considerably increasing the tenseness of the situation here. Another group of foreign missionaries, most of them British, arrived here from the Hinterland seeking safety. The United States submarine tender Canobus and four submarines arrived from Manila on a trip northward for a brief stay and a British submarine tender and five submarines arrived from Hong Kong also on the way north. The arrival of these ships, which officials said, had nothing to do with the emergency here crowded the local harbor here with foreign fighting craft.

WASHINGTON, April 23.—(UP)— Execution of Juan B. Wainwright, a British subject, by Guatemalan authorities for attempting a communist revolution has been reported to the state department. The story of Wainwright's death contains the dramatic qualities of a novel. When his execution seemed certain, he slashed his wrist with a razor blade and wrote in blood on the walls of his cell this final challenge: “Long Live Communism!” Six Central Americans representing several nationalities were arrested with Wainwright, but he alone was executed. Wainwright's execution centered attention on reports to the state department which indicate a quickening of communist activity in Latin America during the last six or eight months. This trend is interpreted in responsible quarters here to be the result of distressing economic conditions, which always provide fertile soil for radicalism. Dispatches to the s

BARRY, Wales (7) — Ten of a crew of 12 men were missing today from the Spanish trawler Upia Mendi, which ran on the rocks off the Pembrokeshire coast and sank. The steamer Daldorch rescued two and landed them here.

NEW YORK, April 23 (AP).— Clocks will jump ahead an hour at 2 a.m. Sunday for 35,000,000 Americans in 15 states, as hundreds of communities go on daylight saving time, the Merchants’ Association estimated yesterday. New York and its environs and a good sector of New England will be on the “fast time” unanimously.

1932-05-17.text: Aden, Arabia, May 17. (4)-Eighty to 100 persons, most of them first class passengers, were trapped aboard the blazing French motorship Georges Phillipar yesterday and some of them must have lost their lives, survivors declared when they arrived here today aboard the British steamer Contractor. The fire, discovered when the ship was off Cape Guardafui, Italian Somaliland, spread with extreme rapidity from the aft of the vessel, driving the passengers toward the bow. There were harrowing scenes as the passengers strove to reach their lifeboats amid the smoke and confusion. Some of them, apparently, were overcome before they were able to do so. No Serious Panic But the survivors aboard the Contractor declared that at no time was there serious panic. Some of the rescued were unable to reach the lifeboats. So they jumped into the shark-infested water and were picked up later. More than 100 of

BOMBAY, May 17. -- Riotous fighting between Hindus and Moslems which caused 80 deaths and 950 injuries in four days spread to the mill area today after armored cars and British troops rushed here had eased the situation in the Hindu quarter. Despite the police and military reinforcements, today casualties were 13 dead and 150 injured. Police fired on mobs looting and burning in 12 different localities. Curfew orders were proclaimed prohibiting free movement, loitering, or the assembly of over five persons in the streets. The second battalion of the Green Howards (Yorkshire) regiment and five armored cars from Poona patrolled native sections. Hindu mill hands attacked a mosque last night. Police were unable to break up gatherings of workers while the military could not be called away from patrol duty. Bombay auxiliary units were mobilized. Tanks were en route here from Poona.

LONDON, May 17. — At least 100 persons are missing from the liner Georges Phillipar, according to a wireless message to the Evening Standard from Capt. Owen of the British ship Contractor, which rescued 75 of the liner’s passengers. Capt. Owen credited Capt. Vica of the Georges Phillipar with the estimate of at least 100 lost. Many first class passengers were reported trapped in their cabins by fire. “Approaching the Georges Phillipar we found a few hundred people grouped on the forecastle head,” Capt. Owen reported. “We lowered two boats and took off 75 passengers. The fire is believed to have originated from a short circuit in an empty deluxe cabin.” “The wireless room and the captain's quarters were said to have been destroyed first. The fire traveled rapidly through all state-rooms fanned by a fresh breeze. My officers on the second journey reported that the French captain was the la

London, May 16 (UP)—A mystery airplane was sighted by two steamships in the Atlantic today, flying from the direction of North America toward the British Isles. The ship was a monoplane equipped with pontoons. The air ministry had no knowledge of any airplanes maneuvering at sea. Other aviation quarters and shipping offices could not identify the plane. The ship was reported by the American steamer Ala, over which it passed at 11:45 a.m. GMT (7:45 a.m. New York time) flying east. At that time it was about 155 miles from Landsend. It had passed the American steamer McKeesport an hour earlier. The latest reported position of the plane was 49.50 north, 9.44 west.

Bombay India, May 17—(#)—The toll of the fierce Hindu-Muslim riots which have made shambles of several districts of Bombay for several days had risen to 71 dead and 700 injured. Seven were killed and 50 injured during the afternoon in spite of the fact the city was patrolled by British tanks and troops brought here last night. Except for the rioters and the troops and police the streets were virtually deserted. The rest of the population stayed indoors as the riot continued. Along the streets garbage and refuse unattended for three days was rotting filling the city with an abominable stink. Bursts of rifle fire broke out from time to time during the day as the troops clashed with rioters. Authorities this afternoon issued a curfew order which prohibits more than five persons congregating at any spot. The riot spread to the mill area, forcing the closing of mills which threw 45,000 men an

BOMBAY, India, May 16 (P)— Three days of murderous strife between Hindus and Moslems, during which British troops fired on the rioters to restore order, had resulted in 60 dead and 700 injured tonight. Today's casualties were 22 dead and 150 injured. Hundreds of families were fleeing the city. Police fired five times in different places today into the crowds which were looting and burning.

Paris, May 11.—(A%y—The office of the Messageries Maritimes said today its latest word of the disaster to the French motorship Georges Philippar was that 420 survivors were aboard the Soviet tanker Sovietskala Neft, 104 aboard the British steamer Contractor and 184 aboard the Mahsud. Announcing that they had received information about a possible attempt to fire the ship, the police said it seemed out of the question that any political group was responsible for the disaster. Believe Most Passengers Saved. The Georges Philippar was homeward bound from her maiden trip to the Orient. When she sailed from Marseilles outward bound she was carefully inspected. Police took extra precautions, identifying passengers as well as members of the crew. The belief was expressed that virtually all the passengers on the ship were saved. (The captain of the ship was quoted in a dispatch to London as saying

BOMBAY, India, May 16. (AP)—Savage attacks and counter-attacks among rioting Hindus and Moslems, interspersed with volleys of rifle fire from the ranks of British troops, raised the death toll to 60 today in the most serious communal strike of recent years. The streets of the native sections of Bombay were littered with the debris of guerilla warfare, murder, arson and pillage which has steadily worsened during three days of rioting. More than 700 persons have been injured. Hundreds of families are fleeing the city. Campaign Futile British troops in armored cars and motor patrols roamed the streets in a concerted but futile campaign to suppress the disturbances. There were many attacks on pedestrians in isolated by-lanes. Victims were butchered by ruthless assailants, houses were set afire and streets sometimes for a distance of almost a mile—were ablaze. Fighting today was even more int

1932-06-20.text: DUBLIN (#) — Ireland gave its heart away today to a smiling man in scarlet, He is Cardinal Lauri. As the Pope’s personal representative he will be the chief figure at the Eucharistic congress here this week. Next Sunday he will celebrate a pontifical high mass before a million people. Long before his ceremonial landing at Kingstown quay this afternoon, where Archbishop Byrne, primate of Ireland, and President De Valera and lesser notables assembled to welcome him, thousands lined the route of the papal legate’s triumphal procession to Dublin pro-cathedral for the solemn ecclesiastical reception.

London, June 20.—(U.P)—The government will consider the advisability of asking the United States to investigate the causes of Violet Sharpe’s suicide in Englewood, N.J., Oliver Stanley, home office undersecretary, told a questioner in the house of commons today. The suicide of Miss Sharpe just as she was about to be re-questioned on the Lindbergh kidnapping case led to charges here that she had been the victim of police persecution. Stanley told Brig. Gen. Howard C. Brown, conservative, that the government had not made inquiries to Miss Sharpe's parents about the matter. Brown then asked if Stanley were aware that “the parents owing to a letter they got from their late daughter, are convinced she committed suicide as a result of the methods of investigation she went through, and are very anxious in the interests of justice that the case should be investigated.” “What the honorable member

By MELVIN K. WHITELEATHER, LAUSANNE, Switzerland, June 19.—(?)—The big four of Europe — Great Britain, France, Italy and Germany, will meet here tomorrow for a private and intensive effort to chart a definite channel for conversations they hope will permanently settle war debts and reparations. Their meeting will come on the eve of plenary debate, which was dropped Friday after the nations represented here agreed to forego an estimated $48,000,000 in war payments for the duration of the conference. As the matter now stands, Great Britain has voiced her willingness to cancel all war payments, Germany has insisted she cannot pay more now, at any rate, and pressed for an end to reparations, France admitted Germany could not pay now, but insisted that treaties must be observed, and Italy had previously come out for cancellation. King Albert of Belgium today (Continued on Page 2: Col 3.)

DUBLIN, June 19.—(#)—Dublin had its first glimpse today of the sheen and luster the Eucharistic congress this week will bring. Many of the prelates appeared in services. In the morning there was general communion of men throughout the island. Retreats for men concluded in the afternoon.

WIMBLEDON, Eng., June 20— Ellsworth Vines, ranking United States tennis player, successfully opened his campaign for the English championship at Wimbledon today, defeating I. Duplaix, a little known French player, in straight sets, 7-5, 6-3, 6-4. Gregory Mangin of Newark, American Indoor champion, won his opening match from L. Hecht of England, in straight sets, 6-1, 6-2, 6-3. Jean Borotra, French veteran, had to go five hard-fought sets to eliminate his young countryman, Andre Merlin, in the first round. The scores were 0-6, 6-1, 1-6, 6-4, 6-2, Merlin winning the first set in the record time of seven minutes. The New Zealand star, Andrews, eliminated another of France's veterans, Jacques Brugnon, 6-1, 6-3, 6-3. Sydney Wood Jr., defending champion, joined the American advance by defeating A. M. Wedd, Cheshire champion, 6-2, 6-2, 8-6 in the final match of the day on the center court.

Dublin, June 20. (P)—Next Saturday promises to be woeful for the milkmen. With the celebration of a pontifical high mass during the eucharistic congress Sunday, the public fears the milkmen won't be able to get through the streets, so folks are ordering double for Saturday.

ST. BEES, England, June 20— (AP) -- Scotland Yard is investigating the discovery of an unexploded bomb yesterday under a platform from which Lord Lloyd, former high commissioner for Egypt, the Bishop of Carlisle and other prominent men spoke during a school commencement. The bomb was discovered after the exercises. A home office official said today that it had been made by an expert.

Tokio, June 20.—The question of confiscation of the Chinese custom revenues in Manchuria by Henry Pu-Yi's government has been called to the attention of Japanese ambassador Dubuchi at Washington by Secretary of State Stimson, it was learned from an official quarter here today. Secretary Stimson, this source said, called the ambassador's attention to American consular reports from Manchuria describing efforts of the Pu-Yi government to establish custom autonomy there and assume control of all Chinese custom offices including that at Dairen which is on Japanese leased territory. The British ambassador, Sir Francis Lindley, also visited the foreign office here and discussed the same situation. It was understood the powers favor the matter threatens the integrity of the Chinese maritime customs by which a large portion of China's foreign indebtedness is secured. The foreign office here takes

1932-04-28.text: Geneva, Switzerland, Apr. 28— (AP)—Henry L. Stimson, American Secretary of State, decided today to postpone his departure from Geneva until Saturday “or later.” Mr. Stimson conferred with Ramsay MacDonald, Prime Minister of Great Britain, and Dr. Heinrich Bruening, Chancellor of Germany, and later lunched with the American delegation to the world disarmament conference. It was not immediately apparent why Mr. Stimson decided to delay his leave taking at Geneva, nor was it revealed whether or not he had also postponed his sailing for the United States, which was arranged yesterday for Wednesday May 4 from Cannes, France on the liner Vulcania. It was assumed however, that he would adhere to his sailing schedule merely holding off on his departure from Geneva for Cannes.

PORT DARWIN, AUSTRALIA, April 28—()—C. W. A. Scott, noted flier, landed here at 10:22 a.m. today after a flight from Lympne, England, in which he recovered his record for flights between England and Australia. He beat the record of J. A. Butter by 5 hours and 40 minutes. Scott's time for the flight was 8 days, 20 hours and 49 minutes.

LONDON, April 28 (U.P)—An Exchange Telegraph dispatch from Geneva reported today some of the bills paid for the Lindbergh baby’s ransom had been changed in Switzerland. Police were searching for the persons who changed them, concentrating in the Canton of Neuchâtel.

DUBLIN, Irish Free State, April 28, (4)—William Norton, leader of the Irish laborite group, tonight announced that the laborites would support President Eamon De Valera’s bill abolishing the oath of allegiance to the English crown, thus practically assuring the passage of the measure in the Dáil Éireann.

DUBLIN, April 27 (AP)— The long-promised fight over President Éamon de Valera's attempt to wipe away the oath of allegiance to the British crown reached its climax today in an exciting session of the Dáil Éireann. As a prelude to the main battle the government was unexpectedly defeated by a vote of 76 to 66 on a side issue connected with the problem of unemployment, but the determined De Valera took that setback in his stride. In the face of opposition cries of "resign! resign!" he moved on to the debate on the oath, a debate raised to new heights by declaring that "the moment the people are ready to stand for an independent republic we will be quite ready to lead them." A round of applause from his adherents greeted that statement. The president made it clear, however, that it was his purpose to abolish the oath now required of all public servants in Ireland—without withdrawing the Free

Dublin, April 27.—(#)—President Eamon De Valera, moving the second reading of his bill to abolish the oath of allegiance to the British crown, told the Free State Dail today that the moment the Irish people are ready for an independent republic, he will be ready to lead them. The abolition bill was brought up immediately after the government had been defeated by 74 to 66 in a division on the unemployment issue. Immediately there were shouts of “resign,” but the president made it clear he had no intention of resigning on that vote.

LONDON, April 28 -- The Daily Herald today said a “secret plan” for institution of a tariff on foreign meat, with preference to meat produced within the British empire, would be submitted to the imperial economic conference at Ottawa next July. The newspaper said the plan had been drawn up and signed by representatives of meat interests in Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Great Britain and approved by the National Union of Farmers.

HARBIN, Manchuria, April 27 (Pj)—Japan’s Manchurian military machine opened today the greatest drive since the capture of Chinchow in an effort to suppress a Chinese revolt against the government of Henry Pu-yi. Three Japanese brigades moved by rail and river boats, in a sweeping “pincers” movement against the rebel forces, estimated at 20,000, along the eastern lines of the Chinese Eastern Railway and in the lower Sungari valley. At the same time lesser Japanese forces sought to crush minor revolts in the Tunghua district, 125 miles east of Mukden and in the (Continued on page Four)

1932-03-10.text: Dublin, March 9, (AP)—Eamon de Valera, New York-born son of a Spanish father and an Irish mother, was elected President of the Irish Free State today by a vote in the Dail Eireann of 81 to 68. With his deeply furrowed face wreathed in smiles at his triumph after years of fighting with his back to the wall, the new chief executive this evening took actual charge of the Dail and presented the names of his ministers. The ministry is wholly Fianna Fail — the de Valera party name, which, translated, means soldiers of destiny. The Labor party, whose handful of votes will be needed to keep the de Valera government alive, was not represented.

LONDON, Feb. 18.—(UP).—The Bank of England reduced its bank rate one per cent to five per cent. STOCKHOLM, Feb. 18.—(UP).—The Swedish bank rate was reduced today by one half per cent to 5 3/4 per cent.

Aboard the Coast Guard Cutter Ossipee, Mar. 10 —(4)—The crew of the disabled collier H. F. De Bardelleben abandoned ship in their own boats at 2 a. m. today. All were taken aboard the British freighter Lagenbank. No one was injured. The position of the De Bardelleben when she was abandoned was latitude 39:36 north and longitude 68:53 west. The Lagenbank is still standing by the abandoned vessel while awaiting arrival of the Ossipee.

Dublin, Mar. 10--Mamou de Valera summoned his cabinet for the first time today and presided over the Republican ministers meeting pledged to break the oath of allegiance to the British crown and to win complete independence for Ireland. De Valera and members of his Fianna Fail Party formally subscribed to the oath when they took their seats in the new dail. They maintained they would act as quickly as possible to remove it from the free state constitution. One of the new government's first acts was expected to be abolition of the public safety act, passed by the Cosgrave government, which established military tribunals for the trial of terrorists. The tribunal was given the power of death sentences for some offenders.

Shanghai, China, Mar. 10—Four kidnappers faced a firing squad today at Trae Ho-King prison in Shanghai. Two of the men were convicted of abducting a compradore (native commission merchant) of the British American Tobacco Company in March, 1929, and the others were convicted of the same offense against a British company in 1930.

Melton Mowbray, England, March 10—Mrs. Marshall Field of Chicago was injured internally today when she was thrown from her horse during a run of the Fernie fox hunt. The horse rolled on her. Mrs. Field was taken home in an automobile.

Berlin, March 10—(”)—Government officials prepared today for any eventuality which might follow next Sunday's presidential election, even a general revolt of Adolf Hitler's national socialists. Some uneasiness developed yesterday over the possibility of an uprising of the Nazis in case the election goes against them. Two Hitlerite engineers, Theodore Eickel and F. Kemmet, were arrested at Ludwigshafen, charged with illegally manufacturing 80 bombs. An editorial in the Nazi newspaper at Halle declared there must be no second balloting even if Sunday's election brings no absolute majority for any of the four candidates. Police chiefs throughout the country assured the people that they were ready to prevent any illegality. Gustave Noske, provincial governor in President Paul von Hindenburg’s home town of Hanover, was especially outspoken. “Before me stand 1,000 steel-hard, trained men,” he

PARIS, Mar, 10—(AP)—The body of Aristide Briand was taken to the Quai D'Orsay this morning without other ceremony than the spontaneous expression of grief which came from many Parisians who lined the sidewalks with heads uncovered. Premier Andre Tardieu and other members of the government attended the removal. The body was placed in the clock room at the Quai D’Orsay where it will remain until the funeral Saturday.

1932-06-29.text: Lausanne, June 29. — Germany demanded revision of the Versailles peace treaty as a price for future payment of reparations of any type. The German demand was made known through an official announcement after it had been made to British Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald by German Chancellor Franz von Papen. The German delegation earlier had issued a communique, in the German language only, declaring bluntly that the Reich did not intend to pay any more reparations. The conversations between German and French delegates seeking an end to the reparations deadlock centered on reaching a compromise on the French demand for economic or political compensation for cancellation of reparations. Then the Germans brought forth their demand for revision of the “discriminator” provisions of Versailles, which include restriction of German armament and the clause holding Germany responsible for the war gui

LONDON, June 29.--(UP)—The suicide of Violet Sharpe, maid in the Morrow home at Englewood, was not caused by police violence in questioning her about the Lindbergh kidnapping, Capt. R. A. Eden, foreign under-secretary, told the House of Commons today. Eden said the British consul-general in New York reported he was satisfied "no physical violence or so-called third degree methods were used by the police."

LAUSANNE, Switzerland, June 29 (UP).—The six inviting powers to the reparations conference met tonight for an important meeting which may settle the fate of the conference. Represented were Great Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Belgium and Japan. Rumors of everything from a complete rupture to a last-minute compromise were current.

United Press Staff, Correspondent WIMBLEDON, June 29.—Miss Helen Jacobs of California won her way to the finals of the English tennis championship women's singles by defeating Mme. Rehe Mathieu of France in a semi-final match today. George Patrick Hughes and Fred Perry of England also reached the semi-finals by defeating Sidney Wood of New York and Gregory Mangin of Newark, N.J., 7-5, 7-5, 6-3.

Geneva, June 29.- Immediate adjournment of the Arms Conference cannot be considered by the United States delegation, Hugh S. Gibson, chief American delegate, informed Premier J. Ramsay MacDonald and Arthur Henderson, president of the conference, tonight. Gibson sought assurances that Britain does not contemplate such adjournment as reported.

(By The Associated Press) Lausanne, Switzerland, June 29.—Unconfirmed reports circulating here tonight said the Franco-German reparations deadlock had been broken with an agreement on the part of the Germans on the principle of 'payment of something on account.' Heretofore Chancellor Franz Von Papen has held that Germany cannot pay under any circumstances. It was learned in French circles that the German chancellor had 'modified his tone during the afternoon' regarding his earlier statement that the allied powers must alter the Versailles treaty before Germany would consider a different attitude toward reparations. These developments indicate that it would seem possible that some agreement might be reached at Lausanne without an adjournment. Von Papen earlier today laid before the powers a demand for revision of the Versailles treaty as a necessary preliminary for German participation in
Bombay, India, June 29.--(AP)— One man was killed and thirty were seriously injured today in a series of vicious riots between Hindus and Moslems.

BERLIN, June 28—Political disorders in various parts of Germany during the last 24 hours piled up a casualty list of four dead and more than 87 injured. Forty-four persons were arrested. Meanwhile President Paul von Hindenburg signed an edict which added to the confusion surrounding regulations restricting the activities of militant political groups. The edict, to be issued tomorrow, asserts federal law supersedes the laws of the states, and hence members of militant factions may wear their political uniforms even in the states which have raised objections to them. At the same time, the decree holds the state governments responsible for maintaining order and reaffirms that, in their discretion, they may ban individual political demonstrations or so far as the National Socialist hope for unconditional freedom is concerned. Three Communists were shot dead and seven were seriously injured,

1932-04-07.text: London, April 8. (4)—The four-power conference called by Prime Minister MacDonald to consider means of extending financial aid to the nations on the Danube ended today without an agreement. A communique issued by the foreign office after the close of the conference said each of our governments, Great Britain, France, Germany and Italy, agreed to address to the other three as soon as possible a statement of its views on points reserved and on the best means of further advancing the proposals considered. The conference adjourned without setting a definite date for the resumption of the parley. The conference also agreed that its work would be continued through the league council at Geneva Tuesday, as well as by negotiations among the governments.

LONDON, April 7 (4)—Representatives of the four power conference considering relief for the Danubian countries failed to reach a complete agreement this morning as they had hoped to do, and a meeting of the full conference scheduled for this afternoon was cancelled. Instead, the heads of the delegations—Prime Minister MacDonald, Pierre Flandin of France, Dino Grandi of Italy, and B. W. Von Beulow of Germany—continued their conversations, trying to reach a basis of agreement.

LONDON, April 7—()—Gloria Swanson and her husband, Michael Farmer, wanted a boy instead of a girl, Farmer revealed today, and Gloria had planned to call the boy “Mike.” They were “just a little bit disappointed,” he said, when a girl was born the night before last. Provisionally, he said, they have been calling the girl “Mike,” but another name will have to be chosen later. “Gloria and the baby are both getting along wonderfully,” he said. Gauzets are different because of an exclusive feature which makes them absolutely moisture proof. 35¢ for package of one dozen. Snow's Drug Store—

LONDON, April 6 (#)—Representatives of Great Britain, France, Germany and Italy, functioning as a kind of executive committee of Europe, today discussed ways and means of remedying the Danubian economic troubles, and they achieved what was authoritatively described as “very good progress.” Tomorrow morning committee meetings will be held for the purpose of examining numerous proposals and reports touching on the questions of guaranteed loans and tariff preferences among the Danubian states. Each of the four governments is appointing a treasury expert to examine the recent report of the League of Nations’ financial committee on the condition of the Danubian countries. These nations—Austria, Hungary, Jugoslavia, Czechoslovakia and Rumania—were not represented at the deliberations. The principal delegates participating in today’s session were Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald, Finance Ministe

St. John's N. F., April 7—(Pj)—Newfoundland’s capital was quiet today under the watchful eyes of 850 special police as citizens awaited political changes expected to result from recent riots against the government of Sir Richard Squires. Sir Richard, who disappeared when the fury of 10,000 rioters seemed to menace his life Tuesday night, slipped back into the colonial building last evening under the cover of the special police officers who had been quickly recruited from among former service men and other civilians. He declined to make any statement as to where he had been or what he may intend to do. Peter Cashin, former finance minister, who made charges of falsification against the prime minister two months ago, said he understood Sir Richard had agreed to submit his resignation or dissolve the assembly within 48 hours. Genoa, April 7.—The police were aghast today when, coming to the end of the trail in a search for counterfeiters, they discovered that excellently-made spurious coins of five and ten lire were being turned out by convicts at Marassi prison and circulated by the warden. The discovery caused such amazement that the chief government prosecutor has taken charge of the case and all the counterfeiters have been placed in solitary confinement.

ST. JOHN'S, N. F., April 6.—While Sir Richard Squires, Newfoundland's prime minister, remained in hiding from an angry populace, war veterans and municipal police late today repulsed a mob which sought to break into the government’s main depot. The crowd, using a battering ram, hurled itself at the depot door, but was driven away by a force of 600 former World War soldiers and police. The street was roped off and by nightfall the veterans and police appeared to have the situation well in hand. Although his resignation was expected momentarily, Sir Richard kept himself secreted as the government charted an uncertain course. Sir William Coaker, minister without portfolio, sounded the keynote of opposition sentiment by proposing a plan for a national government. He would place F.C. (Latted Press Leadacad Wire) BERLIN, April 7.—An "end of reparations" in exchange for German pledges was forecast as a development of the Lausanne debts and reparations conference today in a statement considered semi-official. The statement was part of a story circulated here by the Wolff Telegraphic Agency, generally considered to have sources close to the government. The foreign office, however, promptly denied any connection with the statement. Officials of the press department appeared to have no information regarding its source. Proclamation Expected The statement said it was believed the Lausanne conference would "bluntly proclaim the end of reparations, so far as Europe is concerned." Germany would be expected to maintain her own political situation in order and not to advocate revision of the Versailles treaty for a number of years in exchange for lifting of her reparations burde

1932-10-14.text: PARIS (UP).—Great Britain and France agreed today to hold a four-power conference at Geneva with Italy and Germany to allow the world disarmament conference to be resumed with German participation, the foreign office announced. The foreign office communique stressed the French victory in the London negotiations. It said Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald agreed on Premier Edouard Herriot’s insistence that the conference be held within the League of Nations' halls rather than at London.

HONG KONG, Oct. 14 (U.P)--Passengers aboard the Chinese owned steamer, Helikon, including an American missionary, were robbed today by Chinese pirates. Traveling as passengers, the pirates seized the vessel, which was flying the British flag, and locked her British officers into cabins. Without firing a shot, the pirates leisurely robbed the passengers aboard. Among the victims were Miss E. C. G. Boynton, American missionary and Mrs. Dirk Van Driest, a Canadian. The vessel was bound from Hong Kong to Saigon. The pirates kidnapped five Chinese passengers when they went ashore in a small native craft near Bia Pay.

Hongkong — The British Steamer Helikon, enroute from Hongkong to Saigon, was seized by a group of Chinese passengers and looted, it was reported here Friday. The steamer was held for 36 hours while the loot was transferred to junks in Heichechin bay. The captain was taken off as a hostage, but later released. One of the women passengers, a Miss E. B. Boynton, is an American, and the other, Mrs. Dirk Van Driest, is a Canadian. They were not molested. Both said they suffered great anxiety during the raid but were relieved when the pirates appeared to be amused by their phonograph and finally returned their jewelry.

London, Oct. 13—(@)—France and Great Britain, represented by the two premiers, agreed Thursday that it is essential to get Germany back into the world disarmament conference if that meeting is to achieve any constructive results. All morning and up to late Thursday evening Premier Herriot and Prime Minister MacDonald, with other officials of both governments, talked about disarmament at No. 10 Downing Street. Friday the discussion will be resumed. As often happens in such meetings as this the official communique gave little information. The statement issued Thursday evening said merely that there had been a discussion which was to be resumed. (By The Associated Press) Mukden, Manchuria, Oct. 14. — Japanese headquarters here announced today that airplanes had dropped leaflets printed in English over a number of points in the area west of Mukden, where an offensive against Chinese insurgents is under way, warning all foreigners to withdraw or concentrate in one city. It was estimated the area contains 20 foreigners, including eight American Catholic missionaries from the Maryknoll mission headquarters at Ossining, N. Y. Most of these were believed to be at Fushun, inside the Japanese lines, and out of danger. The Japanese said the drive against the insurgents was proceeding according to schedule. Advancing with unexpected speed in a sweeping enveloping movement from every direction, the Japanese announced they already have captured half of the Tungpien bandit zone which covers 20,000 square miles. It was not possible to estimate at this stage the extent to which the new rates will affect American business, but the experts are preparing schedules upon which such an estimate can be based. Dundalk, Northern Ireland, Oct. 14 (P)—The Honorable Katherine Plunket, said to be Ireland's oldest inhabitant, died at her home here today. On Nov. 9 she would have been 112 years old. This remarkable old lady was widely known throughout the United Kingdom and usually on her birthday there was a telegram from the king and queen.

'ATHENS, Greece, Oct. 14—()—Samuel Insull, wanted in Chicago to answer an indictment in connection with the collapse of his vast public utilities, wrote a letter to the American consul today explaining his reason for refusing to surrender his passport and thus to facilitate extradition proceedings. "Sir," he wrote, "I was very much surprised at your letter of yesterday informing me that the state department had instructed you to take up my passport. "It seems that they don’t know in Washington that my passport is valid until February, 1934 and that by its authority I can stay out of America in any country I choose. Since the passport was issued by the country of which I am a citizen, its withdrawal is impossible especially while I am traveling through foreign countries.
