1932-11-23.text: Washington, Nov. 23. (UP) —Thanksgiving Day at the White House will be observed simply according to the best New England traditions. President and Mrs. Hoover expect only a few personal friends for Thanksgiving dinner. The customary turkey and pumpkin pie are on the menu. In the afternoon the Chief Executive and Mrs. Hoover may attend religious services. A group of 100 children, coming here to protest against "child misery" are expected to present a petition at the White House sometime during the day, but there will be no attempt at picketing, according to Herbert Benjamin of the unemployed councils of America, which has sponsored the march.

Capetown, Union of South Africa, Nov. 22. (4@)--Amy Johnson, who holds the speed record for flight from England to Capetown, said today she will fly home next month in an attempt to set a record for the round trip.

| By The Associated Press. London, Nov. 22.—King George opened parliament today with all the usual dignity and ancient pageantry, but as soon as the ceremonies were over the House of Commons had a rough and tumble debate on the pressing problem of what to do about the unemployed. This issue was discussed at considerable length in the King's speech and subsequently in Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald's exposition of the government's policies. The attack came from George Lansbury, leader of the labor party, who declared that the speech from the throne “was not worthy of parliament or of being put into the King’s hands.”

BOLTON, ENGLAND — The Prince of Wales stepped out of his private railroad car here today to begin a two-day visit among part of the Lancashire unemployed, nearly 150,000 men and women living here, in Liverpool, and in St Helens and Wigan nearby. Thousands of unemployed greeted him at the station, cheering and waving handkerchiefs. Lord Derby, friend of the Prince and mayor of Bolton, greeted the royal visitor. The Prince did not smile often. When he did, it was in response to a cheer for “our Prince” from the unemployed who lined the sidewalks of this small, depressed community.

PARIS, Nov. 23 (#)—Premier Herriott and Lord Tyrell, the British ambassador, talked together for some time today, presumably about the attitude of both governments toward the American debts. They issued no communique but there were indications that France and Great Britain will adopt a common policy with the object of obtaining an eventual adjustment of the entire issue.

NEW YORK, Nov. 23.—(%)— The Evening Post said to-day that according to persistent reports in the financial district, New York banking interests, headed by J. P. Morgan and Company, have assured private London bankers that a substantial credit will be advanced to support sterling, if needed as a result of payments by the British treasury of the $95,000,000 war debt due the United States December 15th. Efforts to obtain confirmation of these reports at the house of Morgan were unavailing, but the Post said they were generally accepted in well-informed circles.

1932-04-05.text: New York, Apr. 5.—(AP)—J. P. Morgan & Co. is mailing checks totaling $20,000,000 to 110 American banks today. The payment is being made by the Morgan firm as the fiscal agent in this country of the British government. It will wipe out the $200,000,000 banking credit obtained last August in Britain's futile effort to avoid being pushed off the gold standard. The credit was arranged to run for a year, but, as a result of recent improvement in Britain's financial condition, she has been able to extinguish her indebtedness four months in advance of maturity. New York bankers say the repayment sets something of a record in international finance. About six months ago the finances of the British government were shaken to a point where a complete breakdown seemed possible. Fawcett, “lost” English explorer, in the Brazilian jungle about 1927, today said the colonel may be a voluntary exile from civilization. “A meeting in the jungle with an Englishman who said he was ‘not going back’ to civilization was described by Araujo, son of a Brazilian rubber exporter and now a resident of Washington. The region where he says he met the mysterious white man is near that in which Stephen Rattin, a Swiss trapper, recently reported meeting Fawcett and receiving from him a message asking to be rescued from “Indian captivity.” Leader Gets Lost Araujo said he led an expedition in 1925 into the Matto Grosso jungle looking for rubber. DUBLIN, April 5.—(UP)—The Irish Free State cabinet approved the government's reply to Great Britain regarding abolition of the oath of allegiance and retention of land annuities today and prepared to send the reply to London. The vote of the cabinet was unanimous, apparently disproving reports of dissension among Republican leaders. There had been rumors that Eamon De Valera, president of the executive council, had been forced to alter his attitude on Republican policies which London holds to violate the Anglo-Irish treaty. The text of the reply will not be made public until exchange of communications between the two governments is completed.

TOKIO, April 5.—(AP)—Possession or domination of the Philippines “would be as great a liability to Japan as it has been to the United States,’ a government spokesman said today, commenting on Secretary of State Stimson’s suggestion that withdrawal of American sovereignty would result in the domination of the islands by some foreign power, “probably either China or Japan.” The spokesman expressed the belief that the Japanese government would willingly enter into a treaty with America perpetually guaranteeing the neutrality and independence of the islands in the event they gain their freedom. The passage of the Hare independence bill in congress yesterday surprised official quarters here, in which Philippine independence has been regarded merely as a possibility for the distant future. Hopewell, N. J., April 5—(AP)— Col. Charles A. Lindbergh, who won his fame in the air, is using that same element in an attempt to get his stolen baby back. Optimism permeates the home on Sourland Mountain as the head of the household comes and goes on mysterious airplane journeys. Twice in three days he has soared away, apparently seeking a yacht off the Massachusetts coast. The trips are believed to have some unexplained connection with rumors that ransom negotiations are being carried on with kidnappers who took Charles A. Lindbergh, Jr., 21 months old, from his crib March 1. WASHINGTON, April 5—()—A veto apparently awaits at the White House for legislation to grant independence to the Philippine Islands. By an astonishing margin—306 to 47—the Hare bill under which independence would come after eight or ten years, passed the House yesterday. Later this session, this bill or a substitute for it will be taken up in the Senate, with fair chances of passage. It may, therefore, be up to the president to meet this long-standing issue. The two members of his cabinet most concerned in the question are definitely and sharply opposed. The House action, taken under the most stringent rules invoked since the Democrats took control, followed reading of a letter from Secretary Stimson in which turning loose the islands was condemned strongly. 1932-11-25.text: LONDON, Nov. 25. (4) —The pound sterling touched 3.22 dollars in early trading on the sterling-dollar exchange today. This figure was one cent below the previous minimum since the country went off the gold standard in September of last year.

London, Nov. 25.—Two of the most important British newspaper groups, controlled by Lord Beaverbrook and Lord Rothermere, united today to declare it impossible for Great Britain to pay her $95,500,000 debt installment, due the United States December 15. At the same time, it was believed in many reliable quarters that the present British strategy has as its major purpose the procuring of the most generous terms possible if and when readjustment (Continued on Page &).

New York, Nov. 25—Trail’s end seemed near today for Eddie Guerin, international criminal who once amazed the world by escaping from Devil's Island. Old and broken in body, he was sentenced yesterday, cablegrams said, to a year in a London jail for snatching a handbag containing $15. Guerin, 72, was caught as a common thief. In the nineties, before racketdom was born, he was the talk of two continents as robber and cracksman. Infatuation for a woman called “Chicago May” Churchill, a pal whose name was written as large on detectives’ memories as his own led Guerin to his first large batch of grief. He followed her from Chicago to New York and then to Europe, where French police arrested him in 1901. A French court sent him to Devil’s Island, the penal colony in French Guiana, for taking $30,000 from the American Express Company in Paris. Four years he served in that sizzling place of horro

TRURO, Nov. 25 (4).—Liquor valued at about $75,000 in 1500 cases was seized along with four automobiles on the beach here today by coast guardsmen. Nine hundred cases were found on the beach and about 600 more on property nearby. Four men were arrested as the guardsmen swooped down on a group of about 20. A coast guard patrolman came upon the group in that section of the Cape Cod Coast known as Long Nook Beach. He notified his station and a squad of guardsmen hurried to the scene. As they charged the group the rum-runners scattered into the sand dunes and nearby woods. The men caught said they were Isaac Warner and Lewis Arnold of Boston, Morris Glass of (126 Market Street) New Bedford, and John Tama of (8 E. 11th Street) New York City. 1932-04-22.text: London, April 21.—(AP)—Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer, explained today that the uncertainty over war debts and reparations caused their omission from the new British budget and that it was “not a notice of a definite policy.” His explanation followed an appeal for a great American-British effort “to revalue commodities to gold up to the level of 1928, to restore world business,” made by Winston Churchill, who was chancellor of the exchequer when the conservatives ruled the British government. Both came out to debate on the budget in the house of commons. Close companionship between Britain and the United States as leaders in the project for a great trade revival, Mr. Churchill said, would bring France, one of the principal holders of gold, and other countries into line. “This would give the producers of commodities, the agriculturalist or the producer of raw materials o

London, April 21,—(A)—The tariff wall around Great Britain, once the leading exponent of free trade, was doubled in height today. The import duties advisory committee recommended that a total duty of 20 per cent be imposed on nearly every type of manufactured goods imported into the nation. The new rates become effective after midnight, April 25. The general tariff law now in effect assesses imports 10 per cent. The advisory committee described the new tariff policy thus: “For most manufactured goods an additional duty of 10 per cent, making 20 per cent in all. On a limited number of others, for which a lower rate seems appropriate, total duty will be 15 per cent, and for certain articles of luxury or semi-luxury character, total duties will be 25 or 30 per cent.”

Moscow, April 22 —-(AP)— The 17,000,000 members of the Soviet Trade Unions stood pledged today to defend their country, if need be, as news dispatches from the Far East told of new charges that Russian "White Guards" were active against the Soviets. The Ninth All Union Congress of the Trades Unions made the pledge for its members last night, and, sending greetings to the Red Army and to Klementi E. Voroshilov, War and Navy Commissar, called for increased watchfulness, especially in the Far East, against the menace of a bourgeois invasion. It also obligated itself to extend military preparedness to the proletariat and the peasants, with a view to greatly enlarging the already comprehensive 'patronage' of the Red Army.

Tokyo, April 22.—-(Friday)—() Four persons died today, 40 were injured and 6,000 were left homeless in a fire that wiped out the greater part of Omiya, a town in the prefecture of Shizuoka, 75 miles southwest of Tokyo. The flames destroyed 1,200 houses.

Bastia, Corsica, April 21.—-(#) The roof of the famous palace of justice collapsed with a roar into a crowded courtroom today, killing 15 persons and injuring 30, eleven of them seriously. Among the dead was Louis Colombani, president of the Bastia Bar association. The accident caught an attorney, M. Bianchi, in the midst of a plea to a large crowd. He also was among the dead taken out by rescuers an hour or so later. The two-story palace, particularly noted for a magnificent colonnade of blue marble, had on its top floor an audience chamber, called the Hall of Bees, after the Napoleonic symbol. This chamber was empty, and the masonry crashed through its floor down to the crowd below. Troops were called in to direct rescue work and continued their search tonight, fearing more bodies would be found.

| BOMBAY, India, April 22 (AP)— Mme. Sarojini Naidu, acting president of the Indian National Congress, was arrested today for defying a government order forbidding her to leave Bombay to attend the annual Congress convention at Delhi. The government also had forbidden the Delhi meeting, but Mme. Naidu said she regarded it as an honor to follow Mahatma Gandhi to jail.

LONDON, Aug. 5. UP)—A “cooperative agreement” on war debts satisfactory both to the United States and Europe is envisaged by Premier J. Ramsay MacDonald, the United Press was informed on unimpeachable authority today. The guiding principles in MacDonald's mind concerning future war debt negotiations were revealed after the Premier's return from Lossiemouth, Scotland, where he rested and meditated. He returned to London greatly benefited in mind and body.

MIAMI, Fla., Aug. 3 (AP).--The story of a woman flier's love for two men was relied on heavily today by the prosecution in its attempt to convict Capt. W. N. Lancaster, former British army aviator, of the murder of Haden Clarke, young American writer. State Attorney Hawthorne called Mrs. Jessie M. Keith-Miller, Australian aviatrix, as one of his first and principal witnesses. Hawthorne's opening argument told of his plan to attempt to show that Lancaster frequently threatened Clarke's life after he learned that the author, who was writing Mrs. Keith-Miller’s life story, had become engaged to the aviatrix during Lancaster's absence on a business trip. She once was Lancaster’s fiancée.

HAMBLEDON, ENG., Aug. 5—()—Mrs. Victor Bruce, who made a false start on Monday in an attempt to set a new endurance flight record, took off this afternoon. She and her husband and a radio operator are using an amphibian plane equipped with a kitchen, dining room and shower bath.

MIAMI, Fla., Aug. 5—(P)— Stories of contemplated suicide and death threats were balanced against each other today by jurors trying Captain W. N. Lancaster, former British army flier, for murder of Haden Clarke, his rival for the love of Mrs. Jessie M. Keith-Miller. It was Mrs. Keith-Miller, petite soft-spoken Australian, who told of discussing a suicide pact with Clarke, her fiancé, less than three hours before he was fatally shot in her home. The two were worried over their plans to marry in the face of the woman’s earlier engagement to Lancaster, her flying partner, she said. For today’s hearing State Attorney Hawthorne indicated he would read Lancaster's personal diary and a mass of letters written by the flier, the aviatrix and the author. Tokio, Aug. 5 (UP)—New Japanese advances into Jehol Province and possibly to the Chinese cities of Peiping and Tientsin were believed impending today. The war office issued a statement denouncing Marshal Chang Hseuh-Liang, Manchurian war lord, for organizing "banditry" in Manchuria. Similar statements in the past have been followed by military action. The rumors of further fighting came thick and fast. They included reports that an additional division would be mobilized for service in Manchuria. There was no confirmation of this report. The Japanese attitude during the occupation of Manchuria has been that Japanese nationals must be protected from roving bands of Chinese. The bands are usually groups of demobilized soldiers, or parts of leaderless armies. The Japanese term for these groups is "bandits." The Chinese call them "patriots" fighting to regain Chinese soil.

Shanghai, Aug. 5. (#)—Fighting between Chinese and Japanese in South Manchuria, which broke out again Wednesday, was spreading over a wider area today, Chinese reports received here said. The Chinese claimed their Manchurian volunteers were driving the Japanese out of Xingkow while other volunteers recaptured Tungliao, important railway terminus northwest of Mukden. The reports said the Chinese sent an ultimatum to General Shigeru Honjo, Japanese commander-in-chief, demanding that the Japanese withdraw from Chinchow within 48 hours. General Honjo was said to have ignored the ultimatum and declared martial law in Chinchow. Fighting also was going on south of Mukden along the South Manchuria railway the Chinese claimed and the Japanese were hard-pressed there and asked for reinforcements.

1932-04-30.text: DUBLIN (AP) - President Eamon De Valera’s bill to abolish the oath of allegiance to King George is safely over what was considered its most formidable hurdle. Waging a bitter battle in the Dail Eireann last night, the president and his Fianna Fail and Labor colleagues carried it on second reading by a vote of 77 to 71, in the face of bitter opposition from former President James T. Cosgrave’s supporters. “We purpose to get the last letter of our legal rights,” De Valera declared shortly before the vote was taken. “If Britain is going to use the Anglo-Irish treaty as a big stick, let her do it in the face of the whole world. If the British government attempts any reprisals it will prove its pretense of co-equality among the nations of the Commonwealth to be bosh. “We are going to test whether co-equality is a deceptive phrase or has solid substance behind it. My aim in life is to defeat t

Geneva, April 29.—(4#)—The statesmen of the “Big Five”—the United States, Great Britain, France, Italy and Germany—and the general commission of the world disarmament conference decided abruptly today to suspend activities for two weeks, leaving the coast clear for a League of Nations decision tomorrow on the Sino-Japanese dispute. A plenary session of the assembly of the league will hear a long report of its committee of 19 submitted as a program to expedite the Sino-Japanese armistice negotiations at Shanghai. DUBLIN, Irish Free State, April 29 (®)—The government bill to abolish the oath of allegiance to the British crown was passed on second reading by the Dail Eireann tonight after prolonged debate in which President Eamon de Valera declared “we proposed to get the last letter of our legal rights.” The vote on the measure, which has been assailed as repudiation of the Anglo-Irish treaty by J. H. Thomas, dominions secretary of Great Britain, was 77 to 71. “I do not fear negotiation with England,” President de Valera told the Dail, “but when we negotiate we will negotiate about a united Ireland and not before.”

Tokyo, April 30. (AP)—Reaction to the bomb attack of Japanese officials at Shanghai yesterday was kept studiously moderate here today in all responsible quarters and it was stated it was not expected it would affect Sino-Japanese relations at Shanghai. No protest was contemplated by the government, since the scene of the bombing was under temporary occupation by the Japanese military and the thrower of the bomb was a Japanese subject.

SHANGHAI, April 30 (INS) — Japanese officials appointed a special committee today to arrange for the funeral of Dr. Kawabata, resident of the Shanghai Japanese residents’ association who died from injuries received in yesterday’s daring bombing in Hongkew Park. An elaborate ceremony was planned at which all of the thousands of Japanese in Shanghai were expected to pay tribute. Mamoru Shigemitsu, Minister to China, showed no improvement during the night, although all of the other high Japanese officials wounded in the explosion were progressing favorably. General Kenkichi Uyeda, second in command of the Japanese Shanghai army, was reported as doing as well as could be expected after an operation in which all the toes of his right foot were removed. Meanwhile, police of the French concession planned further raids similar to those carried out yesterday on Korean houses, which the Japanese c

HONOLULU, April 30 (AP)—With a recommendation for leniency, a racially mixed jury has convicted four Americans of manslaughter for the slaying of a Hawaiian. The jury reported a verdict late yesterday after more than 48 hours deliberation. The defendants are Lieutenant Thomas H. Massie, U. S. N., Mrs. Granville Fortescue, society matron, his mother-in-law; Albert Jones and E. J. Lord, navy enlisted men. The verdict was read in a courtroom tense with silence. First to break it was a sob from Mrs. Thalia Massie, wife of the naval officer, who allegedly was criminally attacked by Joseph Kahahawai, the slain. Conviction set all Honolulu astir with excitement and rumors. Governor Lawrence M. Judd denied the national guard had been summoned but said precautions had been taken against possible emergencies. The governor declined to say what his precautionary measures were. It was no secret the n

WASHINGTON, Apr. 30. (AP)— President Hoover's biggest hope for reducing wasteful expenditure in the government had weathered today the worst of the Congressional opposition. Alone of the important provisions in the once impressive economy bill, the unwieldy Federal machine was passed unchanged by the House late yesterday. To Cut More Savings. The insurgent coalition group remained firmly in the saddle, however, riddling the bill with so many amendments that reductions totaling $67,000,000 have been thrown out so far and only $42,000,000 of economies approved. This accounted for about half of the items in the entire bill and the revolters started work on the remainder today confident that more millions would be slashed from the savings as soon as the section reducing veterans’ allowances is reached. The leaders, however, had not surrendered but clung to the hope that when record votes are

Long of Louisiana, Robinson offered in the senate today to quit his post as minority leader whenever a majority of the democrats desire it. WASHINGTON, April 29.—(AP)—Attacking the democratic leadership, Senator Long (dem.) La., today resigned from all senate committees. In a dramatic flourish, Long stood on the senate floor and sent his resignation from all committees to the desk after attacking the leadership of the party by Senator Robinson of Arkansas, and others. The Louisiana senator shouted, "I want to resign from every committee assignment given me by the democratic party." He announced that if a Senate party re-elections he would vote for the farmer-laborite. 1932-08-10.text: ALBANY, N.Y., Aug. 10. (AP). — Gov. Roosevelt’s last word on the Walker case before tomorrow's hearing on the charges against the New York mayor was a reiteration that politics will have no bearing on his decision. A London newspaper telephoned to the Democratic presidential candidate yesterday to get first hand his position on the matter. The governor said what he had said frequently to American newspapermen, that he would consider the case purely as a judge and that the possible effect of his decision on his presidential candidacy would have no weight. The Albany county Democratic organization, outspokenly anti-Roosevelt in the past, had orders from the county chairman to “greet”

COURTROOM, Miami, Fla., Aug. 10—(UP)—Capt. William N. Lancaster, British flier, recounted from the witness stand today his dramatic story of how Haden Clarke, young writer and rival for the affections of Jessie M. Keith-Miller, was killed in the bungalow where the three lived and denied that he fired the fatal shot. Lancaster said Clarke shot himself and that he typed the suicide notes found later, and indicated he was unable to arouse Clarke to sign them. “I scribbled ‘Haden’ on one note and ‘H’ on another,” Lancaster said, “Something I shouldn't have done.” MIAMI, Fla., Aug. 10.--(UP)-- Positive denial that he killed Haden Clarke was made today by Captain William N. Lancaster, British flier, on trial charged with murdering the young man who supplanted him in the affections of Mrs. Jessie M. Keith-Miller, Australian aviatrix, —**Captain Lancaster, did you kill Clarke?** Defense Co

OTTAWA, Aug. 10. (AP).—The prospect for broad success of the imperial trade conference lay today largely in the hands of Premier Bennett of Canada. Upon his reply to Great Britain, which is expected before the end of the day, may depend the outcome of the effort to conclude a trade agreement between Canada and Britain. This proposed accord has achieved a key position in the conference work. If the accord is to go through, as matters now stand, it is up to Bennett to make further concessions to British industrial imports into Canada. Unofficial observers, for the most part, inclined to the belief that he had nothing further to offer. Conservative newspapers, however, insisted he was ready to give wider concessions to British iron, steel, coal and textile products.

- PLYMOUTH, Eng. (#)—Miss Betty Gow, Scottish nurse in the home of Colonel and Mrs. Charles A. Lind- bergh, landed here today for a visit to her home in Scotland. - She was met by her mother and a group of friends from Glasgow and they planned to motor there from here. Miss Gow refused to talk ex- ‘cept to say that she intends to re- turn to her place in the Lindbergh household in October.

- MIAMI, Fla., Aug. 10.—()—Captain W. N. Lancaster, British aviator, testified in his murder trial today he did not kill Haden Clarke, young author who had supplanted him in the affections of Mrs. Keith Miller: His firm voice gave the answer "No" to the first question asked him as he resumed the witness stand in the eighth day of the trial. Lancaster apparently was prepared for the question. He showed no surprise and went calmly into his answers to ensuing questions by James M. LONDON, Aug. 10--Nancy Hoyt, American writer of sophisticated novels, said today the death of Smith Reynolds at Winston-Salem, N. C., had sent her to London to blot out the memory of her love for the man whose death has resulted in murder indictments against two persons. Miss Hoyt, who recently underwent a major operation, is living here under the care of a trained nurse. She met Reynolds in 1930 when both were bound home from Europe aboard the Leviathan, she said today, and thereafter they were the closest friends. Both were married at the time, but obtained divorces in order to wed each other. “We were both stubborn,” said Miss Hoyt. “One night last September he asked me to fly to Carolina with him to be married. “I wouldn't do it. I thought my friends would say Nancy was marrying for money. Besides, he was eight years younger and I was fool enough to think my friends would talk. “He w

Lancaster, British flier on trial charged with murdering the young man who supplanted him in the affections of Mrs. Jessie M. Keith-Miller, Australian aviatrix. “Captain Lancaster, did you kill Haden Clarke?” defense counsel James Carson asked in opening the second day of direct examination of the accused airman. “I did not,” Lancaster replied,

Plymouth, England, Aug. 9.—Miss Betty Gow, nursemaid in the home of Colonel and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh when their son was kidnapped, wept for joy when she landed here today on her way to visit her family in her native Scotland. Her mother and a group of friends from Glasgow met her. "Oh, mother dear, I'm so glad to be home again!" Miss Gow said as she embraced her mother. The homecomer would say nothing about the Lindbergh kidnapping.

1932-08-16.text: DUBLIN, Irish Free State, Aug. 13. ()--Eamon De Valera, president of the Free State, was beleaguered from two sides to- editorial headed “an emphatic answer to De Valera” that the mere abolition of the oath of allegiance to King George would not alter the republican position. At the same time the newspaper “United Irishman,” organ of former President William T. Cosgrave, conservative leader, attacked De Valera as acting illogically in not declaring a republic. Such a procedure, it said, “would certainly be damaging, but would probably be less so than De Valera’s policy of governing the Free State by a sort of conspiracy with the Irish republican army.” Both incidents followed the announcement Thursday of an organization known as the Free State Comrades Association which was considered in some quarters to be opposed to the republican army.

OTTAWA, Ont., Aug. 15.--(P)-- Canada and Great Britain were reported today to have solved most of their important differences and virtually to have reached an accord on a trade agreement which would include preference in Britain for Canadian farm products and reciprocal favors by Canada for British iron, steel and coal. Delegates estimated that with all the agreements completed the diversion of trade from the United States was not likely to reach more than one-third of the $200,000,000 additional business Great Britain might expect from the Dominions. Under the proposed agreements with Canada and the other dominions, Great Britain recognizes empire preference as a definite part of her fiscal policy. Foodstuffs now on the free list will be brought within the preferential field, Subject to later changes, the tentative basis of the accord was understood to include the following: 1. A duty o

OTTAWA, ONT., Aug. 16.—() The empire trade conference was moving today toward a British five-year plan. Trade agreements negotiated here, it was proposed, will have a duration of five years and will then be terminable at six months' notice. Only the important agreement between Great Britain and Canada remained uncompleted today, but there was no move to change the date of the final plenary session ending the conference, which is set for Thursday, and, consequently, it is indicated the British and Canadians intend to reach a final agreement by tomorrow night. Two Main Difficulties. The question of levying tariff taxes against foreign food products in Great Britain, a move which is generally conceded would be unpopular with the British people, was the chief difficulty the conferees were facing. Miami, Fla., Aug. 15 (P).--Defense Attorney James M. Carson, pleading for the acquittal of Capt. W. N. Lancaster, in the British filers’ trial for the murder of Haden Clarke, today criticized the state's case as the sum of “five disconnected and sketchy circumstances in no way sufficient to give any reason for believing he killed Clarke.” He praised the “bravery” of Mrs. J. M. Keith-Miller, Australian aviatrix, in baring her tangled love affairs with the two men from the stand to aid Lancaster. The state charges the love triangle was the motive for the alleged slaying, while the defense casts the young writer’s death as suicide partly resulting from the snarled affairs of the trio. Carson enumerated five circumstances on which he said the state based its case: 1. Lancaster's love for Mrs. Keith-Miller, whose affections Clarke claimed in Lancaster's absence on an unsuccessful flying ventu

MIAMI, Fla., Aug. 16—W.P.—Anticipating a verdict today, crowds jammed the Dade County courtroom as final arguments were presented in the trial of Capt. William N. Lancaster, British war-time flier charged with the murder of Haden Clarke, young Miami journalist. “The state asks conviction—and the death penalty—on facts utterly foreign from those with which it started out,” James M. Carson, chief defense counsel, said in low tones as he opened the final summation of his case. Carson had charged the state dragged “filth, mud and dirt” into the case to sway the jury toward the charge that Lancaster, angered by the fact Clarke had triumphed over him in a love triangle, killed the youth to get him out of the way. The third member of the triangle was Jessie M. Keith-Miller, Australian flier, Lancaster's air companion and sweetheart for five years.

'By The Associated Press. NEW YORK, Aug. 15.—Business has made a "decided upturn" throughout the country, with improvement greatest in the manufacturing districts of New England, Etnies S. Willis, president of the Associated Grocery Manufacturers of America, said today. The East, in general, was showing the upturn more quickly than the middle and far western states, he declared in an address before the Association of Manufacturers’ Representatives of New York. Willis has completed a survey of conditions in the country’s principal industrial centers.

LONDON, Aug. 16.—(4)—A message to news today from Tokyo said 19 lives were lost when the steamer Hidemaru collided with the Nichifukumaru on the inland sea this morning. The Nichifukumaru sank shortly afterward.

Dublin, Irish Free State, Aug. 15.— A new “white” army is being formed in the Irish Free State with the aim of maintaining law and order. Dr. O'Higgins, president of the volunteer division of the Saorstat Army Comrades association, declared today that his organization is neither a menace nor a challenge to the Free State government. There already are two armies in the Free State—The “green” forces of Saorstat regulars and the “red” Irish republican army which was an illegal organization under the old Cosgrave government. Much interest has been aroused in the new association. “We only stand between the people and the menace of secret organizations,” Dr. O'Higgins said. “Our division is not a military organization likely to precipitate war, and our immediate object is peace.” Dr. O'Higgins asserted that the people were in a state of demoralization as a result of invisible intimidation, and

1932-08-06.text: LONDON (AP)—The Economist, one of Great Britain’s foremost economic and financial authorities, said today it believed the crisis of economic stress in the United States was past. “It would be rash to predict that America is yet within sight of general economic recovery,” it said, in a review of world conditions, “nevertheless, there is reason to think that the giant of the west has passed the crisis of his sickness. “In the spring and summer there were grave symptoms, such as the growth of unemployment, the drain of gold to Europe and the growth of hoarding and the distrustful public. “These were justifiably regarded with serious apprehension, but the period of panic seems to have passed. The process of hoarding is being checked, the banking position is salvaged and the psychology of the people steadied.” There are also indications, the paper said, that “in the world generally, the steep

By The Associated Press. Miami, Fla., Aug. 5.—Captain W. N. Lancaster’s own written record of passionate devotion to Jessie M. Keith-Miller and his anxiety over her relations with Haden Clarke, young writer, was put in the record today at the British flier’s trial for what the prosecution calls a love triangle murder. The former British Army pilot's diary, read by State's Attorney Hawthorne to an intent jury and spectators, also revealed the beginning of the attachment between Clarke and the Australian aviatrix who had been Lancaster's constant companion for five years. Hawthorne declared his motive was to show by the diary that intense love for her led him to murder Clarke in a fit of jealousy. The diary told of the suspicions of friends relayed to Lancaster by letter while he was in the west and repeated the friends’ stories of the drinking bouts in which Mrs. Keith-Miller has testifie

Ventor, Isle of Wight, Aug. 6—Clara Victor Bruce, British woman flier who took off yesterday in an attempt to set a new endurance record, failed again today. Her plane, the City of Portsmouth, which she called her “flying bungalow,” came down on the water near here this morning after being in the air a little more than fifteen minutes. A leak in the main gasoline tank was given as the cause.

OTTAWA, Ont. Aug. 6.—(/)— Plans of the dominions for trade agreements with Great Britain were in the hands of the British delegates today. The British were expected to begin making their decisions next week. The two exceptions were the Irish Free State and India, whose delegates indicated they did not come to the conference to treat with Great Britain. In each of the other instances, the dominions asked the mother country for a protected British market for their products, chief agricultural. There was a tacit promise that the British answers would be transmitted beginning Monday but there was no indication that these would be made public. It was quite plain that to grant their requests Great Britain would have to forsake her time-honored policy of free trade in bread and meat and that her decision would be based on whether the inducements were sufficient. By The Associated Press Miami, Fla., Aug. 6.—Testimony that the body of Haden Clarke, young writer, was bruised and bore no powder marks and that Captain W. N. Lancaster had threatened to “get rid” of him was introduced today in the prosecution's effort to prove the British flier killed Clarke because of jealousy over Jessie M. Keith-Miller, Australian aviatrix. The condition of Clarke’s body was described by K. B. Bess, funeral director, who prepared it for burial. Over objections by defense counsel, he was allowed to testify that in his experience bullet wounds unprotected by clothing always bore powder marks in cases of suicide. He also said he found a bruise on Clarke's shoulder. The defense contends Clarke killed himself because of despondency over financial troubles, a disease he had contracted and remorse for having stolen from Lancaster the affections of his flying partner. MIAMI, Fla., Aug. 5 (#)--Captain W. N. Lancaster’s anguish at hearing Haden Clarke had succeeded him in the affections of Mrs. J. M. Keith-Miller was described to the jury today in a lengthy diary read at the former British army flier’s trial on a charge of murdering his rival. State’s Attorney N. Vernon Hawthorne pointed out his motive in reading the diary was to prove Lancaster killed Clarke because “his beloved had been taken by his best friend.” Hastens to Scene The diary was written by Lancaster between Jan. 1 of this year and April 15. The last entry was made at St. Louis, from which city he hurried to Miami upon learning Mrs. Keith-Miller, his former fiancée and flying partner, and Clarke, a young writer helping her prepare a story of her life, were engaged to be married. Clarke was shot to death in a room he and Lancaster shared at Mrs. Keith-Miller’s home the day after Lancaster

BALTIMORE, Md. (4)—An outbreak of typhoid fever among the crew of the British steamer, Victoria City, was under investigation by agents of the Maryland state department of health. Nine members of the steamer's crew were in University hospital here under treatment for typhoid fever and two other ill seamen remained aboard the boat after she had docked Friday. Dr. Robert H. Riley, state health director, said health agents would board the steamer to take “samples of the Victoria City’s water supply, inoculate these members of the crew not already ill and search for a typhoid carrier or other sources of the outbreak.”

Hamilton, Ont., Aug. .. — Headquarters of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police instructed the local detachment yesterday to arrest a man described as “A Sinn Feiner of the most radical type” in connection with a reported plot to assassinate J. H. Thomas, British Secretary for Dominions. Mr. Thomas, who is attending the Imperial Economic Conference at Ottawa, is expected to participate Saturday in the opening of the Welland Canal. He did not come to Hamilton on the special train for distinguished guests that arrived yesterday, but another train will get in Saturday. An exceptionally large number of Royal Mounted men were on duty here today and a strong guard will be maintained at Thorold today when the formal ceremonies inaugurating the canal are held. As Dominions Secretary, Mr. Thomas has taken a prominent part in negotiations with the Irish Free State over the conflict growing out of the

1932-11-22.text: WASHINGTON, Nov. 21—Czecho-Slovakia aligned itself beside Great Britain, France and Belgium in seeking war debt revision today, in a note asking suspension of the $1,500,000 payment it has due to this country Dec. 15. There will be no publication until tomorrow of this latest communication in the difficulties which President Hoover and President-elect Roosevelt plan to seek to thresh out at the White House. The total obligation of Czecho-Slovakia to the United States stands at $167,071,023. Payments already have been made which aggregate $18,304,178. Along with debt matters, Mr. Hoover and Mr. Roosevelt are expected to discuss tomorrow the probable date of the world monetary and economic conference.

London, Nov. 22.—(AP)—King George ceremoniously opened the ninth parliament of his reign today with a speech touching on major world problems, but he omitted any mention of the momentous war debts issue up before President Hoover and President-elect Roosevelt in the United States. The king, with Queen Mary by his side, proclaimed broad national policies for the coming year, stressing the importance of disarmament, the world economic conference, the need for economy and farm relief, and the solution of the unemployment problem. Ever-old yet ever-new, a pageant of heraldry and history, medieval ceremony marched with modern government for its setting in the house of lords at midday. In fine, deep tones, the words of the royal address came from the king’s mouth, but they were written for him by Ramsay MacDonald, the prime minister, and his cabinet colleagues. “Large numbers of my people are

LONDON. (UP) — King George made a plea for economic restoration of the world in opening the new session of parliament today, although he did not mention war debts directly in the speech he read before a joint meeting of the houses of commons and lords. Couple Cheered The king and queen were driven to the house of lords in their state coach, while thousands along the Mall and near the parliament buildings cheered their majesties in the colorful procession. The king expressed earnest hope that the world economic conference meeting soon "will be able to reach an agreement on measures required to deal with the causes which brought about the present economic and financial difficulties of the world." Referring to the world disarmament conference, the king said "my government will continue full cooperation with all other members of the conference to work for an international convention which wi

PARIS, Nov. 22—The Grand Duke Alexander of Russia, husband of the Grand Duchess Xenia, cousin and brother-in-law of the late Czar Nicholas II, and cousin of King George V of England, is seriously ill from spinal trouble at Nice, it was learned today. The grand duchess was summoned from London. The grand duke is 66 years old. He returned to the Riviera recently after a visit to the United States and reopened his villa.

WASHINGTON, Nov. 21.—A bitter controversy which has raged through the last decade over cancellation of Europe's war debt to the United States seems likely to reach a crisis this winter. Requests by Great Britain, France and Belgium for fundamental debt revision makes it almost inevitable that Congress either shall grant more lenient terms on Europe's $11,000,000,000 (C.B.) obligation or else say; “Pay or default.” When the issue reaches the floor of Congress two opposing schools of thought in America—the cancellationists and anti-cancellationists—are expected to open fire on fellow senators and representatives. They have battled for a decade. Thousands of words have been written and spoken by each side to support its view. ROME.—Italy is taking no action for the moment regarding its debt to the United States, awaiting negotiations between American and France and England. It was said, however, that this country is ready to pay, if the $15,000,000 instalment due Dec. 15, is not postponed.

BERLIN, Nov. 21——)— Adolf Hitler, who has been campaigning nine years to head the German government, finally received a mandate to form a cabinet today. But President von Hindenburg attached to the request certain political conditions which some observers thought would make Hitler's acceptance improbable. The president insisted that the Hitler cabinet be backed by “a majority or almost a majority” of the reichstag. Hitler retired to confer with his advisers, promising to answer before the end of the day. One of his closest associates said this afternoon that “it is obviously impossible for Hitler, who has spent his whole political life in a bitter fight against parliamentary haggling to try to resurrect a system which already is dead. 1932-11-15.text: Washington, Nov. 15.—(A.P.)— The Belgian government today presented a note to the American government on the debt situation. The communication was reported to be similar in tenor to notes presented last week by Great Britain and France. Paul May, the Belgian ambassador, handed the note to Secretary Stimson. No immediate comment was forthcoming from either the ambassador or the secretary, but there were indications the communication would be made public later in the day.

London—Postponement of the next British war debt payment to the United States was regarded by leading British economists today as the first step toward complete debt cancellation. It was held generally that “remedial measures” which Britain mentioned in the note to Washington as necessary for the restoration of prosperity certainly included a suggestion of Chancellor of the Exchequer Neville Chamberlain’s frequently repeated official statement in favor of complete cancellation. Britain refused to consider the possibility that postponement of the December 15 payment might not be granted. The war debt situation today: The Belgian government presented a note to the American government reported similar in tenor to notes presented last week by Great Britain and France asking a moratorium on debts. President Hoover was said to feel the United States should grant the postponement of December payments asked by Europe, pending new negotiations. President-elect Roosevelt accepted Hoover's invitation to discuss the debts with him. The conference probably will be held next week. Most congressional leaders appeared opposed to further concessions and felt debtor nations should be permitted to default if they cannot meet payments. Washington administration sources warned a default might set a bad example that would endanger international credits generally. British official quarters were confident the U. Ten Eyck, president of the New York State Waterway Association, before a senate foreign relations sub-committee. ABOARD PRESIDENTIAL SPECIAL, ENROUTE TO WASHINGTON, Nov. 13.— (UP) —President Hoover has invited President-Elect Roosevelt and his advisers to confer with him this week on the entire war debt question, reopened, he said, by Great Britain in a request for postponement of its December 15 payment. The conference, it was indicated in the text of Mr. Hoover’s message to Governor Roosevelt, would open the way for the incoming policies. The discussions, Mr. Hoover suggested, need not be limited to war debts, but could include any questions of world economic stability and disarmament. Great Britain's payment due December 15 is $95,000,000, the president revealed, however, that "similar requests are to be made by other debtor nations" on installments due December 15. Washington, Nov. 14. (INS)—A hostile reception in Congress awaits any proposal President Hoover may make toward considering favorably the formal request of the British and French governments for an extension of the Hoover war debt holiday and a re-examination of the reparations-debt problem. This became more apparent today as members of Congress, both Democrats and Republicans, gave careful scrutiny to the texts of the British and French notes delivered to Secretary of State Stimson last week, and made public Sunday, while awaiting the return of President Hoover. The sentiment among leaders of both parties in the legislative branch of the government was that the European nations, in presenting their pleas for further leniency on their debts to this country at this time, are following a lost cause. Without the consent of Congress, the executive branch of the government is unable to suspen

BRUSSELS, Nov. 14—The Belgian government today joined France, England and other European debtor nations in appealing to the United States for suspension of the war debt installment due Dec. 15. A note to this effect, said by officials to be similar to the French and British memorandums to the American government, was telegraphed to the Belgian ambassador at Washington.

1932-09-28.text: London, Sept. 28.—(AP)—Three of the important liberal and labor members of Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald's eleven-month-old national cabinet resigned today following a disagreement over the tariff proposals approved at the recent imperial trade conference at Ottawa. The three who resigned are Viscount Snowden of Ickornshaw, lord privy seal, former labor party leader who followed his colleague, the prime minister, into the national cabinet last November, and two noted liberals, Sir Herbert Samuel, home secretary, and Sir Archibald Sinclair, secretary for Scotland. The resignations marked the first break in the national government which was chosen from all three leading parties to meet the financial crisis which Great Britain faced last October. The liberal leaders and Viscount Snowden objected to the tariff proposals as incompatible with their free trade principles. The cabinet met in a

London, Sept. 28—(U.P)—Britain’s ancient battle between free traders and advocates of a protective tariff brought the resignation of three members of the cabinet today, the first open rupture in the national government. Viscount Snowden, lord privy seal and die-hard free trader; Sir Herbert Samuel, home secretary and liberal leader; and Sir Archibald Sinclair, secretary of state for Scotland and prominent in liberal councils, notified the cabinet of their intention to resign. The immediate cause of the resignations was the cabinet’s decision that legislation making effective the agreements of the Ottawa imperial Continued on Page 2, Column * |

London, Sept. 27.—Great Britain’s year old national government faces a fateful session at No. 10 Downing Street tomorrow, with a major reshuffling of the cabinet considered a foregone result but with every indication that Ramsay MacDonald will remain as prime minister. Because of conservative opposition, it was believed unlikely that the prime minister could delay in presenting the Ottawa tariff proposals. Therefore his task seemingly resolved itself into replacing Mr. Snowden, Sir Herbert Samuel and a half dozen liberal ministers who have refused to swallow their free trade principles. Epochal Step Any such program of replacement would mean acceptance of the new empire protection as a basic fiscal policy of the national government.

MANCHESTER, England, Sept. (28. 4)—Work in the cotton mills of Lancashire, which has been suspended for some time as a result of a textile workers’ strike, began generally to be resumed today after the signing of a peace pact yesterday. In Burnley, which was a storm center of the strike area, nearly all the mills resumed operation. The only district in which work has not begun again was around Nelson, where the weavers were holding out for further discussion of the settlement terms.

Herman singled to short center, English singled to right and Ruth muffed the ball, Herman scoring and English racing to third. Ruth was given an error. Cuyler fanned. Stephenson singled off Ruffing’s glove, English scored. Moore fanned. The crowd gave him a big hand as he came to the plate. Grimm fanned. Two runs, three hits, one error, one left on base. YANKEES—Combs was called out on strikes. Sewell flied out to Grimm. Ruth was cheered wildly as he came to bat. Ruth out to Grimm unassisted. No runs, no hits, no errors, none left on base. LONDON, Sept. 27—(AP)—Helen Keller, famous American blind educator, and Mrs. Anne Macy, her constant companion of a lifetime, received diplomas today making them honorary fellows of the Education Institute of Scotland. Only 16 other persons are honorary fellows and Miss Keller and Mrs. Macy are the first women so honored.

Ball two, low and outside. Strike one, called. Foul, strike two, into the screen back of the plate. Ball three, high. Foul, into the stands. Foul, into the lower stands. ATHENS, Sept. 28—Two hundred refugee families from the peninsula of Chalcidici, damaged by a violent earthquake, were reported lost today when the island of Amogiana, where the refugees fled, vanished into the sea. The island is off the Chalcidici coast. Much damage also was reported to relics of monasteries on Mount Athos, the ‘Holy Mountain.’ It was the center of Greek theology and learning in the middle ages. Villages, convents, and quarters for monks are built on the mountainside. According to first reports received here, many survivors of the earthquake were driven mad by the veritable inferno, or were buried alive in mines destroyed at Cassandra and Stagira. Streams of hot, red water were reported spouting from the ground. The village of Stagira was reported completely submerged.

1932-03-18.text: Birmingham, England, March 18 (AP)—Neville Chamberlain, Chancellor of the Exchequer, warned Eamon De Valera tonight that the British government would view with the “gravest concern” any suggestion that the new Irish Free State government suspend the oath of allegiance to the British crown or the land annuities due Great Britain. De Valera pledged himself to effect both these changes in the campaign which ended with his election as president of the Free State. Mr. Chamberlain asserted that any such action on the part of the Irish Dail or president would revive the bitterness which both England and Ireland had hoped they had removed forever. Mr. Chamberlain referred to statements “said to have been made by Mr. De Valera” to the effect that the Free State government intended to withhold the land annuities and abolish the oath of allegiance.

The president spoke through Senator Reed, (R., Pa.), who gave this message to the senate in the midst of a democratic attack against revision of the British debt. It was inspired by an article in today’s Washington Post, which said Ambassador Mellon upon assuming his post in London shortly would open discussions looking toward modification of the British war debt owed America. Not So Senator Reed, coming to the floor after a visit to the White House, interrupted the debate to say: “I am authorized to say that there is not a word of truth in the article.” Senator Connally, (D., Texas), demanded to know by whom Reed was authorized. “By the president,” replied Reed. “I am authorized to say that the subject of debt negotiations or debt reconsideration has not even been discussed with Mr. Mellon since it was first suggested that he should go to London as ambassador.” Senator Robinson, of Arka

Weymouth, Eng., Mar. 18—(#)— The body of a member of the crew of the sunken submarine M-2 was taken out of the vessel today by divers and removed to Portland. It was the first to be recovered. Fifty-six men were lost with the M-2 when she went down off Portland on Jan. 26. For days after the disaster a salvage fleet dragged the bottom looking for the ship, but it was not until Feb. 3 that it was found, wedged in between two other wrecks with the conning tower hatch open. Divers continued their efforts to extricate such bodies as they could reach.

WASHINGTON, D.C., March 18 (P)—The storm which swept the senate yesterday after its members read a newspaper story to the effect that Ambassador Melion was going to reopen war debt negotiations as soon as he reached London, was given its final and official quietus last night by the state department. A formal statement by the department pronounced there was no truth to the rumors and that the basis of it had no foundation whatsoever.

AINTREE, Liverpool, Eng. Mar. 18 (UP)—Forbra, an outsider, won the Grand National steeplechase today in a heartbreaking race in which favorites went down one by one. He was 50 to one in betting odds. It was second and Shaun, a previous winner, was

PREETI BRODUMA, 18, Mar 18.—(AP)—Wilko Drenth, aged father of Harm Drenth who as Harry F. Powers will be hanged tonight, showed no sorrow over his son's fate today when he was interviewed by a newspaper man. “He is getting just what's coming to him,” the father declared. Drenth speaks no English, but communicated his opinion through an interpreter, Powers’ brother-in-law. “He did the things, he should be hanged,” the farmer, who lives two and a half miles southeast of “I haven't heard a word from him until this trouble,” the elder Drenth continued. “In fact, I haven't seen him nor heard from him for ten years. My last meeting with him was in Minnesota. He was a hard worker and bright in school.”

London—(4)—Zaro Agha, the 158-year-old Turk who says he is the eldest man in the world, was in a hospital today with acute indigestion. He collapsed in a restaurant after dinner yesterday. His condition is said to be serious.

Berlin, March 17.— (4?) —Headquarters of Adolf Hitler's national socialist party throughout Prussia were raided today by police, acting on orders to smash what Prussian officials declared was “a plot to plunge Germany into civil war and seize power by force of arms. In addition to visiting the offices of the party, police searched the homes of many Nazi leaders. They confiscated numerous files of correspondence and membership lists. “Storm Troops” Prepared. Prussian officials declared they had established that 500,000 Hitler “storm troops,” including automobile and motorcycle detachments, had been made ready for mobilization at various points throughout the state. A code message—“grandmother dead”—was to be broadcast throughout Prussia, these officials said, and it was to be the signal for each unit to march upon the nearest large city. 1932-03-09.text: DUBLIN (U.P)—Eamonn De Valera, republican leader, reached the climax of his career Wednesday when the Dáil Éireann elected him president of the executive council of the Irish Free State. De Valera, who has said his first official act will be to abolish the oath of loyalty to the king, was elected titular head of the state by the Dáil without a vote. The chamber was the scene of intense excitement as the republican leader finally achieved his goal. The galleries were overflowing. Civic guards in the streets restrained the crowds, which cheered arriving Fianna Fáil members, booed the followers of William T. Cosgrave, the retiring president, and gave De Valera an ovation.

Shanghai, March 9—The Japanese civil and military authorities at Shanghai are prepared to negotiate for peace on the terms of the league assembly’s resolution of March 4, Mamoru Shigemitsu, Japanese minister notified the Chinese today. The notification was sent through Sir Miles Lampson, British minister. Shigemitsu added that in view of the situation at the front, he deemed it a matter of urgent necessity to reach at the earliest possible date a definite agreement for complete cessation of hostilities and then discuss arrangements for the withdrawal of the Japanese forces. The Chinese government considered the way now open for beginning negotiations. The government was understood to be notifying W. W. SHANGHAI, March 10.—(Thursday)—Sir Miles Lampson, British minister to China, transmitted to the Chinese authorities early today Japan's newest proposal for ending the hostilities in this area. The Japanese proposal, in the form of a letter from the Japanese minister, asserted Japan is eager to negotiate a truce because of the "critical situation existing at the front and the imminent possibility that hostilities will break out afresh." Sir Miles laid the letter before T. V. Soong and Quo Tai-Chi, representing the Nanking government here. They sent them on to their superiors at Nanking and Loyang. Washington, Mar. 9 (AP)— By his victory in the New Hampshire primary, Gov. Franklin D. Roosevelt was leading the field today for the Democratic presidential nomination, while his supporters hailed the New England result as a blow to the movement to stop him. The New Yorker's defeat of the forces hind Alfred E. Smith for New Hampshire’s 8 votes brought his total pledged delegates to 24 as against 22 for Gov. “Alfalfa Bill” Murray of Oklahoma. Roosevelt’s friends looked ahead of this and saw in the voting great promises for the future, Senator Wheeler of Montana, who will leave here today to make a campaign speech for Roosevelt at Fargo, N. D., Friday, considered the New Hampshire result a “great victory.” “In my judgment they can’t stop Roosevelt’s nomination,” he said. “It means that if Roosevelt puts up a fight in Massachusetts he can carry Massachusetts.”

DUBLIN, March 9—The supreme moment in the colorful career of Eamon De Valera, Irish republican leader, came today when the Dail Eireann, which once laughed at him, assembled to elect him president of the executive council of the Irish Free State. De Valera’s Fianna Fail party defeated the forces of President William T. Cosgrave in a general election last month. Through co-operation with the labor party, Fianna Fail is assured of a slender majority in the chamber. Final standing of the parties when the dail convened was: Fianna Fail 72; Cosgrave party, 56; independents 13; labor, 7; farmers 4. Fianna Fail and labor thus control 79 votes to the opposition’s 73. One of the first objectives of the De Valera forces in the dail session will be to repeal the oath of allegiance to the British crown. De Valera declared in a recent article written for the United Press that the abolition would enab

Shanghai, March 9 (/P)—Japanese military authorities continued to pour reinforcements and huge quantities of ammunition and supplies into their lines on the western Shanghai front today. Four transports arrived at Woosung during the day with an undetermined number of fresh troops. At least 2,000 of these were landed soon after their arrival and they immediately sloshed off through pouring rain and thick mud toward Kiangwan. A large number of additional soldiers remained aboard the transports, but no announcement was made of the total number still there. It was indicated at the Japanese headquarters that still more reinforcements are expected. A number of bluejackets also were sent forward toward the front lines during the day but where they went could not be learned. All was quiet along the Chapei-Woosung line during the day. Paris, March 8, (.- The body of Aristide Briand, known and loved throughout the world for years as an apostle of peace, lay in state today in the historic foreign office on the Quai d'Orsay, scene of his activities during most of a vigorous lifetime. Preparations were made for the funeral on Saturday after which he will be taken to the little country home at Cocherel in Brittany which constitutes practically all of the estate he left and which is to be his last resting place. In the meantime thousands of messages of condolence and sorrow flowed in from the four corners of the world, from heads of states and common citizens. The funeral services will be held at 2 p.m. Saturday at the foreign office and the body is to lie in state there until then. Premier Andre Tardien will be the principal speaker at the service.

Shanghai in Panic as New Battle - Is Brewing Shanghai, March 9.—(Wednesday) - Wildly circulated rumors that the Japanese planned to occupy Nantao and other large areas on the southern side of Shanghai, along with reports of a new fight brewing along the battle front, stirred the Chinese populace into panic today. Nanking dispatches said the people there also were nervous and a real exodus of inhabitants was under way, due to rumors Japanese soldiers were marching on Nanking. Roads Guarded. Neutral mediators, inactive several days, again took up the task of negotiating an agreement to end a cease-fire. Service was resumed over the Shanghai-Hanghow Railway, which was cut 35 miles southwest of Shanghai yesterday, the track having been repaired. The Chinese Lunghwa arsenal close by was being dismantled. The machinery was sent to Hangzhou. Oceania guarded the roads throughout the areas south

1932-02-15.text: DUBLIN, Feb. 15 (#)—The Irish election campaign, one of the chief issues in which is the question of a closer or more distant relations with Great Britain, entered its last day today with the blood of two citizens, one of them a candidate, across its trail. Patrick Reynolds, a member of the government party in the Dail Eireann and candidate for re-election, and a detective named McGeehan were shot and killed while delivering political addresses at Foxhill, County Leitrim. A man named Joseph Leddy was arrested. — The two men were witnesses the day before at an inquest into the death of James Vauch, a leader of the opposing Republican party, who, it was charged, had been mistreated by guards while a prisoner in more barracks. McGeehan testified that Vauch had been treated in the kindliest manner. President Cosgrave, who after 10 years in office is making his fifth appeal to the country in

WASHINGTON, Feb. 18.—(UP)—The state department announced today that Consul General Edwin S. Cunningham at Shanghai, cooperating with the British consul general, had protested to the Japanese consul general the landing of Japanese troops in the international settlement of Shanghai last Saturday. Attention was called by the state department to the fact that Washington already had protested directly to Tokio on the same subject when other Japanese troops were landed in the settlement recently. Strenuous objection was made to the use of this neutral territory as a Japanese military base. Meanwhile Secretary Stimson awaited a complete report on the beating of American Consul Arthur Ringwalt last Wednesday; it is considered likely a protest to Tokio will be made on this incident. Consul General Edwin S. Cunningham reported the attack on his junior colleague only yesterday, although it is under

Tokyo, Feb. 15—-(#)—-Ambassador W. Cameron Forbes of the United States and Ambassador Lindley and Dey Martel of Great Britain and France called at the foreign office late this afternoon on invitation of Foreign Minister Kenkichi Yoshizawa and it was understood the foreign minister explained the reasons why Japan deemed it necessary to send thousands of additional troops to Shanghai. The foreign minister was also understood to have outlined why Japan believed it necessary to drive the Chinese army back from Shang- Official censorship of news and the troop movement to Shanghai was lifted by the government today and it was also made known that Lieut. Gen. Kenkichi Uyeda commander of the Japanese land forces, at Shanghai was expected to present an ultimatum to the Chinese shortly demanding that they withdraw!

Dublin, Feb. 15—Gunfire which killed two members of the government party Sunday, forecast more bloodshed in the closing hours of the bitter Irish Free State campaign ending in tomorrow's general election. Patrich Reynolds, member of President William T. Cosgrave's Cumann na nGaedheal party, and a detective named McGeehan were shot and killed yesterday while electioneering in Roscommon. Reynolds was a candidate for re-election to the lower chamber of Parliament, from the constituency of Sligo Leitrim. A former policeman named Liddy was arrested. Reynolds and McGeehan were leaving Liddy’s house when shot.

TOKIO, Feb. 15 — Japanese troops in Shanghai will have to be reinforced to meet the menace of gathering Chinese forces, Foreign Minister Wenkichi Yoshizawa announced today. Yoshizawa issued a statement after conferring with the United States, British, French, Italian and German ambassadors. He explained the Shanghai situation to them in detail and reiterated his previous arguments that the protection of Japanese lives is necessary. Because of the increase in the Chinese forces, which are being joined by additional divisions, Yoshizawa said, it will be necessary to reinforce the Japanese units further. After meeting the ambassadors, Yoshizawa conferred with Lt. Gen. Sadao Araki, minister of War, regarding additional troops. NANKING, Feb. 15 — Japanese naval authorities demanded today that the chairman of the provincial government board a Japanese destroyer and apologize for an attack on a

STILLWATER, Minn., Feb. 15. —()—Michael “the gentle-hearted” has learned something about the cost of crime. Twenty years ago he slew Gregori Pellegri at Virginia, Minn., in a quarrel over $80. Since then life for Michael Angelo Gentilcore, whose name in English means “the gentle-hearted angel,” has been one long procession of half soles and heels over which he works in the state penitentiary to earn pennies which he sends to Italy for the support of the widow and two children of the man he killed. Forty-five cents a day is his pay. So far he has sent more than $3,000 to Italy, all of it voluntarily. He was a young man when the crime was committed. Now he is 44. Thrice he has tried for a commutation of sentence, but each time the pardon board has said no.

DUBLIN, Feb. 14.—U.P)—A volley of gunfire which killed one government party candidate and one detective marked the first outbreak of violence today in the Irish Free State campaign for Tuesday's general elections. Patrick Reynolds, member of President William T. Cosgrave’s Cumann na nGaedheal party, and a detective named McGeehan were killed while electioneering in Foxfield. Reynolds and McGeehan were emerging from Liddy’s home when the shooting started. Reynolds was a prominent politician and chairman of the Leitrim board of health. He is survived by a large family. Berlin—President Paul von Hindenburg who led an army in the World War, announced today that at the age of 84, he will obey the mandate of millions of Germans and be a candidate to succeed himself when his term expires in May. He has been president of the German republic for the past 7 years. There is every indication that he will be elected and it was generally believed that if he had thought there was any chance of defeat he would not have offered himself as a candidate. In recent weeks 2,500,000 persons have signed a petition asking him to run.

1932-08-15.text: By The Associated Press. Miami, Fla., Aug. 14.—Mrs. Ida Clyde Clarke will defend from the witness stand tomorrow the memory of her son, Haden, for whose slaying Captain W. N. Lancaster, British aviator, has been on trial since August 2. Mrs. Clarke is expected to testify regarding an alleged statement by Lancaster a few hours after Haden was fatally shot in the home of his fiancée, Mrs. J. M. Keith-Miller, in which statement the aviator was quoted as saying he did not know whether he killed Clarke or not.

Ottawa, Ont., Aug. 15 (UP)—Great Britain today offered Canada preferential tariffs on wheat, copper and lumber in return for preferences on textiles, leather, iron, steel and coal, it was reported on the best of authority. The offer, if accepted, will mean the loss of a hundred million dollars trade annually for the United States, for the States have been heavy exporters of all the items mentioned to both units of the Empire. The United States trade lost in textiles, leather, iron, steel and coal will go to Great Britain. The other trade will go to Canada. The British refused finally, it was reported during the Empire Economic Conference, to place an embargo or quota on imports of Russian wheat, as requested by Canada. Such action, Britain felt, would endanger trade with Russia which already has cut her imports from the United States to one-tenth of what they were two years ago. The fina
ATHENS, Greece, Aug. 15.—A violent earthquake rocked central Greece early today. First reports said a number of houses collapsed, but no casualties were reported.

VIENNA, Austria, Aug. 15.—(Monday)—(AP)—A son was born early this morning to Princess Ileana of Rumania. Physicians reported that mother and child were in good condition. The baby, whose father is the Archduke Anton of Hapsburg, to whom Ileana was married last year, will be christened Stephan.

WARSAW, Poland, (P) — Police investigation of the “Kidnapping” of Patricia McMillin, daughter of United States Consul Stewart McMillin, last Friday, showed tonight that the man who was thought to have kidnapped her only wanted to get a meal. When the little girl strayed from a park where she was playing, it developed, the unidentified man led her to a restaurant where he ordered a hearty meal for both of them and then told the waiter he had forgotten his purse. He said he would go and get some money, and in the meantime left Patricia as surety. He was not heard from again.

WAR CLOUD THINS OUT MOSCOW, Aug. 15.—(AP)—The Russo-Japanese war cloud that has hung over the Far East since the Japanese invaded Manchuria last September had thinned considerably today. Summer orders issued by the Soviet revolutionary war council considerably eased the tension of the military forces and they were accompanied by the announcement that the dispute between Russia and Japan over Pacific coast fishing rights had been settled.

Moscow, Aug. 15 (AP)—Dissatisfied with low wages and inferior living conditions, between 20,000 and 25,000 miners in the Donbas coal field have quit their jobs in the past two months. This is Russia’s chief coal producing area and if its output continues to decline there might be a serious shortage of fuel this winter, placing the nation’s industry in a precarious position. Some of the men are going back to their villages and others to industrial areas hoping to get better jobs. Unskilled workers are now paid 80 to 100 roubles a month. Their food costs a minimum of 70 to 120 roubles monthly.

BOMBAY, Aug. 15 (Monday) — About 100 persons were believed to have drowned today when a ferry boat capsized near Kothapur while crossing the swollen river. A large snake sprang from a floating tree into the midst of the 120 passengers, who all rushed in fright to one side of the boat, turning it over. Part of the crew and some of the passengers reached shore, but it was believed the number was small.

1932-12-02.text: WASHINGTON, DEC. 1. (AP).—The British war debt note today was delivered to Secretary Stimson. The British embassy sent the note to the secretary at his home, whence he went immediately to confer with the President at the White House. The note, however, will be given to the press some time today for publication in newspapers of tomorrow morning. The first note presented by Great Britain asking for an extension of the moratorium and reconsideration of war debt agreements was presented November 10. France made similar representations November 11. Belgium did the same on November 15 and Poland, Czechoslovakia and Latvia sent memorandums to the same effect at later dates. The answer of the United States government to all of these notes was essentially the same. This government declined to make any promises concerning the moratorium and explained that the question of reconsideration of war deb

Washington, Dec. 1—(AP)—Poring over a 6,000 word note from Great Britain, President Hoover and his Secretaries of State and Treasury deliberated today as to what should be America’s next war debts move. The document was carried to the White House by Secretary Stimson immediately after it had been delivered to him at his home the first thing this morning by Sir Ronald Lindsay, British Ambassador. President Hoover at once called in Secretary Mills, who has worked with him closely throughout the difficulties. After an hour with the President, both Secretaries left the White House, smilingly declining to comment. They said the British reply would be made public for tomorrow morning's newspapers. The text was understood to present reasons why Great Britain feels her request for postponement of her December payments and for a discussion of the whole war debt matter should be granted.
