Lancaster, British war flier and third side of the love triangle which collapsed with the death of Haden Clarke, plans to marry Mrs. Jessie M. Keith-Miller—the woman in the case. “I intend to marry Mrs. Keith-Miller whether she wants to or not,” Forrester said the British flier declared. Forrester conducted labor department deportations hearings for both, and his reports await adjudication now in Washington. The declaration was in contrast to the assertion of Mrs. Keith-Miller while on the witness stand in the recent trial which led to the acquittal of Lancaster on a murder charge growing out of the death of Clarke. “I do not love Bill (Captain Lancaster) and had not for the past two years,” she testified, explaining she was only “intensely fond of him.” Captain Lancaster now is in Waterb

London — (AP) — Great Britain faced a country-wide holdup of milk supplies today as a result of a farmers’ decision to inaugurate a “milk strike” Oct. 1. The decision followed a breakdown of negotiations between the farmers’ representatives and representatives of milk-distributing companies over contracts for the forthcoming year.

London, Sept. 20. (AP)—A cry for powder puff and lipstick from a British woman in distress among Chinese bandits in the wilds of Manchuria was reported to the Daily Mail today from Newchang. “Please send me a powder puff, face cream and a lipstick,” Mrs. Pawley, kidnapped by the bandits near Newchang over a week ago, was quoted as writing to a friend from the bandits’ retreat. “I don’t want anything else but a bath.” The letter was received together with a demand from the bandits for 100,000 Chinese dollars as ransom. “The bandits intend to keep moving,” Mrs. Pawley said, “until the pursuit ceases. Please persuade the police and soldiers to keep away, otherwise they say we will be killed. “I feel in a vile temper with the fools. They probably will want an extortionate ransom, but please don’t bust yourselves.” Charles Corkran, another British subject, was kidnapped at the same time as Mr

MOSCOW, Sept. 20. (P)—Rhea Clyman, a Toronto, Canada, correspondent here for the London Daily Express and newspapers in Canada, was ordered expelled from Soviet Russia today on a charge of spreading false news about the country. The order followed recent publication by the Daily Express of a series of articles she wrote after a visit to the northern Russia, purporting to reveal methods employed by the secret police at a prison camp near the area.

WENDOVER, BUCKINGHAMSHIRE, ENG., Sept. 20.—(4)—The little Congregational church in this picturesque village was packed to its capacity of 400 today when Dr. Joan MacDonald, daughter of the prime minister, was married to a fellow student of her college days in Edinburgh, Dr. Alastair Mackinnon. Her father came over from his country place at Chequers and gave the bride away. It was a great occasion for the village people. Many of them left their work early to secure places from which they might watch the bridal procession. The school children, who were given a holiday, lined the roadway to the church and cheered the wedding party when it arrived. Inside the church, which was decorated with lilies and chrysanthemums from the gardens at Chequers and with white heather from Scotland, Ishbel MacDonald, the bride's sister, acted as mistress of ceremonies. The bride was attended by four bridesma

WASHINGTON, Sept. 21.—(P)—General improvement in the world gold situation is reported by the federal reserve board on this anniversary of Great Britain’s abandonment of the gold standard. The United States gold stock, in the board’s latest monthly bulletin, was placed at $4,086,000,000, after a year which began with England's action and included a sharp ebbing in domestic gold supplies, enactment of the Glass-Steagall law to aid the reserve system in handling these withdrawals, and then a return flow of gold. It was on September 20, 1931, that Great Britain gave notice gold payments temporarily would be suspended, effective the next day. Today, the reserve board placed British gold reserves at $676,000,000 for the end of August, the largest total in 14 months. The board said that central gold reserves of all the principal countries outside the United States have increased $1,800,000,000

1932-09-14.text: LONDON, Sept. 14.—(U.P)—Great Britain is preparing to meet fully her Dec. 15 war debt payment to the United States and will not invoke the suspensory clause before the deadline at midnight tonight, the United Press was reliably informed today. Diplomatic quarters here were privately convinced that Britain hoped that the favorable impression created by meeting the payment would hasten readjustment of favorable debt terms at the earliest moment after the American presidential election. While some British quarters apparently have not abandoned hope of a moratorium, the British government is reported to feel that the benefits of a moratorium, despite temporary desirability, would be incomparable to an early, thorough readjustment. A concerted move of other debtors toward suspension, which might follow another moratorium, would damage British financial prestige.

London. Sept. 14.—-(UP)—The monoplane American Nurse, attempting a non-stop flight from New York to Rome, headed toward the Azores Islands today to take advantage of favorable weather. The monoplane was sighted about 450 miles northwest of the Azores by the steamer Ashburton at 4:30 a.m. G. M. T., 11:30 p. m. (E. S. T.) today. Previously the steamship Winnebago had sighted the airplane about 500 miles south of Cape Race and 1,000 miles east of Boston, indicating that the plane was making 100 miles an hour on a due east course. The air ministry reported at 10:35 a.m. today (4:35 a.m. E. S. T.) that moderate southwesterly winds prevailed in the east Atlantic toward the Azores. Winds were fresh from 500 to 600 miles west of Ireland, and strong to the north, toward Iceland. There were considerable clouds everywhere, but no large area of rain. The monoplane is a flying scientific laboratory i

LONDON, Sept. 14. (4)—British motorists were hit today by an increase of nearly 20 per cent in gasoline prices, raising the standard grade to 39 cents a gallon. The London Omnibus company estimated the rise would cause a sharp rise in oil shares on the stock exchange.

nts, ——— London.—(UP) — The monoplane American Nurse, carrying an American nurse, a doctor and a pilot on a non-stop flight from New York to Rome, was eagerly awaited along the coast of Europe today. The plane apparently was making steady progress and, if it holds to its southern course, should be in the vicinity of Cape Finisterre, northern Spain, early this evening, New York time. When last reported to the United Press by the steamer Ashburton at 12:30 a.m., E. S. T., the plane was 450 miles northwest of the Azores, or about 1,600 miles from Cape Finisterre. At an estimated speed of at least 100 miles an hour, the plane should make land before nightfall in New York. As the fuel load decreased, the plane's speed would increase, it was pointed out. There were “considerable clouds” everywhere, but no large area of rain. A Flying Laboratory The monoplane is a flying scientific laboratory i

Aberdeen, Scotland (AP)— The trawler Lord Talbot, which rescued the flying family of Hutchinsons on the eastern Greenland coast yesterday, will arrive here in about three weeks and it was considered probable that the Hutchinsons will be aboard as no Danish boat will be available from Angmagsalik for many months. Foodstuffs and other supplies at the Angmagsalik colony have been reported insufficient to permit the Americans to winter in Greenland.

Landon, Sept. 14 (Py)—It seems the okay folks outnumber the rather, old dear people. Lloyd James, phonetics expert, says more people talk American English than British English in the world today. He foresees radical changes in the language, making it “a strange compromise between future British English and future American English.

PARIS, Sept. 14. (AP).—France exacted the supreme penalty today for the slaying of her venerable president, Paul Doumer, by execution on the guillotine Dr. Paul Gorguloff, Russian physician who shot him May 6. Gorguloff was executed at 5:52 a. m., as he muttered almost incomprehensible references to his “idea.” He was accompanied to the scaffold by Father Gillet, a priest of the Greek church who was his spiritual adviser. The priest kissed him just before the guards fastened on the block under the knife. Dawn was just breaking. The procedure moved swiftly. Only 40 seconds after Gorguloff stepped down from the prison van, his head rolled into the basket. A few seconds were lost in adjusting his huge bulk to the block.

PARIS, Sept. 14—(UP)—The assassin of the beloved President Paul Doumer paid for his crime at dawn today when the sharp blade of the guillotine chopped off his head. Dr. Paul Gorguloff, half-mad Russian, shot down the frail “Pere” Doumer at a benefit book sale for war veterans on May 7. The knife of the guillotine fell at 6:03 a.m. The Russian’s head clopped into a basket and his body thumped over the cobblestones, drawing a closed van that carried the body to a pauper’s grave. “Monsieur Paris,” as official guillotiner Anatole Deibler is called, officiated in a grey suit and derby hat. The execution was completed so quickly that even the group of lawyers, officials and journalists assembled at Sante Prison near the guillotine scarcely saw it. Hundreds, including scores on their way home from cabarets of Montmartre and Montparnasse, tried to break through police lines. Immediately after th

1932-04-18.text: Dublin, April 17, (#).—Two prominent figures in Irish politics died today. Captain William Archer Redmond, member of the Dail Eireann for Waterford, collapsed and died beside the grave of a friend, while Jeremiah MacVeagh, who was an Irish National member of the British House of Commons from 1902 to 1920, succumbed here. Captain Redmond, 46, war hero and long a prominent Independent Nationalist, was attending the funeral of his friend, D. F. Hogan. He had gone to the graveside where he suddenly collapsed and could not be revived. Mr. MacVeagh, who was 61, was a lawyer and a journalist.

Dublin, April 15) Members of the original Sinn Féin movement led by a woman revolted against the rule of Eamon de Valera today. The revolt came as the government prepared legislation for abolition of the oath of allegiance to the British crown to be introduced in the Dáil Wednesday. Headed by M. MacSweeney, Republican heroine who led troops in the Easter Rebellion of 1916, the Sinn Féiners issued a statement challenging de Valera’s right to head the government, declaring that they alone were entitled to rule because “the government of the republic was established on Easter Sunday, 1916. The statement was made soon after an important commercial firm had warned that separation from Great Britain would mean the discharge of about half of its 1,400 employees. If the Free State withdraws from the empire, exports to Ulster will be subject to

By The Associated Press Friedrichshafen, Germany, April 1.--(Monday)--The dirigible Graf Zeppelin left at 12:08 a.m. today on its third trip this year to Pernambuco, Brazil, under the command of Dr. Hugo Eckener. Among its five passengers were Ralph Booth, commander of the British dirigible R-100, and Richard Von Kehler, president of the German Aeropile.

TOKYO, April 18—()—Military preparations of Soviet Russia on the north Manchurian border are taken by Japanese military experts as a clear indication that Russia expects a clash with Japan, a spokesman for the foreign office said today. “Our military experts estimate that the Soviet forces on the Manchurian frontier between Vladivostok and Manchuli now number nine divisions, a total of 70,000 men, with the strongest concentrations in the Pogranichnaya and Manchuli districts, where there are two divisions each,” the spokesman said. “The experts assert the dispositions clearly indicate the Russians are expecting a clash with Japan. Although they are of a defensive nature, they are capable also of assuming the offensive.” Reports from the Japanese consulate at Harbin, Manchuria, said it was indicated the wreck of a Japanese troop train there last week, causing the death of 14 men, was “the

TOKIO, April 18 (.P)—Concentration of 70,000 Soviet troops on the Manchurian-Siberian frontier indicates Russia is preparing to fight "either offensively or defensively," a government spokesman said today. His statement came as he termed "absurd" a New York World Telegram editorial warning against the effect of American toleration of Japanese aggression in North Manchuria, strengthening of these "militarists" might lead them to attempt aggression in Soviet territory, and suggested the outcome of such action would be a Russian-Japanese war, chiefly because of a belief in Tokyo that America would tolerate such action. The spokesman denied any possibility of Japanese aggression against the Soviets, but said the Japanese would intervene in the event of a clash between the Soviets and the new Manchurian state. "Very serious consequences" may result if there are further incidents such as the r

Paris, April Wfo-A belief that the financial crisis in the United States is now passing through its final “healing phase” and America is headed for renewed prosperity was expressed today in the newspaper Le Temps. The newspaper said it thought the American recovery would be achieved without any real inflation. “American money will remain stable,” said its weekly financial review, “Losses will be registered and accepted. "The United States will enter a period of new credits with the likelihood of an economic prosperity less brilliant than before the crisis, but more real and more solid.” The article was signed by Frederic Jenny. Reviewing conditions after the passage of the Glass-Steagall act in the American congress, which permits banks to borrow money on securities other than those stipulated in the federal reserve regulations, M. Jenny said: “This chapter in the financial history of th

STOCKHOLM, Apr. 18 (AP).— New developments in the investigation into the affairs of Ivar Kreuger, Swedish match king who committed suicide in Paris last month, led today to make preparation for a widespread international inquiry which will include the United States. The plans called for a special "Kreuger Department of Police," made up of four lawyers and six detectives. It was understood more arrests were imminent and that the police activities would extend to New York, Berlin, Paris, Amsterdam and Geneva. The investigators were said to have established that the forged Italian bonds reported to have been turned up last week among the documents of the Kreuger and Toll Company amounted to about $100,000,000 and were printed at Kreuger's direction by a private firm here about a year ago. The head of the firm said only the forms of the bonds had been turned out and they bore no signatures o

MOSCOW, April 18. Concentrations on the Manchurian frontier were admitted by Moscow today, although figures were not available. Thorough preparations have been made for national defense, it was stated. The press gave warning that the Soviets will not be caught unaware. The Komsomolskaya Pravda said: “Hired bandits are rushing on our frontiers. They should know there is not a single window through which robbers can creep without risk.” Official circles strongly denied any Soviet connection with the recent wrecking of a Japanese troop train in Manchuria. On the contrary, they insisted the wreck was engineered by White Russian emigres with the connivance of some Japanese military authorities with the object of provoking war with Russia. The press accused Japan of spreading lies about Soviet terrorism to prepare public opinion for “further military adventures.” Tokio, April 18—Concentration

1932-09-26.text: POONA, India, (UP).—The Mahatma M. K. Gandhi abandoned his “fast unto death” today as vitality ebbed steadily from the frail, brown body he had staked against the British settlement of India’s communal voting problem. British acceptance of an agreement reached between caste Hindus and “untouchables” enabled Gandhi to end his hunger strike. Doctors attending the Mahatma at Yerovda prison, where he lay on a cot in the shade of a mango tree in the yard, told Indian government officials that Gandhi's vitality was at its lowest ebb since he ate his last meal at noon last Tuesday. Today was Gandhi's weekly day of silence. He suffered from frequent periods of nausea and fainting spells during the last stages of the fast. His wife rubbed his head with olive oil to restore consciousness when he fainted. LONDON, (UP).—The British government today approved a Hindu settlement of the communal voting

POONA, India, Sept. 26.—The dramatic "fast unto death" undertaken by Mahatma M. K. Gandhi in behalf of India’s "forgotten men"—her 60,000,000 "untouchables"—came to an end this afternoon. One hour and fifteen minutes after Gandhi was informed that the British and Indian governments have approved settlement of the Hindu problem, the Mahatma raised his head from his hard cot under a mango tree in the courtyard of the Yeravda jail and called for nourishment. A glass containing two ounces of orange juice was handed to him by the superintendent of the jail. His thin lips curled over the rim and he took into his frail and emaciated body the first nourishment of any sort in more than 145 hours. Few Persons Present. Only a few persons, including the superintendent and the Mahatma’s doctor, were present at the breaking of the fast. But outside of the prison where Gandhi threw his own life into th

POONA, India. (7. Mahatma Gandhi warned the people of India he would suspend his “fast unto death” only if the compromise electoral plan, accepted by untouchables and caste Hindus, is approved by Prime Minister MacDonald. His voice was barely audible as he neared the end of his fifth day without food. A physician who examined the sixty-two year old nationalist said he would be unable to recover unless he took food soon. “If my fast is broken by virtue of the cabinet's decision, it will be but a suspension,” he said. “Sure as fate I shall take my vow again if the part to be played by caste Hindus is not well played in the coming months.” Mr. Gandhi lay on an enameled bed under a mango tree in the compound of Yeroda jail. The compromise plan, hastily effected in an effort to end Gandhi's hunger strike in protest against the separate electorates set up for India’s untouchables, was cabled t

TOKYO. (Monday). UP. The wireless station at Ochiishi continued throughout the night to cover the north Pacific for news of the Japanese goodwill plane en route to Nome, Alaska, but the efforts were fruitless, and fear was expressed the plane had not survived a weekend storm. The plane hopped off at 5:35 a.m. Friday from Samushiro, and the last word was at 10:16 a.m. the same day, when the plane flashed it was 750 miles northeast of Tokyo. At 12:30 a.m. Monday (9:30 a.m. Sunday, c.s.t.) the goodwill ship had been out nearly seventy-two hours. The newspaper Hochi Shimbun, promoter of the flight, doubted whether the ship would ever be heard from again. Aboard were three aviators, Ejiichiro Baba, pilot; Kiyoshi Honma, navigator, and Tomoyoshi Ishita, radio operator. Their ship was a single motored one and this was the third ill-fated goodwill flight sponsored by the newspaper. Since the for

Cherbourg, France, Sept. 26 (4).— The French submarine Persee sent out a call for assistance today after an accident in which a number of men were injured. Details of the accident were not given. The vessel is of the same type as the submarine Promethee, which sank off Cherbourg last July with heavy loss of life. Incomplete reports said there had been an explosion but the number of injured could not be learned immediately. A salvage tug and an airplane went out. Ministry of Marine officials said they did not believe the accident was serious. The submarine normally carries a crew of about 65 men.

CHERBOURG, France, Sept. 9 —(UP)—The French submarine Persee radioed its base here today that an accident had happened to its machinery and that several were injured. The submarine gave its position as near Jajdheu. Naval vessels located it and were towing it to port. The Persee is one of France's big new cruising submarines, recently completed and is a sister ship of the Promethee, which went down off here this year with a loss of more than sixty lives. The submarine was engaged in its trials—as was the Promethee—when the accident happened. The radio message asked for medical assistance and said there had been an explosion in the engine room.

JRAMAT, France, Sept. 25. —Premier Edouard Herriot declared in a public address today that military experts of unquestionable authority insist Germany is seeking sufficient military strength to defeat "with one thrust the designated adversary." The Premier, whose speech outlined the French conception of disarmament with security, did not name the "adversary." He said the military authorities were trying "to convince us" of the truth of their opinion and then put the question to his audience in these words: "In the same way that, formerly, Prussia took advantage of conditions imposed on her to build a redoubtable army of an absolutely new type, is not German military genius today searching to create an army with the intention of striking to the heart with one decisive thrust the designated adversary, for whom national defense is but one form of patriotism?" The Premier stopped here on his

CHERBOURG, France, Sept. 26 —(AP)—One man was killed and 12 were injured, three critically, in an explosion today in the sheathing engines of the new French submarine Persee, which was making a trial trip off Cherbourg. The injured included two naval officers and several workmen from the Schneider shipyards. It was feared several men might die. The cause of the explosion has not been determined. The ship was not endangered, although a call for assistance was sent out. Naval tugs had her in tow quickly and the doctors they carried gave the injured men first aid treatment. The Persee was cruising on the surface between Guernsey and the French coast, about seven miles off shore, when the explosion occurred. There were about 60 men aboard.

1932-07-03.text: LONDON, (UP).—Former King Manoel of Portugal died Saturday in his home at Twickenham, a suburb. He had been bothered by a throat disorder. Manoel appeared in the best of health Friday when he witnessed the Wimbledon tennis matches Saturday afternoon but a message was received at the club about 1:30 p.m. saying that he was suffering from throat trouble and would not appear. The former queen of Portugal was at Manuel's bedside when he died.

LAUSANNE, Switzerland, July 2.—A plan to settle the German reparations problem was approved by the leading powers today and will be presented to German leaders by Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald, of Great Britain. It was understood to provide for a three year moratorium in Europe with Germany asked to pay approximately 4,000,000,000 marks, or $952,000,000.

WIMBLEDON, Eng., July 2.—Ellsworth Vines, Jr., American champion, today won the prized Wimbledon tennis title, defeating H. W. (Bunny) Austin, of England, in the final match 6-4, 6-2, 6-0. The lanky Vines, white cap pulled down over his eyes, merely toyed with England's leading player, overwhelming Austin with the fierceness of his drives and his masterful court covering. He is the fourth American to win the English title, considered the most prized possession of the world’s tennis courts, and succeeds a fellow American, Sidney B. Wood Jr.

Lausanne, Switzerland—A?—War debts due the United States from Europe were linked with reparations payments Saturday in what may be the last act of the Lausanne conference which met two weeks ago to solve the reparations problem and map a route to world economic recovery. The five principal creditor powers handed to the German delegation last night a proposal for a reparations settlement in which the settlement was made to depend on America’s cancellation of war debts. The proposal was softly phrased, to avoid stirring up American opposition, but it was none the less firm. German sources were responsible for a report that Chancellor Franz von Papen already had informed Prime Minister MacDonald of Great Britain his government would not endorse the plan. It is a miniature Young plan, but it contains no figures. These were left to be filled in later. The core of the proposal is a proviso for

LAUSANNE, Switzerland, July 2—(AP)—The five power scheme which would tie up settlement of German reparations with revision of the allied war debts to the United States appeared tonight to be facing rejection by Germany. In a last minute effort to avert rejection, the creditor countries were understood to have substituted a "gentlemen’s agreement" for the so-called safeguard clause which Germany found objectionable. Under the proposed agreement, said authoritative quarters, the accord would not be ratified until the United States was heard from on the subject of debts. It was explained that the "gentlemen’s agreement" would make the reparations settlement dependent upon Washington without a specific statement to that effect, eliminating the safeguard clause, which would make elimination of reparation payments conditional upon America’s agreement to revise debts. The Washington government

Lausanne, Switzerland, July 2.—Germany has refused to accept any proposal linking up the settlement of reparations with the adjustment of allied debts to the United States, it was reported this evening. The proposal advanced primarily by France is objectionable to Germany even in camouflage form, it was understood. In effect, the suggestion, which has been receiving consideration for the past several days, is that Germany put up a bond of between four and eight billion marks with the World Bank, part to be used in lieu of reparations payment, and the rest for rehabilitation of the economic wreck of Europe. There is in addition a “safeguard clause.” It would make the wiping out of reparations payments conditional upon America’s revision of the debt due her from the World War allies.

Berlin, July 2 (AP)—Four were dead and more than two dozen injured today as a result of political rioting in Germany during the last 24 hours. One was killed in Berlin when police fired on a group of national socialists, two were killed in a battle between communists and Hitlerites at Hattingen and a Nazi at Cologne shot three men, killing one of them.

OSAKA, Japan, July 2.—Fourteen persons were drowned and forty were injured today when the river dike collapsed at Mikimachi, in the Hyogo prefecture. Fifty buildings were washed away, including the railroad shops and a hospital, in the release of the bank full stream. It was estimated that 4,800 houses were inundated in this city following heavy rains throughout the region.

1932-01-08.text: By Tre Arnaewrte fren MBAY, India, Jan. 7.-The legality of the arrest of Mahatma Gandhi, leader of Indian nationalists in their struggle for independence from British authority, will be tested in the courts. Nationalist attorneys announced today they would apply January 11 for a writ of habeas corpus which would call for a high court review of the Mahatma's arrest under an 1827 law. India Remains Tense Meanwhile all India remained tense, but no major clashes between police and nationalist demonstrators were reported. Five powerful bombs were discovered in a first class compartment of the Darjeeling express when the train arrived at Calcutta. Attorneys backing the legal fight to release the Mahatma said he could not be held indefinitely in prison under antiquated and vague laws. The 1827 law has never been challenged in court, and they will attempt to test it before the highest tribunal i

| By The Associated Press. Weston, Super-Mare, England, Jan. 7.—Sir William Mills, inventor of the Mills hand grenade, of which 75,000,900 were estimated to have been used in the World War, died suddenly today. He was 76 years old.

TOKIO, JAN. 8. (AP).—The Japanese government of Premier Inukai, less than a month old, handed its resignation to Emperor Hirohito today shortly after the emperor had narrowly missed becoming the victim of a bomb. The premier was instructed by the emperor to continue in office until further orders. The action of the cabinet in resigning was based on the precedence of the resignation of the “earthquake” cabinet of Premier Yamamoto, which resigned in 1923 after Emperor Hirohito, then prince regent, was fired upon while on his way to open the Japanese parliament. The bomb exploded immediately in front of the emperor's state carriage as he was nearing the palace grounds on the way home from the annual military review. It fell under the carriage of Count Makino, of the imperial household, but injured no one. A young Korean was immediately arrested. A second bomb was found in his pocket.

TOKYO, Jan. 8, (#)—American Ambassador W. Cameron Forbes presented Secretary Stimson's note on the Manchurian situation to the Japanese Foreign Office late today and official circles expressed the view the 'genius operations in Manchuria' are not of a nature to warrant intervention by third powers. Japanese Ambassador Debuchi cabled a text of Secretary Stimson’s note, which invoked the 9-power treaty, and it was reiterated that Japan has made no demands in Manchuria except with respect to her treaty rights and that, even in the face of the representations of other powers, there is little chance that she will modify her Manchurian policy. Government a Masquerade. In this connection it was emphasized that any administrative integrity of China proper in Manchuria prior to Sept. 18, 1931, was not destroyed by the Japanese because, it was stated, Nanking had never exercised any real authority

AVAL E—An attempt to assassinate Emperor Hirohito failed Friday when an assailant said to be a Korean hurled a bomb at the emperor's carriage. The assailant was captured. The attack occurred outside the Sakurada gate to the Chiyoda castle, directly in front of the huge new metropolitan police headquarters. Police said the bomb exploded behind the second carriage of the royal procession in which Minister of the Imperial Household Count Makino was riding. The carriage was seared, but the carriage in which the emperor was riding was not damaged. The emperor entered the imperial palace safely. The assailant gave his name as Rihosho. He said he was a laborer and was born at Seoul. His motive was not revealed. The attack occurred as the emperor was returning to the imperial palace after reviewing troops at the Yoyogi parade grounds. American Ambassador W. Cameron Forbes and other foreign diplo

Berlin, Jan. 7. (4)—By a dramatic turn in politics, fiery Adolf Hitler, former non-commissioned officer in the German imperial army, sat in judgment tonight on his old field marshal, President Paul Von Hindenburg. It was for Herr Hitler to decide whether to command his fascist legions in the Reichstag to prolong for one year Von Hindenburg’s term as president. This shift in the political lineup was brought about by two days of conferences in which Hitler first listened to overtures by Wilhelm Groener, minister of defense, and then talked with Chancellor Heinrich Bruening. The national socialist leader announced he would confer with the chieftains of the nationalist opposition and would make known his decision as soon as he had learned their views. Hitler was called into the government’s counsel to avoid the necessity of a presidential election at this critical time. The fascist leader, t

Moscow, Jan. 7, ().—Fifty persons were killed and many others injured in a rear-end train collision Saturday about nine miles northwest of Moscow, it was learned today. The heavy casualty list resulted in part from the fact that the injured were placed by rescuers along a parallel track to await arrival of medical crews. A freight train came along and before the engineman could stop, plowed through them. Government and railway officials attempted to suppress all news of the disaster so there were no official figures on the total casualties. Some estimates were that several hundred were killed. Two six-car local trains, both packed with passengers, were involved in the collision.

TOKIO, Jan. 8—(UP)—The Japanese government indicated clearly today that it might not hesitate to land marines in China and possibly establish blockades and seize customs in Chinese ports to combat the Japanese boycott in China. The government is increasingly concerned over the movement. Officials said the boycott was increasing rapidly throughout China and that many Japanese firms, threatened with bankruptcy, had asked the government for indemnity.

1932-09-13.text: ANOMAGSALIK, Greenland, Sept. 13—Wrecked on the beach less than 40 miles from here, George Hutchinson and the seven who were flying with him from New York to London, were rescued today by the British trawler Lord Talbot. A leaking gasoline tank forced them down in the water of Itersak, but the plane was wrecked on the reefs which makes navigation perilous. Hutchinson, his wife, their two children, and the crew of four men waded ashore, awoke a tiny Eskimo settlement whose few inhabitants would have abandoned the place and returned to Anomagsalik for the winter in a few more weeks. Eskimo sealers assisted them in saving their instruments and most of their supplies. The castaways were taken aboard the Lord Talbot and Capt. Watson, master of the trawler, awaited orders from the owners in Aberdeen, Scotland, whether to bring them there or drop them at Iceland.

POONA, India, Sept. 13. (AP).— At the very time the Mahatma Gandhi's starvation ultimatum was made public in Great Britain the Mahatma himself was sitting in an improvised dentist's chair in Yero-da prison, having finishing touches put to a new set of teeth. The dentist has been a frequent visitor to the prisoner because the Mahatma has proved a difficult case for him. He has made several dentures for the Mahatma only to have them discarded. The Mahatma’s plan to “fast unto death” unless British communal election plans are abandoned, was expected to bring about his release from prison. Simla authorities were reported as saying they would send him to Sabarmati Ashram, his residence near Ahmedabad.

COPENHAGEN, Sept. 18—The “flying Hutchinsons,” father, mother, two little girls, and a crew of four, missing since Sunday afternoon in their attempt to fly from New York to London, were discovered early today alive and well on the east coast of Greenland. They were found ashore at Ikereak Fjord by the British trawler Lord Talbot, first craft to be in search of them after Colonel George R. Hutchinson sent a distress signal Sunday when his plane was forced down while he was bound for Angmagsalik. The plane is a total wreck, Captain Thomas Watson of the Lord Talbot wired International News Service. The Lord Talbot, according to messages from Iceland, is proceeding slowly to Angmagsalik through the ice field after taking the eight occupants of the wrecked “City of Richmond” aboard shortly after daylight this morning. Copyright International News Service Copenhagen, Sept. 13. (INS) "Flying Hutchinson family" and a crew of four were found well today by the British Lord Talbot. News of the rescue of the "Hutchinsons," including George R. Hutchinson, of Baltimore, his wife, and two small daughters, was flashed to International News Service today in a brief message direct from Captain Watson, of the Lord Talbot. It read as follows: "Located Hutchinson at 1:00 a.m. All well: Now awaiting daylight: Signed, Watson." This would place the rescue at 7:00 p.m. Eastern Standard Time last night, about thirty-three hours after the first distress signals were flashed from the Hutchinson's plane, the "City of Richmond" as it was forced down off the coast of Greenland in a sea jammed with icebergs. ABOARD S. S. DARTFORD (UP)—The monoplane American Nurse, on a projected non-stop flight from New York to Rome, was sighted at 6:05 p. m. Greenwich time (1:05 p. m., E. S. T.) Tuesday, flying very low, heading eastward about 150 miles southeast of Cape Cable, Nova Scotia. FLOYD BENNETT AIRPORT, N. Y. (UP) — The plane American Nurse with two men and a woman aboard took off Tuesday on a projected non-stop flight to Rome, 4,209 miles distant. The huge Bellanca plane roared into the air at 5:17 a. m. CST. The plane started climbing immediately as it circled the field twice, then it headed for Cape Cod at an altitude of 4,000 feet. William Ulbrich was at the controls of the “flying medical laboratory” with Dr. Leon M. Pesculli and Miss Edna Newcomer, nurse, as passengers. The flight was designed to be a scientific expedition with the physician studying the physical reactions of Ulbrich and Mis

Thomas Watson, of the rescue trawler Lord Talbot, cabled the owners today he had landed the crew of the Hutchinson family plane safely and was proceeding with his fishing. He did not say where he landed them, but it was obviously near Angmagsalik. It was reported the Hutchinsons had arrived at Finsbu, near Angmagsalik, where the Norwegian wireless station is located. PARIS, Sept. 13. (®)—Pres. Albert Lebrun rejected the final plea for the life of Dr. Paul Gorguloff, Slayer of former Pres. Paul Doumer, today and the Russian was ordered guillotined tomorrow. Even before formal announcement of the execution, passes were being issued by the prefecture of police for the occasion. Father Gillet, a priest of the Greek Orthodox church, arrived to administer last rites to Gorguloff. The execution probably will take place at dawn.

Announcing that democracy had broken down in Germany, the chancellor gave every indication that he intended to continue to hold the reins under the slogan: “With von Hindenburg for Germany.” In the meantime plans proceeded for taking to the supreme court the issue of the legality of the chancellor’s decree of dissolution, which the opposition contended was presented out of order while a vote was being taken. “The government of the reich,” the chancellor said, “is of the opinion that the system of formal democracy has broken down and is incapable of resurrection.” He earnestly begged private employers to “read the signs of the times aright,” declaring if they did not they would find themselves “ruthlessly swal

1932-09-10.text: Deal, England, Sept. 10 (AP)— After bobbing about in the channel all night in choppy seas, Charles Zimmy, legless professional swimmer of Long Beach, California, abandoned an attempt to swim to France. He was taken out of the water after he had covered 40 miles and eight miles off Calais when he quit.

DOVER, Eng. Sept. 16—Charles (Zimmy) Zibelman, legless American swimmer, was forced to abandon his efforts to swim the English Channel today when eight miles off the coast of France. Buffeted by heavy seas the legless man left the water and returned to Dover on board a tug.
-DAIREN, Manchuria. (). The British consul here refused to pay a ransom of $60,000 demanded by Chinese bandits for two British subjects kidnapped near Mukden last week.

SEATTLE, Sept. 9 ()—Hugh Eugene Wood, aged two years, speaks Esperanto. He speaks “The Universal Language” to his father, an Esperanto enthusiast, and English to other members of the family. Complimented today on his prowess, he said: “Mi est bona, chu ne?” The reporter said yes.

, Tokyo, Sept. 10. — A storm of protest which developed during the last two days over the photographing of a number of Japanese business and industrial buildings by the National City Bank of New York, assumed a more serious aspect today and led to diplomatic action of delegations from several Japanese patriotic societies who visited a branch of the bank at Osaka, and attempted to intimidate its Japanese employees. Osaka newspapers came out again with full pages devoted to protests against the photographing, and printed a number of other reports hinting that the United States is making other preparations for a possible war. Ambassador Grew called on Japanese Foreign Minister Count Uchida. Officials of the bank explained that the photographs were taken to be used in promotional material illustrating the business and industrial development of the Far East. BERLIN, Sept. 10 (UP).—The German government today confirmed that it is planning to ask Washington to postpone the semi-annual payment of 33,000,000 marks due on September 30 as arrears on the costs of the United States army of occupation and other mixed claims. Official announcement, however, has been withheld pending further conversations between the German embassy in Washington and the American government. It is understood that whereas it was first intended to ask a postponement of two and a half years, a longer period may now be requested. If an agreement is reached with the United States it is understood that Germany intends to open negotiations with other creditor nations such as Belgium, seeking to postpone payments due. The government is carefully avoiding the word “moratorium.”

TOKIO, Sept. 10.—A statement absolving the National City Bank of suspicion in connection with a series of photographs of industrial plants it had taken for publication in advertising matter was issued this afternoon by Foreign Minister Uchida after a conference with Joseph Clark Grew, United States ambassador to Japan. Ambassador Grew had called upon the minister for a complete investigation into charges published by the vernacular press that the photographs were for foreign military use. Uchida received the American ambassador at 3 p.m. and informed him that an investigation already had been launched into statements made in certain vernacular newspapers. His formal statement absolving the bank, which is a unit of the National City Bank of New York, was issued a short time later. Minister of War Sadao Araki scoffed at the suspicion cast upon the bank during an interview with the United P

Paris. — (AP) — The council of ministers, with President Lebrun presiding, approved unanimously today the text of the French reply to Germany's aide memoire demanding equality of armaments. The reply, among other things, points out that the German demand calls for a revision of the Versailles treaty and that such a procedure could not be taken by France and Germany, but should be proposed to the League of Nations. The text will be taken to Berlin by a member of Premier Herriot’s staff who will deliver it to the French ambassador there Sunday. The premier said it probably will not be published here until Monday evening. It was indicated that the American government would be provided with a copy of the reply. The note was described as extremely courteous in tone, dealing separately with the points raised. The matter is Geneva, where Germany is a member of the League of Nations council. The

1932-12-04.text: (United Press International Correspondence; Washington, Dec. 3—(UI)—The administration today pondered its reply to urgent British and French pleas for postponement of war debt payments due 12 days hence. Congress warned that recommendations for a further moratorium would be futile. The president was expected to make known his views in a special message to congress next week. While Mr. Hoover and his cabinet advisors studied the new British and French notes, Speaker of the House Garner and Senate Majority Leader Watson warned that congress would not authorize delay of the December 15 debt payments, totaling $124,000,000. Senators Borah, Rep. Idaho, and Bankhead, Dem. Ala. were the only outspoken advocates of relief for the debtors. They attached reservations; Bankhead suggested that only interest be paid on Dec. 15, pending an effort to work a method of payment other than in gold. Reduced

The British public found little encouragement today for any hopes they may have held that the second British debt note would have an immediate effect on Washington. The newspapers advised them that congressional leaders had received with more or less hostility the British arguments for suspension of the war debt payment of $95,550,000 due Dec. 15. A sharp recession in the rate for the pound sterling featured the foreign exchange market Saturday. Opening at $3.21, against an overnight quotation of $3.20 5/8, the rate fell within an hour to $3.17 1/2 on selling again attributed to war debt uncertainties. The closing price was $2.17 1/2.

Geneva, Dec. 3—()—Preliminary discussions began today in preparation for a five-power conference on Monday whose main purpose is to bring Germany back into the world disarmament conference. Norman Davis of the United States, Prime Minister MacDonald of Great Britain, Premier Herriot of France and Italo Rosso, Italy's arms expert, engaged in informal discussion but Foreign Minister von Neurath of Germany and head of the arms delegation was detained in Berlin. He will be here on Monday.

LONDON, Dec. 3 — United States Ambassador Andrew W. Mellon conferred for half an hour today with Stanley Baldwin, head of the government during Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald's absence at Geneva. Baldwin, the first cabinet minister to make a public statement since the British debt note was sent to Washington, indicated yesterday that the government expects the war debts question to be carried over to the world economic conference to meet herein 1933. Baldwin said he was glad to think that "following the Lausanne conference and following this note to America, we shall have an international conference as soon as it can be convened in 1933." "I have no doubt that Americans will give the note the most careful consideration, and I would say that as far as their government is concerned, it will also give sympathetic consideration. They must know that they stand to suffer, just as we stand to

By The Associated Press Washington, Dec. 3.—Several movements were developing in congress today to turn the debts storm into a rainbow with a pot of silver at the end. Chairman Somers of the house coinage committee suggested that Great Britain might be allowed to make her December 14 debt payment in silver; Senator Hayden (D., Ariz.), said he was trying to get some figures concerning his resolution to permit debt payments in the metal; Senator Wheeler (D., Mont.), and numerous others held to a belief that remonetization of silver is essential for economic recovery. But some leaders in both house and senate predicted the silver drive might end at naught, swept aside by other pressing things such as prohibition, appropriations, the budget and relief. Somers’ theory was based on facts obtained in a lengthy study of world monetary conditions made by his committee. He held that the use of sil

WASHINGTON, Dec. 3.—Overwhelming opposition in congress to any postponement, reduction or cancellation of the European war debts left President Hoover today with the knotty problem of replying to the French and British notes in such a manner as not to aggravate still further a delicate situation. Administration officials maintained tight-lipped silence as to whether Mr. Hoover will recommend to the congress the postponement of Dec. 15 payments requested in the notes, pending review of the whole war debt structure. Whether he does or does not, congressional opinion is fixed and seemingly immovable. Leaders without regard to party or faction, as well as the rank and file, are a unit against any postponement, reduction or cancellation. London, Dec. 8—The Shanghai correspondent of the Daily Express reported today that bandits wounded some of the crew of the American steamer Tplnug when the ship fired on 30 miles above Ichang, on the Yangtze.

WASHINGTON, Dec. 3 (IA) — America’s weakened treaty position in warships as compared with Japan and Great Britain was asserted today by Secretary Adams in his annual report to President Hoover. “Curtailment of expenditures has been made principally at the expense of the fighting fleet,” the secretary said in discussing limited congressional appropriations for the Navy. He made no direct recommendations, but presented numerous comparative figures and tables of the strength of the three navies to speak for themselves. In this connection, the report cited that the present building program of the United States does not provide for a treaty navy for the next four years, makes no provision for the replacement of overage vessels, nor the “rectifying of our already seriously impaired position relative to other signatories of the Naval treaties nor the preventing further undermining of that posit

1932-11-10.text: A week-old tropical hurricane bore down on the Bahamas today after killing at least 10 persons, injuring several score, and causing great damage in Cuba and Jamaica. The British funnel line freighter Premius, struck off Nicaragua by the storm, made repairs yesterday and a salvage tug was nearby. The British tramp Ingola, out of Montreal for Montevideo, reported she was drifting in the hurricane without steerage way, but did not ask assistance. The hurricane began to appear in the Virgin Islands No. 2. It dipped southward, wrecking Bahama plantations in Colombia, before starting out on the normal northwest hurricane path. Sunday it was off Nicaragua. It destroyed half the banana cultivations on the island of Jamaica yesterday, and headed through the Bahamas today. The path of the disturbance was northeastward, and was central during the night 150 miles south of Nassau. The United States m

Albany, N. Y.—(A#)—President-elect Roosevelt, asked today regarding reports published in British newspapers that he would visit London before taking office and that he was inclined toward favorable war debts terms with England, said: “Who's looney now?” Mr. Roosevelt's cryptic reply was given to a secretary who submitted the question for newspapermen. The query came as Mr. Roosevelt awakened from a long night's rest. Mr. Roosevelt has not gone abroad since he journeyed to Paris in the spring of 1931 to visit his mother, ill in a hospital at that time.

Stockholm, Sweden, Nov. 10—(F)—The 1932 Nobel Prize for Literature was bestowed today upon John Galsworthy, the British novelist. The author of "The Forsyte Saga" had been mentioned in newspaper predictions as the probable recipient of the award. Last year’s prize was won by E. A. Karlfeldt, of Sweden. Sinclair Lewis, who received the prize in 1930, was the first American to be so honored. Last year’s prize was worth about $31,000. Since 1901, when the prizes were established under the will of Alfred B. Nobel, Swedish scientist who invented dynamite, only two other Englishmen have won the award for literature. Mr. Galsworthy, now 65, published his first novel, "Jocelyn," in 1886 under the nom de plume of John Sinjohn. It was not till 1904 that he attracted general attention with (Continued on page two!)

Stockholm, Sweden (U.P.) — John Galsworthy, English novelist, was awarded the Nobel prize for literature today. His most recent novel, “Maid in Waiting,” was published last fall. The Nobel prize for literature was worth $46,350 when Sinclair Lewis won it in 1930. This year’s prize is expected to be considerably less however, because interest accruing from the $9,000,000 bequeathed by Alfred B. Nobel to establish the prizes has decreased during the past two years.

London. Nov. 10. (UP)—Negotiations for revision of her war debt due to the United States and postponement of the payment of approximately $100,000,000 due Washington on December 15 was forecast in the press today, now that the presidential election is over. The statements in this morning’s papers along that line were so unanimous they appeared to have been inspired, although no official announcement came from government sources. The political writer of the Daily Mail said it was expected the government would address an important communication to Washington soon on the question of war debts.

(By The Associated Press) London, Nov. 10—It was learned this evening that a British note on the subject of debts was delivered today by the British ambassador to Secretary of State Stimson in Washington. No further information was available here, probably because it was not certain whether the American government was willing to have the contents of the note made public.

Storms held sway over a third of the United States today. Warnings were posted along the New England coast in the wake of a terrific gale that lashed New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Long Island, Connecticut, and Massachusetts last night. In the mid-west, snow storms, in some localities of blizzard intensity, brought sub-arctic weather. The tropical hurricane that struck Cuba was passing out to sea east of the Bahamas. Radio Marine, in touch with ships in its area, reported that the tanker Sun Oil had been severely damaged but was riding out the storm. Along the eastern coast, storms brought record high tides that did considerable damage.

London--(?)--The British government officially voiced the opinion today that the drastic reduction in reparations recently agreed upon in Europe “should now become possible,” while the press generally speculated on the effect of the American election on war debts. The official expression came from Stanley Baldwin of the British cabinet, speaking before the lord mayor's banquet last night in place of Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald. Mr. Baldwin said: “It is essential to the world that ratification of the Lausanne settlements on reparations should now become possible, and the work begun there should be completed.” “The gentlemen’s agreement” at Lausanne, provided that the accord cutting Germany’s war reparations payments to a bonded $714,000,000, must depend on a lenient attitude by creditor nations. The United States is the chief creditor nation. Mr. Baldwin said he wished the Lausanne re

1932-05-23.text: | London, May 22.—(#)—Amelia Earhart Putnam, smiling lone flyer of the Atlantic, flew from Londonderry, Northern Ireland, to London today, landing in a terrific thunderstorm at Hanworth airdrome to complete her oversea trip from New York. | “I don't mind the rain,” she said in the downpour in which she arrived. “I got used to it Friday night.”’ She laughed as she said it while a crowd of some 200 swarmed around her and cameras snapped. | Thousands, believing she was coming to Croydon airdrome, gathered there to welcome her. Only a few, including a delegation from the American embassy, headed by Ambassador Andrew W. Mellon, were on hand at Hanworth when the slim blonde flyer arrived in a borrowed plane from Ireland, where she ended her ocean flight yesterday. New York, (f)—A man whose identity police withheld, but who, police said, had a diary or notebook intimating he was in some way responsible for the death of Lord Kitchener, chief of staff of the British army, who lost his life in the North Sea during the World War, was under arrest at police headquarters today. Lord Kitchener lost his life in the North Sea when the H. M. S. Hampshire was lost. Police said the man was being held in connection with the burning of a British vessel, in which several lives were lost, during the World War. Although police declined to disclose the identity of the prisoner, it (Continued on Page 8)

Southampton, England, May 23—The German flying boat Dornier DO-X, en route back to Lake Constance from New York, arrived here at 7:15 p. m. today (1:15 p. m. Defiance time) from Spain. The DO-X left Vigo at 10:45 a. m., en route to its base at Lake Constance. It arrived at Vigo last night from the Azores.

DERBY, England, May 22 -(#)— The heaviest floods in half a century spread through the English Midlands today, marooning thousands in and on their homes, disrupting all traffic, wrecking communications and causing great damage to property. Early reports listed no casualties. The principal cities affected were Derby, Sheffield, Banbury, Northampton, Leicester, Buckingham, Worksop and Ashby-de-la-Zouche. Dozens of other towns and villages were wrestling with high water. Conditions in Derby, where the water in the central streets reached five and a half feet, were illustrative of the situation elsewhere in this heart of the English countryside. Great damage to the goods in stores occurred, phones were put out of action, and scores of houses in the poorer districts were inundated.

London, May 22.—(#) -— Peter Garvie, a little boy who wanted to be a Life Guard, was told by a nurse, as he was having several stitches taken out of a wound, that “Life Guards don't cry.” “Perhaps, if you won't cry the Prince of Wales will make you one of his Life Guards,” she said. The prince visited the hospital a few days later and the little fellow called out: “I want to be a Life Guard.” The nurse told the prince how brave the boy had been. Dream Comes True Two days later a little Life Guard's uniform, complete in every detail, was sent to Peter Garvie with a card: “From the Prince of Wales.”

AMELIA EARHART IN EUROPE (Copyright, The Associated Press) London, May 22 (P)—I will leave Europe for home about June 10 without going back to Ireland, where I landed yesterday after my flight from Harbor Grace, Newfoundland. I sort of hate to leave my plane up there, but there is a man here in whom I have faith to dismantle and pack it, so I am going to let him do it and ship it back to the United States for me. So I won't go back to Ireland after all. But I am going to Rome, prob- ably during this week. First, I am going shopping early tomorrow morning. I had to borrow some clothes from friends at the American embassy, but I can't keep borrowing forever. My start Friday from Newfound- land was delayed a little bit to have time to fix up all the customs re- quirements, they gave me clearance papers just as if I were captain of a ship and I filled a blank space saying I was going to Pari

London, May 23. --- Hundreds of square miles of country in central England were under water today following a series of cloudbursts and consequent overflow of rivers over the weekend. Scores of towns and villages in nine counties were swept by floods, said to be the worst in 50 years. Farmers throughout the wide areas are in a desperate plight.

By HENRY T. RUSSELL, (United Press Staff Correspondent.) ‘Copyright 1932 by United Press.) London, May 22,—(UP)—Drenched by rain but still smiling happily Amelia Earhart Putnam arrived from Londonderry tonight in the midst of a terrific thunderstorm that menaced the last stage of her flight from New York. A great thunderclap split the heavens as the chartered plane carrying the first woman to fly the Atlantic alone raced down to Hanworth airdrome at 6:10 p. m. Rain battered the sturdy craft and soaked the landing field, but about 200 persons out of many at the airport braved the deluge and ran out to shout a wild welcome. Miss Earhart, tall and blonde, was smiling as she stepped from the plane. The heavy downpour drenched her flying costume, water streamed down her face and her boots sloshed in the puddles. But the smile with which she responded to that first shout of welcome did not fad

1932-05-15.text: Paris, May 14. (AP).—At the end of the first two weeks of May there were only 276,125 men out of work in France. In the past week the decrease in the number of jobless has been 5,888. Since the middle of March unemployment has been on the decline, principally because of improved conditions in the textile regions of the north, the east and in Alsace. In the latter part of April M. Laval’s chart showed that business was picking up in 43 provinces of France, was holding its own in 16 others and in 20 provinces no man was receiving government aid. The government aid amounts to 28 cents a day for each person who receives it, plus 20 cents a day for the wife of each married recipient and 20 cents additional for each child under 16.

HOPEWELL, N. J., May 14 (P).—A baby’s ashes in a simple urn rested today in a crematory chapel, the solemn symbol of human helplessness when madmen roam free. These were the ashes of the Lindbergh baby; the body of a murdered child reduced to a tiny pile of dust by cremation. In the lonesome Sourland Hill home Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh lay ill. HOPEWELL, N. J., May 14 ().—The metal scoop of a broken shovel was found in the undergrowth today close to the spot where the body of the Lindbergh baby was discovered Thursday. Police said there were indications it had been used recently. The walled hollow where the body of the murdered baby was found was scraped clear today and the scrapings were sent to experts for analysis in the hope that science might show the way to arrest of the kidnappers. As the little body was being cremated yesterday State police built a two-foot high wall of concrete blocks around the spot where the long hunt for the kidnapped baby ended Thursday afternoon. Previously the police had merely stood guard over the place, but the wall was raised to make doubly sure that no bungling step might destroy possible valuable clues. KENOSHA, Wis., May 14.—(#) Four robbers, armed with submachine guns early today terrorized the village of Trevor, west of Kenosha. They held up the Zmrzlys hotel, herded guests into the lobby and tossed tear gas bombs into the rooms. They blasted two safes in the offices of the Wisconsin Livestock company. The robbers made an assault, almost military in its maneuvers, first on the plant of the livestock firm. Then they laid siege to the hotel. In the office of the livestock company they shot at and then slugged a watchman, Frank Carney. Then, methodically and without any show of haste, they blew open two safes. Cut Telephone Wires. The robbers worked boldly and successfully, secure in the knowledge that the community of 159 could not summon aid. Telephone lines had been cut. Lackmann of the yacht Marion used by Norfolk negotiators in an attempt to contact kidnappers of the Lindbergh baby, today expressed the opinion that the kidnappers intended to abduct Col. Charles A. Lindbergh. “These men asked no ransom before the baby’s delivery,” Lackmann told the United Press. “They said they would return the child safe and sound and depend on Mr. Curtis’ good faith to pay them later. “What could they have been aiming at if not to get Lindbergh?” He revealed officially for the first time that Lindbergh was aboard on some of the frantic cruises in search of the kidnapped child, and that the boat was heavily armed.
