Sunnyvale, May 14.--(AP)--The navy's new lighter-than-air craft base here had its first customer today, the dirigible Akron swinging from a portable mooring mast. Riveters beat a tattoo on the skeleton of the new airship hangar and civic and governmental dignitaries gathered to celebrate the ship's coming. The giant airship was moored successfully last night after cruising all day around the San Francisco bay area. Lieut. Commander Charles E. Rosendahl, master of the Akron, said it would remain here at least for the weekend. He said he was subject to the orders of the commander-in-chief of the United States fleet, Admiral Frank H. Schofield, to whom he probably would report Monday at San Pedro, flying there.

1932-05-09.text: Adele Astaire, 31, who always said a girl ought to marry a man younger than herself, did it today. She was married to Lord Charles Cavendish, three years her junior, a member of one of England's most noted families. It was an exclusive ceremony in the private chapel at Chatsworth House, ancestral home of the Duke and Duchess of Devonshire, her husband’s parents. Only half a dozen of the bridegroom’s family were present. It was in an interview last year shortly after her engagement was announced, that the popular American dancer put her advice to the lovelorn into these words: “Women gain wisdom more quickly than men, their wisdom enables them to fend off age with greater ease to restrain their independence and individuality, they should never tie themselves up to husbands older than themselves. That is an old-fashioned custom and should be discarded.

CROYDON, Eng, May 9—(AP)—The Imperial Airways liner Horatius, bound through the rain for Paris with 13 passengers, was struck by lightning today over the town of Tonbridge, but the pilot turned around and landed here safely. The bolt blew out the cockpit windows, disabled the wireless aerial and damaged two of the four propellers. The uninjured passengers were transferred to another plane and took off again immediately.

LONDON, May 9—(UP)— British babies are now quoted at from $175 to $350 each, according to the Sunday Express, and certain Americans are buying them “like cloth over the counter.” “The reason is that since the war the United States is eager to have British blood to improve her stock,” the Sunday Express said, “One man offered 1,000 pounds for a really blue-blooded baby.” The newspaper said wealthy Americans in the baby market insisted that the babies be of good family.

BERLIN, May 9. — Chancellor Heinrich Bruening, once more today had served notice on the world that Germany can no longer pay reparations. He added a prediction that the European financial conference at Lausanne next month would lead the way either to world recovery or collapse. “The Lausanne results,” he said in an address to German provincial correspondents on the government's foreign policy, “will determine what fate is in store for Germany and the whole world—whether the world will continue to sink into misery, or finally land on solid ground on which alone reconstruction may be achieved.

Paris, May 9.--(AP)—Two candidates to succeed President Paul Doumer, who was assassinated Friday, were officially in the running today. The election is to be held at Versailles tomorrow. Paul Painlevé, former premier, formally consented today to become a candidate. Albert LeBrun, president of the senate, presented his candidacy formally yesterday. The new president will be chosen by a joint session of the chamber of deputies and the senate. At the special request of Madame Doumer, the body of the president will not be interred in the Pantheon with the group of celebrated French heroes which includes Voltaire, Jean Jacques Rousseau, and Victor Hugo, but in the family plot at Vaugirard cemetery, the decision was made this morning. Other arrangements for the national funeral at Notre Dame cathedral Thursday remain unchanged.

| Paris, May 9.—(Monday)—(P)—Premier Andre Tardieu’s government majority of the right center, which has controlled the chamber of deputies for the past four years, was routed in a heavy swing toward the left in yesterday’s runoff election of a new chamber. At 1:30 a. m., today, with virtually all the seats accounted for, including results from the first election last Sunday, the opposition parties had gained control of the chamber, Herriot Victor Edouard Herriot, leader of the radical socialists, appeared to be the dominant figure as his group rolled up a total of 151 seats, representing a gain of 42. The socialists of Leon Blum had 129 seats, a gain of 18, and the republican socialists, also a left group, had 39. The communists got nine seats and dissident communists obtained 12. With the radical socialists wary of the formation of a government in co-operation with the socialists, there

PARIS, May 9.—Thousands of Frenchmen filed through the death chamber at the Elysee Palace today to pay silent tribute to President Paul Doumer, beloved chief of state murdered by a Russian assassin. The body was clothed in formal, black dress with the Grand Cross of the Legion of Honor across the breast. High officers with drawn sabers stood guard at the catafalque, covered with the French Tricolor and surrounded by subdued lights.

(By Associated Press) NELSON, B. C., Canada, May 9 —The capacity of the Nelson jail was packed to the limit today by 209 Doukobors, arrested yesterday for parading in the nude. The Doukobors have a doctrine that they can parade in the naked. The jail already has as prisoners 118 members of the sect, arrested a week ago and sentenced to three years each in prison. Those arrested yesterday were found in the same orchard where the clash between the nudists and police occurred a week ago. Ninety were men, 52 were women and 67 were children 14 years old. Those arrested offered no resistance. Police surrounded them in the orchards and as trucks arrived the nudists scrambled on voluntarily and truck load after truck load set off for the jail.

1932-05-10.text: BASEL, Switzerland. May 9 ()—Directors of the Bank for International Settlements today authorized a three months’ renewal of the bank’s one-fourth share in the $90,000,000 credit extended to Germany in conjunction with the Banks of France and England and the American Federal Reserve. The credit would have expired on June 4. A moratorium of perhaps two or three years on Germany's reparations payments, followed by an attempt to revise the reparations schedules, was predicted today by a source close to the bank. No Settlement The general belief expressed was that the Lausanne conference, which meets next month, would effect no permanent settlement of the reparations problem. Last year the earnings of the World Bank exceeded the profit of about $2,145,000 earned the first year.

Miami, Fla., May 9 (#)—The Dade County grand jury today held that Captain W. N. Lancaster, former British army flier, must stand trial for the murder of Haden Clarke, 26-year-old author and fiancé of Lancaster's flying partner, Mrs. J. M. Keith-Miller. The jurors returned a first degree murder indictment. Circuit Court Judge H. F. Atkinson ordered the British aviator held without bail. He probably will be tried during the term of court opening tomorrow. He has been in jail a week, since his arrest on a warrant sworn out by State Attorney N. Vernon Hawthorne. He could not be seen at the jail immediately after the jury reported, but he had expressed himself several days ago as expecting to be indicted. The indictment was a new chapter in a killing, solution of which has defied authorities since Clarke was found fatally wounded early on the morning of April 21 in the bedroom he and Lancaste

Miami, Fla., May 10 (UP)— Captain W. N. Lancaster, British aviator and manager of Mrs. Keith-Miller, Australian flier, is under a first degree murder indictment today in the death of her sweetheart, Haden Clarke. The indictment was returned late yesterday by the Dade county grand jury, considering the death of the young “ghost writer” April 21. It is believed to presage a trial in which an intriguing love triangle will be revealed.

(By The Associated Press) BAKERWELL, Derbyshire, England, May 9.—Adele Astaire, who danced her way to prominence in theatres on both sides of the Atlantic, was married today to Lord Charles Cavendish in the private chapel of Chatsworth House, the ancestral home of the Duke and Duchess of Devonshire, parents of the bridegroom. Miss Astaire, who is 41, said shortly after her engagement had been announced last year that a girl always should marry a man younger than herself. She obeyed the rule. Her husband is then Scar's juror.

Miami, Fla, May 8—(#)—Capt. W. N. Lancaster, former British army flier, was indicted by the Dade county grand jury today on charges of first degree murder for the death of Haden Clarke, 26-year-old author and fiancé of Mrs. Josie M. Keith-Miller, Lancaster's flying partner. Lancaster is in jail here on a first degree murder charge preferred Monday night by State Attorney N. Vernon Hawthorne, who claims the flier, Mrs. Keith-Miller and Clarke were the principals in a love triangle. The Englishman maintains he is innocent, and Mrs. Keith-Miller joins him in expressing the conviction Clarke committed suicide.

PARIS, May 9. (4)—Defeated by a decisive margin in yesterday’s parliamentary election, Premier Andre Tardieu will resign tomorrow night with a request that his successor be chosen immediately. An official announcement after a cabinet meeting this morning said that the resignation will be presented as soon as the parliament has elected a new president to succeed Paul Doumer. The parties of the left, which have not been in power, except for a few days, since the famous “left cartel” of Edouard Herriot in 1924, swept away the republican majority in the chamber of deputies and left Herriot’s radical socialists and the socialists with a substantial control. On the basis of yesterday’s vote the left groups had 358 seats in the new chamber, compared with the present government’s 244. Excluding the communists, this gave the left a majority of 100 seats. The new chamber does not meet until June 1

LYONS, France, May 9.—(?)— Thirty-eight persons were believed buried today under landslides which swallowed up two apartment houses in the outskirts of Lyons. Twelve injured were removed before rescuers were ordered away by Edouard Herriot, the mayor and former premier, who himself escaped death from another slide only by leaping to safety. Explosions and fires preceded the slides. The first occurred at 9 a.m., while many of the residents were asleep. It cracked the gas mains. The fire department removed the first 12 persons before the second and larger slide tumbled down, crushing both buildings. M. Herriot leaped to the top of the ruins when firemen failed to obey his request to leave. Engineers had predicted a new collapse of the walls. “Do you want to be killed?” he shouted. He himself jumped just in time to escape the crash. About 100 persons were killed in a similar landslide on Fo

(By United Press). Versailles, France, May 10.—Albert Lebrun, 60-year-old president of the senate, was elected president of France on the first ballot today in succession to the murdered Paul Doumer. The official ballot was Lebrun, 639; Fause, 114; Cachin, 8; and Blanes, 49. The Versailles palace, where the senate and chamber, sitting as a national assembly, held the election, was heavily guarded by thousands of troops as a precaution against any outbreak of violence. The election proceeded in good order and was the calmest in history as a tribute to Doumer. Albert Lebrun, new president of France, is a member of the great world-wide Brown family. His name, phonetically, is pronounced “Al-bair Le-Broen.” He has the reputation of being the most distinguished and cultured of all French senators and one of the best orators in the country. The story of his rise in French political life is tha

1932-07-05.text: LONDON, July 5 (#)—Testifying in her trial for the murder of Thomas William Stephen, Mrs. Elvira Dolores Barney told today how she had supported the young man-about-town for nearly two years. Stephen, son of a prominent British financier, was killed in her Mayfair apartment after a party May 31. The defense is that the fatal shot was fired as Stephen tried to disarm Mrs. Barney who had threatened to commit suicide. Mrs. Barney, apparently in complete control of her emotions, was led through a story of the past few years by her attorney, Sir Patrick Hastings, one of England's most brilliant trial lawyers. Four years ago, she said, she married John Barney, an American singer who appeared in England as one of “the three New Yorkers.” He was cruel to her and they separated in 1930. She has not seen him since, she testified. She could not get a divorce because she had acquired American citize

London, England, July 5. (/P)— The House of Commons Monday night overwhelmingly empowered the British government to impose a tariff of 100 percent on imports from the Irish Free State in retaliation against Eamon De Valera’s refusal to pay the semi-annual installment on Irish land annuities. The vote was 223 to 31 for a financial resolution to that end which was moved by J. H. Thomas, secretary for dominions. This surprised the dominions secretary, who said the issue now solely seemed to be the constitution of an arbitration tribunal. He insisted, however, on his resolution. The government’s resolution was supported by a margin of 278 votes in the first test before the House, after it had been proposed to collect the semi-annual installment of some $11,000,000 by the tariff route. An earlier move to delay action was crushed 321 to 43.

Albany, N. Y., July 5. (AP)— Carrying out a four-year old idea, Governor Roosevelt and his four sons will next week go on a short cruise in a forty-foot yawl up the New England coast. The Democratic presidential nominee said today he and the boys, James, Elliott, Franklin, Jr., and John, would put out next Monday from some undesignated point on Long Island with Portsmouth, New Hampshire, as their destination. In addition to Mr. Roosevelt and his sons, there will be one other person on board, a press representative who will meet newspapermen when the boat ties up each night. The nominee explained that in the four years he had been governor he had been unable to have a vacation with his sons. The boat trip was arranged months before the Democratic convention and was to be carried out in event of his victory or defeat. Returning to the executive office with the mantle of his party’s preside

London (U.P.)—Mrs. Elvira Dolores Barney, attractive member of London’s younger set, denied in a broken voice on the witness stand today that she had murdered her lover, Michael Scott Stephen. Mrs. Barney, dressed in black and deathly pale, was on the witness stand for an hour and 45 minutes at her trial for murder in Old Bailey today. She declared she did not shoot Stephen. "I never wanted to shoot him; there was no one I was fonder of," she cried... After her testimony she returned to her place in the prisoners' dock and the defense case was completed.

Jirae Sameera | LONDON. July 6—(P)—Dramatic evidence about “the other woman” was projected today into the murder trial of beautiful Mrs. Dolores Harney of the West End set, who stands accused of shooting her close friend, Thomas William Scott Stephen, after a night of revelry May 31. The witness who told the story was Dr. Durant whom Mrs. Harney called to her obscure but attractive alley apartment on the night of the tragedy. Dr. Durant gave a detailed account of the scene that met his eyes. He said Stephen was dead and Mrs. Harney, overwrought and hysterical and babbling incoherently, again and again kissed the body. The witness said the young woman told him she and Stephen had quarreled the night before over another woman and that a reconciliation had followed, but, the doctor said, Mrs. Harney told him she and her socially prominent companion had resumed the quarrel after a visit to a

NEW YORK, July 5 (AP).—Hope dwindled today for the Ketch Curlew, missing with her crew of six New Yorkers on a race from Montauk Point, Long Island, to Bermuda. Hampered by rain, more than 100 coast guard vessels swept the Atlantic from New London to Norfolk yesterday. If weather permitted, seaplanes were ready to go out today. Skippered by Nat Blum, young engineer who had no ocean racing experience, the 49-foot ketch left with 26 yachts June 25. Only the Curlew and the Bermuda fishermen Spanish Rose are unaccounted for. The Spanish Rose, however, is manned by a seasoned crew.

By United Press BOMBAY, July 4—Five persons were killed and 50 injured today in a renewal of the rioting between Moslems and Hindus. Detachments of British troops were called out to patrol many of the native sections and in some districts police were forced to disperse crowds with gun fire. The casualties today brought the total deaths in the rioting since last May to 22. More than 2600 persons have been injured.

LONDON, July 4 (#)—It was said in authoritative quarters today that Great Britain has decided to build up a disarmament case at Geneva, harmonious with and on the foundations of President Hoover's proposal for reducing the world's arms by one-third. The British delegation at Geneva, it was said, will not advance a distinct program of its own but, using the Hoover plan as a basis, will put forward observations upon it, implementing the American proposals in some cases and amending them in others.

1932-01-13.text: WASHINGTON, Jan. 12. (Pi— Disappointment was expressed today by Senator Bingham of Connecticut, at the report on employment in beer production before prohibition submitted to the senate by the commerce department. In answer to a resolution by the New England republican, the department sent up figures last night showing that malt beverage manufacture employed a maximum of 175,404 persons in 1914. By 1919 the figure had dropped to 42,689, while in 1909 it had been 66,725. This did not include those engaged in distribution, Bingham's complaint, however, was that the report failed to show such industrial consumption items as the amount of coal and the number of freight cars used by the breweries. The information was sought in pursuance of the hearings now on before a senate manufactures sub-committee on bills to increase the legal alcohol content of beer to something approaching pre-prohibit

By ARTHUR BRISBANE Our government must select an ambassador to replace Dawes in London and Forbes in Tokyo, and it is suggested that the chosen must be “men of wealth and suavity.” Suavity perhaps, although a little genuine Americanism might replace suavity. Why is the wealth necessary? Franklin and Jefferson didn’t have it, yet they made good American Ambassadors to France and to England in times just as trying as these. Wouldn't a real American man be as good as a real American pocketbook? The thirty-second national automobile show opens in New York City with interest as great as though the automobile were a new invention. In many respects 1932 cars truly are “new.” Those that have not seen them have surprises in store. It is no exaggeration to say that $700 and less, payable on easy terms, will buy in beauty, comfort, durability and luxury, what $10,000 could not have bought a few yea

AHMEDABAD, India, Jan. 13—(P)—Miss Madeline Slade, once a belle of London society and daughter of a British admiral, made a plea to the nation today to carry on the civil disobedience campaign of Mahatma Gandhi whose devoted disciple she has been since she renounced the drawing rooms of Mayfair. “Now that Gandhi's voice is silenced behind prison walls,” she said in her message to the people of India, “it is all the more our sacred duty to carry out his dearest wish—spinning and weaving homespun.” If Indians had fulfilled this wish previously, she argued, Gandhi would not now be in prison. “If the whole nation wore homespun,” she said, “we would have had strength and unity such as would have made it possible for the British to have piled insults upon our heads.” Before he was arrested the Mahatma instructed Miss Slade, known now as Mira Behn, to do nothing to warrant her own incarceration

By The Associated Press MILAN, Italy, Jan. 13—Premier Mussolini advised Europe in an article in his newspaper, Popolo D’Italia, today to cancel reparations as the first step to the world’s economic recovery. U. S. Should Follow The article, which was unsigned, but was known to be from il duce’s pen, said this undoubtedly would leave the United States in such a position that it would have to follow suit by cancelling war debts. It was Mussolini's pronouncement through his Milan newspaper within three days of his personal views and therefore of the official policy of Italy. The article today was spread across the front page of Popolo d’Italia, which since it was founded by Mussolini has been the nearest to an official Italian organ. The writer pointed out the moral effect that voluntary cancellation of reparations by European states would have on the United States. The American people coul

PARIS, Jan. 12.—(4)—The entire French cabinet today followed the example of Aristide Briand and placed their portfolios in the hands of Premier Laval, leaving him free to do as he wishes in reconstructing the ministry. The action, not altogether unexpected, followed a conversation between the premier and M. Briand, whose ill health impelled him to ask last week that he be permitted to retire as foreign minister. This development, coupled with the sudden death of Andre Maginot, minister of war, precipitated the cabinet crisis. After he had received the ministers, the premier sent for Edouard Herriot, chief of the radical socialists, whose support he needs if he is to form a national union government, something like Great Britain's, to face the impending international conferences. The premier has three alternatives: He may step out in case the radicals should decide to enter the cabinet; h

Tokyo, Jan. 12.—Japan will reply to the recent note of Secretary of State Stimson on the Manchurian situation within a few days, the Rengo News agency said today, and will state it believes the various movements for independence there and in Mongolia should not suffer interference, either from Japan or any other nation. The reply will also say, according to the Rengo News agency, that Japan’s military operations have by no means transgressed the nine-power treaty or the Kellogg-Briand act, which was cited by Stimson in his note. The government would emphasize, the agency said, that it believes the urgent problem at this moment in Manchuria is to restore peace and order, and Japan's aim is to make the territory a safe place in which to live, making possible the open-door policy of equal opportunity.

Paris, Jan. 12, (P)—Premier Laval, who headed the government of France for just ten days short of a year, presented the collective resignation of his ministry to President Doumer at the Elysee palace tonight. The president, who will start early tomorrow morning on the task of selecting a successor, thanked M. Laval and all of his collaborators for their loyal service, and asked that the cabinet carry on the government until a new ministry has been chosen. At the last moment M. Laval decided not to oblige all of his colleagues to go in a body to Elysee palace. Instead, accompanied only by Deputy Cathala, undersecretary of state for interior, he crossed the street from the ministry of the interior to the presidential residence. It was the first time in ten years that a French premier has resigned voluntarily without being overthrown either in the senate or in the chamber. The name of Senat

| PARIS, Jan. 18—(AP)—President Paul Doumer began a series of consultations with political leaders today which was expected to result by night, in his selection of someone, probably Premier Laval, to form a new French cabinet. The quest was made necessary by the resignation of the Laval cabinet last night after radical Socialists refused the premier's offer to name Édouard Herriot, former premier and radical leader, foreign minister in place of Aristide Briand. Briand, whose illness led to his resignation, was reported to be much better today. In the meantime, reliable sources reported that the French reparations plan now being considered by the British cabinet calls for a two-year moratorium on German conditional payments and an issue of German railroad bonds to be turned over to France for the unconditional annuities. 1932-11-28.text: | LONDON, Nov. 28—(UP)—Premier J. Ramsay MacDonald indicated in the House of Commons today that the government would settle the question of paying its Dec. 15 debt installment to the United States without consulting Parliament. Asked by the Rt. Hon. George Lambert if Commons would be consulted before “further payment of war loan interest is made,” MacDonald replied that if requested through the usual channels, it would be given careful consideration, “but it is not to the public interest to have debate at this moment.” LONDON, Nov. 28—(UP)—The new British war debt note, drafted over the weekend, was expected today to claim that if the United States insisted on payment of the $95,000,000 December installment there would be serious world financial repercussions. The question of payment or default would remain unsettled by the note, it was predicted. The Daily Mail understood that Prime Min

King Winter, who has made several sharp thrusts at the nation in warning of what is in store when he officially takes over the weather situation in another three weeks, has been no more bitter than in the attack directed at New England over the week-end. The temperatures dropped precipitately to as low as six degrees below zero, Boston, with a minimum reading of 5 above, marked up the coldest November 27 on record. Atop Mount Washington a reading of 21 below zero was recorded. A biting wind added to the misery. Hope was held out for moderating temperatures today. Below Freezing In South Borne on down the Atlantic seaboard by a northeast gale, the temperature drop spread into 'Dixie, with sub-freezing readings reported at Asheville, Richmond, Birmingham, Little Rock and Memphis. A schooner was grounded at Fernandina, Fla., and small crafts were tossed about at widely scattered points. In

Washington, Nov. 28.—England, which owes the United States $95,550,000 on December 15, is at work on a second note renewing a request for postponement of that payment and for reconsideration of the entire debts problem. After the cabinet approves the text it will be sent immediately to Washington. France, with an installment of $20,000,000 due on the same date, is considering a similar note suggesting postponement of the December payment and prolongation of the Hoover moratorium. It probably will be sent soon after England’s memorandum. Poland, which owes $3,303,000 next month, already has sent a second note to Washington with a full explanation of its request for suspension of the December payment. Italy is ready to pay the $1,245,000 she owes, but although the government has made no official pronouncement, the general sentiment there is that postponement should be granted. No new decis

Washington, Nov. 28. — Holding securely to the position that Europe has failed to produce facts which justify her requests for postponement of war debt payments due next month, President Hoover and his advisors tonight awaited the arrival of additional notes from London and Paris. Secretary Mills and Secretary Stimson talked the situation over with the chief executive today and afterward said no new decisions had been reached and America’s course remained unaltered. “We will know more in 48 hours,” Mills said in reply to newspaper men's questions on what the debtor nations will do on December 15 when the next installments fall due, “Right now we are standing squarely on the president's position that no facts have been presented to warrant suspension of the December 15 payments, and that these payments should be made.” It Is Up to Europe Both the cabinet members felt the next move must co

WASHINGTON, Nov. 28 (UP)— The war debts crisis was thoroughly canvassed again today by President Hoover in a lengthy conference with Secretary of Treasury Mills and Secretary of State Stimson. "We're waiting now to hear more from Britain and the other nations," Mills said at the conclusion of the conference. "We frankly know no more than has been published, but will all know a lot more in the next 48 hours." Mills and Stimson were closeted with the chief executive for more than an hour.

WASHINGTON, Nov. 27 (#)—European optimism that an extension of the moratorium on war debts will be forthcoming has state department officials puzzled, as they await the next move from abroad. The administration is at a loss to understand press dispatches from London and continental capitals indicating a belief prevails in high official circles that some means will be found to postpone the December 15 payments due the United States, despite the polite refusals that already have been sent to Europe. The replies of the American government to the requests of Great Britain, France, Belgium, Poland and Czechoslovakia for an extension of time on the war debt payments due next month were uniformly negative and made it clear that congress alone could alter the debt agreements. However, the European governments apparently still regard the payments as open to negotiation despite Secretary Stimson's

LONDON, Nov. 28—(UP)—British currency declined to the lowest level in history today as the government considered means to meet her Dec. 15 war debt payment of $95,500,000 to the United States. Under steady selling the pound was driven down 3 cents to $3.19 ($4.8665), the lowest level at which it has ever sold at this city. On Feb. 3, 1920, the pound sold as low as $3.18 at New York, but until today the lowest price here was $3.21, reached 12 years ago.

LONDON, Nov. 2 —(P)— Drafting of the new British war debt note to Washington was begun tonight at a special meeting of cabinet members with Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald, Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer; Sir John Simon, foreign minister, and Stanley Baldwin participated in the conference. A full meeting of the cabinet probably will be held tomorrow morning to discuss the note. The document may be dispatched tomorrow afternoon or Tuesday, but it is suggested in some quarters that publication may be indefinitely delayed because of delicate secret information which it may contain. The new memorandum is expected in informed quarters to set forth the British financial position in detail and to indicate, if it does not directly state, reasons why the mid-December British war debt installment of $95,500,000 should be postponed. 1932-02-14.text: LONDON, Feb. 10.—(hi—sensational charges of a secret treaty concluded between Soviet Russia and Japan, giving Japan control of Manchuria and part of Mongolia, were published in the Daily Express today. The Daily Express article asserted that the agreement was concluded by Moscow as an alternative to war over Russia’s waning interests in Manchuria, now occupied by the Japanese. The newspaper said that the desire of some of the Soviet leaders to fight it out with Japan had resulted in a “bitter conflict” in the inner councils at Moscow. Interest to U.S. The Soviet government was declared to be pledged under the pact not to intervene in any affair affecting the Pacific Coast—a purported stipulation of peculiar interest to the United States. LONDON, Feb. 13.—(P)—A lasting solution of the world’s economic and financial ills is the ambitious program set for the adjourned Lausanne reparations conference which, it was officially announced today, will meet in June. In authoritative quarters it was expected that the conference would be shifted to Geneva where, for a period at least, it would overshadow the disarmament negotiations.

Shanghai, Feb. 18.—Japanese airplanes and big guns pounded the wrecks of Chapei and Woosung today with the heaviest bombardment since the fighting began two weeks ago, and the Japanese claimed they had stopped the Chinese counter-attack. Promising reports of peace negotiations through the medium of the ministers of the United States, Great Britain and France were also shot to pieces when American Minister Johnson, who arrived here yesterday with his fellow diplomats, said he knew of no such peace prospects. The voice of a hundred American residents in Shanghai was raised in protest against the Japanese activities in a cablegram to United States Senator Borah. Their protest was against what they called the violence of Japan’s methods. Ten, Chinese delegate to the world disarmament conference, told the conference Saturday morning that its success or failure depends upon the outcome of the conflict between China and Japan in the far east. If the covenant of the league and the Kellogg pact are permitted to crumble over the Sino-Japanese situation the conference will fail, he said. “The outcome of the present struggle to ward off external aggression in the most virulent form,” he added, “must inevitably and largely determine the armament policy which the Chinese nation will pursue.” Want Treaties Honored Dr. Yen dealt more with the far eastern situation in his address than with disarmament. “My country and my people,” he said, “are not seeking pity or soliciting the armed help of other nations in our hour of trial, but we do demand that the nations that have affixed their signatures to these solemn

[Shanghai, Sunday, Feb. 14 (AP). —Fighting all along the Woosung front subsided early today but under cover of darkness the Japanese landed troops and tanks, guns and ammunition from seven transports which moved up the Whangpoo river late Saturday night. Somewhere close to the China coast on the way from Japan more transports were bringing additional men and supplies for the big push the Japanese plan to start as quickly as men and material are ready. Saturday's fighting was limited to intermittent artillery fire although there was one Japanese raid late in the afternoon when 15 men and a sergeant crossed Woosung creek and were beaten off by Chinese defenders. Geneva, Switz, Feb. 13.—The disarmament conference today heard Dr. W. W. Yen of China declare that its success or failure depended on the outcome of the far eastern conflict, and thereby the international statesmen completed two weeks of work in the course of which they have heard 25 speeches. These addresses have clarified the issues before the delegates and have given them some hope that the problems they face will be solved. Meetings Develop Optimism. The conference, which began in deep pessimism, has developed some optimism. A few points, in fact, already are regarded as virtually settled. Two camps have arisen which at first seemed irreconcilable but lately commentators have declared that they might eventually get together. “Security first,” is the slogan of one camp; “disarmament first” of the other. Japanese naval headquarters denied Chinese reports that more than 1,000 Nipponese soldiers had crossed Woosung creek and met a crushing defeat at the hands of the defenders. The Japanese were supposed to have crossed the creek late Saturday, but the press correspondent in the Japanese lines saw no such movement. Foreign observers, who entered the debarkation zone here, despite Japanese efforts to cover their troop movements with secrecy, said they believed 20,000 soldiers had been landed within a few hours. Seven Japanese transports steamed up the Whangpoo river Saturday night under the very noses of silent Chinese guns at the Woosung forts and began d

(Copyright, 1932, by United Press) SHANGHAI, Sunday (UP).—The Japanese and Chinese armies came to grips along Woosung creek on Saturday in the fiercest battle of the Shanghai campaign and the banks of the creek were littered with dead and wounded. - The Chinese at 1 a. m. Sunday reported hundreds of casualties on both sides. The Japanese admitted several officers and many men were killed and wounded, Japs Forced to Withdraw Mayor Wu Teh-Chen announced that the Chinese commander at 9:40 p. m. had reported the Japanese, who previously had crossed the creek and stormed the Chinese positions, had been compelled to withdraw across the creek. The battle began after nightfall and was halted at 11 p. m. while the Japanese reorganized for another attack. The Japanese admitted their casualties included one captain. The relative positions, they said, were unchanged. At midnight, amid resounding fir

1932-03-03.text: (By The Associated Press) London, Mar. 1—One of the biggest bullion firms in London estimated today that the British people own 1,000,000,000 pounds in gold sovereigns and manufactured gold articles. He made his estimate on the basis of the heavy sales of gold objects during the past few days of England's “gold rush.” Owners have sold ancient articles made by the old goldsmiths taking advantage of the high price for gold and at the same time embracing the opportunity to increase the country’s gold supply.

LONDON, Mar. 3 (4---The kidnaping of Charles Augustus Lindbergh, jr., aroused the entire British press to indignant editorial comment today. Under the caption, “A Monstrous Crime” the Daily Telegraph said: “Few more open challenges to civilized government ever have been ventured. Every citizen of America who is able to do so feels he has to play his part in rescuing Charles Augustus Lindbergh and the whole world will enter into the acute anxiety of his parents and share in a hope for the child's recovery.” “If this cruel and miserable method of intimidation with a helpless child as its victim,” the Manchester Guardian said, “is really the work of ‘racketeers’ and if the outcome of it is not a genuine and determined effort to end the whole deplorable business in all its ramifications, then the rot must be sunk very deeply into American life.”

LONDON, March 3.—(UP)—The Daily Express correspondent at Helsingfors reported martial law throughout Finland today with the army mobilized to quell a Fascist attempt to overthrow the government. The correspondent said leaders of the Fascist Lappo party sent another ultimatum to the government demanding cessation of military activities and a new cabinet.

SHANGHAI, March 3 (4)—Admiral Kichisaburo Nomura and General Yoshinori Shirakawa, navy and army commanders, announced tonight they had ordered their forces to cease hostilities in the Shanghai area. The Japanese forces were ordered to consolidate the positions they now hold on the border of a 12½ mile zone around the city unless the Chinese resorted to further hostile action. “I have ordered the army to stop for the time being at the points it occupies,” General Shirakawa said, “and to stop fighting if the Chinese cease hostilities.” The statements of the two commanders followed a confused situation earlier in the afternoon. The Japanese legation issued a statement between 2 and 3 o'clock that hostilities would be ended immediately but Chinese civil authorities said there was no indication that the orders had been put into effect. Nearly two hours later it was announced that the military

Geneva, March 3.—(AP)—Negotiations for an armistice at Shanghai have broken down, Dr. W. W. Yen, the Chinese spokesman, told the League of Nations assembly Thursday afternoon. Japanese terms which were denounced by Yen provided that the Chinese withdraw their troops first to a distance to be determined between the Chinese and Japanese authorities and that thereafter the details and duration of an armistice should be determined by similar direct bi-lateral negotiations.

By The Associated Press SHANGHAI, Friday, March 4—The Chinese government at Nanking notified the League of Nations assembly today that the 19th route army had been instructed to cease hostilities in this area unless it were attacked.

(Copyright, The Associated Press) Shanghai, March 2 (Thursday) (®)—A huge Japanese landing party finally wrested the forts and the village of Woosung from the Chinese under a combined artillery, naval and aerial attack today, while other Japanese forces pushed ahead against the retreating Chinese army on the entire Chapei-Woosung front. The Japanese said they also occupied Nanziang, 15 miles northwest of Shanghai, a new objective in their westward drive to shove the doughty warriors miles away from the battle front here. More Troops Landed Still other forces, newly landed at Litho, on the Yangtse River 20 miles from Shanghai, were approaching Kating, northwest of Nanziang, in an encircling movement southward. While Japanese guns ashore and on destroyers and cruisers offshore, with airplanes overhead, combined to throw a literal rain of shells and bombs into the long-suffering fortificati

(Associated Press) TOKYO — Japanese officialdom, after a harried afternoon today, faced westward to look more hopefully upon the procedure of the League of Nations at Geneva, following an announcement that hostilities at Shanghai had ceased. The announcement of the cessation of fighting was made only an hour or two before the assembly at Geneva convened to work out a permanent settlement of the Sino-Japanese trouble.

1932-02-04.text: Washington, Feb. 4 (A.P.) — A new protest against the use by the Japanese of the international settlement as a base for their attacks upon the Chinese went to Japan today from the British and American governments. It closely followed the announcement in Tokyo of the Japanese reply to the latest Anglo-American overtures for peace. The new representation followed the line of others which had contended that the Japanese were using the American marines in the international settlement at Shanghai as a shield. They have pointed out that the American marines were under orders to fire only under extreme emergencies. The present fear of officials is that fighting across the line between the settlement and the native city might result in a serious battle in which innocent neutrals might be killed. The Japanese reply to the peace proposals was awaited at the state department as a new protest went f

Tokyo, Feb. 4.—(AP)—The Japanese government in a note handed to the American, British and French Ambassadors agreed to cease hostilities at Shanghai if assured the "Chinese will immediately and completely cease their menacing and disturbing activities." A few minutes before the note was made public it was learned the government decided definitely to send a full division of army troops to Shanghai to take the place of bluejackets who have been bearing the brunt of the fighting. The following is the text of the English translation of the note: "First, the Japanese forces at Shanghai will cease hostile acts if it is assured the Chinese forces will immediately cease their disturbing activities, if on the contrary the Chinese including the regular and non-uniformed forces persist in such activities the Japanese government must preserve its freedom of action for its military forces. "Second, i

WASHINGTON, Feb. 15. (AP).— The United States and Great Britain have again protested against Japan’s use of the international settlement in Shanghai as a military base for attacking the Chinese outside the settlement. - The landing of a limited number of Japanese forces in the Shanghai international settlement for the protection of foreigners living there would not be the basis for any objections on the part of foreign powers interested in the settlement. But the landing of forces by the thousands to be used in fighting the Chinese outside the international settlement is considered quite another matter. The consular officers of Great Britain, France, Italy and the United States have repeatedly called to the attention of the Japanese consul general what they regard as misuse of the international settlement as a military base for outside operations.

London, Feb. 4—()—The Admiralty announced last night that the British submarine M-2, missing since it dived over a week ago with 61 men aboard, had been located at the bottom of the English Channel nearly six miles off Portland Bill. The vessel, virtually given up as lost after a desperate search for days failed to show a trace of it, was located by the destroyer Torrid with powerful apparatus which detected tell-tale sounds. Reports received here indicated that the sunken ship was located sometime after 10:30 P. M. last night at a spot 5.8 miles west of Portland Bill, a rocky promontory off which it went down in the treacherous tides of Dead Man's Bay. The spot is near the place where two flags in a canvas bag were picked up earlier in the search and where the captain of a coastwise vessel reported he had seen a submarine dive stern first. Special finding apparatus on the Torrid during

Andrew W. Mellon, secretary of the treasury, Wednesday night accepted the ambassadorship to Great Britain. The acceptance by Secretary Mellon, who has served under three presidents, beginning with the Harding administration, was announced Wednesday night by President Hoover in Washington. Mr. Mellon earlier in the day had admitted after inquiries that the post had been offered him, but he had not made up his mind as to whether he would accept. The president, in announcing that the veteran secretary of the treasury would succeed Charles G. Dawes, who resigned to head the Reconstruction Finance Corporation, said: “The critical situation facing all countries in their international relations, the manifold economic and other problems demanding wise solution in our national interests, call for experience and judgment of the highest order. The importance to our country of the sound determinatio

By The Associated Press. PORTLAND, England, Feb. 4.—Divers today were examining the wreck of the British submarine M-2 which sank January 26 off the coast here and which was definitely located on the bottom of the channel late last night by sub-sea soundings. Admiralty officials said it was unlikely that the hull of the submarine, which went down with 61 men aboard, would be salvaged before next summer. Westerly winds in the channel would be almost certain to interrupt the salvage work if it were begun now, they said. The vessel was located by the destroyer Torrid. The spot where it was found was near where two submarine signal flags in a canvas bag were picked up during the frenzied search last week when hope of saving the lives of the crew was still cherished.

| Shanghai, China, © Feb. 4—(AP)— Japanese naval officials here today denied reports that Admiral Shiosawa, Japanese commander here, had committed suicide. Suicide Report London, Feb. 4—(AP)—A Reuters News Agency dispatch from Shanghai today said an unconfirmed report there said Admiral Shiosawa, Japanese naval commander, had committed suicide. The report was officially denied, but it was widely believed at Shanghai, the dispatch said, because of numerous notable precedents in Japanese history. Students of Japanese psychology said the Admiral would be found to consider himself a failure because of the fact that his attempt to capture the Chapei sector at Shanghai was unsuccessful. Some persons at Shanghai, it said, attributed his succession in command by Admiral Nemura as a personal reflection in spite of assurances from Tokyo that this action was taken only because of the necessity for

PORTLAND, England, Feb. 4 — Divers studied plans for raising the submarine M-2 today, discovered in the wreck-strewn dead man’s bay lying alongside a German U-boat sunk during the World War. The M-2 had been missing since Jan. 26. Rescue vessels had worked over the area where she was found many times, but the sweeps had brought up only submarine signal flags. The cause of the disaster had not been determined nor had divers learned how many of the 60 men aboard the submarine when she dived for the last time were still inside. The M-2 was found about 6.8 miles off Portland Bill, where divers had inspected four wrecks within a radius of a quarter of a mile 24 hours after the submarine disappeared. The M-2 was lying in 108 feet of water.

1932-06-25.text: London, June 24 (#)—The Daily Herald today said conferences have been going on in secret for a week among the former Kaiser, German bankers and monarchist politicians with a view to possible restoring the Hohenzollerns. The dispatch, dated Amsterdam, added that the former Crown Prince had made his first visit to Holland in seven years to attend one of the conferences at Zandvoort, Holland, where the former Kaiser is spending a short vacation.

DUBLIN, June 25.—(P)—A shrill cascade of starch and bright eyes—white dresses and white ribbons and white sashes—spilled into the majestic, colorful pageant of the Eucharistic congress today. It was the children’s day. From all over Ireland—and some from far lands away—they came, a stream of children treble until 10,000 stood in orderly groups before the white high altar in Phoenix Park. By 10 a. m.—an hour before the solemn pontifical high mass began—Dublin seemed a city of children and the avenue leading to the park was almost a solid stream of bobbing heads of motor cars filled with them. In the park, Cardinal Lauri, the pope’s representative at the congress, celebrated the mass, and before that the children sang in Gaelic the hymn “Soul of My Saviour,” led by a choir of 500 children. After the mass the cardinal moved among the miniature battalions which stood stiffly in their places

LAUSANNE, June 25 (AP) Relief was expressed in informed quarters here today that the battle for cancellation is weakening and perhaps lost. Foreign Minister Dino Grandi of Italy restated the Italian position in a memorandum for Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald of Great Britain. The memorandum has not been presented but in it Signor Grandi said Italy wants to clean the slate, but failing that, reserves the right to collect her share of reparations payments. This fits the softening attitude of the British delegation. Five countries had submitted memoranda today, four of which were veritable proposals for a reconstruction of Europe.

| LONDON (#)—Darby and Joan, | who found a thrill on court presen- 'tation nights by gaping unabashed at fashion through limousine win- | dows, had lost their free show to- day. Overturning a precedent which has come down since Queen Vic- toria’s day, King George abolished the customary long wait on the mall before night’s court and the including several American women, were hustled di- rectly into Buckingham Palace, Curiously, the rumble of protest came not alone from the Darbys and the Joans on the sidewalks. There also were discreet plaints from the presentees themselves. Although some of the be-plumed ladies heretofore have declared “their embarrassment at the waiting as a gaping ordeal, some of them ap) / ‘tenda lat ciahe “stop by limousine windows. |

Dublin, Irish Free State, June 24. —(/P)—Irish women, who have sent forth many sons to serve the Catholic church, and women from many parts of the world, assembled more than 100,000 strong tonight before the Eucharistic congress altar in Phoenix Park and heard themselves praised for their religious sacrifices. Speaking from a tiny white pulpit, the Most Reverend Andrew Joseph McDonald, archbishop of St. Andrews and Edinburgh, told them the “destiny of the human race lies largely in the hands of women.” Citing the pope’s recent encyclical concerning the spread of the forces of anti-religion, the archbishop assured his hearers “evil is not cast out except by prayer and penance.” He urged daily communion as the only means of combatting the powers of darkness and pleaded with the women to renew and increase the fervor of their faith in this crisis in the world’s affairs. Their Privilege “In

DOORN, HOLLAND, June 25.—(A7 Former Kaiser Wilhelm came back to his exile home today from Zandvoort, Holland, where he has been visiting Baron Von Ver Heydt. Yesterday there was a report in a London newspaper that his son, the crown prince, had been with him at Zandvoort discussing a project for restoration of the monarchy. The report was denied.

CHICAGO, June 25.—The spectacular factional strife of Louisiana Democracy was added today to the problems and controversies confronting the national convention. Finally in control, the governors of Franklin D. Roosevelt in the national committee last night tentatively seated a delegation headed by the irrepressible, self-styled "Kingfish" Huey P. Long, over the protests of two other groups believed opposed to the New York governor's nomination. In addition they gave official representative status to pro-Roosevelt delegations from Minnesota and Puerto Rico, overruling hostile groups claiming a place in the convention. Rousing Fight It all presaged a rousing fight to be waged Monday before the convention credentials committee and later, in the case of the Louisiana squabble, on the floor of the convention itself. The 50 votes represented by the contesting delegations were critical to the R

Fresh Meadow Country Club, Flushing, N. Y., June 25—(AP)—In one of the most spectacular golf finishes of all time, Gene Sarazen added the United States Open Championship to his newly acquired British crown. His score was 286.

1932-03-02.text: LONDON, March 2.—(P)—Great Britain is repaying $150,000,000 in credits to the United States on Friday, Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer, announced in the House of Commons today. At the same time, Chamberlain said, Britain is repaying approximately 13,000,000 pounds sterling (about $44,200,000 at present exchange) to France, reducing the French credits to 7,000,000 pounds. The $150,000,000 to the United States is part of the $200,000,000 credit obtained last summer to bolster the pound.

SHANGHAI, Mar. 2 (AP) — Japanese forces advanced all along the Chapei-Woosung battle line today and had almost pushed the Chinese forces back to the 12 1-2 mile limit set by them in their recent ultimatum. Woosung alone held out against the relentless march of the Japanese war machine operating in the Shanghai sector. During the afternoon the Japanese troops had reached their objective with Chanju, former Chinese headquarters captured.

SHANGHAI, Wednesday, Mar. 2—(2)— Hammered by the new strength of Japan’s fresh storm troops, the Chinese line in the Kiangwan sector gave way early today and fell back foot by foot, covering the retreat with machine gun fire. Japanese officials claimed late this afternoon the entire Chinese line, from Chapei northward through the western environs of Kiangwan to Miaochangchen, was driven back by their forces in the most terrific battle the Shanghai front has seen. Backed up by 12,000 reinforcements who landed here during the last 36 hours, the Japanese early this morning began a tremendous assault along the whole front. They used artillery, airplanes, machine guns, and a squadron of tanks in the tremendous push which Tokyo expected to defeat the Chinese sooner than League of Nations peace proposals could become operative. Blast Shakes Shanghai A terrific explosion which shook the entire c

(Copyright 1932. by United Press) SHANGHAI, March 2—(UP)—Chinese defense troops evacuated their fortifications around Shanghai under a withering fire from the Japanese today and re-established positions miles to the rear for another dogged stand. Chinese commanders of the 19th route army, principal defense unit, declared "the fight is just begun" as troops completed an orderly retreat to second defense lines. The evacuation began shortly before expiration of a Japanese ultimatum threatening to blow up the main Shanghai railway line. Within a few hours the Chinese troops were solidly behind fortifications 20 kilometers (12 1-2 miles) away, just outside a zone around the international settlement which the Japanese had demanded they evacuate. Japanese merged land, sea and air forces for a driving offensive, seizing quick advantage of the opportunity offered by the Chinese retreat. Soldiers

TOKYO, Feb. 28—(AP)—The foreign office was informed today that 100,000 Soviet Russian troops have been massed in the vicinity of Vladivostok in preparation for what is considered in Russia to be ‘an inevitable conflict with Japan. This information came from Japanese Consul Yamaguchi at Vladivostok, who reported that troops were stationed in that city and along the Ussuri railway near the border of North Manchuria. In a telegram to the foreign office the consul asserted that an iodine factory at Olga Bay was being converted for the manufacture of poison gas and that fortifications at the entrance to Vladivostok harbor and on Russian Island were being strengthened by new heavy guns and anti-aircraft batteries. Basing his report on information which he said he received from a reliable foreign source, M. Yamaguchi declared there were two army corps in the immediate vicinity of Vladivostok an

(United Press Staff Correspondent) (Copyright, 1932, By United Press) Shanghai, Thursday. — (UP) — The native city of Shanghai was in flames today as the torch and incendiary bombs were applied to Chapei in the wake of the retreating Chinese army. Chapei was burning along a mile front in the North Station area. Huge cotton mills exploded with terrific detonations, the flames shooting high in the air. American observers claimed the Japanese were setting the fires because of snipers and machine gun nests remaining after the general Chinese withdrawal to 12-14 miles from the city. Fortunately, there was no wind and the flames did not menace the International Settlement. The bulk of the Chapei area, which housed 600,000 Chinese, appeared doomed. For weeks it has been under withering fire and aerial and artillery bombardment. Shanghai—(UP)— Chinese defense troops evacuated their fortification

(By Glenn Babb, Associated Press Staff Correspondent) TOKYO, March 2.—Japan’s acceptance of the League of Nations proposal for an international conference at Shanghai to attempt to bring an end to hostilities there was announced by the foreign office today but the spokesman said no progress had been made in negotiations for a truce. Terms for an armistice were presented to the Japanese negotiators at Shanghai yesterday by Vice Admiral Sir Howard Kelly, British fleet commander, but the Japanese found these unacceptable and presented a set of counter proposals. Dispatches said the Chinese had assured Admiral Kelly that the terms proposed were acceptable to them, but they had not yet replied to the Japanese counter proposals, the foreign office said. The Japanese counter proposals were not disclosed, but it was said that Japan’s position remained unchanged since the ultimatum of Lieutenant

(Copyright, 1932, by the Associated Press) Tokyo, March 1 -- Acceptance of the League of Nations' proposal for an international conference at Shanghai to end the Sino-Japanese conflict was announced today by the Japanese government. At the same time various government spokesmen made it clear Japan believes a decisive victory in the field will be necessary to pave the way for the conference. The league proposal, made by Joseph Paul-Boncour, French delegate to the league council at Geneva, called for negotiations in which “the United States, Great Britain, France and Italy would participate, as well as Japan and China. It was understood the Japanese government interpreted the suggestion as meaning the conference probably would cover a long period and would seek a permanent solution of the Shanghai problem. In official quarters it was said that a decisive Japanese victory was expected to re

1932-08-27.text: | MANCHESTER, England, Aug. 27.—(#)—Factory whistles at noon today called 200,000 cotton workers throughout Lancashire on a strike which threatens to become the greatest industrial war Britain has experienced since the general strike of 1926. How far the call will be obeyed can not be known until the mills open Monday. The tragic aspect of the grim struggle in which women and children will be the sufferers, is that peace negotiations were wrecked, not on the main issues of wages, but on the reinstatement of about 2,000 strikers.

LONDON, Aug. 27 (UP).—Flying fields in England and Norway that burned flares and beacons all night long, reported no word today from the transatlantic monoplane “Green Mountain Boy,” flown by two young American bachelors. The plane’s fuel supply was long since exhausted, and it was feared that its pilots, Clyde Allen Lee and John Bochkon, who took off from Harbor Grace at 5:01 a. m. (E. S. T.) Thursday, had been forced down at sea. The two carried fuel to keep them in the air 37 hours. That deadline was passed early last night.

Oslo, Norway, Aug 27.—(INS)— More than a dozen ocean liners between Europe and North America scanned the seas closely today for a trace of Clyde A. Lee and John Bochkon, youthful American aviators lost on an attempt to fly non-stop from Harbor Grace, Newfoundland, to Oslo, Norway. The fliers, who took off at 6:06 F. D. T. Thursday, were due in Oslo around noon E. D. T. yesterday. They allowed themselves extra fuel for seven hours flying and this, had they remained in the air, must have been exhausted at 7:00 p. m. E. D. T. yesterday. The airmen have not been reported seen since their take-off. British air ministry officials, convinced the Americans were down, still held out hopes for their safety. There was the possibility they had landed at some remote point in the British Isles or on the continent or, if they had come down on the sea, that they still might be picked up. Their cabin mon

LONDON, Aug. 27.--With all ships off the British Isles instructed to keep sharp lookout for Clyde Allen and John Bochkon, Vermont to Oslo flyers, the plane Green Mountain Boy was still unreported at 5 p. m. today. Neither the British admiralty, the air ministry, or the aerodrome had received any reports indicating the flyers had reached the western coast of Europe. There has been no official order for a search for the men as yet.

He passed on New York street car rob- bery, used him to tell how streaks of rusty rails were down on thirty-fourth street's level surface, and charged to the company at a rate per mile higher than the cost of building over any part of the Rocky Mountains. NEW YORK, Aug. 26 (#)—On the eve of his projected takeoff on the first leg of a return flight to England, Capt. J. A. Mollison tonight received an official greeting from Mayor James J. Walker, A final weather report from Dr. James H. Kimball tomorrow morning, he said, will determine whether he starts his homeward journey then. Captain Mollison plans to fly to Harbor Grace, N. F., tomorrow, stopping en route at St. John, N. B. He said he would not take off across the ocean until Sunday, at the earliest. In greeting the flier and pinning on his lapel a gold medal from the city, Mayor Walker said: “You are the first flier who has come here with a round trip ticket. London, Aug. 27——Europe assumed today that the trans-Atlantic plane "Green Mountain Boy," long unreported out of Harbor Grace, Newfoundland, bound for Oslo, Norway, was down in the Atlantic, and the only hope was rescue by a passing ship. Dawn broke without any news of Clyde Lee and John Bochkon since they took off at 4:02 a.m. (C.S.T.) Thursday with 37 hours supply of gasoline in their plane’s tanks.

WASHINGTON, Aug. 27 (UP)— Andrew W. Mellon, ambassador to the Court of St. James, will return to his post in London either Wednesday, August 31 or the Wednesday following, he said this afternoon after a long conference with President Hoover. When Mellon came to this country from London a few weeks ago there were persistent rumors he would not return.

1932-08-12.text: Ottawa, Ont., Aug. 12.—(P)—Great Britain and Canada, whose problems have constituted the most difficult bridge the imperial trade conference has had to cross, were reported virtually agreed on a trade conference plan today and arrangements were begun to bring the conference to a close next Thursday. The plan is to hold a plenary session of the conference Thursday after which the British will give a ball for the rest of the delegates as a grand finale. Asked if the British-Canadian market Malcolm McDonald, son of the British Prime Minister, said the idea of British preference was not aimed at the trade of any foreign country.

Madrid, Aug. 11—Spain's twenty-four hour monarchist rebellion was smashed by the government today by the arrest at Huelva of its fleeing leader, Gen. Jose San Jurjo. The general fled from Seville shortly before one a.m. after his revolutionary machine, which captured the government of the important southern city yesterday, had crumbled in front of a powerful concentration of government troops which were converging on Seville from several nearby concentration points. Civil Governor Gualio Solsona of Huelva reported a few hours later that San Jurjo was under arrest at the executive palace there. He said he was taken as he was about to enter the city. Three of his chief officers were arrested with him. The governor telephoned the government here of the capture and Minister of Interior Cashers ordered the four officers brought to Madrid (Continued on Page Five)

Madrid, Aug. 12,—(AP)—Rioting and burning reddened much of southern Spain today as the government laid plans to punish General Jose San Jurjo, leader of Wednesday’s abortive rebellion, and his followers. One man was killed and three wounded at Santa Fe when civil guards dispersed a group which burned the Agrarian casino. One workman was killed in a political fight between laborers and employers. A civil guard was killed at Seville when a mob attacked the jail. At Seville, cordons of soldiers were posted around religious houses, and heavy guards patrolled the streets. In the towns of San Lucar and Amacolar, mobs set fire to the churches, but the fires were put out by citizen volunteers. In San Simón Ponce a mob attacked the mayor, seized his cane and beat him with it. Mobs burned a convent at Albacete and a church at Santo Tomás, near Granada and afterwards set fire to a factory. BERLIN, Aug. 11.—(U.P)—President Paul Von Hindenburg, confronted with a rising tide of fascism and the menace of Adolph Hitler's mobilizing "storm troops," will grant an audience to Hitler tomorrow to offer him the chancellorship of Germany. The rapid developments of the last few days have brought the fascist leader at last to his goal. Von Hindenburg, however, was expected to attach four conditions to his offer, and it was doubted if Hitler would accept the terms. The conditions are: 1. The Constitution must be respected. 2. The fascist militia must not be employed as auxiliary police. 3. There must be no equality between the fascist militia and the Reichswehr, or regular army. 4. There must be no party government relying on the "storm" detachments for support.

Berlin, Aug. 11.— (A.P.) — Adolf Hitler’s advance toward the German chancellorship slipped momentarily into the background today as Germany celebrated the 13th birthday of the republic. It was perhaps the strangest celebration of “Constitution Day” in all these 13 years, for outdoor political meetings were forbidden and Republican groups, holding their anniversary exercises under the guise of party assemblies, huddled indoors, forbidden to rejoice openly at the founding of the republic. The outward form of custom was observed in the Reichstag, where Baron von Gayl, minister of the interior, was orator of the day, and President von Hindenburg, tanned and healthy after a vacation in the country, was cheered as he entered the presidential box. Baron von Gayl’s speech was like no other on Constitution Day. He referred but briefly to the country’s economic plight, asserted that the past 10 ye

Madrid, Aug. 12 (UP)—The populace demanded General Jose San Jurjo be executed immediately for his leadership of Wednesday’s abortive revolutionary outbreak, as the general awaited fearlessly and calmly the republican government’s decision today on his punishment. The fat, bald, moustached military leader formerly associated with Primo Rivera, accepted the situation with stoic calm, even though mobs in both Madrid and Seville shouted for his head. His son, Justo, came to him at his summer home in El Escorial, he said, and told him that he was needed to head the monarchist revolt. “He told me,” General San Jurjo explained, “that he wanted me to go to Seville with him—that it was a matter of the utmost importance. On the way to Seville Justo said that the rebellion was absolutely necessary, and that I was needed to head the movement. “I agreed to it. And in spite of the disappointment I hav

ROME, Aug. 12— (*) —Augusto Rosso, director general of League of Nations affairs at the foreign ministry, was named ambassador to Washington today in a far-reaching shake-up of the diplomatic service by Premier Benito Mussolini. The new appointments were not announced officially but the premier informed the cabinet of the changes.

BERLIN, Aug. 12. — CP — A possibility that Germany's next government may be dominated by a coalition of Adolf Hitler's National Socialists and the Centrist party of former Chancellor Heinrich Bruening emerged today as Berlin awaited the return of Hitler to Berlin to confer with President Paul Von Hindenburg. The Telegraphen Union said Hitler would not arrive today; and the conferences would not be held until tomorrow. The Centrists, although their representation in the new reichstag will be comparatively small, occupy a pivotal position. They have made an emphatic demand that the new cabinet be formed on strictly constitutional lines with the Nazis bearing a great share of the responsibility. The same applies to the new break which must be formed in the state of Prussia to replace the present dictatorship under Chancellor Franz Von Papen.

1932-09-20.text: Bombay, (UP) — The Mahatma M. K. Gandhi, an 84-pound man in a loin cloth, staked his frail, brown body and his life against edicts of the British government today in a "hunger strike". Gandhi started his strike "unto death" after his noon meal today at Yerovda prison, where he had been a prisoner of the Indian government at the pleasure of His Majesty, the King Emperor. He was technically freed just before he began his fast but the government did not remove him against his will. With trembling hands, Mahadeo Desai, Gandhi's faithful secretary and fellow prisoner, handed the Mahatma his usual glass of lemon juice mixed with sodium carbonate soon after the last meal. Gandhi, Desai, and Vallabhai Patel, ex-president of the Indian Nationalist Congress and also a prisoner, prayed together when Gandhi announced that the fast had commenced.
