ALGONAC, Mich., Sept. 20 (A) Gar Wood, America’s premier speedboat pilot, drove his Miss America X over a measured mile in the St. Clair River here today at a speed of 124.91 miles an hour to recapture from Kaye Don, British pilot, the world’s hydroplane speed record. Don, who failed a fortnight ago in an attempt to take the Harmsworth trophy from Wood and his Miss America X, established the record at 119.75 on Loch Lomond, Scotland, July 18. Wood went after the record this morning with little preliminary tuning up. He notified the timers he was ready and, despite a drizzle of rain, brought the big 48-cylinder, brown-hulled Miss America out to roar upstream on the first official trial against the record. Swinging around, he shot the craft downstream even faster. The official timers announced that the average for the two trials had set the world’s record at 124.91 miles an hour.

BERLIN, Sept. 20 (AP).—Both the government and the press assailed the British statement of Germany's demand for arms equality, in which the London government took the position that Berlin had no legal right to seek revision of her military status outside the world disarmament conference. “It goes without saying,” said a government spokesman, “that we cannot accept the reasoning of the British memorandum, according to which Germany of her own accord and without compelling reason raised a political issue of vast implications. “The unfriendly form which clothes the charge that we proceeded in a manner tactically wrong and calculated to disturb the harmony between nations does not establish the truthfulness of this charge.” German newspapers, especially those of the extreme right, sharply criticized the British position, although journals of moderate political opinion tempered their criticis

BOMBAY, Sept. 20.—INS—Despite the pleas of his best friends, Mahatma Gandhi, Hindu "saint," today began the fast by which he hopes to starve to death. Gandhi remained at the Yeravda jail at Poona as the fast started at noon, but British government officials said he was free to receive visitors or to leave the prison whenever he wished. His decision to die so that the world might take notice of India’s plight remained unshaken although a deputation of Bombay Hindus argued with him in his cell at Yeravda jail in Poona for three hours, urging him not to make a move that may plunge India into more trouble. The Mahatma has refused to leave his cell or to accept the British government's offer of conditional release. In response to this offer, he replied that only by force could they remove him. He plans to starve himself by eating nothing, dragging out the death-fast by taking water, to which

London, Sept. 20.—(4)—The United Methodist Church, one of the largest Protestant organizations in the world, was created this afternoon at Albert Hall at a ceremony which attracted 10,000 representatives from many nations to witness the union of the three branches of the church. The Duke of York, representing the king, welcomed the delegates. The three uniting branches in Great Britain, after having been split for many years, completed the act of union by signatures to a document expected to become history in the development of Methodism. No longer are there Primitive Methodists, United Methodists or Wesleyans. They are merged in the United Methodist Church. In Great Britain the new church embraces 5,000 ministers, 200,000 Sunday School teachers, 1,250,000 Sunday School scholars and a million church members. Its total property in Great Britain in churches, schools, colleges and missions

London, Sept. 20.—(UP)—Ten thousand persons crowded Albert Hall today and watched leaders of the three chief divisions of the Methodist church in Great Britain sign a deed marking the final union of the branches and making it the largest Protestant church in the world. The act of union, bringing together the Wesleyan, Primitive Methodist and United Methodist branches after years of negotiations, has been widely described as “the most notable event in the religious history of the country since the birth of John Wesley.” After the ceremony, members of the three churches in the audience engaged in handshaking. An estimated community of between 600,000 to 4,900,000 British Methodists and church property valued at more than $200,000,000 will be affected by the union.

Mahatma Gandhi’s starvation campaign is in protest against Great Britain's settlement of the “Communal” voting problem in India, under which upper-class Hindus and the lowest caste, or “untouchables”, vote as separate communities and have separate legislative representation. Gandhi, imbued with the idea of universal brotherhood, contends such a system would tend to perpetuate the cleavage between the classes and keep Hindu India divided. The majority of Indians are Hindus, although the Moslems (Mohammedans) have a fairly large population. The Hindus are divided into two classes, with a vast gulf between. The “untouchables” or depressed classes have a social rating of outcasts, and a high caste Hindu considers himself contaminated by their very presence. Gandhi has become the champion of the cause of raising their status, although many leaders of the untouchables themselves favored the co

London, Sept. 20.—- (Tuesday) — (AP)—Reports from India early today said that Mahatma Gandhi, the famous Indian nationalist, had advised the government he would not leave his jail cell during his projected fast unless he was forcibly removed. The consensus was that the Mahatma would begin his abstention from food at noon in accordance with his declarations. It was understood that the civil disobedience leader was holding to his declaration despite many telegraph and written appeals from friends in all parts of India, and persuasive efforts of Hindu leaders, to desist.

1932-04-20.text: LONDON, April 18, — Revival of trade and employment in the past few months gives Great Britain reason to hope the worst of the depression is over, Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer, told the house of commons. He said there would be no relief from present high taxes for another year.

Senator Borah, the chairman of the foreign relations committee, from the senate floor yesterday turned a smashing attack on the cancellation idea, speaking unexpectedly after it became known that Great Britain had made no budget provision for payment of the debt instalment due the United States next winter. The current moratorium expires in June and despite President Hoover's message to congress last December 10, asking provision for "temporary adjustments" in the war debts, it has been clear that the administration had every intention of heeding the sharp retort of congress that the existing moratorium was the limit to which American public sentiment would go. Borah warned the European nations not to come to the United States for debt relief until they have disarmed, settled reparations and revised the Versailles treaty. In his powerful oratorical voice he told the senate that the world

Dublin, Irish Free State, April 20 —(/P)—President Eamon De Valera’s bill to abolish the oath of allegiance to the British crown was passed on first reading without a division in the Dáil today. This had been expected, but a critical vote is looked for when the bill comes up for second reading next Wednesday.

London, April 19. (4)—Chancellor of the Exchequer Neville Chamberlain introduced another hard times budget in parliament today, balancing the British revenue and expenditure during the coming year at £766,000,000 (currently $2,887,820,000) and providing a small estimated surplus of £796,000 ($3,000,000). No relief was afforded taxpayers from the heavy burdens levied during the national crisis last autumn. The chancellor resisted all temptations to relax efforts which, he declared, had provided such a wonderful revival of public confidence. Pointing out that the last year had been one of "anxiety, difficulty and hardship,” Mr. Chamberlain informed the house that it is “only in the last few months that some revival of trade and employment has led us to hope that at last the worst is over.” “Coming now to the financial year 1932-1933,

London, April 20.—Europe is concerned lest strained relations between Japan and Russia intensified by bitter charges in hostile language unprecedented in peace time, be turned into war by any one of the many explosive factors in northern Manchuria. Foremost among dangerous elements is the present in Manchuria of thousands of ‘white,’ or anti-Bolshevik Russians, who fled from Russia after the revolution. They hate the Soviet regime. Many are reported ready to do anything to involve the Moscow government in trouble. Then there is the Soviet conviction that Japanese militarists believe that difficulties with the Soviets along the Siberian-Manchurian border would afford the excuse for Japan to remain in Manchuria indefinitely to suppress the “red menace.” This, the Soviets believe, would gain the approval or at least the benevolent neutrality of anti-Soviet European powers and dissipate any

London, April 20. (AP)—Majority opinion on the national government’s budget, introduced in the House of Commons yesterday by Neville Chamberlain, Chancellor of the Exchequer, today appeared summed up in the words of one prominent conservative industrialist who described it as “deeply disappointing, but not disheartening—inconclusive, but in some respects hopeful.” Liberal Opinion. Liberal opinion, on the whole, treated the budget favorably, although Major Gwylim Lloyd George, son of the former leader of the party, described it as one of the worst budgets in recent years. Other free-trade liberals expressed themselves as “thankful for small mercies,” and commended the impartiality of the Chancellor in granting no one relief because he could not ameliorate the condition of the unemployed and other chief sufferers from the government economy program. Labor Group. Comment from the labor grou

LONDON (/) — Spirits on the witness stand get no hearing in the court of Justice McCardie of London. The justice granted a verdict yesterday in favor of the London Daily Mail, which was sued for libel by Mrs. Meurig Morris, a spiritualist medium, because of an article in which Mrs. Morris was advertised as “a trance medium found out.” Mrs. Morris went into a trance on the witness stand at the close of the trial and purported spirit voices began to roll forth over the courtroom. The judge was in the midst of his address to the jury. The woman stood up suddenly with her eyes closed and a deep voice boomed: “Hearken to my voice, O Brother Judge!” The judge stopped his reading and ordered the plaintiff to be seated. “Let her speak!” someone shouted. The court then ordered the woman removed, but when the usher approached her the deep voice boomed again. “Do not touch her,” it said, “until I h

(By The Associated Press) DUBLIN, Irish Free State, April 19—Eamon De Valera plans tomorrow to take his first major legislative step toward “a free Ireland,” when a government bill to abolish the oath to the king comes before the dail on first reading. The energetic Republican, who has fought through two decades for his conception of an independent nation of Irishmen, will be carrying out the pledge of the campaign that made him president. Reliable sources have it that there will be no opposition to the abolition bill on its first reading. Nevertheless, intense excitement prevailed throughout the free state, and the demand for tickets to the public galleries for the opening of the dail exceeded the supply. With the recently deposed conservative group of William Cosgrave in opposition, there conceivably might be fireworks.

1932-05-22.text: New York, May 21 (AP)—Word was received here this afternoon that Mrs. Putnam had taken off in her own plane for London. Culmore, Ireland, May 21 (AP) Amelia Earhart Putnam brought down her red and gold monoplane in a field near here this afternoon and became the first woman ever to fly the Atlantic alone. She landed on this side of the ocean five years to the day after Colonel Charles A. Lindbergh arrived in Paris successfully completing the first solo flight across the Atlantic by a man. “Pye done it!” Mrs. Putnam exclaimed when she got out of her ship. She had intended to go to Paris but it was necessary to cut the flight short because her exhaust manifold had burned out and the gasoline line was broken causing a little leakage. Woman Is Unhurt Mrs. Putnam who took off from Harbor Grace, N. F., at 4:51 p.m. Friday got a lift by motor to Londonderry, 5 miles away, where the first thing

hry £920 ASO aetee Fees NEW YORK, May 31—Amelia Earhart Putnam will be heard at 11 a. m. (Central Standard Time) tomorrow in a transatlantic broadcast from London through the Columbia broadcasting company network.

ROME, May 21. (4) — Captain George Endres, who flew from Harbor Grace, Newfoundland, to Budapest with Captain Alexander Magyar last year, was killed with his mechanic when their plane crashed during a practice flight here today. Captain Endres came here to attend a convention of aviators opening tomorrow. Fifty-two men who flew either the Atlantic or Pacific Oceans are at the convention. The plane’s motor failed as Captain Endres was trying to gain altitude over the field.

Stockholm, May 20.—(A, P.)—Ivar Kreuger, the world famous "match king," who until he fired a bullet into his brain in Paris March 12, was considered the greatest financial genius of modern times, died practically penniless and owing $168,300,000, it was revealed today. The announcement was made by the Swedish investigating committee, which has been probing Kreuger’s affairs since his suicide. The $168,300,000 is in personal debts and indirect liability against the match king’s name, the committee said, and there will be little, if anything, left for distribution to unsecured creditors. The committee found that fictitious assets were set up on the Kreuger & Toll books since 1924, and that the state of the books was such that it was extraordinarily difficult to produce a definite balance sheet for the company. “This being the case, the committee considers there is no longer any need for ma

ROME, May 21 (UP).-—Capt. George Endres, who made a trans-Atlantic flight from New York to Hungary in 1931, was killed with another Hungarian pilot named Bituny today when their plane crashed in landing at the Littorio airport. Early reports, which later proved unfounded, said Alexander Magyar, who made the 1931 flight with Endres, was also killed.

NANKING, China, Sunday. May 22 - Three hundred bandits raided Kwochiu and Nauhi, looting more than 100 homes and kidnapping 50 women, while terror-stricken inhabitants tried to flee the area Saturday. The bandits freed scores of convicts, who participated in the raids. Seven persons were reported killed. When the bandits swooped into the district, the local garrison commander and magistrate fled.

Pinsent, a Hungarian army flier who made a successful crossing of the Atlantic last year with Alar Magyar, was burned to death in the crash of his plane here today. His mechanic was killed also. Endres crashed at the Littoric airport on his arrival to attend the convention of transatlantic aviators—the event that brought Mrs. Amelia Earhart Putnam to Europe. The plane, just after his ocean flight, nose-dived from a low altitude and crashed to the ground in flames. Endres and Magyar flew from Harbor Grace, N. F., to Distant, Hungary in July, 1931, and were only 14 miles from their goal.

ATHENS, Greece, May 21 (7) — Premier Eleutherios Venizelios, his position as head of the government made difficult by Greece's financial problems, resigned today because of difficulty in getting parliament to pass legislation he sponsored. He recommended the formation of a coalition republican cabinet under one of the opposition leaders.

1932-04-04.text: GLASGOW, Scotland, April 4. (4) - It was officially reported here today that Major Charles H. Schoeffel of the New Jersey state police will arrive tonight from London. It was understood he was coming to interview a Mrs. Taylor, the mother of the Lindbergh nurse, Betty Gow. There was a feeling among police authorities here that “something of considerable importance” may be the outgrowth of Major Schoeffel’s visit. The city is excited about it and the question is being asked on the street: “Is the Lindbergh baby in Glasgow?” The police have even gone so far as to institute a search for the child. Mrs. Taylor maintains reticence, however. When informed that the New Jersey officer would arrive tonight, she merely smiled and said: “I have nothing to say at the moment.”

LONDON, April 4 (UP).—The trail of the kidnaped Lindbergh baby was followed with vigor today by Scotland Yard and Major Charles Schoeffel, assistant superintendent of the New Jersey police. After a mysterious and secretive trip across the Atlantic, Schoeffel conferred with Yard officials today and then left on an undisclosed mission. He is due in Glasgow tonight to interview Mrs. Taylor, mother of the Lindbergh baby's nurse, Betty Gow.

LONDON, April 4, —Premier MacDonald, after a conference Sunday with Premier Andre Tardieu of France, announced that the four power conference Wednesday will include the whole range of the European crisis, including disarmaments, debts and reparations. Originally it had been intended to discuss only the Danubian states’ economic trouble. Germany and Italy will join England and France in the conference. Subscribe for the News-Miner.

| LONDON, April 4 (CP) — It was definitely settled today that the four-power conference which meets here Wednesday will discuss not only means of extending financial aid to the nations on the Danube, but the whole of Europe's difficulties, including reparations, disarmament and war debts. Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald made the announcement last night after a preliminary conversation with Premier Andre Tardieu of France, who came here yesterday and remained for further discussions today.

SAN PEDRO, Calif., April 4—(?)—In collision with the passenger carrying English freighter, Japanese Prince, on the high seas off Point San Vicente, the navy sub-chaser No. 34 headed to this port today in tow of the coast guard cutter Tamora. Radio reports revealed the navy vessel was badly damaged in the crash last night, but was in no apparent danger of sinking. The Japanese Prince, outbound from San Pedro to Yokohama on a round-the-world trip, was damaged badly. Point Vicente is approximately ten miles northwest of San Pedro. The navy boat was returning from Santa Barbara, from which point it had taken a group of naval reservists on a training cruise, to its base at San Diego.

LONDON, April 4 (INS)—Representatives of Great Britain and France met at 10 Downing Street today ostensibly to discuss the Danubian Federation, but the conversations immediately branched into the wider fields of debts, reparations and disarmament. The chief conferees were Premier Andre Tardieu of France and Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald of Great Britain. While official statements from both premiers so far have dealt solely with generalizations, reports from Paris indicated strongly that Tardieu is here mainly to strengthen the Anglo-French reparations front against the United States. The French Premier, it was understood, is desirous of pinning Premier MacDonald down to a definite declaration that Great Britain and France can pay war debts to the United States only out of funds received in the form of reparations from Germany. Britain’s reparations stand is predicated upon the Balfo

Cork, Ireland, April 4 (?)—The strike of employees of the Ford Motor assembling plant here, who walked out on April 1, collapsed today when the men returned to work on their old wage scale. The management agreed to negotiate for a new scale immediately, a development which was regarded as a victory for the workers. The men walked out in protest over a new wage cut ordered by the management.

BERLIN, April 4. (AP) — Three dead, a score injured, and hundreds arrested today marked the first day of Germany's second presidential campaign in less than a month. The election will take place April 10. While Adolph Hitler denounced the Von Hindenburg government, the Nazis fought communists and both factions battled police and the republic’s Iron Men, leaving a trail of death, blood and broken heads. Hitler began his campaign at noon Sunday, ending a political truce ordered for the Easter holidays.

1932-09-07.text: WASHINGTON—(?)—A flat prediction that Congress will not act to relieve America’s war debtors was made today by Speaker At about the same time, Secretary Stimson at the White House told newspapermen “it may not be necessary to reply” to the latest notes from Great Britain and France asking suspension respectively of payments of $95,550,000 and $20,000,000 due in less than two weeks. Others powerful on Capitol Hill also expressed strong opposition to acceding to the requests of Great Britain and France. The Secretary of State gave the first intimation that the United States might not answer the new debt communications as he hurried back to the State Department after a cabinet meeting at which the war debt situation—and the newly received French note in particular—were discussed. “It may not be necessary to reply,” he told newspapermen over his shoulder, as he left the White House. While he

Godthaab, Greenland, Sept. 7 (AP).—The “Flying Hutchinsons” took off on another leg of their New York-London flight this morning. They headed for Angnagsalik, on the east coast of Greenland. The Hutchinsons, a party of eight, including two pilots, are flying across Greenland, despite refusal of the Danish government to grant permission for a landing. The government explained that should an accident force the plane down in an inaccessible spot, it would not assume responsibility for the safety of the flyers.

Southampton, Eng., Sept. 7 (AP) United States Ambassador Mellon, returning from a visit to the United States, said today that this trip to America had absolutely no significance as a matter of world finances. “Nobody is thinking about war debts now—there is nothing to think about them,” he said in answer to a question. “I have had no serious business to do in America. I went over because I felt that I needed a holiday after a strenuous time in London. I can assure you that my visit had no significance whatever from a financial standpoint.”

RUTLAND, Vt., Sept. 7. (7:—Gov. Franklin D. Roosevelt's conferences with political leaders again bring him to western New England today, this time into the mountains of republican Vermont. He expected to motor from Albany to the state fair here, and to leave later in the day for Bennington, to talk with State Chmn. Park Pollard. Roosevelt was to make a brief speech at the fair. It was expected to be a greeting rather than a political address.

| Ollawa—()—The “Flying Hutchinsons” took off this morning from | Godthaab, Greenland, for Angmagsalik on Greenland's east coast, continuing their flight from New York to London over the Arctic route. Word of their departure reached the department of marine by radio, The Hutchinsons, a party of eight, including two children, are flying across Greenland despite refusal of the Danish government to grant permission for a landing there. The government explained that should an accident force the plane down in an inaccessible spot it would not assume responsibility for the safety of the flyers. When the Hutchinsons landed at Godthaab without permission they were fined approximately $180 by the Greenland government which requested that in continuing the flight the tourists follow the coastline to Angmagsalik instead of starting across the interior.

NEW YORK—50,000 ideas have been submitted, say officials, to the song, slogan and knickknack department at Democratic national headquarters but the most subtle of all is an emblem bearing no words at all—just a rose pinned to a piece of felt. Figure it out for yourself. YORK, England—The woman who is trying to conceal her age should keep an eye on her eyebrows, so to speak. They tend to give the secret away. Prof. V. Suk told the British Association for the Advancement of Science that eyebrows change position with advancing age. They sink below the upper margin of the orbital cavity, or eye socket. LONDON—Londoners who gibe at Chicago as crime town got a rebuke from Mayor Anton J. Cermak, “You Londoners quit maligning us,” the Chicago executive told interviewers. Declaring 10 big American cities had more murders than Chicago last year, he said: “You have 22,000 police in London, I am tol

Mukden, Sept. 7.—Raiding gangs of Chinese bandits swept into Newchwang and Mukden today, kidnapping a young English woman and two Englishmen. Duncan MacIntosh, one of the captives, escaped, but Mrs. Kenneth Pauley, 19, and Charles Corkran were spirited away to bandit strongholds. A large ransom was demanded for Mrs. Pauley’s release. British authorities promptly asked assistance in effecting the release of the two prisoners. Japanese and Manchukuo officials immediately prepared to send troops to the bandit stronghold.

London—(P)—It was said in official quarters today that the British government had received no intimation from the United States regarding postponement of the world economic conference which has been expected to begin in London late next month. Newspaper reports from Washington say the United States desires postponement but preparations for the conference already are under way with a preparatory committee scheduled to meet at Geneva late in September.

1932-12-13.text: WASHINGTON, Dec. 12. (AP) — European nations cannot attach strings to war debt payments due in three days. The United States government made that clear to Great Britain the same time as it advised against setting up reservations which would only increase the "difficulties that must be overcome" in attempting any new study of the debt tangle. In a flurry of diplomatic activity that broke the usual Sunday calm of official Washington, the British government said it would pay in gold the $95,550,000 due Dec. 15, but this was not to be taken as a resumption of payments on the plan existing prior to the Hoover moratorium. Rather it proposed that this remittance be treated as a "capital payment of which account should be taken in any final settlement." Hurried Consultations These proposals were promptly rejected by Secretary Stimson a few hours later after hurried consultations with President H

LONDON, Dec. 12. (AP).—Despite the American government's warning against such a procedure, it was predicted in well-informed quarters today that Britain will pay its war debt installment to the United States Thursday with a reservation that it be credited on a future debt settlement. It was learned that a cabinet session would follow Premier MacDonald's arrival from Geneva which was expected to frame Britain's next move in the high-speed war debts diplomacy. Another way of viewing the situation here was that Britain would make the payment as if to a court and that the manner in which the payment is dealt with in the bookkeeping of creditor and debtor countries.

The issue has not yet reached the parliament of either country, but it must come before the British House of Commons and the French Chamber of Deputies tomorrow or the next day, perhaps this evening. There was a report in London that England will pay the $95,550,000 due on the 15th and a reservation that it be credited as a capital payment despite the clear assertion that the United States is not prepared to receive it as such. In Paris, Premier Herriot said he would not make a final decision of policy until he knew what England was going to do. It was certain the French government would follow the course of the British.

By The Associated Press Icy winds from the northwest carried winter’s second cold snap over a wide section of the nation last night—bearing death and suffering with it. There was snow, sleet and rain in the New England states and California. In the vast section between the two coasts temperatures fell as low as 30 degrees below zero. Traffic accidents caused many of the two score deaths reported, but there were several instances of persons freezing to death. Livestock died on northwestern prairies. The mid-west feared for its winter wheat, although protecting snow fell in several states. The lowest official temperature was 37 degrees below zero at Elko, Nev., while Coalville, Utah, recorded an unofficial 40 below. In Chicago, the temperature hovered near zero. Weather forecasts said the temperature would rise slowly tomorrow. From the Dakotas and Minnesota, the cold wave was reported mov

(By The Associated Press). Great Britain has returned to the debate on the debts with another note to Washington renewing the promise to pay the $95,550,000 due on Thursday, reiterating the British position as outlined in previous notes, and urging again the importance of a conference to reconsider the whole debt system. The government in London has made it clear that although the issue will be debated in the House of Commons tomorrow, no action by Parliament will affect the decision of the cabinet. In France the situation was somewhat different. Premier Herriot, adhering to his policy of following the British lead, prepared for transmission to Washington a note offering to pay the $20,000,000 due this week on condition that the payment be applied against the capital account. The foreign affairs and finance committees of the Chamber of Deputies rejected that proposal, voting in favor of

Washington. Dec. 13.47—The U.S. will send no reply to the latest note from Great Britain on the war debts. After repeated conferences Tuesday between President Hoover, Secretary Stimson and Secretary Mills, the impression in informed quarters was distinctly that the U.S. and Great Britain now understand each other's position. No reason is seen in official circles for the U.S. to reject the payment expected from Great Britain Thursday.

WASHINGTON, Dec. 13, (P).— Great Britain’s explanation that the conditions she is making on Dec. 15 war debt payments need not affect the United States’ stand in accepting the money is considered satisfactory by American officials. This was learned today after Secretary Stimson had held a brief conference with President Hoover. It appeared here that the exchange of notes between the two countries in regard to the debts would now cease at least until after the payment date. Great Britain's third note, delivered to Stimson last night, said that while that government stood by the position that it regarded the Dec. 15 installment a payment to be credited to a new settlement, to be arrived at later, it did not intend this to affect the “constitutional position of the United States,” left officials satisfied that the payment could be accepted as though made without strings, and with no implied

(LOY ASSOCIATED PRESS) London, Dec. 13.—A laconic British note dispatched to Washington today promising to pay the debt installment due on Thursday signified that there has been no change in the basic British policy of cancellation of the war debt, with payments to be made under protest or with reservation. Until that goal, or at least a drastic revision of the debt has been realized, the new note merely affirms in words less liable to be misunderstood, what was set forth in the British note of last Sunday, and completed the exchange of legalistic views. What the note lacks in the eyes of government critics is any notification to the United States that the $95,550,000 payment due this week will be the last Great Britain will make under the present funding scheme. The government meets this criticism somewhat with a renewed appeal to the United States for an early review of the whole probl

1932-12-29.text: LONDON, Dec. 20—Rumors of the possibility of the Mahatma Mohandas K. Gandhi’s early release from prison, for some time current in India and England have been revived with the conclusion here last Saturday of the third India round table conference. A dispatch from New Delhi, India, yesterday recording a revival of the rumor there, stated that official quarters were reticent and it was vocated that the vice

ATHENS, Greece. —(4)— Samuel Insull, who recently made a successful fight against extradition to the United States, said today that while he had made no definite plans to return to America in the near future he contemplated a trip through the continent and England. He said his wife probably would meet him there later. Discussing his recent acquittal he criticized Chicago attorneys for their declaration that they would make diplomatic efforts to obtain his extradition. “What would be the impression in America if a foreign country should threaten to take diplomatic steps against their judicial decision?” Insull asked.

POONA, India, Dec. 29. (UP)~ The Mahatma Gandhi today laid down a new ultimatum to the British government demanding legislation to permit the downtrodden untouchables of India to enter the temples from which they have been barred for centuries. If the government refuses, Gandhi told the United Press, he will begin a new fast in mid-January. Ignoring rumors in London that the government probably would free him and thousands of other political prisoners on New Year's Day, the little man declared he had definitely decided that action must be taken in regard to the untouchables issue.

| LOS ANGELES. .m. The ten ugliest words in the English language, said the National Association of Teachers of Speech, meeting here are: Jazz, plump, gripe, treachery, sap, cacophony, plutocrat, flatulent, phlegmatic, mash.

WELLINGTON, N. Z., Dec. 29. Ten persons were drowned when a launch carrying 380 workers collided today with a small steamer in Napier harbor. The remainder were rescued, several being taken to a hospital.

| Athens, Dec. 28.—Samuel Insull had dinner with friends last night, a free man after a Greek court had refused to sanction his extradition to the United States to answer Cook County (Illinois) charges of mismanagement of the funds of his utilities companies. The court, after having peremptorily cut short the presentation of the defense case, found that depositions brought from Chicago did not support the charges against the former utilities operator. A large crowd had gathered for the verdict and shouts of “Long live Greek justice!” echoed through the building. “I owe thanks to Greek justice for the sympathy expressed,” Insull said. Embezzlement Charged. The charges against Insull in Chicago are grand larceny and embezzlement. They involve payments of $66,000 and $104,000 which, according to a deposition made by Oliver McCormick, treasurer of the utilities companies, were made to broker

TOKYO, Dec. 28.—(/)—Plans to bolster Japan's military strength in Manchuria were announced today by the war office. It was announced that, although the number of units would be but little increased, the quality of equipment of Japan's forces in Manchuria would be greatly improved. For this purpose, the forces remaining in Japan proper would be reduced as much as possible. Funds needed for the readjustment were included in the army's 443,006,000 yen budget for 1933-34 announced Nov. 25. (This is about $4,000,000).

Paris, Dec. 29 —(AP)—Former Premier Herriot today gave his vigorous support in the Chamber of Deputies to a proposed loan of $14,000,000 to Austria, declaring he wanted to assume his share of responsibility for the proposal. Opponents of the loan had said it would be inconsistent for France to lend money to Austria after having defaulted on the December installment of the debt to the United States, but M. Herriot asserted that “it would be better to try to extricate Austria from her difficulties than to leave her to her fate.” Financial aid thus extended by France, he said, would prevent any attempt at union with Germany, “of which France would be the first victim.”

1932-08-31.text: | LONDON, Aug. 31.—(UP)— Capt. James A. Mollison will return to England by steamer, his manager announced today. Scot flier has decided to yield to the pleas of his wife and numerous prominent persons he abandon the return flight.

LONDON, Aug. 31. (4”)—Amy Johnson announced today her husband, Capt. A. J. Mollison, had definitely decided to return to England by steamer, abandoning the plan to fly the Atlantic for his second trip on a round-trip hop. It was reported earlier that Mollison was suffering from nervous exhaustion at Sydney, Nova Scotia.

LONDON, Aug. 31. (AP)—Scotland Yard ringed London today with a blockade against “motor bandits.” Several hundred motor cars were stopped by policemen called secretly into action by Lord Trenchard, Scotland Yard's new chief. At dawn the secrecy was still strictly maintained, and it was not disclosed whether any arrests had been made in the most impressive combing out of its kind London has ever known. Almost every day has brought fresh stories of brutal holdups and assaults by “motor gunmen” who cruise about in automobiles. Lord Trenchard launched his blockade in the early morning hours. There were flying squads of speed cars and motorcycle patrolmen and a large force of patrolmen. All the main approaches to London were posted, as were the bridges and important centers inside the city, and the orders were to halt every car, no matter what it looked like. Hundreds of motorists were stopped

CARNARVON, WALES, Aug. 31.—(?)— Authorities here are keeping a close watch along the north Wales coast and at Cardigan Bay for possible traces of the ‘missing trans-Atlantic fliers, Clyde Lee and John Bochkon, as a consequence of a report that an airplane motor had been heard on the night they were due over England. An automobile association scout inspector reported that on Friday night, while he was walking on the shore of Cardigan Bay he distinctly heard the ‘drone of a powerful airplane engine. It appeared to come from some distance at sea. He heard it for several minutes and then it stopped suddenly. Visibility was poor at the time with mist over land and sea. The automobile association informed the army flying corps of the report immediately, but all the air force planes were accounted for. Clyde Lee and John Bochkon took off from Barre, Vt., on Aug. 23 for Harbor Grace, Newfoundlan

Eo lh Sea! Uh wee )36h—6R Oe eee ical expeditions lined up at dawn Wednesday for the total eclipse of the sun. In a string 300 miles long and 50 wide from Montreal to Cape Cod, they dotted the landscape, mostly in flat New England valleys. Their telescopes were trained low toward the northwest, where the moon covered the sun at 3:30 p.m., Eastern standard time. A few were on high places. One woman astronomer set her telescope on top of a tower 295 feet above the surf on the coast of Cape Cod. Around these astronomers, spectators from many states massed in such manners that state police and town constabulary set up military lines to ensure freedom for scientific work. Several million persons scattered picnic fashion throughout the eclipse areas. They came by special trains from as far as New York City, but mostly in a stream of automobiles.
