MANCHESTER, Eng., Aug. 31 (AP).—The third day of the Lancashire textile strike today showed both sides standing firm with 145,000 operatives, as estimated by the trade unions, participating in the walkout. The number of strikers was swelled yesterday, and strike officials said complete stoppage of the textile industry by the end of the week was expected. The Lancashire weavers walked out in protest against a ten percent wage cut and working conditions.

LONDON, Aug. 31 (P)—Capt. James A. Mollison will return to England by steamer, instead of attempting a return Atlantic flight, the flier told the Evening Standard today by transatlantic telephone from Sydney, N. S. “I have not been feeling too well the last few days and I now realize that I am not so fit as I ought to be to make the flight back,” Captain Mollison said. “The strain of waiting has been simply awful.”

Astronomers literally slept on the ground in New England last night to guard their precious instruments against the millionth of an inch jar that might spoil observations of today’s total eclipse of the sun. Last night’s weather forecasts were for partly cloudy weather in a large part of the American collimation belt. But 200 astronomers cannot all be wrong—that was the big hope. For cannily, months ago they distributed their positions strategically to checkmate just such a forecast. Not for nothing have they observed similar “partly cloudy” days in past trips halfway around the world to gamble on just one minute of total eclipse “seeing.” Last night they were strung out in 26 places in a line about 300 miles long. Auto traffic into the eclipse area was reported heavy. Railroad of.

1932-06-07.text: | SHANGHAI, China, June 7 UP. The Exchange Telegraph reported today that the American gunboat Oahu had fired on Chinese soldiers who were attacking two British steamers, They were attacking the river boats Wanliu and Kiawo, the dispatch said. The Oahu's gunners drove off the attack with many casualties,

(By The Associated Press) NEW YORK, June 6 — The 83rd hour since Stanislaus Pex Hausner, 31-year-old Polish-American flier, took off from Floyd Bennett Field on a projected non-stop flight to London or Paris and Warsaw, passed tonight without word of his whereabouts. Mrs. Martha Hausner, his bride of a year, lost some of the optimism she maintained after the 52-hour limit at which his gasoline supply would last has passed. Her brother, Walter Wages, Jersey City, said she still had hope her husband is alive, believing he may have brought his red monoplane down on the wastes of Iceland sometime Saturday and been unable as yet to communicate his whereabouts. Hausner took off at 7:46 a.m. (central standard time) Friday and never has definitely reported after that although a plane believed to have been his passed over Sydney, Nova Scotia, early that evening.

SANDWICH, Eng., June 7.—(?)— America's “big three” in the British open golf championship—Tommy Armour, defending champion, MacDonald Smith and Gene Sarazen—safely qualified among the leaders today for the 72 holes of medal play proper, but home-bred British golfers furnished all the fireworks. Mac Smith and Armour had 36 hole totals of 146, Mac Smith with 73-73 and Armour with 75-71, and Sarazen, one of the leaders yesterday with a 73, took 76 for a 36-hole total of 149. Alfred Robert Oradbeer, young Somerset professional, held the lead, with only a few scores yet to be posted, with a fine total of 141; adding a 71 today to his 70 of yesterday. The main interest, however, was furnished by Aric McRuvie, young Scotch amateur and Walker cup player, and Don Curtis, English professional, who scored 69s over Prince’s par 74 stretch to break the course record of Jock Hutchinson and Arthur Hayer

Rome, June 6. (4)— Angelo Sbardellotto, who was arrested Saturday on a charge of plotting to assassinate Premier Mussolini, told police today he was chosen by lot to do away with Italy's strong man. His attempt, he said, was a continuation of the “mission” of Michele Schirru, a naturalized American, who was executed in May, 1931, for plotting against the Premier's life. The same group of conspirators who sent Schirru to Italy selected him by a lot at a meeting in Brussels, Sbardellotto declared. He had intended, he told the police, to fling a bomb at the premier Saturday during ceremonies honoring Garibaldi, Italy’s liberator, but was frustrated.

Para, June 7—(/)—Premier Edouard Herriot today made a declaration for the reciprocity in war debt and reparation negotiations at Lausanne June 16th and there was every indication he would receive a heavy vote of confidence from the chamber of deputies. The entire left with the exception of the communists and a goodly portion of the center group applauded the premier’s cabinet seat and his predecessor, Andre Tardieu of the moderate right openly accepted some passages. Premier Herriot opened his Lausanne remarks with the statement that his government would take a determined stand against violation of treaties and contracts between nations. He left the way open, however, for negotiations with the statement that he will be ready to discuss at Lausanne “any project which on a basis of reciprocity seems likely to lead to greater world stability and peace reconciliations.”

PARIS, June 7-(P)—For the first time in two weeks the American dollar showed improvement on the foreign exchange market today. The quotation was 25.3275 as against 25.3250, the level at which it had stood since May 25. The improvement was attributed to the action of the United States Congress in voting the tax.

COLLINGSWOOD, N. J., June 7 (AP).—Five persons were killed and two critically injured today when an ambulance collided with an automobile. The automobile caught fire and burned up. The driver of the car was a student at Georgetown University in Washington, and he and his mother and aunt were returning home after attending commencement exercises at the university yesterday. The child suffered a cut on her forehead in a fall from her crib and was being taken to the hospital for treatment.

WASHINGTON, June 7.—(/)— The new revenue bill is law today, bolstering the credit of the government with the greatest range of taxes ever imposed by this country except during the war. Spartan absence of ceremony, President Hoover transformed this giant legislation into statute by affixing his signature yesterday evening in the presence only of a secretary, less than two hours after the final legislative step had been taken by the senate. The majority of the new rates, excises, tariffs, and stamp taxes will go into effect in 15 days, or on June 21. The treasury will immediately prepare for their collection. The new, high income rates are applicable to the earnings of the current calendar year and will be payable on the next year’s returns, Puts Nation on Cash Basis. The tax law is to pour $1,115,500,000 into the treasury during the fiscal year which begins July 1, and thus restore the na

1932-02-23.text: DUBLIN, Irish Free State, Feb. 23 (P)—President William T. Cosgrave and his cabinet conceded today their defeat in the Irish election held last Tuesday. With the returns from the election completed except for 7 districts in which voting was postponed, Eamon de Valera’s Fianna Fail and its Labor allies had won 77 seats in the new Dail Eireann, as compared with 68 for the Government party and its independent supporters. President Cosgrave said he and his cabinet had definitely determined to go into the opposition. He said reports he was seeking alliance with any group to keep de Valera's Fianna Fail out of power were totally unfounded.

Dublin, Irish Free State, Feb. 22—(AP)—President William T. Cosgrave today promised conditional support of his apparently defeated government party to Eamon De Valera if the latter forms a new Irish government. President Cosgrave, whose party ran second to De Valera’s Fianna Fail in the general election held last Tuesday, said that although his government had “hysterical opposition” during the years it was in power in Ireland, the new government would have from him an opposition which would support it as long as its policies were in the best interest of the country. (Continued: on Page Two).

NEW YORK. (4. Although the great south Arabian desert is now a desolate stretch of sand dotted with dead men's bones, Bertram Thomas, a British explorer, is convinced it once was a fertile, pleasant land in which a now unknown civilization flourished. It was Thomas who last year risked death by murder, starvation and thirst to make a 600 mile trek across that "empty quarter of the world," which had been called the last unexplored strip of the globe. Monday night the bronzed Englishman was guest of honor at a banquet at which half a dozen other famous explorers were present. To make the perilous trip across the desert never before crossed by a white man, Thomas explained, he was forced to spend fifteen years winning the confidence of the natives. He learned their language, adopted their garb and manners, acquired a taste for their food, and grew a beard, which is essential to wear by. On

WASHINGTON, Feb. hostilities between China and Japan were cited tonight by the chairmen of the Senate Naval and Military Committees as reasons why America should be adequately prepared for war. Chairman Hale of the naval committee advocated building the Navy up to London treaty limits and Chairman Reed of the military affairs committee urged maintaining the strength of the Army. They spoke in the Washington Star forum over the National Broadcasting System. "With the world in its present condition," Hale said, "and with the apparent failure of all treaties to guarantee world peace, it is inconceivable folly and no part of real economy to fail to provide in full measure for the national defense of our country." Asserting that no one can say the war in Asia will not spread, Reed warned: "We once thought that a war in Europe could not touch us, and when it did touch us, it found us unprepare

Dublin, Irish Free State, Feb. 22. The strenuous and victorious election campaign of last week sent the fiery Eamon De Valera to bed with a cold today but not until he had hailed “a new era of peace and prosperity for Ireland.” The condition of the Fianna Fail leader was declared not serious by his physician, who said a day or so in bed should conquer his ailment. De Valera’s Fianna Fail party and its labor allies have won 77 seats against 68 for the government party of President William T. Cosgrave. This was shown in complete returns, except for seven districts in which the voting was postponed. De Valera told the Associated Press that he intended to pursue, if asked to form a new government, his campaign policies. He said: “A new era has dawned before Ireland. An era in which the Irish people will enjoy a peace and prosperity so long denied them. “The only way to avoid misunderstanding

LONDON, Feb. 23 — (Lp) — Great Britain’s policy in the Far East will be to co-operate with the United States and the League of Nations in whatever action may be agreed upon, according to Sir John Simon, foreign secretary. It was assumed such cooperation might include an economic boycott. Simon presented Great Britain’s official stand in a statement last night before the House of Commons. He said England is convinced that ‘affirmation of the principles of the League of Nations with boldness and sincerity’ is essential to a solution of the Sino-Japanese question. Simon’s statement was in reply to the insistence of George Lansbury, Labor leader, that the League quickly “decide on some appropriate action.” Lansbury mentioned the possibility of economic measures or withdrawal of ambassadors to halt the fighting.

Tokyo—(f)—The Japanese government decided Tuesday night to double the strength of its army at Shanghai in the face of reports from there saying that the Chinese defenders of the city, during three days fighting, had successfully stopped the power of Japan's attack. The proposal to send additional troops to Shanghai was placed before the cabinet early today by General Sabao Araki, minister of war, following a conference of military leaders which was called (Continued on Page 11)

Shanghai, Feb. 23. (Tuesday) — Chinese headquarters issued a bulletin early today declaring their army was advancing rapidly along the whole front from Chanei to Woosuns, driving back the Japanese despite the arrival of enemy reinforcements. Chinese Artillery Shell Hongkew Area Shanghai, Feb. 22.—Chinese artillery trained on Hongkew, Japanese base, cut loose tonight with the heaviest bombardment in several days, blasting the north Szechuen road. Some shells fell in the Chinese residential area where many householders had refused to evacuate. It was feared that many Chinese civilians had been killed. The shelling was so heavy the ambulances could not get to the wounded. Dozens of fires broke out near the Japanese barracks and the flames spread while firemen stood by helpless. The fire headquarters was struck by a shell and several firemen were wounded. Another shell landed in the isolatio

1932-11-16.text: DAKAR, Senegal, French West Africa, Nov. 16. (?—Amy Johnson, Britain's daring woman flier who is trying to beat her husband’s record from London to Cape Town, has successfully crossed the Great Sahara desert. She landed at Gao, on the upper Niger, yesterday and took off for Douala, on the Gulf of Guinea. Miss Johnson made the 1,400-mile flight from Oran, Algeria, in a little over 13 hours, landing at Gao at 12:30 p.m., yesterday. Miss Johnson is trying to beat J. A. Mollison’s record of four days, 17 hours, 19 minutes, for the 6,200 mile flight to Cape Town.

PARIS, Nov. 16, ()—The formation of a tri-partite economic consortium among France, Germany and Great Britain, and designed to rehabilitate Europe, was announced today by Raymond Patenotre, the American born under-secretary for national economy. The first project will be the offering of a 17,000,000,000 franc loan for the electrification of railways in Poland, Rumania, Irak and Portugal. (This sum is equivalent currently to $680,000,000.) The Paris edition of the New York Herald-Tribune said France and England each would provide 40 percent of the loan, and Germany would contribute 20 percent. The consortium, as described by M. Patenotre on his arrival from Berlin, was said to be purely an economic arrangement, but, as approved by the three governments, the program is an outgrowth of the visit of then Premier Pierre Laval and the late Aristide Briand to Berlin in 1931. Premier Edouard Her

Hy fie Associated Press. Washington, D. C., Nov. 15. While European capitals waited anxiously today for America’s answer to French and British requests for a renewed study of the war debts situation and an extension of the Hoover moratorium, a third request for such action was received at the state department, this one from the Belgian government. President Hoover, meanwhile, was speeding eastward to dig into the problem with his advisors here and to go over it personally with President-elect Roosevelt. The President is scheduled to arrive here at 9 a. m. tomorrow. The date of the latter meeting had not been set, but Albany dispatches indicated it would occur by the middle of next week. Rigid Attitude Needed Administration spokesmen denied reports (not carried by The Associated Press) that Mr. Hoover favored another year of the moratorium. It was indicated that the administration believe

WASHINGTON, Nov. 16 UP— England, France and Belgium stood side by side today, eagerly awaiting the outcome of White House conferences on this nation’s answer to separate but similar requests for a re-opening of the complex international debt problem. As President Hoover was returning to the capital to discuss with government leaders and his successor-elect, Franklin D. Roosevelt, what America’s position should be, Belgium joined the lead of her two fellow-debtors in seeking an extension of the Hoover moratorium and re-examination of the huge war obligations held by the United States.

| Belfast, Northern Ireland, Nov. 15.—(4)— Disturbances broke out tonight on the eve of the arrival of the Prince of Wales to dedicate the new parliament buildings here tomorrow. A British Union Jack was torn down on Falls Road. Republican posters protesting against the visit of the prince were removed by police. Two women were arrested. The officials charged with the prince’s safety declared, however, that with the extensive military and police preparations they had provided nothing alarming could happen. Recent Rioting It was only a short time ago that rioting occurred in the streets here. That was not connected with the visit of the prince, but some of the northern Ireland groups have announced their opposition to his visit. Only the great influence of the Duke of Abercorn, the Ulster gov- (Continued on Page 7)

LONDON, Nov. 16—Mrs. Amy Johnson Mollison, British woman flier, attempting a record flight to Cape Town, landed at Gao, French West Africa, at 12:30 P. M. Tuesday and continued to Duala, an Exchange Telegraph dispatch from Dakar said today. Uneasiness had been felt over lack of news from her since she left Oran, Algeria, for French West Africa late Monday.

PARIS, Nov. 16—()—Greta Garbo has been in Paris since Thursday incognito and wearing the horn-rimmed glasses that disguised her in London, said Paris Midi today. The Swedish movie star was accompanied by the Countess of Wachmeister as companion. She shopped a good deal and planned to leave tomorrow for Stockholm.

London, Nov. 16.—{INS}—Streaking alone across the wastes of the Sahara, Amy Johnson, British aviatrix, landed at Gao, French West Africa, at 12:30 p.m. yesterday, and then took off for Duala, according to an Exchange telegraph dispatch from Dakar this afternoon.

1932-10-11.text: Manila —(P)— Captain Wolfgang von Gronau and three companions abandoned efforts to repair the disabled engine of their globe-girdling airplane, forced down on rough seas of the Indian Ocean, when the British steamship Karagola turned to their assistance today. A cryptic radio message from the German flier received here at 4:11 this afternoon (3:11 a.m., eastern standard time) said: "Steamship Karagola comes to our rescue. Thanks for your help. Sorry could not finish our program." The globe-encircling plane had been forced down earlier in the day 200 miles south of Rangoon by a broken water pump.

LEIGH, Lancashire, Eng. Oct. 10—Nineteen persons were drowned today when a cage conveying 20 miners crashed 700 feet to the bottom of a colliery shaft here. Before rescue parties and doctors could extricate the trapped victims, water in the mine pit had ended their lives. Only one occupant escaped. He managed to smash the cage door and crawl out before being submerged. When the tragedy became known, the pit-head was crowded with weeping relatives of the victims, who were declared dead after two and a half hours of artificial respiration failed to revive them.

NEW YORK, Oct 11 (UP).—A smashing, spectacular drive to win New York and New England for the republicans and keep Herbert Hoover in the White House was led today by two men of widely different personalities--Calvin Coolidge and William J. (Wild Bill) Donovan, candidate for governor. The two will speak tonight in Madison Square Garden. More than 50,000 persons have sought the 21,000 available seats for the opening attack in the republicans' major eastern offensive. Coolidge’s address will be the first public political speech the former president has made since he retired from the White House in March of 1929. The address will be broadcast starting about 7:45 p. m. (CST).

PARIS, Oct. 10.—Premier Herriot is to go to London before the end of this week to discuss with Prime Minister MacDonald Germany’s demand for arms equality and other phases of the disarmament situation. The trip was arranged during an interview with Lord Tyrrell, the British ambassador. After M. Herriot said he would go, Lord Tyrrell telephoned to London to fix a date, and it was understood that the meeting will take place between Thursday and next Sunday. M. Herriot expects to spend two days in London, and it is understood that the conversations will be only between France and Great Britain, with a view to reaching a decision on the attitude of both governments for the forthcoming disarmament discussions at Geneva.

PARIS, Oct. 11 — Premier Edouard Herriot was expected to confer with Norman Davis, American disarmament conference delegate about the proposed new French disarmament plan when he goes to London tomorrow to consult with Prime Minister MacDonald and Foreign Secretary Sir John Simon. French newspapers said today the new French plan consists of five projects: 1. A general convention for the reduction of armaments. 2. A general consultative pact which would include the United States, 3. A regional European pact for mutual assistance and non-aggression, 4. Progressive creation of an international air force to be placed at the disposal of the League of Nations, 5. A protocol on the application of the principle of equality of rights — a measure intended to satisfy Germany. Under the proposed consultative pact, if a nation insisted on war after a warning, mutual assistance would be brought to ope

WASHINGTON, Oct. 10.—Senator Reed, Republican, Pennsylvania, recently returned from a series of conferences with European statesmen, said today he was convinced France and Great Britain intended to pay their war debts to this country. Reed expressed his views at the White House after conferring with President Hoover.

London, Oct. 11—(AP)—An Exchange Telegraph dispatch from Athens this evening said Samuel Insull, detained there pending extradition proceedings, had been set at liberty. The Greek judicial authorities, having examined the evidence in the case, decided that there was nothing to justify his further detention, the dispatch said.

| MANILA, (Tuesday) Oct. 11.—(4) Capt. Wolfgang von Gronau and his three companions on a round-the-world flight have been rescued by the British steamer Karagola and their flying boat taken in tow for Rangoon, a message intercepted by the Radio Corporation of America here tonight said. A wireless message said the Karagola had picked up the four German airmen from their flying boat after it had been forced down in the Indian Ocean by engine trouble and later the steamer reported “the plane O. K., being in tow of Karagola.”

1932-04-26.text: GENEVA, April 26 (—A joint plan of Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson and Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald of Great Britain to bring together, in their presence, Premier Andre Tardieu of France and Chancellor Heinrich Bruening of Germany for an effort at Franco-German reconciliation went awry this morning when Premier Tardieu failed to show up. MacDonald and Stimson thought they had the French premier’s promise to meet them and Chancellor Bruening at Secretary Stimson's villa at Bessingle, but M. Tardieu remained in Paris. Chancellor Bruening was present, however, and conferred with Stimson and MacDonald all morning. The results of the diet elections in Germany Sunday have given cold chills to the leaders here who are seeking a solution of international problems, especially on the eve of the French elections. According to well-informed sources, Secretary Stimson and Prime Minister MacDon

New London, Conn., April 25 (AP)—An explosion in the engine room of the Coast Guard patrol boat CG290, veteran rum craft chaser, while it was taking on fuel today injured seven men and demolished the vessel. The commander and five members of the crew were taken to a hospital, where two were regarded in a critical condition. Another man helping fill the gasoline tanks was slightly hurt. The explosion, just after the fueling had been finished, tore the ship almost in two. The noise of the blast was heard for miles. Its force broke windows in buildings near the pier. Accumulation of gas fumes in the engine room was believed responsible. The twisted vessel sank at the wharf but part remained above the surface because of the shallowness of the harbor.

| NEW LONDON, Conn., April 26.—D)--The coast guard patrol boat CG-290, veteran rum boat chaser, was at the bottom of New London harbor today, and six members of her crew were in a hospital as a result of an explosion which demolished the oath. The explosion, believed to have been caused by the accumulation of vapor fumes, occurred yesterday in the engine room while the boat was taking on fuel. In 1928, the CG-290 engaged in a battle with the rum boat Black Duck during which three of the Black Duck's crew were killed.

London, Ont. — Wallace Ramesboltom of Sarnia, who was 21 years old the day before last, paid the death penalty in the local yard early this morning for the killing of Samuel Weinstein, a London merchant. The 65-year-old grocer was shot close by the heart by a man who fled without loot. Pale but resolute, he faced his fate as he ascended the steps to the gallows. At 12:10 a.m., the Lord's Johnson announced the condemned.

LONDON, April 26. — (») — Eamon De Valera’s bill in the Irish Dáil to abolish the oath of allegiance to the British crown is considered by the British government to be a violation of the treaty which established the Irish Free State, J. H. Thomas, secretary for dominions, told parliament today. De Valera has been informed of that viewpoint in clear and unmistakable terms, he said. The Dáil passed the bill on first reading without a division last week. It comes up for second reading tomorrow, when it will meet stronger opposition.

New London, Conn., April 25 (#) —Seven men were injured, five of them seriously, when the Coast Guard Patrol Boat CG 290 blew up at a wharf this afternoon as it finished taking on gasoline. ‘An explosion in the engine room, believed to have been caused by the ignition of accumulated gas fumes, demolished the center of the boat, which sank. The CG 290 had been outstanding in the Coast Guard’s work of chasing rum boats, and in 1929 was in an encounter with the Black Date, in which three men were killed.

WASHINGTON, April 26 (UP) — Many women prohibitionists are bombarding Prohibition Director Woodcock with letters demanding that action be taken against Ambassador Andrew W. Mellon who announced he would serve liquor at the American embassy in London. Woodcock proposes to do “absolutely nothing” about it. He holds that a question of diplomatic policy and immunity is beyond the province of his bureau.

Sey S24AW SLOAN FLO Washington, Apr. 26—The Hale Bill to build up the navy to the London treaty strength was given calendar preference today by the senate steering committee. The banking reform bill of Senator Glas (D., Va.), was placed second in order, followed by the resolution of Senator George (D., Ga.) authorizing the President to reorganize the executive branch of the government. Fourth on the list announced by Chairman Vandenberg (R., Mich.) came the Democratic emergency road fund bill, long since approved by the house. The resolution of Senator Norris (R., Neb.) providing for government operation of Muscle Shoals, or for leasing the properties under a number of conditions, was made next. Sixth and last was the Hawes-Cutting Philippine independence bill. Appropriations bills pending and in committee will maintain their preference as will the tax bill and conference reports on bill

1932-08-02.text: OTTAWA, Ont.—(?)—The stupendous portion of the trade of Great Britain and Canada which is with the United States proved the greatest stumbling block Tuesday to all negotiations for intra-empire trade deals at the conference here. With all its dominions and colonies, the British Empire handled only about 28% of the world’s trade in 1930 while the United States alone handled 12%, almost half as much. In the United States was sold, in 1930, more than one-third of all the linen manufactures exported by the United Kingdom; 43.2 per cent of all the tin, and nearly 19 per cent of all British exports of leather and leather goods, other than wearing apparel. On the other side of the ledger, the United Kingdom took one-sixth of all the imports from the United States, some of the outstanding items being four-fifths of the American exports of hams, more than half the tobacco, worth $79,400,000, and

Miami, Fla., Aug. 2—(AP)—Captain W. N. Lancaster, formerly of the British Air Corps, went on trial in Dade County Circuit Court today charged with murdering Haden Clarke, a young writer, in a love triangle involving Mrs. J. M. Keith-Miller, the Austrian flier. Clarke was mysteriously shot April 21 in the bedroom he and Lancaster occupied in her home here. James M. Carson, chief of the defense counsel, moved in vain for a continuance of the trial until September 15 as soon as court opened.

OTTAWA, Ont., Aug. 2. UP—Unemployed masses here today sent delegates into the British Empire Economic Conference to give Premier R.B. Bennett their demand for their war-time pay and allowance—$1.10 daily. The deputation, limited to seven, was told it might visit the prime minister today provided the workers’ conference, which the deputies represent, was not a communistic outfit. The hundreds of delegates to the conference are members of the National Committee of Unemployed Councils or the Workers’ Ex-service League, both rated as communistically affiliated.

MIAMI, Fla. Aug. 2—(UP)— Capt. William Lancaster, British aviator, was brought to trial here today on a charge of murdering Haden Clarke, youthful newspaperman, in a bungalow by the side of the sea April 21. As the trial began Judge J. H. Atkinson denied a defense motion for continuance until the next court term on the grounds of absence of a material witness, Dr. Percy L. Dodge. Lancaster and his attorneys declared the defendant could not safely go on trial without the assistance of Dr. Dodge's testimony. Clarke was found dying of a bullet wound in his head on the sleeping porch he occupied with Lancaster in the bungalow home of Mrs. Jessie M. Keith Miller, Australian woman flyer. Lancaster had been Mrs. Keith Miller’s flying partner in a London-Australia flight and other air tours in many countries for five years. Clarke had been engaged to write Mrs. Keith-Miller's biography. When Cla

TIDAL WAVE IN BENGAL LONDON, Aug. 2 (INS)—The loss of 216 lives when a tidal wave capsized a ferryboat at Koakhali in Eastern Bengal was revealed in an exchange telegraph dispatch from Calcutta today. Only 31 passengers aboard the craft were saved.

MIAMI, Fla, Aug. 2—(P)—A jury of twelve men was selected today to try Captain W. N. Lancaster, former British army flier, charged with the murder of Haden Clarke, young author and fiancé of Mrs. J. M. Keith-Miller, Lancaster's Australian flying partner.

WASHINGTON, D. C., Aug. 2—(#)— The United States today accepted an invitation to an economic conference with European nations. - The decision was made in a note delivered to the British charge d'affaires here. It outlined briefly the acceptance of the United States as a participant in the conference on the terms prescribed by the recent British invitation and said the three American members of the separate committees that will be set up to arrange for the conference would be named later. The text of the acceptance note was not made public and it was said this country would leave it to London officials to decide whether it would be...

LONDON, Aug. 2.—(4)—London newspapers professed today to see a tendency toward a return of the monarchy in Germany and a prospect that the country would be governed for a long time without a parliament as the result of last Sunday's elections. “Although the government is undoubtedly monarchist in tendency,” the Times said, “it probably has no present intention of attempting drastic changes in the constitution. It must, for the moment, renounce the role of reformer and diplomatist for the work of the police.”

1932-05-02.text: NELSON, N. C., May 2.—(CP)— British Columbia police used itch powder and short lengths of garden hose as weapons yesterday when they encountered 200 Doukhobors on parade at Thrums, 16 miles from Nelson. Authorities arrested 117 men and women. The Doukhobors, many of whom were nude, fought back savagely. They turned several streams of water on the officers. The police sprang clear of the water and sprayed the powder on the exposed bodies of the men and women, finally herding them into an orchard, where they were held until trucks arrived to bring them here. The prisoners consisted of 33 women and 84 men. They will be arraigned during the week. Persons guilty of parading in the nude are liable to three years’ imprisonment. It was the second demonstration at Thrums in 24 hours. Saturday the Doukhobors, a religious sect which came to Canada from Russia, staged a parade, during which there wa

LONDON, May 2. (AP).—Two young scientists of Cambridge University were hailed today as having achieved a goal physicists have sought to reach for years. They have broken the atom. In announcing details of what he called “a discovery of great scientific importance,” Lord Rutherford, noted scientist, said Drs. J. D. Cockcroft and E.T. S. Walton accomplished the feat after several years of work with apparatus erected under his supervision. Dr. Cockcroft said he and his colleague bombarded hydrogen atoms with a voltage of 120,000 and that under the bombardment the hydrogen atoms began to break up into helium, a still rarer gas. The helium atoms, he said, came out of the bombardment with energies of 100 to 160 times those of the particles fired into them. Only one particle broke up, however, for every 10,000,000 particles used to bombard it, he said. Dr. Cockcroft, the older of the two experi

CAMBRIDGE, Eng., May 2—British scientists have succeeded in splitting the atom and in transmuting elements into other elements. The goal of ancient alchemists and the dream of modern chemists was reached by Dr. F. D. Cockcroft and Dr. J. T. S. Walton in experiments at Cavendish laboratory here. The experiments succeeded in turning atoms of hydrogen into atoms of helium. They used voltages of between 120,000 and 600,000 to send millions of particles a second through a vacuum tube. The particles travelled at the rate of 10,000 kilometers a second, the physicists said. They revealed that for every atom “split” by this bombardment, several million particles were required. Lord Rutherford, one of the founders of the modern atomic theory of physicists, is the director of Cavendish laboratory.

By the Associated Press LONDON, May 1.—Lord Rutherford, one of the world’s foremost scientists, today disclosed that two young Cambridge physicists had achieved one of the greatest goals of all scientific research, They split an atom. (This is not to be confused with the accomplishment of Dr. Carl Anderson at the California Institute of Technology, who devised an electromagnet last year which made possible the photographing of an atom’s nucleus while it was being dissipated by the cosmic ray). In revealing the details of what he termed a “discovery of great scientific importance,” Lord Rutherford said the successful investigators of the atom were Drs. J. D. Cockcroft and E. T. S. Walton, both of whom have been working on their problem for several years with special apparatus erected under the supervision of Lord Rutherford himself. Optimistic scientists long have hoped for the split atom

PARIS, May 2 (AP) — The support of the government of Premier Andre Tardieu was shown to have slipped today, as returns from yesterday's election were completed. "I counted on victory, and it is one," said former Premier Edouard Herriot, M. Tardieu’s chief opponent, at Lyons. "It is a strongly marked swing to the left." With returns from the 615 districts almost completed, the ministry of the interior issued a tabulation today showing that candidates in 244 districts were chosen and candidates in 359 more must go into the run-off election next Sunday, having failed to secure a clear majority. Of the seats which must again be contested, 190 were normally government supporters, 150 normally supporters of the opposition and the rest independent. Premier Tardieu himself was reelected at Belfort by a sound majority as were most of the important members of his cabinet.

BY EUGENE LYONS. (United Press Staff Correspondent) MOSCOW, May 2—Defense of the Soviet Union against its enemies was pledged millions of times today after the great display of military strength and allegiance to the Soviet regime in Red Square here in the first of the May Day celebrations. Today's program consisted chiefly of mass meetings and lectures. Both Sunday and today were legal holidays. The big parade began early Sunday and continued all day. After 35,000 red troops had passed in review before Joseph Stalin, Premier Molotov, Commissar of War Voroshilov, and other leaders at Lenin's tomb, 10 new four-motored bombing planes led 275 war planes over the capital in Russia's greatest display of strength in the air. Hundreds of new tanks and artillery equipment rumbled across Red Square. The parade revealed the progress of mechanization and motorization of the red army. It is an open

Berlin, July 16 (AP)—Two women were killed and two men were seriously injured at Langenselbold last night during a riot between unemployed and police. Numerous others were less seriously hurt. There was a similar clash at Halle, the communist district of Berlin, with numerous injuries. At Nordhorn several were hurt in a yoga demonstration which ended in a fight between Nazis and Communists.

Tokyo, May 2—(4#)—Japanese military forces and Chinese rebels battled over a wide area in Northern and Eastern Manchuria today. A Japanese brigade under Major General Murai fought a 24 hour battle with three thousand rebels near Wukimiho which resulted in a victory for the Japanese. Reports said there were thirty casualties. The Chinese retreated northward. They used machine guns and mortars and took advantage of the heavy forests as screens. A new threat developed at the Unhua end of the Kirin-Tunhua branch of the railway when rebel bands numbering several thousand men, most of them followers of General Wang Teh-Lin, threatened to surround the city. Japanese military reports also said a three hour battle took place northwest of Tungliao yesterday in which several hundred Chinese rebels were killed. The Japanese losses were six dead and sixteen wounded, the report said.

1932-08-29.text: MANCHESTER, Eng., Aug. 20—The gloomy prediction that more than 10,000,000 people within 3 miles of Manchester will see their spending power cut in half if the textile strike just called becomes general, was before the British public today. It was made by Deputy Mayor George Titt, of Manchester, who initiated conferences last week in a vain effort to circumvent a walkout over wages and working conditions. The failure of these meetings resulted Saturday in orders for 200,000 weavers not to return to work today. This strike order on the part of the trade union was the initial

NEW YORK, Aug. 29.—(UP)—Commodity markets in America and abroad surged upward today in a world-wide scramble to buy up raw materials of all kinds. American and British markets were the scenes of lively trading to the accompaniment of reports that a complete liquidation of war debts and reparations were being worked out by bankers of both countries in a program calling for a general rise in the international price of raw goods. “Bull Fever” Spreads. “Bull fever” spread to South America and the Far East. In Yokohama and Kobe, Japan, the silk markets had to be closed because of a buyers’ panic that resulted from a wild rush to accumulate the commodity in belief that a world-wide recovery in trade was imminent. American markets were marked by an unprecedented bull rampage in the New York cotton exchange, where prices shot up almost $2 a bale. Waves of buying orders were inspired (Continued o

MANCHESTER, England, Aug 29.—Thousands of cotton workers in Lancashire's vast textile industry went on strike today in what may develop into the greatest industrial disruption since the World War. Union leaders sent pickets to the mills early this morning. It was estimated that more than 700 plants were picketed by mid-morning. The strikers were, for the most part, weavers in the cotton mills and 200,000 spinners were preparing to ballot on the question of a walkout soon. It is considered likely they will join in the strike. Many mills were not operating today, due to lack of working forces.

NEW YORK, Aug. 29. (U?)—Britain’s return to the gold standard, complete war debt and reparations liquidation through a $3,500,000,000 loan, and worldwide commodity price boosts were believed discussed over the week-end by American bankers and Montague Norman, whose visits always have preceded world-shaking financial adjustments. The governor of the Bank of England, who arrived in this country recently under the name of “Professor Clarence Skinner” to spend a vacation in Maine when there are many vacation spots nearer England, attended a conference at the Federal Reserve Bank here Saturday. And the next day he conferred with other New York financiers, including George L. Harrison, governor of the Federal Reserve, who called the Saturday conference. Within the past few days Norman (Continued on page 5, column 1)

CONWAY, N. H., Aug. 29— Telescopes and long range cameras already trained aloft, New England awaited the awe-inspiring eclipse of Wednesday. This is the area of complete totality. Elsewhere the eclipse will be but partial. Here, however, the show of the moon blots out the glaring sun. And from the world—not alone the United States and Canada, but distant lands of Europe—hundreds of scientists are gathered here. Although astronomers predominate among the hundreds of scientists now waiting in New England, there are also chemists, meteorologists, physicists, zoologists and alienists, all prepared to study the phenomena in the light of their own problems. All of the more than 25 major expeditions encamped in the Conway-Fryeburg area, center of the eclipse studies, were well-established today. The astronomers marked time awaiting 3:30 P. M. EST Wednesday, when for about 99 seconds they expect

LONDON, Aug. 29.—(I.N.S.)—Only the meagerest of hope was held out today for the safety of Clyde A. Lee and John Bochkon, young American flyers, unreported since their take-off Thursday morning on a transatlantic flight from Harbor Grace, Newfoundland, to Oslo, Norway. As the fifth day rolled by with word still lacking the possibility of their having landed on remote soil without means of communication dwindled. Each passing hour also lessened their chances of remaining afloat if they had been forced down on the ocean.

NEW YORK, Aug. 27.—(P)— One of nature's rarities, a “magnetic storm,” is predicted for the total eclipse in New England next week, but it won't interfere a bit with seeing. The prediction is an example of a new kind of scientific forecasting, possibly the first time when advance notice of a magnetic storm has been important to a large number of persons. Magnetic storms are electrical disturbances coming from the sun. Scientists think they are caused both by the invisible ultra-violet rays and by slower moving hypothetical “electrical particles” shot out from the sun. The forecast for the eclipse is made by A. M. Skellett of the Bell Telephone Laboratories, New York. It is important information for the scientists who will use the long twilight of the eclipse, and its momentary “night,” to learn more about the reasons for radio fading and differences between day and night transmission. ST. JOHNS, New Brunswick, Aug. 28 (AP)—Capt. James A. Mollison completed the initial stage of his return flight from New York to London today, landing in a field 18 miles from here at 3:30 P. M. (CST). He brought the tiny airplane "Heart’s Content" down to a safe landing near Nerpis when fog prevented him from making a scheduled arrival at St. John airport. Leaving Roosevelt Field, New York, at 9:50 A. M. (CST), he flew the first stretch of 511 miles and five hours and 40 minutes. After taking care of his plane Captain Mollison went to a nearby house and telephoned the municipal airport here. He intended to motor to this city to spend the night, and leave tomorrow morning for Harter Grace, whence he will take off on the water jump.

1932-05-24.text: LONDON, MAY 23. (AP).—Mrs. Amelia Earhart Putnam, the first woman to fly the Atlantic solo, demonstrated today that she is exactly as efficient at the feminine business of shopping as she is at the hardier pursuit of flying an airplane. After a light breakfast at the American embassy, where she is staying, she sped off to the West End shopping center before 9 o'clock. She completed her purchases in time to attend a luncheon given by the Institute of Journalists—and speed had no check on her efficiency. On all sides she received congratulations on the excellent taste displayed in her emergency apparel—emergency because when she landed in Ireland all she had with her were her flying clothes on her back. Mrs. Putnam wore a blue voile dress with a white neck piece. Ambassador Andrew W. Mellon was present at the luncheon, as was Sir John Simon, British Foreign Secretary. The large assemblage

SOUTHAMPTON, England, May 23,—The German flying boat DO-X narrowly escaped disaster on arriving here this evening after an uneventful flight of 630 miles from Vigo, Spain, in six and a half hours. The giant plane alighted perfectly on Southampton waters and was taken in tow by the Royal Air Force ship Pinnacle, which was to bring her to her moorings. When she was in a position to be moored and the tow-rope had been cast off, one of her navigators leaning over the bows to grasp the moorings fell into the water. With all engines shut off the big ship was helpless in the grip of a fast flowing tide and was being carried toward the Calshot air station jetty. The DO-X mechanics, standing on the wings, strove frantically to get some of her 12 engines working. First one, then another, stuttered and failed. Finally, when only a few feet lay between the DO-X and shipwreck, (Continued on Page 2, C

(By The Associated Press) LONDON, May 23. — Amelia Earhart Putnam shopped today for clothes to augment her flying togs, was toasted by British journalists and gained one of the points of her solo flight across the Atlantic—an admission by a man that women could do something valuable. The slim blonde flier, whose tousled hair and frank smile have captured the fancy of the British public, said feminine resentment at all the “catty things” men say about women drivers and women pilots was the driving urge behind her ocean flight. She Shows 'Em “Where there's a traffic jam on Fifth Avenue, men always comment, ‘Oh, it’s a woman driving,’” she explained. “I have gone up with a mechanic who doesn’t know the controls from the altimeter and when I've come down I have heard people say he probably did most of the flying. “So I determined to show them. And outside of demonstrating that a woman can fl

London, May 24 (AP)—Four persons, three of them children, were known to be dead today as a result of floods which have raised havoc in the English midlands following cloudbursts over the weekend. Ten were injured in an explosion at Derby believed to have been caused by flood waters leaking into a gas main. Reports from the huge flood area were sketchy as communications became increasingly difficult. Telephone and telegraph lines have been damaged seriously by the raging waters which spread over hundreds of square miles, causing damage estimated at nearly $2,000,000. A fund was opened last night to relieve the distress of thousands of homeless persons. Burton, famous Staffordshire brewing town, was reported disappearing under the advancing waters. Roads in the vicinity of Leicester, Nottingham, Worcester and Bedford were covered by four to five feet of water. Central Oxfordshire is a vast

(United Press Staff Correspondent.) LONDON, May 23 — Amelia Earhart Putnam, first woman to fly the Atlantic alone, and wearing clothing borrowed from an Irishwoman at Londonderry, and from members of Ambassador Andrew Mellon's official household, today went on a shopping trip here before her trip to Rome. Miss Earhart went shopping with Mrs. David K. E. Bruce, daughter of Ambassador Mellon, soon after breakfast, and greatly refreshed after a good night's sleep. She was taken to a large Anglo-American department store and made numerous purchases to substitute for her borrowed clothing. Miss Earhart said her plans would depend on answers to several cables she sent to the United States this morning. She was expected to be the luncheon guest with Ambassador Mellon, of the British Institute of Journalists, and to receive correspondents this afternoon. The Rome flight will take her to the cong

LONDON (WP)—Amelia Earhart Tuesday achieved an honor many American girls have sought, a conference with the Prince of Wales. The American woman, who flew across the Atlantic in record time last week, was received at the Prince's residence, St. James Palace, and for 30 minutes discussed her flight with the British heir. The Prince of Wales received Miss Earhart in his own study, where he received Col. Charles A. Lindbergh and other distinguished visitors. Miss Earhart told the press she probably would not go to Rome, as she had planned, but would at least go to Paris on Friday or Saturday.

LAKE GARDA, Italy, (UP).— Kaye Don, British racing driver, Tuesday unofficially broke the world’s motorboat speed record held by Gar Wood of Detroit by sending his Miss England III over Lake Garda at a speed of 131.78 miles an hour. The official record held by Wood is 111.712 established at Miami Beach, Fla., in February. The unofficial trial completed, Don prepared to make an official attempt at the record later in the day.

LONDON, May 4 (UP) — Fierce gunfiring on the north side of the Sungari river opposite Harbin, Manchuria, was reported in Exchange Telegraph dispatches today. Steamers were forced to return to Harbin. Artillery, tanks and airplanes were sent by the Japanese against the Chinese insurgents. Train service to the west was suspended. The tracks have been torn up.

1932-03-20.text: Shanghai, March 18—(®)—Japanese and Chinese authorities met in a new peace conference today at the British consulate and participants in the parleys said progress was being made. Chinese official quarters at Nanking were reported hopeful over the situation. The ministers of the United States, Great Britain and France and the Italian charge d’affaires attended the conference. Chinese officials at Nanking indicated the present parleys, preceded by Japanese troop withdrawals, would be followed by a broader round table conference later, with the world powers sitting in to iron out the details of a permanent solution. Summing up the movements of troops, Japanese headquarters said 55,000 troops arrived here during the time since the hostilities began and that about 20,000 were now being withdrawn, Neutral observers said, however, that although the Japanese forces are being slightly reduced by

TOKIO, March 19 acro— Japan will oppose any effort of the United States to invoke the Nine Power Treaty in Manchuria, a government spokesman said today. Simultaneously the foreign office denied Chinese charges that Japan had formed the new state. The government views the New Manchu regime sympathetically, the spokesman said, and pressure of public opinion may force recognition. Secretary of State Stimson had announced that the United States would not recognize territorial or economic gains by aggression and the announcement of policy was based on certain terms of the Nine Power Treaty. Not Aggressive Japan's announced intention to oppose invocation of the treaty, it was believed, would be based on the argument that its activities in Manchuria were not aggressive but defensive. 'Timmons, Ont., Mar. 19.—(UP)— Seven men, feared lost in a cabin monoplane between here and Toronto, were found alive today near their damaged plane. They suffered slight injuries, first advices said. The plane was piloted by Ernest Levine. Six prominent citizens of Timmins, including a priest, were his passengers. The group set out from Toronto Wednesday after witnessing a hockey game and were few heard from until today.

TIMMINS, Ont., Mar. 19 (AP)-- A cabin airplane missing with seven persons since last Wednesday was found today, forced down on a small lake south of Night Hawk Lake, 30 miles east of Timmins. None of the seven occupants of the plane was hurt. The plane, carrying a pilot and six passengers, took off from Oshawa Wednesday morning for Timmins, a distance of slightly more than 200 miles, and had been unreported since Wednesday afternoon, when a ship was seen flying over Liskeard. Anxiety over its safety led to the inauguration of an air search this morning when planes took off from North Bay.

FORT SMITH, Mackenzie, Mar, 19. UP—Two rock cairns in the haunted Thelon river hills today started the Royal Canadian Mounted Police on another manhunt—one that may take three years and lead them to the Arctic ocean’s border. The cairns mark the bodies of Edward Olson and Emanuel H. Bobe, slain about Dec. 5, 1930, as they slept in their solitary tent on Thelon river, northeast of Great Slave lake, in a country called by the Indians bewitched. For the murder police officers seek Tekaluk, an Eskimo last seen a year ago about to start a long journey to the Arctic coast, 300 miles northward. Graphic Picture Discovery of the slayings gave a graphic picture of the sub-Arctic wilderness where the newest drama of the “mounties” is being played. 'Amsterdam, Netherlands, Mar. 19 (P).—A Dutch trawler pounding along the north Atlantic stopped long enough to fish a package out of the sea and today when it was turned over to the U.S. consulate, it was found to contain papers belonging to Parker D. Cramer, an American flyer lost last August in an attempt to fly across the ocean. Cramer's flying license was among them, a permit for his flight across the Atlantic, a description of his ship and a letter from his mother. The trawler picked them up just east of the Faroe Islands. Cramer started from Detroit secretly and the first thing the world knew about his flight was last August when he landed in Greenland and it was disclosed he was trying to map a route north of the Great Circle between the United States and Europe. On August 7 he was forced down off the Faroe Islands, but flew back and took off again for Bergen and Copenhagen the ne

Berlin, March 19 The certain withdrawal of the steel helmeted, Theodore Duesterberg, from the presidential runoff election April 10, was indicated Saturday night when the nationalist party announced it would not participate in the second contest for the presidency. An official party statement indicated its support would be thrown to Adolf Hitler, the Nazi leader, although it was conceded the reelection of President von Hindenburg was certain. SHANGHAI, Sunday, Mar. 20. (#)—Participants in Sino-Japanese peace negotiations here wound up a long conference late last night without having achieved any definite results, but they appeared optimistic and announced that the parley would be resumed on Monday. Both Japanese and Chinese authorities were present at the meeting in the British consulate and word came from Nanking that officials there were hopeful of establishing a definite armistice within a few days. Nelson T. Johnson, the American minister, said there had been progress on the path to peace. Quo Tai-Chi, China's vice-minister for foreign affairs; Mamoru Shigemitsu, Japan's minister to China; and the ministers of the United States, Great Britain, France, and Italy participated in the conference. Japanese troops continued on the way out of China by transport and headquarters announced that 20,000 of the 55,000 men sent here f

1932-10-27.text: ALBANY, N. Y., Oct. 27 (UP).— Franklin D. Roosevelt today punctuated his national campaign by an interlude devoted to state problems, and then plunged into preparations for his final thrust at the New England states where his supporters are least confident of victory. - Back from an eight-day campaign in the east and south, the democratic presidential candidate announced he would invade Massachusetts over the week-end, to make a major address in Boston on Monday. Proposals to extend the tour as far as Portland, Maine, were being considered. Roosevelt's decision to go into New England was prompted by the desire of his managers to unite any factions of the party, particularly in Massachusetts, still remaining aloof from him because of the wounds opened by the Chicago convention. | Roosevelt was optimistic over his tour of the middle west and south, and if any rumors of party disturbance ov

nea scanners London, Eng., Oct. 27—Thousands of unemployed, carrying red banners and openly flaunting the sickle and hammer of Soviet Russia, marched on Hyde Park today in a desperate demand for government relief. As they marched, headed by banders, banners and red flags, their ranks were augmented by thousands of London's jobless. They were vigilantly escorted by foot and mounted police. All during the morning, Communist workers visited the various starting points of the parade and addressed the demonstrators, but most meetings were without disorder. Soviet banners carried in the ranks urged the marchers to “arise and join the proletariat. Down with petty bureaucracy.”

London, Oct. 26.—()—A movement to have three women and three men plead the cause of the “hunger” marchers before parliament was launched tonight as most of the 2,000 members of the unemployed army camped in London suburbs. Waving red flags, a division of 200 marchers moved into Acton, a London suburb, to the music of a piper. A number of the marchers chased a uniformed soldier and shouted uncomplimentary remarks at him, but he escaped. Pledge of Premier Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald has promised reconsideration of phases of the government’s dole system to which the marchers have objected. They are opposed particularly to the “mean tests,” by which many dole receivers have been stricken from the lists. The tests are to determine if they have any means of subsistence aside from the unemployed benefits.

LONDON, Oct. 27.—(AP)—Wild rioting and attempted looting, seriously taxing the resources of London police, broke out late this afternoon as thousands of hunger marchers and sympathizers surged into Hyde Park for a mass meeting to protest against the reduction in dole. After a series of riots police succeeded later this afternoon in clearing the rear guard of the contingent, which gave way to violent looting. Finally fierce fighting broke out within the gates of Hyde Park, with rioters, completely out of control, tearing up small trees and tipping down iron fences. A heavy police reinforcement eventually succeeded in clearing the area. POOR MARCH ON LONDON. LONDON, Oct. 27.—(AP)—The streets of London resounded with the tramp of marching feet today. Thousands of unemployed marched in military ranks and oblivious to lumbering buses and hooting taxicabs, surged upon Hyde Park for the most in

FOOCHOW, China, Oct. 3.—(4)— American and British missionaries were fleeing toward this city today from a communist army driven into northwest Fukien province by Chinese Nationalist troops. Missionaries of the Congregational church, with headquarters in Boston, and the Northern Methodist missionaries, with headquarters in New York, were reported among the American groups retreating before the outlaw advance. While it was believed there was no danger in this vicinity, it was reported American destroyers now on their way from Shanghai to Mantila may be called in here if necessary. Thousands of Chinese were arriving here from the upper Min river. Reports were received here that American Methodist property at Kenping was occupied by Fukien provincial troops.

NEW YORK, Oct. 27 (4)~-Former Gov. Alfred E. Smith left for New England today to continue his campaign for the Democratic ticket with a speech this afternoon at Providence, R.I., and another this evening at Boston. Before boarding the 10 o'clock train for New England, Smith said that his Providence address would be brief and informal, a speech of greeting in which he would stress the duty of citizens to vote. In the Boston speech, the second major address of his campaigning, he said he would take up the financial aspect of the general situation and would deal with taxation and what he termed Republican neglect to balance the budget. "The Newark speech stands by itself," Smith said of his first major campaign address, in which he spoke of alleged religious bigotry during the 1928 campaign, when he was running for the presidency. Hyde Park; London, Oct. 27, (U.P) — Two hundred police and 6,000 unemployed clashed in a second outbreak at Marble Arch late today soon after police had quelled a riot in which limousines were attacked and windows of homes and business buildings broken. The rioters tore down railings and used stones, sticks and umbrellas in their attack on the police, who retaliated with their batons. London, Oct. 27, U.P — Thousands of unemployed, carrying red banners and openly flaunting the 'sickle and hammer' of Soviet Russia, marched on Hyde Park today in a desperate demand for government assistance. The protests which have been building toward London for weeks from various points in the provinces began marching at noon from their overnight quarters in scattered suburbs.
