1932-06-06.text: LONDON, June 6—Airdromes from London to Warsaw and air officials of several European nations who waited in vain for word of Stanislaus Hausner on his projected New York-Warsaw flight feared he had been lost in the Atlantic. The only possibility was that he might have landed somewhere on the continent where he would be out of communication with the world. His fuel supply would have been exhausted early Sunday. A garage proprietor at Cork, Ireland, over which the great circle route would carry a flier over St. George’s channel, reported he heard the motor of a powerful airplane early Sunday. Officials could find no other residents of the district who reported hearing an airplane. Beacons at airports in Ireland, France, England and Poland were kept lighted throughout Saturday night. Police chiefs throughout Poland were instructed to keep a lookout for Hausner and civil guards in Ireland wer

By Associated Press LONDON, June 6.—Lord Rothermere, publisher of the Daily Mail, telephoned his paper from Berlin today his belief that the Hohenzollerns would again occupy the throne of Germany within eight months. He said the restoration of the monarchy would be peaceful and heartily welcomed by the German people.

London, June 6.--(UP) Thomas, Dominion Secretary, informed the House of Commons today that he and Lord Hailsham, Secretary of State, were going to Dublin to negotiate the Irish situation directly with President De Valera. They agreed after starting the negotiations in Dublin, to come to London to resume the conversations next Friday. Thomas said he had received and accepted an invitation from De Valera for preliminary discussion of the present difficulty between Britain and the Free State, with relation to the Ottawa Imperial Conference. Thomas announced last week that in view of Ireland's action on the oath and land annuities, which he considered a violation of the 1921 treaty, he would not negotiate a new agreement with the Free State at Ottawa.

Sandwich, Eng, June 6—-(P)—A. R. Bradbeer, little known professional from Somerset, today led a fine international field, including three ranking American players, in the first round of qualifying play of the British open golf championship, with a par-shattering 70. Bradbeer finished with the late players to lead Arthur Havers, British winner in 1923 and the last Briton to hold the title, by one stroke. Gene Sarazen, MacDonald Smith and Tommy Armour, defending champion—the three leading American hopes—were right up in the van, Sarazen and Mac Smith with 73 and Armour with a 75. Martell Dallemange, of France, and several native Britons, were just in front of the Americans with scores of 72 while Robert Sweeney, American student at Oxford, scored a surprising 75 to stay with the leaders. London, June 7. (IW$)—Unreported four days after taking off from New York on a solo flight to Warsaw, Stamsiaus Hausner, Polish-American flier, is believed to have met death in a stormy Atlantic. Prevailing bad winds and rain over the ocean, which failed to daunt him despite warnings by experienced pilots, appear to have taken his life. There was a slim possibility that Hausner may have been picked up by a ship without wireless, or may have come down on some remote point on the British Isles. No definite word of Hausner was received after he left New York Friday morning.

London, June 6,—Ambassador Mellon's policy on the issue of trousers versus knee breeches has been refined thus—breeches when he is invited merely as Mr. Mellon, and not as ambassador, and trousers at any function comparable to white house functions. Mr. Mellon wore silk breeches recently at the Derby Day dinner given by the Countess of Ellesmere at Bridgewater House, which was attended by the Queen and the Duchess of York, while the King was host at the traditional Derby Day stag dinner at Buckingham Palace. Ambassador Mellon wore ordinary evening clothes recently when he went to court.

London, June 6.—(4?)—Great Britain has accepted an invitation of the Irish Free State to engage in a discussion of disputes between the two governments. J. H. Thomas, secretary for dominions, informed parliament today that President Eamon de Valera had suggested the discussion as a preliminary to the imperial conference at Ottawa this summer. The principal points at issue are the Irish plan to abolish the oath of allegiance to the British crown and to discontinue payments of the Irish land annuities.

LONDON, June 6.—().--Plans for a world conference on curative economic measures probably will not take definite shape until the debts parley at Lausanne this month is well under way, it was said today on good authority. The British government has not received replies to suggestions regarding such a conference and doubt was expressed whether France, Germany, Belgium and Italy would be willing to commit themselves until after the Lausanne meeting starts.

1932-01-03.text: ABOARD S.S. PRESIDENT TAFT, Jan. 1—Shanghai was a knockout, its Brooklyn gone English. Say, where did they get this Chinese chop suey stuff? I have run the legs off every ricksha motorman in China, and nobody ever heard of it any more than Nevada did Volstead. Another hoax was that a Chinaman's word was as good as his bond. Well, that goes with the chop suey that might have been in the old days, but not since the missionaries and business men came in. Chinese are just as human as anybody now. Yours, WIL.

LONDON, Jan. 2.—(AP)—The world of British journalism mourned today the death of C. P. Scott, editor of the Manchester Guardian, because during 57 years he showed the heights to which journalism based on idealism and humanitarianism can attain. Mr. Scott was 85 years. He took the Guardian, then a little provincial newspaper, and made it into a great editorial medium whose voice reached daily around the world.

COLUMBUS, Jan. 2--(T.R.)--Celebration of the new year’s beginning, an airplane accident and many traffic accidents caused the death of many Ohioans during the last 24 hours. At least 22 persons were killed. When an American Airways Plane crashed in a fog near London, G., four passengers were killed and the pilot was seriously hurt. Three men were killed and two injured when the roof of a cave collapsed at Waterloo, O., where the victims were celebrating the new year. Those killed were Samuel Cooper, 63; Amos Woodim, 36, and Paris Couper, 85. Seven persons were killed in traffic accidents in the vicinity of Cleveland. They were: Miss Eva Wdlemon, 18; Meris Glendon, 22; Arthur Wellman, Curtie Wollard, 40, Edward Ashmorg, 69, Joseph Horsefield, 60, and Fire Lieutenant John McKinney, 58. Three were killed in accidents at Cincinnati. They were: Dr. O.C. Culbertson, Edward Blake, 65, and Thoma

Helsingfors, Finland, () ~ Tabulation of more than one-half the votes in Finland's prohibition referendum showed today that 73 per cent were for repeal, 25.6 per cent for maintenance of the present law and 1.3 per cent for modification to permit light wines and beer. It appeared obvious that the final count would show a substantial majority for repeal and popular interest turned to speculation on what the government would do to carry out the mandate. It was understood the government measure already had been drafted but the course of procedure had not been determined.

Bombay, India—(AP)—Viceroy Lord Willingdon tonight rejected Mahatma Gandhi's terms for settlement of India’s political dispute and grave developments were believed to be imminent. He sent Mahatma Gandhi a telegram warning him that the government would hold him and the congress responsible for any action they may take, and that the government will be ready to meet any action. Gandhi smiled when he read the message.

Paris, Jan. 2:-- (AP) —General Paul Gerald Pau, noted French war commander, died here today, aged 82 years. Since the end of the war, General Pau has devoted himself to looking after wounded veterans. At the time of his death he was president of the French Red Cross. He lost an arm in the war of 1870.

Bombay, India, Sunday, Jan. 3, —Negotiations for peace in India broke down today and the arrest of Mahatma Gandhi was momentarily expected. Viceroy Lord Willingdon rejected the mahatma’s terms for settlement and informed the nationalist leader that he and the All-India National Congress would be held responsible for any action they might take. The government will be ready, the viceroy said in a telegram to Mr. Gandhi, to meet any activity on the part of the Nationalists. The mahatma smiled as he read the message. He expected, he remarked, to be arrested under a law of 1818 which empowered the government to arrest or deport any agitator without trial. The mahatma had told the viceroy he would withhold plunging India into the turmoil of another civil disobedience campaign if the viceroy agreed to an interview with him for the purpose of discussing the recent restrictive ordinances put into

Bombay, India, Jan. 2. —(AP)— Subhas Chandra Bose, former mayor of Calcutta and one of the extremist Nationalist leaders, was arrested today after he had repudiated Mahatma Gandhi's conditional offer to cooperate with the government for the purpose of preventing disorders in India. Mr. Bose was arrested while on a train bound for Calcutta and was taken to a destination not made public. The arrest occurred after he had joined with two other extremists, V. J. Patel, former president of the assembly, and Jamnadas Mehta, president of the Indian Trade Unions, in a statement urging uncompromising battle for complete independence. 1932-12-19.text: LONDON, Dec. 19. — (UP)-- Britain's foremost flying family-- the Mollisons have added two more aviation records to their joint collection. Amy Johnson Mollison landed at Croydon airdrome yesterday from Cape Town to set a new record for the Cape to England flight and a new mark for the round trip. Miss Johnson's time for the return flight was seven days, seven hours and five minutes, compared with the nine and one-half day record held by the Duchess of Bedford and her pilot, Capt. Bernard. Miss Johnson made the round trip in 11 days, 1 hours, and 68 minutes, against the Duchess’ record of 20 days.

WASHINGTON, Dec. 19.—()—Inquiries at the White House and Department of State this afternoon brought the response that there was no information to be given out or reports of an agreement between this country and Great Britain for a joint examination of war debts. Dispatches from London telling of such an agreement were not denied, however. President Hoover was in conference with Secretaries Stimson and Mills at the time, on the war debts topic and the message that he has prepared to send to Congress. None of the three could be reached for questioning as to the report, and lesser officials would only say that they had “no information.”

(International News Service) LONDON, Dec. 19.—Cheers of admirers echoed in the ears of Amy Johnson Mollison today, after she had written another record in her solo flight from Capetown to England. With seven days, seven hours and five minutes of flying time behind her, she put her plane down at Croydon airport, having lopped nearly four days from the previous record for the 5,500 mile air jaunt. The premier aviatrix of Great Britain accomplished this feat despite delays caused by blinding storms. When she landed, her husband, Capt. J. A. Mollison, was the first to greet her. Embracing her, he shouted: “Hello! I’m so proud of you. You've done your stuff!” “Thank you, Jim,” she replied. “I'm pleased for your sake and mine.”

/ London, Dec, 19—(INS)—In a sudden and dramatic move, the Irish republican army turned against President Eamon de Valera of the Irish Free State today, passing a resolution condemning his government, according to a Dublin dispatch to the London Evening News. The action was taken at a mass meeting of the army, roused to fury by the government's arrest and sentencing of members recently convicted of damaging a brewery, the newspaper said. The Irish republican army newspaper, “An Phoblacht,” demanded dismissal of the judge who passed sentence on the convicted army members as well as immediate reprisals, it was stated.

PARIS, Dec. 19 U.P)—The United States embassy was advised today that Dr. Daniel Mahoney of San Francisco had been manhandled by an anti-American mob in Montparnasse, and his front teeth broken off to the roots by fist blows. Dr. Mahoney saw a mob gathered around an Englishman, then heard shouts of “there's another American,” and was felled by a dozen blows. Dr. Mahoney fought with the American army in France and won the French Croix de Guerre for heroism. He was formerly a native of Richmond, Va., and had been engaged in post-graduate study in Paris.

The French love of simplicity and democracy marked M. Paul-Boncour’s accession to power. GENEVA, Switzerland, Dec. 18.—(Instructions from Tokyo setting forth Japan's unyielding opposition to any plan of conciliation which condemns the setting up of the Manchukuo government were conveyed to League of Nations assembly officials today. China's position—that refusal to recognize Manchukuo must precede any attempts by the assembly to conciliate the dispute between China and Japan over the Manchurian trouble—was similarly reaffirmed today. Meanwhile, the drafting sub-committee of the committee of 19, which seeks to arbitrate the dispute, conducted another long session, in which varying views of the apparently irreconcilable conflict were discussed.

PARIS, Dec. 19—Joseph Paul Boncour officially took over at noon today the premiership and foreign ministry from Edouard Herriot, who resigned last Wednesday when the chamber of deputies postponed the December debt payment to the United States. The impression spread in diplomatic circles today that the tendency of the new Paul-Boncour government was to allow the American debt problem to lie dormant for the present, without making any sensational move or trying to secure a reversal of the decision by the chamber. This idea was voiced by the newspaper Paris Midi also, which said a number of ministers believed the problem would be treated by allowing it "to sleep" in the meantime, however, pursuing vigorously semi-official conversations with Washington until the arrival of power of President-elect Roosevelt. BOMBAY, Jan. 10 (P)—Two disturbances, in one of which a crowd estimated at 12,000 persons rescued three prisoners from a police station, were reported Sunday in India's forbidden struggle against British authority. Police charged a crowd at Karachi with staves after a public meeting which had been declared unlawful and 28 persons were injured. The other occurrence was at Spinigar, where an armed crowd attacked the police station and rescued three prisoners charged with attempted arson. They were the only disorders reported and the relative calm that hung over the country was interpreted by observers in two ways.

London, Jan. 11.—(UP)—London doctors worked overtime today combatting an influenza epidemic fatal to 500 while gales and floods caused heavy damage in other parts of the British Isles. Incessant rains and an abnormal lack of sunshine were blamed by health authorities for the influenza wave. Many local hospitals were full of influenza patients. The outbreak was worst in North London where 80 of 350 prisoners and 20 of 80 officials at the Holloway Women’s prison were ill. Work in the prison shops was stopped. Many towns in the Monmouth district were isolated by floods. Four rivers, the Wye, Monnow, Usk, and Trothy, overflowed. The Monmouth electric power station failed. Some streets were under five feet of water. Communications were cut in the region.

Washington, Jan. 11 Reports that Charles Dawes of Chicago announces his intention to resign as Ambassador to Great Britain in order to be free to run for the presidency have caused more surprise than concern at the White House. The rumors of an alleged rift between the President and his Ambassador at the Court of St. James were ridiculed by persons close to Hoover. It was emphasized in a statement on Dawes’ abrupt announcement of his intended resignation that his action had been the subject of discussion frequently since Dawes' return a few days ago from London. Furthermore, friends of both Hoover and Dawes said Dawes and the President have long been close personal friends, and indicated there was no reason to believe anything had occurred to impair that friendship. 1932-02-27.text: Daytona Beach, Fla., Feb. 27—After making new world’s land speed records for five distances, Sir Malcolm Campbell decided today to attempt no further trials this year and said he would ship his 12-cylinder Bluebird racing car back to England immediately. Conditions for further runs were not satisfactory today.

Dock district in the Thames estuary was jammed today with ships from all parts of the world which hoped to pass customs before 5 p.m. Monday, when Great Britain erects her 10 per cent. tariff wall. With the opening of customs houses Tuesday morning a general 10 per cent. tariff will be levied against all imports with only few exceptions, marking the passing of the world’s last great free trade country. 200 Vessels Jam Thames While an estimated 200 cargo vessels stood at docks or in the lower reaches of the Thames awaiting berths, other ships raced against fierce channel gales to reach London, Hull, or other southern British ports to unload before the zero hour Monday. Hong Kong, Mar. 1—(Tuesday)—Foreign lighthouse keepers at Breaker Point lighthouse near Swatow, including an Englishman named Edward, his wife and four children were reported captured today by Chinese communists. The British warship Whitehall at Swatow was reported attempting to locate the victims. The warship Keppel left Hong Kong for the same purpose.

LONDON, Feb. 29,—(4—Ships from all parts of the world crowded the London dock district in the Thames estuary today in a last minute crush to pass the customs before 5 p. m., when the new 10 percent tariff law goes into effect. The number of cargo vessels at the docks or in the lower reaches of the Thames awaiting berths was placed at 200, and other ships fought fierce gales in the channel in an attempt to reach London, Hull or other southern ports before the zero hour. When the customs houses open Tuesday morning and the levy of the new tariff begins it will mark the passing of the world’s last great free trade country.

Shanghai, Feb. 29 (Monday) (Pj)—Attempts to arrange a peace formula were made aboard the British flagship Kent today between Admirals Nomura and Matcuoka, of Japan, and Chinese officials, including Dr. Wellington Koo, former foreign minister, and the chief of staff of the 19th Route Army. The representatives of both sides were invited to the conference by Admiral Kelly, commander of the British fleet in Chinese waters. The result of the conference was not given out.

GENEVA, Switzerland, Feb. 29 (A. P.)—Japan’s representative on the League of Nations council tonight provisionally accepted a proposal for a conference at Shanghai to restore peace between Japan and China. This conference would bring together not only the two belligerents but also the United States, Great Britain and the other neutral powers directly concerned. Sir John Simon, the British foreign secretary, said he had been authorized to pledge the full support of the United States to this concerted move for peace. The plan calls for an immediate end of the armed conflict in the Shanghai area and the simultaneous withdrawal of both the Chinese and Japanese armies.

PARIS, Feb. 28.— (') —Former King Alfonso XIII and his uncle Alfonso Carlos, traditionalist pretender to the Spanish throne, have issued a call to the Spanish people to overthrow the new republic in Spain, a member of Prince Alfonso Carlos’ entourage said tonight. In the manifestos the former king accepted his uncle as head of the family and proposed restoration of the monarchy as a form of provisional government, which would collaborate with legislative chambers representative of the people, (Continued on Page 2. Col. 3.)

Paris—(A)—Premier Herriot said Wednesday he will make no decision regarding the French policy on the money owed the United States until after he talked Thursday with Prime Minister MacDonald of Great Britain. Mr. MacDonald was in town today, but the two premiers will await the arrival of Neville Chamberlain, British chancellor of the exchequer who is due tonight, before undertaking discussion of the situation. M. Herriot quoted Mr. MacDonald as having said the purpose of this Franco-British parley is first to clarify the attitude of France toward England and toward the United States; second, to discuss the debt which France owes England, and third, to talk over the Lausanne accord.

LONDON. UP. Britain and France will talk over the war debt problem Wednesday in conversations in Paris which some members of the British parliament declare may result in the reassembling of the Lausanne conference with a view of resurrecting reparations payments by Germany. The Paris meeting was brought about by the refusal of the United States to extend the debt moratorium over the payments due this month. The British will be represented by Prime Minister MacDonald, who hurried to Paris from Geneva, and by Chancellor of the Exchequer Neville Chamberlain, Premier Herriot will be the chief French official taking part. When plans for the meeting were announced here it was said authoritatively that no attempt was being made to consolidate a European front against the United States. PARIS, Dec. 7—(UP)— The French government reached a crisis today in its efforts to avoid payment of the December $20,000,000 war debt installment to the United States with the knowledge that Italy and Great Britain are ready to pay. Premier Edouard Herriot told the United Press "no definite decision" had been taken after a meeting of the cabinet and the council of ministers. "After an exchange of views with Prime Minister MacDonald and Chancellor of the Exchequer Chamberlain of Great Britain I shall advise the committees of finance and foreign affairs of the chamber of the status of affairs and call a cabinet meeting to decide the government's attitude which will be announced in parliament Friday afternoon," the premier said. MacDonald arrived from Geneva today and Chamberlain was due from London tonight.

PARIS (#) — The higher statesmen of France and Great Britain arrived from Geneva today to discuss war debts due in the United States next week, while parliamentary gossip ranged around the idea of consigning the French debt money to the Bank of France. Some lobby commentators said the cabinet might consider immediately a plan to put the $20,000,000 interest due Dec. 15 in the bank for international settlements. Statesmen who tackled the problem were Prime Minister MacDonald and Chancellor of the Exchequer Neville Chamberlain, of Great Britain, and Premier Herriot and Finance Minister Germain - Martin, of France. As the French leader left the station, he was heard to remark on the “great fidelity” on the part of the British delegation and their “irreproachable loyalty.” There was no immediate explanation. Meanwhile, the French cabinet prepared to discuss debts. It was announced the premie

London —P— Compton MacKenzie, the noted British novelist, was formally committed for trial Wednesday on a charge of violating the dreaded “official secrets act.” The action was taken in police court and the trial was scheduled at Old Bailey in January after the prosecution had alleged MacKenzie had “unlawfully communicated” information gained in the government service. MacKenzie was attached to the British intelligence service in southeastern Europe during the war. The novelist recently published a book “Greek Memories,” dealing among other things with his experiences in the intelligence service. The volume was withdrawn from circulation on the very day of issue and prosecution followed. The author refrained from submitting any testimony in his own behalf, but sought to justify the writing of the suppressed book in a statement to the court. “My object,” declared MacKenzie, “was not finan

RATHENOW, Germany, Dec. 7. Ten workers were known to be dead and a number were buried under debris in an explosion at the L G. Farbin artificial silk works at Premnits today. A 400-pound hydrogen container blew up while workmen were putting finishing touches on an addition to the plant. The fate of those inside the crumbled walls was not known, although ten are known to have been injured. The annex was wrecked, so terrible was the blast. Masons and locksmiths were putting the building in shape, mechanics having just completed installing the machinery.

N. Lancaster, British aviator. "Did you at any time after the shooting tell Mrs. Clarke you thought sometimes that you killed Haden?" State’s Attorney N. Vernon Hawthorne asked Lancaster. "I did not. I never told her any such thing," Lancaster shouted. The flier was called for further cross-examination on the eleventh day of his trial. Lancaster is charged with slaying Clarke April 21 as jealous retribution because Clarke, a young author who was writing Mrs. J. M. Lancaster, British airman charged with murdering Haden Clarke, his rival for the love of Mrs. Jessie M. Keith-Miller, Australian aviatrix. Final arguments began at 11:37 a. m., E. S. T. MIAMI, Fla. COURTROOM, MIAMI, Fla. Aug. 13.—(UP)—Capt. William N. Lancaster, British airman, addressed the jury today and placed in the records several changes in his testimony in his trial on a charge of first degree murder in the fatal shooting of Haden Clarke. He added to his story of the "suicide notes" he admitted forging with Clarke's name with the statement that he had admitted to copying Clarke's signature from a letter he received from the young journalist who supplanted him in the affections of Mrs. Jessie M. Keith-Miller, his former lover and flying partner. He stated he had not thought of having done this until after he left the stand following his last testimony, adding that he understood from Judge Atkinson that he was permitted to correct his statement. Venice, Italy, Aug. 13, —(P)— Mrs. Cecile Kraus, an attractive young widow spending the season at the Lido, nearly monopolized the attention of the Prince of Wales at a dance last night, and swam with him and Prince George this morning before they left by airplane for Corfu to review the British naval squadron. The princes arrived yesterday and met Mrs. Kraus at the dance, where she was with a party at an adjacent table. The Prince of Wales danced almost the whole evening with her and then invited her to swim this morning. Mrs. Kraus, described as well-to-do, lives at Turin. She is understood to be partly of Hungarian ancestry. A dispatch from Corfu said the two British princes arrived there late this afternoon to inspect Great Britain's Mediterranean fleet.

NEW YORK, Aug. 18 (P.— Thomas W. Dunk, Jacksonville, Fla., banker, sailed for Italy with Mrs. Dunk today, complaining that he wished people would stop asking him if his family originated the custom of dunking. “Our family came to England with William the Conqueror,” he said, “and they were Dunks then as they are Dunks now. One of my ancestors was the Earl of Sandwich and on that side of the family we are responsible for the sandwich, but upon no side have we sponsored the dipping of bread into soup and gravy.”

LONDON (UP)—Six world powers have begun a secret race for supremacy in the stratosphere—that freezing region ten miles above the earth where airplanes can attain the speed of bullets. The next war, it has been said, will be fought in the air. The latest scientific discoveries about the stratosphere, which only one man so far has pierced, now make that prediction almost doubly so. Germany, France, United States, Russia, and Belgium are the nations bent on being the first to conquer this new frontier, aided by secret subsidies from their governments. France Builds Craft. France already has finished two planes capable of piercing the stratosphere. With hermetically-sealed cabins to keep their pilots from freezing or dying from lack of oxygen, they are now being tested under the eye of the air ministry. Chatham, Ont., Aug. 13—(AP)—Roy A. Graham, 45, secretary-treasurer of the Graham-Paige Motor Company of Detroit, drowned today in McGregor's Creek. Police said witnesses told them Mr. Graham had returned to his hotel after attending a church service. He remained there only a few minutes before he ran and jumped into the creek. The body was recovered 20 minutes later.

Berlin, Aug. 13. (AP)—President Von Hindenburg talked for 15 minutes this afternoon with Adolf Hitler, head of the national socialist party, and announced after the conference that the present cabinet under Chancellor Franz Von Papen will remain in office. Hitler reiterated his demand that on the strength of his party’s power in the Reichstag he be made chancellor of Germany. The president refused “for moral, reasons and for the sake of the Fatherland.” Not to One Party. With great dignity he added that this conscience would not permit him to entrust to one party the sole responsibility for the entire German people. He entreated Hitler to be content with a cabinet office, but not that of chancellor. The Nazi chieftain refused. He asserted nothing but the chancellorship would satisfy him and that he would not share responsibility with others. He straightened his shoulders, clicked his hee

1932-10-29.text: Albany, N.Y., Oct. 28. Alfred E. Smith and Governor Roosevelt chatted tonight by telephone about the "New England situation," a short time after Smith arrived here declaring "everything's all right over there now" for the Roosevelt-Garner ticket. Roosevelt was preparing to follow the trail that Smith had blazed for him, and with his advisors was working on the speech he will deliver Monday night in Boston—the same city in which Smith had told shouting thousands that they should give their "unqualified, full and complete support" to the ticket headed by his old political ally. Smith had found the trail one of cheering crowds, and he spent much of the afternoon on an observation platform renewing his appeal for a "full" Democratic victory November 8. At Worcester he spoke to a crowd estimated by police at 5,000, and at Springfield, 20,000 to 30,000. Smith's advisors on the train were unite

LONDON, Oct. 28. (AP)—Serious as was yesterday’s riots of thousands of unemployed in Hyde Park, the authorities disclosed today it might have been worse. Sir John Gilmour, home secretary, informed the house of commons that when the police stopped a motor truck accompanying the advancing columns of idle at Hammersmith yesterday they discovered 154 nail-studded ash clubs, and burlap bags filled with heavy chunks of concrete and iron bolts. “I saw those clubs myself,” he said, “and I ask you to believe they were there by deliberate intent. In another truck police found more clubs of various kinds.” In addition to this, an evening newspaper said it had learned the searchers discovered broken glass and lengths of steel wire attached at either end to upright standards, an instrument invaluable in tripping charging police. Men arrested in yesterday’s disturbance were arraigned today. The magist

PARIS, Oct. 29.—(Saturday)—The chamber of deputies early today gave Premier Edouard Herriot a mandate to present at the Geneva disarmament conference a plan which calls for the abolition of all professional armies of Europe—such as the German reichswehr—in favor of a short-term conscriptive system. "The premier had informed the chamber he must have its confidence before he went to Geneva. He got it by the overwhelming vote of 430 to 20. This action probably means that the new French scheme, details of which were officially made public by the premier for the first time, will be submitted in committee at Geneva Nov. 3. Just before the vote was taken at the conclusion of a chamber session which lasted until about 1 a.m., M. Herriot said he had taken note of Secretary of State Stimson's interpretation of the Briand-Kellogg pact—an interpretation he said meant that neutrality no longer is pos

Washington, Oct. 17.—(P)— President Hoover will deliver an address at 8:30 p. m., Saturday in the Olympia arena in Detroit. He plans to leave here Friday, to allow for a series of rear platform appearances along the route to the Michigan city.

Double Plays Yankee Stadium, New York —(AP)—The Yankees gained a commanding lead of two victories to none as young Lefty Gomez shaded Lon Warneke of the Cubs to win the second game of the World Series, 5 to 2, Thursday before a crowd estimated at more than 59,000. Lou Gehrig starred at bat for the Yanks, hammering out a single on each of his first three times at bat. Dickey ripped off two hits. Stephenson and Grimm contributed two hits each in the Cubs’ vain attempt to overcome the lead of the New Yorkers. The Cubs sparkled in the field, pulling off a series of double plays besides playing errorless ball throughout. Herman, at second, handled six chances without a slip. The teams return to Chicago Friday for the third clash of the big series at Wrigley Field on Saturday.

Beverly Hills, Calif., Sept. 29.— It was good yesterday to hear our old friend De Wolfe Hopper recite his epic, “Casey at the Bat.” It was good to hear Graham McNamee who has remained preeminent as an announcer during all these years. Ted Husing was good as usual. The old radio pays for itself every fall during the World Series. We listen to ads, crooners, and politicians all year just to hear, “the count is three and two on Babe Ruth and the pitcher is winding up.” That's America’s greatest suspense, Babe is the only man in the world that was never “tuned out on” when he stepped up to that old home plate microphone. P. S.—Gandhi is eating again; democrats still fasting. (Copyright 1932, McNaught Syndicate, Inc.)

HUTCHINSON, Kans., Oct. 09. (MS) A suit for divorce was filed today by Mrs. Jowett Shouse, wife of the former chairman of the Democratic National Committee. The man is charged with abandonment, lawyers said, and a settlement already had been made and the suit will not be contested.

New York, Oct. 29—A solar plexus blow to a far-flung rum-runners’ ring was the way federal agents described a raid on a hidden radio station as they arraigned seven prisoners today on a charge of breaking radio laws. Two months of investigation culminated last night in a surprise raid on a Coney Island house. In the walls of the place the agents said they found the most powerful unlicensed broadcasting outfit uncovered in years. In the house and in another building near Manhattan Beach, the agents seized the seven men, among them George McDonald, described as an unlicensed radio operator. For more than a year, the agents charged, the station had been directing rum row operations, sending messages to liquor-laden vessels off the Coney Island, Long Island and New Jersey coasts. They said it had guided the smuggling of about $7,000,000 worth of liquor in a year.

1932-08-13.text: London, Aug. 13 (P)— British newspapers criticized President Hoover’s acceptance speech sharply today, especially that part of it referring to war debts and tariffs. Most of them added that the speech seemed “primarily intended to influence votes,” and said “the references to the debts and tariffs showed a determination to ignore the main causes of the depression.” “He was careful, however,” it added, “not to close the door to future negotiations.” The Liberal News-Chronicle, which sponsors free trade, said the speech was intended to encourage the British delegation at Ottawa to keep the door open to possible arrangements with America and also to enable the President to open the door of debt revision. After praising the “admirable record” of the President's foreign policy, the Telegraph rapped smartly at the references to war debts. “It is largely owing to the existence of the debt oblig

MIAMI (4)—Capt. W. N. Lancaster’s attorney called three physicians to court today to support the British airman’s denial that he murdered Haden Clarke, youthful writer. The skull of Clarke, who died of a bullet wound in the home of Mrs. Jessie M. Keith-Miller, Australian flier, already occupied a gruesome niche among the exhibits. It was handed around to the jurors yesterday as Albert H. Hamilton of Auburn, N. Y., defense ballistics expert, demonstrated his contention that the bullet hole in it must have been inflicted by Clarke himself. The defense maintains Clarke was an honor suicide—that he killed himself because he could never marry Mrs. Keith-Miller, whose affections he had won away from Lancaster.

COURT ROOM, Miami, Fla. Aug, 13—Captain William N. Lancaster, British aviator, today told the jury hearing his trial on charges of murdering Haden Clarke how he practiced copying the signature of Clarke so that he could sign his name to suicide notes. The slow speaking Briton changed the story he had previously told about the notes. He related how he had practiced copying Clarke's signature from a letter the young journalist wrote him while supplanting him in the affections of Mrs. Jessie M. Keith-Miller, the aviatrix sweetheart of both. In connection with the jury's visit yesterday to the scene of the tragedy in Mrs. Keith-Miller’s home, Lancaster said: “I was at the Keith-Miller home yesterday and want to state that the bed in which Haden Clarke slept was pulled out farther from the east wall than it was the night of the tragedy.”

BORLIN, Aug. 12. — Adolf Hitler, whose importance in the German political drama is constantly increasing, left his vacation retreat in the Bavarian Alps today to talk with Chancellor Von Papen tomorrow morning. After that meeting he probably will see President Von Hindenburg, and on the outcome of that conference depends Hitler's immediate future.

| WARSAW, Poland (#) — Police, after a night spent in seeking a man they believed kidnapped 45-year-old Patricia McMillin, daughter of United States Consul Stewart E. McMillin, of Lawrence, Kan., said today they believed the child had merely been lost and found. - She disappeared yesterday in a public park where she had gone with a nursemaid to play. Found a few hours later in a shop, she said she had been taken from the park by a man.

| Press} | BERLIN. (AP) —— Adolf Hitler’s brown shirted storm troops are massing and drilling 20,000 strong in Berlin, while their leader awaits a decision on his demand that he be given the nation’s second highest office, the chancellorship. | They have been reported mobilizing as a threat to help their colorful leader gain the power he has sought. There have been conflicting reports on the truth of the reports, I went out into the outskirts of Berlin, the small towns nearby, into corner saloons, into side streets, into some of the larger towns within marching distance of the capital to learn what was the truth. I have seen the brown shirts gathering. I have seen them drilling. They certainly are preparing for action! What action that may be, I do not know. The brown shirts constitute an army of wartime proportions, 500,000 strong in Germany. The most rigorous discipline is maintained.

(By the Associated Press) Ottawa, Ont., Aug. 13—America, observing the work of the Imperial Conference, interpreted a final report of the monetary committee today as a definite bid for continuation of currency on a gold basis and for leniency by the United States in settlement of war debts. The report was prepared for the plenary session expected to end the conference next Thursday. "The conference," the report said, "recognizes the ultimate aim of a monetary policy should be the restoration of a satisfactory national standard." It added that trying to achieve low interest rates and abundance of short-term money should not be predicated on "inflationary creation of additional means of payment to finance public expenditures." WARSAW, Poland, Aug. 12 (AP)-- Patricia McMillin, five-year-old daughter of United States Consul Stewart E. McMillin, was kidnapped from a public park here today and several hours later was found in a shop in a distant part of Warsaw. She tearfully told her parents she had been taken from the park by a man she did not know. "The girl apparently was unharmed. Police were searching for her abductor."

1932-07-06.text: LONDON (U.P)—Mrs. Elvira Dolores Barney, young society beauty, was acquitted by a jury in Old Bailey Wednesday of murdering her lover, Michael Scott Stephen. The jury, deciding one of the most spectacular criminal trials in recent British history, was out one hour and 53 minutes. Its verdict, while acquitting Mrs. Barney of the murder, formally indicted her on another charge, that of attempting to kill Stephen during an earlier quarrel on May 19. When no evidence was offered, however, Justice Humphreys instructed the jury to return a verdict of not guilty on the second charge also.

London, July 5. (®)—Mrs. Elvira Dolores Barney, lovely young society woman, declared in cool, calm tones on the witness stand today that she had been the mistress of Thomas William Scott Stephen, whom she is accused of having murdered, and that for almost two years she supported him. Questioned by her attorney, Sir Patrick Hastings, one of Britain’s eminent trial lawyers, she recounted all details—including some sordid ones—of her love for Stephen. She had been anxious, she said, to keep knowledge of her mode of life from her parents, Sir John and Lady Mullens. They were present in the Old Bailey courtroom as she testified. The 26-year-old defendant retained her composure on the stand until her attorney asked her about the events of the night of May 31, when she gave a smart cocktail party in her flat in which Stephen was found shot to death a few hours later. Tears choked her as she tes

| By Associated Press | LONDON—Great Britain today made good its threat to retaliate against the refusal of the Irish Free State to make further land annuity payments. | A 100 per cent tariff on Free State goods was authorized by the House of Commons by an overwhelming vote.

LAUSANNE, Switzerland, July — Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald of Great Britain became the virtual arbitrator of the debts and reparations dispute today when France and Germany laid their causes in his hands. For days MacDonald has been working at high pressure to effect a compromise between the two nations. Yesterday he delivered what amounted to an ultimatum by declaring that there would have to be a settlement by Thursday because he was going home that night. The French are sponsors of a plan which would make cancellation of reparations conditional upon revision by the United States of the debts due her from the World War allies. Germany has declined to accept any proposal barring reparations and the allies' debts.

LAUSANNE, Switzerland—France and Germany have practically reached an accord on all points at issue in the reparations conference, an official statement from the British delegation said this evening. Earlier it had been reported that a compromise treaty solved the German “war guilt” controversy by insertion of the phrase: “The treaty of Versailles, insofar as it concerns reparations, is hereby abrogated.”

Berlin, Germany, July 6—(UP)— James Mattern and Bennett Griffin, ‘dashing over land and sea in a spectacular race around the world to beat the Post-Gatty record, landed at Tempelhof airdrome at 5:42 p.m. (10:42 a.m. CST) today, already ahead of the Post-Gatty time. They reached Berlin 31 hours and 41 minutes after leaving New York and 18 hours and 40 minutes after leaving Harbor Grace. The Post-Gatty time to Berlin was 34 hours and 34 minutes. Thus Mattern and Griffin had made up the time they lost while wandering in the fog over Newfoundland yesterday, landing here two hours and 53 minutes ahead of Post-Gatty time. Since leaving New York at 4:01 a.m. (EST) yesterday Mattern and Griffin had covered approximately 4,100 miles including 1,150 from New York to Harbor Grace and 2,950 without a stop from Harbor Grace to Berlin. Sydney, Australia, July 4. () — Captain Hans Bertram, German aviator, and his mechanic, whose name is Clausman, were found alive today after having been missing since May 17. On that day they took off in Bertram’s plane from Kupang island on a flight to Darwin. They did not reach there and were given up for lost when a search revealed no trace of them. Two weeks ago natives turned over to a missionary a handkerchief and a cigarette case with Bertram's initials. They said they had found them about 100 miles north of Wyndham where they also had seen the footprints of two men going south. This spurred the search anew and the abandoned plane was found with a message that the fliers had gone into the bush. It was feared that they had been slain by hostile natives, but the search continued. Meanwhile, a tribe of natives had found the men and supplied them with food before sending for help. The

MOSCOW — An unofficial move to re-open the question of formal recognition by the United States of the Soviet government was under way here Wednesday and there was reason to believe it was being met with favor by Soviet officials. The move was made by Colonel Frederick Pope, New York industrialist, acting alone and in a private capacity. Col. Pope presented to Soviet officials a suggestion that the United States send an unofficial commissioner to Russia as a preliminary to negotiations for the establishment of normal relations between the two countries. He laid the matter before a special meeting of ten high in the Soviet regime, among them V. I. Mezhlauk, vice chairman of the state planning commission; V. V. 1932-08-19.text: PORTMARNOCK, Irish Free State, Aug. 18—Captain J. A. Mollison, who left his bride of three weeks today and took off on a projected round-trip flight to New York, was sighted this afternoon 650 miles off Ireland and going strong. His bride, the former Amy Johnson, herself an eminent flier, watched his ship as it disappeared in the west. “A fine start, anyhow,” she said. “I have perfect faith in him and in that little bus. I think he's wonderful.” A few minutes later she got into a plane and sped away to catch up with him and accompany him on the first hundred miles or so of his journey. Mollison, a 27-year-old Scotsman and veteran of the Royal Air Force who already has made a bit of aviation history with record Australia-London and London-Cape Town flights, hoped to be back on this side within two and a half days. Flying in Tiny Plane. The plane on which he is depending to carry him on th

LONDON, Aug. 19. UP—Amy, aviation record holder and wife of Captain J. A. Mollison was with friends in a west end hotel today when word was brought to her that her husband's plane had been sighted over Halifax. “Isn't it wonderful?” she said, “I knew Jim would do it. I feel much easier now. I know the return journey is not easy, but in comparison with the outward trip it isn't so bad. I don’t know exactly what Jim's plans are. If he has enough fuel he may make for New York non-stop.”

OTTAWA, ONT., Aug. 19.—-(A)— The British imperial economic conference, which began a month ago, determined to lift the world’s greatest commonwealth of nations out of economic distress, is expected to end tomorrow claiming a psychological, if not actual, victory. Today it seemed likely Great Britain’s promise, as the greatest consumer of world exports, to take the lead in an international ban against “dumping” would be proclaimed as the chief success of the parley. A formula to prevent price slashing by Russia or any other country, without specifically naming the Soviet Union, was expected to be announced today or at least at the final plenary session scheduled for Saturday morning. GLASGOW, SCOTLAND, Aug. 19—()—Captain J. A. Mollison’s mother, Mrs. Bullmore, was delighted to hear that he had successfully crossed the north Atlantic by plane. “That's wonderful,” she said, “my heart is content. “I haven't slept a wink since he started. The strain of waiting was terrible but I had every confidence in him.” Captain Mollison was born here in 1905, went to school here and never has been in America before.

Halifax, Nova Scotia, Aug. 19 —(P)— Capt. J. A. Mollison, who already holds speed records for flights from Australia to London and from London to Cape Town, today completed the first westward solo flight across the North Atlantic. At 5:45 a. m., E. S. T., just 24 hours and 10 minutes after he left Portmarnock, Ireland, he was sighted over the airport at Halifax, N. S., approximately 2,663 miles from his starting point. His silver grey sports plane, which is little more than a flying gasoline tank, passed over the airport headed west. Apparently, Mollison had omitted a scheduled refueling stop at Harbor Grace, 650 miles east of here.

London, Aug. 19. ()-Captain Mollison’s safe landing at Pennfield Ridge, N. B., caused delight in London and Ireland which regarded his fast Westward crossing as a new record added to the British air achievements.

LONDON. (UP). Amy Johnson, flier bride of Capt. J. A. Mollison, said she was “terribly thrilled” upon being advised her husband had successfully flown the Atlantic. “That's wonderful,” she said. “I knew Jim would do it, I am terribly thrilled.” GLASGOW. | Pennfield Ridge, N. B., Aug. 19.— | (AP)—Capt. J. A. Mollison, 27-year-old flying Scot, the first man to make a solo flight across the north Atlantic, landed just outside this little village at 10:45 a. m. (C. S. T.) today, too tired to go any farther. For more than thirty hours he had pushed his plane, “The Heart's Content,” stripped down so that it was little more than a flying gasoline tank, across nearly 3,000 miles of ocean through weather that was none too good. He had plenty of fuel and but for his own weariness might have gone on to New York, he said. When he got this far, however, and saw through a break in the clouds a broad meadow below him, he dropped down to a perfect landing. Pennfield Ridge is a village of not more than 300 population. Even telephones are scarce, but Captain Mollison was on a long-distance wire reporting his landing a few minutes after he was down. Farme

1932-12-28.text: NEW YORK (WP) — The first shipment of gold paid by Great Britain on its war debt to the United States arrived here today when the Majestic brought $15,000,006 in gold. The shipment was part of $17,005,000 carried by the liner.

Madison—Gov. Philip F. LaFollette announced today that he will visit Washington and England after his retirement Jan. 2, and will return to Madison later to resume his private law practice. Immediately following the inauguration next Monday of his successor, Governor-elect A. G. Schmedeman, Mr. and Mrs. LaFollette will go to Washington to visit Senator and Mrs. Robert M. LaFollette, Jr., and Mr. and Mrs. Ralph Sucher. Early in January the retiring governor will sail for England where he has accepted invitations to lecture, returning to Madison the following month.

NEW YORK, Dec. 29.—(4)— The steamer Majestic brought to New York Wednesday a $15,000,800 shipment of British gold, representing another installment on England's December 15 debt payment to the United States. The gold was consigned to the Federal Reserve Bank. The same ship also brought from Cherbourg $2,500,000 in French gold, said to represent a private franc cartian.

ATHENS, Dec. 28. — Samuel Insull intends to remain in Greece permanently, he announced today after the Greek appeal court had refused his extradition to the United States on charges of embezzlement growing out of the collapse of his utilities interests. Insull, a free man so long as he remains in Greece, returned to the Petit Palais hotel from the hospital where he had been a patient under police supervision.

PARIS, Dec. 28. (@)——France’s unpaid debt to the United States forged to the front again today as a matter for discussion on the floor of the chamber of deputies. The occasion was the opening of debate, which probably will continue tomorrow, on the proposed French loan to Austria. Speaking privately, deputies already have linked the two problems by criticizing the ethics of such a loan after the refusal to pay the United States. For two weeks—since the historic early morning vote December 14 against the debt payment—the chamber has been silent on the American issue. Premier Joseph Paul-Boncour was believed ready at last to take the initiative in an effort to persuade the chamber to reserve its stand. This was reported in highest political quarters after yesterday’s statement by Secretary of State Stimson that the United States will not enter discussions with nations which defaulted Decem

ATHENS, Greece, Dec. 28 (UP)— Further proceedings cannot be taken in Greece against Samuel Insull on the same charges on which a court ruled yesterday he was extraditable, a legal authority said today. The decision was binding upon Greek executive authorities, barring them from further steps should they be so inclined, it was declared. President Georgopoulos, of the court of appeal, said today there has been no attempt by executive powers to influence the court. It ruled Mr. Insull could not be extradited to the United States on the evidence which was intended to show him guilty of larceny and embezzlement in connection with the collapse of his midwest enterprises. “Even had they tried to influence us,” the court president said, “Greek judges, you know, pay no attention to anybody's pressure.” Believes Him Innocent M. Georgopoulos, who is one of the most distinguished Greek jurists, said

CAPE TOWN, Union of South Africa, Dec. 28.—(4)—Finance Minister Havenga declared in an interview this morning: “We are virtually off the gold standard.” Banks will have to “exchange on a new basis,” he said. Commercial banks were dealing in exchange during the morning at last Saturday's rates but transactions were limited to 50 pounds sterling. The reserve bank, however, was prepared to do business in amounts up to 100 pounds sterling. The government organ Die Vaderland said today: “The union has been forced off the gold standard, we are in the same position as

(By United Press). Paris, Dec. 28.—France will be informed soon that all pending Franco-American negotiations, such as debts and the proposed commercial treaty, are to be deferred until France’s Dec. 15 debt annuity is paid. Walter E. Edge, United States ambassador, will impart the information to Premier Joseph Paul Boncour, on instructions of State Secretary Stimson.

SHANGHAI, Jan. 31 (Sunday) — (AP)—The International Settlement was reported shelled today as Japanese invaders held a flame-wrecked area in their grip. Showing outside neutral superiority in the Shanghai settlement, Japanese gained a great slice within the bow, turning it into a base for operations against the army of China from the native city. Two foreigners were reported beaten by Japanese "Reservists" when they protested against the beating of Chinese. The Japanese movement within the settlement, refuge of Americans and other foreigners, carried them toward United States Marines patrolling the southern banks of Soochow Creek. The Chinese government decided to make a formal declaration of war. Then it fled from Nanking to Honanfu, about 450 miles inland, to establish a new seat of government. This declaration came on the heels of hints from authoritative sources that Japan eventually may withdraw from the league if a second commission of inquiry is sent into the field. As a result of this step another commission of investigation may be appointed. “Not Thinking of War” “There is no question of breaking diplomatic relations with China and Japan is not thinking of war with her neighbor,” the war office said. SHANGHAI, Jan. 31—(Sunday) (AP)—Japanese airplanes renewed their activity over Shanghai this morning, 13 planes flying over the city.

Labor, from section hand to engineer, takes a 10 per cent wage cut today, with the hope it will give work to its jobless and speed the return of better times. The agreement which authorized the nation’s railroads to take $215,000,000 out of the pay envelopes of the workers for one year was signed last night by leaders of both sides. It was a voluntary concession on the part of labor at the request of the rails. Had the workers chosen, they could have forced the carriers to take the reduction demand before a board of arbitration with consequent months of delay. Their rate of pay is protected by contract. In return the workers received certain concessions to a compromise program they proposed, chief among them being the assurance the rails would do as much as conditions would justify to use the wage cut savings toward relieving the distress of 700,000 jobless and 1,600,000 only partly empl

By The Associated Press Washington, Jan. 30.—American warship reinforcements pointed toward China tonight, authorized to go into action if the riotous tumult of death at Shanghai should spread to entrap United States citizens. While orders for preparedness to lift anchor were flashed to Manila, this government and Great Britain protested emphatically against the Japanese occupation that has led to ravishment of Oriental sections in the opulent seaport, President Hoover kept even more closely in touch with the acute situation. Early and late he had by his side officials directly concerned with American policy; but neither Secretary Stimson nor Undersecretary Castle divulged his views. The tensity of the situation was reflected at the capitol, where many of the legislators discussed the potentialities privately. One, (Continued on page two)

Plenty of rumors of war were abroad Saturday in the capital. (By the Associated Press) China has decided to make a formal declaration of war against Japan. In preparation for it the seat of the government was moved for safety today from Nanking to Honanfu, in western Honan province. Meanwhile Japanese invaders crushed the authority of the international administration of the foreign settlement in Shanghai. Japanese military rule was made supreme throughout a great slice of the settlement in which the international council, two members of which are Americans, ceased to exercise the slightest semblance of authority. The Japanese arrested whom they pleased and those held were subject to the decision of the Japanese naval authorities. From the supposedly neutral ground of the settlement the Japanese based their operations to clear out of Shanghai the Chinese troops that have abruptly halted their advance. 1932-02-24.text: Washington, (4) — The Senate naval committee today approved the Hale bill to authorize building the navy up to the limits fixed by the London treaty. The bill, sponsored by Chairman Hale, was approved unanimously. It calls for building the navy up to the maximum allowed by the London treaty, but does not carry any appropriations. The cost of the program would depend upon how many years it was spread over. Hale estimated that if it were completed in ten years, the cost would be $980,000,000, but this includes ships now under construction, modernization of ships and replacements. The chairman will ask for early consideration in the Senate. A similar measure faces final disposition in the House. In a speech last night, Hale said there was a necessity for building the navy up to the limits of the London treaty because of the hostilities between China and Japan. Important as the bill is, it i

Daytona Beach, Fla., Feb. 24.—(A, P.)—Sir Malcolm Campbell, famous British race car driver, today hung up a new world's automobile speed record on the ocean speedway here. The veteran 47-year-old racer drove his 12 cylinder Bluebird twice over the course for an average two way speed of 253.968 miles an hour, over an official mile. This exceeded by 8.235 miles an hour the record of 245.733 he established here last year. Campbell was clocked over the mile at 13.46 seconds on his first run south over the course and at 14.89 seconds on his second trip, made north over the beach.

Washington, Feb. 24.—(P)—Mindful of the war in the orient and the arms conference at Geneva, the senate naval committee Tuesday voted for a navy as big and as strong as the London treaty will permit. It approved a bill by Chairman Hale to bring this about. Senator Watson, the republican leader, promptly gave it his endorsement, and indicated the measure would receive early consideration. Spread Over 10 Years The measure is a simple authorization and provides no appropriations. Hale estimated it would cost $980,000,000 to bring the navy up to the treaty strength in 10 years. A similar bill is pending before the house naval committee, introduced by Chairman Vinson. The committee approved it, but voted not to seek enactment at present because of the depleted condition of the treasury. LONDON, Feb. 24. (AP).—Karin Nissvandt, pretty daughter of a Stockholm businessman, who fell in love with His Royal Highness Prince Lennart of Sweden, was in London today with the prince for their wedding, a bit lonely and shy as a result of running counter to the will of the king. After their marriage, which will not take place for two or three weeks, the pretty blonde Karin will not be a princess, for her fiancé is renouncing all rights to his title and will become plain Mr. Bernadotte after the wedding. They looked like an ordinary college boy and his co-ed best girl as they stepped, somewhat abashed, from the train at Victoria station last night into a strange city neither had ever seen before and where no one came to meet them except. There were no representatives from Swedish embassies, for the young man's grandfather, King Gustaf of Sweden, and his father, Prince William, have dis

WASHINGTON, Feb. 24. —(AP)—The Senate naval committee reported to the senate today that enactment of legislation to build the navy to the full strength allowed by the London treaty "will have a stabilizing effect on world affairs." The committee’s favorable report on the bill to bring the Navy up to treaty strength was submitted by Chairman Hale, author of the measure. The report said testimony before the committee showed, "that our navy is rapidly becoming a navy of obsolete ships and will in the near future be entirely inadequate to protect our country, our foreign trade, our foreign possessions and our citizens at home and abroad." Japan, the report said, had approved and appropriated funds for a building program which will bring her navy up to full treaty strength by 1936 except for one aircraft carrier and six destroyers.

LONDON, Feb. 24.—(UP)—Increased prices will be guaranteed growers for home grown wheat which British millers must pay, text of the government wheat revealed today. The payments will be guaranteed on a maximum of 27,000,000 hundredweight any cereal year starting with 1932. A standard price of 10 shillings (about $1.73 at current exchange and $2.50 at par) per hundredweight will be guaranteed.

Geneva—/P—Arthur Henderson of Great Britain, president of the world disarmament conference, today addressed an eloquent appeal to the assembled delegates in behalf of the children of the world, who, he said, are always the victims of war. President Henderson's address marked the closing of general discussions of the conference. “War will inevitably always outrage and destroy the children,” Henderson declared, quoting John Galsworthy, noted British novelist and playwright. “The telegraphic reports from the far east,” he said, “show us the magnitude of the work before us and the terribleness of the war we are seeking to prevent. “The task of the conference,” he continued, “now that general debate has ended, looks very large. “The whole problem of security has been set out very closely as a corollary to disarmament and we owe much to the French and other delegations for making this problem

London, Feb. 23.—(/P) —— Exiled for his love of a commoner from the bosom of his family and his home in Sweden, His Royal Highness, Prince Lennart of Sweden, tonight brought his timid blonde fiancée to London to make her his wife. Looking much like a Texas college boy and his co-ed best girl, the happy but abashed pair stepped from a luxurious continental train at Victoria station into the strange city neither had ever seen to find no one to meet them—except two hotel employees. 1932-06-09.text: SANDWICH, ENGLAND, June 9 — Gene Sarazen, long hitting New York professional, tied the course record at Prince's with a 69 today to take the lead in the second round of the British open golf championship with his 70-69-139. Tommy Armour, defending champion, finished with a 70 and 145 just as Gene was starting out and his fellow American's fine performance stimulated Sarazen to do his best. Gene was out in 35 and home in 34 for a card five under par. Percy Alliss, British professional, was the closest to the American among the early finishers with a 71 for a 36-hole total of 142. Sarazen had birdies at the second, fifth, 12th, 15th, 16th and 17th holes and was over par only once, on the ninth hole. 443 424 455-35 444 433 3453469 to set a new record because he half smothered an approach shot to the home green where he had an easy four in sight for a 68. The ball carried into the crowd.

LONDON, June 9 (7%—John R. Mott, president of the world’s alliance of the Y. M. C. A. and head of the international missionary council, told the Associated Press today that he would welcome a thoroughgoing reconsideration of prohibition as a policy in the United States, on certain conditions. “I am not in favor of repeal of the 18th amendment,” he said. “Because with all its limitations and certain disappointing circumstances in connection with its working I believe its good results far transcended those which have been unfavorable. “At the same time I would welcome a nationwide, thoroughgoing reconsideration of prohibition as a policy on two conditions. Out Of Politics “First, that such a reconsideration be in the form of a popular vote in the various states, in no way related to any political campaign. “Second, that it be in the form of a clear-cut expression of choice between (A) the

London, June 9 (UP)—Dr. John R. Mott, world famous Y. M. C. A. leader, announced today he favors nationwide reconsideration of the prohibition question in the United States. Dr. Mott in a statement to the United Press urged that prohibition be put to a non-political vote of the people after a lengthy educational campaign which would give the electorate a choice between the present system of absolute prohibition and a definite concrete alternate plan. Dr. Mott, who is president of the international missionary council and of the world alliance of the Y. M. C. A., was inspired to make his statement by the recent announcement of John D. Rockefeller, Jr. that he has decided prohibition is a failure. Dr. Mott, however, does not believe that the evils of prohibition have outweighed its good results.

Rome, June 8—Amelia Earhart Putnam received a warm official welcome from General Italo Balbo, air minister, as she emerged from the cabin of an army plane which brought her from Milan. The Atlantic solo flier was hatless and her hair tousled. She was attired in a dark blue traveling dress. Mrs. John W. Garrett, wife of the American ambassador, kissed her and General Balbo and under secretary of aeronautics, Raffaello Riccardi, greeted Miss Earhart in Italian through an interpreter. Premier Mussolini tonight will give a dinner in honor of Miss Earhart, but General Balbo will preside in his stead. Tomorrow the premier will receive Mrs. Putnam and her husband and the Pope probably will give them an audience later.

BERLIN, June 9.—(U. P.)—Though denying the new German government intends to restore a Monarchy, Baron Wilhelm von Gayl, minister of the interior in the Von Papen cabinet, today made a personal declaration of loyalty to the Hohenzollerns in his maiden speech before the Federal council. His address created a sensation in the Reichsrat. “Personally,” he declared, “I consider a Monarchy to be the most suitable form of government for a nation situated in the heart of Europe.”

PETROVSK, Russia, June 9 UP —Another catastrophic wreck on a Soviet railroad in which an undetermined number of persons was reported killed on May 15 was revealed publicly for the first time today when 16 railroad employees went on trial charged with responsibility for the accident. Two crowded passenger trains collided between Kharkov and Dnieper Petrovsk. Scores of victims were crushed beyond recognition. The prosecutor charged the station master and other employees were drunk and mixed the signals. The most recent train wreck was in January when persons were killed in a collision near Moscow. Heavy prison sentences were imposed upon those responsible.

Cleveland, Ohio, June? (AP)—Eight persons were known to be dead and two others were missing in an explosion and fire which swept a downtown apartment early today. Four bodies had been brought out of the ruins and firemen had sighted four others, First Assistant Chief James Nimmo said he was positive two more bodies still were in the ruins. The bodies of two more persons were recovered today from a downtown apartment building which was destroyed by an explosion and fire, raising the number of dead to eight. The two new victims, both women, were found as firemen and police started through the fireswept building searching for a number of residents unaccounted for. The search began five hours after an explosion shook a six-story building in the heart of the downtown area early today. Flames which engulfed the upper five stories, consisting of apartments, had prevented rescue workers from ent

Detroit, June 9.—(#) —Harry Fleischer sought for many months in connection with the Lindbergh baby kidnapping and Detroit-Collingswood apartment massacre surrendered at 10:20 o'clock this morning arriving at police headquarters accompanied by two attorneys. Fleischer well dressed in a light suit and wearing a straw hat appeared extremely nervous. He held a handkerchief over his face as though expecting to face newspaper photographers but none was in the room when he arrived. He was taken to the office of Prosecutor Harry S. Toy who went into conference with Fleischer and his attorneys.

1932-03-27.text: DUBLIN, March 26. (#)—Easter Eve, the sixteenth since the revolution which flared on “bloody Easter week” in 1916, found the republican spirit more active in Ireland today than in years, with some trepidation over the possibility of trouble before the morrow passes. It is the first time in years that republicans, under the organization of the “Irish Republican Army” have been permitted a free rein for their memorial celebrations in honor of the 1916 revolution and the republican leaders who died for the cause. On that fact, however, officials of the government today pinned a confidence that the day would be peaceful. Clashes, they said, were not likely to occur when there was no opposition. As a precautionary measure, however, the regular Free State Army was ordered confined to barracks over the weekend, to prevent any possibility of clashes with the republican irregular forces. The “Rep

DUBLIN, (UP).—Eamonn De Valera, newly elected president of the Irish Free State, reiterated Saturday the government's intention to remove the oath to the king from the constitution. The oath must be removed at all costs, he said. "It is an offensive test which the Irish people cannot tolerate," De Valera said. It was understood the government would not reply before Tuesday to the note received from Great Britain.

Dublin, Irish Free State, March 26. (P)—Ten thousand Irishmen with the flag and uniform of the Irish Republican Army will parade through Dublin tomorrow in company, battalion and brigade formation to celebrate the sixteenth anniversary of the Easter rebellion which brought Eamon de Valera into the spotlight of the world’s news. As president of the Irish Free State, De Valera will not participate in the demonstrations, and he will keep the Free State army confined to barracks to avoid the trouble concerning which there is so much apprehension here. Dublin’s celebration will be one of half a hundred throughout the country and only its lack of firearms in tomorrow's parades will prevent the Republican army from appearing as a rival force to the Free State troops. In Belfast, Antrim, Armagh and Tyrone there will be similar big demonstrations with speeches by the political prisoners whom De V

WASHINGTON, March 26 (UP) Sir Willmott Lewis, correspondent of the London ‘Times, was reported today to have received a third note demanding $1,500 and threatening his five year old son. Police declined to confirm or deny the report. Police doubt the Lewis letters were written by the person who tried to extort $1,500 from Mrs. Alice Roosevelt Longworth three weeks ago.

By The Associated Press Wevbridge, Surrey, England, March 26.--Sir Horace Plunkett, Irish leader who promoted co-operative farming in his country and figured in efforts to settle the political differences between Ireland and Great Britain, died here today at the age of 77 years. He long had been out of active politics, having retired from the Irish Free State senate in 1923, after an attempt was made by Irish irregulars to burn his mansion Kilteragh, in County Dublin. Thereafter he made his home in England. Sir Horace’s important work was as an Irish leader up to and through the days of the World War. At one time he was chairman of the Irish convention which was called into being during 1917—to attempt to reach a final settlement of the Irish political question. He almost achieved success in this convention, but when he became convinced that the maintenance of a union between Ireland and

NEW DELHI, India, March 26 (®) —It appeared today that events were moving to clear the path to peace between India’s nationalists and the British government. Hope for restoration of normal conditions was revived suddenly when it was learned that Mrs. Sarojini Naidu, president of the Nationalist Congress had had a long conference yesterday with Viceroy Lord Willingdon after which she hurried to Benares for a talk with Pandit Maidan Mohan Malaviya who, next to Gandhi, is the most influential Nationalist leader. These conversations, it was believed, were intended to pave the way for resumption of a policy of cooperation and conciliation by the viceroy and Mr. Gandhi. The government policy toward the Nationalists has not been tempered, but those in authority would welcome peace overtures from the Nationalists.

TOKYO, March 26 (UP).—Japan has decided to withdraw from the League of Nations if undue pressure is exerted over settlement of the Manchurian and Shanghai problems, it became known today. Sir Eric Drummond, secretary general of the league, informed the Japanese representative at the league council that section 4 article 15 of the league covenant which provides that non-settlement of a controversy will result in league publication of recommendations deemed proper in the matter might be applied to the Manchurian situation.
