Associated Press Staff Writer ROME, Italy, Mar. 26. ()— Lent was over officially at noon today and church bells and organs, silent since Holy Thursday morning, apprized the capital city of the Roman Catholic world that the time had come to rejoice in Christ's resurrection. Special rituals commemorated the day. In St. Peter's the pope's paschal candle, eight feet high and three inches in diameter, was blessed by Cardinal Pacelli. The cardinal lighted the Easter fire by striking a spark from flint. The “new fire,” as it is called, was Continued on page 2

1932-04-13.text: Berlin — (AP) — Adolph Hitler’s national socialist “storm troops” were declared illegal throughout the country by a government decree today. The ban affects 400,000 “Nazis” organized on military lines and referred to by their political opponents as Hitler's “pretorian guard” and sometimes as “the state within a state.” Chancellor Bruening considered this extraordinary action so important that he delayed his departure for the disarmament conference at Geneva a full day to deliberate its every step and consequence. Immediately after the ban was declared, police throughout the country invaded local and state places of the storm troops to seize their banners and equipment and padlock the premises. This is not only a heavy blow to the Nazi movement, but is a matter of bread and butter for hundreds of thousands of unemployed who receive food and clothing as members of Hitler's private army.

. BERLIN, April 13. (UP) President Paul Von Hindenburg has signed an emergency decree dissolving and suppressing the Brown Shirt Fascist army of Adolf Hitler, it was announced officially today. Police at Konigsberg were reported closing the barracks of the Brown Shirts in East Prussia at once. Similar action, it was understood, would be taken promptly throughout Germany. Hitler's army and shock troops were estimated to number about 200,000 picked men. During the presidential election campaign the Fascist headquarters in Prussia were raided and authorities claimed to have found plans for forcible seizure of the machinery of government.

GENEVA. —(4)—Foreign Minister Dino Grandi of Italy told the world disarmament conference Wednesday Italy welcomed the United States proposal for abolition of tanks, heavy artillery and gas warfare. He added to the American plan a proposal to abolish battleships, airplane carriers and bombing airplanes.

Tokyo, Apr. 13—-(AP)— Two officers and twelve men of General Jiro Tamon's Japanese Manchurian force were killed and more than fifty injured in the wreck of a troop train near Harbin, Manchuria, last night, according to official reports to the war office here today. Earlier press reports of the wreck said it was caused by an explosion, but the official version merely declared the train was derailed and burned, cremating the victims.

TOKYO, April 13, —Dispatches from Harbin, Manchuria, said 11 Japanese soldiers were killed and 50 injured when a troop train was wrecked on the Chinese Eastern Railroad 17 kilometers east of Harbin Tuesday night. Press dispatches said the train was blown up. 14 Killed TOKYO, April 13, — Fourteen soldiers were killed in the wreck.

Tokio, April 13—(UP)—Fourteen Japanese soldiers were killed and fifty were injured in the wreck of a troop train dynamited on the Chinese Eastern Railroad east of Harbin, an official announcement today said. Reports to Japanese newspapers said Chinese Guerrillas had attacked Japanese soldiers at Mukden. The Nippon Dempo agency said Communists of “a certain country” were being sought in connection with the wreck of the troop train. Dispatches from Changchun quoted officials of the C. E. R. as saying they had obtained material evidence against agents of an unnamed foreign country as instigators of a plot to blow up the Sungari Railway bridge.

By The Associated Press Stockholm, April 13.—Police received orders today to search the city for the kidnapped Lindbergh baby. Pictures of the missing child appeared on the front pages of all newspapers.

HARBIN, MANCHURIA, April 13—(UP)—Troops of the Manchukuo government defeated a force of disbanded Chinese today at Taolaichao, on the southerly branch of the Chinese Eastern Railway 75 miles south of here, killing 200 and wounding 150.

1932-08-22.text: NEW YORK, Aug. 22.—Sandy-haired Capt. James A. Mollison, the only human ever to fly alone from Europe to New York, cocked an anxious eye at the sky over Manhattan's towers today and hoped the weather man would let him start his hop home to England in two or three days. “I've just been married, you know,” he explained with a grin. When he finished his precedent-shattering jaunt from Europe at 3.33 p. m. (East Liverpool time) Sunday, Mollison, who is the husband of Amy Johnson, England's most famous woman flier said: “Amy and I have made a pact to make no more extremely long or hazardous trips, once this flight is concluded.” Mollison was in the air 36 hours and one minute between Port Marnock, Ireland, and New York, which showed in his face when he brought his tiny plane “Hearts’ Content” down before 2,000 cheering fans at Roosevelt field. He had made the leg from St. John, N. B., in five

NEW YORK (UP).—Journey's end for Capt. James A. Mollison will be Croydon airport, England, with New York only the western terminus of his trailblazing flight. The intrepid little Scot left no doubt of his intention immediately after arriving here from Pennfield Ridge, N. B., at 4:35 p. m. Sunday. “I'll be back in England in a short time,” was his only answer as to the time of take-off. Mollison landed at Roosevelt Field, L. I., amid scenes reminiscent of those created by Col. Charles A. Lindbergh, crowds surging about the landing field, men trying to shake his hand, women running to kiss him.

Ottawa, Aug. 22.—(P)—A series of 12 trade treaties, designed to promote the economic welfare of the British empire and to demonstrate the unity of its dominions was revealed in part to the world today as the delegates to the imperial conference scattered to the four winds. - The United Kingdom signed seven agreements. These were with Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, India, Newfoundland and Southern Rhodesia. The Irish Free State signed two pacts, one with Canada and another with South Africa. Canada also had agreements with South Africa and Southern Rhodesia, while South Africa struck a bargain with New Zealand. Many of the trade channels between the United States and various British dominions and the United Kingdom will be affected by the treaties. Just how far British preference will cut into American or world trade cannot be determined by the various summaries. Actual pra

London, Aug. 22.—(A. P.)—The heat wave that swept the British Isles last week moved onto continental Europe during the week-end sending the mercury to over 100 degrees Fahrenheit in many parts of France and Italy. Berlin dispatches said Sunday, with 98 degrees, was the hottest day in Berlin in 67 years. Twelve persons were drowned there and five in Munich, seeking relief from the heat. A heavy wind struck Hamburg, damaging 40 houses. Temperatures in the British Isles and northern Germany and France dropped about 20 degrees last night, and there were indications that relief might be expected in other sections soon.

| OTTAWA, Ont., (UP).—Trade agreements between Great Britain and other empire units which may deprive the United States of $100,000,000 or more in trade annually will be made effective after the Canadian parliament convenes October 27. The agreements were published Sunday after 30 days of debate in which every dominion, province, and commonwealth in the British commonwealth of nations participated. The United States was represented by observers. The agreement in brief gave dominions a free trade tariff on their natural products shipped into Great Britain—which means they will go in practically duty free. They gave Great Britain’s manufactured products a free trade tariff on shipments into the dominions, which means the United States product will be handicapped in meeting British

Dublin, Irish Free State, Aug. 22 (A); —Two hundred members of the Irish republican army, most of them armed, moved into Donaman Castle during the night to hold a convention of their organization. The building is unoccupied and there was no resistance to their entry. The government made no attempt to eject them and officials at the republican army headquarters here said it would not be in the public interest to make any statement.
CAPE GRIS NEZ, France, Aug. 22 if Fritz Fisher, a German, entered the English Channel at 10:50 o'clock this morning to swim across to England. At 1:30 he was six miles out.

BEUTHEN, GERMANY, Aug. 22—(#)—Five members of Adolf Hitler’s national socialist party were sentenced to death today after being convicted of acts of terrorism. The trial was in one of the new speed courts established under the emergency decree of August 9 which also provided the death penalty for acts of political violence. Three defendants tried with those who were convicted were found not guilty. The specific charge that the defendants had administered a fatal beating to a young communist living in the village of Potenpa shortly after midnight of the day on which the emergency decree became effective.

1932-11-06.text: LONDON, Nov. 5. (4)—The main body of the 2,000 “hunger marchers” who trekked hopefully into London 10 days ago rode homeward today toward Scotland, Wales and provincial England in comfortable railway coaches attached to regular trains. The railways offered transportation at a low rate and the National Unemployed Workers’ organization, which sponsored the march on London, raised the funds. They got the money by public collections and from sympathetic organizations.

LONDON, Nov. 5.—Thirty thousand trained troops of the Japanese army near Manchukuo have revolted and joined the rebels that defied Japanese forces in the Anacaha region, 85 miles north of Harbin, a dispatch to the Daily Express said today. The Japanese hastily reinforced troops to recapture the city. Japanese sources estimated 1000 rebels were killed.

London, Nov 5 (UP)—London’s hunger marchers began to desert the city today, their invasion which lasted nearly ten days having failed to accomplish anything towards alleviating the reduction of dole benefits. The unemployed army was granted a special rate of one-half penny a mile (about one-half cent at par) by the railroads to get its members home, and all were glad to accept the offer. Many still had to continue their drive for pennies and sixpences by street collections to raise even the reduced fare, however. It was estimated that by nightfall, the vast majority of the marchers would have departed. Three of their principal leaders, Walter Hannington, Sid Elias and Emrhys Llewellyn, were still under charges of London police. Elias was accused of fostering Soviet propaganda and inciting the others to disaffection and revolt.

HOLLYWOOD, Calif. Nov. 5. (P) —John Warburton, young English screen actor, told friends here today he is engaged to marry Estelle Taylor, actress, former wife of the ex-champion, Jack Dempsey. Warburton would not elaborate on the statement. Miss Taylor was reported to be in Chicago filling a vaudeville engagement. The actor has been in this country about three years. He is under contract with R.K.O. studios.

Riv The Associated Press MANCHESTER, England, Nov. 5 —The cotton spinners’ strike ended today and work will be resumed in the mills Monday. The decision was made after a ballot was taken of the union membership. Eighty per cent of the spindles in the Lancashire mills were stopped on October 31 when spinners rejected a wage cut of from 5 to 8 per cent. The strike affected about 150,000 workmen. This was the second walkout in the region in recent months. Weavers struck late in July and were out four weeks before the conflict was settled. Manchester has just settled down to peace when the spinners decided to strike.

Lendon, Nov. 5—The British government does not contemplate under any circumstances asking for postponement of the war debt installment due the United States on December 15, the Daily Telegraph said today. However, when notifying Washington of its intention of paying, the paper said, the government probably will call attention to the onerous circumstances under which it is paying. The depreciation of sterling will be cited, also decreased British exports to the United States and Britain's failure to receive payment from her debtors.

LONDON, (4. Disillusioned but good-humored, Britain's little army of 2,000 “hunger marchers” evacuated London. They left in regular railway coaches provided for them, with banners high and the crowd cheering and singing. They had failed to attain an increase in the dole or any change in the means test but their fighting at the very doors of parliament forced an airing of the unemployment situation in the House of Commons. The three-day unemployment debate in the hex led by the veteran George Lansbury, will be resumed Monday. Most Londoners felt the trouble of the past ten days had been caused by avowed communist leaders aided by members of the London underworld. This feeling was caused by a letter introduced at the trial of Sidney Job Elias, chairman of the national unemployment workers’ movement, which tended to show that Moscow had interested itself in unemployment agitation. It was al

ATHENS, GREECE, NOV. 5. (AP).—The Greek court of appeals this evening confirmed the arrest of Samuel J. Insull, former Chicago utilities operator, indicted for embezzlement, who is held here for extradition to the United States. The court decision means that the financier will be detained while extradition negotiations are proceeding. A physician acting for the court of appeals today reported that Insull was suffering from myocarditis, diabetes, and low blood pressure.

1932-12-18.text: By The Associated Press Winter’s third zero attack in two weeks moved full force into the New England states Saturday night and left most of the remainder of America shivering. Snow in half a dozen states threatened to tie up transportation. It fell at the rate of half an inch an hour in Baltimore, disrupted ocean shipping there, and made highways all but impassable. Northern Texas, Oklahoma, and parts of Illinois already were blanketed with from six inches to a foot, and more was forecast for most of the Midwest. Government forecasters’ predictions of warmer weather brought the temperature higher than 20 above in only a few Midwest states and zero was scheduled for a return engagement from the Arctic Sunday. Danville, Vt., furnished a 40-below reading. It was below zero at Governor Franklin D. Roosevelt’s home in Albany, N. Y., and only 18 above at Washington, D. C. New York City’s lowe

‘Decision to Act at Once Made After Meeting of President and Secretaries Stimson and Mills—England Announces Conference. Washington, Dec. 19 ().—President Hoover will send a message to Congress on war debts this afternoon. Decision to dispatch the message without delay was made at a White House conference through the morning between the President and Secretaries Stimson and Mills. Mr. Hoover informed congressional leaders of his decision, and a full discussion of the debt situation impended on Capitol Hill. Final preparation of the message coincided with announcement to the British Parliament by Stanley Baldwin that the United States had agreed to undertake with Great Britain a joint examination of the debt structure. Secretary Mills said the message probably would be dispatched during the early afternoon, but had nothing to say as to its contents or length. It was believed at the Capito

LONDON, Dec 17—(P)—Andrew W Mellon, United States ambassador to Great Britain, caught an early boat train for Southampton where he sailed today on the steamship Europa for home. He will spend Christmas with his family in Pittsburgh. After a brief stay in Washington, he plans to return to London aboard the Majestic, sailing January 4.

Le Bourget, France, Dec. 17.— (AP)—Amy Johnson, noted flying wife of Capt. J. A. Mollison, British aviator, arrived here at 4:03 p.m. from Oran, Algeria. She left the African city at daybreak on the final stage of her return flight from Cape Town to London. Miss Johnson's landing was without incident, but she was greatly fatigued. It was thought possible she would not continue her flight to London today, as weather conditions were reported unfavorable.

LONDON, DEC. 19. (AP).—While cables told of severe weather in the United States, this country was experiencing the warmest December in seven years today, especially in the south where an average temperature was 57 degrees. In the north, however, rain and flooding on a big scale caused disastrous floods. The lakes of Derwentwater, Bassenthwaite and Thirlmere, familiar to tourists, overflowed following sixty hours of incessant rain and many villages were flooded and hundreds of persons driven from their homes.
SOUTHAMPTON, Eng. Dec. 17. —(UP)—Andrew W. Mellon, United States ambassador to London, sailed on the Europa today to spend Christmas in his home in Pittsburgh.

PARIS, Dec. 17.-(#)—With Joseph Paul-Boncour struggling to form a ministry, indications were today that France still was expecting something more definite from Washington on debt revision if the chamber were to be induced to reverse its decision and pay the December interest. Such was the official view expressed this forenoon. Acting Premier Herriot declined Joseph Paul-Boncour’s offer to enter a new cabinet but assured the premier-designate he could count on Herriot’s cooperation in the chamber. A high official was asked what, from the French view, was necessary to extract the debt problem from its present deadlock, he replied that if the United States, in some form or other, could clearly give the French nation a promise that debts would be revised he believes the French chamber might alter its decision to postpone payment. The opinion was growing here that the Franco-American differen

| SHANGHAI, March 18 (AP).-—A more definite prospect for a Chino-Japanese peace parley arose today at the same time that three Japanese transports steamed down the Whang-poo carrying the first contingent of troops back to Japan. Japanese peace negotiators received instructions from Tokyo saying the government decided to forego “certain conditions” which thus far have held up the peace parleys and is anxious to see the conferences proceed. Two more transports are slated to leave tomorrow and the homeward movement of troops will continue for a week.

1932-04-08.text: | London, April 7.—(4)—Friends of David Lloyd George said today he had decided virtually to retire from the House of Commons. He will devote his time, they said, to writing and farming and only events of outstanding importance will bring him back into the House. Commentators recently have pointed out that it was hard to see what his place could be in the present political scheme with his liberal party split and merged under new leaders in the national cabinet. A suggestion that he cooperate with the labor party opposition in the new parliament has met with little enthusiasm from either side and his vigorous attacks on the national government have left no place for him there.

LONDON, April 5 (-P) - Former Secretary of the Treasury Andrew W. Mellon arrived today to take up his duties as United States ambassador and was given an ovation by a considerable crowd at the railway station. He was welcomed by representatives of Prime Minister MacDonald. As he stepped down from his train, representatives of the American Legion raised the stars and stripes and the Legion flag.

London, April 7 (AP) - The four power conference failed today to agree on a scheme to solve the Danubian economic crisis and tomorrow it will adjourn to resume sessions later, probably at Geneva. Although the meeting here did not achieve the results hoped for, the opinion expressed by the British delegation was that, viewed in large perspective as one step in the slow progress toward the economic restoration of Europe, a measure of progress was attained. Britain, France, Germany and Italy sent representatives to the conference. It was reliably said that France and Britain stood together on the necessity for immediate agreement which would permit the Danubian states themselves to buttress their crumbling economic structures, which one high authority declared were rapidly going to 'rack and ruin.'

Southampton, England, April 8. - Andrew W. Mellon, new American ambassador to Great Britain, arrived here Thursday aboard the liner Majestic. He decided to spend the night on the ship and gave out no statement on his arrival.

ST. JOHN'S N. F., April 7 (FR) Sir Richard Squires today turned a surveying eye on Newfoundland’s embroiled populace, said he would not resign and refrained from outlining his government's future policy. The government, meanwhile, was represented as being unaware of reports in London that the mother government, Great Britain, had ordered a warship to St. John's.

LONDON () — Usually well-informed circles said today the Irish Free State government will insist that any conference with Great Britain on the oath of allegiance and the land annuities must be held in Dublin. President Eamon De Valera, of the Free State, and his adherents are irrevocably opposed to a conference in London.

Shanghai, April 7.—-(AP)--Rumors of impending civil war in China reached here today and centered especially on a report that Gen. Lian Fu-Chu, one of the northern leaders who already is in control of Shantung, has thrown down the gauntlet of battle before the Nanking government. General Han's defection in the north has been known for some time but only today did it begin to receive serious attention in local political discussions. Although he informed Gen. Chiang Kai-Shek he would no longer remain a part of the Nanking government and that he desired the independence of Shantung, he has not yet begun any hostile action. Shantung was quiet today, according to dispatches from Sinanfu and Tsingtao. The gist of recent reports is that the Nanking government is destined for an armed clash with the northern coalition which is said to be planning to overthrow Gen. Chiang Kai-Shek's regime and est

FRIEDRICHSHAFEN, Germany April 13 (-P) — The Graf Zeppelin, German dirigible, landed here this morning at 8 o'clock, ending her second trip of the year to Pernambuco, Brazil. The crossing from Pernambuco was slower than usual, taking 101 hours, on account of heavy fogs.

1932-04-03.text: LONDON —()— Edward Marjoribanks, brilliant young conservative member of parliament from East Sussex, was found shot to death Saturday night in the home of his stepfather, Lord Hailsham, near Hailsham, Sussex. He had been ill and suffering from insomnia. News of the death of the young author and politician caused a sensation in social and political circles. It was reported that a gun was found beside the body in the billiard room of Lord Hailsham's home. The young man had been working very hard of late, and among other things he was writing a life of Lord Carson. Marjoribanks was 32, the son of Archibald Marjoribanks and the former Myssie Brown, of Nashville, Tenn. Mrs. Marjoribanks later married Douglas Hogg, who subsequently became Lord Hailsham. Young Marjoribanks was educated at Oxford, where he attained many high scholastic honors, and was called to the bar in 1924. He was elected to

BERLIN, April 2—Former Crown Prince Friedrich Wilhelm today pledged his support to Adolf Hitler, presidential candidate of the National Socialists, who would ‘repudiate the Treaty of Versailles. Friedrich Wilhelm, hitherto more closely allied with the Nationalist party than with the Hitlerites, announced his position as all political Germany was preparing for a week of strenuous campaigning for the run-off election a week from tomorrow in which the chief contenders are Herr Hitler and Pres. Paul Von Hindenburg.

TOKIO, April 2. U.?)—Heavy Japanese reinforcements were sent into Manchuria today to cope with the growing drive of irregular Chinese armies threatening Japan's hold on that province and the stability of the new Manchurian state of Manchukuo. Engagements in various parts of South and Central Manchuria were reported, with villages burned and aw threatened. It was officially announced that the Korean army had been instructed to send a unit to assist in Manchuria, where the Chinese outnumbered Kirin provincial troops loyal to Japan.

By The Associated Press NORFOLK, Va., April 2—Three Norfolk men, who say they have never lost faith in their efforts, today continued to await further de- velopments in negotiations for the recovery of the kidnaped baby of Colonel and Mrs. Charles A. Lind- bergh. Rear Admiral Guy G. Burrage, retired, spokesman for the inter- mediaries, stated there had been a new development since Thursday morning, but there was no other intimation of what progress was being made. He refused to say what the development was.

Norfolk, Va., April 2. — (#) — John Hughes Curtis, one of three Norfolk negotiators for the return of the kidnapped Lindbergh baby, slipped away today on a mission announced to be in the interest of the negotiations. | Rear Admiral Guy H. Burrage, spokesman for the three men, said Mr. Curtis, a Norfolk boat builder, was “off on business for the case.” He refused to comment further. | Mr. Curtis, whose negotiations (Continued on Page 7)

WASHINGTON, April 2 (PIA) A bipartisan drive to push the billion-dollar revenue raising bill through the Senate was mobilizing today as Secretary Mills gave qualified endorsement to the measure approved by the House. The treasury head spoke of some “serious defects and discriminations” in the legislation but gave it endorsement for sound financial principles. Senate leaders added their pledge to balance the government's income and outgo by next year but the dispute on what is necessary to bring this about developed further today. Mr. Mills challenged sharply contentions of the Democratic House leadership that a $200,000,000 saving in government expenditures next year can be made by Congress—this saving is counted on by the House to balance the budget with the aid of the revenue bill. Senate Republican leaders did agree today, however, with Speaker Garner that a determined drive can put t

BF £20 Hever esteye Free WASHINGTON, April 2—An astounding story of the power of Al Capone and his Chicago gangsters, told in the words of the man who finally made them surrender before the strong arm of the federal government, was made public today by a senate committee. It was the inside story of the government's long battle against Capone and his gang as told by District Attorney George E. Q. Johnson, at Chicago, to the senate judiciary sub-committee considering the nomination of Tuten Tamec 1. Wilkerson to the circuit court. Wilkerson sentenced Capone to 11 years in the penitentiary after overturning an agreement by Johnson to recommend 2½ years if Capone would plead guilty. In his sensational testimony at an executive session of the committee Tuesday, Johnson revealed what he said were the true circumstances of that agreement for the first time. He said Judge Wilkerson approved of t

| WASHINGTON, April 2 (P)—Old man tariff and the comparative youngster—prohibition—are strutting forward in presidential politics as Franklin D. Roosevelt and President Hoover corral most of the nominating delegates to the Chicago conventions. Alfred E. Smith furnished a weekend high spot with a statement denying he would withdraw his name from the democratic convention and resenting reports that he would support Roosevelt in return for a cabinet appointment. Simultaneously, the democrats lost their national committee treasurer, James W. Gerard, who resigned after handling the party’s finances for eight years, because he said the job required more time than he could give to it. Chairman Raskob will appoint a successor to conduct the party’s “victory” fund drive. Republican leaders long ago accepted the democratic challenge to lock horns on the Hawley-Smoot tariff act in the coming campai

1932-03-31.text: DUBLIN, March 61, (F)—Southern Ireland's seven century struggle for complete freedom seems to be nearer its goal, although several more years may be needed to write the end of its independence story. There is every indication that the Irish Free State today is on the threshold of the most significant period in its history. The change that has come over the country in the past five months, and especially since the election of Eamon de Valera as head of the executive council, is unmistakable. To an Englishman or to any other foreign observer this change can mean only that the Irishmen never will be satisfied with anything but complete separation from Great Britain. The wave of nationalistic feeling sweeping over the Free State now is as widespread as that which drove Southern Ireland into rebellion against the British crown. But there will be no rebellion this time. Republicans have learne

LONDON, March 30—Confidence in the American financial situation was expressed today by one of the highest financial authorities in Great Britain, while prospects for a four-power conference here to discuss economic relief of the Danubian countries of Southeastern Europe faded. The financial authority, who would not permit his name to be used, said it was inconceivable that the dollar should go off the gold standard. His comment was on press reports current the past few days of a “flight from the dollar.” “There are all sorts of risks in America, but there are not currency risks,” he said. “I can conceive of bank robberies, kidnappings and gang murders, but not of a collapse of the dollar.” Although a conference on the Danubian situation embracing delegates of Italy and Germany, as well as France and England, was likely to be delayed, Premier Andre Tardieu of France will come over from Pa

New London, Conn., March 30,—(F)—Willard E. Blain promised in police court today that he never again will try to fly like a bird in Connecticut. Blain was nearly drowned Saturday when he jumped from a bridge over the Thames River in his "ornithopter," a motorless airship with bat-like wings. State aviation officials arrested him on charges of flying an unregistered craft and of having no pilot's license. The court fined Blain $100 on each count, but suspended payment on his promise to stay on the ground in the state. Blain, however, told the court he would attempt a flight from the top of the Empire State Building in New York.

Shanghai, March 31.—(AP)—Definite progress towards a settlement of the major issue of withdrawals of Japanese troops from the Shanghai area was made today at the reopening of the Sino-Japanese peace parleys. As a result, a breakdown of the conference, anticipated by some observers during the two-day adjournment, was averted and the delegates resumed their discussions in a more conciliatory mood than since the parleys began. A spokesman for the conference said both sides were gradually approaching an understanding on the question of a time limit for the troop withdrawals, and that mutual concessions were being made. The conference adjourned again to meet Saturday at 10 a.m. The military subcommittee which is meeting at the same time as the main conference also made important advances, it was stated, when the Chinese members showed a willingness to meet the Japanese halfway in settling the

SHANGHAI, March 30 (7) — Peace negotiations here approached a crisis tonight after sharp skirmishes between Japanese and Chinese forces at Chiwangmiao earlier in the day. Chinese and Japanese military leaders still were far apart on truce terms. Chinese newspapers predicted the conference would collapse. A Chinese spokesman said the parleys might reach a critical stage tomorrow, when they are to be resumed without definite recommendations for either side to be discussed. A Japanese officer, meanwhile, sought to wipe out in traditional fashion—by suicide—what he considered the dishonor he had brought upon the army by allowing himself to be captured. Major Noboru Kuga was captured by the Chinese during the fighting around Kiangwan. Released today, he went back immediately to the scene of his capture and ended his life, leaving a note of explanation. A military sub-committee of the peace co

CHANGCHUN, Manchuria, March 31. (P)—The rebel Chinese forces under General Li Hai-Tsing, which have been threatening this new Manchurian capital for several days, apparently had taken Nangun, 35 miles from here, today, and were pressing on to the south. As a result of the increasing danger, several Japanese tanks left here to join the Japanese forces which are approaching the battle zone on foot. The Manchukuo government announced today that on April 1 it would take over all the post offices in Manchuria and place them under the jurisdiction of the new ministry of communications. Previously the customs revenues and the salt collections were absorbed.

SHANGHAI, March 31 (U.P)— Japanese and Chinese armies were constructing military defense works in the Shanghai area today despite assurances of leaders that peace negotiations were progressing satisfactorily. The fifth and 19th Chinese route armies were building trenches along the west bank of the Tsingyang-kiang River in the vicinity of Henli, where foreign residents of Shanghai hold an annual regatta. Japanese troops constructed bulwarks in Kiangwan and other villages surrounding Shanghai, although commanders gave no indication of their purpose. From Chinese sources it was reported Japanese peace conferees desired an indefinite continuation of their occupation in four areas around Shanghai, the Woosung and Yangtzepoo districts, in Chape! from North Sezechechuen road and in Kiangwan eastward from the race course.

Hamburg, Germany, Mar. 31 (A.P)—Max Schmeling, world’s heavyweight boxing champion, sailed for the United States aboard the liner New York to begin an exhibition tour, preparatory to defense of his title against Jack Sharkey in New York City, June 16.

1932-07-20.text: OTTAWA, Ont., July 20. (P)—An inference that the British Empire trade conference, which opens tomorrow, might prove a means for Canada to “break away from the influence of the United States” was plumped into the laps of the empire delegates today. Stanley M. Bruce, former premier of Australia, stabbed through the maze of predictions of success that resound through the corridors where the conference is talked to place in blunt words a question which was uppermost in all minds, “Will a cohesive trade policy within the United States of British Empire be purchased,” he asked, “at the cost of American commercial relations with Canada?” Referring to the United States, Canada’s best customer, as a “major problem,” Bruce said: “There is always that tendency to be absorbed by a bigger country. This ought to be Canada’s chance to break away.” The Canadians, although they are prepared to open the c

GENEVA, July 30 — The big four powers of the world disarmament conference, the United States, France, Great Britain and Italy, met today in another attempt to break the deadlock on the question of abolition of heavy mobile artillery which has prevented the adoption of a resolution to adjourn. The United States delegation was holding out for total abolition of these weapons.

LONDON, July 20. (P)—Prosperity should start coming around the corner this year, the Prince of Wales indicated in a speech at a banquet given by the West African Society, “It is my belief that 1952 will witness the beginning of the return to happier and more prosperous times and a great revival of world trade,” the prince said.

SOUTHAMPTON, July 20--(G5) United States Ambassador Mellor and his son, Paul, sailed today on the Majestic for New York. Nicholas Murray Butler and his daughter, Gladys Schuyler Bailes, were also passengers.

BEDFORD, Ia. (AP)—The body of Thomas J. Allen, 26, farmer near here, was found Wednesday buried in a shallow grave near the place he had been building fence. Authorities were trying to solve the cause of his death and the reason for his slaying. The family was unable to assign any motive, declaring he had no enemies to their knowledge. The spot at which the body was found was within eighty rods of the place where Ely Jones, his father, had been searching for him after he failed to return Tuesday night for supper. Allen’s face apparently had been crushed by a stone. Three sets of tracks were found, each believed

SOUTHAMPTON, Eng, July 20 —(UP)— Andrew W. Mellon, United States ambassador to Great Britain, sailed with his son, Paul, aboard the Majestic today for New York. The ambassador declined any statement, except that he hoped to return in three weeks. His visit was understood to be without political significance.

BOSTON, July 20. (INS)—Dinner pails are rattling again in the New England states as the gates of mills and factories swing open. Reports coming in today to the New England council headquarters and other official sources presented a cheering picture of a slow but sure revival in manufacturing and business generally in this group of six states. Orders were coming into textile mills, shoe factories, hat factories, print mills and jewelry shops calling for an increase in production. A big parade of thousands of workers appeared definitely un-factory in Cambridge prepared for the fall rush. An electric clock company in Ashland received a government order for 2,650 clocks for new government buildings in Washington. Two thousand textile operatives reported back to their jobs in Lawrence. Activity was reported in textile mills in Fall River, Vt.; Wyoming, R.I.; Seekonk and Riverpoint, R.I., and

ROME, July 20. —(A4’) —Dino Grandi, Italian foreign minister, resigned today in a far-reaching cabinet shake-up ordered by Premier Mussolini. Five ministers and 11 under-secretaries were displaced in the shake-up. Mussolini retained for himself two of the vacated portfolios, These constituted the first changes in the cabinet since September, 1929. The shake-up was regarded as another “rotation” to bring new blood into the government without any change of policy. The five ministers who resigned are: Grandi; Alfredo Rocco, minister of, (Continued On Page Eleven)

1932-07-25.text: | London, July 25. (AP)—The Daily Herald said today Ambassador Andrew W. Mellon "is expected to resign" when he arrives in Washington on his present trip to the United States. "It is believed he will tell President Hoover the coming negotiations on war debts should be in hands younger than his," the Herald added. ‘The London newspapers have been making something of a mystery of the ambassador's trip home ever since he left here a week ago today, declaring he was going to the United States for a holiday, taking advantage of a dull period in embassy work: He, himself said the trip had no political significance. Today, however, his leaving was coupled with the departure of the British ambassador, Sir Ronald Lindsay, from Washington and other newspapers besides the Herald printed dispatches from New York and Washington speculating on the coincidence. Before he left here the ambassador indica

London, July 25, — Andrew W. Mellon, former secretary of the treasury, will resign his post as Ambassador during his present visit to America, London newspapers said today, discussing war debts and reparations settlements. The Ambassador feels that a younger man should handle important questions such as war debts which are expected to be discussed by the United States and her European debtors, the Laborite Daily Herald said. The Herald predicted Mellon's resignation would be submitted to President Hoover soon after his arrival in America this week. The Sunday Dispatch quoted official circles as saying that Mellon would not return to his post here. The newspaper commented on the fact that the British Ambassador to Washington, Sir Ronald Lindsay, is now en route to London. The Daily Herald said Sir Ronald would report on the American (Continued on Page Two)

OTTAWA, July 25 (Pp) — Advocates of remonetization of silver at the imperial conference today linked a bi-metalism scheme for the British commonwealth of nations with the idea of a super-empire bank. Here, as in the United States, silver has its champions as medium of exchange and it is considered certain that the silver question will be presented to the conference in connection with a plan to stabilize the unit of exchange within the empire.

BOSTON, July 25 (*)—Business conditions are looking up in old New England. The New England Council reports closed mills re-opening, laid-off employees going back to work and sufficient orders coming into several industrial plants to warrant capacity production in the near future. The good news is probably best in Pittsfield, Mass, where the Berkshire Woolen Company and Glix Underwear Company plants are working at capacity. The Silver Lake Woolen Mills in the same city are employing day and night shifts and the Wyandotte Woolen Mills expect to have a full force operating in two weeks. Two thousand have gone back to the American Woolen Company mills at Lawrence, Mass., and another 2,000 have been taken back by the re-opening of the Nashua Manufacturing Company’s Lowell, Mass., and Nashua, N. H., plants. The Nashua company manufactures blankets. Seven hundred workers are celebrating the re-

CORK, Irish Free State, July 25 — (AP) — James Burke, of Charleville, insisted he could kiss the blarney stone without anyone holding his legs as he hung head downward over the parapet, as so many pilgrims have done. He tried it, slipped, and fell 100 feet to his death at the foot of the ancient castle. Kissing the stone, tradition says, gives the power of eloquent and persuasive speech.

WASHINGTON, July 25. UPR The State Department said today it had no reason to believe that Andrew W. Mellon, ambassador to Great Britain, planned to resign. It characterized British press reports of his resignation as mere speculation. LONDON, July 25. U.P)—Andrew W. Mellon, former secretary of the treasury, will resign his post as ambassador during his present visit to America. London newspapers said today in discussing war debts and reparations settlements.

Bright spots studded the American business picture Monday. More than 15,000 idle New England workers have returned to work recently as a result of a business pickup in that section, a survey showed. Although the textile and shoe industries hired the most men, the spurt extended into almost a dozen other lines of trade. The Department of Commerce in Washington reported a sharp reduction in business failures for the week ended July 16, and the largest increase in commodity index prices since the depression started. Other important developments were: An increase of 85,144 in car loadings. Increased gray iron production and a 1 percent increase in steel operations. Several companies reported increased earnings.

London, July 2d. (AP)—"Borah's conversion," as London newspapers called the senator's suggestion for a conference on war debts, was hailed here today as "a considerable straw in a wind that is beginning to blow" in the United States for debt revision. "Europe will welcome wholeheartedly so notable a conversion as Senator Borah’s," the Telegraph said. "His courage and candor will receive unstinted recognition in this country and elsewhere." "What Borah says," the News-Chronicle commented, "is generally what the mass of Americans is thinking. It is therefore supremely welcome that he now publicly declares in favor of a conference." The Daily Express said it was too early "to read into Senator Borah’s words a determination of the American people to face the debt problem in a realist way," but it added that "Borah is a shrewd man, and a fairly considerable straw in the wind that is beginning

1932-06-08.text: (By United Press London, June 7.—The United States gunboat Oahu opened fire with heavy machine guns on a large band of Chinese regular soldiers on the Yangtze river, forty miles below Chungkiang, causing many casualties, an exchange telegraph dispatch from Shanghai said today. The Chinese had tried to compel the surrender of the stranded British steamer Wanliu, carrying $110,000 in specie. The British ship was transferring the passengers and specie when the Chinese fired from the river bank. The firing was renewed later and continued until the Oahu silenced it.

DUBLIN, June 8 (UP) — The senate by a vote of 30 to 22 rejected the vital section two of the oath abolition bill today. The senate action means that the oath remains in the constitution as far as the senate is concerned. Thus the bill as passed by the dail is rendered practically useless.

Sandwich, Eng. June 8—(AP)—Gene Sarazen, New York, professional and American favorite for the title, today scored a 70 for the first round of the British open golf tournament, to take the lead with most of the field in. Sarazen went along easily in the two qualifying rounds for a 78-76 and then got “hot” today to break par by four strokes in one of England’s most difficult golf tests. His score was one stroke better than those of MacDonald Smith, another American favorite, Charles Whitcombe and W. H. Davis, British professionals, who had been tied for the early lead. Sarazen was out in 35, one under par, and home in the same number of strokes, three under “perfect” figures. Sarazen’s finish was as spectacular as if the title itself depended on the first round. The gallery gave him a big cheer as he finished. Percy Allis, British professional, posted a 71 to make it a four-way tie for sec

SHANGHAI, June 7.—A dispatch telling of heavy casualties inflicted by the U.S. gunboat Oahu on Chinese soldiers who were attacking two British steamers in the upper Yangtze river was published today by the Exchange Telegraph agency. The gunfire, the dispatch said, was for the purpose of protecting the steamers Wanliu and Kiawo. The Wanliu, which had $110,000 in cash aboard, ran aground 40 miles below the town of Chungking and when the Kiawo came alongside to take off the money, cargo and passengers, a considerable force of Chinese soldiers intervened. Demands Refused The Exchange Telegraph agency said the soldiers were men of the regular army. Their demands for the money were refused and gunfire resulted. Thereupon the master of the Kiawo signaled for assistance. The Oahu came alongside and stood by during the night. This morning the firing was resumed by the Chinese, the dispatch said,

Dublin, June 8.-(-—Possibility of a “new Anglo-Irish treaty to iron out dif-ferences over the oath of allegiance was Mentioned among the m@)1,.eumors which circulated here today over the outcome of the conference yesterday between President De Valera and two British cabinet ministers, Officially, no hint was given either about the subjects discussed at the conference, at which Great Britain was represented by J. M. Thomas, secretary for the Dominions, and Lord Ha} - Sham, secretary of state for war, or about the progress made. Nothing was known definitely, however, except that De Valera would go to London Friday to continue the par-leys there. In other quarters it was said yesterday's meeting resulted in a complete deadlock.

BOSTON, JUNE 8. (AP).—New England shivered today in unseasonably cool weather which brought frost, damaged crops and in Boston drove the mercury down to 42 degrees, the lowest June temperature recorded in 48 years. Frosts were reported from the Connecticut valley in the vicinity of Springfield, damaging young crops. The Massachusetts State College at Amherst reported an all-time frost record for the date with 36 degrees. The college's records cover forty years.

DUBLIN, Irish Free State, June 7--President Eamon De Valera and James Geoghegan, his minister of justice, talked for an hour today with two members of the British cabinet about the differences between the two countries. J. H. Thomas, British secretary for dominions, and Lord Hallsham, the secretary for war, came over from London last night with the primary purpose of arranging for a meeting at the end of the week between Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald and Mr. De Valera, who is going to London on Friday.

London, June 7 (AP)—Aviators here have virtually abandoned hope for Stanislaus Hausner, the American aviator missing on a solo flight from New York to Warsaw. There was a possibility that he might have been picked up at some vessel without wireless, but the general sentiment was that the chance was remote.

1932-03-07.text: | LONDON, Mar. 6~-(P)—Hetty Gow, the Scottish nurse of little Charles Lindbergh, had a “premonition” that something unusual was going to happen in the Lindbergh home. It was revealed today. Mrs. Taylor, Miss Gow's mother, a resident of Glasgow, Scotland, told the Sunday Express that Betty had recently written her expressing the fear that “something was going to happen.” The nurse had given this statement to her mother in promising to come home soon. Mrs. Taylor told the Express that she was sure her daughter “had never dreamed of the baby being kidnapped.” Mrs. Taylor revealed yesterday that she had feared for her daughter's safety ever since another of her children, a son, was accidentally killed by an electric shock in the United States last September. “Betty is my youngest child,” Mrs. Taylor said, “and she went to America three years ago. Ever since my boy was electrocuted I have bee

GENEVA, March 7.--(i§)—Great Britain today turned thumbs down on the effort of a group of smaller powers in the League Assembly to obtain an immediate pronouncement against Japan in the Shanghai war and to propose measures to force her to cease hostilities. Sir John Simeon, the British foreign speech was greeted with silence and was scarcely applauded.

Paris, March 7.—(AP)—Aristide Briand, “apostle of peace,” died at 12:45 o'clock this afternoon. “He died in a coma,” said Dr. Marx, his personal physician, “after a stroke from which he did not regain consciousness. “He passed away peacefully without suffering. Professors Dozelot and Vaquez and I saw him at 9:30. He was no worse then than he had been for several days and we did not imagine the end could come so quickly. “He died at about 12:45.” It was the end of one of the most active careers in modern French political history. The bent shaggy-haired old statesman—he was 69—had occupied the post of foreign minister in one cabinet after another for so long that he had made the office almost his own. It was in that capacity that he participated in the Briand-Kellogg pact outlawing war as an instrument of national policy. It was from that office that he played so important a part in the ma

(Associated Press Staff Writer) PARIS, March 7 (4)—Aristide Briand, France’s most prominent statesman in the international field and symbol of her post-war striving for peace, died just before 1 P. M. today in his modest bachelor flat not far from the Arc de Triomphe. The man who 12 times was chief of his country’s government and was a leading spirit in activities of the League of Nations, passed away as a simple member of the chamber of deputies. M. Briand, who would have been 70 years old May 28, succumbed to a heart attack. The nation he served as premier during the dark days of Verdun as well as throughout the efforts to stabilize peace in Europe during the last 11 years, will accord him a state funeral. The services will be held at 2 P. M. Saturday at the foreign office in the Quai d’Orsay. The body will lie in state there. Andre Tardieu, premier of France, will be principal speaker

Shanghai, March 7—(/)—Japanese authorities declared today their troops would be withdrawn from Shanghai as soon as it was made certain the Chinese army would not again enter the 12% zone and the offer re Chinese and Japanese peacemakers together again in a hopeful atmosphere. The declaration stimulated hopes of softening the attitude of the Chinese government which rejected former peace proposals, declaring the Chinese army would not be evacuated except on withdrawal of the Japanese forces. The indications were late this afternoon that the proposed round table conference of the neutral powers would be discarded in favor of a direct Sino-Japanese parley. Up To Chinese Mamoru Shigemitsu, Japanese minister, declared Japan was willing to withdraw its troops at the earliest practical moment. He said that although the time and place for a new conference between Chinese and Japanese authorities

TOKYO, March 7.—Agitation for withdrawal of Japan from the League of Nations increased today as officials and the public digested reports from Geneva describing a condemnation of Japan's invasion of China by smaller nations in the league assembly last Saturday. Plan Garrison Even in official quarters the opinion was heard that Japan should withdraw from the league as soon as the present conflict with China is settled. One official said Japan proposed to retain a garrison in Shanghai's International Settlement after withdrawal of the main force now there. Officials said the status of this force would be the same as that of the American and British troops which have been stationed there since 1927. May Quit League Although Foreign Minister Kenkichi Yoshizawa said Feb. 21 Japan had no intention of quitting the league, advocates of withdrawal said the foreign minister was "not permanently in

SHANGHAI, (Monday). (Copyright 1932, by (.) The arrival of more Japanese reinforcements and an admission that one or two more divisions were en route from Tokyo prompted Chinese government circles to charge that they feared Japan might attempt to capture Nanking. The possibility of further inland invasions, the Chinese announcement said, led a plenary session of the central executive committee to designate two cities as temporary capitals of China. Honanfu (Loyang) has already been designated as the temporary capital, and Monday Sianfu, the capital of Shensi province, was announced as a co-capital to be known as the western capital. While Chinese sources continued to charge that skirmishes had been occurring beyond the twelve and a half mile zone around Shanghai and Japanese denied them, the Japanese admitted the rest of the Fourteenth division had landed on Sunday. Admitting that one or

SHANGHAI (PR) — Edwin S. Cunningham, United States Consul General, still was awaiting a reply today from Japanese authorities to whom he protested against the beating of Miss Rose Marlowe, American mission teacher, by two Japanese in civilian clothes last Friday. Miss Marlowe was pummeled by the Japanese when she entered the compound of the school where she had taught to inspect the damage caused by the hostilities. D. Robinson, United States trade commissioner, whose home is at Salt Lake City, Utah, said today the incident Saturday in which he was beaten by armed Japanese civilians was “trivial.” He said he reported the incident to the United States consulate, but not to the Tonaneca.

1932-03-30.text: NEW LONDON, Conn., Mar. 30. (AP)—The Game Cock, described by officials as a British liquor supply boat, and the yacht 247 of Boston, were seized last night by coast guard patrol boats from the New London base. They carried liquor valued by authorities at $150,000. Thirteen men comprising the crews of the captured craft were arrested. Coast guard officials said the Game Cock was a contact boat.

LONDON, March 23. (4%—Great Britain, by the aid of economies and taxes, will end its fiscal year Thursday with a small surplus in its treasury. Thus Britain will be one of the few countries in the world that has paid its way in the past year. But all is not unalloyed satisfaction. The Daily Herald, organ of the Labor opposition to the national government of Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald, puts the surplus at between £40,000,000 and £50,000,000 (nominally about $200,000,000 and $250,000,000) and says it will probably endanger the unity of the cabinet because demands are going to come from all sides for some of the money. The hero of the budget balancing is the income tax, which was paid up promptly. The taxpayers’ sacrifice saved the situation. Since December 1931, British income taxpayers have parted with more than £200,000,000.

Cannes, France, March 30.—(P) American and British society folk kept their heads and helped to stem a panic at a restaurant here last night when a performing lion broke out of its cage. Seven hundred guests began to stampede when the beast leaped clear upon the dancing floor. Billy Arnold, of Patterson, N.J., leader of the orchestra, set his men to playing as loud as they could for such of the guests as continued dancing. A fire hose was turned on the lion and it was herded back to the cage.

WASHINGTON, March 20.—Andrew W. Mellon, new ambassador to the court of St. James, paid his farewell to President Hoover late today prior to sailing for London Friday on the S.S. Majestic. The former secretary of the treasury said there had been no special emphasis upon the question of war debts during his conferences with Washington officials.

LONDON, Mar. 30. (AP).—Complete confidence in the financial situation in the United States was expressed today from one of the highest financial quarters in Great Britain, but without authority to disclose the source. Commenting on press reports of the last two days discussing “a flight from the dollar,” this source said: “There are all sorts of risks in America, but there are no currency risks. I can conceive of bank robberies, kidnappings and gang murders, but not of a collapse of the dollar. It is inconceivable that the dollar should go off gold.

London, Mar. 30.—Prospects for a four-power conference here in connection with the economic position of the Danubian countries faded today, but arrangements were completed for a meeting between Prime Minister MacDonald and Premier Tardieu of France, who will come over from Paris on Monday. Tardieu will talk with Mr. MacDonald, Sir John Simon, the foreign secretary; Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer, and perhaps Walter Runciman, president of the board of trade. Pierre Flandin, the French minister of finance, is coming with him, and these officials will discuss the whole range of European problems, particularly that of Danubian reconstruction. Although Mr. MacDonald invited Germany and Italy to participate, the foreign ministers of those countries will not be able to be present. The four-power conference, therefore, will be held probably at Geneva sometime next month.

SHANGHAI, March 30 (4)~A sharp clash between Japanese and Chinese forces at Chiawangmiao took place today, according to Japanese military authorities, punctuating a lull in the peace parleys which are slated to be resumed again tomorrow. The Japanese said the Chinese were driven to the south side of Soochow Creek, on the north side of which they were reported last week to have been digging trenches and erecting defenses. The Japanese notified British authorities then that drastic measures might have to be taken to force the Chinese to observe the limits fixed in General Uyeda’s ultimatum of last February. Japanese peace negotiators, meanwhile, charged the parleys were being delayed because the Chinese delegates lacked responsibility and authority to make decisions and the Chinese countered with a charge that the Japanese were trying to break up the conference. Chinese officials expressed

OSLO, Norway, March 30.—(?)—A family tragedy, in which a young man of 21 killed his father, mother and five brothers and sisters with an ax and then set fire to their home was discovered at Verdal, near Trondheim, today when the sheriff answered a mysterious telephone call. A youthful voice had called the telephone exchange. The sheriff was notified and rushed to the house immediately. Neighbors said the young man had shown signs of increasing nervousness during the last two days.

1932-12-25.text: Washington, March 25.—(#)—A kidnap scare swept the capital today after police disclosed that extortion notes, accompanied by threats, had been received by Mrs. Alice Roosevelt Longworth, Sir Willmott Lewis, the London Times correspondent, Ben Lyon of the movies, and others. Police, however, predicted an early arrest. They were working on the theory that one man was responsible for several if not all of the threats, which involved promise of kidnaping Sir Willmott’s young son unless $1,500 were paid. A police guard was placed at his home, and detectives also are watching Mrs. Longworth’s home. She too was told to pay $1,500, but Paulina, her seven-year-old daughter, was not threatened directly. Definite instructions were received by her twice as to how to pay the money. An agent followed the instructions, driving slowly in a taxi by the chosen spot for depositing the amount, but the promi

Bethlehem, Dec. 24.—Hundreds of Americans are celebrating Christmas in the Holy Land amid familiar scriptural surroundings. They are tourists on a world cruise aboard the liner Empress of Britain, and arrived in Jerusalem today. This evening automobiles carried these tourists and pilgrims to worship at the cradle of Christ's birth here. When Wise Men Came Above them was a starry sky which recalled the actual night of the nativity 1932 years ago, when Three Wise Men of the East came to the manger bearing gifts of frankincense and myrrh for the newly born savior. Brighter, however, than all the stars tonight was the electrically lighted cross above the Church of the Nativity which, from a distance, resembled a large star hovering above the darkly silhouetted rooftops of Christ's town. Birmingham, Eng., Dec. 24.— Seven of the nine children of an unemployed and crippled World War veteran, ranging in age from three to 13, were burned to death today in a fire that destroyed their two-room tenement home. The father, Patrick Weir, his wife and eight of the children were sleeping when the blaze was discovered. Weir managed to carry his wife and their youngest child, seven months old, to safety before he was overcome by smoke. He was later found crying and almost naked in the charred entrance of the tenement. He and his wife and the rescued baby were taken to a hospital suffering from severe burns. The other child who escaped the fire had spent the night with relatives.

LITTLE ROCK, Ark: Dec. 24. — Striking in three widely separated sections of Arkansas late last night and early today, tornadoes caused considerable property damage and injury to at least three persons. The town of England in Lonoke county bore the brunt of the storm. A tornado unrooted or otherwise damaged more than 30 dwellings there and injured two persons. At Hampton, in Calhoun county, the Baptist church and a filling station were wrecked and several houses damaged. Mrs. C. L. Poole, wife of a state senator, was injured. A tornado struck a mile north of Mountain Home, in Baxter county, wrecking a house occupied by Bill Hubbard. A bed on which members of the Hubbard family were sleeping was hurled through the front part of the house but no one was injured.
