Lee emphasizes the great resemblance between “the early books of the Old Testament and the Popol Vuh, Mexico's book of ancient legends

SHANGHAI, March 25. (#i— Sino-Japanese peace negotiations lagged perceptibly today, while armies of the two nations engaged in sniping and skirmishing a few miles outside Shanghai. Each blamed the other for a clash between outposts near Kating, and neither had an official explanation of sniping between troops in the vicinity of Chiawangmiao, incidents which added to the general uneasiness. The Chinese defied the 13% mile limit ultimatum of the Japanese when they occupied Chia-Wangmiao recently, and they have shown no disposition to retire across Soochow Creek as the Japanese have demanded. The delegates—Chinese, Japanese and neutrals alike—emerged from a three hour session of peace negotiations with weariness written on their faces, although the official communique noted, as usual, “some progress was made.” The Chinese insisted there was no advance in negotiations.

SHANGHAI, Dec. 24. — Richard Stewart Hooker, commander of American marines stationed in the Shanghai area, dropped dead at his home here today a few minutes after he had returned from a Christmas shopping trip with his wife. Heart disease was believed to have caused his death. He had been in apparently excellent health.

Bombay, India, March 29.—(#)— Meher Baba, the Indian spiritual leader whose disciples call him “The Messiah” and “The God Man,” left here today for a new crusade in America. He intends, he said, to break down all religious barriers, destroy America’s materialism and amalgamate all creed into a common element of love. For eight years Meher Baba has been observing a vow of silence, which he said he would break upon his arrival at Harmon, N. Y., where he plans to establish a spiritual retreat similar to Mahatma Gandhi's in India. Giving his first interview to an Associated Press correspondent by means of a blackboard, Meher Baba, who in the eyes of his followers has performed many miracles, said Gandhi had promised to come with him to the United States as soon as his political work has been finished a year hence. Many Indians regard Meher Baba as Gandhi's guru, or spiritual adviser. Meher B

1932-04-17.text: STOCKHOLM, April 16.—()—Three men alleged to have been connected with the operations of the Kreuger interests were under arrest today after new developments in the investigation of the affairs of the late Swedish match king, who committed suicide in Paris March 12. Another important development in the inquiry was a report that a large amount of forged Italian government bonds had been found in Mr. Kreuger’s effects. The three arrested were Carl Lange, a director of the Garanta company of Amsterdam, Sven Huldt of the Nederlanska Bank for Scandinavian Commerce, and a man named Victor Holm, described as a director, whose connection with the Kreuger interests was not explained.

WINNIPEG, Man. —(#)— One prisoner was killed and two others were wounded in the first serious riot in the history of Stoney Mountain penitentiary late Friday, Warden William Meighen announced Saturday. Chief Keeper Thomas Clayton also was injured. Mike Bihun, imprisoned for bank robbery, was shot in the chest and killed in the prison yard by guards stationed on the prison wall. T. Jones and William Corda, charged by prison officials with having been the leaders in the uprising, were wounded in the legs by bullets from the guns of guards.

AUCKLAND, New Zealand, April 16.—The mayor of Auckland issued an order today prohibiting all public meetings, in the face of threats by unemployed rioters to hold an assembly tomorrow. At the same time, the mayor announced he would read the riot act to keep spectators off the streets where they hampered efforts of the police by affording a retreat within their own ranks for the rioters. His action followed renewed fighting yesterday between mobs of unemployed and forces of police, marines, and special constables on horse and foot, in which 58 plate glass shop windows were broken. For three hours again last night there was pandemonium in the streets as the unemployed throngs renewed their battle. After order was restored, a check-up showed that 130 rioters and 2 police had been hurt. Property damage was estimated at over $500,000.

SHANGHAI, April 17. (Sunday) — Twenty Japanese soldiers were killed, the Chinese military authorities announced today, in a skirmish with a detachment of the 19th Route Army at a place called Yanglingkow, northwest of Liuho. The Chinese said the Japanese attempted an advance which the Chinese repulsed. There also was another skirmish near Nanziang, but none was killed.

BUCHAREST, April 16 (AP)—The royal chateau of Foisor, summer residence of King Carol at Sinaia, was destroyed by fire early today. The fire is believed to have been caused by carelessness of workers who were repairing the chateau.

Stockholm, Sweden, April 18 (AP)—Forged bonds, dummy directors, fictitious assets and non-existent features "among the mounting allegations piled up" today in connection with the investigation into the affairs of the late Ivar Kreuger, Swedish industrialist, whose suicide in Paris last month precipitated one of the sensational financial dramas of the last few decades. Experts who have completed their investigation into the alleged forgery of Italian bonds said that $3 Treasury bonds of £500,000 each were forged by Mr. Kreuger and that he alone was responsible. Computed by normal exchange rates, these bonds would aggregate about £100,000,000. "The experts asserted that only Mr. Kreuger knew the truth concerning the bonds, which were in English and ostensibly signed by the Italian monopolies board. The forged signature of Ricci Decili on the papers was clumsily done; the errors being easil

BERLIN, Apr. 16 — President von Hindenburg, who dissolved the national socialist storm troops by decree this week, today instructed the authorities to investigate accusations that other political units are maintaining military relations calculated to undermine the authority of the state. His order mentioned no names but it was understood that the investigation would be directed particularly into charges against the republican Reichsbanner.

Washington — Activity toward resubmission of the Eighteenth Amendment showed itself Saturday as an increasing factor in the political preparations for the June conventions of the Republican and Democratic parties. At the Capitol, where hearings are in progress looking to an early vote by the Senate on resubmission, the two Wyoming senators joined in announcing themselves desirous of placing the prohibition question before the people. Both Kendrick, the Democrat, and Carey, Republican, have dry records behind them. In Richmond, Va., Bishop James Cannon, Jr., one of the most active dry leaders, announced himself in substantial agreement with the "basal features" of the plan advanced by Former Governor Harry F. Byrd at this week’s Jefferson Day Democratic rally in Washington to make possible a popular vote on prohibition. Hearing of this, Byrd said he believed that having extreme drys as (C

1932-09-02.text: BISHOP, Sept. 2.—To the Editor of The Californian: Everybody has been denying that they saw this fellow Norman, the head of the Bank of England. Hoover says if he saw him it was under an assumed name. Melion says he never heard of him, so the whole thing is just a rumor. Mr. Norman wasn’t in America at all. The orange squeezers out in California went for the Democratic ticket here the other day like they did in the old days when they were Republicans. The rest of the country certainly got even with California. They had an eclipse and if you ever saw a thing leave anyone flat, it left us. The chamber of commerce has already taken it up. New England got the whole thing. It's their first show since the Plymouth Rock 'fiasco.' Yours, WILL ROGERS.

BROOKLINE, Mass., Sept. 2.—(P) — The United States today clinched the Walker Cup, British-American golf trophy, as Captain Francis Ouimet halved his 36-hole singles match with Tony Torrance, British leader, after six successive victories in the two-day competition for the home forces. It was the seventh straight triumph in the international series for the Americans in ten years.

(By the Associated Press) Harrisburg, Sept. 1—Robert S. Gawthrop of West Chester, a member of the Superior Court for 11 years, today was appointed counsel for the special committee, named by the Senate to investigate the Public Service Commission. Gawthrop is in London. A relative at West Chester said tonight that he did not know whether the appointee would accept the place, which would require his resignation from the Superior Court bench. Committee members said he had not been consulted in advance of the appointment, so they too were uncertain whether he would take it. He is due to retire from the Superior Court in January, having lost a campaign for Republican renomination in the spring primary. Split Over Selection The Republican organization approved the investigation in the closing week of this summer's eight weeks’ session of the legislature. Its hand was forced by Governor Pincho

Quebec, Que. Sept. 1. ()—Captain J. A. Mollison, trans-Atlantic flier, landed his tiny plane at St. Louis airport here at 5:25 p. m. (Eastern Standard Time) today after a flight from Sidney, N. S. The British aviator, who abandoned his plan to fly back to England at the request of his wife, the former Amy Johnson, and the advice of his physician, will go home by steamer from here.

QUEBEC, Sept. 2 (UP).—Captain James A. Mollison, first man to fly the Atlantic westward alone, arrived late yesterday from Sydney, N. S., and will go home tomorrow aboard the Empress of Britain. He abandoned his projected return flight at the behest of his wife, the former Amy Johnson, and a physician.

York, England, Sept. 2—(P)—If engineers and scientists ruled the world, there would be no depression, no poverty, and much more happiness, Prof. Miles Walker today told the British Association of the Advancement of Science. He suggested that the British government organize an experimental, self-supporting colony under the auspices of engineers, scientists and economists "to ascertain how far it is possible with our present knowledge and the best methods of manufacturing to enable a group of 100,000 persons to maintain themselves and continually increase their wealth when freed from restraints and social errors of modern civilization." If the experiments proved successful on a small scale, it could be gradually extended to cover the entire world, he said. Answering the question "what is wrong with the world?" Prof. Walker listed three evils; poverty in material possessions, poverty in out

BERLIN, Germany, Sept. 2.—The five fascists who were condemned to death at Beuthen last week on a charge of murdering a communist during a political brawl, received a commutation to life imprisonment when the federal commissioner reviewed their case today. Chancellor von Papen presided at the conference which decided to show mercy to the men who were condemned under the emergency decree of Aug. 9, providing capital punishment for crimes of political violence. The men were charged with the murder of a communist. During the trial, it was established that the crime was committed only a day and a half after the emergency decree became effective. With that fact in mind, the commissioners decided to yield to the petitions for clemency which had been submitted by numerous organizations. It seemed likely that they were influenced also by the consideration that Adolf Hitler's national socialists

BERLIN (U.P) — Death sentences given to five members of Adolf Hitler’s fascist party were commuted Friday to life imprisonment. The five men were convicted of political terrorism by the special court at Beuthen. They were sentenced to be executed by axe men. The sentences, passed Aug. 27, had been the cause of further serious political troubles.

1932-12-21.text: Paris, Dec. 21—(2)—Great Britain will informally counsel France against pursuing an idea under consideration by officials of having the question of payment of the December interest on the American debt submitted to arbitration, according to reports in diplomatic circles. It is stated that the British feel this would not in the long run contribute to successful settlement of the debt problem and that resort to arbitration would be undesirable because it would be founded on the presumption that the question cannot be settled through the regular diplomatic channels. However, the British are said to be strong for the French idea that a general conference or general negotiations should be adopted for treating the debts. The general situation lined up today about as follows: First, the French attitude is to keep negotiations with America actively going. Second, eventually to try to move toward

LONDON, Dec. 21, — (U.P) — Crown Prince Michael of Roumania disliked the nose on a bust of himself, almost completed, so he knocked the nose off with a hammer, the Daily Mail correspondent at Vienna reported today. Servants found the noseless bust at Bucharest and called police, who began an investigation of a supposed political outrage, the correspondent said. Later the prince told his father, King Carol, that he was the culprit.

London, Dec. 21.—(#)—Lady Furness, an American beauty who married into the English peerage, filed suit for divorce today against her husband, the shipbuilding magnate, The Associated Press was informed that the grounds for the suit will be misconduct. The suit is expected to be heard at the next term of court, but the hearing probably will be quiet, with no more publicity than is necessary. Lady Furness, formerly Mrs. Thelma Morgan Converse, is a sister of Mrs. Reginald Vanderbilt of New York and of Mrs. Benjamin Thaw, Jr., of Pittsburgh. She was married to Lord Furness in 1926.

LONDON, Dec. 21--(AP)—The use of wheat as a basis for money would double the price of the grain and provide a swift avenue for return of prosperity, believes J. P. Darling, a director of the Midland Bank, and of England’s important financial institutions. Darling, who would link wheat to gold and silver, believes "that in wheat as a basis for currency we possess an even more powerful instrument for raising prices and stimulating world trade." "Wheat," he declared when announcing the plan, "has in a marked degree one of the qualities of a currency basis in that it is in universal demand and has a worldwide market." There would be a central superbank as custodian for such wheat and gold and silver as formed the basis for the currency. His plan—as advanced—considers only the British Empire and would use 300,000,000 bushels of wheat. "Debts could then be settled by a debt and credit in the l

CHERBOURG, France, Dec. 21 — The liner Majestic is sailing today with 139 cases of gold valued approximately at $3,500,000 consigned to American banks. A large shipment of gold from the British government in payment of the Dec. 15 war debt interest also was reported to be aboard the Majestic. DOORN, Holland, Dec. 21 (?).— The former German Kaiser Wilhelm II, suffering from a cold and rheumatism, was confined to his room in Doorn Castle today by order of his court physician.
Seaham, England (UP)—The captain and seven men from the crew of the British steamer Gateshead were drowned today when the steamer sank near here after a collision with a Norwegian boat.

Paris.—(AP)—Another phase of France’s financial dilemma—a proposed loan to Austria—pressed forward today for a decision while responsible leaders hoped for early settlement of the American debt problem. The two problems were linked by deputies who asked how France could make the loan to Austria when it refused to pay a sum only twice as great to the United States last week. The League of Nations approved a $43,000,000 loan to Austria last July at the Lausanne conference, to be raised by member nations. France's share in this loan, intended to save Austria from a perilous financial situation, was 250,000,000 francs, or about $9,750,000. Within the next ten days a decision is to be reached by the French government on whether the loan should be made. Deputies who favored making the interest payment of more than $19,000,000 to the United States last Thursday raised the question of grounds fo

Doorn, Holland, Dec. 21.—The former German Kaiser Wilhelm II, suffering from a cold and rheumatism, was confined to his room in Doorn castle today by order of his court physician. Measures to guard him against future intruders have been again intensified. (A German, believed by the police to be mentally deranged, was caught crouching in a castle room recently with a dagger and pistol on his person). All locks to outer gates and also to some of the doors of the castle itself have been renewed. Dogs on Job Chains by which the dogs were kept in the grounds have been lengthened in order to enable the animals to intercept suspected persons at longer range.

1932-12-22.text: By The Associated Press Athens, Greece, Dec. 22—Hearings in extradition proceedings against Samuel Insull will begin Tuesday it was decided today by the court of appeals. This date was fixed after attorneys for Insull requested time to study the defense and prepare the case.

PARIS, Dec. 22. — The ministerial declaration prepared by the new cabinet says the Paul-Boncour government will bend every effort to a general settlement of the war debt problem. But in view of the political situation in the United States, the declaration warns, the negotiations must be conducted with extreme prudence. The text of the declaration on debts reads: "The second of the essential tasks imposed upon us is the general settlement of the war debt question.

PARIS, Dec. 22—Joseph Paul-Boncour's new cabinet made its bid for support of the chamber of deputies today in a vague declaration of policy that dodged immediate consideration of France’s default on her overdue $20,000,000 debt payment to the United States. The new government's declaration pledged it to seek ‘a general settlement’ of debts that will be ‘mutually satisfactory’ to the nations involved, but promises little more than continued negotiations on the question of intergovernmental obligations. The ministerial declaration, published before its presentation to parliament, cited the present domestic political situation in the United States as one reason for moving slowly. “We believe,” it said, “that the present domestic circumstances, as well as the complexity of the political situation in the United States, require extreme prudence in the negotiations whose course was marked by th

Paris, Dec. 21.— (4) —Premier Joseph Paul-Boncour spent the day putting the finishing touches with his cabinet to the ministerial declaration which will be presented to parliament tomorrow, two of the chief problems being debts and the budget. Best informed quarters expect he will refer to the debts briefly, taking the position that it is indispensable to continue negotiations with the United States. The chamber of deputies’ recent vote deferring payment undoubtedly will be accepted as the guide for these negotiations. No interpellations on debts have yet been introduced, but it is likely Louis Marin and Henry Franklin-Bouillon, both bitterly hostile to payment, may press the premier to explain conditions under which negotiations are proceeding. It is expected M. Paul-Boncour in his reply will tell the chamber he will report when he has something definite. The disposition continues in ch

Berlin, Dec. 22.—An alleged widespread plot against the Soviet dictatorship of Joseph Stalin, resulting in scores of arrests and deportations, was reported by the Czarist Russian newspaper bulletin here today. The newspapers charged that among these exiled to Siberia was Gregory Zinovieff, former president of the Communist Internationale. Reports spread through Europe a few weeks ago that Zinovieff had died suddenly but the Soviet foreign office denied them. In addition, the bulletin charged three members of the Soviet council of commissars have been taken into custody for alleged complicity.

: Pella, Ia., Dec. 22—(U.P.)—Not content with a 10 per cent cut in water and electricity rates three months ago, the city council has lightened December bills to city residents by 50 per cent, a total of $3,500. The city owns its own utilities.

ROME, Dec. 21. (AP) — An unexplained explosion in a dump of 100 aeronautic light flares at Fort Appio killed seven persons tonight. Eighteen laborers were missing. - Suspicion was aroused that the explosion may have been of criminal intent. Simultaneous with this blast, the explosion of an artillery projectile on a practice field forty miles away killed five soldiers.

WASHINGTON, Dec. 22. (UP)—A presidential veto today appeared to be the one real obstacle in the way of swift modification of national prohibition. Authoritative polls indicated the Senate, after much argument, probably would follow the lead of the House which, with unprecedented speed, passed the Collier bill legalizing 3.2 beer. The dramatic House vote yesterday was the first genuine wet victory in Congress since passage of the Volstead Act more than a decade ago. Yet anti-prohibitionist leaders, elated as they were, felt they had won a sham battle as far as this session was concerned. Authoritative and undenied information has reached the Capitol that President Hoover under no conditions will sign any sort of a beer bill. Modificationists, although now in the majority, lack the two-thirds strength necessary to override a veto. Hence it is believed beer will have to wait for the new Dem

1932-12-30.text: NEW DELHI, INDIA, Dec. 3.—()—Reports from London that the viceroy, the Earl of Willingdon, was to resign and that Mahatma Gandhi was to be released Jan. 1 were described here today as “pure inventions.” It was stated authoritatively that the government of India has received no communication from London authorities about Gandhi, who is imprisoned at Poona, and that there has been no change of policy in this matter.

Moscow, Dec. 29.—(AP)—Russian housewives who now may purchase for themselves small rations of bread and sugar from the government stores, will lose that privilege after Jan. 1, and thereafter will have to earn those commodities by working in the factories. The government decreed today that after the first of the year all housewives under the age of 56 will be deprived of the cards which entitle them to purchase sugar and bread. In the category of housewives are included all healthy women not engaged in ‘socially useful’ work. The wives of a number of high government officials are in this class. “No Work—No Food” The new order reflects the continuing food shortage and is an extension of the government’s ‘no work-no food’ policy. Its object, apparently, is to bring more women into industrial occupations with a view to ultimate abolition of the home as the unit of family life.

ADELAIDE, Australia, Dec. 30, (P)—Unemployed white men, who have “gone native” and joined roving aboriginal tribes, may have a profound influence on these stone age nomads. L. A. Wells, explorer, who has returned from a trek through the wildest parts of Australia, says he was surprised to find that many tribes included one or two white men. They were naked and almost black from exposure to the sun and were living in accordance with native customs. They were able to improve on the age-old methods of hunting and trapping and had brought to the tribes a knowledge of the conservation of food and cultivation of vegetables. By making the tribal food supply more plentiful and certain these whites, it is believed, may save many of the tribes from decay and extinction.
PARIS, Dec. 30 (AP) — Parliament adjourned today until Jan. 10 after both houses had approved a government proposal to participate to the extent of $14,000,000 in aid to Austria.

Johannesburg, Dec. 30.—Mrs. Daisey de Melker, wife of a well-known rugby football player, was hanged here today. A jury had convicted her of putting poison in her son's coffee. She previously had been acquitted on charges of murdering her two former husbands.

Phoenix, Ariz., Dec. 30.—(A. P.)—J. J. Halloran, Phoenix lumberman and sportsman, was indicted by the grand jury today in connection with the Winnie Ruth Judd murder case, and shortly afterward accepted a bench warrant, charging he was an accessory in the slaying of Agnes Anne LeRoi and Hedvig Samuelson. Halloran appeared at the courthouse and posted $3,000 bond. He was released pending preliminary hearing next Tuesday. The charge against the lumberman was based on alleged attempted concealment of a crime. He was not charged with implication in the slayings themselves. The maximum penalty upon conviction would be five years’ imprisonment. The indictment came two days after Winnie Ruth Judd, condemned to die Feb. 17 for the slaying of Mrs. LeRoi, and under a second charge of murder in connection with the death of Miss Samuelson, appeared before the grand jury. Specifically, the true bill

FORT HUACHUCA, Ariz., Dec. 20. (P)—The brooding of a Negro soldier over his demotion from sergeant to private was advanced today as a possible motive for the negro’s slaying of two army captains and their wives at this historic post. Another white officer was wounded late yesterday before the soldier was shot and killed by a negro corporal of the Provost guard. Although the official statement suggested no motive, the investigating board of officers was emphatic in stating “no breach of discipline” was involved. The dead: Captain Joseph P. Wessely, 45, of San Antonio, Tex., 25th infantry, assistant to the post quartermaster, Mrs. Wessely, wife of the slain officer, of Cedar Rapids, Iowa. Captain David A. Palmer, 42, of Beverly, Mass., in command of Company M, 25th infantry. Mrs. Palmer, wife of Captain Palmer, the former Miss Mary Lowden of Dedham, Mass. James H. Abernathy, negro private,

WASHINGTON, Dec. 30. (AP)—General reorganization of the federal government in the interests of economy will be undertaken by President-elect Roosevelt after he takes office March 4. This became evident after house democrats had proposed that he be given such broad authority and word came from Albany that the governor was ready to assume full responsibility. To this end, the democratic leaders prepared today to block the regrouping program submitted to congress in a special message by President Hoover. A resolution will be offered in the house soon after Jan. 1 for this purpose and, with democrats in control, its adoption seems assured. Parley to Hew Course. The reorganization proposal was put forward yesterday as one means of bringing the federal budget into

1932-12-15.text: England, America’s largest European debtor, has decided to pay in gold the debt installment due today. Italy already has paid, France and Belgium have decided not to pay and Poland has indicated that it will default. In London the chancellor of the exchequer told Parliament default on this payment was unthinkable, that arrangements have been made with the Federal Reserve Bank to meet it, but that this device was not to be interpreted as meaning a return to the debt system in operation before the Hoover moratorium. France was without a government, Premier Herriot having been overthrown by the Chamber of Deputies. He sent word to Washington that he can carry on only current affairs now and that it will be up to the next government to continue the debt negotiations. At Rome there was an announcement that Italy already had paid the $1,245,437 interest installment she owed. In Brussels a new

LONDON, Dec. 15. (4—Great Britain today paid its war debt installment of $95,550,000 in gold to the United States. It was a routine banking transaction, completed as the tumult of the controversy which raged for the past month subsided and merged into the beginnings of the Christmas season. No flourish of gold pen, no clicking cameras, no grouping of high officials marked the event which may be epochal in international financial relationships. It was only a routine banking matter to the men who carried the transaction to completion at the Bank of England while federal reserve officials in New York and Washington acted for the United States government. The old lady of Threadneedle Street, who never is loquacious, held her tongue so well today that no one could say exactly at what moment the payment was completed. No dramatic circumstances accompanied the payment. The House of Commons, hav

BOSTON, Dec. 14 — The Coast Guard put to sea today to intercept one of the greatest rum running invasions ever attempted in the history of prohibition. Coast Guard headquarters was aware of the presence of 66 liquor-laden craft off the New England coast and southward to Cape May, N. J., and there was good reason to believe other contraband-carrying vessels soon would join the fleet. All the liquor-laden fleet was said to be well outside the 12-mile limit and it was to keep it there that five destroyers and nine 125-foot offshore patrol boats left this port. Other government craft will hasten to join the blockade. The rum fleet, according to Captain William H. Hunter of Coast Guard headquarters, includes motor ships, schooners and various other types of shipping. Off the Massachusetts coast alone, he said were 22 vessels with liquor cargoes.

Oran, Algeria, Dec. 14. ()—Unfavorable weather forced Amy Johnson, flying from Cape Town to England, to land today at Beniqunif, Morocco. She planned to resume her flight across the Atlas mountains to Oran as soon as the weather cleared. Miss Johnson, the wife of Captain J. A. Mollison, British trans-Atlantic flier, took off from Gao, French West Africa, Wednesday morning, hoping to reach Oran by night. She is attempting to make the Cape to England flight in less time than it took her recently when she set a new record from England to the Cape. That record is 4 days, 6 hours and 55 minutes.

LONDON, Dec. 14.—(AP)—England will pay its $95,550,000 debt instalment to the United States in gold tomorrow, Neville Chamberlain informed parliament today, communicating the decision which the government had reached independent of the House of Commons. The cabinet was unable even to contemplate default, he said, "for default by the British government on a sum which they could not truthfully say they were unable to pay would rebound all around the world. It might have been taken as justification for other defaults." Instead, he explained, arrangements for payment have been made with the Federal Reserve Bank. Tomorrow that institution will provide the amount of gold required by the American government, and the Bank of England simultaneously will earmark here an equivalent amount of gold for the account of the Federal Reserve. Later the gold will be shipped to the United States as required

Washington, Dec. 15—(U.N.)—The United States will carry on business as usual with nations which have defaulted war debt payments, Secretary of Treasury Mills said today after announcement of the payment of $95,550,000 due from Great Britain. The British ambassador, Sir Ronald Lindsay, called at the treasury to inform Mills that the $95,550,000 installment had been paid. A number of smaller European countries which owe smaller amounts were expected to make their payments through the federal reserve bank in New York later during the day. ‘Will Increase Treasury Deficit Mills said “the defaults by France and other countries will increase the deficit for the fiscal year 1933 by the amount they fail to pay.” In declaring the United States would carry on business as usual with defaulting countries, Mills cited the example of Russia and declared; “Russia has never paid a nickel on debts owed ma

LONDON, . 15—Deep in the vaults of the Bank of England, gold bars to the value of $95,550,000 were transferred from one storage place to another today, marking Britain’s payment of her debt installment to the United States. The momentous transaction, which has been the subject of international concern for weeks, was carried out without ceremony. The only outward evidence of the transfer behind the massive, unwindowed walls was a sheet of paper which was posted, containing the bank's weekly statement. The gold was earmarked as belonging to the Federal Reserve Bank of the United States. The Bank of England notified the Federal Reserve that it now owned the gold, and instructed the Federal Reserve to place the amount to the credit of J. P. Morgan & Co., financial agents of the British treasury in the United States. The Morgan house will pay it to the United States treasury at once. Brokers

WASHINGTON, Dec. 15—(UP)—Treasury officials today believed action looking toward revision of Great Britain’s war debt may be instituted soon in the Senate. Congressional leaders are quietly making a thorough study of the revision question, particularly with reference to Britain. Senator Pat Harrison, Dem., Miss., and several of his colleagues have called frequently at the Treasury during the last few days seeking data, the United Press learned. Payment Helps Cause The fact that Great Britain today is paying its full installment of $300,000 in gold, while France is defaulting on $19,000,000, is expected here to make for more favorable consideration of the British case. The 3.96 per cent interest rate charged Britain, contrasted with 1.64 per cent for France, also is an important factor. Treasury and Commerce Department officials feel that France’s default is “the least excusable of any Eu

1932-08-01.text: OTTAWA, Ont. Aug. 1—(P)— Heavy and open pressure was brought upon Great Britain's delegates to the Imperial conference today to force the hand of the mother country on what tariff preferences she is willing to give. N. C. Havenga of the South African delegation, in a blunt statement yesterday, virtually called upon the British delegation to quit talking about favors already shown the dominions and to get down to facts, The statement linked South Africa with Australia in the movement to bring the conference down to brass tacks, Havenga charged that Stanley Baldwin did not give a true picture of the situation when he declared last week that the union of South Africa had a favorable trade balance against the United Kingdom. Many delegates already have begun to talk of leaving here not later than August 15 and there was evidence today that the sub-committees were preparing to get down to ser

WASHINGTON, Aug. 1. —(P)—Ways of increasing the use of the five day week in industry and of spreading employment among a larger number of workmen were sought today at a conference with cabinet members by a group of New England leaders. Preliminary to a discussion with President Hoover tomorrow, the New Englanders conferred with Secretary Lamont at the commerce department and later with Secretary Doak at the labor department. The chief executive, resting at his mountain retreat on the Rapidan river, named the cabinet members to act for him until his return to the capital. He has promised to meet with the delegation.

Ottawa, Ont., July 31.--(AP)— South Africa fired a shot at the United Kingdom today in a statement construed here as virtually calling upon the British delegations to quit talking about favors Great Britain has shown dominions and get down to the business of the Imperial Economic conference. Thus the Union of South Africa joined Australia today in differing with Stanley Baldwin on the point of the United Kingdom's attitude toward the dominions as expressed in statistics of exports and imports, Stanley Bruce of Australia at the outset declared the United Kingdom had been tardy in reciprocating preferential treatment by the dominions, Not So Today N. C. Havenga of the South African delegation denied the Union enjoyed a favorable balance of trade with the United Kingdom. He took to task the British view as expressed by Baldwin last week that the record would not substantiate any claim that

Not Cramer's Clothing, London, Aug. 2---Clothing worn by a dead aviator picked up off the Scottish coast indicated the body was that of an obscure Englishman or Scot, and not Parker Cramer, American flier lost on a Detroit-Copenhagen hop a year ago.

Hitler’s push for complete power in Germany was stopped today. The question, after yesterday's elections, was whether the present government under the Junker-Soldier Gen. Von Schleicher would continue or whether Hitler could negotiate an alliance with former Chancellor Heinrich Bruening. Hitler and his Nazi followers doubled their strength in the Reichstag over four years ago, but fell far short of achieving the clear majority they sought, receiving little more than one-third of the total vote. The official apportionment of seats indicated the new Reichstag will have 607 members, distributed among the parties as follows: Nazis 230, socialists 133, centrists and Bavarian people's party 2, economic party 2, agricultural alliance 2, farmers’ federation 2, communists 89, nationalists 37, populists 7, Christian socialists 4, state’s party 2, farmers’ party 2. HARBIN, Manchuria (#7) — General Ma Chan-Shan, unlettered former governor of the province of Heilung-Kiang and twice leader of the Northern Manchurian armies against Japan, is dead, his body riddled with Japanese bullets. He died with his boots on, they said, this former bandit whose name blazed briefly across the first pages of newspapers throughout the world last Fall when the Japanese invasion of Manchuria began. His body was found last Wednesday in a mud hut in the squalid little village of An-Kuchen, 40 miles northeast of Hailun, his staff officers piled in pools of blood around him, his army, which once numbered 20,000 men, entirely wiped out. Trapped between two Japanese divisions which had relentlessly pursued him since the day he left the cabinet of Henry Pu-Yi at Changchun and went back again to the north to renew his fight against the invaders, he and his army fought gallantly

(WORLD COPYRIGHT, 1932, BY THE UNITED PRESS) Paris, July 30,—(UP)—America need have no fear that a European bloc has been formed to drive a bargain with the United States on payment of war debts, Premier Edouard Herriot said today in an exclusive interview with the United Press. In doing so, he said: 1—The impression that France has an agreement to act jointly with Britain in dealing with war debts owed the United States is false. 2—The Lausanne settlement is provisional within the framework of a world settlement of the question of international debts. 3—So far as Herriot is concerned, no further move will be made regarding the debt situation until after the presidential election in the United States, he said in his office at the Quai D'Orsay. Herriot himself offered a contrast with the gold and crystal atmosphere of the office. Herriot was informed that many conflicting reports regardin

BERLIN, Aug. 2—-(Monday)— (AP)—The German people brought to an end a bloody election campaign today with a forthright refusal to entrust the fate of the nation to any one of the 21 political parties of the Reich—not even to the Nazis of Adolf Hitler. This means that the so-called “neutral cabinet” of Franz Von Papen, with the strong shadow of General Kurt Von Schleicher behind it, probably will continue to rule Germany. But the brown-shirted little Nazi, who promised the voters he would rule Germany alone after the elections of yesterday, gained a tremendous victory compared with his standing in 1930. Hitler will hold 229 seats of the 589 seats in the new Reichstag, whereas he held only 107 in the 1930 Reichstag. But Hitler’s strength represents only 37 per cent of the entire vote and the only way he could ascend to immediate power would be to join a coalition, and he solemnly promised n

1932-09-25.text: MOBCOW, Sept. 24. UP Rhea Clyman, expelled for articles she wrote for a newspaper, left tonight for London. A representative of the British Embassy accompanied her.

SHANGHAI, Aug. 22 (4)—Chinese dispatches from Peking and other North China points today said the Japanese forces in Manchuria had launched a strong military thrust into Jehol, the province that borders on China proper. The dispatches said fighting was going on along a “broad portion” of the Jehol eastern border, with the Chinese falling back before Japanese artillery, airplanes and machine guns. Japanese bombing planes were reported as spreading terror among the border population, which was streaming into the open country seeking safety.

POONA, India, Sept. 24 (P.— Physicians attending Mahatma Mohandas K. Gandhi, who is fasting for the principle of citizenship equality in India, tonight announced their patient’s blood pressure had increased, and that continued absence from food 48 hours longer would endanger the life of the 62-year-old nationalist. This announcement came as the Mahatma, lying on his bed under a mango tree in his yard, had raised his weak body on his elbow and smilingly signalled assent to a compromise Indian electoral plan designed to put an end to his death fast. The compromise had been effected by leaders of the caste Hindus and the untouchables who had been striving for three days to reach an agreement acceptable to Gandhi. Gandhi was so weak he was not bothered with the detail of watching the formality of signatures. Indian leaders, uneasy as to whether the British prime minister, Ramsay MacDonald, w

GENEVA, Dec. 8. (*)—Yosuke Matsuoka, Japan's special counsel, threatened “unforeseen consequences” if the assembly of the League of Nations adopted a proposed resolution condemning Japan’s policy in Manchuria. He made the statement to the assembly today. Matsuoka demanded that the authors of the resolution withdraw it or that the assembly vote on it immediately. Some observers present recalled that authoritative sources in Tokyo said Japan may be forced to withdraw from the league if her Manchurian policy was endangered. Matsuoka said the assembly's purpose should be to seek a conciliatory settlement and that the resolution, submitted by Spain, the Irish Free State, Sweden and Czechoslovakia, would be hostile to this purpose. “If it is adopted it will have consequences unforeseen by the authors,” he said. Geneva, Sept. 4.—(P)—The League of Nations council today postponed consideration of the Lytton report on the Sino-Japanese conflict in Manchuria until Nov. 14, giving Japan and other league members six weeks to study this important document after its publication Oct. 1. China's plea as voiced by W. W. Yen, that only the assembly itself was competent to make such a decision, was denied. H. Nagaoka, the Japanese delegate, did his utmost to obtain further time. He spoke of floods, slow transportation, translations and the like, and his anxiety to stretch the delay became so obvious that the councilmen joined the public in general laughter. The Japanese himself smiled amiably, "Nothing to say." The critical Far Eastern problem was not the only one placed in suspense today. DES MOINES, la., Aug. 24—(/P) —Two victories marked the course of the Mid-West farm strike for higher prices today, as the movement spread in some quarters and receded in others. Interference with rail transportation continued. Both victories were scored in Nebraska, where milk producers gained higher prices for their products. At Omaha, officials of the Iowa-Nebraska Cooperative Milk Association consented to pay $2 a hundredweight for milk, compared with a previous top of $1.45, while at Lincoln milk dealers agreed to pay $1.80, an increase of 49 cents over the previous figure. More than 1,900 agriculturists were assembled in camps along the main highways leading into Omaha, but there were reports that some of the picketers were in a dispute as to the best method of enforcing the farmers’ holiday. GIBRALTAR, Aug. 22 -- Five young landlubbers, all undergraduates of Princeton University, have conquered the Atlantic on a two-master in 49 days despite storm and calm. The adventure began in New York July 2, and will end, for the time being at least, in Marseilles, when the craft reaches there. The venturesome team lost five sails in a heavy blow and spent 14 days in various spots of dead calm. They are: William Drewrey, New York; William L. Crow, New York; Standish Backus, Detroit; Ashley Hardy, Boston, and Robert Keldle, Baltimore. Here is the story of the adventure from Drewrey: "We sailed from New York July 2, reaching Marblehead five days later. We made the Azores July 28, leaving for Tangiers July 31, and arriving there Aug. 16. We reached Gibraltar Saturday for provisions. 1932-10-09.text: NEW YORK, Oct. 13. (4—Alfred E. Smith, beginning next week, will make six speeches in behalf of the Democratic State and National tickets, his office announced today. Smith will speak in New England, New Jersey and in New York State.

The search for Samuel Insull extended across Europe Saturday while his brother, Martin J., went home from a dingy Canadian jail cell. The search for the one-time London office boy who became one of the world’s greatest financiers was concentrated in the fast continental trains that speed across the South of France, bearing strangers to the gaming tables of Monte Carlo and the Riviera. Both Missing No trace had been found of either Samuel Insull or his son. The wife and mother was in their Paris hotel. She would not say where they were. The search was localized largely in Portugal and Italy. Meantime, Martin Insull was freed from the jail to which he had been taken as a result of the inquiry into conditions of the companies he once headed. He still said he would not come back to the United States willingly to face charges. The Chicago phase of the Insull attack progressed slowly. A court

BARRIE, Ont., Oct. 8. Martin J. Insull’s plea that he is a sick man and that it would be impossible for him to escape from Canada, won him freedom in $50,000 bail today pending a hearing on extradition proceedings that will determine whether he must return to Chicago to face an indictment for embezzlement and grand larceny growing out of the collapse of the Insull utilities empire. The Chicagoan’s plea was presented by J. C. McRuer, Toronto attorney, who submitted medical affidavits saying that if his client spent any more time in jail his health would suffer. Mr. Insull has been imprisoned since Thursday night. The granting of bail was a set-back for the prosecution, Edward Bayly, assistant attorney general of Ontario, appearing before Justice ~~, Holmes as special counsel for the state of Illinois, asserted that the court had exceeded its jurisdiction by liberating Mr. Insull. Paris, Oct. 8.—(#)—Dispatches from Geneva tonight said the French delegation there had formulated a plan linking the ideas of universal security and progressive disarmament over a 10-year period. The Havas (French) agency in a Geneva report said Premier Edouard Herriot of France would make a speech in Alsace tomorrow that would contain special mention of the French suggestion. It was added that the plan would be offered to the world disarmament (Continued on Page 3. Sec 2)

By The Associated Press Cleveland, O., Oct. 8.—Two gunmen attempting to rob a downtown jewel house were run down by police today and one of them killed after a mad three mile automobile chase across town in which seven other persons, including a mother and her daughter, were shot or injured. The dead bandit was identified by the bureau of criminal identification as Norman Townsend, 34, of Detroit, suspected bank robber. The injured are: Herbert Quinlan, 38, jeweler, shot through abdomen, condition feared fatal, Patrolman Fred Blazier, shot through abdomen, also believed fatally injured. Miss Beverly Martin, 15, injured when she jumped from a careening commandeered bandit car. Mrs. Florence Martin, mother of Beverly, injured in crash of bandit car. Detective Roy Heisley, shot in jaw. Francis (Mack) Bush, captured bandit and convicted bank robber, injured in jumping from bandit car. (Bush

CHICAGO, Oct. 8—(AP)—Frank McErlane, ruthless, mad killer who cheated the enemies that tried to kill him in his own way, died in bed today. Prosecutors of two states had tried to put him away for murder. His common law wife had shot and wounded him. Gunmen sought him out in his hospital bed, but their bullets failed. Pneumonia took him at last, in a hospital down at Beardstown, Ill., but a peaceful death was denied him even though it was natural. In his last hours he struggled violently, screamed in his delirium—fearing, perhaps, the foes of the underworld in which he had lived a violent life; fought against four strong men who endeavored to quiet him in his cot, and knocked out a nurse at his bedside. For 21 years he had been feared and hated as a cruel, wanton slayer. He had been the inventor of the gangland death ride, had helped engineer a famous jail-break, but had never been convic

JACKSONVILLE, Fla., Oct. 8 (A) —Testimony that bruises, which could not have been suffered in attempts to escape, covered the body of Arthur Maillefert, young New Jersey convict, after he was found strangled to death in a sweat box at a prison camp near here last June was given by undertakers today in the murder trial of two former convict guards. The testimony followed that of prisoners who said yesterday that the body bore the marks of whippings, and that camp officials hastily dressed the corpse to cover up bruises. Whipping is illegal in Florida prisons. Rules out Testimony Judge George C. Gibbs ruled out testimony that Maillefert had been whipped, but permitted to stand a statement that Solomon Higginbotham, one of the defendants, donated a shirt to dress the body because he was “anxious” to cover the George Courson, acting captain at the camp when Maillefert died, is the other defe

Hyde Park, N. Y., Oct. 8. (PF) — With Alfred E. Smith definitely aligned on his side for the remainder of the campaign, Franklin D. Roosevelt spent today among his neighbors of Dutchess County and recommended to them his old co-worker, Herbert H. Lehman, for the governorship. Appearing as the honored guest of the Franklin D. Roosevelt Home Club on a flag-swathed platform in the county fairgrounds at Washington Hollow, the Democratic presidential candidate told the several hundred persons of his home county about the cross-country campaign trip just finished and of his ideas of the economic interdependency of all sections of the country. The crowd grouped before him, lining the fence about the race track, sitting on the grass that bordered the track and half filling the bandstand behind him as the candidate outlined his views that all prosperity must flow from the raising of the economic

1932-03-29.text: Yesterday took at least 16 lives and caused widespread damage. Northern New England was speckled with stalled automobiles in snow several feet high. There and in upstate New York and Pennsylvania many communities were isolated. Schools didn’t keep, telephone poles toppled, blue birds met death in freezing winds, snow and rain. High waves gnashed at the Maine coast. At Harrisburg, Pa., a murderer got two and a half hours extra life when the current to the electric chair failed. A tornadic wind ripped down buildings in three towns near Richmond, Va., doing $100,000 damage. Leslie Dishman, 8, was killed when his home was shattered at Loretto, Va. Gov. Roosevelt was “snowbound” at Hyde Park, N. Y., and snow turning to rain undermined a five-story building at Peekskill and it collapsed. Cold rain kept all but 11,000 youngsters from the egg-rolling on the White House lawn. Last year there were

New York, March 28. (7)—Blizzards buffeted New England, gales swept the eastern seaboard, snowdrifts marooned Easter holiday motorists as Easter Monday became a belated winter day. Snow from 7 to 12 inches deep, the heaviest fall of the winter blanketed New Hampshire. In the Berkshires, drifts blocked many highways, and school children were gleeful over unexpected extension of Easter holidays. Many vacation parties were held snow-bound in the Pocono mountain resorts in Pennsylvania. Railroads sent out snow flangers for the second time this winter, and snowplows charged the wet drifts on highways. North of Lowell, Mass., a storm felled twenty-five telephone poles, cutting the city off from communication to points north. It blew down trees and ripped an advertising sign off a building. Game wardens at North Adams, Mass., reported flocks of early robins, bluebirds, and song sparrows died in

LONDON, March 29. (INS)— The shortest story which ever appeared in the Evening News was carried on its front page today in “covering” the Lindbergh kidnaping. It is doubtful whether a shorter story ever appeared anywhere. Under the heading “Lindbergh Baby,” the story simply said: “No news.”

LONDON, Mar. 29. (LP)--Popularity of the United States in Europe, at its highest peak of recent years when President Hoover announced his moratorium proposal, is heading rapidly toward a new low. Failure so far to balance the budget has resulted in many dire predictions. Abandonment of the gold standard: “Flight from the dollar,” complete impoverishment of the once mighty financial colossus; these are some of the forecasts one hears in London and continental capitals. Londoners refer to the gain of the pound sterling as “the fall of the dollar” instead of a rise in sterling, claiming that Europeans are selling out their dollar holdings and that Americans themselves have lost confidence and are buying sterling and Canadian dollars. The press has taken advantage of the situation to revive the anti-dollar campaigns which began when the United States failed to rehabilitate stricken Europe, a
| SHANGHAI, March 29.—British-owned newspapers here featured rumors today that the United States was preparing to go off the gold standard.

TOKYO (#)—It is learned the government has decided to refuse to furnish the League of Nations with a statement of its side of the controversy with China as required when China invoked Article 15 of the league covenant recently. Many observers believe the decision may result ultimately in Japan's withdrawal from the league. It is predicted that the Japanese delegation would not attend the next league session.

By The Associated Press Shanghai, March 29. —A new rupture in the Sino-Japanese armistice negotiations was threatened tonight with the issuance of a statement from the Japanese consulate ascribing the repeated delays in the conference to the fact that no Chinese delegate seems to be in a position or to be willing to assume responsibility.

Friedrichshafen, Germany, Mar. 29. (AP)--The Graf Zeppelin landed on her home field at 4:30 this afternoon, completing a round trip to Pernambuco, Brazil, with passengers and mail. It was the first of a series of South American flights scheduled for this spring.

1932-09-11.text: PORTLAND, Ore., Sept. 10. () —Action placing the American Legion on record in favor of immediate cash payment of the soldiers’ bonus was indicated tonight as delegates gathered for the 14th national convention opening Monday. Instructions given by state conventions, which with few exceptions, demanded payment at recent sessions, seemed to assure a reversal of the national organization’s attitude of last year when the bonus proposition was rejected after the legionnaires listened to an appeal from President Hoover and others at Detroit. Rank and File Adamant Sentiment among the rank and file for cash payment of the adjusted service certificates has grown steadily since a year ago, as evidenced at the department conventions, many of them held since the eviction of the bonus expeditionary force from the national ant. A floor fight on the bonus question is in prospect, however, as the vetera

NEW YORK, Sept. 10. (®)— Reiterating his prediction that Franklin D. Roosevelt will carry New York in the presidential election, James A. Farley, democratic national chairman, tonight expressed confidence the governor leaves on his western trip Monday with the state situation considerably improved by developments of the week. The chairman discussed the situation informally after his return from the state committee meeting in Albany. His optimism apparently was based on three developments: The state committee’s unanimous vote on a resolution introduced by John F. Curry, Tammany chief, which pledged New York democracy to the “active and loyal support” of the Roosevelt-Garner ticket. The good-will call which Curry and John H. McCooey, Brooklyn leader, made on the governor. McCooey’s visit to national headquarters, first made by any City organization leader—and his agreement to occupy a desk

By The Associated Press New York, Sept. 10.—Four men, including the co-owner of the old wooden steamer Observation, were held today as material witnesses in connection with the explosion of the ship yesterday which killed at least 41 workmen. Alexander Forsythe, whose father, George, lost his life on the boat which they owned together, was arraigned at a hospital and held under $25,000 bail. The others held were Walter Larsen, 27, and Victor Michaelson, former fireman on the Observation, who resigned after a few months’ service, and Otto Nelson, a deckhand who stayed on the pier to haul in the line when the vessel put out on its last trip. District Attorney Charles B. McLaughlin, who ordered the former firemen held, did not disclose why they had quit their jobs but said they gave him “valuable information.” They were ordered to appear before a grand jury Tuesday. In a federal investigati

AUSTIN, Tex. (AP)—Mrs. Miriam A. Ferguson, claimant to the democratic nomination for governor of Texas, lost her effort in the state supreme court Saturday to compel the party managers to certify her name as the nominee. Primary election, however, by her action a definition of lawful rules that guide the canvassing board which virtually precludes any contest of the tight race before the party executive committee or the state democratic convention on the grounds of ballot irregularities.

By The Associated Press DETROIT, Sept. 10.—One man was killed and 20 men and boys were injured, several seriously, when the roof of a shed from which 150 persons were viewing an automobile race collapsed today at the state fair grounds here.

Washington, Sept. 10.—()—The nation’s political focal point will shift Monday to Maine for the general elections there and then will pass on during the week to eight state primaries. Seven states, Arizona, Colorado, Vermont, Michigan, Washington, New Hampshire and Louisiana hold their primaries Tuesday and Georgia follows on Wednesday. Watch Maine. Unusual interest has been manifested in the Maine elections where a governor and three house members are to be chosen. National leaders of both parties have stumped the state in the most brisk campaign of many years. The Democrats are seeking to win the gubernatorial race with Louis J. Brann over Burleigh Martin, president of Maine’s Republican Senate. Republicans, however, (Continued on Page 1, Sec. 2)

| BRECKENRIDGE, Texas, Sept. 10, — Doy Arnold, 24, once sentenced to die for criminal assault and who later was pardoned from the Texas penitentiary, beat his ex-wife to death Saturday afternoon on the streets of Breckenridge, according to a complaint filed against him after he had surrendered. Court records show that the woman obtained a divorce from Arnold Friday. His ex-wife, Mrs. Zelma Arnold, 28, died from being struck over the head with a rock according to physicians who examined her at a hospital here. She lived only about 4 minutes after the attack. She also was stabbed in the abdomen but the physicians said this wound did not produce death. Arnold Surrenders Soon after the woman was injured, Doy went to Sheriff J. W. Morrow's office and surrendered. Witnesses who said they saw the beating stated that Arnold and his ex-wife had been standing on the street corner talking for about

By THE ASSOCIATED PRESS. Out of conflicting reports of operations in the long contested Chaco region of South America, there appeared evidence yesterday that Paraguayan and Bolivian troops were waging a bloody struggle for the strategic Fort Boquerón, in the heart of the lower Chaco. The struggle began on Friday and dispatches from Asuncion soon claimed Paraguayan troops had dislodged the Bolivian garrison at Boquerón. Paraguayan dispatches about the next phase of the situation stated that fighting continued Saturday near Boquerón. Bolivian Reports, Bolivian army communiques, however, told a different story. La Paz dispatches quoted them as saying Bolivian troops had routed the Paraguayan besiegers, and that there were many casualties.

1932-02-17.text: Bombay, India—/P—Madeline Slade, former London society girl who is now one of Mahatma Gandhi's chief aides and almost the only one still at liberty, was ordered by the government today to leave Bombay within 24 hours and to abstain from all unlawful activities. The order was signed by Sir Patrick Kelly, commissioner of police, and was issued under the emergency powers ordinance promulgated to put down Gandhi's civil disobedience campaign. Miss Slade, the daughter of a British admiral, was ordered not to return to Bombay without official permission. “Come any time Thursday morning and you will find me still here,” she was reported to have declared when confronted with the government’s order. “I don’t propose to leave Bombay to oblige the police commissioner and I shall carry on with my usual work. “If you are going to arrest me please don’t disturb my sleep at midnight.

Dublin—(A)—Intense excitement prevailed throughout the free state Wednesday as the people awaited the result of the count of ballots cast in yesterday's elections upon which hangs the fate of the government of President Cosgrave. Most observers expressed the belief that the margin for the winner, whether President Cosgrave or his rival, Eamonn De Valera, leader of the Fianna Fáil, would be very small. Some of the returns might be delayed for days, they said. Two boys, one 13 and one 16, were permitted to vote in Dublin when they appeared at a polling place and their names were found on the lists. A two-year-old baby whose name was inadvertently placed on the list was carried to a booth and voted.

DUBLIN, Irish Free State, Feb, 16, (P—-The Irish Free State, with intense excitement and sporadic disturbances, cast the heaviest vote in many years Tuesday in deciding whether President William T. Cosgrave should stay in office or turn over the power to Eamon de Valera and his Fianna.

(Copyright 1932, by Associated Press) Shanghai, China, Feb. 17. — (Wednesday) — Big guns blazed in battle over the entire Shanghai front today after an all-night artillery duel that shook the city, hurled shells into the area patrolled by United States marines and wounded two British bluejackets. Japanese naval headquarters said the Chinese had unlimbered the heaviest artillery thus far used in a tremendous attempt to wipe out the Japanese-occupied Hongkew section of the international settlement, causing Japanese casualties and considerable damage. Chinese Bombardment Severe The battle was fought along a line reaching from Chanei to Kiangwan, halfway to the Woosung forts. The Chinese bombardment around Kiangwan was described as severe by the Japanese. Rifle and machine gun barrages were laid down with the falling shells. “Although the Chinese are now using shells of great explosive power

Berlin, Feb. 17—(AP)—Sir Edgar Speyer, 69, former Privy Councillor of Great Britain who resigned his post at the beginning of the World War in 1914 after he was charged with disloyalty, died last night at a clinic here. He was born in Germany. British newspapers accused him of being pro-German in 1915 and he resigned, afterward going to the United States to live. He was a prominent figure in British financial circles and was chairman of the London Underground Electric Railway Company, which operates the equivalent of New York's subway system. He arrived in New York in June 1915. A short time later he was ordered by the Lord Chief Justice to authority for a claim to membership in the Privy Council and a hearing was begun in November of that year. It was decided he was entitled to his seat but the matter was taken up again in 1921 and his British naturalization was revoked, resulting in hi

London, Feb. 17 (A.P.) — Two British sailors wounded when shells from the Chapei area fell on the Shanghai waterfront where they were on patrol duty died of the wounds today, the admiralty office announced. Able Seaman H. A. Francis died soon after he was taken to a dressing station and a few hours later Able Seaman John Prior died. Both were members of a landing party put ashore from the British cruiser Suffolk.

Dublin, Irish Free State, Feb. 17.—(UP)—Tabulation of ballots in Ireland's record-breaking general election, the most sober and orderly in history, was underway today but complete returns on Eamon de Valera’s sensational fight for the presidency may not be known until Saturday. Early results were expected during the afternoon, and the trend of the voting as between de Valera’s Fianna Fáil party and President William T. Cosgrave's government supporters may be shown by them. The result will determine whether Ireland is to renew her 700-year fight for complete independence from England advocated by the de Valera party.
