1932-04-29.text: ‘NEW YORK, April 29—(UP)—John Milton, who wrote “Paradise Lost” and who died in 1674, received a letter today at Columbia University. The letter was from a young salesman, employed by a press clipping bureau. The salesman, it seems, had recently read some favorable comment on the English poet’s work. Learning that the Columbia University Press is bringing out a volume of Milton’s poems, he wrote to ask if Milton would not like to subscribe to his clipping service, so he might see how the literary critics view his work.

Ottawa, April 29—(@T)—A 12-year-old Eskimo boy took a high place today in the long roster of heroes of the far north. Harnessed to a sled with two ailing dogs, he saved his sick mother’s life by pulling her over 160 miles of ice and snow to safety at Wager Inlet post. The feat, performed in the midst of winter, the wildest time of the year, was described by Constable J. W. McCormack of the Cherfield Inlet post in the annual report of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Eladenac, father of the unnamed boy, died in 1980. His wife Kudluk stuck to her oath not to remarry, and her son took up the task of hunting food. But his luck was bad, meat was scarce, and his mother became seriously ill. Then the dogs began to die of distemper, until only two were left, so, when he saw his mother was getting no better he put her and his 3-year-old brother on the sled and started the terrible journey, from

TOKYO, April 29. (P)—A two-day battle between General Murai’s brigade of Japanese troops and Chinese rebels in which 200 rebels were killed without decisive advantage to either side, has been fought near Hailin, Manchuria, Japanese dispatches from Harbin said today. The battle continued all Wednesday night and Thursday morning, the Rengo News agency reported. Afterward, it said, the insurgents, estimated to number 6,000, held their strongly entrenched position four kilometers from Hailin. Correspondents of local newspapers, as well as the Rengo agency, said the insurgents apparently attempted to use poison gas. They also were reported to be using improvised tanks, constructed on motor trucks.

| Shanghai, Saturday, Apr. 30.—The man who threw a bomb into the midst of the highest ranking Japanese officials in China, seriously wounding five of them yesterday, was identified by the police today as Yin Kitsu, a Korean revolutionary who came here last August from Manchuria. The man was dragged off to a police station immediately after he had thrown the bomb, but not before he had been severely beaten by the mob which closed in around him. Today there were reports that he had died of his injuries, but these were not confirmed. His victims hovered between life and death in hospitals early this morning. Y. Kawabata, president of the Shanghai Japanese Residents’ association, was worse off than the others and the doctors feared he would die before the end of the day. Mamoru Shigemitsu, the Japanese minister to China, had 32 pieces of shrapnel in his body and was in critical condition. So

TOKIO, April 29—Bodies of thirteen passengers on the coastal steamer Kurenai Maru number 5 had been recovered today and thirty-seven were missing after the ship collided with the Nagato Maru and sank off Hiroshima. Thirty passengers were rescued,

Paris, April 29.—(AP)—(Friday)—Former President Jose Francisco Uriburu, 64, of Argentina, died early today after an operation for stomach ulcers. His wife, son and daughter were with him. The ailment which caused the operation on the former dictator appeared shortly after he came to Paris on a two-years' vacation.

TOKYO, April 29. (®)—The news of the wounding of Japan’s four outstanding military, naval and diplomatic leaders at Shanghai by a bomb blast was a tremendous shock to Tokyo. Newsboys, shouting extra editions on the streets, broke the stillness of the capital’s holiday in honor of the Emperor’s birthday. Pending official reports of the bombing the government gave no indication of what its action would be, although the belief was expressed in unofficial quarters that the signing of a Sino-Japanese truce, which was expected to occur tomorrow at Shanghai, would be delayed because Mamoru Srepoenitan and General Kenkichi Oeda, two of those injured, presumably would have been the Japanese signers.

SHANGHAI, April 29 (UP) — Peace negotiations between Japan and China at Shanghai probably will not be broken off because of today’s bombing in which five Japanese officials were injured, it was believed tonight. The bomb was thrown at the reviewing stand in Honkew during the Japanese celebration of the emperor's birthday. The five high officials wounded were: Minister Shigemitsu, right leg broken; Admiral Naraura, commander of naval forces, wounded in the face and eyes, may lose eyesight; General Shirakawa, commander of Japanese troops, wounded in the face; Consular General Murai, left leg injured; General Uyeda, who commanded the 98th Division in the Shanghai fighting, left arm injured. In addition, H. Tomono, general secretary of the Japanese Residents Association, was wounded slightly in both arms. Several spectators were slightly hurt. A reliable source said Kazuo Merive, consular of

1932-02-10.text: LONDON, Feb. 10.—(AP)—The British government is considering renouncing the trade treaty with Soviet Russia, made by the late labor government, the Daily Mail said today, to stop the “dumping” of Russian goods on the home market. The announcement would be made, the paper said, shortly after the return of Foreign Secretary Sir John Simon from the disarmament conference at Geneva. The British trade balance is imperiled under the present condition, it said, with imports of Russian goods exceeding British exports to Russia by nearly $100,000,000 a year. Besides, the Mail added, most British goods bought by Russia have been purchased on credit and Russia now owes Great Britain about $200,000,000, while Russian goods have flooded the home market at prices sometimes 40 per cent below British prices.

LONDON, Feb. 10—(?P)—London newspapers expressed much gratification in editorials today over the disarmament proposals of the United States as outlined at Geneva by Ambassador Hugh Gibson, acting chief of the American delegation at the conference. The press generally hailed the Gibson proposals as closely coinciding with the British plan outlined the day before by Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary. The Times said the American plan left a deep impression on the delegates and was assured of a ready response throughout the British empire.

| London, Feb. 10 (#).—Intense cold came to most of Europe today accompanied by snow flurries, and numerous deaths were reported from various cities. London had its first snowfall of any consequence while some of the rural districts of England were hampered by a foot or more of snow. All small craft in the English Channel were driven to shelter. Paris reported brisk snow flurries this morning, marking the coldest day of the winter. The temperature was 23. Bucharest dispatches said the bitterest cold in years prevailed in many sections of Rumania with numerous deaths from freezing reported. Eleven persons succumbed on a wagon near Chisinau, Bessarabia. Two families were reported found frozen to death in another Bessarabian village and the Danube was frozen from bank to bank.

TOKYO. (UP). Hope for a peaceful solution of the Shanghai situation faded in government quarters because of the Chinese refusal to withdraw from the foreign area in the beleaguered city. Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary, was informed that Japan feared the situation could not be solved peaceably. A government spokesman commenting at the same time on the Geneva report that the Soviet government was reorganizing its border garrisons, said this means the Japanese army cannot withdraw from Harbin. WASHINGTON. (IP). The opinion is growing in Washington that China and Japan must fight out their differences in the Shanghai area and reach a military decision before further peace overtures can well be made to Japan by foreign governments. Through fourteen days of fighting, the international peace plan and various attempted local truces have failed and there seems little the United States,

LONDON, Feb. 10 (UP)—One of the most severe blizzards of a decade swept over the British Isles and northern Europe today, with heavy snow, sleet and bitter gales plunging Britain into arctic weather. Most channel vessels were unable to leave port.

WASHINGTON, Feb. 10 (UP) More than 20 shells have fallen within the international settlement at Shanghai during the last 24 hours, Consul General Edwin S. Cunningham reported today to the state department. One of the shells injured a British woman. Meanwhile communist agitators, Cunningham reported, have been distributing circulars urging Chinese policemen, soldiers and the masses to seize arms from the "Imperialists and Kuomintang government," and convene a mass meeting to organize their own government. "Chinese artillery," Cunningham said, "opened fire on the Japanese position at Chapei Tuesday night and during the ensuing bombardment some 23 shells exploded in the vicinity of the Dixwell police station, which has been evacuated by police. "The Chinese artillery does not seem to have damaged the Japanese positions very materially."

Geneva, Feb. 9 With a significant veiled reference to Soviet-Russia, the spokesman of Japan laid his country’s view before the World Disarmament Conference here today. Tsuneo Natsudaira, Japanese Ambassador to Great Britain, and chief of the Japanese delegation to the arms parley, declared that “notwithstanding the unfortunate situation far out in Eastern Asia, Japan was as eager as ever to further the cause of disarmament.”

HOLLYWOOD, Feb. 10—Edgar Wallace, 57, English author and playwright, died today at his Beverly Hills home. Wallace had been in a coma since Monday with double pneumonia following an attack of influenza. Shortly before he died, Wallace opened his eyes and smiled faintly to acknowledge he understood his secretary, Robert Curtis, who brought word that Mrs. Wallace had sailed from London today. At Wallace's bedside were Curtis, Dr. E. C. Fishbaugh, and Walter Huston, the screen and stage star. AWAIT INSTRUCTIONS Wallace's body was to be removed to a Hollywood mortuary to await funeral instructions from Mrs. Wallace. Coming to Hollywood three months ago to write “Thrillers” for a motion picture company, Wallace amazed the producers and other authors by the speed with which he wrote his plays. He completed three and was preparing to start work on a fourth when he became ill last week with a co

1932-08-09.text: | OTTAWA, Ont (AP)—A rift be- 'tween the Canadian and British delegations over terms for trade agreements cast a shadow over the imperial parley here Tuesday. Malcolm MacDonald, son of the British prime minister and press liaison officer for the delegation, issued an announcement Monday night, however, emphasizing that the differences which had arisen were not such as to threaten a deadlock such as occurred in the ge conference at London in The negotiations between Canada and Great Britain have been the most important phase of the conference and the two delegations have made no secret of the fact that they were out to drive the best bargain possible. The British have had to consider the effect of empire preferences on Britain's isolated position, the possible political consequences of arrangements which would cause higher food prices at home and also British trade relations with Russia,

By United Press LONDON, Aug. 9.—Between 20,000 and 30,000 Chinese have died in floods which virtually destroyed the Manchurian district in Manchuria, the Mukden correspondent of the Daily Express reported today. The floods covered an area of about 180 miles along the Sungari River east of Harbin.

PORTSMOUTH, ENG., AUG. 9. (AP). - Mrs. Victor Bruce took off today in her third attempt to establish a new endurance flight record. In the past week two attempts ended in failure because of mechanical difficulties in her plane. Flying with two co-pilots, she is using an elaborately equipped amphibian plane.

Dover, Eng., Aug 9—Lily Copplestone, of New Zealand opened the channel swimming season today though she failed to reach Dover from Cape Grisnez. Miss Copplestone entered the water at midnight. Four hours and fifty minutes later she gave up the attempt to beat the record established by Gertrude Ederle.

(By The Associated Press) Miami, Fla., Aug. 9—Capt. W. N. Lancaster, former British army aviator, was called to the stand Tuesday to tell his own story of the strange shooting of his rival in love, Haden Clarke, with whose murder he is charged. Lancaster, in direct examination was to describe events of the night of April 21 when Clarke, who recently had replaced the Briton in the affections of Mrs. J. M. Keith-Miller, Australian flier, was shot in the room the two men occupied in her home.

COURTROOM, MIAMI, Fla, Aug. 9—Capt. William M. Lancaster, tall, quiet British flier, dramatically sketched his romance with Jessie M. Keith-Miller today: from the witness stand as he fought to free himself of the charge that he murdered young Haden Clarke, his rival for her affection. “We suffered a lot together,” he testified when recalled to the stand today after adjournment cut short his story late yesterday. Clarke, a Miami newspaperman, was fatally shot in a sleeping porch he occupied with Lancaster in the Keith-Miller home here last April 21, Lancaster contended Clarke committed suicide. The state contends Lancaster killed Clarke because of jealousy. Captain Lancaster said he and Mrs. Keith-Miller fell in love in Australia after a flight from London. “We had suffered a lot together on the flight,” Lancaster said, “Our relations became more than friendly in Sydney, Australia. We adm

COURTROOM? MIAMI, Fla. (UP) - Captain William N. Lancaster, British aviator, told today of “his love for Mrs. Jessie M. Keith-Miller, his Australian flying partner, from the witness stand in defense at the charge he murdered Haden Clarke, his rival for her affections. Clarke, a young Miami newspaper man, was fatally shot in a sleeping porch he occupied with Lancaster in the Keith-Miller home last April 21. Lancaster contended Clarke committed suicide. The tale contends Lancaster killed Clarke because of jealousy. Captain Lancaster, resuming his testimony today, said that relations between himself and Mrs. Keith-Miller became more friendly in Australia, after he had completed a flight down.

TOKIO, Aug. 9 (UP)—Explanations will be asked of Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson regarding his speech before the Council for Foreign Relations in New York, Japanese government spokesmen indicated today. Viscount Yasuya Uchida, foreign minister, was reported indignant over Secretary Stimson’s speech, in which the United States’ attitude toward the Kellogg peace pact was clearly defined. It was understood the government would cable Ambassador Debuchi in Washington, requesting a statement from Stimson. In his speech Stimson indicated that world moral pressure might be exerted against the Japanese occupation of Manchuria. He characterized the Kellogg treaty as more than a pious promise, and denounced nations engaging in war as “lawbreakers.”

1932-04-06.text: LONDON, April 6. (UP)—Gloria Swanson and Michael Farmer received congratulations from all over the world today on the birth of a blue-eyed curly-haired daughter who cried so lustily Miss Swanson remarked, “Well, she seems wired for sound.” The daughter was born late yesterday. She weighed 7 pounds 2 ounces; Arrival was almost a month early. Farmer had rented a house for the event. Miss Swanson married Farmer after she was divorced from the Marquis de la Falaise. She has one other daughter, named Gloria, and an adopted son.

London, April 6.—(A.P.)—Gloria Swanson and her husband, Michael Farmer, wealthy Irish sportsman, were getting acquainted today with a new daughter, born last night at their home on Farm Street, in the fashionable Mayfair section of London. The noted film actress and the baby were both very well, Mr. Farmer said. The baby was born a few hours after the parents had moved into their new home, from the hotel where they had been living since they came to London several weeks ago. It is Miss Swanson's second daughter. Her first child, Gloria, daughter of her second husband, Herbert Somborn, film executive of Chicago and California, was born ten years ago. She also has an adopted daughter. She and Farmer were secretly married at Elmsford, N. Y., last August. Their wedding was not announced until November 6, when it was disclosed by the officials who (Continued on Page Eight.)

LONDON. (CP), Great Britain has declined to recognize the existence of the new state of Manchouku, set up under the government of Henry Pu-Yi, the House of Commons was informed. The Undersecretary for Foreign Affairs reported that his department had received a "communication purporting to be from the foreign minister of the new government of Manchuria, regarding the opening of formal diplomatic relations with Great Britain." He said no answer had been returned. One of the members asked the reason for the delay in replying. "There has been no delay," said the Undersecretary, "No answer has been returned."

LIVERPOOL, Eng. (4)—Professor James Foote, master of science at a local technical school, died in his classroom today when he picked up a beaker of acid from his desk, mistaking it for water, and drank it. He fell to the floor, writhing in agony, and died in a few moments. He was in the midst of a lecture and reached for a drink of water to ease his throat.
LONDON, April 5 (—A daughter born tonight to Gloria Swanson, American moving picture actress. Miss Swanson has been in London for some time with her husband, Michael Farmer.

(By MSBOCTIACCG) LONDON, April 6.—King George's crown, made for Queen Victoria in 1839, is back from the cleaners ready to do service for another 100 years or so. It had threatened to lose its shape, so it was reblocked, new gold added, and its 3,000 jewels polished.

LONDON, Apr. 6 (#)—J. H. Thomas, secretary for the Dominions, told the House of Commons today that Ireland’s second note regarding abolition of the oath of allegiance to King George, and also dealing with suspension of land annuities, has been received and is being studied. Contents of the note were not disclosed.

London, April 5 ()—A daughter was born tonight to Gloria Swanson, the American film actress, and her husband, Michael Farmer, at their new home in the fashionable Mayfair section of London. Mother and child were both "very well," Mr. Farmer said. He and Miss Swanson, who had been staying at a hotel since they came to London after their marriage in the United States last year, moved into the house on Farm Street, where the baby was born, yesterday. The child is the second born to Miss Swanson. Her first, Gloria, now ten years old, is the daughter of Herbert Somborn, film executive of Chicago and California, who was Miss Swanson’s second husband. She also has a third child whom she adopted. The actress and Mr. Farmer, wealthy Irish sportsman, were married secretly at Elmsford, N. Y., last August. 1932-12-10.text: GENEVA, Switzerland, Dec. 10.—Plans for a Japanese navy almost equal in strength to the American and British navies were revealed officially today at the disarmament conference. The official Japanese plan envisages a fleet nine tenths as effective as either the British or American naval arms. It proposed that the United States and Great Britain each reduce their capital ships from 15 to 11, with Japan reducing capital ships from nine to eight. Under this plan, the total tonnage of Great Britain in capital ships would be 276,000 tons, and the U. S. would have an equal tonnage. Japan would have 200,000 tons and France and Italy 150,000 each.

Toronto, Ont. Dec. 10.—(AP)—A new monetary system for the world, a system in which wheat, silver and gold would be the vital factors, has been presented to financiers in America, Great Britain and other countries by Frank O'Hearn, former vice president of the standard stock exchange. Proffering it not as a panacea, but as a plan intended to aid farmers and silver currency nations, O'Hearn has drawn up the suggestion in outline and mailed it to leading economists and money experts. The first aim would be to arrive at a commodity valuation to stabilize that would be a standard to which all other commodities and services would have a permanent relative valuation. The second would be to elaborate the gold monetary system to fulfill efficiently the requirements of modern business and the needs of the people. This, O'Hearn believes, calls for two primary requisites. (1) A fixed monetary valuat

As in the case of Great Britain, the United States for the second time answered “No” yesterday to the plea of France for suspension of the war debt payment due next Thursday. In Paris the question of making or refusing to make the $19,261,000 payment reached the stage of parliamentary consideration. Premier Herriot clearly indicated he desired to find a formula of payment which parliament would approve. The British House of Commons probably will debate the issue next Tuesday, but the storm which may be aroused will not alter the government’s intention of making the $95,550,000 payment due from Britain. Indications in both Paris and London were that some sort of reservation would be insisted on by both governments. A declaration against further payments pending general revision was especially suggested. The second American note to France asserted that a “more favorable situation for any s

- WASHINGTON —U.P)— Administration quarters today considered it virtually assured that France and Great Britain will pay their debt instalments to the United States next Thursday. Their combined instalments account for about $115,000,900 of the $125,900,000 due from Europe then, leaving only $10,000,000 open to default. This is owed by smaller countries. The administration fully expects that Britain and France, after paying, will press vigorously their plea for revision of the debts. Officials feel, however, that this will be primarily a problem for the Roosevelt administration to handle. While President Hoover has (Continued on page 19 column 1)

LONDON, Dec. 10 — British gold for payment of the December war debt installment may be sent to the United States on the biggest and fastest battleship available, flying the Union Jack, financial agencies understood today. Many quarters, resigned to the fact that Britain is to pay the $95,550,000 annuity, urged that if the gold was actually to be transferred, the operation should be completed with as much publicity as possible. This resulted in the proposal to rush the yellow metal across the Atlantic on a British man-of-war. The method of payment remained secret. Although it was expected that the gold would be taken from the reserves of the Bank of England, it was understood that Chancellor of the Exchequer Neville Chamberlain discussed the possibility during his recent visit to Paris of obtaining enough gold from France, to be shipped direct to New York. London, Dec. 10 (INS)—With debt discussions virtually at a standstill until the cabinet meets, the government’s decision to pay the December 15 instalment to the United States will be formally ratified next week, officials said today. The government was faced with a growing revolt in the House of Commons, where members of all parties brought strong pressure to bear for a full-dress debate on the entire debt question. Many members of the House expressed strong disapproval of Britain’s decision not to claim payments from her European creditors. They maintained it was unfair to expect already burdened taxpayers in Britain to "hold the bags." It was evident the government does not want the matter to come up for parliamentary debate until after December 15, but a strong move is afoot backbenchers to thresh out the issue on Tuesday. On that day Winston Churchill expects to demand assurance fro
LONDON, Dec. 10.—By a vote of 137 to 40 the House of Commons yesterday rejected a measure to establish a six-hour working day with no decrease in wages. It was sponsored by a Labor member.

1932-01-07.text: Bombay, India, Jan. 4—The renewed struggle between India’s Nationalist millions and the British government, brought to a head with the arrest of Mahatma Gandhi, drew its first blood today. In a clash between police and Nationalist demonstrators at Allahabad, two men were killed, one of them trampled to death. Many others were injured and 30 were arrested. The British government armed itself for the renewal of the fray with a group of drastic new ordinances, one of which authorized a declaration that the Working Committee of the All-India National Congress was an organization wholly without the law, and could be so treated. Police Charge Crowds At Cawnpore, city of a tragic reputation for successive outbreaks and disorders starting with the Indian mutiny, police armed with lathis (staves) twice charged crowds of demonstrators. Throughout India there was great tension and anxiety. Meanwhil

BOMBAY, Jan. 6.—(4)—All turbulent India was in what amounted to a state of siege today as the British government's extraordinary summary measures, dealing with every phase of nationalist activity, became operative. New and sweeping special decrees, covering the whole Bombay presidency, outlawed 500 nationalist organizations, including such institutions as anti-drink leagues, spinning schools and boys’ boarding schools. All citizens were warned that, without trial, they might be sentenced to two years of hard labor for peaceful picketing, persuading anyone not to pay taxes, boycotting British goods or public servants, or contributing funds to the nationalist cause. Other ordinances, operative in all India, empowered the authorities to fine even children for nationalist activities, the fines being collectible from their parents. Collective fines may be imposed on whole villages and towns.

Washington, Jan. 7.—(4)—Definite action in the Manchurian situation has been decided upon by the interested powers. Decision has been reached after conferences between Secretary Stimson and the British, French and Italian ambassadors. In view of a probable declaration on the subject, state department officials declined to comment on the nature of the action except to say it was “sweeping and unmistakable.” The secretary called a special conference with American correspondents for late today at which, department officials said, he would discuss the Manchurian situation.

LONDON, Jan. 7, (P)—Several deaths were caused by the terrific Storm of wind and rain which swept western Europe and neighboring seas yesterday, strewing a large part of the British Isles with wreckage and causing severe floods in low-lying areas. Every craft afloat in the channel during the gale underwent a terrific buffeting and the cross-channel steamers were tossed about like corks, although all reached port safely. Reports from inland districts told of furious winds and torrents of rain. A number of rivers overflowed, causing floods which inundated hundreds of houses and business buildings and practically halted traffic on the roads.

WASHINGTON, Pps AD — An undercurrent of tension pervaded official Washington today as the State Department continued conversations with Britain, France, and Italy regarding concerted action to bring peace in the Far East. Augmenting the serious tone about the State Department was the feeling that the last word had not been said in the exchange over the beating administered by Japanese soldiers to an American consul in Manchuria. While Secretary Stimson said yesterday he considered Japan's official "regrets" as tantamount to an apology, he indicated the case was not yet closed. He is still waiting for a detailed report from Mukden. Stimson has indicated he would have a statement soon regarding possible action of the western powers in Manchuria. Yesterday, Japanese Ambassador Debuchi and Italian Ambassador De Martino discussed the situation with Undersecretary Castle. Previously, Stimson h

By The Associated Press. NEW DELHI, India, Jan. 7.—Reports from London today that an attempt had been made here on the life of Viceroy Lord Willingdon were described this afternoon as absolutely without foundation.

By The Associated Press London, Jan. 7.—Storms from Portugal to Scandinavia and floods in many parts of Europe caused six deaths yesterday and distress for several ships. The British steamer Jersey City sent urgent calls for help from a position near the Scilly islands, saying it was out of control with its machinery broken down. A motor barge sank in the Thames Estuary, but the crew of three was saved. The Grecian steamer Alexandria grounded two miles off the coast in Gunganess bay in the English channel and later was refloated. The wind had reached a force of 80 miles an hour over some parts of Great Britain last night, while the Scilly islands were lashed by a 93 mile gust. The battleship Royal Sovereign and the cruiser Exeter went to the assistance of the British freighter Trevaylor, which had lost a propeller and was drifting in peril off Plymouth. The tremendous gales were accompan

Tokyo, Jan. 7. (AP)—Sir Oswald Lindley, British ambassador, called at the Japanese foreign office today to inquire about impairment of the British interest in the Mukden railway in Manchuria by the action of the Japanese army in retaining the railway’s receipts. It was understood an undersecretary explained the army has sequestered the money temporarily in order to keep it from falling into the hands of Marshal Chang Hsueh Liang, but now that Marshal Chang has withdrawn it would be handed over. The French and American ambassadors also visited the foreign office but it was authoritatively stated the objects of their visits were not related in any way.

1932-01-14.text: BOMBAY, Jan. 14 The hand of the British government’s drive against the Nationalists fell on children again today when four boys under 10 were fined 25 rupees each at Surat for urging that their school be closed in protest against the arrest of Mahatma Gandhi. The fines were paid by their parents. A 5-year-old boy was sentenced to four years in the state reformatory yesterday as a Nationalist delinquent.

Doorn, Holland, Jan. 13.—(AP)— Former Kaiser Wilhelm of Germany, whose sister, former Queen Sophie of Greece, died tonight at Frankfort-am-Main, was himself suffering from an obstinate attack of bronchitis. He had been suffering with a cold for several days. Frankfort-am-Main, Germany, Jan. 13.—(AP)— Former Queen Sophie of Greece, 61, sister of former Kaiser Wilhelm, died at a clinic here tonight from cancer.

TOKYO. Jan. 14 (®.—Japan's reply to the recent American note invoking the Nine-Power Treaty in the Far East probably will be given to United States Ambassador Forbes tomorrow, it was said this evening. The note was to have been delivered today but the plans were changed at the last moment after Mr. Forbes had called at the foreign office to receive it. The postponement was decided upon so that Kenkichi Yoshizawa, the new Foreign Minister who arrived from Mukden tonight, might deliver it personally.

FRANKFORT-ON-MAIN, Germany. Jan. 14 (AP)—Former Queen Sophie of Greece, 61, sister of former Kaiser Wilhelm of Germany, who died last night, will be buried at Florence, Italy, beside her husband, the late King Constantine. The former queen, married to King Constantine in Athens in 1889, had been ill for a long time but on last Monday she suddenly grew worse. After the death of King Constantine at Palermo in 1923, Queen Sophie took up her residence at Florence where she remained until last November when she came here to consult a specialist.

BY THE ASSOCIATED PRESS. Paris, France, Jan. 13—Pierre Laval, sturdy little Auvergnat, who was President Hoover’s guest at the White House last autumn, again became head of the French government as premier in the reorganization of his cabinet tonight. He also took over the portfolio of foreign minister, held for so long by Aristide Briand, and induced his old-time friend and predecessor in the premiership, Andre Tardieu, to accept the post of minister of war, vacated by the death of Andre Maginot. Succeeding Premier Laval in the all-important post of minister of the interior, on which the outcome of next spring’s legislative elections may hinge, is young Pierre Cathala, a disciple of Laval and Tardieu. To succeed Tardieu in the agriculture department, which controls and cares for France's great rural population, the premier selected Achille Fould, young former under-secretary, who was gi

PARIS, Jan. 14.—(UP)—Pierre Laval headed a new French cabinet today formed rapidly to solve the debts, reparations and disarmament problems. Laval succeeded himself as premier and also became foreign minister, replacing Aristide Briand. He appointed ex-premier Andre Tardieu minister of war to head the disarmament delegation to Geneva. Tardieu performed a similar duty as premier at the London naval conference. The new cabinet was identical with the old Laval regime except that Pierre Cathala succeeded Laval as minister of the interior and Achille Fould succeeded Tardieu as minister of agriculture. Both new ministers were under-secretaries in the previous government.

| MILAN, Italy, Jan. 14. (AP)— Italy’s policy for the Lausanne conference was indicated today through an editorial in a newspaper by Premier Mussolini, calling on Europe to cancel reparations demands, assuring that in such a case the United States would refuse to appear as the only profiteer of the world war. The article, which was unsigned, but was known to be from Il Duce’s pen, said this undoubtedly would leave the United States in such a position that it would have to follow suit by cancelling war debts. It was Mussolini's second pronouncement through his Milan newspaper within three days of his personal views and therefore of the official policy of Italy.

1932-08-03.text: OLYMPIC STADIUM, Los Angeles, August 2 (4) — Under another beaming sun, the world’s greatest collection of track and field talent ran wild today in the Olympic championships in a record-battering jubilee featured by the 800 meter triumph of Tom Hampson, British school teacher, in the world record time of 1:49.8 and climaxed by four successive record reaches in the 200 meter quarter finals. Eddie Tolan and Ralph Metcalfe, the twin American negro thunderbolts, who ran one two in the 100 meter final yesterday, came back with a rush to lower the 200 meter Olympic mark to 21.5 seconds. No sooner had a crowd of 45,000 finished cheering these stars, however, when Carlos Luti, Argentine, and Arthur Jonath of Germany came along to cover the same route in 21.4 seconds each, in the remaining heats, to finish the wreckage of an Olympic record that has stood since 1904. By The Associated Press Miami, Fla., Aug. 2. — Threats against Haden Clarke by Captain W. N. Lancaster, former British army flier, when the latter learned of a growing attachment between the young writer and Mrs. J. M. Keith-Miller, his flying partner, were charged in the prosecutor's opening statement today as Lancaster went on trial for murder. Earlier, Judge H. F. Atkinson overruled a defense motion for continuance to September 15 to permit attendance by a physician on whom Lancaster's attorneys said they relied heavily. Selection of a jury and opening statements by opposing counsel took up the first day of the trial.

HARBIN, Manchuria (4) — Twenty-one days of uninterrupted rain have converted North Central Manchuria into a vast lake and brought about a national disaster. Tens of thousands of square miles of rich harvests have been destroyed and enormous stocks of grain and soybeans lost. Thousands of farmers and other residents have lost their homes and are flocking to the cities from the terrible inundation. The material damage is estimated at several hundred million Mexican dollars (a Mexican dollar is worth approximately 21 cents) and the floods threaten to rival even those of 1914, the worst in Manchuria’s history. Harbin is isolated from the rest of the world by rail and mail. All three branches of the Chinese eastern railway are paralyzed and all communication with Siberia is cut off.

(Copyright, 1932. by United Press) ROME, Aug. 3—(UP)—War apparently cannot be abolished and Fascism does not stand for pacifism, Premier Benito Mussolini declares in a frank and astounding article to be published tomorrow in the Popolo D’Italia at Milan, and later in all Italian newspapers. When considering the future development of mankind, the Premier writes “Fascism does not believe in the possibility or utility of perpetual peace.” Fascism, he said, “casts aside pacifism, which implies renouncement of struggle. Only war brings human energies to their full force, placing the seal of nobility on people who have the courage to face.” The article, signed by Mussolini and entitled “Political and Social Doctrine,” disapproves of doctrinaire attempts to create an atmosphere of world peace. “Such organizations are useful to certain situations,” he said “but vanish before the wind of a tempes
By United Press GENEVA—Paraguay is willing to submit the Gran Chaco dispute with Bolivia to arbitration, the Paraguayan government notified the League of Nations secretariat today.

Tokio, Aug. 3 (P)—A force of Japanese bluejackets has been landed at Yingkow, Manchuria, to assist local troops in beating off an attack by Chinese bandits, the navy office announced today. A cruiser and several destroyers were sent with the bluejackets to the port city from Port Arthur, the announcement said. The Chinese invaded the outlying streets, the announcement said, and clashed with the Japanese near the Japanese consulate and the Japanese hospital, but they were driven back. The cabinet declined today to call a special eight-day session of the Diet Aug. 22 to pass legislation necessary to begin a national relief program, of which farmers, fishermen, and small merchants would be the chief beneficiaries.

BERLIN, Aug. 3.—(1M$)—Bursting bombs and pistol fire took three lives and injured a dozen persons today as National Socialist sympathizers embarked anew on a campaign of terrorism against Socialists and Communists. The campaign took on a more sinister hue when Nazi rioters singled out Jews for their attacks in a number of localities, carrying out the antisemitic doctrines which Adolf Hitler has preached from the beginning of his career.

SHANGHAI, Aug. 3—Chinese dispatches from Manchuria today said there was sharp fighting between Chinese and Japanese forces at Yingkow. Chinese volunteers, the report said, entered the city, burned the Japanese police headquarters and forced the Japanese consul to take refuge aboard a gunboat. Forty per cent of the Japanese forces were disarmed, it was said, and heavy Japanese reinforcements were on the way from Port Arthur. There were reports also that there was fighting between Japanese and Chinese volunteers 30 miles south of Mukden, interrupting service of the South Manchuria railway.

1932-04-11.text: WASHINGTON, Oct. 6 (UP)-- The weather bureau today ordered southeast storm warnings posted along the New England coast from Block Island to Eastport, Maine. The bureau said a disturbance over southeastern Pennsylvania was moving north-northeastward with increasing intensity and would cause strong south winds, probably reaching gale force this afternoon.

By Associated Press LONDON. — Gloria Swanson’s baby daughter will be named Michele Bridget, it was announced today. The baby was born last week at the home of Miss Swanson and her husband, Michael Farmer, wealthy Irish sportsman, here.

By United Press LONDON, April 11.—Britain, in its reply to President Eamon de Valera of the Irish Free State on the oath of allegiance and land annuities, reaffirmed in unmistakable language that it will stand absolutely by the treaty settlement,” J. H. Thomas, dominions secretary, told the House of Commons today. Thomas’ announcement was a reply to a question by Arthur Lansbury, Laborite. He said that in view of the great importance of the communications between Britain and the Free State, the government had decided to make the texts available immediately as a ‘white paper.” Therefore, he would not attempt to summarize them himself.

LOS ANGELES, April 11 (P— The body of John David Guelph, who laid claim to the English throne, was embalmed today, his widow accepting the word of physicians that he was dead. Guelph was pronounced dead last Wednesday, but the widow declared her husband was in a state of suspended animation, a condition she said he had been in on five previous occasions. She kept a vigil at his bier in the undertaking parlor until convinced early yesterday that he would not return to life. Guelph claimed to be a son of King Edward VII by a morganatic marriage.

Ennis, County Clare, Irish Free State, April 10.—President Eamon de Valera of the Irish Free State vigorously restated today his position that his country should stand firmly for abolition of the oath to the king and against payment of land annuities. Those who heard the fiery republican in a vigorous speech here today interpreted his assertions as disposing of all rumors that the latest Irish note to Great Britain had showed a weakening of the Irish attitude.

BERLIN, April 11—(P)—Field Marshal Paul Von Hindenburg, second president of the German republic, settled back in his presidential chair today at 84 years of age for another term of seven years. In yesterday’s run-off election he rolled up a plurality of nearly 6,000,000 votes over Adolf Hitler, National Socialist candidate, his chief opponent. The vote, as announced early today, was: Von Hindenburg ...... 19,359,642. Hitler ................ 13,417,460 Thaelmann (Communist) ....... 3,706,388 Invalid: ............... 8,204 Total ................ 36,491,694 Chancellor Heinrich Bruening, at President Von Hindenburg’s request, consented to remain in office as chancellor. He offered a formal resignation when he congratulated the president on his victory, but withdrew it later. The winner will have the satisfaction of knowing he is a majority president. Although he failed to get a majority in t

GENEVA, April 11.—Abolition of tanks, of heavy mobile artillery and also of gas was advocated today by Ambassador Hugh S. Gibson in an address to the disarmament conference. Gibson, ambassador to Belgium and acting head of the American delegation to the conference, said it is obvious that abolition of these weapons can in no sense prejudice any other plan for achieving security.

1932-04-02.text: Shanghai: April 2 UP = Chinese and Japanese peace negotiations were in somewhat closer agreement,” it was announced after today’s conference at the British consulate, but their opposing attitudes on the main issue of troop withdrawals remained unreconciled. They adjourned for the weekend in order to consider the possibility of further concessions. The parties will be resumed Monday afternoon.

New York. Today.— (4)— Andrew W. Mellon is on his way to take up his post as ambassador to England. He sailed late yesterday, declining to answer questions and declaring he would utter no “platitudes.” INSURE with HAMMAR,

LONDON, April 2—(#)—It was authoritatively stated at Scotland Yard today that the police have no information that any agent is on the way to London here as an emissary of Colonel Charles A. Lindbergh or of the American police in connection with the kidnapping of the Lindbergh baby. Reports from the United States said Major Charles H. Schoeffel of the New Jersey state police was on his way to England in connection with the crime.

By The Associated Press. New York, April 1—Andrew W. Mellon, new United States ambassador to Great Britain, sailed today on the Majestic for London, convinced he will enjoy the experience that awaits him. "I have spent a great deal of time in England and of course I will like it there," he said as he stood at the door of his luxurious suite bidding goodbye to friends that filed past. The former secretary of the treasury who celebrated his 77th birthday last week, was asked a long list of questions about taxation, reparations, balancing of the federal budget and national politics, but as he waved them aside with his hand he said: "Any statement I might make at this time would be just a lot of platitudes and why talk platitudes? Schoeffel of the New Jersey State Police was nearing the shores of England aboard the Mauretania today, following up what is believed to be an important lead in the kidnapping of the Lindbergh baby. Major Schoeffel is making extraordinary efforts to conceal his identity, despite the fact that wireless reports from New York declared official announcement had been made of his sailing. He appeared startled when questioned concerning his mission and stoutly denied having anything to do with the Lindbergh case. He sailed under the name of Carl Schoeffel, and his name does not appear on the passenger list. When approached by questioners, Schoeffel declared he was simply travelling for his health. HOPEWELL, N. J., Apr. 2 (UP) News of the departure of Major Charles Schoeffel for England indicated today the police are following hitherto unrevealed clues in the Lindbergh kidnaping case. Colonel H. Norman Schwartzkopf, in a press bulletin yesterday, revealed that Schoeffel sailed on the Mauretania Monday. Schwartzkopf's only comment was: “Major Schoeffel is under special instructions, and no further information will be given out until he returns.” It was assumed Schoeffel would confer with Scotland Yard authorities in London. There were unconfirmed reports at one stage that the baby had been smuggled out of the country. Meanwhile a new development in the negotiations at Norfolk, Va., with men claiming to be the kidnappers was hinted by Rear Admiral Guy Burrage. He declined to discuss it, however. . LONDON, April 1 (P)—The pretty girls who used to know the Rev. H. F. Davidson when he was Vicar of Stiffkey are parading through the courtroom where the 62-year-old clergyman is being tried on charges of immorality. Today Dorothy Burn, who used to work in a tearoom at Lyons, said the minister used to follow her around the restaurant taking her by the hand and showing her pictures of actresses. “He told me,” she said, “that he used to visit them frequently to forgive their sins.” Violet Lowe, formerly a waitress in a Chinese restaurant, said Dr. Davidson used to come there frequently and one time she saw him kiss one of the other girls.

1932-06-04.text: London, June 4.—(AP)—Mrs. Elvira Dolores Barney, beautiful young London society woman, collapsed in Westminster police court today when she was formally charged with the slaying last Tuesday of William Scott Stephen, 26-year-old socially-prominent Londoner. The young woman, daughter of Sir John Mullens, wealthy London stockbroker, was arrested last night. Stephen was shot and killed following a cocktail party in her bizarre west end apartment early last Tuesday morning. She is the former wife of John Sterling Barney, an American singer, and was once a London actress. She appeared scarcely able to walk when she was brought into the prisoner's dock this morning, led by her mother, Lady Mullens, and a prison wardress. After brief testimony by the police officer who arrested her last night, she collapsed completely, fell out of the dock and was carried from the courtroom by the wardress and

Suspended installments will be paid over a one-year aging beginning next

Heavy clouds with visibility between two and three miles in the middle and eastern Atlantic, and wind between northeast and east, with a velocity of 15 to 20 miles an hour, were reported. Then at 9 a. m. British summer time (4 a. m. New York time) the air ministry reported overcast weather and a drizzle in the Atlantic from 600 to 700 miles off Central Ireland. Visibility was about 12 miles with moderate northeasterly winds. From Southern Ireland to a.m. miles at sea, rain, low clouds, and some fog prevailed. There was poor visibility, with rain and low clouds in Southwestern England. The weather in Western Ireland was "reasona

Washington, June 4 (AP)—Great Britain and Italy today signed the formal agreement postponing international debts for one year from last July 1 under the moratorium proposed by President Hoover. The British agreement, signed by Sir Ronald Lindsay, British ambassador, called for the payment of $158,520,000 and the Italian agreement signed by Ambassador Giacomo de Martino calls for a payment of $14,706,000. The postponed debts are to be repaid over a period of 10 years the first payment to be made on December 15, 1933. The signing of the formal agreements, which are to repay the postponed debts at four percent interest, carries out the agreement reached last June by the nations which were parties to the postponement. The signing today makes six nations which have formally accepted the postponement. The others are: Austria $287,556; Finland $55,000; Greece $1,109,000; and Germany $6,000,000.

Washington, June 4—(A.P.)— Great Britain formally agreed today to the repayment over ten years of the $159,520,000 which it owed this country this year, but the handing over of which was deferred under the Hoover moratorium. Sir Ronald Lindsay, the ambassador, signed the document at the treasury. Interest will be at four per cent over the decade, the first payment to be made next December. Other nations which have signed the formal postponements, which merely put into effect the agreement last June, have been Greece for $1,109,000, Finland, $55,000 and Germany $6,000,000 for the postponed payments on army costs. Treasury officials expect the remaining nations which agreed to the postponement of international debts, to sign the formal agreements during the coming week. France with the largest payment, had $50,000,000 postponed.

LONDON, June 4.--(UP)--Staa-ley Hausner, Polish-American flier, seeking to fly from New York to Warsaw had been unreported for 30 hours at 5:46 p. m., (11:46 a. m. PST). Coast guard and wireless stations of the French government and the meteorological service were without any reports on his progress and the same held true of similar aer-vices in the British Isles. Paris reported a thick fog and heavy rain late in the Atlantic and up the Seine valley, the route he normally would take enroute to Paris. Visibility was poor. If all went well and he followed the usual course, he should have been over Ireland during the afternoon in his plane, Rosa Maria. Last weather reports from the Irish coast showed low clouds and gentle winds.

LONDON, June 4. —(#)—Coastguards in Ireland and southwestern England and airport officials in both countries were on the alert this afternoon for the appearance of Stanislaus Hausner, flying from New York to Warsaw. The sky was overcast, but pilots at Croydon said that would not cause any serious difficulty to the flight.

1932-07-21.text: OTTAWA, July 21—(P)—A definite offer proposing wider preferences for British goods in exchange for greater British preference to Canadian imports was made today by Premier R. B. Bennett of Canada immediately after he was chosen chairman of the imperial economic conference. Any such program of preferences would have considerable effect on the trade of the United States. The premier declared such a system of preference exchanges should be enduring. Representatives of the dominions, he said, must decide now what course they intend to take and follow it without deviation. WASHINGTON (UP) — The Interstate Commerce Commission Thursday approved the four-party plan of consolidation of all eastern railroads, excluding those in New England territory. Under the proposed plan, all the railroads east of the Mississippi River, north from the Ohio River, and southern territory, exclusive of New England, may be consolidated under the banners of the New York Central, the Pennsylvania, the Baltimore & Ohio, and the Chesapeake & Ohio. Commissioner Eastman dissented from the findings of the commission. The commission modified the railroads' plan in some particulars, and insisted that each of the four systems have full access to coal supplies for fuel and for substantial participation in the commercial distribution of coal.

OTTAWA, ONT., July 21—(4)—The shadow of Mahatma Gandhi and the boycotts of India moved over the British empire trade conference and its formal opening today. During the days of conversations and published statistics, stress was placed on the trade of Canada and other dominions. Today it began to be remarked that, whereas Canada has a population of 10,000,000, India has 300,000,000 and the Indian delegation represents two-thirds of the empire’s 450,000,000 people. But for the passive resistance of Mahatma Gandhi, now silent in Yeroda jail, and his followers, it was estimated, India would be taking millions of dollars worth more of British goods than it now absorbs. SILVER BAY, N. Y., July 21 (AP) — Describing “all politicians high and low” as the chief beneficiaries of the “relief racket,” Roger W. Babson, economist, today told members of the Silver Bay Institute that the United States today is as much on a dole as England and asserted that until public attention is focused on men instead of money “the world will continue to suffer.” “Money,” said Mr. Babson, “will no more succeed in getting us out of the depression than it succeeded in keeping us out. Nor does the solution lie in building more non-productive public works, but in getting the unemployed back to their old productive jobs.” “Organized relief,” he said, “is benefiting the politician more than the distressed unemployed. It is the biggest racket in the country and all politicians high and low are its chief beneficiaries.” Mr. Babson urged a “quota plan” for bringing business back to norm

Ottawa, July 20 (®)—Nine nations of the British Empire will hoist their banners above Canada's Parliament building tomorrow and set about the very serious business of bettering economic conditions for their 450,000,000 people. In a sense they will be as much at war with a common enemy as when their colors were massed on the battlefields of France. Certainly their determination of purpose is as profound. The United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Newfoundland, South Africa, India, Southern Rhodesia and the Irish Free State—all of them subscribe to the tenet of J. H. Thomas, British Secretary for Dominions: “We will not think of failure. We will not talk of failure. The people want us to succeed and we intend not to deceive them.”

BOSTON, July 20 (P)—President Hoover Wednesday was asked by a New England conference on re-employment to consider calling a national conference which would effect an organization sponsoring the flexible work day and week as a partial solution of the unemployment problem. The conference was attended by more than 100 widely known executives, economists, labor and industrial leaders, college presidents, and social workers. The conference found that "unemployment continues with increasing problems, despite all efforts to curb the lessening of business activity and.... cooperative national action to achieve job security by job sharing seems imperative." At the opening session of the conference, Stanley Baldwin of Great Britain offered to the delegates representing the far flung nations of the Empire comprising one-fourth of the people of the world, a “wide extension” of tariff preferences in dealing with Britain. OTTAWA, July 21 — (AP) — Prime Minister R. B. Bennett of Canada sent the British Empire economic conference off to a business start today when he proposed at the opening session a wide extension of the Empire preferential tariff system. Bennett spoke in the House of Commons chamber, as official host to the 275 delegates. Instead of the usual formal speech of welcome, he outlined what Canada has to offer other Empire units and what she expects in return. Stanley Baldwin, head of the British delegation, followed Bennett and announced that Britain, with her tariff system, was prepared to grant "wide expansion" of tariff preferences to the Dominions. Re-submitting his plan for preferential tariffs, which was offered unsuccessfully at London in 1930, Bennett said: "We will propose that the United Kingdom shall extend the principle of her present tariff preference to natural products. 1932-06-12.text: LONDON —(#)— Dramatic details of what took place in the apartment of Mrs. Elvira Dolores Barney, young London society woman, when the body of Thomas William Scott Stephen was found there on the morning of May 31, were told Saturday at a police court hearing into the murder charge against her. Dr. T. Durant, who was called to the bizarre flat where the prominent young man had been shot, after a cocktail party, said he found the accused slayer in the grip of beside the body, the physician testified, and repeatedly kissed the dead man. As this story was unfolded, Mrs. Barney, beautiful auburn-haired daughter of a leading stock broker, sobbed unrestrainedly.

J., June 11.—44--The yearning for green hills far away brought Violet Sharpe from the placid English farm lands to sudden suicide in one of hurly-burly America’s most sensational mysteries. Only a few years ago she was an English “outdoor girl,” gaily chugging on a motor bike over the moors and hills of her native land. A chestnut-haired, shy girl of bovish demeanor, Her picture, telephoted throughout the land, shows a smiling, happy girl, clad in knickers and sports jacket, leaning against the motor bike in which she delighted. Persons who knew her said her eyes had a violet tinge. Perhaps they gave her her name. She was born in Tuls Clump, Bradfield, seven miles west of Reading, England, in 1904, and came to the United States, through Canada, about two and a half years ago. By The Associated Press STOURBRIDGE, Eng., June 11. Violet Sharpe, maid in the Morrow home at Englewood, N. J., killed herself because the police "drove her crazy" with their constant questioning about the kidnaping of the Lindbergh baby, her sister Emily Sharpe declared today. "It's all so cruel," the sister said. "Violet would never have done anything to that child or help anyone who wanted to harm it." At the time of the kidnaping, Emily was working for a New York family. She went to Englewood to see her sister who, she said, "swore to me that she knew nothing about the child's disappearance." Emily was interviewed as she was leaving Stourbridge for her family home in Beenham. Her father had summoned her upon learning from police in the United States that Violet killed herself yesterday. LAGOS, Nigeria, June 11. (P— Ninety passengers on the Spanish steamer Tiede which was wrecked Wednesday off Fernando Po Island were saved by the tremendous burst of sailing speed of the 19-year-old British steamer Appam, it was learned here today. The old Appam, steaming through the tropic night with flames belching from her funnels and the needles of her pressure gauges teetering around the danger mark, covered 104 miles in less than 7½ hours and arrived just in time to rescue the ninety from the sinking ship. Among Sharks As a result of the old ship’s dash the total casualties in what threatened to be a major sea disaster were limited to the loss of five natives, four of whom jumped overboard in the shark-infested waters. The fifth died on board. About 700 other passengers got away in lifeboats shortly after the ship struck.

Berlin, June 11—(UP)—Lt. Col Franz Von Papen, head of the German "all monocle" government, announced today that the new regime intends to exercise dictatorship unfettered by political ties but "naturally adhering to the framework of the constitution." The chancellor made the pronouncement in his first public speech since he assumed office. He addressed the agricultural council, the central body of all German landowners, angrily waving away news photographers. Von Papen, sleekly tailored, spoke with the crisp enunciation of a Prussian officer. He was interrupted by occasional bravos from his audience as he proclaimed the breach with the past system of parliamentary democracy. "The formation of the new government has little in common with the usual change of parliamentary cabinets, but involves a fundamental departure in the leadership of the nation," the Chancellor said. 1932-05-26.text: The Associated Press. PARIS, May 26.—A debt agreement with the United States, similar to that negotiated by Great Britain this week will be signed by France next week, providing for payment of its war debt annuity which was waived by the Hoover moratorium, the foreign office announced today. The Agence Economique et Financière said today the arrangement would provide for repayment of the French annuity at four per cent over a period of ten years. At the American embassy it was stated all the negotiations are being carried on at Washington.

LONDON (UP)—Great Britain has made no arrangement to pay war debt annuities to the United States after expiration of the Hoover moratorium, Maj. Walter E. Eliot, financial secretary of the treasury, informed the House of Commons Thursday. Eliot was asked by George Lambert if an arrangement had been made to pay the annuities after expiration of the moratorium, in addition to the agreement for paying the annuities suspended during the moratorium. Eliot merely referred him to the budget speech of Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer, and the statement of Sir John Simon Wednesday. Eliot said British debt payments to the United States to date total £326,200,000, while British receipts from reparations and war debts totaled £200,782,000. “The deficit, including interest at 5 per cent, on both sides of the account is about £200,000,000,” he said.

It is reported seriously that England, France and Italy have united to "bar the payment of debts to us." They are said to have arranged what might be entitled a "Welching Bloc" as though three bookmakers should agree not to pay what they owe, hoping to make the welching less unpleasant by making it co-operative. This welching plan by European friends that came hat in hand, tears in their eyes, begging for help in the war, may hurt them more than us. We can afford a ten billion welching process if we must whereas on future occasions the welchers may discover that deliberately swindling a good lender, with plenty more that might be lent, is not profitable. Also, there are several ways of killing a cat, and several ways of recovering a debt. Some day a forceful American government may reveal some methods of debt recovery to the "welching bloc." | LONDON, May 26—(7)— Queen Mary celebrated her 65th birthday today. Members of the royal family were invited to luncheon at noon. A salute of 21 guns in Hyde Park was the only formal ceremony authorized. The royal servants at the palace, according to an old custom, drank the queen’s health in champagne furnished by the king.

Boston, May 26—(4)—Wireless stations along the New England coast were listening today for a repetition of SOS calls which sent coast guard craft scurrying to the aid of the steamship Europa’s mail plane while the German flyers sped toward Boston without knowledge of the search. The plane arrived at the Boston airport yesterday and the pilot professed ignorance of the SOS calls. A shortage of fuel brought her to Boston. She was expected to proceed to New York today. Two coast guard destroyers ordered to search for the plane when the calls were received yesterday remained at sea today in the belief that some ship may have sent the call for aid. Radio officials of the department of commerce meanwhile conducted an investigation to determine whether a hoax had been perpetrated.

London—(AP)—Amy Johnson, Great Britain's noted airwoman, and Mrs. Amelia Earhart Putnam, America's woman trans-Atlantic flier, met Thursday for the first time. Miss Johnson, accompanied by her fiancé, J. A. Mollison, famous British long distance flier, went to the American embassy at Prince's Gate to see Mrs. Putnam. They chatted for a long time and posed for photographers in the garden of the embassy. Miss Johnson, who has flown in record time from England to Australia alone, paid the visit at Mrs. Putnam's expressed wish.

BY ASSOCIATED PRESS. LONDON, May 26.—Hornby, Hemelryk & Wo., one of the oldest cotton firms in Liverpool, suspended today. Its accounts are considered solvent, but suspension was decided upon for the protection of everyone. Prices declined from 50 to 65 cents per bale, following the announcement on the New York cotton exchange.

SHANGHAI, May 23. (®)—General Yoshinori Shirakawa, supreme commander of the Japanese army forces during the battle of Shanghai, who was critically wounded April 29 in a bomb explosion at Hongkew park, died today.
