DUBLIN, Irish Free State, Nov. 11.—(AP)—Sharp fighting occurred in the streets of Dublin tonight when the police broke up a parade of several thousand young men of the Irish Republican Army. After the demonstrators had marched around St. Stephen's Green and Merrion Square they attempted to pass Trinity College. A large force of police blocked their way. Finally the police drew their batons and charged again and again to break up the demonstration. Many persons were injured and removed to hospitals. Several were arrested. Members of the crowd threw stones at shop windows displaying armistice day poppies and snatched poppies from the lapels of pedestrians. The police said that numerous young men were equipped with brass knuckles and other weapons. The situation became so ugly all available police reserves were called out. As the night advanced the police charges became more and more freque

Washington — (AP) — Secretary Stimson told newspaper-men today that the British debt note has been submitted to President Hoover, but that it would not be made public for two days at least. The Secretary of State said the British communication would be published in America and England at the same time through an agreement between the two countries. Secretary Stimson said he has not received a note concerning debts from the French government.

EUROPE HOPES for a visit from Gov. Roosevelt before March 4, and London hears that he is “indulgent on debt,” is going over to get first hand information. The average American thinks first hand information is right here in America now. ‘There is no doubt that we LENT the money no doubt that they owe it. There is considerable doubt about their paying it, and the question is whether the new President of the United States would rather have Europe’s debts paid by Europe or paid by American taxpayers. You will be pleased to know that Gov. Roosevelt is not going to Europe. * THE FRENCHMAN who bosses the Lebanese republic, where cedars of Lebanon once grew so beautifully, finds Lebanese unfit for parliamentary government. Their politicians acquire big fortunes, create new offices and impose heavy taxes. That to America is amusing news. More serious news and sad tells about the cedars of Lebanon

DUBLIN, Nov. 12.—(INS)—One member of the Irish Republican Army died today from injuries received in rioting, which followed a police attempt to break up a marching demonstration past Trinity College. Several more members of the organization, a volunteer army supporting the faction of President Eamonn De Valera, lay seriously injured in hospitals. Many were trampled. Scores were arrested in the melee, during which the police made several baton charges.

Dublin, Irish Free State, Nov 12 (AP)—Twenty persons were reported injured in hospitals today due to fighting between Irish Republican Army men and police on Armistice evening. The riot began apparently as a protest against the wearing of armistice day poppies. The young men went about the downtown sections in military formations singing songs early in the evening.

PARIS. Nov. 12 (*).—With debt revision back in the forefront of European discussion, there was a prediction from unofficial quarters today that Italy and Belgium soon would present notes to Washington dealing with payments due the United States. Already France and Great Britain have presented their views on the status of war debts to the United States, and although secrecy about them was strictly adhered to, it was known they dealt with payments due Dec. 15. The suggestion that France and Belgium will follow the lead of Great Britain came from "Pertinax," the usually well-informed political writer. "If America’s debtors pay up on Dec. 15, they will be obliged to call back reparation agreements made with Germany," he said in Echo de Paris. "This means the whole structure built up in July (at the Lausanne Conference) will collapse. If the United States does not wish to destroy the entire w

1932-06-01.text: - Washington; May 3 - The United States has consented to attend an international economic conference in London, sponsored by Great Britain for the purpose of considering methods of stabilizing world commodity prices. The date of the conference and its program have not been announced, but the State Department made it clear today that the American acceptance of the invitation was, with the understanding that only economic questions shall be considered and political questions such as war debts and reparations barred. Study Monetary Reforms, Sir Ronald Lindsay, British ambassador in Washington, asked Acting Secretary of State William R. Castle, Jr., a fortnight ago to give consideration to such a conference. Meanwhile, Ambassador Meilon discussed the subject with Sir John Simon, British Foreign Secretary, in London. Today, after Secretary Stimson and Secretary Mills talked with President Hoo

EPSOM DOWNS, Eng. June 1— April The Fifth, an outsider owned running of the English derby before a crowd of some million, including the king and queen. Dastur, carrying the silks of Aga Khan, was second and Lord Roseberry’s Miracle, the second choice, third. Orwell, the favorite, was not in the money. Quoted at 100 to 6, April The Fifth was quoted at 100 to 6 in the betting. Dastur was 18 to 1, and Miracle 100 to 9. Twenty one ran. April The Fifth, given only an outside chance in the pre-race betting, is by Craiganeran out of Sold Again. He won by three quarters of a length with only a head separating Dastur and Miracle. Royal Dancer, the only entry ever to win a race over the Downs course previous to today, was fourth, with Firadussi fifth. The time for one and one half miles was two minutes and 43 seconds. Favorite Defeated Orwell, owned by W. M. G. Singer, former New York business man

London, June 1--(7)—The Daily Telegraph said today Mrs. Amelia Earhart Putnam, American trans-Atlantic flier, danced three times with the Prince of Wales last night at a hospital charity ball at which she was a guest. The prince danced the first dance and two others with her and they chatted animatedly, the paper said.

LONDON, May 31.—(#) — The haunts of Mayfield were stirred today by the fatal shooting of Michael Scott Stephen, son of a London banker, after a gay cocktail party. The tragedy occurred in the apartment of Mrs. Elvira Dolores Barney, beautiful golden-haired divorcee and daughter of a knight, whose former husband is John Sterling Barney, an American singer. No Charges Filed. No charges had been filed tonight against Mrs. Barney, in whose flat in Williams Mews the young man was shot and killed at about 4 a. m. The story it is understood Scotland Yard investigators will tell at an inquest next Friday is that during discussions in the long hours after a cocktail party Stephen brandished a revolver which was accidentally discharged, killing him. Meanwhile astonishing stories were heard of parties which were held in the gayly decorated back-alley flat in Williams Mews, the London counterpart of

London, June 1—(4)—The British government is consulting the nations of Europe about the value of a world conference in ameliorating the general economic crisis. This was revealed today by Sir John Simon, the foreign minister, in parliament. The consultation was inspired, he said, by a request from Andrew W. Mellon, the United States ambassador.

Washington, June 1.—(UP)— The two greatest commercial nations of the world, Great Britain and the United States, were united today in support of an early world economic conference to seek means of insuring work, food and clothing for the common man. Great Britain suggested that such a conference be held in London, Secretary of State Stimson instructed Ambassador Andrew W. Mellon to say this country thought the British idea a good one provided war debts and reparations were not discussed. That is as far as the plan has gone. Details wait, presumably, on conferences among Great Britain, France and Italy. Pending further information, officials here forecast: That the London economic conference, if agreed to by France and Italy, will be held soon after the meeting on reparations at Lausanne June 21. Then Europe will know what to expect from Germany and will have some idea what it will ask th

WASHINGTON, June 1, (4)—The United States has formally consented to take part in an international economic conference to consider methods of stabilizing world commodity prices. This willingness was expressed to Sir Ronald Lindsay, British ambassador yesterday in response to an invitation presented by Great Britain. The meet will be held in London after the Lausanne conference.

| EPSOM DOWNS, Eng., June 1-- (UP)—April the fifth upset all expectations by winning the 153rd renewal of the derby today before a vast throng of half a million which had come to see the expected triumph of Orwell, the favorite. Dastur was second and Miracle third. Royal Danger finished fourth and Firdaussi fifth. Orwell was never in the lead and could not get up. April the fifth finished three-fourths of a length in front of Dastur, which led Miracle to the wire by only a nose. One of the greatest crowds in the long history of the world’s greatest horse race was gathered on the rolling downs. The entire royal family was there, and Amelia Earhart, first woman to fly the Atlantic, attended with Lord Astor.

1932-01-20.text: London, Ky., Jan. 20.—(AP)—The toll of Kentucky's worst gun battle in recent history, the feud shooting in the New Salem churchyard—was brought to five with the death last night of “Little Henry” Johnson. The other victims were ‘Big Henry’ and Earl Johnson, brothers, and cousins of the latest victim, and Forrest and Homer Crook, brothers who were neighbors of the Johnsons. Willie Johnson was the only member of the two families present who survived, though wounded in the arm. The Crooks accused him of wronging their 17-year-old sister Ruby. The girl said she and Willie were principals in a mock wedding which she thought was legally solemnized.

Bombay, Jan. 19.—(4?)— Ramdas Gandhi, youngest son of Mahatma Gandhi, was arrested today in the village of Hartpura for taking part in the nationalist activities against the British government. This put three members of the Gandhi family in jail. The Mahatma was arrested Jan. 4 and placed in prison at Poona, and his 60-year-old wife, who pleaded with the police to take her with him, was taken into custody a week later. The principal member of the Gandhi household closely identified with the nationalist cause who remains free is Miss Madeline Slade, the English woman who assumed the garb of India and became one of the foremost disciples of the nationalist leader. Within 22 minutes today, 19 prisoners who had been arrested for picketing at the government mint, were convicted and sentenced to six-month prison terms. Most of them were women. They had been attempting to stop the shipment of g

LONDON, Jan. 20. (INS)—The International reparations conference scheduled to meet at Lausanne, Switzerland, next Monday disappeared into thin air today. International News Service was informed by a reliable authority that it would be impossible for the conference to meet on Jan. 25 as scheduled. Officials refused to commit themselves as to whether the meeting would be postponed merely for a few days or put off to an indefinite date. Germany Abandons Hope BERLIN, Jan. 20 (PS) The German government abandoned hope today that the Lausanne reparations conference would meet on schedule and were openly skeptical that it ever would convene. Replying to a French inquiry concerning Germany's attitude toward prolongation of the Hoover moratorium, Chancellor Heinrich Bruening informed Premier Wavel that prolongation cannot be considered as a solution of the reparations problem, inasmuch as this coun

Rutland, Vt, Jan. 20. (PJ) They're moving the kitchen and pantry in Jahn Segale’s home into the dining room. The kitchen and pantry have been padlocked, reducing Segale’s quarters to four small rooms. The padlocks were attached following raids for liquor. ‘BUY BRITISH’ UNTO DEATH London, Jan. 20, (AP)—The ‘buy British’ movement has reached the graveyards. The Central Council for the Churches calls attention to “really deplorable” foreign monuments, in many churchyards and says they show “decay in public.
LONDON—A resolution proposing intercommunion between the Church of England and the old Catholic churches of Europe was passed unanimously today by the upper house of the convocation of Canterbury.

SHANGHAI, Jan. 20 (U.P)--Japanese demonstrations demanding that additional warships be sent to Shanghai paralyzed business today in part of the international settlement and caused settlement authorities to order precautionary police mobilization. Tramcars were stoned. Windows of shops were broken after a mass meeting of 2,000 Japanese, called after Japanese mobs burned two Chinese factories here last night. Two Chinese policemen and one Japanese national were killed in fighting. Japanese marines patrolled areas considered dangerous. Sino-Japanese tension increased rapidly as authorities attempted to restore order. Four Japanese warships were lying off Shanghai with their crews still aboard. The Japanese demonstrators demanded cessation of anti-Japanese movements and that Chinese respect the Japanese flag and the emperor.

Premier, chamber for the first time since the formation of his new Cabinet, declared flatly that France would forego none of her rights to reparations from Germany. After he had made his statement of policy the chamber, without a word of protest from the government, put off until Thursday consideration of a question of confidence in the new ministry. No U.S. Encouragement. In Washington no encouragement was accorded the latest French overture for war debt postponement. In response to an inquiry from Premier Laval, the government is informing Paris that the place to settle Europe's vexing problems is in Europe, not here. Satisfaction over this American attitude was expressed in British political circles. London expected the Lausanne conference to be held as

Shanghai, Jan. 20.— Japanese mobs burned two Chinese factories here early today, killed two Chinese policemen, and wounded a member of the police force of the International settlement. One of the Chinese killed was attached to the International settlement gendarmerie. The International settlement police fired on the rioters and killed one Japanese. The rioting was believed to have been in retaliation for a recent attack here on five Japanese monks. Japanese residents called a mass meeting to consider the situation which admittedly was tense. No Japanese warships here were ordered to prepare for possible emergencies.

1932-08-30.text: The solar system's free show is about to begin and the giant ‘midway of the total eclipse’ that runs across New England is crowded with scientists and laymen. The scientific instruments of 43 expeditions are in place and last minute adjustments have been made. It’s the weatherman who is worrying the astronomers. He predicted “Wednesday, partly cloudy” for Maine, New Hampshire and Vermont — states where the majority of scientific camps are located. For Massachusetts, a corner of which lies in the path of the total eclipse, the prediction is “fair and warmer” for eclipse day. Thirty aviators stood by at points along the 100-mile wide belt of the eclipse, ready to carry scientists to heights above the clouds if a haze or rain should interfere. Hundreds of thousands of dollars have been expended over a period of weeks to provide the scientific setting for the 90-second spectacle. While each

SYDNEY, N. S., Aug. 29 (4)—Captain James A. Mollison, homeward bound to Great Britain on a return crossing of the Atlantic, triumphed over rain and fog today and brought his tiny plane to rest in a field near here. The Scottish pilot landed on the Stewart farm three miles from the city at 2:30 P. M. (CST), after a four and a half hour flight from St. John, N. B. Tomorrow, he will proceed to Harbor Grace if flying conditions are propitious and refuel for the final takeoff toward London.

OTTAWA, Sept. 2 (?)—The “Flying Hutchinsons,” a party of eight, on the way from New York to London over the Arctic air route, took off today from Hopedale, Labrador, for Godthaab, 700 miles across the Davis Strait on the west coast of Greenland. They had been fogbound at Hopedale since Tuesday. Word of their departure was received by radio from a government icebreaker in the Hudson Strait.

- LONDON, Aug. 30.—An airplane, possibly that of Clyde Allen Lee and John Bochkon on their attempted transatlantic flight, was heard off the Welsh Coast Friday by a patrol of the Automobile Association, officials of the Association announced today. The plane was well over the sea, the patrol reported, when the noise of the motor suddenly ceased. Lee and Bochkon were not reported after leaving Harbor Grace for Oslo early Thursday in the monoplane "Green Mountain Boy." The patrol was on duty on the shore

(By the Associated Press) New Englanders will first see the total eclipse at Derby, Vt., at 3:30 pm (EST) Seven minutes will elapse from the time the eclipse becomes total at the Canadian border in Vermont until it is seen at Provincetown, Mass., the last New England community to view it. The eclipse will be total over a belt 100 miles wide. The center line of totality runs down from Canada through Derby, Vt., across the White Mountains in New Hampshire, through Fryeburg and Biddeford in Maine and out across Massachusetts Bay. Along the New England coastline, the 100-mile belt extends from Beverly, Mass., to Wiscasset, Me. In the area of totality, the sun will be blotted out for 100 seconds in Canada and about 90 seconds in New England. From beginning to end, the eclipse will last approximately two hours. Outside of the area of totality, there will be a partial eclipse in every part of t

MANCHESTER, Aug. 30. (4)— Estimates of the extent of the Lancashire textile strike ran as high as 90 per cent today as ten ranks of the strikers increased due to the intensity of picketing at operating mills. Union leaders asserted that by tomorrow the walkout would be 100 per cent effective among the 200,000 weavers in the manufacturing section of the industry.

Conway, N. H., Aug. 30—About 200 astronomers are lining up in a 350-mile path running from Montreal to the Maine coast to answer the question “what does an eclipse mean?” They will view the total eclipse of the sun which comes down from the North Pole across Canada and New England Wednesday afternoon, a football-shaped shadow, nearly 100 miles long and 60 miles across. This shadow will blot out the sun for 100 seconds in Canada and about 90 in Vermont, New Hampshire, Maine, a corner of Massachusetts, and Cape Cod. In many towns they will work behind ropes, a protection against over-eager spectators whose advance reservations already have pre-empted all hotel space and many private homes, and who promise to arrive in droves in addition for the day only by automobile and special trains. Airplanes will fly aloft in the shadow as high as 5 miles. At least three of the scientific expeditions

New York, Aug. 30 (AP)—Hope for further increase in employment is seen by the financial district in the recent buoyancy of the textile and commodity markets. Some of these markets have climbed more than 10 percent above their depression lows. Silk, rayon, cotton and woolen mills in New England and other sections report a rush of orders, large numbers of employees recalled and, in several instances, operating schedules stepped up to a 24-hour basis. The firming trend of textiles is being reflected in various wholesale dry goods organizations in the east. One large New York firm has announced an 8 percent increase in wages and salaries. During the past week, officials of this company said between 10,000,000 and 15,000,000 yards of goods were moved. Raw silk has appreciated in value more than 90 percent in three months. Raw cotton is up more than 80 percent above the year’s low. One of the

1932-06-23.text: DUBLIN, June 23.—(Qj)—Massed in military formation before the high altar in Phoenix Park, a quarter of a million men will lift their voices under the stars tonight in one of the most inspiring moments of the eucharistic congress. It will be strictly an affair for men only. The singing will be led by a special choir of men and carried to the vast congregation through a microphone system. Cardinal Lauri, the papal legate, will preside at the meeting, and at its conclusion pass among the battalions. A solemn pontifical mass at 12:30 a.m., and another at 11 o'clock this morning, were the religious high spots of today’s program. But the thousands of visitors spent a busy day with meetings for each nationality and general meetings at which the theme was the doctrine of the eucharist—the bodily presence of Christ in the blessed sacrament which is the central foundation of the eucharistic congre

MIAMI, Fla. (UP)—Mrs. Keith-Miller, British aviatrix, was held in jail here Thursday on complaint of the United States Department of Labor, charged with entering the country illegally from Australia. Her bond was fixed at $1,000. Mrs. Keith-Miller said she was “not worried,” and added, “I will be out as soon as my attorney, James Carson, returns to the city.” She said she came to the United States four years ago “with proper credentials.”

By United Press | GENEVA, June 23.— Premier Edouard Herriot of France and Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald of Great Britain today agreed tentatively that Germany cannot be asked to pay her reparations debt now or during the period of recovery from the world crisis.

LONDON, June 22 (AP)—Prince of Wales will be 38 years old tomorrow and he is going to take a day off. For once his program has been kept clear of official engagements. As usual, he will himself read thousands of congratulatory messages coming from all parts of the world.

DUBLIN, June 23. (P)—Thousands of Catholic pilgrims crowded St. Mary's pro-cathedral today for the celebration of pontifical mass on the second day of the International Eucharistic Congress. General meetings and lectures in which the holy eucharist and its significance were discussed were held at local theaters and at University College. The papal legate, Cardinal Lauri, was to take the salute this afternoon from thousands of men participating in a mass meeting at Phoenix Park.

(By) Cut Bite Press. ’ Geneva, June 23. —— Premier Edouard Herriot, of France, and Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald, of Great Britain, today tentatively agreed that Germany cannot be asked to pay her reparations debt now or during the period of recovery from the world crisis. An agreement between the powers of Europe to allow Germany a moratorium on reparations has been culminating for some time. It is believed any moratorium favoring Germany will mean further demands on the United States to give more time on world war debt payments, and actually, it is believed this is the beginning of a determined effort to force the United States to a cancellation policy.

London, June 23—()—Adele Astaire, who will not soon be forgotten on Broadway, will be presented tonight or tomorrow night to the king and queen, but the name the lord chamberlain will call out as she enters will be Lady Cavendish. The Omaha girl who danced to stardom with her brother, Fred, is making her court debut as the bride of Lord Charles Cavendish, who was one of England’s most eligible young bachelors. Ten other American women will be presented tonight by Mme. De Fievriau, wife of the French ambassador. One is the former Kathryn Bache, now Mrs. Gilbert Miller, wife of the New York and London theatrical producer. Others are Miss Anne Bissell, of Grand Rapids, Mich.; Miss Joan Mehl, of Pittsburgh; Miss Marjorie Sawyer Goodman, of Chicago; Mrs. Herbert S. Howard, of Washington, D.C., and Miss Kathleen Knox, of Washington; Mrs. Thurston Macaulay, of Atlanta, wife of a member of the N

Geneva, Switzerland. June 23— (AP)—Avoiding discussion of the Hoover armament proposals for the present, American, French and British delegates to the disarmament conference today considered the French suggestion for reducing arms by cutting budgets. The French explained their proposal further but refrained from mentioning any definite percentage figure for global arms cuts.

1932-05-14.text: BOMBAY, May 13. (/P)—Mahatma Gandhi has deserted his spinning wheel and is learning to sew on a sewing machine. A recent visitor to Yerovda jail, where the Mahatma is interned as a result of his civil disobedience campaign against the British government, said he has been devoting far less time to his spinning but is spending hours every day working with a new sewing machine of well-known make.

PIMLICO RACE TRACK, Baltimore, May 14. (£)—E. R. Bradley’s Burgoo King, winner of the Kentucky Derby, today won the 42nd running of the Preakness before a crowd of 40,000. Tick On, the favorite, was second, and Boatswain, an outsider, third. Burgoo King, ridden by Eugene James, came from behind in the stretch to beat Tick On by a half length. Tick On just managed to beat Boatswain, a son of Man o’ War, which set the pace to the final strides. The winner ran the one and three sixteenths miles in 1:59 4-5.

| By United Press . | DORTMUND, Germany — Seven miners were killed today when the elevator in which they were descending to the Dortmund Colliery of the Gelsenkirchen mine crashed to the bottom of the shaft.

WASHINGTON, May 14—-(/)— A house vote on a beer-for-revenue bill was assured today when 145 members signed a petition to force the ballot, Sponsors of the petition said the vote will be had Monday, May 23. ‘The vote will be taken on the bill sponsored by Representatives O’Connor (D., N. Y.), and William E. Hull (R., Il), members of the organized wet bloc. It would legalize beer and ale containing not more than 2.75 per cent alcohol by weight and apply a tax of three cents a pint,

Norfolk, Va.—(?)—An investigation into the Norfolk angle of the Lindbergh kidnapping case was started today at the request of New Jersey authorities, it was announced by Director of Public Safety Charles B. Borland. Col. Borland, who conferred this morning with Chief of Police S. W. Ironmonger, said Colonel H. Norman Schwartzkopf, New Jersey state police head, had requested the investigation. The Norfolk officials said their investigation would not involve the questioning of the intermediaries for any information they may have obtained, but would be conducted along other lines. Two of the intermediaries here, Rear Admiral Guy H. Burrage and the Very Rev. H. Dobson-Peacock, were in Norfolk today but were non-committal. The third of the trio, John Hughes Curtis, who was with Colonel Lindbergh in an effort to renew contact with the supposed kidnappers yesterday, was in New Jersey today. Col

TRENTON, N. J., May 13. (AP). — Colonel Charles A. Lindbergh arrived late today to see the body of his kidnapped baby, taken to Linden for cremation. The body had been placed in a casket and a hearse was waiting at the door of the undertaker's establishment where the autopsy was performed when Colonel Lindbergh drove up in an automobile alone and entered the building. It was not known whether or not he viewed the body before it was taken out to the hearse. Previously it had been announced that neither Colonel Lindbergh nor his wife would view the body.

Hopewell, N. J, May 18 (P)—The picture of a father standing alone before the body of his slain son, a mother secluded in grief and a President calling for action inspired the highest law enforcement agencies of the nation tonight to catch the murderers of baby Lindbergh. Meantime the wide-flung man hunters were gripped with the growing belief that the criminals who stole the infant March 1 sought ransom. The focal point of this school of thought was the little white cover-all sleeping suit the child wore on the night of the kidnaping. This was missing when the battered body, wasted to a skeleton, was stumbled upon in a woods by a truckman yesterday less than five miles from the Lindbergh home. Garment Furnishes Clue And—a garment purporting to be this same sleeping suit was the “token” by which Colonel Charles A. Lindbergh and his 72-year-old agent, Dr. John J. Condon, were brought to pa

BOARD S.S. President Roosevelt, enroute to New York, May 14——(UP)—Lou Reichers, young New Jersey flier who lost a gallant fight to span the Atlantic, was under care of ship’s surgeon today, pulled out of an angry ocean by America’s most famous maritime rescue team, Capt. George R. Fried and Chief Officer Harry Manning. The Fried-Manning combination, already honored for its phenomenal ability to be in the right place at the right time for a sea rescue and to do its work precisely in the face of danger, “clicked” again. Reichers’ airplane “Liberty,” the highest powered aircraft ever to venture over the Atlantic, was claimed by the ocean. Manning's lifeboat also was abandoned after Reichers had been taken out of his gold and black speed machine, his nose broken and his face lacerated. The flier said he landed because one wing of his plane was damaged and his fuel supply was almost gone. He

1932-01-30.text: WASHINGTON, Jan. 30.—(4?)—On the heels of vigorous protest by the United States and Great Britain against the Japanese seizure of Shanghai, the navy today ordered its Asiatic fleet to stand ready to protect American lives in strife-ridden China. "Our fleet," Admiral William V. Pratt said, "will be ready to evacuate our nationals or to protect them if a crisis arises where mob rule prevails. "Our forces will go in and take whatever steps are necessary to protect our people." He pointed out there are a large number of American women and children in China. He also said that the ships of the battle force will leave San Diego Monday for winter quarters off Hawaii as scheduled, but will not go beyond those islands at present. Eight destroyers are now being prepared at Manila to leave at a moment's notice, but no specific orders have yet been issued for departure. Four are now en route from the

By the Associated Press These were today’s outstanding developments in the Sino-Japanese trouble: The United States and Great Britain filed a formal protest against Japan's occupation of Shanghai. The entire American Asiatic fleet was ordered to stand by to evacuate or protect Americans in China. The highest officials of the Chinese government decided to declare war on Japan, but the actual declaration was not made. The Shanghai Municipal Council asked that additional American and British troops be sent to Shanghai. Fourteen Japanese in civilian clothes were captured in the American area of Shanghai, after two shots had been fired at a United States marine. Shanghai was a nightmare of chaos as Japanese swarmed through the northern section of the international settlement, beating and killing Chinese. The Chinese section of Chapei was still in flames and the fire threatened the internation

Portland, England, Jan. 29 (/P) The flotilla searching for the sunken Submarine M-2 discovered 11 new objects on the bed of the channel off Portland Bill today, but divers, investigating under ideal conditions, found all of them to be old wrecks. Some of the finds were the remains of ships sent to the bottom by German U-boats during the war. Although all hope of rescuing alive any of the 61 men on the M-2 has been abandoned by admiralty officials, the search is to be continued. Large quantities of oil bubbled up to the surface in the West Bay but it was impossible to establish whence they came. The ideal diving weather came just at the expiration of the time limit in which the men of the M-2 might have been found alive.

PORTLAND, England, Jan. 30.— Salvage crews sweeping the English Channel for the sunken British submarine M-2 have found eight obstructions, all of them old sea wrecks, without finding a trace of the lost craft with its crew of 60. The searching flotilla will continue its efforts over the weekend until virtually every inch of the west bay area is dragged regardless of the fact that all hope of finding the men alive has been abandoned. In contrast to the previous blustery weather, today was fair with the advantage of the clear atmosphere to join in the search. Four naval craft were used. The abandoning hope for all aboard the M-2, the admiralty made plans for an impressive naval funeral at sea, over the spot where the submarine made its last dive. Relatives of the victims will be taken to the scene in tenders.

HALIFAX, N. S., Jan. 30.—(P)—The rescue of nine men by the American steamer Fluor Spar from the sinking British auxiliary schooner Ruth F. was reported in advices reaching the East Coast Radio Signal Service today from its Cape Race, N. F., station. The position given by the Fluor Spar was: latitude 45 degrees, 42 minutes north, and longitude 55 degrees, 32 minutes west. This would place the scene of the rescue approximately one hundred miles southeast of St.

SRINAGAR, (*). Additional British troops were requested to halt disturbances which have been going on the last few days and began spreading over a wider area. Several villages have been burned and plundered by Muslims. A number of persons were killed. The Maharaja, Sir Hari Singh, is rushing military reinforcements to the affected area where Muslims are fighting with hatchets, swords and bludgeons. NEW DELHI. (7%). The British government is sending troops into the state of Kashmir to restore order. The troops were dispatched at the request of Maharaja Sir Hari Singh.

WASHINGTON, Jan. 30 —-(UP)——A formal protest to Japan has been made by the United States and Great Britain as the result of Japanese military action at Shanghai yesterday. This was announced by the state department today. The protests were made on the basis of reports from the consuls at Shanghai. The American consulate said that after the mayor of Shanghai had made a favorable reply to the Japanese demands and the consulate had announced the reply was favorable, the Japanese nevertheless occupied Chapel, attacked civilians with planes, and landing forces. The state department explained that the protest was made primarily because the Japanese operations endangered the whole port of Shanghai, including the international settlement, where 5,000 American citizens live. State department officials objected also to the manner in which the Japanese attack was made. They said it came after a fav

PORTLAND, England, Jan. 30 (#) Search for the ill-fated submarine M-2 concentrated tonight three miles off Abbotsbury where sweepers earlier in the day encountered a new large obstruction. Although there remains no hope that any of the crew of the submersible would be alive, diving operations were to continue through the night if weather and current permitted. Naval officers attached importance to the obstruction and the rear admiral of submarines was taken to the scene from Portsmouth by the Adamant.

1932-05-21.text: Palmer Putnam was informed by telephone from London today in a conversation with the London Daily Sketch that Amelia Earhart, his wife, had landed in Ireland. The Sketch told Putnam that its correspondent at Londonderry had interviewed Miss Earhart after she “Of course, I'm overjoyed.” Putnam said, “but we who know her well were sure she'd do it. “She has more calm courage than any person I ever knew. Please let me thank the Associated Press warmly for being the first to break the news to me.”

WENTWORTH SURREY, England, May 21—A United States team of women golfers today defeated an English side led by Joyce Wethered in a series of nine matches. Virginia Van Wie and Mrs. Leona Cheney made victory sure when they won their singles encounters to make it five American victories. Virginia defeated Wan.

Worth, Surrey, Eng, May 21. AP—Miss Wethered maintained her golf mastery over Collett Vare, former American champion, today, to defeat her, six and four, in the first singles match of a team series between the United States and Great Britain. The two rivals have met several times before in the British championship, and always the tall English girl has won. The jinx held good today, as she took a four-up lead over the American girl in the first nine holes, made it five-up at the 12th, and ended the match on the 18th green. Mrs. Vare won only one hole, the 4th, Miss Wethered won seven, and the others were halved.

LONDON, May 21.—(P)—The press association reported from Londonderry, Ireland, this afternoon that Amelia Earhart Putnam, solo trans-Atlantic flier, had landed there. Mrs. Putnam, the news agency said, was unhurt. She had had trouble with her exhaust manifold, which had burned out. Her monoplane was reported undamaged. “I had this trouble (with the exhaust manifold) for about ten hours,” the press association quoted Mrs. Putnam, “and for a lot of the way I was flying through storms—mist, rain and a little fog.” When Mrs. Putnam landed, the press association said, she declared: “I've done it.” Landed In Pasture “I had to land here in the pastures outside Londonderry,” she continued. “I'm not a bit hurt and I think the plane is all right. I had trouble with my exhaust manifold, which had burned out. “In addition the gasoline gauge had broken, probably in the storm last night, and there was

HALIFAX, N. S. May 21, 4). — The government wireless station announced receipt of a report that the German airliner DO-X, flying to the Azores, was 300 miles southeast of Cape Race at 8 a. m., eastern standard time. Mrs. Putnam was nearing Ireland, where she later landed this afternoon, when the DO-X, fueled to capacity, raced its 12 motors and taxied to a take-off on Mrs. Putnam's trail at 3 a. m., eastern standard time (2 a. m. C.S.T.) today. The DO-X, the largest heavier-than-air machine in the world, was bound for the Azores. She carried 7,000 gallons of gasoline, and her commander, Captain Frederick Christiansen, estimated she would use in a single hour more fuel than Mrs. Putnam's single motored monoplane carried for a 20-hour flight. The DO-X, however, was not expected to make half as fast time as the smaller, swifter plane of Mrs. Putnam. The DO-X has 14 persons aboard, including

STOCKHOLM, Sweden, Mar. 29—UP)—A Swedish investigating committee today revealed Ivar Kreuger had $168,300,100 in personal debts and indirect liability against his name when he fired a bullet into his brain in Paris March 12. Pointing also to "deliberate falsification" of the books of Kreuger & Toll, the match king’s main company, over a period of at least eight years, the committee recommended bankruptcy. "There will be little, if anything, left over for distribution to unsecured creditors," the report concluded. The committee said gigantic fraud to the manipulations of this man, who up until the first of this year was regarded as one of the most powerful financial geniuses of modern times. Fictitious assets for large sums were created on the Kreuger & Toll books since 1924, the report said.

ST. JOHN’S, N. F. May 6 (Sat):—(P)—The 12-motored flying ship DO-X was refuelled with 7,000 gallons of gasoline early today and placed in readiness to leave at daybreak for the Azores on her flight to home waters in Switzerland. The German craft lay at anchor near Flolynopd at the head of Conception Bay.

HORTA, Azores, (UP).—The German flying boat DO-X was expected to arrive in the harbor here between 4 and 5 p.m., EST, this afternoon on the basis of navy reports sighting her about 300 miles away shortly before 2 p.m. The sea was calm and there was a slight south wind. Visibility was fair. A social reception for members of the crew has been arranged for by the German vice consul.

1932-12-16.text: WASHINGTON, Dec. 15 (AP).—The United States today collected war debt payments from six nations while five, unable to pay or determined not to, went into default. Great Britain was first to have its transfer announced, Secretary Mills receiving official word that the Bank of England had earmarked $95,550,000 of gold for American credit and had instructed the Federal Reserve Bank of New York to remit to the treasury. Through the same New York agency the treasury expected to get Italy's $1,245,437; Czechoslovakia’s $1,500,000; Finland’s $186,235; Latvia's $148,852 and Lithuania’s $92,386. Not officially in default until the treasury books are closed for the day, nevertheless France, Belgium, Poland, Esthonia, and Hungary let their opportunity to pay go by and the treasury was prepared for the $26,212,511 due from these countries as unpaid. London, Dec. 15.—(4)—Bernard Shaw's farewell jest to London as he left today with Mrs. Shaw, en route to the south of France to join a round-the-world liner, was, “Give Ireland to the United States and liquidate all the war debts.” The Shaws will visit the Holy Land, India, Siam, China and America. “I intend traveling around the world without giving a single autograph,” Shaw told a girl who held out an autograph book to him at Victoria station.

‘London, Dec. 15. -4()--By the simple process of “ear marking” an imposing pile of gold bullion bars lying in the Bank of England, Great Britain was paying the United States today $95,550,000 due on the British war debt installment. The Federal Reserve Bank of New York was supplying the gold for the actual payment to the United States government on the date the agreement stipulated and the gold “ear-marked” here for the Federal Reserve Bank will be shipped later by the Bank of England as required by the American bank. Announcement that Great Britain was sticking to the letter of the agreement made in the House of Com- mons last night by Neville Chamber- lain, Chancellor of the Exchequer, brought cheers. He added that Great Britain would continue to press for more lenient debt terms.

Washington, Dec. 15 (#)—The treasury’s books tonight recorded France, Belgium and three lesser European nations in default on their obligations to the United States while opposite the names of Great Britain, Italy, Czechoslovakia, Finland, Latvia and Lithuania was written the word “paid.” Thus the first general war debt payment date since inauguration of the Hoover one-year moratorium on intergovernmental debts—mid-summer a year ago—found the nations owing America sharply divided into two groups. Excepting Italy, the paying nations, like the defaulters, had protested and employed all diplomatic means to win postponement of today’s instalments and reconsideration of their entire war debts. However, upon America’s insistence that they pay, they chose to keep their credit standing with this country unmarred. In so doing they heeded the reiterated urging of Secretary Stimson that such action
ORAN, Algeria, Dec. 16 (P)—Amy Johnson, flying from Cape Town to London, reached here this afternoon. She plans to resume the flight at dawn tomorrow.

America’s war debt accounts, cast up at the treasury fast might, definitely classed five nations in default, while six others led by Great Britain were marked as honoring the bond of their international obligations. Nearly 100 million was paid, virtually all of it in gold or U.S. bonds, at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. In London, a stack of gold bars was rolled from one side of an underground vault to the opposite wall, to await the reserve bank's withdrawal. Paris, for more than 24 hours with only a shadow government, since the debt payment issue had overthrown the Herriot ministry, witnessed efforts of Camille Chautemps, minister of the interior under Herriot, to form a new government. Defaulting nations are France, Belgium, Poland, Hungary and Estonia. Paying are Great Britain, Italy, Czechoslovakia, Finland, Latvia and Lithuania.

AMARILLO, Texas, Dec. 16. M— Ralph Montee, transport pilot for Transcontinental-Western Air, died in a local hospital at 9:20 a.m. from injuries received Wednesday night when his tri-motored plane crashed near English field during a snowstorm. His co-pilot, J. E. Bowen, who was with Montee when the plane cracked up, died yesterday. Montee had been unconscious since the time of the crash. Montee and Bowen left the local field about dark Wednesday in an effort to get their mail and express cargo through to Kansas City, after transferring their passengers to a train. A few minutes later, visibility became so bad they tried to return, overshot the airport about a mile and crashed in a plowed field. Montee’s widow is ill in Kansas City. He is also survived by a daughter, Lucille, who is visiting in Los Angeles. Bowen is survived by his widow. He will be buried at Tulsa, Okla., today. Montee h

1932-07-26.text: OTTAWA, July 25—British Imperial economic conference down to brass tacks today when Canada laid before the other delegations her celebrated list of 8000 import commodities which are expected to serve as the basis for her bargaining with the other powers of the empire. This list has been accepted as the key to important trade agreements likely to be drawn up between Canada and the United Kingdom to the possible detriment of the United States and other non-Empire nations that trade with the Dominion. One of the items on it is anthracite coal. This means that Canada is willing to increase its empire importations of anthracite, which is now largely supplied by the United States. In 1931 the United States shipped in 2,230,000 tons, the only competitor being Wales with 870,000 tons. In general, the Canadian list contains commodities not produced on a large scale in the Dominion, and from which

H. C. Bywater, British naval expert, says Italy is building warships in secret, cruisers and destroyers "of phenomenal speed." The same Mr. Bywater criticized United States’ 10,000 ton cruisers. He also "accused" this country of experimenting with the largest, most deadly torpedo in the world, electrically impelled, with high explosive power, to be launched against ships by entirely new methods. Let us hope that accusation is sound, and that we are trying to do something to defend the country. It is not likely that Mussolini is building his ships "secretly." He has always said to the rest of Europe: "You attend to your business, and I'll attend to Italy's business," and unlike ourselves asks no one’s permission to build ships or anything else. LONDON, July 26 — (INS)— George Bernard Shaw reached the ripe age of 74 years today. He had to be reminded of it and wasn't a bit cheerful over passing another milestone in his picturesque life. The famous playwright and author was reached by telephone at Malverne, Worcestershire, where he is attending the annual literary festival. “Why, so it is,” he remarked when informed that it was his natal day. And then as an afterthought, he roared into the mouthpiece: “And I don't thank you for reminding me of it.” With that he banged down the receiver.

Dublin, Irish Free State, July 26. (CP) The Anglo-Irish trade war began officially today, but there were rumors of another attempt to reopen negotiations. The Free State government levied its prohibitive schedule of duties against British imports last night by publishing the list embraced in the special tariff bill passed by the Dail Eireann last week. The rumors of new negotiations resulted from the departure of Hugo Flynn, parliamentary secretary to the ministry of finance, for London last night.

KIEL, Germany, July 26 (AP)—Struck by a heavy storm in the Baltic Sea today, the German Naval Training Ship Niobe, a three-masted sailing vessel, went to the bottom. Forty of the 100 cadets aboard her were saved. Sixty were missing and naval craft were searching the waters in the vicinity. It was about 2:30 p.m. when she keeled over in the storm and sank. The steamer Therese Russ, which was not far off, picked up forty of her survivors. Among the rescued was Captain Ruhfus, the master of the Niobe. The gale struck the vessel only a few minutes after the great seaplane DO-X, flying from Travemuende to Kiel had passed over, and dipping low, had signalled a greeting. She went over on her side and sank in three or four minutes. The DO-X came down safely after a stormy flight.

The veteran of three westward crossings by the northern route brought his flying boat down in Independence harbor at 5:45 p. m., Eastern Standard time yesterday after a 600-mile water hop from Ivigtut, Greenland. The ship covered the 600 miles in easy fashion, taking eight hours and twenty minutes. The distance from here to Montreal, the next leg of the flight is 1,000 miles. Captain von Gronau is demonstrating, as he was in his previous flights in 1930 and 1931, the feasibility of a trans-Atlantic air route from Europe to the United States by way of Iceland, Greenland and Labrador. He took off from List, Isle of Sylt, Germany, last Friday. His crew consists of a second pilot, a mechanic and a radio operator. The mechanic and radio operator also made last year’s flight with him.

BERLIN, July 26.—(#)—Chancellor Franz von Papen, securely installed as federal commissioner for Prussia, today ended the state of martial law established in Berlin and the province of Brandenburg six days ago. Franz Bracht, former mayor of Essen, remains as the chancellor's deputy, however, with the authority of a dictator. The Prussian coalition ministry has been ousted and most observers agreed that the reichstag election next Sunday is not likely to put them back in office. In an emergency decree President von Hindenburg ended martial law at noon. Army Kept in Background. Outwardly there was no change in the city, but even during the past six days the lives of the people have not been materially affected by military government. Berlin, July 26—(UP)—modified martial law was lifted in Berlin and Brandenburg today as politicians saw in a government “deal” the possibility that Gen. Kurt Von-Schleicher, two-fisted militarist, and the dapper Adolf Hitler, Nazi Chief, might share power over Germany. The end of armed resistance to Von Papen’s seizure of power in Prussia, upholding of the legality of the “Putsch” in the Supreme Court, and a sudden decline in political disorders explained President Von Hindenburg’s removal of military control. Civil authorities were in full possession of executive power and police control. The ban on newspapers inflicted for demanding a general strike and criticizing the military was not removed. 1932-11-27.text: WASHINGTON. (Copyright by UP). A high official informed the United Press the administration favors a lump sum settlement of Europe's 11 billion dollar war debt in order to end the vexing problem of American-European relations. Great Britain and France, with whom the idea has been discussed informally over the last year, also were said to favor it. However, the plan is envisaged as one for the future rather than the present. The plan would contemplate determination of a lump sum to satisfy the debts and then probably floating of bonds on the world money markets to provide the funds from which the payment would be made. Meanwhile state department officials studied the speech of Prime Minister MacDonald, Great Britain, insisting America must be lenient. Government ministers sacrificed the British weekend to discuss Secretary Stimson’s note and the nature of Britain’s reply. The ministers retired to various retreats to study the problem and will meet at number 10 Downing Street tomorrow evening, at which time Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald will return from his country place, Chequers Court. Rome, Nov. 26. (?)—Within a few months ultra-short wave radio telephone service is likely to be in everyday commercial operation, Guglielmo Marconi said today as he left for London. Here, before a meeting of scientists, he will make an address in which he is expected to reveal some secrets of his revolutionary method of transmission. The world’s first ultrashort wave wireless telephone, invented by Marconi, now is operating only between Vatican City and the papal summer home at Castel Gandolfo. This system is complete except for the substitution of permanent wiring for temporary wiring, but it will not be formally inaugurated until the inventor returns from London. Marconi has no doubt about the practical application of the system, the present apparatus is small, reasonably simple and quite cheap in comparison with long-wave commercial systems. President Von Hindenburg closed a week of fruitless negotiations over the cabinet stalemate by sending out two political scouts to determine whether it would be possible to call an armistice for the winter. The men charged with this mission are Gen. Kurt Von Schleicher, the defense minister, and Dr. Otto Meissner, the president’s political secretary. Indications were that the president would postpone for several days the appointment of a chancellor to succeed Franz von Papen, resigned. If the “armistice” feelers prove successful, it was possible that the Von Papen interim cabinet might attempt to weather the winter. If, however, a man is found whose personality would command the toleration or the approval of the Reichstag, he would, of course, be asked to form a cabinet. PARIS, Nov. 26—The new Franco-Russian pact of conciliation and non-aggression, which has been approved by the French cabinet and is to be signed Tuesday, was hailed by the Paris press today as an important instrument of stability in Europe. Each country undertakes in the treaty never to resort to arms against the other, either alone or in conjunction with a third power, and each promises to respect the territories under the sovereignty of the other. The pact also provides that if a third power attacks either of the signatories, the other will aid the aggressor neither directly nor indirectly. And neither France nor Russia will make any international agreement hampering the commerce of the other or interfering with the granting of credits. Diplomatic circles attached considerable political importance to the pact as it was learned the negotiations have just been begun in Paris for a Franco

BERLIN, Nov. 26 (UP).—President Paul von Hindenburg decided tonight to give Germany’s warring political factions one more chance to form a working truce and permit parliamentary government before he forms another “presidential” cabinet to rule with semi-dictatorial powers. Von Hindenburg conferred today with his chief advisers and postponed a final decision until next week, intending first to sound out the various parties again on their attitude. Those at the conference included Chancellor Franz von Papen, who resigned but is holding office provisionally, and General Kurt von Schleicher, war minister. The presence of von Papen at the meeting was interpreted in some quarters as forecasting retention of the present ministry, but the decision to confer again with party leaders seemed to indicate that von Papen’s reappointment was doubtful, especially in view of the general opposition to him

By The Associated Press. Detroit, Mich., Nov. 26—Henry Ford, stricken suddenly with the first serious illness of his 69 years, underwent an emergency operation this afternoon at Henry Ford hospital. An announcement from the hospital said that Mr. Ford was operated on at 5 p. m. for strangulated femoral hernia, and that at 8 p. m. his pulse and temperature were normal and that he was resting well. The operation was performed by Dr. Roy D. McClure, head of the hospital into which the motor magnate put $28,000,000 during the World War. Complained of Cold Mr. Ford, who on the occasion of his 69th birthday last July 30 spoke of his unusually vigorous health, complained of a cold yesterday and left his office at the Ford Motor Company. The operation was decided on after an examination this afternoon. He was accompanied to the hospital from his Dearborn estate by Mrs. Ford, his son, Edsel Ford,

WASHINGTON, Nov. 26 (P)— A movement for early Senate action on prohibition repeal developed today following announcement of plans of Speaker Garner to have the House pass on the proposition on the opening day of the short session. Senator McNary, of Oregon, assistant Republican leader, said he favored Senate consideration of a repeal resolution as soon as possible after Congress convenes December 5. Support for quick Senate action was given by Senator Harrison of Mississippi, Democratic spokesman. He told reporters he had “no doubt” there were enough votes there to submit a repeal amendment. Speaker Garner said ‘both parties have demanded an opportunity to vote and I'm going to let the House vote on it on December 5.” Snell Questions Plan Although favoring early action on repeal, Representative Snell of New York, the Republican leader, expressed doubt as to the “propriety” of bringing it

WASHINGTON, Dec. 1.—The British Embassy today delivered to the Secretary of State Stimson at his home a second note regarding the British war debt to the United States, Stimson immediately took the note to the White House to discuss it with President Hoover. Undersecretary of State Castle announced that the new British appeal would be made public in tomorrow morning’s newspapers.

London, Dec. 1.—The new British note on the war debt issue, which replied to the refusal of the United States to postpone the $95,550,000 payment due Dec. 15, was dispatched Wednesday night by cable to Sir Ronald Lindsay, British ambassador at Washington, for presentation to Secretary of State Hughes today. The contents of the note were not divulged, but it was understood on good authority that Britain had presented a simplified explanation of its case for an extension of the moratorium rather than a formal diplomatic thesis. In official circles it was said the purpose of the memorandum was to reach President Hoover and Congress and to present arguments that would affect the great mass of the American people. It was generally expected to be Britain’s most important document since the World War, going beyond the question of the $95,550,000 payment due December 15, with a direct economic appeal to the American people. A new French note, which it was learned authoritatively would insist that the $20,000,000 payment due from that country Dec. 15 must be postponed, was outlined at a cabinet meeting in Paris. It was expected it would be sent to Washington before the end of the week. Open debate on the issue was curbed by vote in the chamber of deputies. BERLIN. (®). If Germany's political chiefs do not watch their step they may find the Fatherland without a president as a result of the possible resignation in disgust of the aged Paul von Hindenburg. For several days there have been whispers in political circles that the president was sick and tired of party bickerings over the formation of the next cabinet—that he was disgusted at the inability of the rightist parties to form a “ministry of national concentration.” These whispers were boldly reported by Der Deutsche, official organ of the Christian trade unions, representing 500,000 workers. Asserting that the president had seriously considered resigning, the paper said that was exactly what the monarchists desired, for it would open the way for a vice regency. | By The Associated Press. | Montreal, Que., Nov. 30.—About 20 persons were injured, including 10 who were trapped in the ruins of a three-story building which collapsed tonight when a series of explosions in sewer and gas mains plunged a northern area of Montreal into darkness. Scores of homes were menaced by fire, and the three-story building, made up of three dwellings and an ice cream parlor, burst into flames when it collapsed. 1932-01-28.text: Portland, Eng.— () —Seaplanes flying over the English channel off Portland today discovered a large patch of oil on the water which pilots believe might indicate the presence of the sunken submarine M-2. One pilot reported that oil was constantly coming to the surface from below. In the center of the patch was something which looked like a fender but could not immediately be identified. The patch covered an area of four or five square miles and was located about three miles south of Portland Bill, some distance from where British ships have been searching. Diver Searched Bottom Meanwhile, for the first time since the search began, a diver was able to reach the bottom of the channel at a point where one of several objects was being investigated. LONDON. (Thursday.) (?). Search for the missing British submarine M-2 was being made in the wrong place, nearly six miles from where it disappeared, Captain Howard of the steamer Tynesider told the Gravelines correspondent of the Daily Mail. Captain Howard said he saw a submarine submerge stern first and had no doubt that it was the M-2, as he clearly read the mark "M." Her head was rising out of the water and before the Tynesider could approach she sank rather suddenly. He had never seen a submarine dive and therefore did not pay much attention, he said, as he supposed it was all right. "But the position the admiralty gave is not a good one," he said. "When I saw the M-2 she was approximately eight miles northwest by north from Portland bill and two and a half miles from shore. I am afraid they are searching in the wrong place." If the dog had two pups and they were expecting more, they will show in some way where the debt settlement was directly responsible for this canine delinquency. But the other day was the best one. London, Jan. 27—(#)—The British Admiralty announced at 1:30 this afternoon that the submarine M-2, which failed to come up from a dive off Portland yesterday, had not been located at that time. "No communication has yet been received from the M-2," the admiralty statement said, "and in consequence great anxiety is now felt for the safety of those aboard." Earlier the Evening Standard said the submarine had been located at the bottom and lighters were on the way with lifting tackle, but efforts to establish contact with the crew had failed. Wives of all the men aboard the M-2 received telegrams today signed by the commanding officer of the H.M.S. Dolphin, reading, "I regret to inform you that your husband is missing and feared drowned in the submarine M-2 which is believed to have sunk off Portland on Tuesday."

London, Jan. 27.— The British submarine M-2 dived Tuesday off Portland, failed to come up, and hours later was believed to have been located at the bottom of the English Channel. Salvage craft and divers were sent to the spot from nearby Portsmouth, chief English naval base. Fears were expressed for the safety of the crew, normally six officers and 48 men, although officials said the submarine could remain under water for 48 hours. The M-2 dived at 10:30 a.m. Tuesday five miles west of Portland in 18 fathoms of water. When she failed to return on schedule, four destroyers and two submarines went to search for her. Two lighters joined the flotilla later to attempt to raise the submarine if found on the bottom. Here is the big British submarine M-2, reported missing in the English Channel with a crew of 54 men within its hold. It is the only aircraft-carrying submarine in the world, carrying a small fighting plane in a hangar on its deck. This official government photo shows the plane being taken from its hangar.

1932-02-06.text: Tokio, Feb. 6—(A.P.)—A pledge that the military reinforcements which are being sent from Japan to Shanghai will be withdrawn as soon as their object is accomplished will be contained in an explanatory statement by the Japanese government which will be published in London, Paris, Geneva and Shanghai tomorrow, it was stated on good authority here today. The statement, which was originally intended to be issued today but which was delayed for some reason, possibly because of the chance of a reduction of the number of troops to be sent will attempt, it was understood, to remove misgivings of the powers and to explain the reason which led to the sending of the reinforcements. It is being issued as a result of action of the British and American governments, which were understood to have conveyed “expressions of disappointment” to Japan on learning of her intention.

Washington, Feb. 5 (?)—Andrew W. Mellon today gave over the destinies of the treasury he has directed for almost eleven years to accept formally his Senate-approved commission as Ambassador to Great Britain. In the chamber where his name and policies have been the center of many vigorous and vitriolic debates, rules were waived to speed through the ambassadorial nomination as a final courtesy to the 76-year-old public servant. A few minutes later President Hoover transmitted for confirmation the name of Mellon's successor, Ogden L. Mills, of New York. Senator McKellar (D. Tenn.), one of the most bitter foes of the former Secretary of the Treasury, announced briefly and in a mild voice that he was voting against confirmation. Then the Senate approved him as ambassador to the Court of St. James with a chorus of “ayes.” Speaking at his regular press conference, President Hoover said he was

ABOARD S.S. EUROPA— This is just a little note to “Uncle Andy” Mellon, the first man to step down in order to take the ambassadorship to Great Britain. Mr. Mellon, you saved us taxes, and you made us money, and we like a lot of “yaps” went and blew it in. When it was all gone we took it out on you. The thing busted in your face the same as it did in ours. This is a crisis where the bigger you were the harder you fell. We are mighty poor losers if we can’t remember what you did and thank you and wish you well. So good-bye, Andy, take care of yourself. If you put on knee breeches be sure and put on long woolens underneath and always remember if we had saved what you saved for us we wouldn't need saving now. Yours, WILL ROGERS

WASHINGTON, Feb. 6.—()—Confirmed by the Senate as ambassador to England, Andrew W. Mellon ceased today to be Secretary of the Treasury, a post he has filled for nearly 11 years. In a tribute to the man which was recognized even before President Hoover pointed it out, the Senate approved his selection for America’s most important diplomatic post within four hours of the time the president submitted his name. A chorus of “ayes” at the end of yesterday’s session cleared Mellon’s path to London. “This is a real tribute to Mr. Mellon,” said the president. Within minutes of this action, Mr. Hoover had submitted the nomination of Ogden L. Mills to be secretary in Mellon’s stead, but the Senate had adjourned and approval may wait until Monday. Mellon will receive shortly the commission of his new office but he will not sail to present his credentials for some weeks. He needs a rest which he expe

Washington, Feb. 6. (P)—In rapid communication with foreign capitals Secretary Stimson today was perfecting plans which should result in new peace proposals to Japan and China within the next two days. There still was no indication as to what line would be taken by this government and Great Britain in getting around Japanese objections to the first plan for ending hostilities at Shanghai, Despite the tenseness there, accentuated by continued preparations for more fighting, the despatch of a Japanese army contingent, and the flight of Chinese refugees to the international settlement, there was marked optimism at the state department. Latest reports from Consul General Cunningham showed Shanghai had for its Chinese population a rice supply adequate for two weeks at best. Unemployment was severe, estimated at 162,000. Formal announcement that Japanese troops would go to Shanghai was deliver

SORE EE GRY LEP Shanghai, Feb. 26 (Saturday) (Pi—The United States destroyer Whipple was badly damaged in a collision today with the British steamer Rosalie Moller in the lower Whangpoo river, two miles from Shanghai. A hole was torn in the bow of the destroyer above the waterline. The British vessel also was damaged in the bow.

By THE ASSOCIATED PRESS. The Greeks, who had a word for almost everything, may take the credit or the blame for that interesting combination 'Sino-Japanese' which has appeared in print so often during the past few months. In the old Greek, 'Sinal' meant Chinese. In the new English, the old word has been lifted and, changed somewhat in form, hitched to another for the sake of convenience. You can still call it Chinese-Japanese if you want to.

Washington, Feb. 5. — (AP) — Shanghai’s critical situation monopolized the attention of the state department today. Secretary Stimson was in communication with London and the other capitals interested in bringing about immediate peace for the protection of the international settlement at Shanghai. Counter proposals to Japan's declination of two of the points in the original plan probably will be framed and forwarded to Tokyo within two or three days. The state department made no comment on the nature of possible alterations in the original plan. There was an air of optimism in the department, however, in spite of the movement of additional Japanese troops toward Shanghai and evidences of continued preparations which the American-British peace plan sought to avert. 1932-03-11.text: LONDON, Mar. 10 (AB). Bank of England reduced its discount rate from 5 to 4 per cent. The bank’s former gesture of confidence when the bank rate was reduced from 6 to 5 per cent on February 18 received such a favorable reaction everywhere that the further reduction today was decided upon by the directors.

Lendon, March 11—(AP)—Prince Lennart, of Sweden, renounced his royal rights and married Miss Karin Nissvandt, a commoner, today despite refusal of the duchess's mother, the Grand Duchess Marie, of Russia, to attend her son's wedding. The prince and his commoner sweetheart were married at the prince’s local register office. It was understood that the prince refused to have a church wedding, and as a result the duchess refused to attend the civil ceremony. Meanwhile, the attitude of the prince’s grandfather, King Gustav of Sweden, remains uncertain. He originally opposed the match. It was reported recently he had displayed a conciliatory feeling after a conference with Prince Wilhelm, Lennart’s father, on the French Riviera. The Grand Duchess had traveled from New York to London to attend the wedding. She said on her arrival that she had come here “to hear wedding bells.” It was understood

DUBLIN, March 10—The gates of three Irish prisons opened wide today for 20 Irishmen with 22 serving long jail sentences for political offenses. They owed their freedom to the election of Eamon de Valera as President. Many thousands outside Arbour Hill prison, where Mr. de Valera himself once was incarcerated, cheered wildly as the 17 men appeared at the portals. The released inmates were hoisted to shoulders and carried to waiting automobiles. The cars, adorned with large tri-colors, carried signs reading: "Welcome home, republican prisoners." There was a great parade through the streets of Dublin between rows of cheering throngs, and the prisoners were taken to a hotel for a public reception. George Gilmore, one of the men released, was sentenced to five years several months ago in connection with the discovery of a dump of guns. Gilmore bore obvious traces of his ordeal. Throughout his

New York, March 10—(INS)—Although fluctuating reports whispered that the kidnapped Lindbergh baby was the center of protracted negotiations, or was even en route home, search for the missing child today spread to the seas and overseas. British authorities searched the liner Ile De France when she docked at Plymouth. Other European ports also conducted a child hunt on incoming ships from the United States. Today’s bombshell report (there has been at least one full-fledged one every day) came from Atlantic City where it was said that the Lindbergh tot was captive on a boat offshore. They said some coast guard men had heard it scream. A house-to-house search was conducted through sections of the resort by police following the report. New York coast guard headquarters said that all government vessels had been instructed to be on the lookout for the kidnapped Lindbergh child. However, Command

Vice President of the United Press LONDON, Mar. 11. WUP)--The League of Nations Program to end warfare and conflicts in the Far East is under way despite a delay asked by Japan today, and it is modelled to fit the pattern of the American Far East policy, in the opinion of informed British leaders. That program, it was pointed out, left America and not Great Britain initiating sometimes economically distasteful plans and policies; it held the League to action it knew the United States would support; it prevented smaller powers from forcing the League into some move the United States would not support. The cautious policy of Great Britain was formulated in the keen legal mind of Sir John Simon, one of Britain's most brilliant attorneys. The result of that British policy at Geneva, it was felt by many, was to offset the feeling among some Americans that Great Britain was “double-crossing” A

Dublin, Irish Free State, Mar. 10. (AP).—Twenty political prisoners jailed under the emergency ordinances enacted by the Cosgrave government were released today from Arbour Hill prison by order of the new De Valera regime. It was one of the first acts of the Fianna Fail government and in line with De Valera’s campaign pledge to revoke the emergency laws as quickly as possible. Early today automobiles began arriving from many parts of Ireland, carrying flags and streamers on which had been inscribed welcoming slogans for the prisoners whose release was even then expected.

London, March 11 (UP)—Prince Lennart of Sweden renounced his royal rights and married Miss Karin Nissvandt, a commoner today despite refusal of the Prince’s mother, the grand duchess Marie of Russia, to attend her son's wedding. The prince and his commoner sweetheart were married at the Prince's row register office. It was understood that the prince refused to have a church wedding, and as a result, the duchess refused to attend the civil ceremony.

Then we may discuss and determine arrangements for a withdrawal of Japanese troops. “Japanese authorities have presumed all along that the Japanese attitude in this matter was understood by the Chinese. 1932-01-02.text: BOMBAY, India, Jan. 2 (AP).— There are indications today that a truce might be reached by Mahatma Gandhi and the British government in India to avert resumption of the civil disobedience campaign. Powerful influences are at work to persuade Viceroy Lord Willingdon to receive Gandhi without placing any restrictions upon the matters to be discussed. Heretofore the viceroy has insisted that he will not permit discussion of the recently-enacted provincial ordinances extending the power of local authorities to deal with political disorders. Telegrams Are Sent Many telegrams have been sent to Willingdon by business interests which feel that another nationalist campaign would precipitate a grave economic crisis, and Sir Tej Bahadur Sapru was active in negotiations to prevent war. It was Sir Tej Bahadur who, as peacemaker, saved the negotiations between Mahatma Gandhi and Lord Irwin, former vice

Fayetteville, Ark. Jan. 1. ()—A shot that merrymakers first believed was a firecracker exploding early today killed Roland Benjamin Schaefer, 25, of Milwaukee, instructor in English and German at the University of Kansas. He shot himself to death after the young woman he escorted to a party went home with another man. Schaefer left a note, a poem and a hastily written will. The will directed that an engagement ring he had be returned to a jeweler. The contents of the note and the poem will not be made public.
