HELSINGFORS, Finland, Jan. 1. —(AP)—Finland stood today on the threshold of 1932 and looked for a wet year, after twelve years of prohibition. Prohibitionists and anti-prohibitionists alike admitted the prospect as returns from the country on the advisory referendum Tuesday and Wednesday continued to be counted. With about one-fifth of the vote counted, 75 per cent of the ballots were registered for repeal of the dry law, 24.2 per cent to retain it and 0.8 per cent for modification to permit the sale of wines and beer. Observers were most surprised because 60 per cent of the repeal votes in early returns in Helsingfors were cast by women. The largest newspaper here estimated on the basis of a poll of its own in various sections of the country; that the final vote would show a majority of 68 per cent for repeal. Prohibition headquarters showed disappointment over the trend, but leaders in

Bombay, India, Jan. 1.-Mahatma Gandhi tonight issued one more warning to his people to be ready to resume the civil disobedience campaign, and packed up his collection of joint cists and spinning wheels in preparation for another term in jail. The congress party working committee meanwhile addressed an appeal to merchants to abandon their trade in foreign cloth and cooperate with the congress, at the same time asking all Indians to make only the very minimum use of the government railroads, post-offices and other bureaus. The Mahatma issued a statement of his own "on the eve of the new era to which India has been summoned," inviting all free peoples to study the progress of the civil disobedience campaign as a possible "effective moral equivalent for war."

PARIS, Jan. 2.—(U.P.)—General Gerald Pau, a famous world war figure, died at his home here today. He was 83. As a 22-year-old second lieutenant in the war of 1870, General Pau lost his right arm at the battle of Froeschwiller. He later went to the colonies where he rose to fame as a colonial administrator and conqueror. In the world war he was past the military age limit and did not get into active service but was a member of various military missions sent abroad to deal with allied and neutral countries.

'By The Associated Press. MELBOURNE, Australia, Jan. 1. —Australia today was in the grip of one of the worst heat waves in its history. At Adelaide the hot spell was the worst in 50 years and the temperature remained at 80 degrees at midnight, sending thousands of people out of doors to sleep.

SHANGHAI, Jan. 2.—A new threat of civil war in China loomed today as nine provincial governors issued a round robin telegram denouncing the new regime headed by Lin Sen and Sun Fo, blaming it for permitting the Japanese to capture Chinchow. Immediately upon its receipt the central political council of the Nationalist party called an emergency meeting, following which they telegraphed Chiang Kai Shek, former president, urging him to emerge from his retirement and come immediately to the capital.

1932-08-25.text: Fort Ménier, Anticosti Island, Quebec, Aug. 25.—(AP)—The flying family of Hutchinsons, en route from New York to London via Greenland, were guests of lonely islanders today before taking off on the third leg of their adventure. George Hutchinson, head of the family, and his crew of four men brought the amphibian down in the harbor at 4:45 p.m. yesterday after a smooth trip from St. John, N.B., 325 miles away. They had flown from New York to St. John Tuesday. The take-off for Labrador, in preparation for the 600-mile water jump to Greenland, was arranged for today if weather conditions remain favorable.

WASHINGTON, Aug. 24.—(?)—The Interstate Commerce Commission today notified southern carriers that they might put into effect reduced rates on cotton from the south and southwest to New Orleans, New England and Canada. The new rates become effective to New England points from Arkansas, Southern Missouri and Western Louisiana on August 27 and from other points on September 6. The rates for the first time in the history of the cotton industry are established on a carload basis. Heretofore cotton rates have been on what is known as an "any quantity" basis. One bale could be shipped at the same rate as a carload. Under the new rates the cost is scaled downward from 45 cents for a minimum carload of 25,000 pounds to 30 cents for a 60,000 pound load. The commission last week held a conference with cotton men and railroad representatives at which the rates were thoroughly investigated. Some larg

LONDON, Aug. 24.—It was learned on high authority today that the Prince of Wales intends to visit Sweden some time in October but that no definite date for the trip has been fixed. The information recalled frequent rumors in the past that the Princess Ingrid of Sweden might become the Prince's bride.

CLEVELAND, Aug. 25.—Chartered ocean liners will take nearly 60,000 delegates to the 45th international Moose convention at London, Eng., next summer, the supreme council of the order announced in convention here today. With $100,000 already subscribed to defray the convention expenses abroad, the Moose delegates will take part in the breaking of ground for a British Mooseheart, located near Cardiff, Wales, similar to the children’s home in Mooseheart, I. E. Morgan-Willmott, supreme dictator of the British Moose, invited the convention to London and assured part of the expenses of the meetings.

BERLIN, Aug. 24.—(AP)—Enraged by the imposition of a death sentence on five fascists convicted of political murder, hundreds of National Socialist storm troops staged a demonstration today at Beuthen where the sentence was passed on Monday. They turned out in defiance of a government declaration that the iron fist will fall upon all those guilty of political violence. The occasion was the arrival of Captain Ernst Roehm, an emissary of Adolf Hitler, to confer with defense attorneys in an effort to liberate the condemned men. Cops Have Hard Time Police had difficulty keeping the crowd in hand. Wilhelm Frick, chairman of the Nazi party in the Reichstag, sent a telegram today to Chancellor Von Papen warning that disastrous consequences would result if execution of the five men was carried out. Germany was told by manifesto today that the government of Chancellor Franz Von Papen would permit

Madrid, Aug. 25. (AP)—Jose Sanjurjo Sacanello, one of the most famous Spanish soldiers of modern times and commanding general of the army, was sentenced to death today for leading a rebellion against the republic. A mixed civil and military tribunal of the supreme court reached the verdict after 20 hours of deliberation, while the nation waited and demonstrations for and against the "hero of Morocco" were restrained with difficulty by government forces. General Sanjurjo’s lifelong friend and companion-at-arms, General Herranz, received a prison sentence of 30 years which, in Spanish law, is equivalent to a life sentence. Lieutenant Colonel Infante was sentenced to 12 years. General Sanjurjo’s son, Justo, a captain, was given his freedom. General Sanjurjo’s attorney immediately started efforts for clemency. He appealed to the president against a sentence he called “a disgrace, against the

TOKIO (UP)—Japan’s foreign minister, Yasuya Uchida, spoke out boldly Thursday in defense of her Manchurian occupation, virtually defying the League of Nations or any other "machinery of peace" to interfere with her policies including the Japan crisis. Support will not be favorable to Japan. He arose in the imperial diet and announced the nation’s intention of establishing what was Manchuria as a member of the Japanese Society of Nations. American Policies Criticized. Uehida’s pronouncement including criticism of American policies outlined by Secretary of State Stimson, and conflicting with the league commission’s findings, inevitably will result in important world-wide repercussions. Stimson’s assertion that Japanese "aggression" constituted a violation of the Pact of Paris aroused indignation in official quarters here. “There are those who argue,” the foreign minister said, “as though t

Tokio, Aug. 25.—(A.P.)—Outlining her foreign policy, Japan today declared the world’s peace machinery offered no remedy for “the chaotic condition of China,” and announced formally her intention to recognize the new Manchurian state, Manchukuo, in the near future. The declaration was made by Baron Yasyua Uchida, the foreign minister, before an extraordinary session of the house of peers, and its text was cabled to many foreign capitals for distribution. Formal recognition of Manchukuo, the foreign minister said, was “the only means of stabilizing conditions in Manchuria and establishing permanent peace in the far east.” “There are those in other countries,” Uchida went on, “who do not fully comprehend the attitude of Japan toward China nor the measures she has taken. x x x. “It is an indisputable fact that the chaotic condition of China and the so-called revolutionary policy carried on b

1932-02-20.text: DUBLIN, Irish Free State, Feb. 19 ()—Revisions and accumulations of returns from Tuesday's election showed William T. Cosgrave’s government creeping up slightly on Eamon de Valera and his Fianna Fáil. De Valera lost three seats on revision alone under the proportional representation voting system. The Government party picked up four seats by accumulation and the independents held ten already credited to them, Labor allies of the Fianna Fáil retained but five seats on the revision. The count stood Fianna Fáil, 45; Labor 5; Government 38; and independents 10. Thus the Fianna Fáil and allies held 50 seats while the Government and its supporters held 46 seats. These returns showed the Independent Labor party without two seats previously accredited to it.

DUBLIN, IRISH FREE STATE, FEB. 20. (AP).—Eamon De Valera, leader of the Fianna Fail, gained steadily today as the count of ballots cast in Tuesday's general election neared a close, and it appeared almost certain he would be asked to form a new government. The Fianna Fail and its supporters had a total of 71 seats in the Dail Eireann, a margin of 12 over the 59 seats won by President Cosgrave’s governmental party and its independent allies. Results from 23 contests were still out.

DUBLIN, Feb. 20.—(?)—Eamon de Valera’s Fianna Fail party and its labor allies had a lead of 10 seats in the Dail Éireann over the supporters of President William T. Cosgrave today, with only 23 of the 153 seats still to be decided after the vote in Tuesday's general election. In spite of de Valera's lead, however, the possibility of a deadlock in the presidential election by the Dail was discussed in political quarters. It was suggested that although the country will have elected a parliament, the Dail may fail to elect a government if any shift occurs in the alignment of the secondary parties. One of the notable results last night was the defeat of T. J. O'Connell, labor leader in the last session of the Dail.

Dublin, Irish Free State, Feb, 19, (P)—Partial returns from Tuesday's general election indicated late tonight that, unless there is some unexpected development, Eamonn De Valera's Republicans, with the assistance of Labor, will be in position to form the next Irish government. With 120 seats accounted for—leaving 32 still to be decided—the Fianna Fail (De Valera party) and Labor had a lead of 10 over the supporters of President William T. Cosgrave and the Independents and Farmers. The party standing was: Fianna Fail, 56; Labor, 9; Government, 48; Independents and Farmers, 12.

LONDON, Feb. 20—(UP)—The British War Office, Admiralty Office, and Cabinet were prepared today for any emergency calling for a warlike move in the Far East. For the first time since the World War, the Admiralty and War Offices were open all night long. They will continue to operate until the emergency has passed. And an emergency cabinet committee has been formed with full authority to deal with any critical situation which may arise during the Chinese-Japanese conflict at Shanghai involving British interests. Great Britain has announced that she will hold both Japan and China fully responsible for any loss of life among her nationals in Shanghai, and for any British property loss in that area.

PARIS, Feb. 19.—_(UP)—An English beauty and heiress, a princess of Borneo who some day may rule over savages, revealed today why she left England as a Christian in an airplane speeding 100 miles an hour and landed in France a Mohammedan after a ceremony in mid-air in the flying mosque. “I chose the air for my conversion because I wished it to be performed in no earthly territory,” the heiress, Princess Muda of Sarawak, Borneo, and daughter of the late Sir Walter Palmer, said. “The fore compartment of the ‘Silver Wings’ liner of Imperial Airways was converted into a mosque. The ceremony was carried out 5,000 feet in the air, halfway between England and France. Dr. Khalid performed the ceremony as solemnly as possible under the circumstances. Princess Muda wore a black fur coat and a black frock. The red fez worn by Dr. Sheldrake was the only eastern touch to the scene.

LONDON, Feb. 20. (AP).—Weekend holidays were cancelled today by members of the British cabinet which was formed some time ago to keep a close eye on events in the far east in order that they might watch the developments in the Sino-Japanese battle at Shanghai. The members of the committee resolved to stay in or near London so that they might take any action that became necessary in the emergency. Stanley Baldwin, conservative leader, presided over the sub-committee in the absence of Prime Minister at Shanghai to do his utmost to ensure the safety of British nationals there, estimated to number 9,

Shanghai, Feb. 19.—(AP)—Chinese guns boomed a heavy tattoo today as a prelude to battle. Three Japanese bluejackets were killed. Under cover of the bombardment, Chinese made hasty but elaborate preparations for the expected attack tomorrow when the Japanese ultimatum expires. Beginning of the Japanese offensive tomorrow morning was considered made virtually certain this afternoon when General Uyeda said unless the Chinese had withdrawn from their front line positions at Chapei, Kiangwan and Woosung by 7 a.m. (5 p.m., C. S. T. today) "the Japanese will take independent action." "Thus far," he added significantly, "we see no sign of a Chinese withdrawal." There was no sign that the Chinese had any other intentions than to fight it out to a finish. The bombardment was interpreted by Japanese officers as a gesture of defiance. They said the Chinese guns hurled shells over the Japanese consul

1932-02-19.text: Bombay, India, Feb. 18--(INS)— Miss Madeline Slade, British girl disciple of Mahatma Gandhi, was arrested today for her nationalist activities and sentenced to three months simple imprisonment. Miss Slade, or Mira Bai, as she now is known, defied a warning by the Bombay chief of police to leave the city by last night, threatening arrest if she should refuse. All of the Gandhi household now is jailed for their congress activities. In addition to Miss Slade, who is Gandhi's personal attendant, the aged leader himself, his wife, and two sons are imprisoned. Miss Slade pleaded guilty to defiance of the government’s orders prohibiting participation in national demonstrations.

Boston, Feb. 19—(A.P.)—The Boston Post in a copyright story today injected a new theory into the circumstances surrounding the death of Elizabeth Barrett Cook aboard the British freighter Chinese Prince—the theory that she was the victim of her own hunger for the dramatic. The Post says that passengers who sailed with the girl to Europe December 12 revealed to the paper that they were convinced that Miss Cook herself wrote the “hoax” cablegram. The copyright story also says that another hoax message was received by Miss Cook while she was in Wiesbaden, Germany. The Post quotes passengers as saying that Miss Cook went ashore at Lisbon during the trip across, visited a telegraph office and returned to the ship. A short time later, the paper says, a cablegram was delivered to her saying that a mythical sweetheart she named Malcolm had died. Passengers, the Post says, informed the paper that

PRANUAAL Fen. 19 (UP) — American Hongkew and Yangtze-poo districts of the international settlement were notified by their consuls to evacuate today, in anticipation of a Japanese attempt to crush Shanghai's 10,000 Chinese defenders. Edwin S. Cunningham and John F. Brenan, United States and British consuls-general, respectively, issued a statement advising evacuation and stressing the danger from falling shells in the districts. Cunningham urged that American women and children be transferred to places of safety before Saturday morning. The orders from the British and American officials followed similar action by the Japanese in clearing their nationals out of the danger zone, the Hongkew district where Japanese troops have been massed for an attack. Chinese Deliver Reply. The Japanese announced officially that they would be ready for the offensive at 7 a.m. Saturday (5 p.m. Friday, CST)

DUBLIN, Feb. 19. (®)—Eamon De Valera, leader of the Fianna Fail, Irish republican party, appeared riding the tide of ballots toward the next presidency of the Free State as returns from considerably more than half of the election districts were tabulated today. The republicans had a lead of 9 seats in the Dail over the government party on the basis of these returns. There were about 69 districts still to be reported, however, and both sides continued to express confidence of winning. De Valera’s Fianna Fail had reported 45 seats and his labor supporters had 5. President Cosgrave’s government party had 86 seats and 10 were held by independents, who usually have supported the government. Thus the Fianna Fail and allies held 50 seats while the government and its supporters held 46 seats. DUBLIN, Trish Free State, Feb. 19—If the Fianna Fail party led by Eamonn De Valera, ardent Anti-British Republican, holds the lead it is piling up hourly in the Free State general elections, it will introduce at once a measure to abolish the oath of allegiance to the King of England, it was understood today. The returns will be complete by Saturday, it was believed. With practically two-thirds of the 146 parliamentary seats accounted for, the De Valera party was leading President William T. Cosgrave’s government party by a 14-seat margin. The returns, with 96 seats accounted for, were: Fianna Fail—46. Government Party—32. Independents—10. National Independents—2. Official Labor—3. Farmers—1. The Independents may be counted on to support Cosgrave, and the Laborites have issued a statement indicating they will back De Valera. Dublin, Irish Free State, Feb. 18-- Eamonn de Valera, the lanky Spanish-Irishman who once was condemned to death for his unending battle against England, tonight became a real possibility as the next president of the Irish Free State. All day long the tellers counted the ballots in Tuesday's general election, and the more they counted the farther ahead went de Valera’s Fianna Fáil ticket.

DUBLIN, Feb. 19.—(UP)— Eamonn De Valera, whose dream of an Irish Republic never has died, proclaimed today that his Fianna Fail party had gained a workable control of the government in the general election to the Dail. “The moment we are returned to power, even though the majority will be a small one,” he told the press, “you will find we have a ‘tremendous moral majority that will give us full support.” With returns for 99 of the 146 contested seats now in, the race between the Fianna Fail and President William T. Cosgrave’s government party continued close, the Fianna Fail and its Labor allies having a majority of five seats over all other groups. By The Associated Press. London, England, Feb. 18.—For the first time in eighteen years the Bank of England today cut its rediscount rate by a full one per cent, reducing it from 6 per cent to 5 per cent. Usually the rate is stepped down a half of one per cent at a time, and today’s action gave an immediate fillip to industrial issues on the stock exchange where cheaper money acted as a valuable stimulus to trade.

1932-09-30.text: H Lewes, Del., Today. — () — Disaster has overtaken another quest for the Spanish gold that is believed to have lain at the bottom of the sea since the British sloop De Braak sank off the Delaware capes 139 years ago. The latest effort to salvage an estimated $16,090,000 worth of doubloons and pieces of eight and gems that went down with the De Braak was suspended today following a fire that burned one of the salvaging ships, the Katie Durm, to the water line last night. The vessel, fired by an overturned lantern, sank within a short time after it was swept by the flames, and the members of the crew were rescued by the Cape, a sister ship, and landed here. One of the crew was burned about the arm. The Katie Durm and the Cape, owned by the Baltimore Derrick and Salvaging Company, had been at work two weeks in quest of the gold that has defied dozens of salvaging efforts over a period of m

ATHENS, Sept. 30. (AP)—The count of victims of the week’s earthquakes at Chalcidice, set yesterday at more than 200 dead, continued to rise today as many dead and wounded were found under crumbled ruins in the city. Meanwhile, shocks continued at Salonika and most of the frightened people spent the night in the open air. A crevasse 16 miles long and of great depth has been opened in the quake area. From the sea the great fissure can be seen climbing the side of one mountain and the inhabitants of the district were terror-stricken today lest the mountain slide and engulf them. British sailors continued distributing food and medicines to the stricken people.

Athens, Sept. 30, UPi—The number of dead in the earthquake of Chalcidice peninsula was nearly 500 today, with the death of 35 injured persons and the discovery of more bodies in ruined dwellings. Some geologists feared that the peninsula might become an island due to gradual sinking. The island of Amogiana, off the Chalcidice coast, was reported soon after the quake to have disappeared into the sea with 200 refugee families. Earth shocks continued on the peninsula and spread throughout Macedonia. Many survivors were made ill by infected water.

Geneva, Switzerland (U.P.) — Division of armies into police forces necessary to maintain internal order and defense forces large enough to protect against external aggression was proposed to the world disarmament conference today by the American delegate, Hugh Wilson. Wilson asked the subcommittee on effectives of the general steering committee to "examine as expeditiously as possible the proposal of President Hoover with the view of bringing about strict limitation and real reduction of effectives." The American move was considered unusually important because the subcommittee is composed of political members and not experts and also because if the powers decide to disarm, they must agree to methods of slashing land forces and navy personnel. The outstanding proposal of the Hoover plan was a straight one-third armament cut. The memorandum submitted today established the guiding principle

Athens, Sept. 29.—()—The series of earthquakes that have caused death and destruction in many parts of Greece during the last few days continued today when five violent shocks caused considerable damage at Salonika.

HAMILTON, Ont., Sept. 29——(AP) The United Church of Canada, representing the largest group of protestants in the dominion, was urged by its board of evangelism and social service today to place its stamp of approval on birth control. Every Christian married person has the right to determine "in the light of the facts and obligations involved how far precautions against reproduction shall be employed in his or her own life," declared a report adopted by the board. The general council of the United Church, which includes the bulk of Presbyterians in Canada and all the Methodists and Congregationalists, referred the report to its committee on evangelism and social service. Another proposed declaration by the church, as recommended by the board, was that civil marriages should be established in all provinces. (In some provinces only marriages by ministers of religion are permitted). It also

NEW YORK, Sept. 29—(p)—On the heels of a court decision calling for a mayoralty election in November, the name of former Mayor James J. Walker was mentioned in political circles today as a possible candidate for re-election. The Herald Tribune said Tammany Hall had revived its plan to support Walker, who resigned following an investigation into the city administration, and had timed a convention of county committeemen, called to nominate a candidate, to coincide with the return of the former mayor from a vacation abroad.

BOSTON, 7. Calvin Coolidge Thursday night called upon republicans of Massachusetts to conduct a “fighting campaign” for the re-election of President Herbert Hoover and the Massachusetts state ticket. The Coolidge call to arms was contained in a letter to President Judson Hannigan, of the republican club of Massachusetts, which was read at the “night before” dinner of republicans here for Friday’s state convention. Hannigan had invited Coolidge to be present. The former president said in his letter, which was sent from his summer home in Plymouth, Vt., that “if I thought I could be of any particular benefit to the cause I should try to be present” at the dinner. Through a change in plans former Congressman Philip P. Campbell of Kansas supplanted Senator Hastings of Delaware as the principal speaker at the dinner. A feature of the gathering was receipt of an address by President Hoover, wh

1932-01-19.text: Washington, Jan. 19.—President Hoover has asked Charles G. Dawes, resigned United States ambassador to Great Britain to become head of the two billion dollar reconstruction finance corporation. Secretary of State Stimson would succeed Dawes as head of the American delegation to the Geneva arms conference. Eugene Meyer, head of the Federal Reserve board, has been named chairman of the board of directors of the finance corporation, the president announced. Dawes' appointment was looked upon as substantiation of denials both at the White House and by Dawes that Dawes’ dramatic announcement of his retirement from the realms of diplomacy indicated a disagreement between him and Mr. Hoover which might lead Dawes into the presidential field. Whether Stimson eventually will actually go to Europe remained conjectural. Dawes was at the office of Secretary of State Stimson when the announcement was

(By Associated Press) France has made overtures for extension of the Hoover moratorium on intergovernmental debts in a semi-official note and in diplomatic feelers sent to Washington. The note said the British and French governments favored renewal of the moratorium on payments due from Germany for six months or a year from next July 1, when the moratorium would otherwise expire. The extension would be worked out by financial experts. The American government in turn would be asked to give European creditors of Germany who are American debtors an extension on their war debts for the same period. Authoritative quarters in London had earlier denied that overtures would be made to America for possible extension of the moratorium but it was indicated that the world reparations conference at Lausanne would consider extending the moratorium for six months. The conference is tentatively schedule

Paris, Jan. 19 () (Tuesday) —France wants the Lausanne reparations conference postponed and the moratorium on reparations and war debts extended until next year, it became known today. The British and French governments, said a semi-official note, seem to be agreed on a renewal for six months or one year of the Hoover moratorium on payments due from Germany. The present moratorium will expire next July 1. Under the French plan, as announced in the note, a meeting of financial experts would be called to prolong the Hoover moratorium. The United States would be asked by France and other European debtors, who are creditors of Germany, to be given a moratorium on their war debts on the same terms. Elections due this year in America, Germany and France were given in the note as reasons for the contemplated “provisional postponement” of the world reparations conference, which is tentatively sc

Edinburgh, Scotland, Jan. 9 Prince George, youngest son of the King, escaped injury by a scant few inches today while he was making a tour of the industrial districts of this city. As he walked into one workshop, a heavy plank which had been used to prop open a window fell at his feet. He jumped back quickly, but made light of the incident and went on with his tour of inspection.

Paris, Jan. 19—(UP)—Minister of War Andre Tardieu was named today to head the French delegation to the world disarmament conference at Geneva. As premier, Tardieu was chief delegate to the London naval conference for 1930. He was expected to carry out the “big army” policies of his predecessor at the war ministry, the late Amire Matiaot. Joseph Paul-Boncour will be vice president of the delegation which will include Minister of Navy Charley Dumont, Minister of Air Jacques Dusmenil, Dean Fabry, Paul Reynaud, and C. I. Gignoux. Experts who will accompany the delegates will be named later.

Bombay, India, Jan. 19—(A.P.)— Another member of Mahatma Gandhi’s family went to prison today when his youngest son, Ramdas, was arrested in the village of Haipura for engaging in nationalist activities. The Mahatma was taken several weeks ago, then his 60-year-old wife was sentenced to three weeks in jail. Nineteen prisoners, most of them women, who were arrested for picketing outside the government mint today were tried, convicted and sentenced to six months in prison in the remarkably short time of 22 minutes.

Paris, Jan. 19.—(4)—Premier Laval, introducing his new cabinet to the chamber of deputies today, said flatly that France will not forego her claim to reparations from Germany. France faces a double duty, he said, "the duty toward the generation which went through the war, to sacrifice nothing of what is due us without a corresponding remission of our own debts; and the duty to future generations, to subordinate all agreements to a just balance between conditions of

MADRID, Jan. 19. (4)—Rioting, burning and labor troubles in dozens of places throughout Spain during the past twenty-four hours was followed today by threats of a general strike next Monday. In several sections of the country city workers moved out upon the land and began to till it, the owners, in most cases, offering no changes. The workers declared they were ploughing only enough to provide themselves with food. The general strike reports, which could not be confirmed, said Communists and syndicalists were organized for a concerted revolutionary attempt to implant “literal Communism” in Spain. Superiors of the Jesuits, following a revival of the anti-Catholic demonstrations which resulted in several deaths in rioting and the burning of buildings, ordered 200 novices at the Loyola Novitiate at Bilbao to pack their clothing in

The statement was drawn from Whitney near the close of a long day of spirited cross-examination, but the stock exchange president would not agree that the ban on short selling was ordered because of a fear that the bears would demoralize the market. He insisted that the prohibitory rule was adopted to make the shorts buy to cover and thus provide a bolstering factor in the market. “God only knows what would have happened,” Whitney said, “if short selling had been allowed.” Hearing Room Crowded The hearing room was again crowded with spectators today, impatiently waiting for the names of the big short

United Press Staff Correspondent. LONDON, April 19—(U.P)—Britain’s expectation of a revision or cancellation of war debts this year was clearly indicated today by Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer, in introducing his 1932-33 budget in the House of Commons, providing for expenditures of $2,908,140,000, the smallest since 1924. Chamberlain reiterated his Feb. statement of reparations and war debts policy, namely, that Britain stands for general all-around cancellation. He said he had not included in this estimated receipts anything from reparations or war debts owed to Britain by her dominions and former allies, and likewise had made no provision to meet payment of Britain’s war debt to the United States. “After the deliberations at Lausanne,” Chamberlain told the crowded and expectant House, “I shall submit to Parliament whatever proposals may be necessary to give effect to

LONDON, April 19 (INS) Early retirement of Prime Minister J. Ramsay from active political life was advocated by politicians of all parties today on the heels of an official announcement that he had suffered a relapse in the eye ailment which recently necessitated a delicate operation. Intimates of the Prime Minister admitted that the state of his eyes will prevent him from doing any large amount of documentary reading in the future. As such work is regarded as essential in the post of Premier, his resignation is expected to follow in due course.

Geneva, April 19 (A.P.)—Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson appeared at the session of the world disarmament conference today and took his seat with the American delegation. His arrival caused a lively hum of excitement among the delegates and spectators. Secretary Stimson entered the session of the general commission of the conference two hours after the session opened. The debate was on criteria of arms reduction. He was escorted to his place at the table beside Ambassador Hugh Gibson by members of the American delegation.

Harbin, Manchuria, April 1.—(AP)—A twenty-year-old Chinese girl, known among natives as a modern Joan of Arc, is playing a prominent part in the insurgency along the eastern section of the Chinese Eastern railway, according to Chinese reports. As near as could be learned here, the girl is the leader of 1,900 Chinese volunteers opposing the Manchoukuo authority in northern Kirin province, which borders on Soviet Russian territory. Reports today said she led her band against the detachment of Chinese provincial forces in that area with such enthusiasm, that the Manchoukuo troops retreated in haste before the fiery attack.

GENEVA, April 19—(UP)—Secretary of State Stimson appeared for the first time at the world disarmament conference today soon after the general commission approved the American claim that armament reduction to the possible level be the first

ORBETELLO, Italy, April 18— (AP) —Lieutenant Colonel Guascone Guasconi, one of Italy's foremost speed pilots, who participated in the Schneider Cup races at Norfolk, Va., in 1926, was killed with two other men when a seaplane plunged into the water here during a demonstration flight today. The other dead were Engineer Domenico Vurlan of the Fiat Automobile company and Naval Mechanic Vittorio Maietta. Five army and navy officers who completed the group in the plane were injured, one seriously.

GENEVA, April 18. UPI--Secretary of State Stimson, the victim of an annoying cold, remained in his sixteenth century villa all today while the disarmament conference debated a proposal for reduction in arms to be achieved by successive stages.

These thirty-four seats were divided as follows: Fianna Fáil (De Valera)... 31 Government (Cosgrave) . 12 Independent 6

Dublin, Irish Free State, Feb. 18 —(U.P)—Eamon De Valera and his Fianna Fail party were increasing their lead today over President William T. Cosgrave’s government candidates, as returns in the Irish Free State general election trickled in. Latest tabulations showed a margin of three districts for De Valera, with independents and labor candidates also gaining. They were: Fianna Fail, 22. Administration, 12. Independents, 6. Labor, 2. There are 153 seats in the lower house (Dail), of which Cosgrave formerly controlled 65 and De Valera 56. Both De Valera in County Clare and Cosgrave in Cork were overwhelmingly re-elected. Cosgrave’s total poll reached 18,125 votes. De Valera’s chief lieutenant, Sean Lemass, was elected from South Dublin, where Cosgrave had been conceded a clean sweep in what practically amounted to his home district. To offset this, General Richard J. Mulcahy, minister of

LONDON, Feb. 18. (#)—The Bank of England extended a helping hand to the commercial community and a financial gesture of confidence to the world today by reducing the bank rate from six to five per cent. The six per cent rate was imposed on September 21, 1931, when the country went off the gold standard. Soon after the announcement in Threadneedle Street word came from Stockholm and from Oslo that the bank rate in both Sweden and Norway had been reduced from six per cent to five and a half per cent. The improvement in the international outlook and the result of preliminary conversations regarding the “Lausanne conference” were taken to be one of the guiding factors in the bank rate reduction, but the chief reason is cheaper money and the fact that market discounts have fallen to such a low level as to make a six per cent rate ineffective. Retaining the higher rate, it was decided, is no l

Dublin, Irish Free State, Feb. 18.— Eamon De Valera’s Fianna Fáil and its allies of the Labor party were running ahead of President Cosgrave's government ticket by 25 to 22 seats in the new dáil at mid-afternoon with returns from 47 of the 145 precincts counted. The standing at that point was Fianna Fáil (De Valera) Labor Independents 6 Even though he was running ahead, De Valera thus far in the count had not registered the heavy vote his followers had predicted and some commentators thought that even if he should win it would be by so narrow a margin as to create a stalemate in the dáil, possibly necessitating a new election in the fall.

TOKIO, Feb. 18 @P~The British naval command holds Japan responsible for Chinese shelling in which two sailors were killed. The shells fell in the international settlement. A government spokesman revealed today that Vice-Admiral Sir William Kelley had protested that ‘Japanese landing in the settlement were responsible for the Chinese fire in which the sailors were fatally wounded.

Bombay, India, Feb. 18.—(Thursday)—Miss Madeline Slade, who forsook London society to become a follower of Mahatma Gandhi, was arrested tonight for disobeying a government order that she stay out of Bombay. She went down to Poona, where Mr. Gandhi is in jail, and courted arrest by returning to Bombay yesterday with the declaration that she was determined to carry on her work.

BUDLEN, Feb. 17—(Thursday)—st William T. Cosgrave and Eamon De Valera, leaders of the two strongest parties in Free State politics, achieved personal triumphs in Monday's general election, by being returned with enormous leads to their seats in the Dail Eireann. Tabulations early this morning showed 28 of the 153 seats in the Dail distributed as follows; Fianna Fail party (De Valera, 12; Government party (Cosgrave), 10; Independent, 5; Labor, 1. Mr. De Valera topped the poll in Clare and was elected on the first count. He received almost double the quota under the proportional representation system. In Cork Mr. Cosgrave had an enormous excess over the next candidate, T. P. Gill, a Fianna Fail candidate, and both were declared elected.

Washington, Feb. 17—Japan's possible responsibility for damage to life and property in the conflict at Shanghai is a problem receiving attention in the world’s principal capitals. The killing of two British sailors in Shanghai's international settlement by a shell from a Chinese gun, presumably aimed at Japan's warships, intensified official Washington's interest in the question. This incident is regarded by officials as one of hundreds which will arise if there is continued heavy fighting. For a week or more state department officials in Washington as well as in Japan and China have been discussing informally with Japanese officials the possible damage claims which would arise if the Shanghai clash should involve the international settlement. Other powers have been engaging in similar conversations. The state department has sent no note as yet to Japan on this question. Press dispatches

1932-06-16.text: Lausanne, Switzerland, June 16.—Europe cannot act alone but must have the help of the United States in solving the world’s economic troubles, Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald of Great Britain asserted today as the delegates of thirteen nations opened a conference on reparations and war debts here. “This is a time for bold proposals,” he said. “The United States has encouraged us to believe it will cooperate in some of the wider problems and join us in devising a policy for the encouragement of trade and the enrichment of nations.” His address, after his election as chairman of the conference, was the only one of major importance in a session which lasted a little over an hour. The continuing economic crisis, he said, is the worst with which the world has ever been afflicted. It amounts to a “world catastrophe.” “The world looks on not only in need but in impatience. My appeal to you is to

LAUSANNE (UP) — Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald of Great Britain, chairman of the Lausanne "reparations conference to end reparations," Thursday pleaded that nations speedily settle the reparations question to "avoid world catastrophe." "We have met today in the shadow of the most ominous economic crisis that ever afflicted the world in time of peace," MacDonald said. "The whole world looks to us as it has never looked at an international conference before to find an agreement which will help end existing distress. "What I wish to emphasize is that this is a world catastrophe. "I repeat that in this, there is no France, no Italy, no Germany, no United States, no Great Britain apart from the rest of the nations," MacDonald said. "None of us can stay out of the restoration and reconstruction because none of us can stay out of the miseries which are gathering about us. "Today we have met to

MANILA, P. L., June 16,—(P)— Hope was raised today that Glenn Brophy, English flier who disappeared March 18, 1931, is alive among the pagan savages of Yami, northernmost of the Philippine Islands. A Japanese fishing boat and Filipinos reported a strange figure was seen signalling from the shore of the island. Strong currents, heavy waves and fear of the savages prevent small boats from approaching to investigate. Brophy vanished between Macao, China, and Luzon, P. L., while on a flight from Shanghai to Manila.

Englewood, N. J., June 15 (4)-- Violet Sharpe, English servant girl in the home of Mrs. Dwight W. Morrow, was buried today after a brief service attended by fellow members of the Morrow household and the acting British consul-general. The British official has been instructed to make a report on the girl’s suicide five days ago. The simple cloth-covered casket was borne by four men employees to a grave in Brookside cemetery, where rests the body of the late Senator Dwight W. Morrow, grandfather of the murdered Lindbergh baby. No member of the Morrow or Lindbergh family attended the final rites, although they were represented by Arthur Springer, the late senator's private secretary, and Mrs. Josephine D. Graham, Mrs. Morrow's private secretary. Gerald Shepherd, the acting British consul-general at New York, immediately after the funeral went to the Morrow estate to confer with Springer, fr

RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil, June 15 (AP) — The Greek freighter Artemis sank off Southern Bahia, Brazil, today and her crew of 31 was saved by the British motorship Eastern Prince, which responded to SOS calls.
LONDON, June 15 - Sir Donald MacLean, 68 years old, president of the board of education in the MacDonald cabinet, died today.

LAUSANNE, Switzerland, June 16 (P)—Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald of Great Britain told delegates of 13 nations at the opening of the conference on war debts and reparations today that the present economic crisis is “the worst with which the world has ever been afflicted. The conference opened at 10 A. M. He was elected president. "It is a world catastrophe with which we have faced,” he said.

| LAUSANNE, Switzerland, June 15 —(AP)—A request that the United States cancel all war debts was being discussed tonight as the 600 delegates of thirteen nations assembled here for tomorrow's opening session of the conference on debts and reparations at which a way to world economic recovery will be sought. The request to the United States in the event it is decided on—will be presented to the conference in the form of a resolution. Whether such drastic action would be advisable was the topic of debate tonight at numerous private gatherings of the delegates. Meanwhile Prime Minister Ramsey MacDonald of Great Britain, who is slated to serve as president of the conference, prepared the keynote speech with which he will open the proceedings. British spokesmen were authority for the statement that MacDonald was determined to lead the way to some definite accomplishment before the conference

1932-03-21.text: OP 440 news (et ew £1 | Belfast, Northern Ireland, March | 20.—Authorities of Northern Ireland | today watched with anxiety and ‘alarm an increasingly serious situation in the Irish Free State, where | President Eamon De Valera is intent upon further severance of the ties to England. Drilling has been resumed illegally by De Valera’s Irish Republican Army in various parts of the Free State, officials said. There was a feeling that the attack from ambush on a party of men cycling to an Hibernian hall in County Londonderry on St. Patrick's Day might be made a pretext for active aggression in the northern territory. A machine gun has been used in Irish Republican Army maneuvers in at least one instance close to the border. The automobile of Coroner J. H. Murphy was stolen at Dundalk last week and was understood to have been used with two other cars for the transportation of rifles into Nort

CHICAGO, March 21 (#)—The Chicago police last night heard a bedtime story from 7-year-old Gertrude Luchsinger, that left them pop-eyed. They found her wandering around in a park. “I was born,” she said, “in New York. My mama's name was Jean, and my daddy was killed in a war in England. Four years ago my mama gave me to another lady and came to see me once in a while from Philadelphia. “My second mama lived in New York, but she came to Chicago three weeks ago on a train, but started back three days ago. At the railroad station mama put me and a little dog and a little baby on the floor and bought the tickets. Then she picked up the baby and the dog and forgot me. Since then I've been shifting for myself. Last night I leaned up against a shack all night.” The wires hummed to New York and Philadelphia, but meanwhile the telephone rang. “My daughter,” said Mrs. Luchsinger, “has been missing

London March 20. (#) — Brecqhou, one of the smaller channel islands, described as a “Paradise” and a “gem set in the azure seas,” has been advertised for sale in London. It is a little kingdom in itself, 160 acres in area. The owner is his own taxing and licensing authority, and is entitled to a seat in the Parliament of Sark. There are only two buildings on Brecqhou—a stone house and a four-room bungalow. The buyer will have to produce his own electricity and draw his water from a well. There are plenty of fish and rabbits, and the taxes levied total only $10 a year in normal times.

LONDON, March 21.—INS—Nel. Ne Richards, 63, old-time American vaudeville star who popularized the song "Johnnie Get-Your-Gun," was found dead in her one-room apartment in the West End today. The room was filled with gas, Police said a tea kettle, which stood on a stove in the room, apparently had boiled over and extinguished the flame on the burner beneath, while Miss Richards was asleep in her bed nearby.

Shanghai, Mar. 21--China and Japan reached a temporary truce in their conflict over control of Shanghai today, when both sides agreed to refer details of a peace pact to a joint commission. The Japanese consular paved the way to an understanding by acceding to Chinese demands that all the Mikado's troops withdraw from Shanghai, leaving Chinese defensive forces in their present position, outside the city. The truce was reached with unexpected suddenness after a day of inactivity.

en, March 21.—(UP)—The Graf Zeppelin was en route to Pernambuco, Brazil, today on the first commercial flight of the spring and summer season. Commander Hugo Eckener chose a route across southern France and Spain towards Gibraltar, after which he intended to head toward either the Cape Verde or the Canary Islands. The ship was due at Pernambuco at 11 p. m. Tuesday. The Graf carried nine German passengers and 100 kilograms of mail. Officials of the Zeppelin works revealed after the start of the flight that a man named Amann, from Augsburg, was discovered trying to stow away and was arrested. Return passage has been booked in the name of William R. Leeds, American millionaire. The Zeppelin made a perfect start in favorable weather and Valence, in southern France, early today.

(Copyright, 1932, by United Press) GENEVA, March 21— (UP) — Japanese proposals for security arrangements in the Far East against China and Russia, rivaling France’s demands for security in Europe, have been prepared for submission to the world arms conference, the United Press was informed today. The Japanese military experts met last night and drafted the proposals for submission to the Secretariat on April 4. The conference will be requested to consider the “special situation” in the Far East, where Japan has two neighbors—namely Russia, whose political, social and military organization differs from all other nations, and China, which is unable to maintain order in its own domain. The proposal asks the conference to consider such special conditions when discussing disarmament of Far Eastern nations, implying Japan will not be in a position to limit armaments unless her security is assu

Nice—(#)—Prince Nicholas of Rumania told the Associated Press Monday he was going back home to take up his old place in the court of his brother, King Carol. He made this disclosure of his plans when he reached here at the wheel of the automobile he drove down from Paris in the grueling Paris-Nice motor race. He was well up in the running, but the official results will not be announced until Friday. Prince Nicholas angered King Carol by marrying Madame Jana Deleti, a commoner, against the king’s wishes. There was some talk of stripping him of his royal prerogatives, but the prince left with his bride for Paris and Carol took no drastic action. Recently the king sent an emissary to see Nicholas, and presumably it was he who succeeded in patching up the quarrel.

1932-02-21.text: DUBLIN, Irish Free State, Feb. 20. — Victory for Eamon de Valera’s Fianna Fail party was unofficially conceded today as returns from the Free State election gave him a certain plurality over the administration party of President William T. Cosgrave. With all but 16 of the 146 seats in the Dail accounted for, the Fianna Fail—which is sworn to abolish the oath of allegiance to King George—held a lead of 16 seats over the Cosgrave party. Minister of Education J. M. O’Sullivan and Minister of Fisheries Fionan Lynch, both of the administration party, have been reelected from County Kerry. All ministers except Minister of Industry and Commerce McGolligan have been reelected. The count in McGolligan’s constituency was expected late today. The Fianna Fail vote has already shown an increase of 120,000 over its total in the previous general election. All members of De Valera’s tentative cabinet ha

London, Feb. 20 — (AP) — The will of the late Sir Thomas Lipton, filed for probate today, showed an estate valued at £566,068, worth $1,953,000 at current quotations. The duties will amount to £925,006 ($776,250).

WASHINGTON (BP)— American Minister Nelson T. Johnson of Shanghai reported to the state department Saturday that he, with the British, French and Italian ministers, had made representations to the Japanese minister concerning danger to American life and property and also had made eleventh hour efforts to maintain peace. The four western spokesmen pointed out to the Japanese that they “could not avoid a large measure of responsibility for the jeopardy to foreign life and property at Shanghai.” The Japanese consul replied that the issue rested with the Chinese. In another report, Johnson said the American, British, French and Italian military attaches made representations to the Chinese General Tsai Ping-Kai against artillery fire into the Yangtze Poo section. The Chinese general replied that he would not fire into their section again if he were assured the Japanese artillery had not taken

Princetown, England, Feb. 20 (CP) Dartmoor prison, where a mutiny broke out recently among dangerous convicts, was seething with unrest tonight. Fifty ringleaders of the mutiny, who are kept in solitary confinement with three empty cells separating them from each other, raised a pandemonium of shouts, curses and banging of their cells. The uproar had occurred for several nights, arousing the villagers of this nearby place. They were greatly alarmed last night, but the authorities said they were ready for any eventuality. Police and troops were available if needed.

DUBLIN, Feb. 20.—(#)—Eamon De Valera appeared to be “in” tonight with only fourteen constituencies missing from the 152 which voted in the Free State general election on Tuesday. At that point his Fianna Fail and its labor party allies had 72 seats in the new Dail between them. President Cosgrave’s government ticket and the supporting independents had 66. The party standing was: Fianna Fail 63; labor 9; government 49; independents 17.

DUBLIN, Feb. 20.—U.P)—Eamonn de Valera, stern prophet of the Irish republic and implacable foe of Great Britain, today was the first man in Ireland as results of the dail elections continued to increase the lead of his Fianna Fáil party over the administration party of President William T. Cosgrave. With scattered results coming in, a tabulation tonight showed Fianna Fáil the strongest party in the Irish parliament, lacking only one seat of being even with the combined strength of all the other parties, except Labor, De Valera’s ally, but with the co-operation of the Labor party and its seven votes, De Valera had little to fret over in this lack of a clear majority.

Dublin, Irish Free State, Feb. 20.—Eamonn De Valera said tonight his Fianna Fail party was victorious in the Free State general election and that “now or later Ireland will win her complete independence.” The republican leader appeared to be “in” with only seven constituencies missing from the 145 which voted in the election Tuesday. The election in seven other constituencies was postponed until next month on account of the assassination of a local candidate. De Valera needed 77 seats in the new Dail before he could be expected to form a government and take over the power. His Fianna Fail and its labor party allies had 72 seats between them. President William T. Cosgrave’s government ticket and the supporting independents had 66. De Valera, interviewed today, reit- Continued on Page 2, Column 3.

PARIS, Feb. 20. (4)—Former Premier Paul Painleve abandoned today his attempt to form a cabinet to succeed the government of former Premier Pierre Laval which resigned earlier this week. In announcing his failure to construct a government, M. Painleve attributed it to the refusal of M. Laval and former Premier Andre Tardieu to join with him in a cabinet of leftist complexion. He left for the Elysee Palace at 4 a.m. to inform President Paul Doumer of his decision. The president was expected to renew his search for a premier later today and in political circles it was considered likely he would call on M. Tardieu who returned from Geneva when the cabinet crisis developed. Before turning to the left, M. Painleve had tried to gather together a "cabinet of conciliation" but M. Tardieu brought this attempt to naught by declining to accept a post as minister of state without portfolio, to which

1932-10-06.text: LEICESTER, ENGLAND, Oct. 6—WU.P—The Labor party, holding its annual conference, passed a resolution today unanimously demanding immediate negotiations for cancellation of war debts and reparations. The resolution stipulated that Britain should not pay or receive another single pound in reparations or war debts.

London, Oct. 5. — A spirit of cordiality not associated recently with Anglo-Irish relations prevailed during a conference at the dominions office today at which President Eamon De Valera and Dominions Secretary J. H. Thomas agreed to negotiate the controversy over unpaid Irish land annuities. The negotiations are scheduled to start October 14. De Valera and several of his ministers will come to London to take part in them. Although the possible basis for settlement was a question neither side would discuss publicly, the fact that negotiations are to be resumed gave rise to reports that a method for composing the dispute had been found. Pending final agreement the Free State will continue to keep possession of the disputed funds and the British retaliatory tariffs, leveled against the Free State when Dublin first defaulted, will remain effective.

London, Oct. 6.—(?)—Information from Downing Street today indicated that the prospects are anything but bright for the four-power conference proposed by Great Britain to consider Germany’s demand for arms equality. Italy has accepted an invitation but neither France nor Germany had accepted up to this afternoon and the unofficial view, based on comment in Paris and Berlin, was that there was not much hope for acceptance. Great Britain, however, merely offered her good offices in this matter and if acceptances are not received the disarmament situation will remain just as it was before the conference was proposed.

Toronto, Ont., Oct. 6. — Cook county’s guest for Martin J. Insull, former utilities magnate, turned to Toronto again today when assistant state's attorney John Hampton of Chicago decided to appeal for a fugitive warrant to authorities here instead of at Barrie. Hampton arrived here by motor at 7 a.m. from Barrie after abandoning his plan to seek the fugitive warrant from County Judge Dudley Holmes there. Hampton planned to ask Deputy Crown Attorney General Edward Bayly of Ontario for the fugitive warrant on the ground that Insull's refusal at an early morning conference to return to Chicago made him a fugitive or would-be fugitive because of the indictments and capias Hampton brought with him from Chicago. The Cook county attorney was constantly on the move after his arrival here at 2 a.m. from Chicago by airplane. He drove to Barrie to seek the fugitive warrant, but changed his mind wit

TORONTO, Ont. (P)—Deputy Attorney General Edward Bayly, K.C., of Ontario, was retained Thursday by Cook County, Illinois, to seek a warrant in Canadian courts for the arrest of Martin J. Insull, as a fugitive from justice. Bayly consented to represent the county in Canadian courts, after a conference with Assistant State’s Attorney John Hampton of Chicago. Hampton flew here early Thursday with indictments and a subpoena:

Orillia, Ontario, Oct. 6. (IMS)—Martin J. Insull, former Chicago utilities multi-millionaire, was routed out of bed early today by Chicago officials who offered him the alternative of returning to the United States voluntarily or facing arrest here under a provisional fugitive warrant. Insull elected to remain in Orillia, where he has been in retirement since the $2,000,000.00 crash of the Insull combine. The former magnate said he will resist extradition. Insull is under indictment in Chicago on charges of embezzlement and larceny, Assistant State's Attorney John Hampton, of Cook County, announced he will go before Judge Dudley Holmes, of Simcoe County, today, and ask for a warrant for the arrest.

PARIS, Oct. 6 (UP).—Reports that Samuel Insull and his son, Samuel, Jr. had left France so they might escape extradition to the United States were under investigation today after the father and son disappeared. The Insulls were believed to have left their hotel early Wednesday. Officials at Le Bourget airdrome had no record of their departure by air. They would be safe from extradition if they reached Luxembourg.

- Burlington, Ia., Oct. 6—()—Former Judge Luke Palmer, 80, well known attorney, died at his home here today after an illness of ten days. He was a native of Burlington. After attending the public schools he attended Knox College and Harvard Law School and was graduated from the Boston Law School in 1883. Three years later he went to Colorado, where he was elected judge. After serving two years of his second term, he resigned and returned here because of illness and business affairs. The widow and one daughter survive.

1932-04-27.text: Washington, April 27.—(A.P.)—Franklin D. Roosevelt's rush for the Democratic presidential nomination met its first direct check today when primary returns showed Massachusetts had pledged its entire 36 convention votes to Alfred E. Smith. To what extent that New England defeat may be mitigated by the results coming in slowly from Pennsylvania, with Roosevelt gaining on Smith in the presidential reference vote, only complete returns from the Keystone state can determine. The Roosevelt forces still claimed he would have more than 60 votes from the Pennsylvania delegation of 176 on the first ballot at Chicago. The preference vote there is not binding on the delegates. Smith’s First Votes, Excepting the Pennsylvania contest for the time being, yesterday’s results gave former Governor Smith his first definite place with pledged votes in the Democratic convention. So far as numbers are concern
DUBLIN, Irish Free State, April 27 (%.--The government of President Eamon De Valera was defeated in the Dáil Éireann today in a division on the unemployment issue. The vote was 74 to 66.

Dublin, April 27.—President Eamon De Valera was defeated in the Dail today during debate on the bill for abolition of the oath to the crown. The bill, by a vote of 74 to 66, rejected his motion to discuss the second reading of the bill ahead of other business. Since the vote was not on a major issue, it was believed the government’s resignation was unlikely.

| GLASGOW, April 27. (AP) — Drouth-stricken counties in northeastern Montana may stage a comeback this year, Because of the availability of federal seed loans, the reopening of certain credit channels and a wide distribution of garden seed and seed potatoes by the American Red Cross, the outlook has taken a decidedly optimistic turn in the last week. On the heels of timely rainfall have come reports of renewed agricultural hopes. These reports were brought here today to national officials of the Red Cross by chapter chairmen of the seven stricken highline counties of Montana. They were presented at a meeting Tuesday called to formulate plans for terminating the relief agency’s program on May 1. Without exception the chapter officers reported that soil conditions, garden prospects and the general farming outlook of their counties are the best in recent years. The counties represented were

Geneva, Switzerland—(4)—Henry L. Stimson, the American secretary of state, is sailing for the United States next Tuesday, it was announced Wednesday. It was understood that the secretary of state would sail on the Vulcania from Cannes, France. Twice within the week that the secretary has been in Geneva to attend the world disarmament conference he has been unable to bring together various diplomats representing the "Big Five" in disarmament conference negotiations. He has sought to break the existing deadlock on the French and American disarmament schemes. San Felice, Binckstone, Dutch Master Henry George, Havana Ribbon Cigars. (advertisement)

Harbin, Manchuria, April 27. — (Wednesday — (AP) — The Japanese army began today its largest offensive since the capture of Chin-Chow last December, when three brigades under Lieutenant General Hirose moved out against a force of Chinese rebels estimated to number 20,000. The Japanese armies moved out into northern and eastern Manchuria by rail and by river boats, executing a huge ‘pincers’ movement, in the hope of crushing the rebels. The whole of the northern and eastern portions of the province were aflame with revolt and it was especially violent along the Chinese Eastern railway lines and in the Sungari area. At the same time, lesser Japanese forces were attempting to crush other rebel groups in the Tunghua district, 125 miles east of Mukden. (This should not be confused with Tunhua, eastern Kirin province.)
Friedrichshafen, April 13—(UP)—The Graf Zeppelin was moored here today after completing a trip of 101 hours from Pernambuco, Brazil. The ship carried 11 passengers and made the trip.

PARIS, April 27. A new hand reported for work at 8 o’clock this morning in the Ford plant outside Paris and punched the clock as Mr. Oricans. In better days his chief claim to distinction was that King Alfonso of Spain was his first cousin and that Isabelle II of Spain was his grandmother. That was when he was Infanta D'Orleans, prince of the Bourbons. He wrote Henry Ford some time ago for a job at Detroit and Mr. Ford offered him a place in the French assembling plant. He accepted, hoping that he will be transferred to the home factory later. He is a clerk now but will have a working permit in two weeks and will move to a job in the plant. He reports at eight in the morning, has luncheon in the workmen’s canteen and quits at 5:00 p.m. His mother, the Infanta Eulalia, approved of his job. “Work is a lifesaver,” she says. Her son is 45.

1932-01-21.text: LONDON, Jan. 20 (4)—Postponement of the Lausanne reparations conference was regarded in British official circles today as inevitable because of the French political situation. With the debate in the French Chamber of Deputies carried over until Thursday, Downing Street considered it impossible for the arrangements for the conference to be completed and give time for the delegates to arrive at Lausanne by January 25, the date set for the meeting.

London, Jan. 21.—A new German reparations scheme calling for payment in railroad bonds instead of cash was reported here today coincident with postponement of the Lausanne debts and reparations conference. The Daily Express said Germany had suggested the elimination of Young plan reparations payments and the fixing of a figure payable in the form of German railway bonds. The Daily Express said the British cabinet had sympathetically considered the plan and forwarded it to France, with alternative suggestions for a year’s postponement of the scheduled international debts and reparations conference. A brief foreign office communique said that because intergovernmental conversations had not been completed it was impossible that the Lausanne conference began on Monday, as had been scheduled, but it was hoped that an agreement on procedure would be reached within a few days. Lendon, Eng., Jan. 20.-The British government, bowing to the inevitable, announced tonight in a foreign office statement it was “evident” the Lausanne reparations conference could not begin next Monday, as originally planned. The announcement raised doubts among responsible commentators about whether the conference would be held at all, and on this point the official statement was extremely guarded. “The conversations which have been taking place between the governments chiefly concerned with the conference at Lausanne are not yet concluded and it is evident that the conference cannot be begun as early as next Monday, the date which had been provisionally arranged,” the statement said. “Further conversations are now in progress and the British government entertains the hope it may be possible to come to a satisfactory agreement as to the procedure to be adopted in the course of a few day

BOMBAY, Jan. 20.—(/?)—A hundred thousand persons are expected to assemble illegally tomorrow to voice their protests at the arrest of Mahatma Gandhi and Great Britain's stifling at the civil disobedience movement.

The meeting of the world reparations scheduled for next Monday at Lausanne seemed certain to be postponed, with a possibility that it might be abandoned altogether. The British government announced it was evident the conference could not begin next Monday, as conversations between the governments chiefly concerned were not yet concluded. Premier Pierre Laval of France had to wait until today to learn whether the new government had the confidence of the French parliament and that was another factor in the delay. The British announcement was not expected, even in Germany, which declared its inability to resume reparations payments at the end of the Hoover moratorium, which expires soon. France has suggested that the Hoover moratorium on German payments be extended another six months to a year by a proposed meeting of financial experts, providing the United States also granted a similar ext

New London, Wis., Jan. 21—An investigation into the sudden and unexplained death of Edward Hidde, 42, of Manawa, an important state witness in the case of Edward Riske, charged with causing the death of two men, was ordered today by District Attorney L. D. Smith of Waupaca county. Hidde, taken ill Monday afternoon, died a few hours later. Authorities learned of his death yesterday and today the investigation got under way when District Attorney Smith ordered an autopsy, to be followed by an inquest later this afternoon. At his office in Waupaca today, Smith said the "sudden and unexplained death of Hidde for which doctors can offer no reasonable explanation warrants the calling of an inquest." Smith was expected here shortly after noon today. Hidde was one of the important witnesses at the trial of Riske in November. Riske was charged with placing poison in a bottle of moonshine whisky w

LONDON, Jan. 20.—(AP)—The upper house of the convocation of Canterbury took what the archbishop described as an “historical step” today by adopting unanimously a resolution proposing intercommunion between the Church of England and the 'Old Catholic' churches of Europe. This designation is the name which was assumed by those members of the Roman Catholic Church who refused to accept the Vatican council decision of 1870 regarding papal infallibility, and organized a separate ecclesiastical structure. The archbishop in presenting the resolution for a vote, made it clear that he looked upon it as a first step in the establishment of a great world organization of churches, each maintaining its individual independence, but all united by a “definite unity of structure in faith and order.”

WASHINGTON. (?). With its position on debts and reparations now clear to Europe, the American government assumed an outward attitude of disinterest to the whole problem. Word of the postponement of the Lausanne debt parley was received by the state department from London. Officials declined to comment on the postponement on the grounds that the United States had no interest in the parley since it was a strictly European conference.

1932-07-04.text: LONDON, July 4.— (#) — Mrs. Elvira Dolores Barney, former actress and one of England's most beautiful women, stood in the historic dock of the old Bailey criminal court today and calmly answered ‘not guilty’ to the charge of having shot and killed Michael Scott Stephen, London society man, in her apartment May 31. The old courtroom was packed with Londoners who fought their way in to hear the testimony in the murder trial of the pretty actress. A tense silence pervaded the room as the murder charge was read. Mrs. Barney, whose husband, from whom she is estranged, is an American singer, stood in the dock, dressed entirely in black, her face ashen, and heard the charge intoned. She braced herself at the end of the reading, and her voice rang clearly through the courtroom as she answered ‘not guilty!’ With Justice Humphreys on the bench, the prosecutor, Sir Percival Clarke, then proceeded t

LAUSANNE, July 4—(UP)—Germany virtually had rejected today the reparations conference project unanimously devised by Great Britain, France, Italy, Belgium and Japan in the hope that it would make possible a final solution of Europe’s economic problem. The German objection to the tentative agreement was revealed after German Chancellor Franz von Papen met in conference with the British Prime Minister J. Ramsay Macdonald to discuss the plan. It was reported that the German delegation did not consider the proposed solution a “definite and final solution.” THREE POINTS PLAN 1—The total of 4,200,000,000 marks (about $1,000,000,000) which it was proposed the Reich should pay into a European reconstruction fund in lieu of reparations. 2—The new form of the so-called “safeguarding clause,” which would loosely bind Germany to pay more if Europe's war debts to the United States are not readjusted.

MAO OANNE, SWITZERLAND, July 3.—Germany's acceptance, with reservations, of the major proposals offered by creditor countries for an eventual settlement of reparations by a bond issue was freely predicted today. Not until the United States acted on a proposed revision of war debts, however, would the sum of the final settlement be decided. Thus the agreement, as now drafted after lengthy conversations by the various powers, was understood to allow Chancellor Franz von Papen of Germany to claim that reparations are ended, while at the same time Premier Edouard Herriot could hold that France was safeguarded against the United States in the matter of debts. The final amount of the bond issue, which would be guaranteed by Germany partly to take the place of reparations and partly for the economic reconstruction of Europe, is expected to be between 3,000,000,000 marks and 4,200,000,000.

With the force of a real stampede, he swept through the convention as the favorite sons announced one after another their withdrawal from the race, and turned their votes into the swelling Roosevelt column. He was declared the nominee on the fourth ballot, the first taken last night.
