CHICAGO, July 4—()—The nation’s organized drys were on the war path today against both party platforms on prohibition. A proclamation by the National Prohibition Board of Strategy declared unalterable opposition to repeal or submission of any repeal or modification proposal which would weaken or destroy the dry laws and concluded “We urge all friends of the 18th amendment to devote their best efforts to the election of dry candidates to both houses of Congress and to the state Legislatures.” Although taking no stand on the presidential contest the board said it would recommend and publish at an early date the “procedure and active steps to be taken in the conduct of the campaign.” The drys “heartily” agreed with that portion of the Republican plank declaring for “obedience to and enforcement of the law and the preservation of gains admittedly accomplished under the 18th amendment,” but o

July 4. ()—Governor Franklin D. Roosevelt, democratic presidential candidate, homeward bound after his acceptance speech to the national convention of his party, today began consideration of the campaign which he believes will land him in the White House next March. The governor, enthused by his reception in Chicago, immediately after his arrival in Albany this afternoon, will begin to set up the machinery for the campaign. Within the next two weeks he expects to meet with leaders of the national committee either in New York or at his Hyde Park home and draw up a “blue print” for the campaign. Section-by-Section Appeal. * The governor said before leaving Chicago that he intends to aim each particular section at the issues in which the section is interested. There are, he explained, several issues, prohibition, the economic situation, the tariff and international relations, to be expounde

CHICAGO, July 4.—(4#)—The democrats were bearing homeward from convention today to bind up the wounds of the recent fray and unite in a solid front to carry the Roosevelt-Garner pennant to that victory they have predicted for November. Aside from the deep breach between Franklin D. Roosevelt and Alfred E. Smith and the unanswered question of whether the latter will support the nominee, there were few traces of the recent conflict. Such disaffection as remained appeared to be concentrated in the Eastern die-hard states that clung stubbornly to Smith to the end of the balloting. Like Smith, Frank Hague, the mayor of Jersey City and Smith's floor manager in the fight just ended, went home in silence. There was a conciliatory gesture today from Senator Walsh of Massachusetts, another one of the Smith states, in the form of a statement calling upon Massachusetts democrats to support the ticke

WASHINGTON, July 4—The coast guard today ordered 165 cutters and two destroyers to search for the yacht Curlew, missing participant in ocean races from Montauk Point to Bermuda. The coast guard issued its orders after parents of persons on the boat had definitely established that she was missing. The Curlew, the coast guard was informed, left Montauk Point June 25 and was at first reported safely in Bermuda. Later advices said she was not there. The entire cutter fleet of 165 was ordered out by the commander of the New York division of the coast guard. Some of them may not have enough fuel aboard to participate in the search.

1932-07-11.text: BASLE, Switzerland, July 11 (UP)—The board of the World Bank voted unanimously today for a resolution recommending a return to the gold standard as the best solution of the world crisis. Montagu Norman, governor of the Bank of England, was one of those endorsing the resolution.

PORT JEFFERSON, N.Y. July 11. — Governor Franklin D. Roosevelt boarded the yawl Myth II during the noon hour today and prepared to leave on a week's sailing trip up the New England coast with three of his sons. The departure was delayed while baggage from the governor's automobile was loaded into the low-hulled yawl.

LONDON, July 11—(UP)—Confirmation in British circles that a ‘gentlemen’s agreement’ had been reached at Lausanne under which the reparations settlement will not be ratified until a satisfactory debt agreement is reached with the United States, induced some feeling of doubt today about the merits of the Lausanne treaty. The Evening Standard was prompted to stigmatize it as a diplomatic version of the famous saw—‘If we had some eggs we could have bacon and eggs if we had some bacon.’ Ministers privately characterized the government as a “buck passing” act, under which the United States in reconsidering debt settlements with individual nations does not scale down to what the debtors consider a satisfactory level, it will be held to blame for frustrating the revival of prosperity. Reparations Out European statesmen unanimously and publicly reiterated prosperity is possible only when “common

NEW BEDFORD, Conn... July 1 —(UP)—A British Naval commander was perhaps fatally injured and two New Bedford men were drowned today when their seaplane was pitched into the Acushnet river as it tossed about in a wild hail storm.

Moscow, July 19, (*). — Dirty, weary and disappointed, James Mattern and Bennett Griffin stepped off a train today, shook hands with a few fellow countrymen and streaked for a bathtub. A little later, with most of the grime scrubbed off, they told of the wreck of their round-the-world flight ambition in a Russian peat bog, and of their determination to try it again, if not this summer, certainly next year. “We got a tough break, that’s en,” they said. “We're going home as soon as we can, but we'll tackle it again this year if it’s not too late; certainly next summer if we can get a plane.” It developed that Mattern was piloting when the “Century of Progress,” booming over western Russia between Berlin and Moscow, began misbehaving. Something went wrong with the steering gear, but it wasn’t serious. “So, I looked around,” said Mattern, “and I hollered back to Griff that we were coming dow

BASEL, Switzerland, July 11 (#)— Officials of the World Bank for International Settlements, as trustee of the proposed bond issue of 3,000,000,000 marks with which Germany has agreed to settle her reparations claims, began today to set the machinery in motion to carry out the Lausanne Plan. The World Bank, it was officially stated, is proceeding as though there were no "gentlemen's agreement" making the effectuation of the Lausanne settlement dependent upon debt revision by the United States. Premier Herriot of France said at Paris yesterday, on his return from Lausanne, that the final solution of the problem now rests with the United States and that by the "gentlemen's agreement" a way had been left open for Europe to return to the original position on reparations if no agreement is reached with America. The "gentlemen's agreement" means nothing, said one authority of the World Bank. "T

Shanghai, July 11. (AP).—An epidemic of cholera which has been spreading from Canton to Peiping is increasing sharply and large numbers are dying every day. An intense heat wave is sweeping all China, apparently speeding the march of the disease. In the large cities, hundreds of new cases are reported each day, and many hundreds of thousands have received injections of anti-cholera serum. Among the rural districts, western Honan province seems to be the hardest hit. Virtually no medical aid is available there and the disease is reported to be 100 per cent fatal.

PARIS, July 11—(UP)—The Lausanne agreement to end reparations depends upon reduction of war debts by the United States, Premier Edouard Herriot said when he returned from the conference. “In case the United States does not agree to debt reduction, France will remain in her previous position,” the Premier said. That means that the entire reparations problem would have to be gone over again on the basis established by the Hoover moratorium. The cabinet heard Herriot’s report today and unanimously approved his accomplishments at Lausanne, particularly the “gentleman's agreement” regarding reduction of war debts. “That was the extent of our engagement at Lausanne,” Herriot continued, “Everything else is subordinate to the French parliamentary vote.” The Premier said that the importance of the Franco-British cordiality at Lausanne must not be overlooked. “We worked in full agreement. The Brit

1932-09-17.text: ROME, Sept. 16-(f)--The Italian air force and the Government continued its wide search over land and sea today for the missing New York-Rome airplane American Nurse and its three occupants, two men and a woman. Last night the Nicholas lightship, in the North Sea about a mile off the British Coast, reported that an airplane had come down on the water, taxied a short distance and exploded. A lifeboat and a tug from Yarmouth found no trace of the plane, the air ministry had no record of a missing ship but it was reasoned that the plane reported by the lightship could hardly have been the American Nurse for the incident occurred many hours after the American plane must have run out of fuel.

By The Associated Press LONDON, Sept. 16—Sir Ronald Ross, whose discovery that the anopheles mosquito carries the malaria parasite was responsible for controlling one of the world's most terrible scourges, died today at the age of 75.

NEW YORK, Sept. 17, (/)—Kaye Don, British speed wizard of motorboat and auto racing fame, sailed for Europe today—no longer the “bachelor” he liked to call himself. ® Last night Mr. and Mrs. Leonard J. Martin, of Greenwich, Conn., socially prominent, disclosed that Don and their daughter, Aileen, 21, were married in Greenwich Friday morning. “Of course, we're married but we wanted to keep it secret,” said the bride as she sat at a farewell dinner with her husband last night. A few hours later Don sailed on the Olympic. Mrs. Don will follow him next week and they will spend their honeymoon on Lake Como.

LONDON. Sept. 16. (4).—President Eamon de Valera of the Irish Free State will spend Monday in London on the way to Geneva where he will preside at a meeting of the League of Nations Assembly. No arrangements have been made for him to see Prime Minister MacDonald, but it was thought likely that he would call on J. H. Thomas, Secretary for Dominions, to discuss outstanding issues between the Free State and Great Britain.

Berlin, ()—Germany has informed the chairman of the disarmament conference that she will not participate in the next meeting, on Sept. 21, the government announced this evening. Konstantin von Neurath, in his note sent yesterday to Arthur Henderson, chairman of the conference, reiterated the German view that all the nations must be subject to equal rules of disarmament and that no discrimination may be shown. TO BUILD THIRD NEW BATTLESHIP Berlin, .—The admiralty today ordered the keel to be laid October 1 for Germany's third “pocket battleship,” to be known for the present as “Armored Ship C.” The order followed closely the dispatch of a letter yesterday to Arthur Henderson, president of the world disarmament conference at Geneva, which was unofficially reported to contain notice that Germany would sit in the disarmament deliberations no longer unless her claims for arms equality were re

Berlin, Sept. 16.--(4)--Germany, having turned her back on the world disarmament conference, will begin on October 1 to build her third “pocket battleship,” another of the 10,000-ton cruisers said to be as efficient as a battleship of twice the size. The admiralty issued an order today for laying of the keel. A few hours later the government published the text of a note to the chairman of the disarmament conference notifying him there will be no German representative present next Wednesday when the conference is resumed at Geneva. “Germany cannot be expected to take part in negotiations with regard to measures of disarmament,” Foreign Minister Von Neurath wrote to Arthur Henderson, the conference chairman, “until it is established that the solution which may be found is also to the advantage of Germany.”

BERLIN, Sept. 17.—The government decided today to hold the new Reichstag elections November 6, subject to approval of President Paul Von Hindenburg. The president is expected to approve the date. The short-lived Reichstag recently was dissolved by Chancellor Franz Von Papen, on authority of the president, during a tumultuous session in which it attempted to pass a vote of misconfidence in the

Geneva, Sept. 17 (P)—Germany read herself out of the world disarmament conference late yesterday as a further step in her campaign to eliminate the arms restrictions placed on her by the treaty of Versailles. The effect of this move was to

1932-08-08.text: LONDON, Aug. 8.—King George and Queen Mary returned to London today after a fortnight’s holiday at Cowes for the races. Last week was one of the most successful the king has ever had on the water, for his yacht Britannia won four out of six races.

PORTSMOUTH, O.---UP)—Paul Kilby, 33, railroader, who was arrested several weeks ago for chaining his son, Andrew, 13, to a post in the hot sun as a disciplinary measure, has been exonerated of charges of cruelty. The probate court, after investigation, committed the boy to the Lancaster industrial school as an incorrigible. The chaining incident gained official note when the boy’s screams for water aroused neighbors, attracting wide interest.

London, Aug. 4.—(/P)—Kaye Don, world speed boat record holder, plans to sail for the United States on the steamer Majestic Aug. 10 to race his boat, Miss England II against Carl Wood's Miss America for the British international trophy.

LONDON, Aug. 8—(#)—Adverse London criticisms of George Bernard Shaw's new play “Too True To Be Good,” gave the veteran playwright a Shavian laugh today. “As usual,” he said, “The majority of the critics have not been equal to the occasion. I cannot help being about 50 years ahead of them.”

BAR EMEREREE LEKSS OPUItS Lalor OLYMPIC STADIUM, Los Angeles, Aug. 7.—Cheered on by more than 300,000 spectators, including 75,000 in the big stadium, Juan Carlos Zabala, 20-year-old Argentine runner, outraced two British rivals and a pair of Finnish challengers today to capture the classic Olympic marathon in record time. First South American to capture the crowning honors of Olympic foot racing, Zabala justified his position of favorite by running a front race nearly all the way, outlasting all rivals in an exciting battle over the last six miles and finishing strongly, in the stadium, amid a tumult of acclaim. Ripping off the handkerchief bound around his head, Zabala acknowledged the big crowd's roar as he swung around the last turn and broke the tape in 2 hours, 31 minutes, 36 seconds. His time for the 26 miles, 385 yards surpassed the previous Olympic record of 2:32:35.8 set by Han

BERLIN, Aug. 8 —(#)—Germany’s most powerful political leaders began to gather in Berlin today for a series of conferences likely to determine the ultimate position of Adolf Hitler in the new government. Chancellor Franz von Papen returned yesterday from a brief holiday and Hitler himself, General Kurt von Schleicher, minister of defense, former Chancellor Heinrich Brüning and Alfred Hugenberg, nationalist leader, are due to arrive in the next day or two. President Paul von Hindenburg will return from his summer estate at Neudeck on Constitution day, August 11,

Gothenburg, Sweden, Aug. 8.— (AP)—A hundred straining policemen, reinforced by strong-armed dockhands, were required to restrain thousands of ardent admirers of Greta Garbo when the liner Gripsholm arrived here this noon. True to the legend of elusiveness, Garbo did not make an appearance until long after the gangplank was lowered. Swedish and American flags flew from the pier in the great popular welcome, and dozens of small craft swarmed around the vessel as she steamed up the harbor. Her nonappearance gave rise to a report that she had left the Gripsholm at sea and had come in by speed boat, but a quarter of an hour after everyone else had left the ship Garbo came ashore. Her brother Sven and a party of newspaper men had boarded the vessel before it docked, but at first she refused to see the reporters. Finally she admitted them to her cabin. Ottawa.—(#)—A prospect that the imperial conference would limit itself to bi-lateral agreements between the dominions and leave the rest of the agenda for the coming world economic conference at which the United States will sit appeared as the conference began its third and perhaps final week today. The general belief was that Great Britain would do something to open her doors wider to the products of the dominions, but that in doing so she would be inclined to confine herself to measures looking to an international revival of trade rather than to purely empire benefit. Need World Markets. It was recalled that the Prince of Wales, on the eve of the opening of the conference, referred especially to the undesirability of damaging the empire's world trade. “Canada and Australia,” he said, “cannot dispense with their world market for wheat. 1932-07-09.text: LONDON, July 9—(#)—The London Press today welcomed the reparations settlement at Lausanne as a “great achievement,” a “happy omen,” and “the world’s best news since the war,” but added that it was only the first step toward a settlement of the world’s economic troubles. Eyes would now be turned across the Atlantic, the papers said, to see what the United States would do on the question of revising the war debts.

LONDON, July 8—(e)—An ecclesiastical church court today decided that the Rev. H. F. Davidson had been guilty of immorality while posing as a reformer among unfortunate girls. Chancellor P. E. North of Norwich diocese, who presided at the trial of the gray-haired elderly rector of Stitkey, said sentence would be pronounced later by the Bishop of Norwich. The minister may appeal. The Rev. Mr. Davidson heard the verdict with his son and daughter and was immediately surrounded by a sympathetic group. One girl rushed up and kissed him. Then he left the courtroom on the run. Chancellor North declared the defense of the preacher was a "tissue of absurdities" and the rector a discredited witness upon whom reliance could not be placed. The court was referring to the minister's defense statement that he was a friend of fallen women, that he had been framed, and that he had come to London from his

New London, Conn., July 8, (2) ——The Ketch Curlew, missing since she entered the Montauk-to-Bermuda race eight days ago, was found safe tonight off Davis South Shoal by the coast guard patrol boat Marion from the local base. The Marion radioed headquarters the Curlew, with all members of her crew accounted for, was proceeding to New York under her own sail.

It probably will be presented early next week. Meanwhile, the American representatives were trying to get him to embody in this declaration the principle of a one-third reduction as the basis for a disarmament treaty. For this purpose Norman H. Davis, one of the American contingent, visited Prime Minister MacDonald at Lausanne. Later he expressed satisfaction with Mr. MacDonald's endorsement of the American view.

Associated Press Staff Writer MOSCOW, July 8—The globe-circling adventure of James Mattern and Bennett Griffin, which started in New York with a blaze of speed, has come to an abrupt end in western Russia with only one-third of the flight behind them. The American pair cracked up their racy monoplane just over the Polish-Russian border, 500 miles east of Berlin, yesterday morning but word of the mishap was received today. Neither Badly Hurt Neither was seriously injured in the forced landing near Borisov, Russia, 50 miles from Minsk. Their “Century of Progress” was believed to have developed control trouble. The pilots probably mistook the lights of Borisov for Moscow, and circled for an emergency landing. The end came in a peat bog, the most likely place they could find to set the ship down, and she cracked up in the soft surface. The plane was too badly damaged to proceed. The men spen

Cherbourg, France, July 8.—(?)— Strong currents and a rising tide halted efforts to salvage the sunken French submarine Promethee today and small harbor craft, unequipped for their heavy task, sought shelter in the harbor. Early tomorrow, they will load chains and cables and heavy lines and steam out again to the spot, seven miles off Cape Hevir where the Promethee lies in 40 fathoms. Italian Ships to Aid. It is hoped that some time in the forenoon the Italian salvage ship Artiglio II and her sister ship, the Rosto, will be there to help. The naval authorities asked for their assistance today and the Artiglio II started immediately from Brest. The Rosto headed for Cherbourg from Havre where she was refueling. The agreement moved toward the end of reparations, the greatest financial puzzle of history. A new effort for peace in relations among nations is commenced, the document went on, on the basis of reciprocal confidence. 1932-01-27.text: Portland, England —(P)— Hope of saving the 56 men in the Submarine M-2 which sank off Portland yesterday dissolved with the fading day. The wives of the crew, most of them watching operations of the salvage vessels from the docks, received telegrams from the commander of the submarine’s mother ship, the Dolphin, that he feared the men were lost. Even the women who had borne up most bravely gave way to despair at this. There were rumors the ship had been located on the bottom by airplanes especially equipped for the work, and communication had been established with the men inside, but these reports were denied by the Admiralty office. Another rumor said one of the planes had sighted a large patch of oil on the surface, but it developed it was only mud stirred up by drags scraped along the bottom by the salvagers. Seek Information The Admiralty office sent a man over to Calais to talk to t

SHANGHAI, Jan. 2/.—(#)—A force of about 2,400 United States and British marines prepared today to take over the defense of the international settlement in Shanghai as approximately 10,000 Chinese troops were deployed, apparently determined to defend the city from occupation by the Japanese. Late in the afternoon Japanese consular officials said a representative of Mayor Wu Teh-Chen had stated unofficially that a reply would be issued accepting the Japanese demands in their entirety. At the same time, however, it was learned that Japanese authorities today began to evacuate their nationals from nearby places in the Yangtze valley. The American marines numbered about 1,200 and have been here since 1927, when Chiang Kai-Shek’s nationalist northern drive menaced Shanghai. The British have a similar force. Precautionary Measures The United States troops began to erect barbed wire entanglement

ORTLAND, Eng. Jan. 27— (UP)—The British submarine M-2, with 54 men aboard, lay at the bottom of the English Channel today while a fleet of ships worked frantically with rapidly fading hope of rescuing her crew alive. A spot of oil on the surface gave a depressing clue to the submarine’s probable position and led naval officers to fear that the double hull of the underseas boat had broken up. The oil was discovered in West Bay, off Portland Island, by a naval seaplane and H. M. S. Blackwell was sent to the spot. Twelve naval vessels, including destroyers, mine sweepers and patrol boats, cruised over a circle of two miles around a buoy marking the supposed location of the submarine. They swept over the sandy bed of the channel, 102 feet deep at the point, with nets and cables, trying to hook the lost ship. Among the wreckages of the war with which this “dead man's” bay is strewn, the task

Portland, England, Jan. 27—(UP)—Fifteen naval craft sought the British submarine M-2, with fifty-four men aboard today, three miles off Portland, where the submarine was believed disabled seventeen fathoms (102 feet) under the choppy seas. The men aboard the M-2 were equipped with the Davis apparatus for escape from submerged vessels. Experts believed they could stay below forty-eight hours and survive. It was emphasized that they would use the Davis apparatus as a last resort, for its use is necessarily hazardous. Five mine sweepers, five destroyers, two submarines, two salvage boats, and the submarine depot ship H. M.S. Adamant circled the two buoys near which it was hoped to reach the sunken vessel. The sea was choppy and blowing up. The destroyer Sabre was sent from Portsmouth with specially trained deep sea divers immediately after the news of belief that the M-2 had been found. Two

MIAMI BEACH, Fla. — (4) — Streaking his Miss America IX across placid waters of Indian Creek at an average speed of 110.785 miles an hour today, Gar Wood exceeded by a scant half mile an hour the world’s speedboat record of 110.223 miles an hour held by Kaye Don of England. Wood's speed was obtained by averaging his time for north and southbound runs over the measured nautical mile course. His first run was clocked by electric timing devices at 11.08 miles, with an elapsed time of 37.32 seconds for the 6,080 foot mile. The second run was at a rate of 110.49 miles with an elapsed time of 37.52 seconds. He was accompanied by Orlin Johnson, his mechanic. Not yet satisfied with the speed he attained, Wood said he would discontinue trials today in order to make repairs on the hull of the Miss America IX and probably would seek to raise his speed tomorrow.

Portland, Eng., Jan. 27. (Wednesday) (*)—The British submarine M-2 dived near Portland yesterday, failed to rise and early today was feared to be lying disabled at the bottom of the English Channel with 54 men aboard. Searching ships, rushed to the scene, touched an object with their instruments which they believed to be the vessel. It was in 17 fathoms of water three miles west of Portland Bill, a rocky promontory, and gave a metallic ring when struck. It could not be established before daylight if the object really was the submarine. Meanwhile, an anxious crowd on the coast watched a circle of flickering lights from the flotilla of salvage craft about three miles off Chesil Beach. West Bay—which locally has the sinister name of Dead Man's Bay—is the area where the search was conducted. It has an evil reputation owing to many wrecks. The dispatch said the Chinese mayor will reply to the Japanese during the day, agreeing to all their demands, but that an occupation of some points is expected, nevertheless. The defense force of the international quarter has been mobilized, it was said.

By the Associated Press Two thousand American and British marines stood by to defend the international settlement at Shanghai today - five times that many Chinese soldiers prepared to protect the area from Japanese occupation. Word from Harbin told of a battle between Chinese factions near that northern Manchurian city, giving alarm to both Russian and Japanese authorities. Meanwhile, at London, the British government gave serious consideration to the situation in Shanghai as the result of conversations in Washington between Secretary of State Stimson and the British ambassador. 1932-07-16.text: London, July 16. (AP)—Field Marshal Lord Plumer, one of the chief commanders of the British army during the World War, died today after a long illness. Few British commanders won such renown as he during the war. He was made a baron after the conflict. Lord Plumer was 74 years old. He was first commander of the fifth army corps and then of the second army of the British expeditionary force in France. Later he commanded the expeditionary force in Italy. From 1919 to 1924 he was governor and commander in chief at Malta, and he followed Sir Herbert Samuel, now home secretary, as high commissioner of Palestine. Since 1918 he had devoted himself to the interests of disabled ex-service men.

Paris, July 15 (?)—French governmental circles today emphasized that it was far from the intention of European powers to form a united front against the United States on the matter of war debts. Any assertion, it was added, that Great Britain under the recent Franco-British consultative pact, would be restricted in dealing with British debts to the United States, was palpably absurd. Such a statement—that Great Britain could not settle her American debts without consulting France—was attributed to Premier Edouard Herriot on Wednesday by the Havas (French) news agency and was considered semi-official at the time. The French government did not issue a denial that the Premier had made such an assertion in reporting the accord to the finance committee of the Chamber of Deputies. But it was officially stated that considerable embarrassment had been caused by the importance given by the press

Paris, July 16.—(AP)—The storm raised abroad by the report of Premier Herriot’s statement on the connection of the post-Lausanne accord with Great Britain and American debts continued to preoccupy official circles today in spite of an official announcement yesterday intended to clarify the situation. Yesterday's statement, officially sponsored, and following by one day President Hoover's letter to Senator Borah declaring the United States would not be influenced on the debt question by any united front in Europe, emphasized that it was far from the intention of France to form such a front. Any assertion that the recent Franco-British accord would restrict Great Britain in making new arrangements for war debt payments to the United States was palpably absurd, it said. The principal Paris newspapers carefully avoided comment on these developments today, but some of the extreme nationalist

EN ROUTE WITH FRANKLIN D. ROOSEVELT, Marblehead, Mass July 16. (UP)—Franklin Roosevelt today was near the end of his cruise up the New England coast in the 40-foot yawl Myth II. He remained at anchor in Marblehead harbor last night after a 55-mile voyage from Marion, Mass., under variable weather conditions, and was in fine fettle as he pointed the yawl's prow northward. “We plan to go as far as possible today,” the New York governor declared. A destination was not named. Roosevelt indicated he would immediately plunge into his campaign after returning to Albany.

London, July 16—(P)—All efforts by Prime Minister MacDonald and President De Valera of the Irish Free State to avert an Anglo-Irish economic war, with tariffs as the weapons, failed Friday night, and today Mr. MacDonald flew to Scotland while Mr. De Valera returned to Dublin. The Irish reprisal duties bill, drawn up by the De Valera government in retaliation against the 20 per cent tariffs imposed against the principal imports from Ireland into Britain, goes to the Irish Senate on Monday. Early next week it may become effective. The controversy between the Free State and Britain rests on two main causes. One of these is Mr. De Valera’s insistent attempts to eliminate the oath of allegiance to the British Crown and the other is his refusal to continue payments of land annuities to the London government.

Marblehead, Mass. July 16—(AP)—With Governor Franklin D. Roosevelt at the helm, the yawl Myth II weighed anchor and set sail from Marblehead Harbor today on the final hitch of its cruise along the New England coast to Portsmouth, N. H. The Democratic presidential nominee and his sons, who spent the night aboard their craft, anchored among the yachts in the harbor of this old sailing port, expected today to continue on to Gloucester and Portsmouth in the hope of reaching the New Hampshire port sometime late today or tonight. Marblehead yachtsmen predicted it would be late at night, even if the breeze held out, before the Myth II could reach port, and that it might not be able to make Portsmouth unless the wind picked up.

3. ky ky JULY 1st, UP—The Republican party's plank on prohibition was called a fraud and a deception by Mrs. Charles H. Sabin, national chairman of the women's organization for national prohibition reform, in an address here last night. Mrs. Sabin, a Republican, warned that the plank “launches us upon an experiment far more uncertain and confusing than the 18th amendment itself, which at least is specific in its terms.” “The Republican plank,” Mrs. Sabin said, “states that the gains under the 18th amendment must be preserved. What gain do they mean? The speakeasies, gangsters, hypocrites, and law-breakers? The whole thing is absurd and impossible.”

BERLIN, July 18.—Political terrorism flamed through Germany today and the government took drastic steps to put down disorder after a week-end in which probably twenty or more dead and dozens wounded were added to the heavy casualties of the last few weeks. After an emergency cabinet meeting, outdoor demonstrations were forbidden throughout the reich in an order by Baron Wilhelm von Gayl, minister of the interior. Proclamation of a state of siege or martial law was discussed, but the cabinet was reluctant to take such a step. As an alternative, it was proposed that the federal government take over police functions in Prussia. That would give the reich control of the 90,000 Prussian police, largest armed force in Germany outside the regular army, and would abolish states’ rights for a territory comprising two-thirds of Germany. 1932-01-05.text: Bembay, Jan. 1.—(AP)—Mahatma Gandhi sought today to enlist the Christians of India in his fight against the British government, calling it a Christian "struggle of Peace." In the meantime the battle was well begun with Nationalists and their followers pressing a strict boycott on British and foreign goods and the government retaliating with more group arrests. With one blow 45 organizations affiliated with the Nationalist Congress in Calcutta and its suburbs were declared unlawful by the government. In his appeal to Christians Gandhi said: "I have full trust that in the present struggle you who tender loyalty to one whom you call the Prince of Peace will not be behind any other community in a struggle which is essentially based on peace." He urged Christians to adopt the spinning wheel and homespun garments and to renounce drink. In a farewell telegram to Lord Irwin, former Viceroy with

The British government in India has extended to every important city its new ordinance outlawing Mahatma Gandhi's nationalist congress party and forbidding contributions to its funds. Everywhere police stood by waiting for trouble but although there were preliminary demonstrations at several points there was no fighting such as that at Allahabad yesterday where two persons were killed and many injured. From his prison at Poona, Gandhi issued an invitation to the Christians in India to join his "struggle of peace" for independence from Great Britain. Merchants in big cities began to worry in earnest over the economic consequences of a boycott against their goods. The nationalists have decided also to boycott the round table conference committees which are going out to India to continue the work begun in London, and from New Delhi came an offer by a section of the All-India Muslim conferen

Washington, Jan. 5.—Secretary Adams, speaking for himself and the Navy department as a whole, gave his approval today to a bill calling for a ten-year naval program which would bring the Navy up to the London treaty limitations. Testifying before the House Naval Committee, Adams said: “Personally I think we should build a navy that meets the requirements of the London Treaty.” He added that the Navy department as a whole felt the same way. Adams said a ten-year program was ‘more acceptable from a practical viewpoint than a one-year authorization. I think there are advantages in knowing about where you are going,” the Navy secretary said. The secretary asserted that if the budget bureau approves the Vinson bill “the Navy department will be favorable to” the program the Vinson bill lays down a ten-year building program.

WASHINGTON (UP). — Charles G. Dawes, former vice president and now ambassador to Great Britain, told the United Press Tuesday that under no circumstances would he approve the entry of his name in the presidential primaries in Illinois. Reports have been current that certain political leaders desired that his name be entered.

BOMBAY, Jan. 4. -(U.P)— Bloodshed marked the resumption of India’s “spiritual” warfare against British rule today, with three killed and four seriously injured at Allahabad, and widespread disorders and arrests in other cities. The conflict at Allahabad arose from a forbidden demonstration by members of the national congress, in protest against the imprisonment of Mahatma M. K. Gandhi. Police armed with staves charged into the mass of demonstrators and in the melee the postmaster and two others were killed. The riot was in the heart of Allahabad, (Combinatorial on Sale @ Col. 3).

WASHINGTON, Jan. 5—(UP)— President Hoover today began consultation with the members of the American delegation to the Geneva Arms Limitation Conference. Charles G. Dawes, American Ambassador to Great Britain and head of the delegation, and Norman Davis, member of the delegation, met with him immediately after breakfast today and discussed the program for the conference.

New York, Jan. 4 (4P).-- Expressing hope for a satisfactory outcome of the disarmament conference in Geneva next month, Gen. Charles G. Dawes, Ambassador to Great Britain, arrived on the liner Europa today. He will confer with Secretary of State Stimson on the attitude of the American delegation to Geneva, which he will head. "Ridiculous!" was the word he used when a reporter asked something about a possible ‘presidential boom.’

TORYO, Jan. 9 (UF) - Japanese troops from Chinchow advanced today on Shanhaikwan, on the northern boundary of China proper. Capture of the city will mark the first Japanese invasion of strictly Chinese territory. It was announced that the southward movement was ordered to effect a junction with a large Japanese garrison at Shanhaikwan, recently augmented by the arrival of several Japanese warships. Heavy fighting was expected at Hungohian and Sunshang, where there are large Chinese forces. Shanhaikwan, where the great wall of China meets the sea, is considerably south of what is generally regarded as Manchuria and only a short distance from the important city of Tientsin, where Japan and other foreign governments have concessions.

1932-09-15.text: London, Sept. 15. (UP)—The British Government will let the Mahatma Gandhi out of jail when he begins his threatened “fast to death” in protest against the India settlement, the India office announced today. When Gandhi, pitting his frail body against an Empire, actually begins his fast, he will be removed from Yerovda jail to “a suitable place of private residence” and ordered to remain there.

Nanking—(P)—The Chinese government opened a counter-attack on the signing of the treaty between Manchukuo and Japan today in the form of notes of protest to London, Paris, Washington, Rome and Geneva, charging Japan was violating China's territorial and administrative sovereignty by recognizing the new state. The notes demanded immediate international action. A cablegram also was addressed to the League of Nations calling its attention to the Chinese claim that Japan’s action is incompatible with the spirit of the league covenant and a direct violation of the resolutions of the league assembly. It urged the league to take immediate steps. READING, Sept. 14.—(AP)—The family doctor is coming into his own again, in the opinion of Dr. Walter F. Donaldson of Pittsburgh, speaker at a district meeting of the Medical Society of the State of Pennsylvania today. Dr. Donaldson, secretary of the organization, explained that in more prosperous times, the family doctor turned over to the specialist or hospital man small cases which he might well have retained himself, as he is learning to do today. “Had this practice been curtailed,” he said, “there would have been a saving for the patient.” Dr. William H. Mayer of Pittsburgh, state president, spoke on “traditional values.”

Rome, Sept. 15—Apprehension grew apace at Ciampino airport today as dawn approached without recent word of the progress of the trans-Atlantic plane, the American Nurse, which left New York bound for Rome more than 40 hours ago. At 4:16 a. m. Thursday, the plane had been out exactly 40 hours. The last reports of her were made by the liner France at 4:50 p. m., Greenwich time, or more than 10 hours before. At that time the plane had traveled 2,800 miles at a speed of a little less than 100 miles an hour. Some authorities felt she could last 43 hours before her gas gave out, but others placed the limit at 40 hours. In the absence of incontestable proof that the various sightings of a plane over the Atlantic and Mediterranean actually involved the American Nurse, officials declined to speculate as to what may have occurred.

Rome, Sept. 15 (UP) — The monoplane, American Nurse, en route from New York to Rome was feared a victim of the Atlantic today, hours overdue and not reported seen at any point on the European coast. Italian officials did not believe that the plane had fuel for more than 40 hours flight. This period ended early today, while beacons at airports from Rome to Paris flooded the sky. The veritable flying laboratory, aboard which a physician hoped to record the reactions of trans-Atlantic fliers, left New York at 6:16 a.m. EST Tuesday. It was known to have reached a point 450 miles northwest of the Azores. The plane had altered its course to the south to take advantage of favorable weather.

ROME (U.P.)—The air ministry canvassed the whole of Italy and islands in the western Mediterranean Thursday for information about the trans-Atlantic airplane American Nurse, long overdue on its attempted flight from New York to Rome, without result. They were convinced the plane must be down and only hoped it had landed possibly in some inaccessible spot in Spain or Corsica. The veritable flying laboratory aboard which a physician hoped to record the reactions of trans-Atlantic fliers, left New York at 6:16 a. m. EST Tuesday. It was known to have reached a point 450 miles northwest of the Azores. The plane had altered its course to the south to take advantage of favorable weather. Aboard the plane are William Ulbrich, pilot; Miss Edna Neweomer, nurse and co-pilot; Dr. Leo M. Piseulli, New York physician, and ‘Tail wind,’ a mascot woodchuck.

ROME, Sept. 15. (AP).—The monoplane "American Nurse," carrying two men and a woman on a non-stop flight from New York to Rome was missing today. Although due to arrive here around midnight last night, no report of it has been received since 11:50 a. m. yesterday, E. S. T., when the liner Paris reported sighting a plane believed to be the "American Nurse" 400 miles off the southern coast of Ireland. Gas Gives Out. At 1:16 a. m. today the 43 hours given as the limit of time its gasoline supply could last had passed. Officials at the Ciampino airport here, where lights were kept burning through the night, expressed deep concern over the fate of the fliers. They are William Ulbrich, pilot of Mineola, N. Y., Miss Edna Newcomer, 28 year old undergraduate nurse of Williamsport, Pa., and Dr. Leon M. Pisculli of Yonkers, N. Y., the commander of the expedition. The chief anxiety was that the plane

1932-06-02.text: LONDON, June 2 Russian attempt to land arms in southern Ireland for the Irish Republican Army, the Daily Express said today, was thwarted by the British navy over the past weekend. The arms, the paper said, were intended to be used by the Republican forces, who were placed under the ban of the government during the previous regime of President Cosgrave of the Free State, in the event of a conflict between the Free State and Ulster. The tramp steamers carrying the arms, it said, were warned by radio of the activity of British warships which set out to head them off at Irish ports, and they returned to the foreign ports, where they were chartered. The Irish Republican Army took on a new lease of life after the election of President Eamon De Valera as president of the Free State. London - (U.P) —The first woman to fly the Atlantic was the first choice dancing partner of the Prince of Wales at the Derby ball and she agreed with the Prince after dancing to "The Tiger Rag" that "We need more dances like that." Amelia Earhart Putnam left the Grosvenor House festivities in the early morning hours Wednesday, after dancing three foxtrots in succession with the heir to the British throne. She also danced with Prince George. Beginning with "Home," taking an encore on "Day by Day," and ending with the lively "Tiger Rag," the Prince remarked to Miss Earhart, "We need more like that." The orchestra leader apparently sensed the Prince’s desire for another dance, for he repeated several choruses, and then asked the dancers to proceed to the supper room. LONDON, June 2. (#)—United States Ambassador Mellon appeared in silk knee breeches last night at the derby day dinner given by Lady Ellesmere at Bridgewater House. Queen Mary and the Duchess of York were there but the king was entertaining racing friends at the traditional derby day stag dinner in Buckingham Palace. Invitations to the dinner at Bridgewater House specified court dress.
By The Associated Press Saunton, England, June 2.— Enid Wilson today retained her British women's golf championship, defeating Miss Clem Purvis-Russell-Montgomery, a Scottish player.

LONDON, June 2—(B)—Mrs. Amelia Putnam, American Transatlantic flier, will cross the channel to France tonight aboard a private motor yacht to meet her husband, George Palmer Putnam, who is on his way from New York. She will go aboard the Evairie owned by C.-R. Fairey, president of the Royal Aeronautical Society, at Hamble, near Southampton, where Amy Johnson, noted British woman flier, and others prominent in aviation will be in attendance. London, June 2,—(Thursday)—The London Express said today a Russian attempt to land arms in southern Ireland had been aborted by unusual activity of British warships over the past weekend. The arms were intended as equipment for the Irish republican army in the event of a conflict between the Irish free state and northern Ireland, the newspaper said. It reported that tramp steamers, carrying the weapons, were warned by radio of the British naval activity and returned to foreign ports where they had been chartered. Dispatches from Belfast said it was reported there that two British destroyers from the Portsmouth naval base put to sea on short notice, while vessels at Cobh, near Cork, were held in readiness. (AP)—There was evidence today that British official circles were inclined to encourage the possibility that the United States government would participate in the second half of the Lausanne debts and economic conference this month instead of insisting upon a separate meeting in London to consider remedies for the world’s economic crisis. Berlin, June 2. (4) — President Paul Von Hindenburg summoned the new German cabinet headed by Count Franz Von Papen to meet at presidential palace at 5:30 p.m. today to take the oath of office. The formal swearing in of the new ministry was to be followed at 6 o’clock in the afternoon by its first session in the chancellery. The cabinet list, completed in skeleton yesterday, was filed in today with the acceptance of Baron Constantin Von Neurath, German ambassador to London, as foreign minister, Count Lutz Schwerin Von Krosigk as finance minister and Franz Guertner as minister of justice.

Thomas as Great Britain’s members of the important committee on commercial relations with foreign countries was heard with satisfaction today by American observers at the British imperial economic conference. Because of their affiliations they are expected to oppose any move by the conference which would result in high food costs to British consumers. First Impression Removed. It has been the impression here ever since Premier Bennett said Canada would expect preferential treatment of exports to the United Kingdom in return for tariff readjustment on imports from there that he contemplated asking the British to raise import barriers against non-empire countries behind which the dominions might find guaranteed markets. That, it was argued, could mean nothing less than discrimination (Continued on Page Five)

Ottawa, Ont., July 23—(UP)— Three principal dominions have demanded that Great Britain restrict imports chiefly from the United States, Argentina, and Russia, and increase imports from Canada, New Zealand and Australia. These forcible demands that the mother country give them preference in importing meat, wheat, wool, dairy products, wines, base metals, sugar, fruit and lumber have been made with the British Empire Economic Conference only two days old. Other demands are to follow. Their very nature is evidence of Great Britain’s foresight in sending seven of her most capable cabinet members and more than seventy assistants to Ottawa to deal with the trade problems arising here. Each Dominion is willing, for a consideration, to make concessions that will favor British manufactures over those of the United States. BY 400 Associated Press Dublin, Irish Free State, July 23— The Irish Free State's tariff bill, authorizing duties on imports from Great Britain, became a law today when it was approved by Governor General James McNeill. President De Valera was expected to issue the first list of duties late today.

Ottawa, July 23—The insistence of Australia upon effective assistance from Great Britain in marketing Australian products threw into bold relief tonight the differences of opinion on the matter of granting empire preferences. At the outset the British delegates declared themselves for the general principle of lowering tariff walls for empire nations, as opposed to raising such walls against foreign countries. The demand voiced by Premier Stanley Bruce of Australia for preference on chilled beef in effect means Great Britain would have to raise her tariff walls against foreign countries if she satisfied Australia on this point. At present chilled beef enters Great Britain free of duty. The Australian’s statement served to link the needs of Canada, Australia and New Zealand, in bargaining with the United Kingdom, although there was no official indication of this. Ottawa, Ont AU.FJ—Four great producing dominions set the pace for the British Empire economy conference Saturday night, with demands for concessions from Great Britain that struck at the trade of the United States, Argentina, Soviet Russia, Poland, Denmark and other world nations. The world depression and the ever-present ideal of making the empire a real family of nations were linked up by chief delegates with the concessions they have granted, and are ready to extend, to the mother country, whose manufactures they use. Stanley Bruce, Australia; N.C. Bhavenga, South Africa; R.B. Bennett, Canada, and J.G. Cotes, New Zealand, were the pacemakers. They asked consideration for British preferential tariffs, or for actual arbitrary restriction of foreign imports, in the instance of wheat, lumber, dairy products, fruits, tobacco and other commodities. GENEVA, SWITZERLAND, JULY 23. (AP).—The world disarmament conference which began its work February 2 adjourned today for an indefinite period after adopting a resolution promising substantial reduction of armaments in its deliberations. Soviet Russia and Germany voted against the resolution. The Russian delegation previously had described it as not substantially specific and the German representative objected to its omission of any reference to the equality of all nations in the right to arms. During the recess important committees of the conference will continue their negotiations on various phases of disarmament.

GENEVA, July 25.-—The resolution adjourning the World Disarmament Conference until autumn and embodying the work of the conference to date was adopted today. The vote by the general commission was 41 to 2, with eight abstentions. The resolution provided that the work of the conference be carried on in negotiations during the summer recess. It left many important points to be settled before the conference reconvenes. The conference adjourned at 12:40 p.m. after setting the date of the next meeting of the steering committee for September 21. The committee was instructed to reassemble the conference within four months after that time.

Paris, July 23 (UP) — Representatives of the leading oil companies of the world signed an agreement today for a general restriction of production through which it is hoped many ills of the industry will be solved. The agreement was reached after several weeks of discussion during which time the Roumanian interests were reluctant to sign pending assurance that Russia, which was not represented, would also cut her production. Great satisfaction was expressed by the American delegates to the conference.

1932-05-29.text: WASHINGTON, May 28. (>)— A raging controversy over sales tax-focusing on President Hoover and the press-swept the senate today and temporarily stalled the billion dollar revenue bill. The upshot of the furious debate was a demand from Senator Connally, Democrat, Texas, for a statement by the president on his position and the circulation of a round robin petition pledging members to vote against the disputed levy. Intimations reached the capitol that Mr. Hoover was prepared to take a hand in the tax contest and a message from him next week was expected. Challenge Received Senator Harrison of Mississippi, Democratic tax leader, challenged the proponents of the sales tax for an immediate showdown and then drew up the round robin petition. He claimed 84 Democratic signatures tonight and predicted more than 50 of the senate—a majority—would be pledged by Monday noon, when the president’s mess

FLEMINGTON, N. J., May 28.—(4?)—John Hughes Curtis of Norfolk will go on trial the week of June 27 for hoaxing the Lindberghs and police seeking the kidnap-murderers of their baby son. Prosecutor Anthony Hauck made this announcement after indictments were handed down today by the grand jury which pondered the Curtis case Thursday. Three indictments were presented to Justice Thomas Trenchard by the foreman of the grand jury. Only three cases had been considered by the grand jury at its most recent sitting, a murder case, a manslaughter case, and the Curtis hoax.

New York, May 28.—- (AP) — Stanislaus Felix Hausner, ‘mystery flyer’ of Newark, N. J., returned to Floyd Bennett field at 9:20 p. m., (Eastern Standard time) tonight, slightly more than six hours after he started on a projected non-stop flight to Europe. Hausner said he had got about 800 miles out to sea and was flying in a blind fog when the artificial horizon, the “brains” of an aviator’s blind flying instruments, stopped functioning. He turned his heavily loaded flame-colored monoplane about and “felt” his way back to Floyd Bennett field as best he could with the aid of a compass only. His return, despite such odds, made those who had murmured “flying fool” when he hopped off at 3:05 p. m., despite warnings against hazardous conditions, wonder if Hausner, the silent, non-committal amateur pilot, possibly knew more about aviation than they had given him credit for.

WASHINGTON, May 28 (*.— Speaker Garner slapped back Saturday with a stinging thrust at President Hoover and proceeded with plans for speeding his relief bill through the house. To the president's charge that the public works phase of the speaker's two billion dollar relief bill was “pork barrel” legislation, Garner replied that the same appellation might be applied to the reconstruction corporation for which non-partisan support was elected by Mr. Hoover. M’KINNEY, May 28. ()—Art Goebel, widely known aviator, was injured, and his mechanic, R. L. Riss, was killed when their plane struck a tree as they took off from the airport here today. Riss was killed instantly, his head being crushed by wreckage of the plane, which was demolished. Goebel, winner of the Dole derby from San Francisco to Honolulu, suffered a broken leg above the knee and facial lacerations. Goebel had come to McKinney, where he recently gave an air circus, to visit friends. During the day he performed some stunts over the courthouse square. About 3 p.m. as a heavy rain was falling, he prepared to return to Dallas. The field was soggy as a result of rain, but he seemed to have no difficulty getting into the air. When about mid-field and at an altitude of about 35 feet, the plane struck the top of a tree and crashed, strewing wreckage for many feet. It did not burn. Riss wa

WASHINGTON, May 28.—(AP)—With the recording of 20 convention votes from Colorado and Utah for Gov. Franklin D. Roosevelt today, the Democratic presidential nomination race came to its first full pause since the New Hampshire primaries March 8. During the next week no primaries nor state conventions are scheduled in either party, although a total of 122 Democratic delegates and 42 Republican remain to be selected. At this point in the pre-convention campaign, Roosevelt still is far in the lead for the Democratic nomination with 418 of the 770 delegates necessary to win formally pledged or instructed for him. In addition, his supporters lay definite claim to 181 more delegates already chosen and confidently expect to pick up, virtually undisputed, a maximum of 98 of the remaining 122 to be named. This would bring the Roosevelt total to 697, or only 75 votes shy of the necessary two-thirds.

NEW YORK. Intense curiosity was manifested in political circles over what Governor Roosevelt’s answer will be if he is asked to remove Mayor Walker, and how his stand on the question might affect his drive for the presidential nomination. From Tammany Hall, where the interest is particularly acute, to the governor's own campaign headquarters, the discussion transcended all other political talk. Samuel Seabury, counsel for the Hofstadter legislative committee, which has spent nearly $750,000 in the last fourteen months investigating Walker's administration, has not indicated whether he will make a demand for the mayor's removal. But Walker himself and democratic members of the committee have said publicly that such is his aim. The general opinion is that when Seabury rounds out the part of the inquiry centering on the mayor personally, he will send his findings to Roosevelt, with a strong

Washington, May 28, ()—A plea from three children for their father's freedom was so appealing today that President Hoover promised to consider carefully the case of an obscure prisoner in a Detroit jail. Busy with many things, President Hoover laid them aside to listen as blue-eyed Bernice Feagan, 13, told him with convincing fervor that her father, Charles R. Feagan, is innocent and should be released. Feagan is charged with unlawfully transporting an automobile. Bernice's younger sister, Irene, 11, like Bernice an unmistakable blonde, and a brother, tow-headed Clifford, 10, nodded vigorously as Bernice stood on tiptoe in her earnestness and begged the president to help her father go free. Mr. Hoover listened intently. Then he smiled. His manner and words which followed brought smiles to the faces of the children. “He told us we could go home cheerful,” Bernice said confidently before l

1932-06-19.text: LONDON, June 18. ()—Mrs. Elvira Dolores Barney, socially prominent defendant in the 'cocktail shooting case', collapsed at her arraignment today during the reading of love letters exchanged by herself and Thomas William Scott Stephen, whom she is accused of murdering. At the conclusion of the arraignment the court held her for trial on two charges—that she murdered Stephen May 31 in her apartment and that a few weeks previous she shot at him during a quarrel. In one of Stephen's letters read in court Mrs. Barney was referred to as 'baby, little fatable.' He asked her to forgive all the 'dreadful horrible things I have done' and promised 'to be better and kinder so you won't be frightened any more.'

Loudon, June 17. (AP)—Eamon De Valera’s ultimate aim is a united Irish republic with King George as its head, J. H. Thomas, secretary for dominions, told parliament today. Mr. Thomas said the Irish president told him, while he was in Dublin last week, that the republic which Mr. De Valera envisions would dictate terms and would be called, understood and accepted as a republic. However, said Mr. Thomas, there might and probably would exist certain circumstances in which the whole of the British Commonwealth would act in unison for external purposes and then His Majesty the King would be recognized under those circumstances as the head. Mr. Thomas said he told President De Valera that it wouldn't do any good to talk about such things because neither the present nor any other British government could or would agree to any such proposal. keynote that President Hoover must accept responsibility before the voters without any plea for pity was sounded Saturday night by Jouett Shouse, chairman of the Democratic National Executive Committee. As Democratic leaders assembled early for their national convention which begins here a week from Monday, it was apparent that the Democratic campaign will aim its guns straight at the White House and keep them trained there throughout the campaign. Herbert Hoover is to be the Democratic issue. This was forecast in an address by Shouse Saturday night. Charges Partisanship. "Whatever the faults of Democratic members of Congress," Shouse said, "whatever the faults of Republican members of Congress, in either house or senate, Herbert Hoover cannot escape the responsibility that was his, the duty that he neglected to attempt to find sane and reasonable remedies for the situation that existed.

Chicago (UP) — Charles G. Dawes, retiring president of the Reconstruction Finance Corporation, expressed belief on arriving here today that the country has reached “the turning point” in the depression. Dawes based his prediction on the general improvement in the small business enterprises of the country in a formal statement issued here which was treated with a good deal of significance because of the close insight he had had into business conditions as head of the Reconstruction Finance Corporation. “Coming as I do from my work in Washington on the Reconstruction Finance Corporation where one gets into a fair perspective of the general business situation in the country, I believe that we have reached the turning point in the depression,” said Dawes. “The recovery in the depression will start from the bottom up, not from the top down. Washington, June 18.— (#) — With the bonus bill out of the way and adjournment next week within easy reach, congress got a running start today on its last major legislative worries—unemployment relief and government economy. The senate opened debate on the controversial $2,000,000,000 democratic unemployment relief bill, which its sponsors claim will provide work for the jobless and set new blood running through the nation’s industrial veins. In the house, the conference report on the badly battered national economy bill was presented, preparatory to consideration Monday, when a settlement of the disputed governmental pay cut controversy may be reached. Data Gathered. Meanwhile, President Hoover began gathering from his departmental heads, in response to a senate inquiry, recommendations for further governmental economies. Washington, June 16.—(2)—A call for recruits to fill widening gaps in their ranks and swell their numbers to 150,000 was issued Saturday night by leaders of the veterans' army, disappointed and disgruntled by the Senate's defeat of the bonus measure. The number of former service men here, which had been estimated at 20,000, diminished somewhat during the day as the more discouraged groups refused to heed the urging of stump speakers that they remain to carry on the fight for $2,400,000,000 on their bonus certificates. By nightfall police trucks had evacuated 200 and the roads leading from the capital were dotted with members of the shattered army plodding homeward. The 1982 revenue act, signed on June 6 by President Hoover and designed to raise a total of $3,261,500,000 to meet the government's expenses in the 1933 fiscal year, puts most of the new levies in force at that time. Nearly every citizen, from five and ten cent store girl clerks to the multimillionaires, will start contributing to the increased levies. 1932-11-19.text: CAPS LOW, UNION OF SOUTH Africa, Nov. 19—Amy Johnson, 23-year-old British flier, took the England-to-the-Cape speed record away from her husband, Captain J. A. Mollison, by bringing down her tiny monoplane "Dégert Cloud" at the Cape Town airport this afternoon four days, six hours, fifty-five minutes after her takeoff in Britain. She was tired—but not too tired to dab some powder on her nose. “Three cheers for our British Amy!” shouted a woman spectator as Miss Johnson climbed out of her plane. Many Cheer Flier A crowd of 2,000 persons cheered the flier, and there was a great din of motor horns. Miss Johnson's first thought was to communicate with her husband back in England. London, Nov, 17 (*—Prime Minister MacDonald opened the third Indian round table conference today, welcoming the delegates to what he called “these familiar scenes” and expressing the hope that before the end of next month they will have succeeded in formulating a constitution extending a degree of autonomy to India. Reduced in number and shifted from the ancient grandeur of St. James’ palace to four drab rooms in the House of Lords, the 40 delegates who will participate in this meeting have been called a “hand-picked” group because Mahatma Gandhi and his Nationalist Congress party are not represented. Today’s meeting and another scheduled for tomorrow are for organization purposes. The main work of the conference will begin next week. Berlin, Nov. 18--(#)--The full weight of Germany's domestic crisis fell upon the aged President von Hindenburg today as he set out grimly to attain his cherished ideal of national concentration government tolerated, at least, by the deadlocked Reichstag. The president started alone on the difficult road he has charted for himself as a result of the resignation of the Junker cabinet of Franz von Papen. That government stepped aside yesterday after two elections had failed to give it a working hold on the Reichstag. Only the president's secretary was called to accompany the president at conferences with various party leaders—each in private. Selected for these talks today were Alfred Hugenberg, the nationalist party leader, Eduard Dingeldey, the German people's (populist) party chief, and Dr. Ludwig Kaas, acting for the Catholic centrists' party. TORONTO, Ont., Nov. 18. (4)—Death, stealing upon them from a world they shut out for 30 years, has struck down the Misses Emma and Amelia Richardson, spinster sisters for whom time stopped at the year 1902. In an old house which they had made a hermitage of Victorianism, a bewildering world of modernity, the sisters, 76 and 73 years old, were found dead yesterday, clad in the bustles and ruffles of a vanished day. Blamed on Gas Today authorities decided that it was gas, one of the few conveniences in that quaint house, that caused their death. A partly opened burner on the kitchen range and the positions of the frail bodies told the story. Miss Amelia, the younger sister, had fallen in the old-fashioned kitchen. Her hand clutched a box of pills, as though she had felt herself growing faint and misunderstood the case. Miss Emma is believed to have smelled the fumes as she lay in an upstai

BERLIN, Nov. 18. (4)—Adolf Hitler came to Berlin today prepared to meet President Von Hindenburg in a private audience tomorrow to lay before him the program of the powerful National Socialist party for dealing with the stalemate in the Reichstag. The Hitlerite organ, the Völkischer Beobachter of Munich, remarked in connection with the Nazi chieftain’s trip to Berlin that it was not asking too much to expect the powers of the nation “to hearken to the masses” and entrust Hitler with the formation of the new cabinet. Commenting on the resignation yesterday of Chancellor Franz Von Papen, the Nazi organ said that “his chancellorship has proved the time of experiments and halfway measures is over.” Herr Hitler, whose party is the most powerful in a Reichstag in which no party or group is able to swing a majority, arrived in Berlin after President Von Hindenburg had personally taken the task

By 2 ASSN Press. Berlin, Germany, Nov. 18.-The political spotlight shifted once again today to Adolf Hitler, leader of the national socialist party, who came to Berlin by airplane for a conference with President Von Hindenburg tomorrow at which he will set forth the course he purposes to follow in dealing with Germany's cabinet problem. The Nazi leader kept his own counsel. At his party headquarters, it was said that even his closest advisers did not know what line he would follow when he faced the venerable field marshal. But all commentators were agreed that Hitler would do his utmost to overcome the president's personal misgivings about him. For the first time the president today took personal charge of the negotiations with party leaders looking toward the creation of a cabinet which would have the toleration if not the active support of the stalemated reichstag.

NAPLES, Nov. 19.—Leon Trotsky, exiled Soviet leader en route to lecture at Copenhagen, left the steamer Praga here today to visit the ruins of Pompeii, reversing his decision to remain in seclusion during his voyage. Trotsky appeared in excellent health. His personal bodyguard accompanied him on his trip to Pompeii by automobile. Reporters who boarded the Praga here were told by Trotsky’s secretary that he would not leave the ship. But later he emerged from his cabin, preceded by his bodyguard and accompanied by his wife, and walked briskly down the gangplank. Trotsky’s cheeks were ruddy and he appeared to be in good humor. Italian authorities treated him with the greatest courtesy. One automobile carrying Italian police and another Trotsky’s bodyguard accompanied the party. The Praga sailed for Marseilles at 6 p.m.

Paris, Nov. 19 — (AP)—Reports from official circles said Premier Herriot is ready to pay the $20,000,000 interest installment due next month on the American debt if the United States should decide to prolong the Hoover moratorium. The premier’s friends said he believes he can get the money from the treasury without previously obtaining the consent of parliament. He is described as wishing to respect international engagements, but hopeful that the debt negotiations eventually will produce a satisfactory solution.

LONDON, Nov. 11.—(/P)—A solemnly majestic ceremony at the Cenotaph this morning marked England's Armistice Day remembrance. King George, for the first time since his illness which followed a chill at the 1928 Armistice Day ceremonies, laid a wreath at the base of the sad symbol. His son, the Duke of York, laid another. Queen Mary took no part in the service, but watched from an overlooking window. A brigade of red-coated guards in their huge bearskin hats were drawn up in precision around the Cenotaph, forming a hollow square. Within were the king and the duke, representatives of the army, navy and various military organizations, a military band and a vested choir. The prayers and the religious service were conducted by the bishop of London.

1932-01-16.text: NEW LONDON, CONN., JAN. 16. (AP)—The coast guard vessel Herndon, disabled in a collision with the collier Lemuel Burrows, arrived at New London harbor this morning. She was in tow of the coast guard tug Acushnet, which had taken her over from the Burrows five miles inside of Montauk Point. The helpless destroyer, which collided with the Burrows yesterday in a heavy fog between Montauk Point and Block Island, was escorted by several other government craft. A cursory examination showed the destroyer was more badly damaged than at first believed. A fifteen-foot jagged hole was torn across her port side near the bow. A collision mat was stretched across the hole at sea, but this failed to hold. Members of her crew, wearing life belts and many wrapped in blankets, were on deck as the destroyer was towed slowly up the harbor to the coast guard base. New York, Jan. 15 (A) Somewhere off New London, Conn., tonight two crippled ships were limping into port. One was the Coast Guard destroyer Herndon, with a gaping hole in her forward fire room. She was being towed by the collier, Lemuel Burrows, which rammed her in dank fog between Montauk Point and Block Island early this afternoon. The Herndon carried 85 men and eight officers and the Lemuel Burrows, a coastwise steamer, usually carries 58 men. The Coast Guard men said they had been unable to establish if any persons were killed or injured in the crash. The enter Champlain, hurrying to the scene at 16 knots from a position 60 miles away, wirelessed that she had no information on this point, though she apparently had been in communication with the two vessels. Washington, Jan. 15. — Throwing his usual diplomatic caution to the winds, Henry P. Fletcher came out openly today as a candidate for appointment as American ambassador to Great Britain, and sought political backing for the post. A telegram from Fletcher asking the delegation to “unite” in a petition to President Hoover for his appointment was received and went unheeded by the 33 Republican members of congress from Pennsylvania. While acknowledging Fletcher's fitness for the job, leaders of the congressional group were not disposed to seek a joint representation to the White House in Fletcher’s behalf. Almost as soon as the telegram arrived the word went around that the president “has some one else in mind.” Its receipt revealed Senator Reed of Pennsylvania had already urged the Fletcher appointment on President Hoover. London—(/)—Great Britain’s delegates to the Lausanne debt conference are continuing preparations for the opening of that meeting on Jan 25 despite reports in Paris that it might be postponed. In official British quarters postponement was not expected. There still has been no indication from Downing St as to what the British policy will be, but an influential section of the press, basing its comment on hints from official quarters, has indicated a growing support for the views expressed a few days ago by Sir Walter Layton against a reparations moratorium of one or two years. Instead of advocating a five-year respite for Germany, as was the consensus until recently, opinion is now veering to a plan for making the Lausanne conference a mere formal gathering for receiving a report from the Young Plan advisory committee which met some weeks ago at Basel.
