Washington, May 7.—(#)— Charges that the United States Steel Corporation carefully timed its announcement of a 15 per cent cut in wages to fit with President Hoover’s message rebuking Congress were flung in the House today by Representative LaGuardia, (R., i P They came as the House still smarted under the lash of criticism in the chief executive’s message Thursday, urging passage of the revenue bill in the Senate and for $709,000,000 in cuts in appropriations. Attack Hot Although defended by Representative Snell of New York, the Republican leader, the president was flayed by LaGuardia and Representative Bankhead of Alabama, a Democratic leader. The latter de- (Continued on Page 1, Sec. 2)

Washington, May 7. — (AP) — President Hoover’s caustic criticism of the Democratic House for failure to point the way to a balanced budget and Speaker Garner’s primary victory in California stirred presidential politics to a new speculative peak this week. With little interest manifested in the remaining pre-convention primaries and conventions, politicians have settled back to weigh the consequences of these two important developments. As to the first, President Hoover struck with such force in his message to Congress on Thursday as to surprise even his staunchest followers. Placed on the defensive, Democratic leaders immediately replied in kind in both houses, while one opposition chieftain heard the message as the opening gun in Mr. (Continued on Page 1, Sec. 2?)

1932-07-02.text: Wimbledon, Eng., July 2.— Playing before an overflow crowd which included the King and Queen of England, Ellsworth Vines of California, U.S. national champion, today won the English Tennis title in the final match with Henry Wilfred (Bunny) Austin, British player. The scores were 6-4, 6-2, 6-0. While Vines did not play as brilliantly as he did in defeating Jack Crawford of Australia, he was well able to defeat the clever English player. He lacked some of the accuracy which had marked earlier play at Wimbledon, but much of this was due to the high and gusty wind. Austin repeatedly played for (Continued..On Page Nine),

LAUSANNE, July 2. UP—A detailed plan for mobilization of credits for European restoration through a “restoration fund” bond issue was submitted today to delegations to the reparations conference. The plan was drafted by inviting powers of the conference, Great Britain, Italy, France, Japan, and Belgium and awaited the approval of the sixth inviting power, Germany. The “restoration issue” would be backed by the German government as a substitute for resuming reparations payments. It was understood that Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald preferred not to mention any escape clause through which Germany's creditors might be safeguarded in the event an agreement on debt payments is not reached with the United States. The memorandum outlining the restoration plans contained ten essential points covering the European situation. The restoration issue was expected to be absorbed by European banks due

Cobh, Irish Free State, July 1. —(/P)— The big four-masted wind-jammer Melbourne and the tanker Seminole were in collision today off Fastnet light, and 11 men of the Melbourne's crew drowned before the Seminole could rescue them. Fifteen of the crew were saved, however, and transferred to a tug for disembarkation here. The Seminole was slightly damaged at the forepeak. The Melbourne sank.
Friedrichshafen, July 2 (UP)— The Graf Zeppelin left for England today, planning to land at Hanworth Airdrome, near London, and take passengers for a 24-hour cruise over the British Isles.
By Associated Press LONDON.—The Prince of Wales who has been suffering for two days from a chill, continued to make good progress today, but he remained in bed.

| Lausanne, Switzerland, July 1.— A reparations formula, softly phrased to avoid stirring up American opposition, but none the less firmly linking together the problems of reparations and war debts, was submitted by five creditor powers tonight to the German delegation. The next move was up to Chancellor Franz von Papen of Germany, German sources were responsible for a report the chancellor had informed Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald of Great Britain the program outlined in the formula was not acceptable to his government. The formula is a miniature Young plan containing no figures and no safeguarding clause which would protect the European creditor nations in the event the United States refused to scale down debts. The figures and the safeguarding clause will be filled in later. Authorities of the reparations conference explained that the relationship between the debts owed to America

BOMBAY, India, July 1 (#)—The enmity between Moslems and Hindus which has long harassed police authorities throughout India broke out into riots yesterday and today which resulted in ten deaths and a casualty list of more than 200. So fierce were the religious combatants that all shops and markets of Bombay were forced to close, and armed police took control of the streets of the city. The cause of the initial outburst was not immediately determined, but fuel was added to the flame when 1,000 Moslem mourners started a funeral procession through a Hindu section of the city. Many clashes flared and six times police had to fire on mobs before they could disperse them and stop the incidental looting.

TOKYO, July 2—(P)—The Japanese foreign office sent its instructions today on the Hoover disarmament plan to Ambassador Tsuneo Matsumoto, spokesman at Geneva. A foreign office spokesman described the instructions as "equivalent to a flat rejection of the Hoover plan."

1932-07-07.text: London, July 7.—(AP)—Great Britain told the world today she was ready to go a long way with Mr. Hoover on his proposal to cut armaments by one-third, but there were certain limits below which the number of units in the British navy could not be cut. This message was contained in a paper read by Acting Premier Stanley Baldwin in parliament, in which it was stated the British government desires to contribute all it can to effect practical application of the Hoover proposal. Geneva, July 7.—(AP)—Frank B. Kellogg, former American secretary of state, added his prestige as co-author of the Kellogg-Briand anti-war pact and as a justice of the world court to the American proposal for a one-third reduction of armaments at a dinner here Wednesday night. Guest of the United States delegation to the world disarmament conference, Mr. Kellogg talked personally with the chiefs of the other important de

LONDON, July 7. — Great Britain cordially welcomes the Hoover disarmament plan, Stanley Baldwin, acting Prime Minister, announced in the House of Commons today. However, he indicated, Britain is unable to accept the plan unconditionally. She agrees on the interconnection of the problems of military naval and air disarmament, he added. The United Kingdom proposes a reduction of capital ship tonnage by 195,000 tons as opposed to the 175,000 tons proposed by President Hoover, Baldwin announced. Submarines should be entirely abolished and aerial bombing completely prohibited, Baldwin said. Baldwin proposed capital ships be limited to 22,000 tons and to carry guns of a maximum caliber of 11 inches. He proposed that cruisers be reduced to a maximum of 7,000 tons with a maximum caliber of 6.1 inches. Aircraft carriers would be limited to 22,000 tons with a maximum caliber of 6.1 inches.

London, July 6.—(AP)—A jury of 10 men and two women found today that Mrs. Elvira Dolores Barney, 26 year-old daughter of a wealthy baronet, was not guilty of the murder of Thomas William Scott Stephen, her lover, who was shot to death in her bizarre flat after a cocktail party May 31. The verdict, reached after one hour and 53 minutes of deliberation, brought to a close England's most sensational murder trial in decades. Defendant Collapses: Mrs. Barney collapsed when she heard it. A short time later, wholly freed, she escaped from the Old Bailey by a ruse, and went to the home of her father and mother, Sir John and Lady Mullens, in swagger Belgrave Square, not far from the little garage flat in the Mews where Stephen was killed. Her future plans remained unannounced. The jury also acquitted Mrs. Barney on two other charges—one of manslaughter and another of intent (Continued on Page 2)

LONDON, July 7.—(®)—Stanley Baldwin, head of the conservative party and president of the council in the MacDonald cabinet, told parliament today that the British government desires to contribute what it can to effect practical application of the Hoover disarmament proposal. The government welcomes Mr. Hoover's plan to reduce the world’s arms by one third and associates itself with Mr. Hoover's conceptions of the problem, he said.

LONDON, July 7 — British brewers, anticipating the possibility of a change in the American prohibition laws, are seeking permission to display their wares at the Chicago World’s Fair, it was learned today. Their representatives have approached Lieutenant Commander Langworthy, representative of the fair in London. No action has been taken.

BALTIMORE, July 6 (#) — The story of a five-day battle with death, with physician and patient never nearer than 100 miles, was told here today when the Baltimore mail liner, City of Hamburg, docked. A sailor on the British freighter, Aracataca, was the patient and Dr. Vernon H. Condon, medical officer of the City of Hamburg, the physician. The Baltimore liner was off the Grand Banks of Newfoundland when a radio message from the Aracataca was intercepted. The message said: “Seaman aboard = critically ill. Temperature 104°. Delirious. Breath short.” Dr. Condon radioed for further information and then diagnosed the ailment as pneumonia. As both vessels were moving eastward, they were almost abreast for five days. Dr. Condon several times each day received information and prescribed for his long distance patient. On the fifth day, this message was received: ‘Patient resting well. Pulse, resp

United Press Staff Correspondent) LAUSANNE, Switzerland, July q—The international debt and reparations conference was saved from failure today and a tentative agreement was reached. The United Press was informed on high authority that the French and German deadlock over removal of the 'war guilt' clause of the Versailles peace treaty was broken and an agreement achieved. Drafting of the agreement will be rushed through tomorrow and a final plenary session held Friday night or Saturday night. The war debt accord reached today is a virtual extension of the June 16 suspension of such debts until Washington acts on the problem. It will be the third document of the agreements reached here which also include unwritten accords. The achievements of the conference follow: 1. The general convention on war debts, including the 'war guilt' question and Germany's payment in lieu of reparations. 2. A

Lausanne, Switzerland. July 6. (>)— The reparations conflict reached a crisis tonight when six-power negotiations, started with confident predictions that a final agreement soon would be reached, broke up within fifteen minutes. Spokesmen for France and Germany, whose deadlock has made accord difficult, expressed pessimism as the delegates of the six leading powers abandoned for the night their attempt to get together. The British retained their optimism, expressing hope an agreement would be completed tomorrow. Before the delegates of the six leading powers sat down together for what turned out to be a surprisingly brief session, it had been said that they would stick it out until dawn, if necessary. Premier Edouard Herriot of France and Chancellor Franz Von Papen of Germany refused to yield on the amount of the final settlement and on the political clauses. They will meet alone tomorro

1932-12-05.text: ROVER VU RRR Be BOAR Ree WASHINGTON, Dec. 2 (A%—The leaders of Congress, and rank and file as well, roared back an emphatic “no” today to the new British and French pleas for postponement of the December 15 war debt payments. With the door to immediate debt relief slammed shut on Capitol Hill, a hint came from the White House that formal answers may not be forwarded by this government in response to the European arguments for help. Produce No Change. Leaving the regular cabinet meeting, Secretary Stimson told newspapermen “it may not be necessary to reply” to the communications. Speaker Garner for the House and Senator Watson, of Indiana, the Republican leader, for the Senate, reported the French and British notes had produced no change of sentiment in Congress and that there was no prospect there of sanction for the December 15 postponement. Mingled in the varied and emphatic declaratio

London, Dec. 5 (UP) — Acting Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin was understood today to have told Ambassador Andrew W. Mellon that Great Britain does not plan a “punitive” tariff policy against American products if postponement of the December war debt payment is refused. Mellon's visit to Baldwin on Saturday was understood to have followed a request from Washington for clarification of the reference to tariffs in the British debt note. The ambassador was understood to have outlined the gist of President Hoover’s message to Congress and the general attitude of the American administration on the British note. It was reported Baldwin said any fiscal action by Britain would be purely precautionary to the making of the December payment of $95,950,000. British Ambassador Sir Ronald Lindsay was expected to clarify the point to officials of the State Department. The American reply to the British re

LONDON, Dec. 5 (England has settled down to a period of watchful waiting while the American congress deals with the debts and Prime Minister MacDonald takes part in the new disarmament negotiations at Geneva. A visit by Ambassador Mellon on Saturday to Stanley Baldwin, who is acting head of the government in Mr. MacDonald's absence, was understood to have been for the purpose of acquainting Mr. Baldwin with the procedure to be expected in Washington this week. The hope that there might be any yielding by congress on the payment due this month is decreasing, but there is still confidence that the British viewpoint eventually will prevail.

DUBLIN, Irish Free State, Dec. 4—(AP)—Irish railroad workers, meeting here today, decided to call a general strike at midnight December 11 as a protest against the decision of a wage council to cut wages 10 percent.

WASHINGTON, Dec. 5——President Hoover, Secretary of State Stimson and their advisors devoted much of the weekend to continued study of the plea of Great Britain and France for war debt revision and postponement of payments due just 10 days hence. The progress of the conferences was not revealed. The president is expected to make known his views in a special message in Congress, perhaps late this week. He has previously indicated he will ask Congress to re-establish a commission to consider the debts anew. In view of the strenuous congressional opposition to postponement, it is believed in some quarters that Mr. Hoover merely will lay this phase of the question before Congress without recommendation.

Manchester, Ia. Dec. 5—Luther Tesch, 25, Hopkinton, was sentenced to life imprisonment at the state penitentiary at Fort Madison, following his conviction on charges of murdering his father, Louis Tesch, on Aug. 28. A motion for new trial was overruled by Judge A.B. Lovejoy. He was convicted by a jury in the last trial following a sensational trial in which the youth repudiated an alleged confession he had made. The state built up a case in which it claimed that the youth had allegedly connived with his step-mother to kill the elder Tesch. The father's body was found in the Wapsipinnicon River Aug. 28 by fishermen. Police traced the movements of Luther and Mrs. Tesch and they were arrested. In the purported confession, Luther was alleged to have said that he shot his father and drove with his step-mother and the body to the river, where the father's body was thrown into the water.

Tokyo, Mar. 5.—(4)—Baron Dan, managing director of the house of Mitsui, which controls one of the world’s greatest fortunes and is Japan's leading commercial organization, was shot and killed today in the heart of the financial district of Tokyo. The assassin, Guro Hashinuma, 21, was arrested. He is a farm boy from Ibaraki, the prefecture, a rural district north of Tokyo from which came the slayer of Innuye, former minister of finance who was shot last month. Baron Dan was shot as he alighted from an automobile in front of the magnificent Mitsui bank building at 11:00 a.m. The youth fired one shot from a revolver which struck the baron in the right breast. He was carried to a medical room inside the building and died forty minutes later. His wife and son were with him when he died.

TOKIO, Dec. 5.—(UP)—The 900-ton Japanese destroyer Sawarabi went down in a storm off Foochow, with more than 50 missing, it was announced today. Fourteen were rescued. A navy office bulletin describing the sinking said: “The destroyer Sawarabi was shipwrecked while adrift in a storm at 2 p. m. Monday, 100 nautical miles off the northern extremity of Formosa. “Fourteen were saved. Accompanying destroyers are trying to effect a rescue. Two cruisers have been rushed from Makao.” The Sawarabi is one of the second class destroyers laid down under the 1921 naval program. It is 275 feet long. The scene of the disaster is between Foochow, South China port in Fukien Province, and the outlying island of Formosa.

1932-09-22.text: Newchang, Manchuria, Sept. 22 (AP)—A poignant appeal for the rescue of herself and Charles Corkran, another British subject who was captured by Chinese bandits more than a week ago, was received today from Mrs. Pawley, who said the bandits planned to shoot them in a week, after cutting off their ears. The note was received by Mrs. Pawley's father, together with another exorbitant demand for ransom. "Get us out as soon as possible," the note said. "They are going to cut off our ears and I rather want to keep mine. For God's sake be quick. We have a week to live before we are shot. "These fellows are really serious, I am filthy and long for a bath. The food is awful."

Paris, Sept. 21—(4#)—France and England were understood in authoritative American circles tonight to have given Senator David A. Reed an impression of “caution and reserve” on the subjects of Manchuria and Japan. This became known as the Pennsylvania senator left for the Riviera after conversations in London and Paris with Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald and Sir John Simon, home secretary of Great Britain, and Premier Edouard Herriot of France. Not on Official Mission, It was emphatically pointed out that while Reed had no official mission nor authority to conclude agreements, he did receive first-hand knowledge in his capacity as a senator. It was believed the Pennsylvanian found both France and England “attached to the sanctity of treaties” and displaying as well, “a certain caution and reserve as to what concrete attitudes will be adopted in the Manchurian affair.” The impression glea

GENEVA, Switzerland, Sept. 22 —(4)— Arthur Henderson, chairman of the world disarmament conference bureau, spiked a move by England and France today to prevent the bureau from discussing outstanding political questions involved in disarmament. LOS ANGELES, Sept. 22—(4)— Ellsworth Vines, Jr., world tennis champion, was eliminated from the singles competition of the Pacific Southwest tennis tournament in the quarter-finals today by Jiro Satoh, brilliant Japanese star, 6-4, 6-4.

BOMBAY, India, Sept. 22.—(UP)—The Bombay conference tonight decided to cable the British government urging the immediate withdrawal or suspension of its arbitrary Indian communal settlement to prevent the death of Mahatma Gandhi, nationalist leader. Gandhi, who started a voluntary fast “unto death” in protest against the settlement, appeared to be willing to cancel his fast if the government consented.

WINNIPEG, MAN., SEPT. 22. (AP).—John A. Machray, custodian of trust funds of the University of Manitoba and the Church of England, pleaded guilty today to the theft of $901,175 from the university and of $60,000 from Heber Archibald, his former law partner, Machray, 67 years old, was sentenced to seven years’ imprisonment on each charge, the sentences to run concurrently.
Liverpool, Eng., Sept. 22. UP Rioting among the unemployed broke out again today in the Islington district. Several persons were injured when mounted police charged a crowd, dispersing them.

PLYMOUTH, England, Sept. 21 (7 —The Italian salvage ship Artiglia today deposited at this port a fourth cargo of gold retrieved from the sunken liner Egypt. The latest haul was the equivalent of $450,000, making the total salvaged $3,250,000 out of the $5,000,000 in bullion in the Egypt's strong-room when she sank in 1922. The latest haul was snatched up from the bed of the sea in the short span of five hours, all the time divers were able to work during the last three weeks. Weather conditions have been bad.

(United Press Staff Correspondent) WASHINGTON, Sept. 22 — U.P— The mystery surrounding Senator David A. Reed’s talks with British and French officials was cleared up today when it was learned that he is on an important mission for the State Department. Pennsylvania’s senior senator is sounding out the Paris and London foreign offices on their Far Eastern policy. He is expected to report to Secretary Stimson on what the two major powers are prepared to do to uphold the Kellogg and nine-power treaties in Manchuria. Reed's report will probably have an influential bearing on future American policy. He is a member of the Senate foreign relations committee. A student of Japanese affairs, Reed conducted the naval negotiations with Japan at the London naval conference. He is a trusted advisor of Pre (Continued on Page Two)

1932-12-17.text: LONDON, Dec, 17 (#)—Marilyn Miller, stage and screen actress, and Don Alvarado, the actor, sailed on the Europa from Southampton today for New York, Miss Miller announced her engagement to Don Alvarado eight days ago.

‘Winter's “flail stung the ‘North Atlantic seaboard’ Saturday, dashing Virginia with unwonted snow. Most of the states still smarted under low temperatures, but the focus of sub-zero had moved into New England. Boston plunged at zero. Outside the window of Henry Ford's Way- side Inn at Sudbury, Mass., a thermometer registered 22 below. Thermometers that had enough levels recorded 40 below zero at Danville, Vt. and 36 below at St. Johnsbury. Moderating in West, Throughout the nation temperatures were still low, but moderating in the west—Florida and California, however, were up to normal warmth. New York had a touch of the chills with a minimum of 12 above, and Washington went pale with snow that sent automobiles skidding perilously. Five inches of fresh snow lay on the capitol grounds this morning and the weather bureau forecast more throughout the day. Bonus seekers got jobs with shovel

' Po The Associated Press. Paris, France, Dec. 16.—Dynamic Joseph Paul-Boncour, who astonished the world by declaring France was ready to place its army at the disposal of the League of Nations, tonight was trying his hand at forming a French government and settling the serious problem of France’s debt to America. Camille Chautemps had failed. The young radical leader gave up the task of constructing a cabinet because he could not find a compromise between the former cabinet's decision to pay America and the chamber of deputies’ resolution to postpone payment pending examination of France's debt with a view to revision. Having failed to find this compromise, which would be acceptable to parliament and presumably agreeable to Washington and would assure belated payment to America, M. Chautemps definitely lost the collaboration of Edouard Herriot, the retiring premier. Then he surrendered.

Athens, Greece, Dec. 17.--(AP)— The American government's papers in the case of Samuel Insull, wanted in Chicago on embezzlement and larceny charges, are now in the hands of Greek authorities, who were making all preparations today to expedite hearings on the extradition application.

Paris, Dec. 16.—Joseph Paul-Boncour tonight undertook the task in which Camille Chautemps failed—to give France a government likely to find the best solution to the war debt problem. Late tonight, he accompanied retiring Premier Edouard Herriot to Elysee palace where the latest information on Washington’s attitude toward the debts, cabled by Ambassador Paul Claudel, was shown to President Albert Lebrun. Washington View Indicated. It was said in official circles that the ambassador's cablegram indicated that Washington, to which was submitted the chamber of deputies resolution against making the December 15 debt payment, was willing to continue negotiations on the subject of the payment, although the due date is passed. So far as was made known, no mention was made of the American attitude toward a general debt conference. After an hour’s talk with Lebrun, Paul-Boncour left for home, anno

GENEVA, Switzerland, Dec. 16 —(AP)—Attempts to solve the Sino-Japanese problem may be postponed until after Christmas because of the hostility Japan and China showed today towards a resolution for conciliating the dispute regarding Manchuria. Japanese representatives here said they do not want to have the provisional text of the resolution discussed in the absence of Sir John Simon, English delegate, who is in London. China dislikes having the discussions continue in the absence of Eduard Benes, Czecho-Slovakian delegate, who tonight planned to leave for Prague, and Salvador Madariaga, who will resume his post in Spain’s embassy in Paris Monday. Uncertainty as to who will be the next foreign minister of France is another factor in the general tendency to delay. After Chinese and Japanese representatives had expressed their disapproval of the tentative resolution, the document was sent ba

PERPIGNAN, France, Dec. 16 (P) —Seven persons were killed today and twelve were injured when an express train from Paris was derailed at Maury, near Perpignan. The wreck was caused by a washout resulting from floods which have caused considerable damage in this region. Among the dead were three members of the train crew.

ROME, Dec. 17. (AP)—Fascism, which has absorbed all other Italian activities, now is Italy's Santa Claus. The Fascists’ smooth-running organization, furthermore, will be a bigger Santa than ever, because more people otherwise would lack the means for making merry. Depots have been opened in all the large cities and gifts of clothing, food, toys, and money are pouring in. Many Fascist syndicates of workmen have voted to give a day's wages to these agencies. At Christmas, thousands of poor persons eat dinners, thanks to the Fascist-inspired depots. Distribution of the gifts, however, will not be made until Epiphany, January 6, when Premier Mussolini himself will open the distribution here. Italian children put it all over their American cousins in receiving presents. Christmas, New Year, and Epiphany are all special gift days, and relatives are free to send presents any time. Christmas is

1932-07-22.text: Ottawa, July 21.—Canada struck deep into the heart of the problem of the imperial economic conference at its opening session today by proposing to lower her own tariff walls for British Empire products, if the Empire would do the same for her exports. But through her premier, R. B. Bennett, she warned there should be no preferences that would isolate the British Empire from the rest of the world. This qualification was particularly significant, since 70 per cent of British Empire trade in the past has gone to foreign countries. American interests were vitally involved because the United States in 1929 got a major share of the commerce of the British Dominions. Comes Big Chief The Canadian premier’s proposal followed an impressive opening (Continued on Page 2.)

WASHINGTON, July 22 (UP). The navy department was advised today that a group of Nicaraguan insurgents had sacked two stores in Bluefields in eastern Nicaragua, killing eight employees. Three of the dead were thought to have been British.
MANCHESTER, Eng., July 22 ()—Cotton mill unions today called a strike for tomorrow morning as a protest against proposed wage reductions. The walkout would affect between 15,000 and 20,000 men.

LONDON, July 21—(AP)—Mrs. Elvira Dolores Barney was fined 50 Lbs. and costs today for owning a revolver with which a jury decided two weeks ago she did not murder Thomas William Scott Stephen, her lover, in her fashionable West End apartment. The fine and costs amounted to about $205. Mrs. Barney, daughter of Sir John and Lady Mullens, admitted that she had not had a license for the revolver. At her murder trial, the jury verdict indicated acceptance of her story that the weapon was discharged while she and Stephen were struggling for it. There were numerous allusions to the death of Stephen in court today and Mrs. Barney sobbed unrestrainedly. At the end of the case, she collapsed and had to be helped out of the courtroom.

WICK, Scotland, July 22. (P)—At 8:40 a.m. G.S.T. today Captain Wolfgang von Gronau, flying from Germany to Chicago by way of Iceland, reported his position as 58 degrees 30 minutes north latitude and two degrees 15 minutes west longitude. This would place him at a point just east of the Orkney Islands.

New York, July 21. —-(#)— A parade of witnesses marched in and out of the grand jury room today as Nassau county authorities pressed for speedy indictments against 18 policemen involved in the third degree killing of Hyman Stark. State police superseded county officers in the case as the grand jury session began. District Attorney Elvin N. Edwards said he requested this move to free county police from any embarrassment they might feel in working on the case. Stark died of strangulation after being subjected to questioning in connection with an assault upon a detective’s mother. Indictments charging second degree murder were being sought against four policemen. The others have been charged tentatively with assault and conspiracy to obstruct justice. The Killing Dr. Otto A. Schultze, who performed an autopsy on Stark’s body and announced the youth had suffered broken neck bones, causing st

Ottawa, Ont.—(4)—The Irish Free State and the Union of South Africa gave indication of balking at the principle of preference tariff dealing as the imperial conference settled down to work today. In the objection of the Irish Free State, as voiced by Sean T. O'Kelly, head of the delegation, there was an echo of the brewing tariff war between the Free State and Great Britain over President De Valera’s refusal to pay land annuities. Need Outside Trade. “Special difficulties,” O'Kelly said, “have recently arisen which affect about 85 per cent of our external trade and which may involve substantial changes in the form and direction of that trade, as well as the economic structure of the country.” N. C. Havenga, South African minister of finance, emphasized that South Africa could not subscribe to the theory of a self-contained and isolated British Empire. “None of its members,” he said, “can

Berlin, July 22. — Hugo Hermannsberg, chief of Berlin police, was tumbled out of bed at 5 o'clock this morning by a squad of soldiers and was led to the military prison on suspicion of contravention of the present decree of imposing martial law in Berlin. Hermannsberg, one of the most popular members of the police force, was arrested Wednesday along with Albert Grzesinski, commissioner of Prussian police, when Grzesinski and chief assistant refused to relinquish their jobs at the demand of General Von Rundstedt, who is in charge of the execution of the martial law. The charge placed against the men was not disclosed.

1932-03-26.text: Dublin, Irish Free State, March 25.--(AP)— Little imitation Easter lilies, made of muslin, which were sold all over Dublin today and worn in hundreds of buttonholes, may bring trouble to Ireland before this week-end is over. The flower has been chosen as the emblem of Irish republicanism, for it recalls the Easter uprising of 1916. The boutonnieres bear the white, green and orange colors of the republican flag. As a precaution against a repetition of the 1916 trouble, troops of the Irish Free State army will be confined to barracks Easter day. The Irish republican army and the Cumann na mBan, an organization of women republicans, organized the lily sale and plastered the town with posters reproducing the proclamation of the republic of 1916. It’s a Revolt The posters called on the Irish people to unite in “one supreme effort” to break the connection with the British empire and establish

| London, March 26.—(AP)— The British government has invited Premier Tardieu of France and representatives of the German and Italian governments to come to London early in April to discuss the question of an international agreement among the nations on the Danube. | The prime minister's invitation was sent to the foreign ministers of Germany and Italy at the same time that his invitation to Premier Tardieu went forward, Paris advices said there was every likelihood Premier Tardieu would accept the invitation. No replies have yet been received from Germany and Italy. Final details for the conference are not arranged but it was officially stated the meeting would be held ‘early in April.’ Parliament will resume its sessions April 5 and it was expected the conference would be held before then. This pointed to the probability of the conferees meeting next Friday and the following Monday. The

LONDON, March 28, —The British government invited Premier Tardieu of France and representatives of Italy and Germany to come here early in April to discuss the question of an international agreement concerning Danubian nations. Paris advices said Tardieu would accept the invitation. The plan is a movement toward Briand’s dream of a United States of Europe. The first stage would be a tariff agreement between countries on the Danube.

(By The Associated Press) Shanghai, Mar. 26.—Negotiations for a Chinese-Japanese armistice were very near a breakdown today as the delegates of the two countries adjourned until Monday in order to refer controversial issues to their respective governments. The meeting today ended with a deadlock on the issue of withdrawal of Japanese troops and only the possibility of substantial concessions on both sides offered any hope of saving the conference. The negotiations reached a crisis late yesterday, it was understood, when Lieutenant General Kenichi Uyeda, chief of the Japanese delegates, informed the conference that the Japanese would not withdraw before six weeks and then only to a so-called secondary defense line running through Chenju, Tachang and Tsetzeling. The Chinese delegates immediately prepared to leave the conference, it was learned, and agreed to remain only after Nelson T. Joh
FRIEDRICHSHAFEN, Germany, March 21 (UP).—The German dirigible Graf Zeppelin left here early this morning on its first 1932 non-stop flight to Pernambuco, Brazil.

NEW DELHI, India (#)—Hope for peace between the government and Indian Nationalists was suddenly revived today when it was learned that Mrs. Sarojini Naidu, president of the Nationalist Congress, had a long conversation with Viceroy Lord Willingdon yesterday. After the conference Mrs. Naidu hastened to Benares where she had a five-hour talk with Pandit Madan Mohan Malaviya, Nationalist member of the roundtable conference. The belief was expressed in political circles that the conferences were intended to pave the way for co-operation and conciliation between Gandhi and the viceroy. Pandit Malaviya, who is next to the Mahatma in influence in Nationalist India, was reported now on the way here from Benares to confer with Lord Willingdon. Additional significance was given the Nationalist move when the Rev. Charles F. Andrews, Gandhi's biographer, who is now at Delhi, cancelled a proposed tri

—— Shanghai, China, March 25. (?)— There was shooting a few miles outside Shanghai today where two restless armies are lined up awaiting the outcome of the peace negotiations which have been going on here for many days. It was only a minor skirmish and each side blamed the other for starting it, but the incident increased the general uneasiness in the city. The peace parleys lagged, each side sticking to the program it outlined at the beginning of the conferences. The principal point at issue seemed to be the method of troop withdrawals and the policing of the evacuated Zone.
CUXHAVEN, Germany, @P — A 12,000 pound whale strayed into harbor here Saturday from the North Sea and disrupted regular traffic until it was captured.

1932-06-11.text: Stourbridge, England, June 11 — Edina Sharp, sister of Violet who committed suicide in the Morrow home at Englewood, N. J., denied today that she knew anything about the kidnapping of the Lindbergh baby. "I know nothing whatever about the kidnapping," she said as she left for her parents' home in Beenham, "What is more I’m quite sure my sister Violet knew nothing about it either."

LONDON, LP, There was no attempt to disguise the impression in government circles that Europe was on the verge of important developments in the war debts and disarmament fields, and the sum total of reports flying about spelled compromise. But just what turn affairs would take was a matter of pure speculation, twelve hours before Prime Minister MacDonald goes to Paris for preliminary discussions with Premier Herriot of France. France and Great Britain long have been at odds on war debts and disarmament, the French standing for absolute security and an armed League of Nations, while the British want to wipe out war debts and reparations in one sweeping gesture. The British also have rejected the armed league idea. Suggestions, however, contained in Premier Herriot’s recent speeches that he was prepared to take drastic action to help clear up the European economic muddle was warmly welcome

NEW YORK, June 11—(/P)— The light of law, hunting the Lindbergh baby’s kidnapper-killer, burned inquiringly and in sharp focus today upon an ex-convict, Ernest Brinkert. The sudden suicide yesterday of an English servant girl in the home at Englewood, N. J., of Mrs. Dwight Morrow, the baby’s grandmother, and the arrest several hours later in New Rochelle, N. Y., of the “Ernie” with whom she said she went motoring the night the baby was kidnapped, gave the investigation into the crime new impetus. The girl, a waitress at the Morrow home for more than two years, was Violet Sharpe, 28 years old. She was English-born, as was Betty Gow, the slain baby’s nursemaid who was among the first questioned after the kidnapping. Police had questioned her before. They said she was the only one of the servants at the Morrow home in Englewood and at the home of the Charles A. Lindberghs near Hopewell, N.

Wimbledon, Eng., June 11—(AP)— The United States successfully defended the Wightman Cup, women’s international tennis trophy, today as champ Wills Moody, the American champion, defeated Dorothy Round of Great Britain. It was the fourth straight victory and clinched the series. Mrs. Moody was victorious over Miss Round by scores of 6-2, 6-3. The American team had captured all three matches yesterday.

Suicide of Violet Sharpe and arrest of Ernest Brinkert brought about accelerated police activity in the United States and England today in an attempt to solve the kidnapping and murder of Charles Augustus Lindbergh Jr. Brinkert was arrested shortly after Miss Sharpe, a maid in the home of Mrs. Dwight Morrow and "under suspicion" committed suicide. He was being questioned at state police headquarters at Alpine, N. J., March 1, the date of the kidnapping. In England, Scotland Yard detectives sought information on Miss Sharpe and her sister, Emily, who left the United States four days after Dr. John F. Condon paid ransom to men who claimed to be the kidnappers. In Washington it was disclosed Emily sought permission to leave for England March 1 but sailed in April. Emily in a press interview said she knew nothing of the Lindbergh case, but that her sister had complained of the "awful police

| WIMBLEDON, Eng., June 11—(UP)—The United States won the Wightman Cup tennis competition with Great Britain for the sixth time in 10 years today when Mrs. Helen Wills Moody of California defeated Miss Dorothy Round, 6-2, 6-3. Mrs. Moody's victory coupled with the United States' clean sweep of yesterday's three matches, gave America the four points necessary for victory. Today’s other three matches, therefore, will be nothing more than exhibitions.

Brest, France, June 10 (4)—The stubborn hull of the sunken liner Egypt, clinging to five million dollars worth of gold and silver bullion these ten years, today yielded up £45,000 to tenacious Genoese divers. Fifteen lives and two strong ships have been lost in the two years’ quest for the precious metal by an Italian salvaging crew. Today's haul, while very small, apparently heralded ultimate victory in a spectacular battle of man against the waves. The ship was sunk in a collision in 1923 forty miles off Brest.

WASHINGTON, June 10, (P)—The capital's “army of nearly 160,000 bonus payment seekers ate well Friday night from enhanced food stocks bought from an enlarged treasury. Their mess fund was raised to $7,000 by a $5,000 gift from Father Charles E. Coughlin, Detroit “radio priest.” It was conditional that communist propaganda be kept from the camps and that Brigadier General Pelham D. Glassford, Washington police superintendent, administer it. The veterans agreed and General Glassford was reinstated as unofficial treasurer, a position he “washed his hands of” several days ago in an effort to get the army from under the protective wing of police assistance. With their own funds and truck loads of food donated by merchants, organizations and individuals both in and out of Washington, the army fared better Friday night.

1932-05-18.text: BOMBAY, India, May 17 (®) — Hindu and Moslem mobs were quieted tonight by the rifle fire of British troops after four days of communal rioting that took 58 lives and wounded at least 850 persons. — Twenty-four were killed today and 200 injured. The Royal Irish Fusiliers fired tonight on a mob of Moslems in Bombay who were looting and burning shops in the Bhendy Bazaar, the center of the worst of the riots. All was quiet afterward, for the first time since Saturday, when a Moslem group first attacked some Moslem youths, although the rioting had forced the closing of mills, throwing 40,000 men and women out of work. For the most part during the day the populace shuddered indoors as blood continued to flow in the shambles of several Bombay districts. Garbage and refuse, unattended for days, rotted in the streets, causing an abominable stench.

By The Associated Press Paris, May 18.—Ninety-one persons who were aboard the French motor ship Georges Philippar when she burned Monday on Italian Somatnd still are unaccounted for, owners of the vessel said today.

Tokyo, May 18—(#)—Leaders of the Seiyukai party decided today to offer the olive branch to the army and proposed a compromise on a coalition party government to succeed the cabinet of the slain Premier Suyoshi Inukai. The compromise proposal followed an ultimatum from the army yesterday demanding a non-partisan, national government. Army officials threatened to boycott a party government if one was formed. At the same time, it was indicated that the controversy over the new cabinet would not be settled until the last of the week. Prince Saionji, the aged sole survivor of the powerful Japanese genro, or elder statesmen, announced that he would not come to Tokyo from his villa at Okitsu until Thursday. The aged prince is coming to advise the emperor on the selection of a new premier. He intended, the announcement said, to let the situation crystallize further before making his decision. Th

HARBIN, May 18. (AP)—A fierce battle between Japanese and Chinese insurgents in which both sides lost heavily, raged today along the north bank of the Sungari river, just north of here. The battle began yesterday evening. Eighteen Japanese were killed in the opening clash at Sungpu. A force of 600 rebels attacked the nearby town of Machuangkou but the Japanese infantry, aided by airplanes, routed them. The Chinese lost 50 killed, the Rengo news agency reported. The Chinese retreated down the river toward Fuchin, 100 miles from the Soviet border town of Khabarovsk. The massacred Japanese had been held prisoners for more than a month by the Chinese.

BOMBAY, May 18—(AP)—The list of casualties of the Hindu-Moslem riots which entered their fifth day here today was increased to 92 dead and 910 injured when four persons were killed and 60 injured as the rioting broke out afresh. The fighting had subsided overnight and the city was quiet until shortly after daybreak.

PARIS, May 18, —Owners of the maotership Georges Philippar, which burned in the Arabian Sea Monday, announced 50 passengers and members of the crew are known to be missing. They said the num- ber might be more when the check is complete. Six hundred and seventy-six per- sons are known to have been res- cued. No Americans were on the list. There was such an uproar of gaiety aboard when fire bells sounded that passengers failed to realize their significance, surviv- ors at Aden declared.

TOKYO, Wednesday, May 18—tAP—In the face of an army demand for a non-partisan nationalist cabinet, the Seiyukai party indicated today its willingness to compromise and form a coalition government. The Seiyukai party, nominally in power because the assassinated Premier Suyoshi Inukai was its president, sought to retain governmental power by permitting the chief opposition, the Minseito party, to place members in the cabinet, and also by inviting the House of Peers to take part in forming a new government. The Seiyukai group hoped such a combination would be acceptable to the military authorities, who are able to block any ministerial formation they wish to, because the minister of war must be a general in the army. The attitude of the army toward such a coalition remained obscure. Although Kaku Mori, one of the principal Seiyukai leaders, held a long conference during last night with Gene

HOPEWELL, N. J., May 18—(AP)—John Hughes Cur- tis, fake Lindbergh baby negotiator, is being watched closely by the police for fear his “remorse” may tempt him to commit suicide, a high official revealed today. Curtis’ every movement is being watched, it was stated. Gov. A. Harry Moore of New Jersey said it was probable that Curtis would be arraigned today after a complaint had been sworn out against him by the police. A report disseminated by a news service (not The Associated Press) that Curtis had actually attempted to take his life was officially denied at the state house. HOPEWELL, N. J., May 18.—(AP)—An elaborate lie, blown into a bubble of hope that hoaxed the civilized world, exploded today on the penpoint of the man who invented it. Police called it an “enormous deception” to which John Hughes Curtis, 47-year-old boatbuilder and Lindbergh kidnapping “intermediary” confessed late

1932-04-24.text: NEW YORK, April 23—They’re getting taller and taller in the fashion parades. Marie Early, who hails from North Dakota, is six feet one. So is Joan Saffelle of London. The manikins will meet here in June to talk height to the dress trade. They believe in it. Marie suffered the pangs of the gangly at 14, when she was as tall as she is now. She wanted to be a dancer. Her family merely laughed. But she has the laugh now, for she is much sought to model extravagant gowns, luxurious wraps and costumes of the present slinky, streamlined molds. “Tall women ought to play up to their height,” she says, “and not slump to try to look shorter.”

ADY 281 serene Soe STATFORD-ON-AVON, England, April 23—The prince of Wales flew here from Windsor today and, with a golden key, opened the new $1,000,000 Shakespeare memorial theatre. It was a day of colorful pageantry and ceremonial tribute to the genius of England's greatest bard. Ambassador Andrew W. Mellon represented the United States at a truly international celebration in which the flags of America, Japan, Russia, France and many other nations—70 in all—flew side by side to honor the poet. The United States, from which came a good part of the funds for the memorial, got special mention in an ode written for the occasion by John Masefield, poet laureate, and in the speech of the prince of Wales. “In describing this theatre as a world tribute to Shakespeare,” the prince said, “I would like to mention Britain's special appreciation of the very generous help which has been forthcoming

BERLIN, April 23 (#)—For the third time within six weeks five-sixths of Germany's voters will cast ballots tomorrow to decide a struggle for supremacy in which the Republican parties and Adolf Hitler's National Socialists are the chief opponents. The elections will determine the political complexion of the diets in Prussia, Bavaria, Wurtemberg, Hamburg and Anhalt. The bitterness of the campaign, which followed on the heels of two presidential election struggles from which Paul von Hindenburg emerged victorious over the fiery Hitler, was illustrated by the fact that in Berlin alone 190 persons were arrested last night. In Cologne 20 National Socialists, headed by Robert Ley, a member of the Reichstag, were jailed in connection with an attack on Otto Wels, chairman of the Socialist party, and Otto Bauknecht, chief of police. “Beer mugs and tear gas were employed as political arguments in a

WASHINGTON, April 23.— The object for days of an unavailing senate search, two of Wall Street's big bear traders—Thomas E. Bragg and Bernard E. Smith—calmly walked into a committee room today and proceeded to tell a story packed with startling surprises for their eager inquisitors. John J. Raskob, chairman of the Democratic national committee, Fred J. Fisher, W. C. Durant and W. F. Kenny, they testified had been associated with them in a gigantic $32,000,000 pool on Anaconda Copper in 1929. They lost heavily. In addition, they said Mrs. Michael J. Meehan, whose husband was a specialist in radio on the floor of the stock exchange, engaged in a pool on that stock in 1928 and 1929. A subpoena has been issued for Meehan. Associated Press Staff Writer NORFOLK, Va., Apr. 30. —(#) — The oft-hoped-for climax, screened behind a curtain of secrecy, and with the sea again serving as the probable scene, was believed to be near tonight in the efforts of three Norfolk men to restore the Lindbergh baby to its parents. The feeling of hopefulness, repeatedly recurring with the coming and going of the intermediaries during the long weeks of their negotiations, reached another high peak with the absence of John Hughes Curtis, presumably seeking another contact with the kidnapers of the Virginia. Although his movements were guarded with utmost secrecy, the Norfolk boat builder was reported to have engaged upon his new mission aboard the yacht Marcon, shortly after returning from a trip by plane. The boat, placed at the disposal of the intermediaries by Colonel Charles H. Consolve, sailed on its third mysterious cruise a

WASHINGTON, April 23 — A wary and much-harassed economy committee whipped the far-reaching $200,000,000 omnibus retrenchment bill into final shape today for ne into the house on Monday. The bi-partisan group planned to work over the weekend to prepare for the expected heated battle over the controversial measure when its consideration is begun Wednesday. As drafted it contains the proposed consolidation of the war and navy departments and the McDuffie federal wage cutting plan, to both of which the administration is opposed, and President Hoover's requested authority to reorganize the government. While house factions set themselves for the impending conflict, plans of the chamber of commerce of the United States to launch a national drive to marshal public sentiment for reduced public expenditures in federal, state and local governments were made known. The campaign will be inaugurated b

(Associated Press Staff Writer) - NORFOLK, Va., April 23 (P) — Maneuvers by three Norfolk men seeking to bring about the return of Charles Augustus Lindbergh, Jr., were accelerated tonight as at least one of the principals indicated their negotiations were moving towards a climax. While maintaining his usual silence regarding details, the Very Rev. H. Dobson-Peacock intimated that some important development was expected soon as a culmination of three secret missions undertaken this week. Dean Dobson-Peacock said he could not tell what progress had been made and when conclusion of their negotiations might be expected. “I don't know myself,” he said. He then intimated, however, that some important development might be expected soon. It could not be learned if a secret mission engaging John Hughes Curtis and a flight made today by the clergyman were to points near those which Mr. Curtis wen

HOPEWELL, N. J., April 238 (#) — As intermediaries seeking the return of the kidnapped Lindbergh baby worked Saturday night behind a veil of secrecy, it was learned the state police plan soon to close the headquarters they have maintained on the flier’s estate since March 3. The baby was stolen from his crib late the previous night. The police telephone lines, machines, desks and other equipment installed in the famous flier’s garage will be loaded into trucks early next week, and carted away to a destination as yet undecided definitely. The move was described as having no particular significance, being the inevitable consequence of the gradual lessening of the intense concentration of police minds which marked the early part of the investigation. It will be made, not because police feel the investigation has come to a standstill but to relieve the family of as much strain as possible an

1932-09-01.text: SYDNEY, N. S. (AP)—Captain J. A. Mollison, abandoning his plan to fly back to England, took off Thursday for Quebec where he will start for home by steamship.

NEW YORK, Sept. 1—(4)—Andrew W. Mellon is on his way back to resume his post as ambassador to the Court of St. James. Before sailing last night he denied a report he had conferred with Montagu Norman, governor of the Bank of England, who is visiting this country.

SYDNEY, N. S., Aug. 31 (®) — Importuned by his wife, his physician and his flight backer, Captain J. A. Mollison, the first airman to make a westward solo crossing of the north Atlantic by air, today abandoned his plan to return to England by plane. Tomorrow Mollison will fly to Quebec and embark on the liner Empress of Britain. His wife, the former Amy Johnson, herself a noted distance flier, had beseeched him to choose the more prosaic steamer passage after learning from his physician that his nerves were in a bad way. Dr. Freeman O'Neil, Captain Mollison’s host here had insisted the flier rest for at least three or four weeks. Exhaustion plus lack of fuel made it impossible for the airman to reach his goal of New York when he made his westward crossing, and Aug. 19 he landed in a meadow at Penfield Ridge, New Brunswick. Subsequently he continued on to New York and on Monday, while en

PARIS. (AP) Premier Herriot, back in Paris for a cabinet meeting which will consider Germany's formal demand for equality in armament, conferred Thursday morning with the British charge d'affaires before summoning his ministers. The government was uncommunicative regarding details of the demand presented by the German ambassador, but it was understood its principal points are these: First: Modification of the Versailles treaty with a provision for a twelve year service basis in the German army. Second: Amalgamation of compulsory military service and the period served by the militia. Third: Permission for Germany to maintain heavy, light and coastal artillery. Fourth: Permission for maintenance of tanks by the German army. Fifth: Establishment of a complete German military aviation corps. Sixth: Establishment of a school for military pilots. Seventh: Extension of the German navy by the ad

A total eclipse of the sun swept across New England Wednesday - only a partial success from the scientific standpoint, but a magnificent spectacle to millions. A sky, darkened in some sections by huge banks of clouds, and partly or entirely clear in others, made results uncertain from the standpoint of the 66 or more scientific expeditions scattered from Canada to the end of Cape Cod, Massachusetts. For some it meant almost complete failure despite months of planning. At Magog, Quebec, where were gathered expeditions from Cambridge and London, England, and from the University of Virginia, clouds hid the sky and the Virginia expedition reported failure. Clouds in War At Conway, N. H., the center of the largest concentration of scientific observers, the results were dubious. The eclipse was a hit and from the layman's standpoint was not a failure, but scudding clouds interfered with the wo

Hawarden, Ia., Sept. 1.—(A.P.)— A loss estimated at more than $20,000 was suffered here late last night when fire burned two business places in the downtown district. The business houses destroyed were the C. J. Dirks hardware store and Ellebrock women’s apparel store. The fire began when a gasoline tank exploded while Mr. Dirks was pumping air pressure into it.

Germany has renewed, in a communication to the French government, her demand for revision of the Treaty of Versailles to permit German equality with the other nations of Europe in the strength of her land and sea armaments. German officials explained that the communication was not a formal note but that the foreign minister merely provided the French ambassador with a "loose aide memoire." The disclosure that the issue had been discussed formally created deep interest in Paris. The French government would say nothing about details, but the cabinet was summoned for this afternoon. Great Britain has been kept fully informed of the negotiations, under terms of the Franco-British consultative pact but is taking no part in discussions. It is expected however that she will be drawn in shortly.

By The Associated Press. | Berlin, Ger, Aug. 31.—Chancellor Franz Von Papen will refrain from dissolving the new Reichstag only if his cabinet is empowered by a special emergency law to govern for six months without parliamentary support. The Associated Press learned of this decision today as officials of the new Reichstag, which held its first session yesterday, were attempting to obtain an immediate audience with President Von Hindenburg for the purpose of attempting to convince him that the legislature was able to carry on parliamentary government. Audiences Requested Immediately audiences were requested by Speaker Hermann Wilhelm Goering, a member of Adolf Hitler’s National Socialist Party, in a telegram sent to the president’s home in Neudeck, East Prussia. The aged field marshal replied that next week, when he will be in Berlin, would be time enough for this conference. Government

1932-08-07.text: BERLIN, Aug. 6—While a wave of political terrorism swept through Germany today, the groundwork was laid for negotiations aimed at bringing about participation in the government by Adolf Hitler, leader of the turbulent National Socialists. Hitler's headquarters in Munich made a great secret about where he was spending the weekend, but political Berlin was convinced that in one of the Baltic seaside resorts tomorrow he will tell Gen. Kurt Von Schleicher, the real power in the present ministry, what price the government must pay for his support. The latest suggestion in political circles is that Hitler will be brought into the ministry with the post of vice-chancellor without portfolio and that his leading lieutenants—Hermann cabinet positions. BERLIN. (UP) — German political unrest, which has cost hundreds of dead and injured in recent weeks, entered a new phase Saturday with terroristic bombings throughout the country. Bomb outrages spread during the night in Brunswick, Kiel, Mülheim, Breslau, and Schwerin, chiefly in private homes and shops. Several deaths and many injuries were reported. Homes Riddled Homes of Republican and Nazi leaders were subjected to volleys of shots. In the town of Hindenburg, upper Silesia, 20 communists stoned the Hitlerite militia headquarters, injuring one Nazi. At Liegnitz, in Silesia, the Nazi “Brown House” was fired on. NEW YORK—(44)—In a bitter attack on his accusers, Mayor Jimmy Walker Saturday night said he would appear at a public hearing called by Governor Franklin D. Roosevelt for next Thursday and would bring out “the real truth” about “these foul and outrageous accusations” on which his removal is sought. He charged the testimony produced against him at hearings of the Hofstadter legislature committee had been purposely manipulated. He said the governor's hearing would be his first opportunity to confront “those witnesses upon whose one-sided and hearsay testimony my political life is sought.” He declared he would examine the witnesses himself in order to bring out the entire truth. By The Associated Press Washington, Aug. 6.—With the presidential campaign about to swing into the faster stride that will carry to November, the leaders and rank and file alike have riveted attention on three prime matters fraught with political potentialities. Above all, of late, has the rising stock market been watched by those who see a relationship between its behavior and public sentiment toward the party in power. More and more, too, has interest dwelt on what President Hoover will say about prohibition in his speech next Thursday accepting renomination; and on how Governor Roosevelt will dispose of the case against Mayor Walker of New York. May Affect Vote As to the market, the only unanimity is that time alone can tell the extent to which the shifts and levels will affect the vote. Aware that a great deal can happen in many fields in the number of weeks between now and balloting

SEATTLE, Wash., Aug. 6. —(7)— Downtown buildings were shaken by an earthquake at 2:17 p. m. today. The earth movements lasted only a few seconds. The quake was the most violent felt here in a number of years, the north-south movement being quite noticeable. Hundreds of telephone calls were made to newspaper offices and police stations as residents inquired concerning the shock. No damage was reported.

By The Associated Press Louisville, Ky, Aug. 6. — An army reserve officer and his student pilot were instantly killed late today when their plane went into a 220-foot nosedive and crashed near Bowman field. The dead are Lieut. Earl C. Gibson, 28, Kenton, Ohio, a reserve officer of the 325th observation squadron, army air corps, and Shereley Pope Monroe, 23, of Lebanon Junction, Ky., a civil engineer for the Kentucky highway department. Witnesses said the plane veered upward, slipped into a left bank, then crashed nose first.

Johnstown, Pa., August 6. (7)— The last units of the bonus expeditionary force steamed out of Johnstown today, only a few minutes after hearing the news that their former chief of staff, Doak Carter, had asked for a haven in Mexico. Shouting, cheering, singing, some 500 veterans, members of the Pennsylvania, New York, New Jersey and New England contingents, marched from their squalid billets to be loaded on a train, amid cheers of crowds lining the tracks. As the train puffed eastward, its whistle shrieking, the last chapter of the Johnstown encampment was written in smoke in the dying rays of a broiling sun. A fife and drum corps escorted the marchers to the train. They sang while the corps played patriotic airs, said “so long” to Mayor Eddie McCloskey—and were gone. The same air of uncertainty pervaded among the departing horde as marked the first arrivals after McCloskey invited them

By The Associated Press Louisville, Ky., Aug. 6.—Light voting marked Kentucky's primaries today for United States Senate and the lower house of Congress, although ideal weather prevailed over the state. Counting of the ballots, which begins Monday, will determine the Democratic nominee for the Senate and the nine nominees of each party for the House. The Republicans will nominate their candidate for the Senate in the state convention here September 7. All three Democrats seeking the senatorial nomination and all but one of the 27 seeking congressional nominations are listed as against the 18th amendment. A majority of the 22 Republicans seeking nomination to Congress are listed as favoring the amendment. 1932-08-20.text: ST. John, N. B. (#)—J. A. Mollison, youthful British aviator, the first person to fly alone across the North Atlantic from east to west, has postponed until tomorrow the continuation of his flight to New York. Mollison came here last night from Pennfield Ridge, N. B., where he landed yesterday after flying from Portmarnock, Ireland. He was too tired to go farther. He had a His crossing of the Atlantic was “the toughest flight” he ever made, Mollison said, and he was “Jolly well all in.” He talked by trans-Atlantic telephone with Amy Johnson, his three-weeks’ bride and herself a noted distance flier, and she promised to sail today for New York to join him. Later she changed her mind and said she would not come to the United States. “I was lucky,” he said. “For hours at a stretch on the way across I couldn't see the water below me and I didn’t know whether the wind was changing and blowing

Utlawa, Ont., Aug. 20 (AP)— Trade treaties between Great Britain and her dominions which will become effective when ratified by the respective parliaments were signed today at the final session of the imperial economic conference. Delegates gathered about the long table for the ceremony which ended a month of bargaining. There was a resolution of loyalty to the king and another expressing appreciation for the work of Premier Bennett of Canada, official host. Then the signing of the treaties began. Stanley Baldwin, lord president of the council in the British cabinet, signed for the United Kingdom with the several dominion premiers affixing their signatures to the agreements in which they are concerned. Premier Bennett signed the five-year trade pact between Canada and Great Britain, with Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer, signing for the United Kingdom. There were other tr

VIENNA, Aug. 20.—(#)—Dr. Johann Schober, 58, twice chancellor of Austria and the man who shook Europe last year with his plan for an Austro-German Customs union, fell dead last night at a sanitarium near Gutenbrunn. He began life as a policeman. Born in Perg, Upper Austria, in 1874, the son of a post office employee, he studied law at the University of Vienna and after graduation, entered the police service. He became chief of police immediately after the World War and so reorganized the department that it became the government's mainstay during the most critical period. In June, 1921, he became chancellor, remaining in office until May, 1922. He was chosen to head the cabinet again in September, 1929, and continued in office for a year, holding also the post of foreign minister. He continued as foreign minister until January of this year.

ST. JOHN, N. B., Aug. 20. (4)— Fog interfered with the plans of Capt. J. A. Mollison today, preventing a flight from Pennfield Ridge, where he completed his trans-Atlantic solo hop yesterday, to the Canadian Air carnival at Montreal. It was too foggy for the short trip, so he left the plane in the field where he landed yesterday and returned here by automobile this afternoon. "I’ll be in New York by 5 o’clock tomorrow," he said. He disclosed that he had cabled his wife, advising her against sailing for New York because he intended starting his return flight for Europe before she could make the journey by ship. She is in London.

ST. JOHN, N. B., Aug. 20, (Pj) Captain J. A. Mollison, who spent the night here after his trans-Atlantic solo flight, left this morning for Pennfield Ridge, 40 miles down the Bay of Fundy, where he landed yesterday. There was a light rain, but he said he would fly the ship up to Montreal, where scores of fliers are gathered for the fourth annual Canadian air carnival... Tomorrow he is going to New York where he will remain a few days before starting his flight back to Europe. That will be his last long distance trip, he said this morning, but he will not abandon his career in aviation. Despite the somewhat unfavorable weather Mollison brought his record-breaking plane from Pennfield Ridge in time to appear as the honor guest at a luncheon. ST. JOHN, N. B., Aug. 20 — (INS) —— First solo conqueror of the treacherous westward crossing of the Atlantic, Capt. James A. Mollison, young Scottish flyer, had the world at his feet today. Messages of congratulation stormed him from all over the world. From many cities in the United States and Canada came invitations for visits. One of these, coming from Montreal, was accepted. Mollison, only a day after arriving at Penfield Ridge near here from Ireland, planned to take off at 2:30 p.m. today for the Canadian city in the same tiny 'flying gasoline tank' in which he fought storms and fog to defeat the ocean. He will go to Montreal as the honored guest of the fourth Canadian air pageant, Colonel W. A. Bishop, famous Canadian flying ace of the World War, and J. A. Wilson, controller of civic aviation for Canada. Earlier plans to fly to New York today were changed, and Mollison now believe

MILAN, Italy, Aug. 20—(/P)—A small steamer which has been hovering suspiciously near the salvage ship, “Artiglio II,” which is retrieving gold from the hold of the sunken steamer “Egypt” near 43°50' France, is believed by the Artiglio’s crew to have piratical intentions, the correspondent of the newspaper “Corriere Della Sera” said today. Commander Quaglia of the Artiglio had distributed revolvers to the 24 members of his crew, the correspondent said. A total of 250 pounds of gold is now aboard the salvage vessel, stored in an armored cabin below decks. Yesterday morning the suspected ship passed very near and closely scrutinized the salvage ship.

PARIS, Aug. 20 (Dr. Paul Gorguloff, who was found guilty July 27 of the premeditated assassination of President Paul Doumer last May, must die on the Guillotine, the court of appeals decided today. The court rejected his demand for retrial. Gorguloff's defense was mentally irresponsible when he shot the president at a charity gale of books for war veterans,

1932-12-03.text: The answer of Congress to the renewed British and French pleas for postponement of the war debt installments due December 15 was emphatically “No.” This was apparent from comments yesterday by Speaker Garner, Republican Leader Watson and Chairman Borah of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. France’s second note, which was in President Hoover's hands yesterday, threatened rejection of the Lausanne agreement cutting down German reparations if payments were required. Commerce Department economists said Britain’s warning that payment would mean restriction of American trade was not a specific threat against this country. Both Britain and France anxiously awaited replies to their renewed pleas, but Secretary Stimson indicated Washington might consider it unnecessary to answer.

GENEVA, Dec. 2—(4—American delegates to the Disarmament Conference told the British, French and Czechoslovakian members today the time was ripe to register a forward step in the direction of armament reduction and at the same time spike rumors circulating in the European press that the United States might withdraw from the conference. Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald and Foreign Minister Sir John Simon of Great Britain, Joseph Paul-Boncour, French Minister of War, Edouard Benes, Foreign Minister of Czechoslovakia, and Norman Davis, the American delegate, started conversations for the Five-Power party at a luncheon today. Premier Herrio, and the Italian delegate are expected tomorrow and the Germany Foreign Minister is due Sunday night or Monday. A series of interviews will then begin in an effort to get Germany back into the Disarmament Conference.

Berlin, Dec. 2.—General Kurt von Schleicher, who calls himself a 'man without nerves,' was commissioned by President Paul von Hindenburg today to form a presidential cabinet—that is, a cabinet responsible to the president himself. As chancellor, the general, who served as defense minister in the Von Papen cabinet, will face the task of leading a disunited nation, exhausted economically and morally by partisan strife, into a quiet period of economic advance and social appeasement. At Weimar, Herr Hitler issued a statement categorically refusing to tolerate a Von Schleicher cabinet. But it was learned on good authority that the chancellor-designate was confident he could come to some sort of terms with the Nazis by which they at least would help in adjourning the Reichstag for several months.

PARIS, Dec. 2—(4—France sat back tonight and anxiously awaited America’s reply to the second French request for postponement of her war debt installment due this month. Premier Herriot had a long talk with Henri Berenger, president of the Foreign Affairs committee of the Senate, and it was said afterward that the debt situation, especially America’s reception of the French note which was delivered in Washington today, was the main topic of discussion. The tone of the note was generally praised in the press tonight which said that the next move was up to the United States. The general theme throughout the press was that the Lausanne accords might be jeopardized if the United States insists upon payment and that the possibility for development of policies leading toward a return of prosperity and toward the organization of peace faced destruction.

BERLIN, Dec. 2—(UP)—General Kurt von Schleicher, who is cast in the image of Bismarck, today was placed at the helm of a disunited Germany. President Paul von Hindenburg, “after long deliberation and with a heavy heart,” appointed him as chancellor. Thus the man who has been content over a period of at least 10 years to stand in the wings and direct the show of government without drawing attention to his personality becomes virtual dictator—the first military man to head a German cabinet since Prince von Bismarck and Wilhelm II parted ways in 1890. General von Schleicher retains his post as defense minister and becomes quasi-dictator of Prussia.

VANCOUVER, B. C.—In a WIRE section, extending from 100 miles east of Vancouver to Alberta and south into the Okanagan valley, a survey of storm damage was underway today. Swirling down from the north Friday, the early winter storm, which almost reached blizzard proportions in some sections, crippled wire communications for many hours, delayed train service and tied up highway traffic. Communication with eastern Canada was reestablished last night, and trains were making their way into Vancouver after long delays. In contrast, the weather was clear and mild on the coast, while in the Pitt Meadows area of the lower mainland flood conditions prevailed today. Loss to cattle herds is reported.

Washington, Dec. 2.—(?)— Nine women, seeking presidential help for the demonstrators now marching on Washington, found today the social register holds no key to the chief executive’s office. The group, including several of social prominence, was informed by Theodore Joslin, President Hoover’s secretary, that it would be impossible for them to see the president. Meanwhile, Herbert Benjamin, one of the sponsors of the march, encountered difficulty in his plan to feed and house the groups. Food supplies which Benjamin had talked of earlier in the week failed to reach his expectations. A vacant warehouse, on which he had depended for shelter, was found already occupied by none less than the federal government itself. He appealed to several local churches for shelter, but gave up that idea (Continued on Page 7)

WASHINGTON, Dec. 2.—(/P) Bipartisan moves to slash federal appropriations went forward on Capitol Hill today as the daily treasury statement revealed a deficit of $750,000,000 for the first five months of the fiscal year. Republicans and Democrats alike waited to see what President Hoover has to say on the subject in his message to Congress next week. But in preliminary conversations and committee meetings, it was agreed that heavy sacrifices in all allotments of federal funds must be made if an appreciable curtailment of the deficit is to be accomplished. Both parties are pledged to rigid economy, but where the axe is to fall will probably not be known until after the budget message makes its annual journey to the Capitol about next Wednesday. 1932-01-23.text: London, Jan. 22 (#)--Prime Minister MacDonald saved his cabinet from breaking up today with a political stroke as swift and unexpected as that with which he formed the present national government. Divided against itself as to whether the country will have a general tariff, the ministry not only remains in existence, but will face parliament when it opens on February 2 with the breach still unhealed. For two days the ministers argued the tariff program, but when they adjourned today it was announced officially they had been unable to reach a unanimous agreement.
