DETROIT, Jan. 23.—Bantam Fords similar in size to the Austin have been shipped to England secretly according to a story appearing today in the Michigan Manufacturer and Financial Record. The article stated that twelve of the tiny cars were produced secretly at the Ford laboratories here and shipped a few days ago. The machines, the paper said, are less than ten feet in length from bumper to bumper, have a fender width of 55 inches and a height of 53 inches. The engine has a small bore and is exactly eleven inches long, the magazine added. “A new car of the type shipped from Detroit last week,” stated the Record, “would put Ford in direct competition with the cars of minimized bore, stroke and wheelbase, produced in Europe. In absence of any official statement by the company, it is presumed that the machines will be made in volume at the Ford Dagenham, England, plant and at other European

| Paris, Jan. 23,—(4)—Premier Laval, functioning for the first time as foreign minister, said today he expected to confer with Prime Minister MacDonald of Great Britain on reparations within a week. | He had asked Mr. MacDonald to come to Paris, he said, but is willing to accept some other meeting place if the British prime minister is too occupied. He implied a definite date and place would be decided upon today. : This afternoon he talked with Premier Venizelos of Greece, a country which is deeply concerned in whatever decision France reaches in handling the reparations problem. Greece is one of the recipients of the German payments.

Paris, Jan. 922.—(#)—After Premier Pierre Laval had rededicated France to a policy of refusing to forego German reparations unless there is a corresponding reduction in the debts France owes, the chamber of deputies voted confidence in his new ministry tonight. The government majority was thirty-eight in a vote of 303 to 265. Immediately thereafter, the premier sponsored a resolution declaring France would be: “faithful to a policy of international collaboration and the organization of peace, of which respect for contracts is the necessary base.” On that resolution he won a majority of fifty-one. After its double-barreled expression of confidence, the first test of the new Laval cabinet in which Aristide Briand was dropped after seven years in the foreign office, the chamber was adjourned until Tuesday. Shanghai, China, Jan. 22--The danger of conflict between Japanese naval forces and foreign troops of the international settlement charged the atmosphere with foreboding tonight. Rear Admiral Shiosawa, commander in chief of the Japanese fleet regularly stationed in the Whangpo river, issued a virtual ultimatum today demanding the immediate suppression of anti-Japanese organizations in the foreign settlement as well as the native cities. Simultaneously, a group of Japanese naval officers called on the editor of a Chinese language newspaper, the Republican Daily News, in the heart of the settlement, and gave him until Saturday to apologize for an article offensive to them on pain of adopting "suitable measures." Barcelona, Spain, Jan. 23.—2—The revolt of extremists in the province of Catalonia, which Friday was thought to have been put down by the vigorous action of the military forces of the republic, promised fresh trouble Saturday as Syndicalists and Communists joined here in declaring a general strike, effective Saturday morning. By way of preparation for trouble, the force of police guards was doubled. Street cars stopped running. All political meetings were suspended in Barcelona Friday, a Communist newspaper was suspended and 27 arrested. The civil governor telegraphed Premier Azaña Friday this area was quiet, but labor leaders expressed fear there might be more trouble Monday, when a general extremist strike throughout the country was slated to begin. MOSCOW, U.S.S.R., Jan. 22 (®)—Lifting of the Soviet worker’s standard of living to new heights was pledged by the state today in an extensive outline of the second five-year plan. First instructions for executing the successor to the present five-year plan, now drawing to a conclusion, were contained in reports by Premier V. M. Molotov and V. V. Kuybishev, head of the state planning commission. They were approved by the political bureau of the communist party and published in Moscow newspapers. A speedier rise in living standards than under the first five-year plan must be assured, the reports stated, and the population must be supplied with the principal articles of consumption from two to three times the present schedule. Madrid, Jan. 22 (#)—Convinced that the Catalonian movement has been crushed, the Spanish government directed its attention tonight to Andalusia, Galicia and this city where extremist propaganda apparently was spreading. Officials were assured by advices from Barcelona that the revolt in that area was in a state of collapse and civil guards and government troops were mopping up on what few insurgents were still showing fight. Nevertheless, it is the government’s opinion that strong and prompt precautions will be necessary to forestall a nationwide strike next Monday, and other quarters were fearful of extremist leaders' apparent determination not to heed the official warning.

1932-06-05.text: The hour at which Stanislaus Hausner, Poland-born American pilot, was due over the British coast on his New York-to-Warsaw flight passed yesterday without word of his whereabouts. No immediate concern was felt for his safety, however, because he had estimated the 525 gallons of fuel he carried would keep him aloft for 52 hours, or until 12:46 p.m. eastern standard time today (Sunday). He had hoped to reach the British coast in 31 hours, or by about 5 p.m. Saturday; Paris by 5 p.m., and Warsaw by 6 a.m. Sunday. The reticent amateur flier of Newark, N.J., who held only a private pilot’s license, was highly optimistic when he flew away into the northeast at 8:46 a.m. Friday. Since then only two reports of the 31-year-old adventurer have been received. At 3 p.m. Friday his monoplane was sighted over Halifax. Two hours later he was reported over Sydney, Nova Scotia. London, June 4,—(AP)—London society people got the thrill they were looking for today when Mrs. Elvira Dolores Barney was formally charged in Westminster police court with the murder of Thomas William Scott Stephen. When the judge ordered her to Holloway jail at the conclusion of the hearing, Mrs. Barney, her face dead white, crumpled up and fell out of the prisoner's dock. Mrs. Barney is the daughter of Sir John Mullens and Stephen also had an assured place in London society. Sir John sat impassively during the hearing in one of the seats reserved for witnesses. Lady Mullens showed great distress, Stephen's body was found Tuesday morning in Mrs. Barney's flat in the fashionable west end. A few hours before the flat was the scene of a cocktail party. LONDON, June 4—(UP)—Word of Stanley Hausner, daring Polish flier was sought in vain along the coast of Europe tonight. Hausner set out in his red monoplane alone to fly the 4,250 miles from New York to Warsaw at 2:48 p.m. He had been gone from New York 20 hours and should have been over the coast of Europe unless his speed was greatly reduced by contrary winds. The weather off the west coast of Ireland and England was not unfavorable. Low clouds prevailed and gentle northeasterly winds. French wireless stations, however, recorded fair conditions further south with thick fog over the Atlantic and heavy rains in the valley. Visibility was poor. Word of the flier has been received since a plane was reported over the south coast of Newfoundland last night, presumably Hausner. ST. JOHNS, Nf. The decoration, plus a speech by Paul Painleve, minister for air, reduced Miss Earhart to blushes and stammers. “Five years ago I had the great pleasure of decorating Col. Edge. Charge D'Affaires Norman Armour was host in the absence of Mr. Bage, who is on his way home. J., aviator. Thirty-seven hours after he lifted his four-year-old red monoplane from the concrete runway of Floyd Bennett Field, New York, the 31-year-old Polish-American was unreported either on land or sea. He had hoped to reach London in 31 hours. All Beacons Lighted In the British Isles and in France beacons cut welcoming ribbons of light in the darkness, but at 9 p. m. (C. S. Washington, June 4 (P)--The billion dollar revenue bill to balance the budget sped to the threshold of congressional completion today as the house adopted the compromise measure with a shout of 'ayes.' A few minutes later the senate gave unanimous consent for consideration beginning Monday noon and leaders of both parties confidently predicted the gigantic tax raising legislation would be in the hands of President Hoover by Monday night. The bi-partisan drive on Capitol Hill to put the government on a paying basis by next year continued with accelerated momentum. The senate voted down overwhelmingly attempts to modify the ten percent salary cut of government workers—the heart of the national economy measure, which is needed to help the revenue bill wipe out the treasury deficit. WASHINGTON, June 4—In a whole-hearted move to slash government expenditures and balance the budget, the Senate today voted a 10 per cent cut in all civilian federal pay including its own. Only employees receiving less than $1,000 annually escaped the one year reduction, estimated to save the taxpayers $117,000,000 and help the new revenue bill bridge the deficit. By a vote of 39 to 27, a coalition of Democrats and Republicans shoved through the recommendation of its bi-partisan economy committee after rejecting numerous alternative plans for a graduated scale of reductions bearing most heavily on the larger salaries. Still remaining to be voted upon as a substitute was the Hoover plan of furloughing government employees without pay for 30 days each year instead of cutting their salaries. Washington, June 4.—-(4)— The bonus march on Washington was denounced today by Senator Borah as new hordes of World War veterans—riding and walking—invaded the capital hourly. “Not a dollar for the veterans as long as they remain in Washington,” the Idaho senator said emphatically. “I will not vote for the soldiers’ bonus bill,” Borah said, “and even if I had been for the passage of such a bill, I would be against it now with these veterans in Washington, seeking by their bodily presence and numbers, amounting to force, to compel Congress to pass this legislation. Nor will I vote a dollar for them for any purpose while they remain in the national capital.” Senator Harrison also reiterated his opposition to a soldiers’ bonus at a time when “the federal treasury is facing a deficit.”

1932-06-26.text: Lausanne, Switzerland, June 25.— The possibility of reducing interest on Germany's private debts, a large part of which are owed in the United States, has been discussed by the German and British delegates to the reparations conferences here, it was learned today from German sources. The suggested reduction would be part of a general agreement to be reached at the conference. A general pool to support public credit by guaranteeing the debts of nations now on the verge of financial bankruptcy was suggested today for study by delegates to the conference. The French, who believe the failing countries of the Danube need credit more than they do cash, were the prime movers in this plan. Experts held that if the nations now in financial difficulties could pay their debts and maintain their credit there would be a revival of private business.

DUBLIN, June 26 (AP).—A signal honor was conferred on American Catholicism today when Archbishop Michael J. Curley was selected to celebrate the solemn pontifical high mass which will climax and conclude the Eucharistic congress tomorrow. The archbishop characterized the congress as the greatest demonstration of faith he ever had seen. Today was children’s day. Some 150,000 of them gathered in Phoenix park at noon when Archbishop Kelly of Sydney celebrated pontifical mass. During the service the vast crowd of children was disciplined and reverent. The girls were in white dresses with gay sashes and the boys were attired in their Sunday best. Cardinal Lauri, the papal legate to the congress, presided over the services. The bill was vigorously defended by Speaker Garner of the House and Senator Wagner, Democrat, New York, as the House and Senate conferees began negotiations which President Hoover hopes will result in a re-written measure. FLEMINGTON, N. J., June 25. (?)—John Hughes Curtis, confessed hoaxer of the Lindbergh case, next week will battle a charge of obstructing justice without the personal assistance of the two Norfolk, Va., men once associated with him. Lloyd Fisher, attorney for the shipbuilder, sought unsuccessfully today for a bill of particulars in the case and then let it be known Rear Admiral Guy H. Burrage of Norfolk had declined to come to Flemington as a witness for Curtis, who recently repudiated his sensational confession. Curtis’ other associate, the Rev. H. Dobson-Peacock, declined to come here for questioning but offered to meet representatives of New Jersey authorities in Norfolk. Dismissal Sought. Simultaneously, Fisher announced plans to seek dismissal of the Curtis indictment and removal from the prosecutor's staff of Harry Stout, one of the county’s oldest active lawyers, when the trial st

BANGKOK, Siam, June 26—(Sunday)—King Prajadhipok cordially accepted today the end of his absolute power and the establishment of a constitutional monarchy by leaders of the people’s party. In a telegram from Huahin, on his way back to the capital, he said he was in entire agreement with the requirements of the new form of government set up by an almost bloodless revolt of the army and navy Friday, aimed at ridding the country of what were described as “certain grafting and extravagant princes.” (The revolution was attributed by the Siamese legation at Paris to the economic crisis, which in Siam was largely caused by the inability of the peasants to sell rice and rubber. The salaries of government employees were cut six months ago, causing further dissatisfaction.) King Prajadhipok was willing, he said, to act as head of the new administration.

Waters, the Portland, Ore., war veteran who originated the bonus army movement, resigned suddenly as commander-in-chief and left behind him a surprised group of advisors and a downcast rank and file of men. | In giving his resignation to his executive committee, he referred to “considerable feeling in the ranks” that all had not had a voice in his selection, It was the second time he had quit the post. He resigned several weeks ago, claiming ill health, but was reinstated within a few hours when his successor, George Alman, also of Portland, Ore., was unseated because of what were described as radical public statements. By The Associated Press. | Chicago, Ill., June 25.—Roy Parks, ill, penniless and exiled from home, wiped out his own family with a revolver today, killed a neighbor who tried to stop him, and then committed suicide. His victims were: His wife, Ida, 43, from whom he was estranged. His son, Robert Parks, 17, just out of high school. Mrs. Barbara Endre, 27, mother of two small children. The man, said by police to have been an ex-convict, left home four months ago after quarreling with his wife. Two months ago she got a court order restraining him from entering the house. Later he took their automobile and started for Minneapolis but returned it voluntarily even as his wife sought police aid to recover it.

1932-02-28.text: TRUCE RUMORED London, Feb. 27.—A Reuters News Agency dispatch from Geneva this evening said strong rumors were current there that an immediate truce was in prospect at Shanghai.

Miami, Fla., Feb. 27 (4).—A one-armed grocer who turned bandit leader was killed and T. Philip Perkins, former British amateur golf champion, and five others were wounded early today in an attempt by a robber band to hold up the gambling casino of the fashionable Embassy night club. Perkins, a guest of the club, was wounded in the thigh by one of the bandits, who used the husky, six-foot Englishman as a shield in a gun battle with two policemen and casino watchmen. The gunfire frustrated the hold-up and no money was taken. The policemen were eating in the kitchen as the robbers entered. They were lined up with the patrons, but they caught the bandits off their guard and opened fire. Perkins was to have played in a final match of the Dixie amateur golf tournament here today, but officials gave the title to Tommy Goodwin, Monroe, N. Miami, Fla., Feb. 27.—(INS)—A Chicago gunman, leader of a stickup mob preying on the wealthy winter society set, was slain and five persons, including T. Phillip Perkins, former British amateur golf champion, were wounded in an unsuccessful holdup of the exclusive Embassy club here early today. Riddled with bullets, A. Y. "Wingie" Yarbrough, wooden-armed Chicago gunman, was killed as he coolly directed the holdup of the ultra-fashionable night club and gambling resort. The wounded: T. Phillip Perkins, former British amateur champion, wounded in the thigh. George Meyers, 40, Tulsa, Okla., one of the bandits, shot in the mouth, and dying. Gene Eckman, 30, Miami, bandit, shot in the chest, and dying. Frank Wood, Embassy club kitchen boy, shot in the shoulder. An unidentified bandit, believed critically wounded, who escaped. Fifteen airplanes from the emergency flying field behind the lines scattered explosives over the Chinese positions, setting new fires flaming over Miaochungchen, source of the beleaguered garrison’s supplies. Aided by air and artillery bombardment, the Japanese made numberless assaults on Kiawan and have issued numerous claims of victory, but neither shells nor communiques dislodged the defenders. Japs Claim Disproved The Japanese announced that during yesterday’s fighting they finally had succeeded in surrounding the village. Their infantrymen already were in the western end, they said, and were proceeding to mop up the rest of it. By The Associated Press. | SHANGHAI, Feb. 28.—(Sunday)—Mamoru Shigemitsu, Japanese minister to China, said today there was no prospect of an immediate truce nor material change in the situation at Shanghai.

TOKIO, Feb. 27 (*)—Japan is ready to use her air force and her navy in interior China to prevent the Chinese from reinforcing their line at Shanghai, it was learned Saturday on high authority. The navy will be ordered to stop troop movements down the Yangtze river and air raids will be employed to discourage the Chinese from bringing up reinforcements by land. The policy already has been put into effect on a small scale. The recent raids by naval planes on the Chinese air bases at Soochow and Hangchow were cited as examples of the method in which the air forces will be used. There is no likelihood that Japan will court another international crisis with Russia, government spokesmen said in commenting on the questions addressed by Russia to Japan in regard to Japanese military operations in northern Manchuria. War office and foreign office spokesmen said that Russia's "nervousness" over Ja

Shanghai, Feb. 27.--(4#)—Every one of the 1,200 officers and men of the 31st U. S. Infantry was ordered vaccinated today. Numerous cases of smallpox in Shanghai caused army physicians to take this measure as a safeguard against the danger of a possible epidemic.

1932-04-16.text: BOSTON, April 16.—(#)—Customs and immigration officers searched in vain among the passengers of the British steamer Fernfield which arrived here today from Halifax, N.S. for Harry Fleischer, alleged member of the Detroit Purple gang, who was wanted for questioning in the Lindbergh kidnapping case. Although a search was made at Halifax for Fleischer by authorities there, the government officials here decided to search the vessel again and scrutinized the disembarking passengers.

STOGUMBER, Somerset, England, April 1—(AP)--A moratorium is feared because the parish council here got reckless and spent 15 shillings. Apart from the clerk’s salary, which is about $20 a year, the council usually spends two shillings and six pence. But because of the extravagance this year the budget won't balance, and the clerk may not get his pay.

‘The Associated Press, GLASGOW, April 16, — The arrival of the liner Duchess of Atholl today aroused some interest because of rumors that Fleischer, reputed gang member mentioned in connection with the Lindbergh kidnapping case, was aboard. Captain McQueen said, however, that the ship was searched when he received a radio message asking for details but that Fleischer was not found.

Paris, April 16—French newspapers were filled today with accounts of the disarmament talks between Premier Andre Tardieu and Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson, but comment was generally guarded. Although definite progress toward eliminating differences between the disarmament views of the two nations was reported after Secretary Stimson left for Geneva last night, Pertinax, political commentator, said in the Echo de Paris this morning that the French and American viewpoints were so far apart it would be surprising if the slightest progress were made. Le Matin said Secretary Stimson "gained precious information" during his conferences with Premier Tardieu. A member of the American delegation accompanying Secretary Stimson, and assigned to speak for him, said the conversations cleared the atmosphere and resulted in a decision to go further into the problem in Geneva. Mr. Stimson and the

GENEVA, April 16. (4)—Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson arrived from Paris this morning at 8 o’clock and went immediately to the villa a mile east of the city which he had engaged as a residence during his stay here. He planned to spend the day in a series of introductory conversations with Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary, Chancellor Bruening of Germany and Signora Motta of the Italian delegation to the disarmament conferences.

| AUCKLAND, New Zealand, April 15 (F)—There was pandemonium tonight in the streets of Auckland. The 'Sanitation unemployed,' who fought the police yesterday, stormed through the streets again, looting stores and defying the forces of order. “If this goes on,” the mayor said tonight, “I shall read the riot act.” The mayor called for civilian volunteers yesterday when the police were unable to hold their own against the rioters. A landing party was sent ashore from a British cruiser in the harbor to restore order and guard property. Tonight men and women fought with sticks and stones and their fists, holding off police, volunteers, and sailors. While fighting was going on, the Church of the Epiphany was badly damaged by fire. Police said the rioters had started the fire.

Moscow, April 16. — Soviet Russia’s alarm over the possibility of serious disturbances in Manchuria was reflected today in newspaper headlines while editorial comment accused Japanese militarists of seeking a pretext for war with the Soviets. An editorial in Pravda said “Japanese imperialists are preparing for further war activity outside Manchuria. If they need a pretext, it will not be difficult to create provocations. The imperialists' policy follows a definite purpose—to transform occupied territory into a hotbed of further adventures.” Pravda concluded that if “the peaceful spirit of the Soviet Union is interpreted by the Japanese imperialists as proof of our weakness and our inability to defend the frontier, it is so much the worse for them.”

Geneva, April 16—(A.P.)—The League of Nations committees of nineteen, appointed to consider the Sino-Japanese conflict, failed to reach any conclusion after a long discussion today. Most of the debate was concerned with fixing a time limit for the withdrawal of Japanese troops from the Shanghai area. Most of the committee were opposed and Great Britain, France and Italy indicated a preference for leaving the solution to negotiators at Shanghai.

1932-11-21.text: GENEVA, (UP) — Citing the American, British and French interpretations of the Kellogg pact to prove that Japan was not guilty of treaty violation in Manchuria, Japanese delegate Yusoke Matsuoka told the League of Nations council today that Japan cannot consider any substitute for the present government in the Manchurian state of Manchukuo. Voice Rises Matsuoka’s voice rose nearly to a shout when he read the United States senate’s ratification of the Kellogg pact recognizing that the right of self-protection may be extended beyond the borders of a country.

NANTES, France, Nov. 20—(4)— Premier Edouard Herriot and a large official party escaped possible death at Ingrandee, 13 miles from here, early today when the railroad track over which their special train was to pass was dynamited. Track guards heard two explosions and rushed to the scene in time to stop the premier’s train and avoid possible catastrophe. M. Herriot and his party were on their way to Nantes for the celebration of the 400th anniversary of the union of France and Brittany. Seven Arrested - Unruffled by the incident, the premier made his public appearance as scheduled. Seven Breton autonomists were arrested in Nantes last night, but so far they have not been connected with the criminal attempt. They were suspected of having come here to conduct a manifestation in favor of separation from France. Autonomists were charged with wrecking a monument at Rennes last August on the s

GENEVA, Nov. 21. (4).-—Defending Japan’s course in Manchuria at the bar of the League of Nations council, Yosuke Matsuoka today rejected the findings of the Lytton commission and pleaded for the patience of the western world until his country can prove its policy of peace in the far east. His address was similar in all respects to the official ‘observations’ published yesterday as Japan’s answer to the Lytton commissioner's report, but he finished with a conciliatory appeal which is not to be found in previous Japanese utterances upon the conflict with China. He cited the American punitive expedition of 1916 in Mexico as a precedent for Japan’s attack ‘in legitimate self-defense’ upon Mukden in September, 1931. "We have violated neither the covenant of the league, nor the nine-power treaty, nor the pact of Paris,” he said. “I ask of the council a little patience. If the western world wil

GENEVA, (UP)— Japan refused before the League of Nations council today to relinquish her position in Manchuria, and China retorted by threatening to extend the Chinese boycott against Japanese goods. The position of the two nations was outlined in speeches by Yusoke Matsuoka for Japan and Dr. Wellington Koo for China. Their deadlock created a grave crisis for the league, with the withdrawal of Japan from membership threatened.

PARIS, Nov. 21.--(UP)—Breton separatists and autonomists bombed the railway near Nantes over which Premier Edouard Herriot was traveling "as a demonstration of the strength of their movement" and not as an attempt against Herriot, the ministry of interior announced today. It was believed the Breton sect "Gwenn Ha Du," meaning black and white and similar to the Irish Black and Tan, would be dissolved. The sect encourages Bretons to speak the native Gallic language and scorn everything French. The bombers sent letters throughout Brittany Saturday announcing their plans to impress the chief of the French government with their strength, the ministry of interior said.

'RETURN MAY BE OBJECT; Paris, Nov. 21.—The arrival to power of Adolf Hitler in Germany, either as chancellor or minister, was declared by the newspaper Ere Novelle Monday to mean the preparation of the way for the return of the Hohenzollerns.

GENEVA, Nov. 21—The League of Nations’ attempt to settle the Manchurian conflict appeared doomed to failure today in view of Japan’s vigorous denunciation of the Lytton report, which was intended to give a true picture of the quarrel between China and Japan. As the League council assembled today to consider the report of the international committee, it found not only Japan rejecting the commission’s findings, but China threatening to resort to “the evils of militarism to drive out the invader.” In her arguments against the Lytton commission’s findings, Japan cited a resolution of the United States Senate and clauses of the Kellogg anti-war pact as (No. & continued on Page 2)

1932-02-02.text: WASHINGTON, Feb. 2. (?)—Guns bellowing at Shanghai sharpened suspension here today as officials impatiently waited to learn whether American and British moves at Tokyo would lead to peace. The United States and Great Britain submitted to the Japanese and Chinese governments detailed proposals designed to end hostilities. France and Italy were expected to do likewise. While gunfire again raked sections of wealthy Shanghai, President Hoover and his cabinet waited anxiously for word whether the peace efforts would have fruition. The far eastern authorities took them under consideration, The proposals were: No more warlike preparations. Withdrawal of combatants from points of contact. Neutral zones to protect the international settlement. Prompt negotiations for permanent peace. The text, made public here, did not mention what further steps would be taken if the proposals proved unacceptable

Washington, Feb. 1 (AP)—Japan’s refusal to heed the protestations of western powers gave rise to fears of carnage in China, and evacuation of Americans soon may begin. After anxious days through which the United States and Great Britain stood alone, France and Italy formally united with them against Japanese use of the international settlement at Shanghai as a base from which to attack the Chinese. Even while this array took form, warcraft from Tokyo opened fire on Nanking in such manner as to cause the American destroyer Simpson to shift "to safer berth"—as the Navy was advised. And hundreds of miles away from the shooting on the Yangtse, violence so threatened the coastal cities of Swatow, Amoy and Chefoo that alarm was felt for the safety of foreigners. United States destroyers will head at once wherever needed to transport citizens of this country to safety. Lieut. Commander Rutledge

WASHINGTON, Feb. 2.—A five-part proposal for restoring peace between Japan and China was submitted to the two nations today by the United States and Great Britain. This action was taken after both the Chinese and Japanese foreign offices had appealed for intercession. The Chinese asked that hostilities be ended. The Japanese asked that the United States use its good offices to induce the Chinese not to reinforce their troops in Shanghai. Italy and France are expected to join the U.S. and Great Britain with similar proposals soon. The program, submitted by the British and American Ambassadors at Tokio and Nanking, follows: 1. Cessation of all acts of violence on both sides forthwith on the following terms: 2. No further mobilization or preparation whatever for further hostilities between the two nations. 3. The announcement was made by J. H. Thomas of Great Britain, who said that the two powers also had asked that negotiations begin immediately to settle the conflict in the spirit of the Kellogg treaty against war. The council met in a sudden extra session, called by Great Britain to consider the Chinese situation. Opening of the world disarmament conference consequently was postponed until 4:30 p. m. WASHINGTON, Feb. 2—Reports from Geneva that the United States, Great Britain, France and Italy were adopting a strong front and demanding peace were received by the United States high officials with alarm. First, it was pointed out that the United States was not represented officially at Geneva. Second, it was said that the United States was using its good offices at the request of China and Japan, and not making any "demands."

GENEVA (W.P)—‘Exert all influence to avert war in the far east,’ Arthur Henderson of Great Britain, president of the world disarmament conference, told representatives of seventeen hundred million people assembled here Tuesday. His address opening the conference came as war clouds, the blackest since before the World War in 1914, gathered in the orient. “I feel bound to refer to the tragic fact that at the moment that this conference—the very purpose of which is to take steps toward the maintenance of peace—begins its work, we are confronted with a situation of such extreme gravity that now exists in the far east. “It is imperative that all signatories to the League of Nations covenant and the Kellogg-Briand pact should make it their business to insure the strict observance of these two great safeguards against acts of violence and war.” Henderson said the conference included spokesmen f

(Copyright, 1982, The Associated Press) TOKYO, Feb. 1.—Protests by the United States, Great Britain and France against the use of the Shanghai international port by Japan as a base for operations against the Chinese were followed today by a statement from the foreign office that there was no reason for any change in the Japanese policy. The ministers of war, navy and foreign affairs recommended to the cabinet that a full army division be dispatched immediately to the Shanghai area. These troops, it was said, would replace the 5,000 Japanese bluejackets now at Shanghai. Final decision about whether they would be sent rested with the cabinet. A foreign office spokesman, commenting on the American, British, and French protests, said “Japan is determined to show China that she will stand for no nonsense.” The Tokyo government, he explained, does not consider its cause justified.

1932-02-25.text: DAYTONA BEACH, Fla., Feb. 24. Sir Malcolm Campbell of England today wrote another thrilling chapter to his years of racing history by hanging up a new world’s automobile speed record of 253.968 miles an hour over a mile route. The 47-year-old driver who has been blazing new speed marks down the “roaring road” for a quarter of a century drove his 12 cylinder Blue Bird car twice over the ocean course to surpass by 8.235 miles an hour his former record of 245.733, established in the same car here last year. On his first run made southward over the beach Sir Malcolm attained the speed of 267.45 miles an hour. Upon reaching the south end of his course he immediately turned his bullet nosed machine around and shot back northward over the beach at a speed of 241.773. He covered the mile on his first run in 13.46 seconds and flashed across that distance on his second trial in 14.89 seconds for a

London, Feb. 25.—(44)—The steamship Aggersund was reported badly damaged in the north Atlantic, with all lifeboats gone, in a radio message from the station at Valencia, an island off the west coast of Ireland. The message, received at Valencia from the steamer Montcalm, said the Aggersund was listing at an angle of 45 degrees. Its position was given at 62 degrees, 20 minutes north latitude, 21 degrees west longitude, which is about 500 miles west of the Irish coast.

United Press Correspondence, Daytona Beach, Fla. Feb. 25.—(UP)—Dissatisfied with his three world automobile speed records set yesterday, Captain Sir Malcolm Campbell, hawk-faced British racing driver, was determined to bullet over the beach today in his supercar Bluebird for six new world records. Flashing over the white coral sands yesterday like a blurred, blue streak, Sir Malcolm and his car established the following amazing record average speeds for three distances: (1) One mile—253.968 miles an hour, bettering his own record by 8.235 miles an hour, (2) One kilometer—251.340 miles an hour, bettering his own record by 5.254 miles an hour. (3) Five kilometers—241.569 miles an hour, bettering his own record by 22.524 miles an hour. Only a broken timing device prevented him hanging up a new mark for five miles. One of the traps broke. Timers were unable to clock him for that distance. Al

LINCOLN, Neb., Feb. 24—(7)—Two University of Nebraska instructors who were arrested recently in a liquor raid at the university coliseum have been suspended until Sept. 1, 1932; Chancellor E.A. Burnet announced today. They were Dr. L. C. Wimberly, professor of English, and N. E. Eliason, instructor in the English department. At a special meeting yesterday the board of regents of the university heard testimony of officers who participated in the raid and from the instructors. Dr. Wimberly will continue as editor of the Prairie Schooner, a literary publication in which the university is interested. Eliason’s plans were indefinite. Neither commented on the action of the board except to again deny they had any connection with the liquor seized in the raid which resulted in the filing of a federal complaint against Alan Williams, a former university student. (International News Service) LONDON, Feb. 25.—Russia today warned both China and Japan that unless they ceased encroaching upon Soviet rights in northern Manchuria, she would be forced to suspend traffic on the Chinese eastern railway there, Exchange Telegraph dispatches from Riga said. Russians Planning. SHANGHAI, Feb. 25.—The possibility of a Russian attack upon Japan in northern Manchuria, to be launched when Japan becomes a little more embroiled in the Shanghai warfare, was a topic of wide discussion in foreign circles here today. Linking the pleas this week of the Soviet minister of war for a strengthened Red Army to protect Soviet interests in the Far East with the reports of renewed attacks against the Japanese forces in the Harbin area, foreign diplomats conjectured that Russia may attack Japan in Manchuria. WASHINGTON, Feb. 25.—(UP)—Admiral William V. Pratt, chief of naval operations, commenting on press reports of Japan’s naval construction program, said today that it is ‘undoubtedly true’ that Japan is building her navy to the full strength permitted under the London naval agreement. He added that ‘there is no evidence that Japan is attempting to go beyond that limit.’

LONDON, Feb. 23, (Pi)—Police broke up two demonstrations of unemployed in England Tuesday, heading off marchers on the houses of parliament in London and on the city hall at Bristol, where the ‘paraders put up a wild fight. A small group of mounted police, riding at full tilt down each side of Whitehall, scattered the London crowds. The unemployed were on the way to send in a deputation to the minister of labor. Several leaders of the unemployed later were allowed to enter the house of commons, where they had an interview with George Lansbury, leader of the labor party. The marchers at Bristol, announcing they intended to present a list of grievances to the city officials, started to the city hall with clubs and heavy instruments. They ran into a police line and the fight began. Thirty of the crowd and several policemen were injured. The crowds reassembled late Tuesday night and dashed t

LONDON, Feb. 25 (AP).—The Landsend wireless station received a radio message today from the tug, Humber, saying it had left the Azores islands to go to the assistance of the Danish steamer, Aggersund, which reported itself in distress in the Atlantic 500 miles off the Irish coast. Distress messages from the steamer last night said all her lifeboats were gone and she was badly damaged, listing at an angle of 45 degrees. The Aggersund, a freighter, sailed from Grangemouth, Scotland, February 10 for Boston.

Washington, Nov. 14. — The fate of Europe’s plea for war debt revision depended in large measure today on President-elect Roosevelt's answer to President Hoover’s precedent shattering invitation to a White House conference. Great Britain and France put the debt reduction issue squarely up to this country in notes made public by the state department. They asked fundamental revision of their $5,000,000,000 obligation. Pending negotiations to this end, they requested delay on December 15 payments of nearly $124,000,000. Mr. Hoover, speeding east from California, asked Mr. Roosevelt and his advisers to meet with him at the White House late this week. The President wants “his successor’s ideas on war debts and other economic issues because these questions are certain to carry over into the Roosevelt administration. Any debt settlement will rest finally with the Democratic congress. Confined

LYMPNE, Eng. Nov. 14.—(AP)— Amy Johnson, England’s premier woman flier and in private life Mrs. J. A. Mollison, took off today for a long flight to South Africa in an attempt to beat her husband's record of 4 days, 17 hours and 19 minutes for the same trip.

Washington, Nov. 13. — (#) — America’s two biggest war debtors—Great Britain and France—have asked the United States to relieve them of their payments due next month and enter into a discussion of the whole debts question. No sooner was this disclosed today at the state department than President Hoover, speeding back from the west, wired President-elect Roosevelt to confer with him at the White House on this and other governmental matters. Confirmed reports that the French and British governments were seeking to reopen the question for discussion with a view to revision and in the meantime requesting an extension of the Hoover moratorium of June 1931, to cover the Dec. 15 payments. Up to Congress Such questions can be passed upon finally only by congress. The French and British move is regarded as only a part of a concerted effort by America’s war debtors to obtain a complete overhauling

WASHINGTON, Nov. 13—(AP)—The French and British governments have requested an extension of the Hoover moratorium on intergovernmental debts pending a re-examination of the subject. The request was transmitted in notes made public at the State Department today. The British note said: “The hopes which were early realized, and the economic troubles which it (the moratorium) was designated to alleviate have not come to an end.” It expressed as its “immediate objective” the suspension of the next installment of the British war debt, due December 15. The British government expressed the belief that “the regime of intergovernmental financial obligations as now existing must be reviewed.” “Today many thoughtful men throughout the world,” said the note, “are convinced that if the depression is to be overcome, further remedial measures must be sought.” The French note proposed that the American an

LONDON, Nov. 14.–(AP)— The British government proceeded on the assumption today that an announcement postponing further war debt payments pending a final settlement, would speed up world trade and help regain confidence. The British proposal for suspension of payments due December 15 and amounting to $95,550,000 as made public in Washington was officially described here as a business-like move in the interest of the whole world. The officials believed, they said, that announcement will have the salutary effect of stabilizing world confidence and promoting recovery of world trade. While admitting Great Britain will keep in close touch with other nations owing money to the United States, British sources were emphatic in professing that no united front has been formed by European debtors to press the issue. London, Nov. 14—(U.P)—The stock exchange opened quietly steady today apparently uninfluenced by the French and British war debts notes to Washington. British gilt edged securities were idle. International industrials were slightly irregular. The pound sterling opened at $3.31 1-2, only three-quarters of one cent above Saturday's close, apparently merely a continuance of a recent gradual improvement uninfluenced by war debts developments.

The Georgetown woman was mentioned by three attorneys attempting to collect a fee of $15,000 for negotiating a $140,000 settlement for Mrs. Shouse and obtaining her divorce here, October 29. F. Dumont Smith, one of the attorneys, testified Shouse agreed to pay Mrs. Shouse $985,000 in cash and $50,000 in 10 yearly installments, only after an alienation of affections suit against the Georgetown woman had been prepared for filing. Two boatloads of men came ashore first, fighting as soon as they stepped on Chinese soil. It was not known whether these were soldiers or bluejackets, but there were several hundred men supported by several Japanese armored cars. The first force landed west of Woosung, on the north bank of the Whangpoo River, and at once endeavored to push through the city of Woosung. The men arrived at the Woosung Railway wharves in two Chinese river steamers. It was believed they had commandeered the boats. SHANGHAI, (Sunday), Feb. 7.—The Chinese strongholds in the shambles of Chapei defended by fresh troops from China’s mighty reservoir of man-power, were battered early this morning by the heaviest Japanese bombardment they have undergone during the nine days of the Shanghai battle. It was impossible to penetrate the zone of action, but the heavy rumble from the region of the Japanese headquarters on the northern edge of the international settlement indicated six-inch guns had been set up there to blast the Chinese from their positions about the north station in Chapei, only half a mile away. Shelling Continues. There were two significant features about this heavy cannonading. Hitherto the Japanese guns have been quieted along about midnight, but today they roared on through, laying down more explosives than they did during the bombardment Saturday afternoon and evening. PARINAS Shanghai, Feb. 7.——(Sunday)— (P)— Three days of bombing and shelling have caused terrible havoc in the Woosung forts, but the red, blue and white flag of China still waves over their torn walls. This I discovered today when I penetrated to the forts in an effort to settle rumors that the strategic position at the mouth of the Whang-poo river had fallen into the hands of the Japanese. Not only do the Chinese remain, but the elaborate defense works they are constructing indicate they have no intention of evacuating. Guns Silenced Although at least four of the forts’ six-inch guns have been silenced and many of the remainder are so antiquated that they are useless, the Chinese garrison is prepared with rifles and machine guns against Japanese warships to land troops. SHANGHAI, Sunday, Feb. 7.—(U.P.)—The roar of artillery shattered the air in Shanghai again today as the Japanese launched a new attack. From 11:30 last night to 1 a.m. today a furious attack was made on the Chinese lines. It began with rifles and machine guns and soon heavy artillery joined in. The Japanese apparently suspected the Chinese might attack before the Japanese reinforcements arrived today and The fighting centered at the North Station, directly bordering the International Settlement where a battle has raged intermittently for days. The reverberations awakened the sleeping foreigners, who had settled down to enjoy a peaceful night after earlier indications had been that the celebration of the Chinese New Year would cause a real lull in hostilities. Donaldson, Third, son of a socially prominent family. The tall, thin young defendant shook like a leaf as he stood up to hear the jury’s verdict. Boy Near Collapse When he heard the words “not guilty” he almost collapsed, but he quickly recovered. Several persons started to cheer the verdict and a dozen bailiffs yelled ‘order’ quelling the incipient disturbance. “Who started that?” asked Judge Harold G. 1932-11-29.text: LONDON, Nov. 29.—Default on the December debt payment to the United States appeared out of the question today as cabinet members completed their arguments for postponement which are to be presented to Washington. It was reported that Britain might suggest payment of $66,550,000 interest and postponement of the $30,000,000 payment on principal. Financial quarters insisted, however, that Britain had the money to pay, and political sources said default must be avoided to protect British credit and empire trade. The pound sterling, after opening at $3.19%, dropped rapidly below the all-time low of $2.17 to $3.15%. Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald was said to consider default "intolerable." Most members of parliament were said to hold a similar view. There was no definite indication of what the government intended to do, however, if the United States rejected the neat postponement plea. SMUIGOM, NOV. 6—(AP)— The pound sterling reached a new all-time low record of 3.14 5-8 today under the influence of continuing uncertainty affecting the war debts, but rallied slightly and closed at $3.1514. The Prime Minister, Ramsay MacDonald, today was devoting his entire time to the preparation of a new note urging for the second time extension of time for the December payment. All morning he was consulting with cabinet members and other visitors, and it was possible a formal draft of the communication would be ready for a Cabinet session tonight. It was more likely, however, that the note would be taken up at the regular weekly meeting tomorrow. It was pointed out in official quarters, however, that a formal cabinet meeting will be unnecessary since no high question of policy is involved in this note alone. Washington, Nov. 29 —(AP)— With the administration expecting the next European move for war relief within a matter of hours, importance was attached today to the latest conversations on the subject held by Sir Ronald Lindsay, British Ambassador, and Secretary Mills. Whether the Ambassador sought additional information on the American position or discussed specifically the $95,000,000 payment Great Britain must make December 15 or default, was not revealed. Under the debt funding agreement, the $30,000,000 principal of that installment may be waived upon proper application, but the $65,500,000 in interest is not postponable. Sir Ronald called at the Treasury yesterday a short while after Mills and Secretary Stimson had conferred with President Hoover on the debts question. Emerging from the White House, Mills said in response to questions as to what foreign nations would do on December 15

LONDON, Nov. 20. (UP)—The British cabinet completed late today its note to the United States, explaining the need for postponement of the $95,000,000 debt installment due Washington Dec. 15. But not in any way threatening to default. Premier J. Ramsay MacDonald visited Buckingham Palace and was conducted at once to the king’s private apartments, where he acquainted the sovereign with the contents of the note. A special cabinet meeting was called in the House of Commons for 9 p.m.

LONDON, Nov. 28.—(?)—While the king of England talked with Chancellor of the Exchequer Neville Chamberlain in a special audience tonight, Prime Minister MacDonald continued conferences with cabinet members which were expected to conclude tomorrow with completion of a new note to the United States requesting an extension of war debt payments.

LONDON, Nov. 20.—(UP)— A special cabinet meeting was summoned for 9 a.m. today in the House of Commons to discuss the debt question. Britain's note to America probably will be submitted to the cabinet meeting. The king was scheduled to grant an audience to Premier J. Ramsay MacDonald at Buckingham Palace this evening.

Washington, Nov. 29. (INS)—Further moves on the war-debt chessboard awaited today the receipt of a new British note which London dispatches indicated would be sent to Washington tomorrow. Until that is received and studied nothing will be initiated here to grant the relief insisted upon by the debtor nations in their notes of last week. The American reply to those communications was that they presented nothing to warrant the United States postponing the December 15 payments, amounting in all to some $125,000,000. It is expected the new British note will present a gloomy picture of Britain’s present financial situation, coupled with a strong argument that world-wide economic recovery will be hastened by readjustment of the whole of the war debts. London, Nov. 29.—Chances for payment by Britain of the December war debt installment to the United States brightened today. Government officials declared it appeared Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald, with the aid of Stanley Baldwin, had finally triumphed over the treasury contention that payment of the installment would be more disastrous to the nation than default. The new British note to the United States, further expanding previous pleas for suspension of the payment, still remained incomplete and lacking approval of the full cabinet, however. Cabinet approval of the note appeared imminent following reports MacDonald’s view had met with considerable support within the cabinet during the past two days. (#)—Germany’s forty-four million voters must choose between Paul Von Hindenburg who is dedicated to the preservation of the young republic, and Adolf Hitler, apostle of its destruction. The presidential election tomorrow, the twelfth anniversary of the Kapp rebellion in which the very forces now opposing the venerable field marshal tried to usurp power. The voting takes place exactly two years after President Von Hindenburg signed the Young Plan. His signature to that document, which continued the payment of war reparations, is one of the items in his record on which Hitler’s fascists have centered their attacks during the bitter election campaign. Although five candidates are running, the real issue lies between Von Hindenburg and Hitler. HANGHAI, March 12.—(AP)—The Japanese consulate announced Saturday that a 15-day jail sentence had been imposed on a Japanese civilian responsible for the beating administered a week ago to Miss Rose Marlowe, an American missionary teacher. In a letter to the United States consulate, the Japanese authorities expressed regret about the incident and asserted they had warned their nationals against any repetition. Reports from the front indicated everything was quiet but the Japanese were moving in large reinforcement units with great quantities of war material. The defense line from Nanjing northward to the Yangtze was strengthened by detachments from the 3,000 reinforcements landed early Saturday morning at Woosung. PARIS, March 12 (4)—Ivar Kreuger, 52-year-old Swedish "match king," international banker and one of the world’s richest industrialists, was found dead in an apartment here today, with a bullet through his heart. Police said he had killed himself. It was understood he left a note saying he was tired out. (Officials of the Swedish match trust, which he headed, at Stockholm, attributed the suicide "to the superhuman burden of work he had borne in the past few months and which resulted recently in a nervous breakdown while he was in New York.") The body of the man who loaned millions to European governments and in return received the match monopolies which his company holds, was found early this afternoon in a furnished flat at 5 Avenue Victor Emmanuel by M. Littorin, a friend and associate. Mr. Kreuger returned from the United States yesterday, and those who saw him said he appeared to be w

PARIS, March 12. (U.P) — Ivaar Kreuger, head of the great Swedish match trust, committed suicide today by shooting himself through the heart in his Paris apartment. The mysterious, reserved financier, little known to the public, although the power of his vast wealth reached into every corner of the globe and swayed the destinies of governments, was found by his valet, in bed, a revolver in his hand. He left a note in which he said that because of his “family and business it would be better for me to disappear.”

STOCKHOLM, Sweden, Mar. 12. (UP)—The premier and cabinet in an emergency meeting tonight decided to call a special session of parliament at midnight Sunday because of the suicide in Paris of Ivar Krueger. Parliament will be asked to vote on a government loan and a moratorium to private companies to save the Kreuger and Toll interests. The death of Kreuger was regarded as a national catastrophe. Major Ferrander, a director of the Swedish Match Company, collapsed and died when informed that Kreuger had taken his own life. It was revealed that the National Bank of Sweden recently loaned 100,000,000 kroner to the Swedish Match Company. Headquarters of the Swedish Match Company said Kreuger had broken down from overwork. Paris, March 13—The world and his Homeland gave final honors today to Aristide Briand. Half a million persons lined the streets of Paris as his body was borne from the foreign office, over which he presided so many years, to Passy Cemetery. Because Briand was the “Apostle of Peace” he was accorded a peace-lover's funeral. Instead of the usual gun carriage, an ordinary horse-drawn coach bore him to his grave, and the part played by the military arm of the nation was cut to the minimum. In a funeral oration at the foreign office, Premier Andre Tardieu called Briand the “prince of orators.” At his funeral, he received the last applause of his people. Last Applause. The half million, massed the length of the majestic Champs Elysees, stood bareheaded and watched the hearse go slowly by. Stockholm, Sweden, March 12.—(#)—The government, following the death of Ivar Kreuger, match magnate, at Paris today, introduced a bill in parliament tonight for a moratorium on Swedish debts abroad. The government would be authorized to suspend payment of Sweden's foreign debts for one month under the bill, which will be considered in an extra session of parliament tomorrow. Severe Blow Enforcement of the measure, intended to protect the vast Kreuger industrial and financial interests in event of a panic, would be left to the discretion of the government. The national bank director said that so far as could now be seen the debts of Mr. Kreuger could have no serious consequences for Swedish banks. Berlin —UP—Germany, with her towns and cities under heavy guard against fighting, was ready Saturday night for the momentous presidential election, in which Adolph Hitler, picturesque fascist leader, will try to wrest power from the aged but indomitable President Paul von Hindenburg. Forecasts of Sunday's polling were that it would be a close race, with the idolized von Hindenburg stemming the fascist tide by a narrow margin, although not by enough to re-elect him. Unless Hindenburg or Hitler obtain a majority over all other candidates combined, a second poll will be necessary. Betting among stock brokers on the Bourse favored Hindenburg for a good lead over Hitler. A United Press tabulation of forecasts from politicians of all parties resulted in an average prediction that 34,500,000 votes would be cast, so that any candidate to be successful on the first ballot would have to poll 17,25

Meanwhile at Plymouth the cruiser Vindictive shipped ammunition and departed with relief crews for service in China. Members of the cabinet's “Shanghai committee,” which was appointed to take care of any exigency over the week-end, were prepared to meet at a moment's notice if necessary. The oath of allegiance to King George is obligated by Article 17 of the Constitution. We propose to remove that article. We have a constitutional right to do so. Regarding separation from Great Britain: Our objective is independence, but in this election we asked for a limited mandate and we intend to proceed within the terms of that mandate. The oath of allegiance is not obligated by treaty. The insistence on this oath prevents a considerable portion of the people from being represented in Parliament. STOCKHOLM, Sweden, Feb 21 (AP)—Prince Lenhart, a grandson of King Gustaf, started for London tonight with his boyhood sweetheart, Karin Nisswandt, to be married in spite of royal disapproval. The romance has touched the hearts of the Swedish people and a great crowd assembled at the station to wish the pair good luck, almost smothering the bride-to-be in flowers. After the marriage in a registry office, the couple plan a honeymoon tour of Europe under the names of Mr. and Mrs. Bernadotte. They will live in a castle on an island in Lake Constance, Switzerland. The prince will lose his royal prerogatives and his tenuous rights to the throne inasmuch as King Gustaf has refused his consent to the marriage unless his grandson agreed to a long delay. Miss Nisswandt is not of royal blood.

SHANGHAI, Feb. 22.—-(UP) —Chinese artillery began a heavy bombardment of the Japanese positions in Hongkew, just outside the International Settlement tonight. At 8:45 p. m. the Chinese were pumping the heaviest shells yet fired into the area. The reverberations were terrific and foreigners in the settlement were more alarmed than at any time in the last two weeks. Dozens of foreigners telephoned the United Press offices, asking whether the battle was inside the settlement. Simultaneously with the artillery attack, Chinese infantry attacked the Japanese positions on the Kiangwan road, which runs alongside Hongkew park and the rifle range just to the north of the settlement. The Japanese were using machine guns and rifles to maintain their positions. (Copyright, 1931 by United Press) SHANGHAI, Feb. 22 (U.P.)— American and other warships in the Whangpoo River were in the line of fire early today as the Chinese opened a heavy artillery attack on the Japanese lines. The cruiser Houston, Admiral Montgomery M. Taylor's flagship, and several nearby American destroyers were within range, although so far the shells were falling short.

(By The Associated Press) Moscow, Feb. 22—The Soviet government has formally decreed the banishment “for all time” of Leon Trotsky and 36 other Russian émigrés now living abroad. The action was taken by the presidium of the central executive committee of the Soviet Union yesterday. In Trotsky’s case, it was a mere formality for he was banished from Russia three years ago after an open split with Joseph Stalin. He went to Istanbul, Turkey, where he has since lived. TOKYO, Feb. 22—(Monday)—() The Seiyukai party of Premier Suyoshi Inukai was leading in returns today from Japan's general election by such a margin that its leaders claimed the government had remained in power by an unprecedented victory. The party of Japan's 'grey fox,' the 76-year-old Inukai, took over the power last December with a minority in the House of Representatives, which made the election test of its control inevitable. The returns up to midnight gave it a lead of 36 seats over the Minseito, the principal opposition. With 160 out of the diet’s 466 seats reported, the standing was: Seiyukai 96; Minseito 60; others four.

Changhun, Manchuria, Feb. 28, (AP)—A bitter battle raged today between Chinese and Japanese forces at Tunhua, strategically the most important town in the province of Kirin, which is now a part of the new federated state of Manchuria, called “the land of peace.” The battle began early today and soon became so serious that the Japanese, protectors of the new State, sent heavy reinforcements from nearby Kirin city. A force of 508 Chinese troops under General Wang Teh-Lin, foe of the regime of Hsi Hsla, Kirin governor, who was one of the founders of the new state, attacked a small Japanese detachment which has been garrisoned at Tunhua since February 17 when Wang Teh-Lin's rebellion began to look dangerous. 1932-12-12.text: Washington, Dec. 12—The British-American debt debate reached a crisis today after a swift dramatic exchange of notes. London offered to pay $95,550,000 next Thursday—conditionally. Secretary of State Stimson promptly rejected the conditions. Great Britain seemed to face a choice between unconditional payment and default after Stimson had refused to take the payment as an advance installment under a future debt agreement. He insisted the money must apply on Britain's $4,600,000,000 debt as funded in 1923. Congressional reaction supported him. Never in recent diplomatic history have two powers exchanged views on a major problem so quickly as did America and Britain. Stimson had just finished his Sunday dinner and prepared for a quiet afternoon when Sir Ronald Lindsay, British ambassador, called at Woodley, Stimson’s estate, with the British note. Stimson hurried at once to the State Depart

(By The Associated Press) A quick passage of notes across the Atlantic yesterday gave notice that Great Britain intended paying its $25,960,000 war debts installment due Thursday and that the United States would not accept the gold with reservations proposed by London. Again suggesting revision of the total debt, the British note proposed that the payment be treated as “a capital payment of which account should be taken in final settlement.” Within six hours the American reply was in the hands of the British ambassador. Written by Secretary Stimson, it said: Has No Authority. “I must call your attention to the fact that the Secretary of the Treasury has no authority to accept payment from your government, except as provided under the terms of the funding agreement. ... The sum... must be credited to principal and interest as provided therein.” In Paris, meanwhile, the French cabinet deci

LONDON, Dec. 11--(AP)—Great Britain notified the United States government today that it will pay in gold the $95,550,000 due next Thursday but that the money is not to be regarded as the resumption of payments on the scale used before President Hoover’s moratorium. Instead, the new note, dispatched to Washington this evening, says the remittance is to be treated as “a capital payment of which account should be taken in any final settlement.” The decision to pay in gold was taken, it was stated, since “under the circumstances this would be the least prejudicial of methods now open.” In its first paragraph the document expresses the pleasure of the British government that “the United States government welcomes the suggestion for close examination” of the war debts problem. Further, the note urges “the importance of an early exchange of views with the object of concluding the proposed discu

LONDON, Dec. 12—The British government prepared for an urgent cabinet meeting today to decide between further negotiations on payment of its $95,550,500 war debt installment and outright default. The government was jolted into such action by the suddenness with which the United States government in a record-breaking exchange of diplomatic notes rejected proposed payment 'with reservations.' Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald.

By The Associated Press Washington, Dec. 12.—The customs bureau today ordered collectors of customs to suspend decision on coal imports from Germany and Great Britain pending a decision by the attorney general as to whether the product was taxable under the 1932 revenue act. The action does not rescind last month’s order permitting free entry and does not levy the duty, but leaves the question in a status where the government can later assess the duty if the attorney general holds that it is required. A tax of two dollars a ton was placed on coal in the billion dollar revenue bill passed by the last congress. Last month the customs bureau ordered this suspended after Great Britain and Germany complained that it violated favored nations clauses of their treaties with the United States. Protests from Senator Reed, Pennsylvania and other congressmen from coal producing states caused the mat

PARIS, Dec. 12—(P)— Premier Herriot announced today after a cabinet meeting that France will wait and see what England does before stipulating her own reservations in the payment of $20,000,000 due the United States on Thursday. He said that inasmuch as France and England have been working together closely on this whole matter, France will await the British decision before making her own.

History was written today in the capitals of Great Britain, France and the United States. The governments at London and Paris debated the momentous question of paying their war debt installment to the United States. The decision was expected to have a tremendous bearing on the future of the world. Literally billions of dollars in tangible gold was at stake, but perhaps even more important was the question of principle—the sanctity of international obligations and the relations, social, economic and trade between the United States and Europe. The French parliament was in a hostile mood, many of its members anxious to default but more cautious ones fearing the consequences. British parliamentarians were stunned by the swift and incisive refusal of Secretary Stimson to accept the payment with the proviso that it is the last until a new deal. But the British were expected to accept the Unite

LONDON, Dec. 12.—Debate on the general question of war debts will start in the House of Commons on Wednesday, Stanley Baldwin, acting prime minister, announced in the House today. An appropriate statement explaining the government's policy will be made, probably by Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer, he said. Baldwin's announcement signified that the government had yielded to the insistent demands of George Lansbury, Labor leader, and members of other parties, that a general war debt debate be held before the December 16 payment is made. The government previously had hoped to get through without debate, having made up its mind to pay. Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald returned from Geneva at 3:52 p.m.

1932-01-10.text: Great Britain refused yesterday to follow the lead of the United States in invoking the nine-power treaty in the Manchurian conflict. The British foreign office announced that there appeared to be no need for sending a note to Japan similar to the one sent by Secretary of State Stimson, because the Japanese government has given assurances of its intention of continuing the open door policy in Manchuria. The Stimson note resulted in an authoritative statement in Tokyo that Japan might try to revise the nine-power pact through the conference method. The purpose of the revision would be to define the “administrative integrity” guaranteed by the treaty to China. At the urgent command of the emperor, the Japanese cabinet, which had resigned en bloc because of the bombing attempt Friday on the emperor's life, decided to remain in office.

By The Associated Press. BERLIN, Jan. 9.—Chancellor Heinrich Bruening declared today the continuation of reparations payments is impossible and any attempt to maintain them "must lead to disaster not only for Germany but for the whole world." This declaration was included in an interview with the chief editor of the semi-official Wolff News Agency. The chancellor said at the impending Lausanne conference Germany would urge the abandonment of reparations. In the interview, which apparently was prompted by the fact the gist of the chancellor’s statement to the British ambassador yesterday had leaked out, Dr. Bruening avoided anything that might look like an ultimatum. He had told Sir Horace Rumbold, British envoy, that for the present and for an indefinite time to come Germany would be unable to pay. By The Associated Press WASHINGTON, Jan. 9— Governor Theodore Roosevelt of Porto Rico was promoted today by President Hoover to America’s highest colonial office upon the resignation of Dwight F. Davis as governor general of the Philippine Islands. Accompanied by Hurley, Davis presented his resignation to the chief executive at the White House. The Secretary of War, who controls affairs of most of America's insular possessions, accompanied him to the White House for a final conference before his retirement from office. The announcement of Davis’ resignation was followed immediately by one naming the son of the late president to govern the millions of people his father fought to free from Spanish rule. Davis was sent to the Philippines from the position of Secretary of War. Personal reasons were given by Davis in resigning. He will sail immediately for Paris to visit his wife and daughter

WASHINGTON, Jan. 9.— (#) — The scant democratic majority scored its first victory over the administration forces on a major political issue today by forcing a party tariff bill through the house. It voted 214 to 182 to revamp administrative features of the Hawley-Smoot law dealing with the flexible tariff powers of President Hoover and went on record favoring an international conference to revise tariffs downward. The bill now goes to the senate, where passage is probable. However, congressional administration followers are convinced if the measure is sent to the White House it will be vetoed. Twelve republicans and one farmer-laborite, Representative Kvale of Minnesota, voted with the democrats. Not one democrat voted against the bill. Washington, Jan. 8 (4)—Through a torrent of oratory and a profusion of amendments, the two billion dollar reconstruction finance corporation moved ahead today toward a critical vote in the senate Monday. After five hours of debate, which wandered off into a heated discussion of prohibition, the senate agreed to act on the mammoth economic rehabilitation measure by the end of its next legislative day. At the other end of the capital the measure made definite progress with final approval by the house banking committee and decision to bring it up for debate on Monday. In the senate only two of the many amendments offered reached a vote. Both were rejected. One, by Senator Bratton, Democrat, of New Mexico, to permit the corporation to loan to irrigation and reclamation districts failed by the slimmest possible margin. Under senate rules an amendment is defeated unless a majority votes for it

WASHINGTON, Jan. 9. UP—A tariff bill sponsored by the Democrats and constituting their record on this controversial issue was passed by the house tonight over protest, after a two day debate. The measure, which now goes to the senate, strikes directly at Republican tariff policy by taking away from the president his power to raise or lower tariff rates 50 percent upon recommendation of the United States tariff commission. It also asks President Hoover to call an international conference to reduce present high tariff barriers over the world. The vote was 214 to 182.

1932-08-28.text: Manchester, England, Aug. 27.—()—The chimneys of Lancashire, those tall, gaunt piles of stone which for months have belched smoke symbolic of Britain's reawakened cotton manufacturing industry, will stand stark and idle in the North country's half-light Monday. Two hundred thousand workers men, women and children—left their looms at noon today and, rather than accept a 10 per cent wage cut, will not go back when the mill doors open with Monday's dawn. The walkout threatens to become the greatest industrial war Great Britain has experienced since the nationwide general strike of 1926. Orders for gingham and calico, which have been coming into Lancashire in heightened quantities since Britain's lapse from the gold standard, gave her an artificial advantage in the markets of the world, will remain unfilled for a few days and then be turned over to factories elsewhere—in America, in Japan an

| Manchester, Eng., Aug. 27.— Two hundred thousand employees of the British cotton milling industry officially went on strike as they left factories throughout Lancashire at noon today, ending the working week. It was the beginning of what may prove to be the greatest industrial war in Britain since the general strike of 1926. Despite the seriousness of the situation and the desperate economic plight of the workers’ families involved, no disturbances were reported as the walkout began.

LONDON, Aug. 27 (UP).—Europe came to the reluctant conclusion today that two young American airmen had suffered the fate of others who sought to conquer the Atlantic, and abandoned hope that Clyde Allen Lee and John Bochkon had reached the Old World in their monoplane, Green Mountain Boy. Cold facts and figures—elapsed time, the amount of fuel in the tanks, flying conditions—stood against the slimmest of hopes that the flyers might have come in some secluded spot, far from communication, in the British Isles, or on the mainland. Barring this, there was the possibility that Lee and Bochkon might have been picked up at sea by a vessel not equipped with wireless. But as the time passed and radio stations queried ships at sea for word of the airmen, this hope also dwindled. MANCHESTER, Eng. Aug. 27.--(UP)—The Lancashire cotton industry, a distressed and battered casualty in the world’s economic upheaval, entered one of its blackest periods today with the strike of 200,000 cotton workers. The strike became effective technically at noon, the end of a 13-day period of grace in which owners and operators in the great cotton mills failed to reach an agreement on wages and hours. Saturday is nominally a half holiday, and the full effect of the stoppage could not be estimated accurately until time for the workers to report Monday morning. The strike was expected to spread eventually to 500,000 mill hands for the union officials and the cotton owners have laid their plans of battle well, and neither side shows any signs of retreat. Employers decided to end the 1919 wage agreement and tried to find a substitute suitable to the unions. The owners wanted another 16 pe

OSLO, NORWAY, Aug. 27.—The pilots of the airplane Green Mountain Boy, unreported more than 60 hours on a trans-oceanic venture from New York to Oslo, were feared tonight to have been lost somewhere on the Atlantic. A slim hope was expressed that Clyde Lee and John Bochkon had come down in good order and were floating on the water or that they had landed in some isolated spot in which communications are scant. When they left Harbor Grace, Newfoundland, early Thursday morning they carried fuel enough to keep them in the air 37 hours, seven hours longer than they needed for the jump, but in the ordinary course of events this would have been exhausted early last night.

Berlin, Aug. 27.--(?)—A new German cabinet which would include Adolf Hitler’s closest associate, Dr. Gregor Strasser, as chancellor was envisaged in political circles tonight on the basis of persistent rumors that the national socialists and the centrists had at last laid the groundwork for a coalition in the Reichstag. According to the best available information, such a ministry would have former Chancellor Bruening as foreign minister, and Defense Minister Kurt von Schleicher, the strong man of the present government, in an equally important post. By The Associated Press Clermont, Ferrand, France Aug. 27—Etienne Michelin, son of Edouard Michelin, tire manufacturer, was killed today when his plane was forced down by a storm.

| By United Associated Press. Des Moines, Ia. Aug. 27—The picket lines of the farmers holiday movement slowly tightened about this capital city of Iowa today as the center of activity in the fight for higher farm prices shifted for the third time in the last two weeks. Peaceful blockades were established on six main farm to market routes and the pickets carried on a “persuasion” campaign to induce truckers carrying farm products to return home. Those who refused were warned that “this is the last time” and that they would not be permitted to pass the lines with more goods. Plans were being laid for extension of the picket lines to include all of the 29 highways leading into the city. Leaders said they expected to have camps established on every one of the roads by Monday morning. Asserting that any new limitation should mean greater sacrifices for larger navies than for smaller ones, the Japanese presented concrete reduction suggestions which would make the ratio 10-10-8.7 in total tonnage instead of the existing 5-5-3. The number of units would be on a basis of 11-11-8.
