At the same time, the "Big Five" Britain, the United States, Germany, France and Italy—announced completion of a tentative formula for security and equality which will be submitted to the governments of France, Germany and Italy as a long step toward a disarmament agreement. PARIS, Dec. 10. uPi — Although Premier Herriot has yet to announce the fact, it was asserted in official circles tonight he undoubtedly will recommend to parliament that next Thursday's payment of interest on the French war debt to the United States be made with reservations. These reservations, it was said, will follow those Great Britain is understood to be formulating. It was asserted the cabinet had arrived at this decision but the reservations it will recommend have not been fully decided upon. One of them is likely to be that this payment shall be the last one until a general and final revision is made.

Berlin, Oct. 27.—(AP)— Prof. Albert Einstein will sail for the United States on the steamer Oakland December 10, the Jewish Telegraphic Agency reported today. He will travel to California by way of the Panama Canal to resume his work at Mt. Wilson Observatory before beginning his new duties as head of the mathematics school of the Institute for Advanced Study.

PARIS, Dec. 10—(AP)—Premier Édouard Herriot and two important committees of the chamber of deputies worked separately today in an effort to find a formula under which the chamber would be willing to vote for payment of the $19,261,000 war debt interest payment due the United States next Thursday. They were not wholly successful. The foreign affairs and finance committees of the chamber worked out a resolution providing for payment—but only on the condition that the United States agree before Thursday to a debt conference which would liquidate the entire problem. Members of the delegation which presented this resolution to the Premier quoted him as saying: "I intended toward the government’s intentions," although he made reservations because negotiations still are continuing with England over a policy acceptable to both nations. STOCKHOLM, Sweden, Dec 10 — Nobel prizes were awarded tonight to one American and three Englishmen at a stately ceremony attended by the royal family of Sweden and by a distinguished audience of scholars, diplomats and government officials. The prize in chemistry went to Dr. Irving Langmuir of the General Electric Company at Schenectady, N. Y., for his discoveries in surface chemistry. The other recipients were John Galsworthy, literature; Sir Charles Sherrington, medicine, and Professor Douglas Adrian, also medicine. Sir Charles and Professor Adrian were recognized for their research into the function of the nerve cell and its processes. Mr. Galsworthy was unable to be present because of illness, and his certificate of award was received from King Gustaf by Archibald J. Kerr, the British minister. Moscow, Dec. 10, (4) — The foreign office published tonight a sharp exchange of notes between the Soviet and Japanese governments in which Moscow categorically refused to surrender the Manchurian insurgent General Su Ping-Wen and his army or to prevent their departure from the Soviet Union. General Su recently fled before Japanese forces in the Manchuli region in northwest Manchuria and crossed the Russian border. H. M. Kharakhan, assistant peoples commissar for foreign affairs said in the exchange that Russia not only was unable to comply with the Japanese request, but it could not entertain the question of extradition inasmuch as Russia has always maintained strict neutrality in Manchurian affairs.

Some 200 or more people rushed from the church building and scattered in all directions. They described the firing as sounding for a few minutes as though machine guns were in use. Men of the Johnson and Crook families were standing in the church yard during the services, according to the story told Sheriff W. H. Steele. He was told one of the Johnson boys approached Homer Crook and said “Let's have peace,” only to be told “there'll be no peace” followed by a burst of fire. London, Ky. Jan. 16. ()—A mountain feud which flared in a peaceful churchyard while worshippers were leaving services claimed four lives today. The trouble resulted, witnesses said, from the accusation of one family that a member of the other clan had wronged a 17-year-old girl. The dead are “Big Henry” Johnson, 35, and Earl Johnson, 25, brothers, and Homer Crook, 32, and Forrest Crook, 30, brothers. “Little Henry” Johnson, 21, a cousin of the dead men and said by witnesses to have taken no part in the shootings, is in a hospital here critically wounded in the abdomen. An emergency operation was performed tonight. Willie Johnson, 21, a brother, was wounded in the hand. The shooting occurred in front of a mountain mission church at New Salem, seventeen miles east of here. HELSINGFORS, Finland, Jan. 16. —(AP)—The cabinet’s prohibition repeal bill, which would set up a government-controlled source of liquor supply without private profit, was made public today. It will be presented at a special session of the diet Tuesday. The measure, drawn up in compliance with the wishes of the voters as expressed in the recent referendum, would set up an intermediate company for the importation, manufacture and sale of intoxicating beverages in which the controlling interest would be held by the government. BOARD OF SEVEN The affairs of the company would be supervised by a governing board of seven members appointed by the cabinet for three-year terms. The sale of intoxicants is to be so arranged, the bill says, so that consumption will be reduced to as low a figure as possible, and the illegal use of intoxicants will be halted, as far as possible. Giendora, Miss., Jan. 16 ()— Water from the swirling Tallahatchie, Coldwater, Yalobusha and Yazoo rivers spread out today in six Mississippi counties, marooning hundreds of persons. Levees crashed after a month of severe strain and residents took to high ground to await rescue. Reaching out into Louisiana, rains kept the Ouachita river in the Monroe section rising upward, and levee crews continued to raise the dykes to prevent inundation of West Monroe. Fear Great Disaster Shreveport, in northwest Louisiana on the upper Red river, reported the flood spreading below there. At least 20,000 acres of lowlands between Gilliam and Shreveport are under water and 200 families, most of them negroes, have fled their homes. By The Associated Press. WASHINGTON, Jan. 16.—The emergency two billion dollar reconstruction finance corporation stumbled over parliamentary obstacles in the senate today but President Hoover went ahead with plans to put it into operation next week. Hoover is selecting the board to direct this gigantic relief corporation and it seemed likely tonight that Eugene Meyer, governor of the federal reserve board and chairman of a similar post-war organization, the war finance corporation, would be at its head. Senator Blaine, Republican, Wisconsin, took advantage of the parliamentary tangle involving the legislation to block a move in the senate today to send the separate senate and house bills to conference for adjustment of differences. Nevertheless, congressional leaders informed the president of every confidence the huge reconstruction corporation would receive final congressional approval

Winter is coming back to the east after hardy thrusts at other sections of the United States. Signs of spring along the Atlantic seaboard Saturday before rapidly falling temperatures. Conditions improved elsewhere, except for flood conditions in the south and scattered snowfall in the west. The abrupt turn from high temperatures was halted at Lake Placid, N. Y., where snow and ice is needed for the winter Olympics. Army airplanes were called into service to carry food to hundreds of Indians snowbound in isolated settlements of the Navajo reservations in northern Arizona and northwest New Mexico. Homes in nine Mississippi counties flooded by the Tallahatchie River. There were minor flood troubles or threats in Tennessee, Oklahoma and Texas. By the Associated Press A brigade of Japanese infantrymen marched westward from Chinchow, Manchuria, yesterday to avenge the slaying of 20 of their countrymen last week by Chinese irregulars. The brigade had orders to clear 15,000 Chinese soldiers from the area between Chinchow and the border of Jehol province—and perhaps to press on into Jehol, Chinese sources said, although this was denied by Japanese authorities. Mukden army headquarters of the Japanese relayed reports that rewards totaling $100,000 had been offered to Chinese guerrilla bands for harassing the Tokyo army. Meanwhile observers in Harbin expected General Mash Chan-Shan, enemy of the Japanese in the Nonni-Tsitsihar campaign last November, to emerge as the leader of a new army that will cooperate with the Japanese-supported regime in the province of Hellungkiang. LONDON, May 30. (@)—Conversion of the coming Lausanne conference on war debts and reparations into a conference on world trade was sponsored today by Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald in an interview published in the London Daily Mail. If the suggestion gains support, the newspaper said, it may completely alter the complexion of the conference and cause the United States to sit in as more than an observer.

BERLIN, May 30.—(UP)—The cabinet of Chancellor Heinrich Bruening resigned today. President Paul Von Hindenburg accepted the resignation. He requested the cabinet to continue in office provisionally. Bruening had delivered virtually an ultimatum to President Paul Von Hindenburg that army leaders stay within the army and refrain from politics, else he and his cabinet would resign. Following a second conference today, he tendered the resignation of the entire cabinet. Recent political events have indicated a tendency by the military for a right wing government to replace that of Bruening with the military a dominant force in the government. General Wilhelm Groener recently resigned as minister of defense and it was reported at that time that army men headed by General Von Schleicher were attempting to force the right wing cabinet. By The Associated Press Paris, May 20.-The newspaper Le Temps in a leading article today entitled “The American Crisis,” declared it was impossible to solve such problems as disarmament, reparations, debts, and the “new economic order” without the help of the United States. The article drew a conclusion of hope that the troubles the United States is undergoing “will recall its rulers to present realities.”

Soviet Russia drew up to render salute to a royal visitor today, the second such personage to pay a state visit to the stronghold of Communism since the czar was overthrown 14 years ago. The visitor was the Emir Faisal, viceroy of Hedjaz, and son of the all-powerful Ibn Sa'ud of Arabia. Two of the highest officials of Communism were sent to greet the princely tourist at the railway station, where a royal carpet was spread for him. The welcome was the ceremonious kind reserved for personages of high rank, and apparently far outdid the reception accorded then King Amanullah of Afghanistan four years ago. Wearing a native costume, a flowing old-braided tan robe and a burnoose, but the modern shoes of the west, the prince and his party were greeted by two vice commissars of foreign affairs, L. M. In the marble amphitheater that looks upon the unknown Soldier's grave at Arlington, former Senator Jas. A. Reid of Missouri mingled with tributes to the soldier heroes a plea for reliance on the stout heart and unyielding sword of our gallant sons. He was the chief speaker at a national memorial service. 1932-12-26.text: PARIS, Dec. 25.—(4)—Forecasts that France may adopt temporarily a system of “decree laws” as a means of expediting national affairs were heard in Parisian drawing rooms during Christmas family reunions, with the suggestion that, if introduced, this system might provide a method of settling the payment of interest on debts due the United States. Apparently the government has taken no action whatsoever on the question of decree laws, although persons close to the government have been discussing it as a possibility. It was pointed out that such a move might permit Premier Joseph Paul-Boncour to pay America when he believes the spirit and the letter of the ideas on debts in the chamber of deputies have been met or are likely to be met and without specifically referring the question to parliament. MOWEAQUA, ILL., Dec. 26. — (PP) — Twenty-seven miners were found dead in the south wing of the Moweaqua coal mine today, making the death toll all 54 of the men caught in the tragedy of an underground explosion. Deadly after-damp finished the work of the searing blast that had killed those in the north wing. The death list may reach 56.

(BY We Associated Press.) Along the roads of the nation, Christmas weekend brought many deaths and injuries, inevitable by-products of a holiday that lured thousands to city boulevards and country pikes. The tabulation from Associated Press reports across the 48 states indicated a loss of more than 200 lives, incidental to heavy travel or accidents that might have occurred at any time. By far the greatest price was exacted in motor traffic accidents. Many parts of the land enjoyed bright, warm weather, some of the warmest Christmas days they had known. In other regions, icy roads tricked motorists with tragic results. At least 100 persons died in automobile mishaps during the double holiday. Moweaqua, Ill., was smitten with the greatest single sorrow as it hunted through tangled debris deep underground for the bodies of its dead. Washington, D. C.—(AP)—Legislation to regulate and insure 'time deposits' in banks was advanced today by Senator Vandenberg, Michigan Republican, as a means of preventing hoarding, creating confidence and relaxing credit. Saying he is 'irrevocably opposed to a general federal guaranty of bank deposits,' Vandenberg proposed to create a gigantic fund for the protection of time deposits and to distinguish these from demand deposits. The Michigan senator would define time deposits as those turned over to a bank for at least ninety days and insure them up to 75 percent through a federal 'time deposit insurance fund.' 'Such a system, if practicable, would end 95 percent of the threat of 'runs',' he said. Washington, Dec. 26—(AP)— The contest for speakership of the next house has been enlivened by informal statements from three leading Democratic candidates expressing confidence in their chances for the nomination. Representative Rainey of Illinois, the Democratic floor leader, told newspapermen he has received indication of support from "160 members, three more than necessary." Representative McDuffie, of Alabama, Democratic whip, and Representative Byrns, of Tennessee, chairman of the appropriations committee, were equally optimistic. In the next house there will be 313 Democrats, 117 Republicans and five Farmer Laborites. The election of a Democrat is assured in view of this majority. The other Democratic candidates are Representative Rankin of Mississippi, chairman of the veterans’ committee, and Representative Crosser, of Ohio, who is being backed by his state delegation.

Washington, D. C.--(AP) — Levi Cooke, prominent Washington attorney and legislative representative of the United States Brewers’ Association, died yesterday from a heart attack. He was 50 years old. He was one of the leading advocates of modification of the Volstead Act and testified three weeks ago at hearings on the Collier beer bill. He held a prominent place in the American Bar Association and also was widely known at the British Bar, having recently spent much time in England. In 1920, Cooke was appointed master by the Supreme Court of the United States in a natural gas case involving Pennsylvania, Ohio and West Virginia. Cooke was born in Way, Ohio, and was a newspaperman in his early life. The widow and two daughters survive. The funeral will be held Tuesday, with burial here.

HYDE PARK, N. Y., Dec. 26.—(7)— Great piles of Christmas gifts were stacked in the library of President-Elect Franklin D. Roosevelt’s home today, their gay holiday wrappings unbroken, while the New York governor prepared to hurry back to Albany. His yuletide visit with his family was interrupted by pressing affairs of state. ‘I’ll never get them all opened, that’s all,” he said as he surveyed the scene. In the center of the big, homey room was a Christmas tree reaching almost to the ceiling, and bedecked in tinsel and colored bulbs. Every hour brought scores of holiday greetings, by mail and telegraph. Hundreds of Christmas cards for Mr. Roosevelt and his family flooded into the big house on the Hudson. With President Hoover off Georgia Coast—Deciding suddenly in favor of fishing in warmer waters, President Hoover Monday gave orders to his small fleet for full speed southward toward Florida. The chief executive expected to cruise as far as St. Augustine, Fla, before dropping anchor and probably will continue southward Tuesday in search of game fishing. Sunday night's plans called for the presidential party to make a stop at the huge Sea Island hunting preserve, an area of 63,000 acres, but Hoover desired to get as far south as possible and no halt was made there.
